Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul and created from it its mate and dispersed from both of them many men and women. And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs. Indeed Allah is ever, over you, an Observer.﴾ (1) ﴿And give to the orphans their properties and do not substitute the bad [i.e., your worthless things] for the good [i.e., their valuable things] and do not consume their properties into your own. Indeed, that is ever a great sin.﴾ (2) [An-Nisa' 1-2].

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted said: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾. This surah is Surat an-Nisa', and it is Madani. According to the majority of scholars, the Madani is what was revealed after the Hijrah, and the Makki is what was revealed before the Hijrah. So the Madani is what was revealed after the Hijrah even if it was outside Madinah, and the Makki is what was revealed before the Hijrah even if it was outside Makkah. On this basis, the determining factor in identifying the Makki and Madani is time, not place. The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, have mentioned criteria for the Makki and Madani, and they have mentioned well-known distinguishing features of the Makki and Madani in the science of the principles of tafsir. Among them:

That in Makki verses, the predominant features are brevity and strength, the strength of style, and their subject is usually Tawhid and what relates to it. As for Madani verses, the predominant features are ease and length of verses, and their subject is in secondary matters, such as sales, etiquette of gatherings, etiquette of seeking permission, and other things.

In Makki surahs, the address is usually to all people: ﴿O mankind﴾, because most of those addressed by it were not believers. In Madani surahs it is ﴿O you who believe﴾; this is the general rule, because those addressed in them are all or most of them believers.

This surah is Surat an-Nisa'. It is named so because of the mention of women in it. As you know, it begins with the origin of the creation of the children of Adam: from where they were created. Then it mentions the wombs (kinship ties) and what relates to them of inheritance and other matters. Then it mentions what relates to marriage, because marriage is a connection between people just as kinship is a connection between people, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And it is He who has created from water a human being and made him [a relative by] lineage and marriage﴾ [Al-Furqan 54]. Then what relates to addressing the Jews and the hypocrites, and what relates also to the situations of dispute between spouses, as will pass with us, Allah willing.

This surah is the third after al-Fatihah: al-Baqarah, Ali 'Imran, and an-Nisa'. It is narrated in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of Hudhayfah: "That the Prophet ﷺ recited al-Baqarah, then an-Nisa', then Ali 'Imran"[[Recorded by Muslim (772 / 203) from the hadith of Hudhayfah.]]. This was at the beginning. Then later, in the final arrangement, it became al-Baqarah, then Ali 'Imran, then an-Nisa', and the Mushaf compiled by Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and then 'Uthman ibn 'Affan settled upon this.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. The basmalah is an independent verse that is recited at the beginning of surahs, except for one surah, which is (Bara'ah) (at-Tawbah), for no basmalah was revealed for it. Had a basmalah been revealed for it, it would have been preserved and placed in its position, because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ [Al-Hijr 9]. However, the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, were uncertain whether it was an independent verse or part of Surat al-Anfal, so they placed a separator between them only because of this uncertainty. As for whether there is doubt about the revelation of the basmalah or not, there is no doubt about this, because if the basmalah had been revealed it would have been preserved just as other verses of the Qur'an are preserved. The correct view is that the basmalah is not part of the surah before it nor of the surah after it, and it is not counted among its verses, neither in al-Fatihah nor elsewhere, contrary to some scholars who said: it is a verse of al-Fatihah and not of other surahs. On this basis the printing of the Mushafs has proceeded, for in printing the Mushafs they made the basmalah a verse of al-Fatihah only and not of others. The correct view is that there is no difference, and that the basmalah is not part of al-Fatihah. The evidence for this is what is established in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah the Exalted said: I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves. When he says: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, He says: My servant has praised Me."[[Recorded by Muslim (395 / 38) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] And the basmalah is not mentioned. What also indicates this is that if al-Fatihah is divided between Allah and the servant into two halves, it is not correct for the basmalah to be part of it; for when we count the verses we find them as follows: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ is one verse, ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is one verse, ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ is one verse; these are three. ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ is one verse; this is the fourth, and it is the middle, which is divided between Allah and the servant in two halves. ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ is one verse, ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾ is one verse, ﴿Not of those who have earned Your anger or of those who are astray﴾ is one verse. Thus the verses are consistent: the right of the Creator, the Exalted, is three independent verses, which are the first, and the right of the servant is three independent verses, which are the last verses, and the seventh is between them; its first part belongs to what? To the right of Allah, and its second part belongs to the right of the servant. By this it is known that the basmalah is not part of al-Fatihah. Its grammatical analysis has already passed with us. So what does the prepositional phrase attach to?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: There is something better.

* Student: A delayed verb, deleted, estimated according to context.

* Shaykh: According to context. What is context?

* Student: If there are indications, or its object.

* Shaykh: That is, according to what one begins with or what one invokes the name over. So the basmalah is a prepositional phrase attached to a deleted element, and this deleted element is a delayed verb estimated according to what is named over. If I want to read, the estimate is: "In the name of Allah I read." If I want to slaughter: "In the name of Allah I slaughter." If I want to perform wudu': "In the name of Allah I perform wudu'," and so on. The verb was chosen to be delayed for the sake of seeking blessing by beginning with the name of Allah in one respect, and for conveying restriction in another respect, what? Because placing before what should be delayed conveys restriction, so it is as if you say: "I do not read except in the name of Allah." It was chosen to be a verb, not a noun, i.e., we do not estimate "In the name of Allah is my reading" or "In the name of Allah is my beginning," because the basic principle in governing is verbs, not nouns, and for that reason you do not find a noun governing except under conditions, unlike verbs. It was estimated as fitting what is named over because it is more suitable. And because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever has not slaughtered, let him slaughter in the name of Allah"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (985), and Muslim (1960 / 1) from the hadith of Jundub ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Sufyan.]]. He said: "Let him slaughter in the name of Allah," so a specific verb was estimated, which is slaughter. As for the word Allah, it is a proper name specific to Allah the Mighty and Majestic alone, and it is not named by it anyone else, by consensus. As for ﴿Ar-Rahman﴾, it is also a proper name specific to Allah, not named by anyone else. As for ﴿Ar-Rahim﴾, it is a proper name for Allah, a name from the names of Allah that is a proper name for Him, but it may be applied to others, as Allah said about the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; it grieves him that you suffer; he is anxious over you and to the believers, kind and merciful﴾ [At-Tawbah 128].

By what do the People of the Sunnah explain ﴿Ar-Rahman ar-Rahim﴾? They explain (ar-Rahman) as the One possessing mercy, which is a necessary attribute related to the Essence of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and from its effects are bestowal and goodness. The people of ta'til explain it as goodness, so they say: ﴿ar-Rahman﴾ is the Benevolent or the Bestower, or by the will of goodness or bestowal; i.e., the one who wills goodness, the one who wills bestowal, because they do not describe Allah with the attribute of mercy. The same is said of ﴿ar-Rahim﴾.

If someone asks: Are (ar-Rahman) and (ar-Rahim) synonymous?

The answer: If one of them is mentioned alone without the other, it includes the other. If both are mentioned together, then (ar-Rahman) refers to the attribute, and (ar-Rahim) refers to the act; because (Rahman) is on the pattern fa'lan, indicating a quality, like ghadban (angry), sakran (drunk), nashwan (elated), and similar words, and (Rahim) indicates an act. So this (Rahman) is in regard to the description of Allah the Mighty and Majestic with mercy, and (Rahim) is in regard to His act, i.e., in regard to His mercy toward whom He shows mercy. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 21].

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾. This sentence is a vocative sentence introduced by (ya), and the vocative is (ayyu), which is built on damm in a position of nasb, and (ha) is for alerting, and ﴿an-nas﴾ is an adjective of (ayyu) or an explanatory apposition, so it is built on damm in a position of nasb.

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾: Allah directed the address to mankind even though the surah is Madani, to show that the message of the Prophet ﷺ is general for all people.

As for ﴿an-nas﴾, it has been said that its origin is unas, and the hamzah was dropped for frequency of use, as lightening, as the hamzah was dropped from (shar) and (khayr), whose origin is (asharr) and (akhyar); you say: "This is better (khayr) than this," i.e., more excellent (akhyar) than it; "This is worse (shar) than this," i.e., more evil (ashharr) than it, but the hamzah was dropped for lightness because of frequency of use. It is derived from al-uns (companionship), because human beings, as it is said of them, are social by nature and need to be at ease with one another, and for this reason you will not find anyone who loves seclusion except for a cause, a cause external to what Allah has created people upon.

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord who created you from one soul﴾. Taqwa comes from waqayah (protection), and it is that a person takes a protection from the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. The Rabb in His saying ﴿your Lord﴾ is the Creator, the Owner, the Manager, so it includes these three meanings: Creator, i.e., the originator after non-existence, i.e., the one who brings into being from nothing; second, Owner, whom none shares in His dominion; third, Manager of affairs according to what His wisdom requires.

﴿who created you from one soul﴾: ﴿alladhi﴾ is an adjective of (Rabb), but it is a clarifying adjective. By our saying "clarifying," we mean explanatory, explaining this lordship or some of its meanings. We excluded by the word "clarifying" that it be "restrictive," because if we made it restrictive there would be two lords: a lord who created us from one soul and a lord who did not create us from one soul, and the matter is not so; rather, the One who created us from one soul is one Lord. So the adjective here is an adjective of what type?

* Students: Clarifying.

* Shaykh: Clarifying, i.e., explaining the meaning of lordship or some of its meaning.

﴿created you﴾: brought you into being. ﴿from one soul and created from it its mate﴾: Is this soul intended as a specific soul, or is the intended meaning of "soul" the species?

The apparent is the first: that the intended soul is a specific soul, namely Adam, peace be upon him, the father of humanity, whom Allah created from clay with His noble hand, and taught him the names of everything he needs; because he was created without anyone to teach him language, so Allah taught him the languages he needed. So the meaning of His saying ﴿He taught Adam all the names﴾ [Al-Baqarah 31] means: of what? Of what he needs. Yes.

As for His saying ﴿and created from it its mate﴾, i.e., He created from this soul its mate, and it has come in reports that she was created from his right rib, and Allah knows best, but it is established in the Sunnah that "the woman was created from a rib"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3331), and Muslim (1468 / 59) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].

﴿and created from it its mate﴾: and it did not say "its wife," because the classical language is that zawj applies to both man and woman, and its root is the opposite of witr (odd), because when a wife joins her husband she becomes a partner to him after having been solitary, and for this reason it is said: the wife is a partner of her husband in life, because each of them joined the other. ﴿created from it its mate﴾ means by it, or it refers to Hawwa'.

﴿and dispersed from both of them many men and women﴾: (baththa) means to spread out and bring forth. ﴿from both of them﴾, i.e., from the soul and its mate, ﴿many men and women﴾. The children of Adam do not go beyond these two categories. As for what has come regarding the khuntha (hermaphrodite), the khuntha is either male or female, or a combination of both, but it does not go beyond maleness and femaleness.

His saying ﴿many men and women﴾ does not say "many women" because multiplicity among men is a source of honor, unlike multiplicity among females, although in reality women among the children of Adam are more numerous than men, as Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, inferred from the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed, most of the people of the Fire are you [women]"[[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (2613) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]], and "the people of the Fire from the children of Adam are nine hundred and ninety-nine out of a thousand"[[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (3168) from the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn.]]. So if they are most of the people of the Fire, and the people of the Fire from the children of Adam are nine hundred and ninety-nine out of a thousand, it follows that they are more numerous than men, and this is the reality. But multiplicity among men is a matter of honor and pride, and people take pride in it, unlike women, for multiplicity among them is a burden, toil, and hardship. ﴿and dispersed from both of them many men and women﴾.

﴿And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another﴾: He repeated the command to fear Him, the Mighty and Majestic, because of its importance; for when a person is granted success in the fear of Allah, his religious and worldly affairs are set right. And His saying ﴿through whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾: regarding ﴿tasa'alun﴾ there are two readings: the first is ﴿tasa'alun﴾ as it is in the Mushaf, and the second is ﴿tassa'alun﴾, and the origin of ﴿tassa'alun﴾ is tatasa'alun.

﴿through whom you ask one another and the wombs﴾: i.e., one of you asks another by Him for protection, saying: "I ask you by Allah to save me," "I ask you by Allah not to harm me," "I ask you by Allah such and such," of what is asked; so Allah the Exalted is the One by whom people ask one another.

And His saying ﴿and the wombs﴾ has two readings: in the genitive (bil-jarr) and in the accusative (bil-fath). If it is in the accusative, it is coordinated with His saying ﴿Allah﴾, meaning: "and fear the wombs, do not neglect them, do not fall short in their rights." And (al-arham) is the plural of rahm, and they are kin, so there is in the verse a command to maintain ties of kinship and to fulfill its rights.

As for the reading in the genitive: ﴿wal-arhami﴾, it is coordinated with the pronoun in (bihi), i.e., "you ask by Him and by the wombs." How is asking by the wombs?

Asking by the wombs is that it is a custom among the Arabs that one says: "I ask you by Allah and by the womb," or says: "I ask you by the womb that is between me and you," and they, out of their tribal solidarity, esteem the womb greatly and respect it and regard its protection as obligatory, and for this reason Allah the Exalted reminded them of it, saying: "Fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs."

If someone says: Is there any contradiction between the two readings ﴿wal-arhami﴾ and ﴿wal-arham﴾?

The answer: No. The two readings in reality make the word into two words; either the reading is an explanation of one of the two readings, i.e., each reading explains the other, or the second reading comes with a new meaning. Here the two readings: is one of them explaining the other, or does each one come with a new meaning?

* The students: Each one came with a new meaning.

* The Shaykh: Each one came with a new meaning. The reading in the accusative contains the command to beware of the wombs, i.e., to beware of neglecting their rights, and the second verse contains the reminder that people ask one another by the wombs, and they only ask by them because of the great importance of their right among them. Yes.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 1 (part 2 of 3):**

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Watchful over you.﴾ When He had commanded them to fear Him, the Mighty and Majestic, twice in the verse, He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Watchful over you.﴾ That is, He observes you in all your conditions: Have you feared Allah or not? Have you feared the ties of kinship and fulfilled their duties or not? This is the meaning of His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Watchful over you.﴾ Concluding the verse with this sentence is intended as a warning against opposing Him. If you say to one of your sons, "Do such-and-such, for I am watching you," what does that mean?

* Students: It is a warning to him.
* Shaykh: It is a warning to him not to disobey, and that if he disobeys, he will find his punishment.

* Several benefits are derived from this noble verse:

* First: The obligation of taqwa (God-consciousness, fear of Allah) upon all people. From where is this taken?
* Student: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul and created from it its mate...﴾
* Shaykh: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾, where He addressed the address to all people.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration that people were brought into existence from nothing: ﴿who created you from one soul﴾. It also contains a refutation of the atheistic idea that people evolved from monkeys into humanity. From where is this taken?
* Student: ﴿from one soul﴾.
* Shaykh: We know of no soul except Adam, from whom we descend. As for whoever claims that the origin of the children of Adam is a monkey, we say to him: your admission against yourself is accepted, but against others it is not accepted.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a reminder of Allah's blessing in creating spouses for us. His words are: ﴿and created from it its mate﴾. The word (min) here is for partition (partitive), and it may also be explanatory, meaning "of its own kind." This is a great blessing. If our spouses were of a kind other than ours, could we find comfort in them? Never. A person finds comfort only in one of his own kind. If they were of the kind of cattle or of sheep, could a person find comfort in them?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: It is impossible. Rather, a person would recoil from them with intense aversion.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the origin of this humanity, whom none can count except Allah, what is their origin?
* Students: Their origin is one.
* Shaykh: Their origin is one. If you wish, say: their origin is two: a pair and a pair. From them Allah produced these many men and women, a humanity that none can count except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as He said: ﴿and dispersed from both of them many men and women﴾.

* Among its benefits: that the abundance of men is more important than the abundance of women, as indicated by His words: ﴿many men﴾. Specifying the abundance of men indicates the importance of this abundance.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the importance of taqwa, and for this reason Allah repeated the command to it twice.

* Among its benefits: an indication that taqwa is obligatory by the requirement of rububiyyah (Lordship) and by the requirement of uluhiyyah (divinity, the right to worship).
* Student: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾ is by the requirement of rububiyyah.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: ﴿And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and [due regard for] the wombs﴾ is by the requirement of uluhiyyah.
* Shaykh: Yes, exactly.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that asking one another by Allah is a known and established practice among the Arabs, as in His words: ﴿through whom you ask one another﴾.
But may a person ask another by Allah?
We say: If the intention in doing so is reminder, there is no harm. If the intention is compulsion, there is room for consideration. If he says, "I ask you by Allah," meaning "I remind you of Him so that you respect Allah's greatness and His right," there is nothing wrong with that. But if the aim is to compel him, that is an embarrassment. Some people do this at times, for example, those who present their questions in lectures and say: "I ask you by Allah to answer me," or say to the presenter: "I ask you by Allah to present it." This is an embarrassment. The one answering or the presenter may judge it better not to present this question or not to answer it. So if someone asks by Allah, is it obligatory to respond?
We say: If he asks by Allah for something prohibited, he has no honor and it is not permissible to respond, as if he said, "I ask you by Allah to enter so-and-so's orchard and bring us oranges and apples." Is this permissible or not?
* Students: It is not permissible.
* Shaykh: No, it is not permissible, and there is no honor in it.
If he asks by Allah for something that harms me, saying, "I ask you by Allah to give me half your wealth" (this one is greedy), is it obligatory on me to respond?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: No, because there is harm to me in it.
If he says, "I ask you by Allah to give me my due right that is obligatory upon you."
Some students: It is obligatory that I give it to him.
* Shaykh: Here it is obligatory, for two reasons. First: it is a right that is owed. Second: he asked by Allah. Some scholars said that the meaning of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: «Whoever asks you by Allah» [[Narrated by Abu Dawud (5108) from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, and Ahmad (5703) from the hadith of Ibn Umar, the wording is his.]] means: whoever asks you for a right that Allah has made obligatory upon him, which Allah has made obligatory upon the one asked. So the meaning of his words, "Whoever asks you by Allah," is: whoever asks you by the law of Allah, that is, whoever asks you a request that the Shari'ah requires you to answer, then answer him. The meaning is not: whoever says, "I ask you by Allah," because whoever says "I ask you by Allah" may intend a meaning that is not valid at all. That is, if he says, "I ask you by Allah," intending to make Allah an intercessor with this one being asked, this is forbidden, because it is not permissible to seek intercession with Allah over His creation. The station of Allah is far too great to be an intermediary between you and creation.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to honor the ties of kinship, as in His words: ﴿and [due regard for] the wombs﴾ according to the reading in the accusative (naṣb). Likewise, there is an indication of honoring the ties of kinship according to the reading in the genitive (jarr). That is, just as you respect them and ask by them, honor them and give them their due.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning against opposing Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. From where is this taken?
* Student: From opposing Allah, glorified and exalted be He.
* Shaykh: The warning against opposing Allah.
* Student: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Watchful over you.﴾
* Shaykh: From His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Watchful over you.﴾ Whoever believes in this, that Allah is watchful over him, will be cautious about opposing Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Do we derive from this verse the affirmation of Allah's name al-Raqib (the Watchful)?
Yes, the scholars derive from it the affirmation of a name of Allah.
Now, do we say that (kāna, "is/was") here is meant in its temporal sense or not?
No. If its temporal sense were intended, the watching would have already passed. Rather, it is intended to establish that the one described has the attribute that is the predicate of this sentence. So it establishes that Allah is Watchful over us. Likewise His words, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾; the meaning is not that He was and then ceased, but the establishment of His being characterized by forgiveness and mercy. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Watchful over you.﴾

Student: Is the nominal sentence stronger than the verbal sentence?
* Shaykh: It is stronger in terms of permanence and continuity. But in a context of warning, it is stronger because it indicates renewal, occurrence, and continuity. That is, whatever you do at any time, the watching is constant.

* Student: Shaykh, when a person says to his companion, "I ask you by Allah," and he means to get something from him, even if (...), like saying, "I seek intercession with Allah over you"?
* Shaykh: No, no. "I seek intercession with Allah over you" is forbidden, it is not permissible. But if he says, "I ask you by Allah," some people intend this meaning, that is, they intend to seek intercession with Allah over the one asked. If this is his intention, it is forbidden. At other times he says, "I ask you by Allah," meaning "by the right of Allah," that is, "I bind you by what Allah has as a right over you, that you give me such-and-such."
* Student: But Shaykh, this is very rare.
* Shaykh: Where is the rarity?
* Student: This second case.
* Shaykh: If he intends the first meaning, it must be forbidden.
* Student: So then it is not permissible (...).
* Shaykh: If his intention is seeking intercession. But in my view, those who say, "I ask you by Allah," intend to bind you by the right of Allah, that is: if Allah is esteemed by you, then I ask you by Him. But if he intends to make Allah an intercessor, that is, a means between you and Him, this is forbidden.
* Student: (...) Shaykh, is the permissibility of asking by Allah derived from this? Can the permissibility of asking by the ties of kinship be derived from the second reading?
* Shaykh: Yes, but do not join it with Allah.
* Student: How?
* Shaykh: He says, "I ask you by the kinship between me and you," as if reminding him of the bond between them, so that he does not wrong him.

* Student: May Allah reward you, Shaykh. Regarding the recitation of the basmalah (the phrase "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate"), some scholars affirm the hadith that «the Prophet (ﷺ) recited the basmalah aloud», [[See al-Tirmidhi (245), from the hadith of Ibn Abbas.]] while some scholars weaken this hadith. Yet one may use this hadith to argue that the basmalah is part of al-Fatihah. How would you answer with this hadith?
* Shaykh: Since it is a weak hadith, we are spared from it.
* Student: But some scholars have authenticated it.
* Shaykh: Whoever has it as authentic may make it part of al-Fatihah. But the fact that the Messenger (ﷺ) recited it quietly at times and aloud at other times indicates that it is not part of al-Fatihah, because if it were part of al-Fatihah, he would have recited it aloud always, as he recited al-Fatihah aloud.
* Student: (...) those who say the hadith is authentic have it that its chains are many.
* Shaykh: I say it is authentic. But did he recite it aloud and not quietly?
* Student: The Prophet recited the basmalah aloud.
* Shaykh: And not quietly?
* Student: He recited it quietly at times.
* Shaykh: Good. His reciting it quietly at times indicates that it is not part of al-Fatihah, because if it were part of it, he would have recited it aloud always, as he recited al-Fatihah aloud. This is one point.
A second point: that reciting it aloud indicates it is part of it is only a possibility. But the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: «I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves» [[Narrated by Muslim (395/38) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] has no such possibility.
* Student: Shaykh, (...) is it a descriptive adjective (na't) or an explicative apposition ('atf bayan) (...)?
* Shaykh: Or. It is a difference of opinion, to vary the disagreement. The preferred view is that if what follows is a derived noun (mushtaqq), it is a descriptive adjective, like ﴿O Prophet﴾. If it is a fixed noun (jamid), like ﴿O mankind﴾, it is an explicative apposition. Is that clear?
* Student: Yes.
* Student: (...) the Messenger (ﷺ) recited the basmalah aloud (...) and was silent about it at times. From this is derived the lack of embarrassment for the ummah, ﷺ, he considers (...). Is this meaning derived from it?
* Shaykh: This meaning may perhaps be derived, perhaps. But many scholars weaken the hadith about reciting the basmalah aloud. Note this.
* Student: Shaykh, the saying of some people: "By Allah upon you, give me such-and-such," would this be a case of seeking intercession?
* Shaykh: Yes, this is asking by Allah, and it may also be seeking intercession by Allah. For this reason, the speaker must be asked: What do you mean by "by Allah upon you"? He may say, "by Allah upon you" meaning "I swear by Allah upon you," so it would be an oath. Yes. The closest meaning is: "I swear by Allah upon you," or "I seek intercession by Allah upon you." Yes.

* * *

* Student: ﴿And give the orphans their property, and do not substitute the bad for the good, and do not consume their property into your own property. Indeed, that is ever a great sin. (2) And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphan girls, then marry those women who please you, two or three or four. But if you fear that you will not be just, then [marry only] one, or those your right hands possess. That is more suitable, that you not incline [to injustice]. (3) And give the women their dowries graciously. But if they give you willingly a part of it, then consume it with satisfaction and pleasure.﴾ [An-Nisa 2–4].
* Shaykh: Enough. I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾ and so on. First: is this surah Meccan or Medinan?
* Student: Meccan.
* Shaykh: Meccan.
* Student: Because it begins with ﴿O mankind﴾.
* Shaykh: With ﴿O mankind﴾, yes.
* Student: Medinan.
* Shaykh: Medinan. What is the difference between the Medinan and the Meccan?
* Student: It has been said: the Medinan is what was revealed after the Hijrah, even if it was revealed outside Medina, and the Meccan is what was revealed before the Hijrah, even if it was revealed outside Mecca.
* Shaykh: This is the correct view, this statement is the correct one. His words, exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul﴾ ﴿who created you﴾. Is this attribute called a descriptive attribute?
* Student: Explanatory (kāshifah).
* Shaykh: Explanatory. And what is the meaning of an explanatory attribute?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, how?
* Student: An explanatory attribute.
* Shaykh: Yes, in this verse.
* Student: In this verse, it is not restricted to saying that Allah, our Lord, is the One who created us. Although our Lord is the One who created us, the apparent meaning of the verse is restrictive. There may be for people two lords: a lord who created them, and a lord who did not create them.
Shaykh: Then what is meant by "explanatory"?
* Student: It clarifies (...).
* Shaykh: It clarifies something from the aspect of Lordship: that He created us. Good. What is meant by the single soul?
* Student: The single soul has two possibilities: either it means the kind (genus), or it means the very individual (...).
* Shaykh: Yes. Either the meaning is the kind or the individual. If we say the kind, the meaning is of one kind. If we say the individual, the meaning is Adam. This is the correct view.
His words: ﴿and dispersed from both of them many men﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿dispersed from both of them﴾?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿many men and women﴾. He did not say "many women" (in the feminine plural). Is this an instance of sufficiency, like His words: ﴿and He made for you garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [An-Nahl 81], meaning and the cold, or is this a pointer to something?
* Student: (...) to indicate that the abundance of men is a source of strength, and it is not the same with women, therefore (...).
* Shaykh: Well said. Now His words: ﴿through whom you ask one another, and [due regard for] the wombs﴾: there are two readings?
* Student: Yes, ﴿tasā'alūna﴾ and ﴿tassā'alūna﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿tasā'alūna﴾ and ﴿tassā'alūna﴾. What is the root of ﴿tassā'alūna﴾?
* Student: "Tatasā'alūna" (you ask one another).
* Shaykh: "Tatasā'alūna." Now, what is the meaning of asking by Allah?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That is, seeking intercession by Allah, making Allah an intercessor for you with this person? No.
* Student: The matter has detail: if he seeks intercession by Allah...
* Shaykh: We are not seeking the ruling. What is the meaning of ﴿through whom you ask one another﴾?
* Student: "I ask you by Allah."
* Another student: Some of you ask others by Allah.
* Shaykh: Some of you ask others by Allah. For example?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: "I ask you by Allah to do such-and-such," or "I adjure you by Allah," or something similar. Good.
What is the connection between His words, ﴿And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another﴾, and the command to taqwa, and their asking by Him?
* Student: Their asking by Him indicates that they worship Him (...).
* Shaykh: Exactly. Because their asking by Him indicates that He is great in their eyes, and what is great must be feared. Good. Now His words: ﴿and [due regard for] the wombs﴾: the governing element. There are two readings.
* Student: ﴿wal-arḥāma﴾ and ﴿wal-arḥāmi﴾ (...).
* Shaykh: No, wait. Give us the reading first, and then we will see its explanation.
* Student: ﴿wal-arḥāma﴾ in the accusative, ﴿wal-arḥāmi﴾ in the genitive (...).
* Shaykh: In the genitive? According to the reading in the accusative?
* Student: ﴿And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾, that is: fear the wombs (...).
* Shaykh: Well said. Fear the wombs: how do we fear them, that is?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but what is the meaning of fearing them? What is the meaning of fearing them?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That is, do not sever them. Good. And according to the genitive reading, ﴿wal-arḥāmi﴾?
* Student: (...) they ask by the right of the womb, and this was well known among them in the pre-Islamic period, that the womb held a high status among them (...). What is the meaning, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: The meaning, the meaning would be what? ﴿And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs.﴾
* Student: The meaning is that they ask by the wombs, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: They ask one another by the wombs, so it would be a conjunction to what?
* Student: To the pronoun, Shaykh, in (bihi, "by Him").
* Shaykh: To the pronoun in "bihi," so?

Right. As for the Almighty's words, ﴿Indeed, Allah has ever been over you an Watcher﴾ — the particle (kana, "was") indicates past time. Does this mean that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, was a Watcher and then His watching ceased?

A student: No. (...) He was and still is continuously (...)

* The Shaykh: So this means it is stripped of time, stripped of indicating a time frame, and what is intended is to affirm that He is characterized by this attribute. There are parallels: ﴿Indeed, Allah has ever been Forgiving and Merciful﴾. The meaning is not "He was in the past," but rather: it is established that He is Forgiving and Merciful. Do you understand?

Now, there is a problem with the reading in the genitive (al-jarr) from the standpoint of grammatical rules, because the grammarians say: if you conjoin to a attached pronoun, bring the detached pronoun, or repeat the preposition, and say: "you ask one another by Him and by the wombs." So do we say that there is in the Qur'an something that departs from the rules? No. We say: the Qur'an is the judge and is not judged. As for the grammarians saying, "This is shādh (anomalous)," we say: the anomalous one is you. There is nothing anomalous in the Qur'an at all. The Qur'an is in clear Arabic tongue. And if this usage is rare among the Arabs, then with the revelation of the Qur'an using it, is it many or few?

* The students: Many.

* The Shaykh: It becomes many, which people recite at every time and in every moment. For this reason, al-Razi and Muhammad Rashid Rida, and other scholars, strongly objected to the grammarians on this and said: how can they say that there is something anomalous in the Qur'an?! The Qur'an judges and is not judged. Rather, when a construction appears in the Qur'an that was not known in the Arabic language, the credit goes to the Qur'an for reviving that construction. Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said that it is not necessary to repeat the preposition, and he said:

"It is not binding in my view, since it has come / established in verse and in correct prose."

This is the correct view. Based on this, we say concerning every verse that the grammarians claimed to be anomalous: the anomalous one is you; there is nothing anomalous in the Qur'an. Everything in the Qur'an is in the eloquent language, in clear Arabic tongue. The rules must be taken from the Qur'an so that it judges by them and upon them, not that rules be derived from modern technical terminology and then one says: the Qur'an, what? Anomalous.

A student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy. ﴿O you who have believed, fulfill [all] contracts. Lawful to you is the animal of grazing livestock except for that which is recited to you [in this Qur'an], not permitting hunting while you are in the state of ihram. Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills. (1) O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah or the sacred month or [neglect] the sacrificial animals and garlands [or] those coming to the Sacred House seeking bounty from their Lord and [His] approval. And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt. And do not let the hatred of a people for having obstructed you from al-Masjid al-Haram incite you to transgress. And cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in penalty.﴾ [al-Ma'idah 1, 2].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted said, in the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy: ﴿O you who have believed, fulfill [all] contracts﴾. Firstly: this surah is Madani, and it is among the last of what was revealed of the Qur'an. For this reason the scholars said: whatever is lawful in it, consider it lawful, and whatever is unlawful in it, consider it unlawful. No ruling in it is abrogated; rather all the rulings in it are muhkam (established), and it is Madani because it was revealed after the Hijrah, and everything revealed after the Hijrah is Madani, even if it was revealed in Makkah. Otherwise, there is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you and have approved for you Islam as religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3]. That was revealed at 'Arafah while the Prophet ﷺ was standing there.

The basmalah needs no repeated discussion, since it was already discussed: that it is a verse of the Book of Allah, independent, not part of the surah before it or after it, and it is recited at the beginning of every surah except Surat Bara'ah (al-Tawbah). It is connected to an omitted element, and this omitted element is estimated as a delayed verb suited to the subject that the basmalah introduces. This is the best of what has been said about the connection of the basmalah. Accordingly, if you want to read, you say: the prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted verb whose estimate is?

* Students: "I read."

* The Shaykh: "In the name of Allah I read"; meaning the estimate is: "In the name of Allah I read." If you want to perform ablution, you say its estimate is: "In the name of Allah I perform ablution." If you want to slaughter a slaughtered animal, you say: "In the name of Allah I slaughter." This is the estimate.

He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿O you who have believed﴾. Know that when speech is introduced with this phrase, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, then, as 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Give it your attentive hearing" — meaning, pay attention to it — "for it is either good that you are commanded to do, or evil that you are forbidden from"[[Narrated by Sa'id ibn Mansur in al-Tafsir (50) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud with the wording: "Then lend it your ear, for it is good you are commanded to, or evil you are turned away from."]]; or a report containing benefit for you, such as the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, indeed the polytheists are unclean﴾ [al-Tawbah 28], and similar. The point is that it must be for good, or for evil, or for a report that includes good or evil. Know also that when speech is introduced with it, it indicates that what follows is among the requirements of faith: affirmation of it if it is a report, and acting upon it if it is a command, and that opposing that is a deficiency in faith. Know also that Allah the Exalted opens address with it to stir the one addressed, since when it is said, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, it is as if He says: your faith obliges you to do such and such, or to abandon such and such, according to context.

﴿O you who have believed, fulfill [all] contracts﴾: fulfill them, i.e., bring them complete and full, without deficiency. Allah the Exalted has explained the threat against those who take full measure from contracts yet do not give them in full, in His saying: ﴿Woe to those who give less [than due], who, when they take a measure from people, take in full, but when they give [a measure or weight] to them or weigh for them, they cause loss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 1-3]. So "awfu" means what?

* A student: Bring them.

* The Shaykh: Bring them complete. From this is His saying: ﴿And fulfill the covenant﴾ [al-Isra' 34], ﴿and give full measure when you measure﴾ [al-Isra' 35], and similar. "Al-'uqud" is the plural of "'aqd," which is what a person concludes with another. Its opposite is "hall" (untying). You say: "I tied the rope" and "I untied the rope." So "al-'uqud" means what a person binds himself to with others, and there are many kinds: sale, hire, pledge, endowment, marriage, and other things.

As for His saying: ﴿Fulfill [all] contracts﴾, this is general: any contract must be fulfilled. But it must be restricted by what the Shari'ah has brought, namely that the contract is not prohibited. If the contract is prohibited, the texts indicate that it is not to be fulfilled, indeed that fulfilling it is forbidden, due to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Any condition that is not in the Book of Allah is void, even if it were a hundred conditions"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2729) and Muslim (1504/8) from 'A'ishah.]].

Then He said: ﴿Lawful to you is the animal of grazing livestock﴾. ﴿Uhilla﴾ is a verb in what form?

* Students: The passive form (for which the doer is not named).

* The Shaykh: The passive, for which the doer is not named, though its doer is known and not unknown, because the doer here is Allah the Mighty and Majestic, as Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And do not say about what your tongues describe, "This is lawful and this is unlawful," to invent falsehood against Allah﴾ [al-Nahl 116]. So the one who makes lawful here is Allah.

As for His saying: ﴿bahimat al-an'am﴾, "bahimah" is that which does not speak; every animal that does not speak is a bahimah, because what speaks or is spoken is clear and not ambiguous, so it is a bahimah.

As for His saying: ﴿al-an'am﴾, it refers to three kinds: camels, cattle, and sheep. The idafah (construct) of "bahimah" to "al-an'am" is of the type of attributing a thing to its genus, as you say "a ring of iron," "a door of wood," and similar, as if He said: the bahimah from among the an'am. When we say "bahimat al-an'am, namely camels," when we say "namely camels, cattle, and sheep," do we explain "bahimah" or "al-an'am"?

* Students: "Al-an'am."

* The Shaykh: "Al-an'am," namely camels, cattle, and sheep.

﴿Except what is recited to you﴾ is an exception from His saying ﴿bahimat al-an'am﴾, because "bahimat al-an'am" is a singular noun in construct, so it is general for everything. From "bahimat al-an'am" He said: ﴿except what is recited to you﴾, and what is meant by that is what comes in the following verse in His saying: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion, blood﴾ up to the end [al-Ma'idah 3]; this is what is recited to us.

And ﴿not permitting hunting﴾ is an exception...

Almighty Allah says: ﴿And give the orphans their properties﴾. ﴿Give﴾ (ātū) means "hand over" or "give."

* Students: "They came."

* The Shaykh: They came. In his words ﴿the orphans﴾ is the first object, and ﴿their properties﴾ is the second object. This verb (ātū) takes two objects that are not originally a subject and predicate.

His words ﴿the orphans﴾ are the plural of yatīm (orphan), derived from yutm, which means being alone. In technical usage it refers to one whose father has died while he is still a minor who has not reached maturity, whether male or female. Once he reaches maturity, his orphanhood ends according to the technical and legal ruling. For this reason it is reported in the hadith: "There is no orphanhood after reaching puberty"[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (2873) from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.]], meaning after reaching maturity, because once he reaches maturity he is independent.

His words ﴿give the orphans their properties﴾: ﴿their properties﴾ means those that belong to them, whether they are in your possession as guardians or whether they are not in your possession but you have taken them unlawfully.

His words ﴿give the orphans their properties﴾ mean: do not betray any part of them, do not conceal any part of them, do not spoil them, but return them as they were.

The command ﴿give the orphans their properties﴾ does not necessarily mean that we hand the money to them while they are still orphans, because an orphan's property is not handed over until he is tested, as Allah says: ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them sound judgment, hand over to them their properties﴾. Here there is a difference between handing the property to him and keeping the property for him until it is given to him in full. So in the verse before us, is the intended meaning the first or the second?

* Students: The second.

* Students: The first.

* The Shaykh: Apparently you do not understand the first and the second; you have forgotten them.

Is there a difference between ītā' (giving) and daf' (handing over)?

We say: Yes, there is a difference between them, because daf' means: do not give him the property until he reaches maturity and sound judgment; ﴿until, when they reach marriageable age, if you perceive in them sound judgment, then hand over to them their properties﴾. As for giving the property, the intended meaning is that we keep the property for them in such a way that we give it to them in full when handing it over becomes obligatory.

﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾, meaning: do not take the good in exchange for the bad. ﴿Do not substitute the bad for the good﴾, that is, do not take the bad in place of the good. How can we not take the bad in place of the good?

The meaning is that we do not give them bad things from our property and take good things in exchange; this is the meaning of the verse.

It has also been said: its meaning is, do not take their property so that you may become rich by it instead of the good; because wealth taken unlawfully is forbidden, and the forbidden is bad. So there are two views:

The first view: that you do not take the good from their property and give them the bad. Example: an orphan has fat, good sheep, while his guardian has lean, inferior sheep; he takes the good sheep of the orphan and gives him the inferior one. This is forbidden. Or he has pure, good wheat and takes it and gives him inferior, mixed wheat, and similar things. So the meaning is: ﴿do not substitute the bad for the good﴾, that is, do not take the good and give them the bad. This is one view.

The second meaning, or second view: do not take anything from their property, because their property is forbidden to you, and the forbidden is bad. The meaning of the verse then is: do not take their property so that you become independent of the good that you earn by lawful means.

Both matters are forbidden; that is, whether you take his property without giving him anything in return, or you take his good property and give him inferior property, both are forbidden.

﴿And do not devour their properties together with your properties﴾. Regarding ﴿ilā﴾, the scholars said it means (ma'a), "with"; that is, do not devour their properties with your properties. It has also been said that ilā retains its original meaning, but ﴿devour﴾ has been given the meaning of (tadummū), "to add"; that is, do not add their properties to your properties so that you devour them. This last view is more correct, because giving a verb the meaning of another verb is common in the Qur'an, while using ilā to mean ma'a is rare, and interpreting the verse according to the more common meaning in the Qur'an is preferable to interpreting it according to the rarer meaning. This is one of the principles of tafsir: that interpreting a verse according to the meaning most common in the Qur'an takes precedence over interpreting it according to a rare meaning, because when it is the common usage in the Qur'an, it becomes the Qur'anic terminology and the Qur'anic reality.

﴿ilā amwālikum, innahu﴾: the pronoun refers to the preceding act, which consists of two things: substituting the bad for the good, and devouring their property along with ours. ﴿Innahu﴾ means this act; the pronoun refers to the act understood from what came before.

﴿Innahu kāna ḥūban kabīran﴾: that is, it was with Allah ﴿ḥūban﴾, meaning a sin or a wrong, and "great" is the opposite of "small," because sins are divided into minor and major sins, and this is among the major sins.

* This verse contains several benefits:

* Among them: the demonstration of Allah's mercy, in that He enjoined care for these orphans, because the orphan is a object of mercy; his heart is broken, he has no father, and perhaps no mother either. Therefore Allah enjoined care for them and for their property.

* Among them: the obligation to protect orphans' property. What is its basis? Because giving them their property necessarily requires what? It requires protection; for if he neglects and is careless and the property is lost, he has not given them their property.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the orphan owns property and his ownership is complete, because of His saying what?

* Students: ﴿their properties﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿their properties﴾. From this benefit it follows that zakat is obligatory upon them, because zakat follows ownership. Allah says: ﴿Take from their properties a charity﴾ [al-Tawbah 103], and the Prophet ﷺ said to Mu'adh ibn Jabal when he sent him to Yemen: "Inform them that Allah has enjoined upon them a charity in their properties"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (1395) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]]. So when ownership is established, the obligation of zakat is established. Do you understand? Good. This refutes the view of some scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, that zakat is not obligatory on orphans' property because the orphan is a minor and not legally responsible. We answer this by saying: zakat is not purely a legal obligation on the person; rather it is an obligation concerning the right of others, namely the poor. So it resembles a debt. For this reason it is obligatory on orphans' property and on that of the insane, even though they are not legally responsible.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the maintenance (nafaqah) must be paid from the orphan's property by those obligated to maintain him. From where is this taken? From establishing that he has property. Maintenance is obligatory on every wealthy person for every poor dependant. So if the conditions of maintenance are met and only puberty remains, we say that puberty is not a condition, because Allah has established property for orphans, and when property is established, the consequences that apply to property-owners apply to them.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to fulfil trusts, because of His saying: ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾.

* Among its benefits: applying the term (khabīth, "bad") to inferior things, is that correct? According to one of the two interpretations of the verse. Allah has explicitly stated that inferior things are called bad, saying: ﴿O you who believe, spend of the good things you have earned and of what We have produced for you from the earth, and do not aim at the bad of it, spending from it﴾ [al-Baqarah 267], so He called it bad, that is, He called the inferior bad. And the Prophet ﷺ called onions and the like bad[[See Musnad Ahmad (17741).]], and he said that it is lawful[[See Musnad Ahmad (23507).]], even though he applied the description "bad" to it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of adding an orphan's property to the guardian's property when the intention is to destroy it. From where do we take this?

* Students: (...).

* The Shaykh: ﴿And do not devour their properties together with your properties.﴾ As for adding his property to one's own not with the intention of consuming and destroying it, but with the intention of preservation or trade, this is not objectionable; indeed it may even be required of a person. If he adds an orphan's property to his own with the intention of preservation or trade, this is a kindness to him and does not fall under the prohibition, because Allah said: ﴿And do not devour their properties together with your properties﴾; He did not say: do not mix them. This is why Allah said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Reforming them is best; and if you mix with them, they are your brothers. Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer. And had Allah willed, He could have put you in difficulty. Indeed Allah is Almighty, Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah 220]. However, when adding property to property for the purpose of preservation or earning, a person must be careful in recording the orphan's property that he has combined with his own, and the full precaution is to have witnesses to this. For example, he says: I added such-and-such of the orphan's property into my property with which I bought the land, bought the cars, and similar things by which one earns.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that aggression against orphans' property, by taking the good and giving the bad, or by devouring their property, is among the major sins; because of His saying: ﴿Indeed it was a great sin﴾.

If someone asks: Why did the Almighty not say: ﴿And do not devour their properties﴾ and stop there, without saying: ﴿together with your properties﴾? The answer: If He had said, "And do not devour their properties, indeed it was a great sin," that would have sufficed. But He said ﴿their properties together with your properties﴾, because a guardian of an orphan may conceal, may hide and add the orphan's property into his own, and who would know about it? For this reason He said: ﴿do not devour their properties together with your properties﴾. Accordingly, this phrase ﴿together with your properties﴾ is not a restriction, such that we would say: if he devours his property without adding it to his own, it is permitted. No, we do not say that. Rather we say: Allah mentioned this only because some guardians conceal, adding the orphan's property to their own, and no one knows about it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 3 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphan girls, then marry from among the women what pleases you﴾. The first verse concerns the wealth of orphans, and the second concerns the marriage of orphan girls (al-abda', meaning the private parts, here used for marriage). He said: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what pleases you﴾. ﴿Al-yatama﴾ is the plural of yatim (orphan), and what is meant by it is orphan girls.

And His saying: ﴿If you fear that you will not act justly﴾. Some of them said: "Fear here means knowledge, i.e., if you know that you will not act justly," and they cited His saying: ﴿So whoever fears from a testator an injustice or sin and makes reconciliation between them, there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqarah 182]; the meaning of ﴿whoever fears﴾ is "whoever knows." But the correct view regarding this verse of an-Nisa' ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly﴾ is that what is meant is fear even if one does not know. Rather, whenever a person fears that he will not act justly regarding orphans, let him do what Allah has mentioned.

And His saying: ﴿that you will not act justly﴾ means: that you will not be just regarding orphans. Here there is a difference between (aqsata) and (qasata). What is the meaning of aqsata?

* A student: (qasata) means "to be just."
* The Shaykh: (qasata) means "to be just," and (aqsata) means "to be unjust."
* The student: "to be unjust."
* The Shaykh: But if you reversed it, you would be correct.
* The student: (qasata) means "to be just."
* The Shaykh: No, (qasata) means "to be unjust," and (aqsata) means "to be just." For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly﴾ [al-Ma'idah 42], and He said: ﴿And as for the unjust, they will be fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Jinn 15]. Therefore ﴿that you will not act justly﴾ means: that you will not be just regarding orphans.

In the Jahiliyyah, when a man took charge of his paternal cousin's daughter, he wronged her: he would marry her while she disliked it, or marry her without a dowry or with a small dowry, or marry her while he disliked her but wished to keep her confined, or other kinds of oppression and injustice. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, guiding His servants, said: if you fear the absence of justice, the door is open: ﴿then marry what pleases you from among the women﴾. That is: women are not non-existent apart from these orphan girls; rather the matter is broad. Avoid them. Avoid them obligatorily or recommendedly?

* Students: Recommendedly.
* The Shaykh: No, obligatorily. If he fears he will not be just to the orphan girl, it becomes obligatory upon him to avoid her; correct? Based on His saying: ﴿then marry what pleases you from among the women﴾, meaning: leave them and marry what pleases you from among the women. (Ma) some of them explained as (man): "marry whoever pleases you." Why? They said: because a woman is rational, and the rational takes (man) while the non-rational takes (ma). So they said: (ma) here means (man), i.e., marry whoever pleases you. But this view is weak. Rather, we say: if the matter is intended as a description, then a description is not of rational beings, so (ma) is used. Here, does a woman please a man for her person or for her qualities? The second; for her qualities, and for this reason (ma) was used. It was said: a woman's selection is for the qualities that she possesses which make her chosen. So the correct view is that (ma) here is in its proper place and does not mean (man).

And His saying: ﴿what pleases you﴾. ﴿What pleases you﴾ means what is good and what you see as pleasing, and what your souls are content with. Do not compel yourselves to marry those whom you do not desire and who do not please you, because a person compelling himself toward one who does not please him is like a man compelling himself to eat food he does not crave; when a person compels himself to eat food he does not desire, that food becomes like stones in his stomach, i.e., the stomach does not digest it. Rather, marry the one with whom your soul is content. With what does the soul become content? With beauty, yes. "A woman is married for four things: for her wealth, her lineage, her beauty, and her religion" [narrated by al-Bukhari (5090) and Muslim (1466/53) from Abu Hurayrah]. And from wealth: her position; women are married today for their job, because a job is a means of acquiring wealth, is it not? So a woman pleases a man by one of these four qualities, and these are the majority qualities; otherwise a man may marry a woman for reasons other than these, for other causes, but this is what is generally the case.

﴿So marry what pleases you from among the women﴾. The scholars call (min) what? 

* A student: Explanatory (bayaniyyah).
* The Shaykh: Explanatory, because it comes after a vague noun, which is a relative pronoun, so it explains this vague noun. Whenever (min) comes after a conditional noun or relative nouns, it is what? Explanatory. ﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾ [al-Baqarah 197]: this is explanatory, and likewise here.

Student: (...) if we say, regarding His saying (...) the view of some scholars that it is abrogated by His saying ﴿And if you mix with them, then they are your brothers﴾ [al-Baqarah 220].

* The Shaykh: A question says: some scholars said this verse is abrogated by His saying: ﴿And if you mix with them, then they are your brothers﴾.
The answer: this speaker erred, erred greatly, because His saying ﴿And if you mix with them, then they are your brothers﴾ is not the consuming that Allah forbade here, so that we would say there is a contradiction between the two verses. Allah says: ﴿And do not consume their wealth﴾, meaning by mixing it in order to consume it. As for mixing it for reform or for a benefit, you know that this is not objectionable. But some scholars, may Allah pardon us and them, when they are unable to reconcile two texts, say: this is abrogated. I say: when they are unable, because there may be no contradiction between the two texts; each text may be understood as carrying a meaning. This is a very dangerous matter, extremely dangerous, because the meaning of abrogation is denying the abrogated ruling; take care, this is not a trivial matter. The meaning of abrogation is that I deny the abrogated and do not regard it as a legal ruling. So the matter is grave, and for this reason it is not permissible to claim abrogation when reconciliation is possible, ever.

Student: Now, if we supposed (man) in place of (ma), the context would be clearer than the other reading.

* The Shaykh: La ilaha illa Allah. So this is a disparagement of the Qur'an. Seek forgiveness from Allah. Say: "O Allah, forgive me." It is not clearer; rather this is an indication from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as will come in the benefits, that a person should focus on meanings and qualities.

Student: If we supposed (man) instead of (ma)?

* The Shaykh: If we supposed (man), its meaning would be only specification.

Student: But if we supposed the description, how would the context be?

* The Shaykh: If we supposed what?

* The Student: If we now put a description, how would the context be?

* The Shaykh: A description?

* The Student: There is the description of women.

* The Shaykh: But a description must have something described, and the description is not what is married; rather the meaning is that a woman is married for her qualities, not for her person.

* Student: (...), we have a problem that the Messenger ﷺ and the Companions were truly Arabs (...) the villages, and would one derive that the difference of people is considered (...) the Arabs?

The Shaykh: It is what?

* The Student: I say: at the time of the Messenger ﷺ they were truly Arabs (...) the meanings, if they say this is from other than the Arabic language.

* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. The reason is that the Qur'an was revealed in their language. Now, if I speak to a commoner in the colloquial dialect, will my speech be difficult for you? It is not difficult; in their time the standard Arabic was like our colloquial language today.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, some hypocrites cite this verse ﴿So marry what pleases you from among the women﴾ to claim that Islam is unjust. We said: why? They said: because when a man marries two, three, or four, it is injustice to this woman; it causes resentment and harm. They cite this verse. So how should we respond, may Allah be good to you?

* The Shaykh: Its time has not come; its time is in the benefits, God willing.

* Student: Shaykh (...) it may be required to combine the wealth of an orphan (...) trade?

* The Shaykh: It may be required to combine his wealth?

* The Student: For trade, for example.

* The Shaykh: No, no. If there is an oppressor who takes orphans' wealth under the pretext that he will preserve it, while we know he does not want to preserve it but to consume it, and someone comes and combines it with his own wealth, this is obligatory for him.

* Student: Shaykh, peace be upon you. If one combines an orphan's wealth with his own and then loses in his own wealth, does he compensate the orphan's wealth?

* The Shaykh: (...) he says: if one combines an orphan's wealth with his own and then loses in his own wealth, is he liable to the orphan or not?
We say: as long as, when he did it, he believed that this was the most beneficial, but matters turned out otherwise, there is nothing upon him; no sin and no liability, because He says: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [at-Taghabun 16]. This is a principle: every person who has authority in disposing (...) there is no liability upon him, let alone when matters come out differently from what was expected.

* Student: Shaykh, what is the benefit of specifying consumption, ﴿do not consume﴾?

* The Shaykh: The benefit of mentioning consumption is that it is the most common, the most general of benefits, and because it is what the body benefits from directly. Clothing you benefit from but externally. Therefore you find that the verses generally express it with "eating": ﴿Indeed, those who consume the wealth of orphans unjustly﴾ [an-Nisa' 10], ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume usury, doubled and multiplied﴾ [Ali 'Imran 130], and similar.

* * *

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the outcast. ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphan girls, then marry from among the women what pleases you, two, three, or four; but if you fear that you will not be just, then one, or what your right hands possess. That is more suitable that you not commit injustice. And give women their dowries graciously; but if they give you willingly a part of it, then consume it with satisfaction and ease. And do not give the foolish their property which Allah has made for you a means of sustenance, but provide for them from it and clothe them and speak to them kind words. And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them sound judgment, release their property to them. And do not consume it excessively and hastily, [fearing] that they will grow up. And whoever is wealthy – let him refrain; and whoever is poor – let him eat according to what is reasonable. And when you release their property to them, have witnesses over them; and sufficient is Allah as Accountant﴾ [an-Nisa' 3–6].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the outcast. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And give the orphans their property, and do not substitute the bad for the good﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿give the orphans their property﴾?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: That is: give them their property in full, without reduction.
Now, does this mean we should hand them the money while they are orphans?

* Student: Yes, we hand them the money.

* The Shaykh: While they are orphans?

* Student: No, we do not hand it over.

* The Shaykh: We do not hand it over. Then how does He say "give them their property"?

* The Student: That is, we preserve it for them.

* The Shaykh: That is, by preserving it for them; and handing it over does not occur?

* The Student: Only after he reaches maturity and sound judgment.

* The Shaykh: Only after maturity and sound judgment. His saying ﴿give the orphans their property﴾: "orphans" is the plural of what?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The orphanhood has ended. Now, if the child's mother died, is he called an orphan?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Why?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, but why do we consider one whose father died an orphan, and one whose mother died not an orphan?

* Student: Because his father is the one who provides for him through earning and care.

* The Shaykh: Because his father is the one who provides for him in care and earning, unlike the mother.

His saying: ﴿And do not consume their property along with your property﴾. How did He say ﴿along with your property﴾?

* Student: (...) do not combine your property with their property.

* The Shaykh: So that you would consume it. Good.
If he combined his property with theirs for preservation, is this forbidden?

* Student: It is not forbidden.

The Shaykh: What is the evidence from this verse?

* Student: ﴿And do not consume﴾ (...).

* The Shaykh: That is, it indicates that the intent is combining them for consumption. Now, is there a verse from the Qur'an that indicates this?

* Student: For preservation?

* The Shaykh: For the permissibility of adding orphans' property to our property, not for consumption but for preservation.

* Student: ﴿And if you mix with them, then they are your brothers. And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer. And if Allah had willed, He could have put you in difficulty﴾ [al-Baqarah 220].

* The Shaykh: ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Reforming them is best. And if you mix with them, then they are your brothers. And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾ [al-Baqarah 220]. Right. Now, what is meant by "the bad" in His saying ﴿and do not substitute the bad﴾?

* Student: The bad, Shaykh, which he explained: it was said: "the bad" means the bad of your property, which you exchange for the good of their property; and it was said: "the bad..."

* The Shaykh: Good. And according to this opinion, what is meant by "the bad"?

* Student: The inferior.

* The Shaykh: The inferior. Good. And what was said?

* Student: It was said: "the bad" means the forbidden.

* The Shaykh: The forbidden.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The meaning is that if you take orphans' property, it is bad.
According to the second view, is it bad in itself or bad because of how it was acquired?

* Student: Because of how it was acquired.

* The Shaykh: Bad because of how it was acquired.
The clause ﴿Indeed, that is a great sin﴾: what is its place relative to what precedes it in meaning?

* Student: Explanatory, an explanation of some of what preceded.

* The Shaykh: No.

* Student: Causal.

* The Shaykh: Causal: ﴿Indeed, that is a great sin﴾.
Does ﴿Indeed, that is a great sin﴾ indicate that combining orphans' property with ours in order to consume it is one of the major sins?

* Student: Yes, because of His saying: "Indeed, it is a great sin" (many).

* The Shaykh: It is recited as ﴿kabiran﴾ (great).

Then He said, Exalted: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphan girls, then marry from among the women what pleases you﴾. ﴿If you fear﴾ means you feared and anticipated. It was said: the meaning of ﴿if you fear﴾ is "if you know"; and the correct view is the first meaning, i.e., you feared.

And His saying: ﴿that you will not act justly﴾, i.e., that you will not be just ﴿regarding orphans, then marry...﴾ and so on. In the Jahiliyyah, a man would have an orphan girl under him, i.e., in his care, then delay her marriage for himself until he married her, or he would marry her while disliking her, but out of his guardianship and provision for her. So Allah clarified in this verse that if they fear they will not be just regarding orphans, then let them turn away from them.

﴿If you fear﴾ means you feared and anticipated; it was said the meaning is "if you know," and the correct view is the first, i.e., you feared.

And His saying: ﴿that you will not act justly﴾, i.e., that you will not be just, ﴿regarding orphans, then marry...﴾ and so on.

In the Jahiliyyah, a man would have an orphan girl under him, i.e., in his care, then delay her marriage for himself until he married her, or he would marry her while disliking her, but out of his guardianship and provision for her. So Allah clarified in this verse that if they fear they will not be just regarding orphans, then let them turn away from them, to what? He said: ﴿then marry what pleases you from among the women﴾, meaning: marry the woman who pleases you, i.e., whom you see as good and find attractive; therefore He said: ﴿what pleases you from among the women﴾, using (ma) rather than (man), because (man) is for a rational being when the individual is intended, but if the quality is intended, (ma) is used.

They said: among it is the Arab saying: "Glory to what subjected these to us," meaning the camels, intending "Glory to Him who..." i.e., "Glory to Allah," but when this speaker intended the quality, namely the perfection of Allah's might and His subjugation of things, he used (ma).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 3 (part 2 of 3):

He said: ﴿So marry what seems good to you of women﴾. And His saying: ﴿what seems good to you of women﴾. Is it connected to (*unkiḥū*, "marry"), meaning: marry from among the women what seems good to you; or is it an explanation of (*mā*, "what") in His saying ﴿what seems good to you﴾? The second is closer, and the first is permissible, but the second is closer, meaning: marry those women who are good for you.

﴿Two, three, or four﴾. The grammarians say that these three words are not declinable (*lā yanṣarif*, diptotes). What prevents them from taking tanwīn is descriptiveness (*al-waṣfiyyah*) and deviation from the original form (*al-'adl*). The meaning of ﴿two﴾ (*maḥnā*) is two by two, ﴿three﴾ (*thulātha*) is three by three, and ﴿four﴾ (*rubā'a*) is four by four. So what prevents them from taking tanwīn is descriptiveness and deviation.

On this basis we say: ﴿two﴾ (*maḥnā*) is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to ﴿women﴾, meaning: while they are two, three, or four. That is, marry two each, or three each, or four each. The meaning is not "marry two, three, and four," contrary to those who claim that and say that the verse indicates the permissibility of marrying nine, since two and three make five and four makes four, all together nine.

This is far from the style of the Arabic language. This style is one of distribution (*taqsīm*): some of you marry two each, some of you marry three each, and some of you marry four each. This is because the address ﴿marry﴾ is addressed to a group, and an address to a group is not to one person. So when the address is to the group, distribute ﴿two, three﴾ among the group, and the meaning becomes: some of you marry two, some of you three, and some of you four. This is supported by the hadiths reported from the Prophet ﷺ that a man may not marry more than four.

As for the Prophet ﷺ, he was singled out with several special privileges regarding marriage. Among them: he could marry more than four; he could marry by gift; according to one opinion, the obligation of equal division (*qasm*) did not apply to him; and after he gave his wives the choice and they chose God and His Messenger, it became forbidden for him to marry others than them until he died. Among them also: his wives may not be married by anyone after him. So the Messenger, peace be upon him, was singled out with privileges not found in anyone else.

In terms of its indication, this verse is like His saying: ﴿Who made the angels messengers having wings, two, three, or four﴾ [Fāṭir 1]. Had God, exalted is He, wished to explain to His servants the permissibility of women up to nine, He would have said: "So marry what seems good to you of women, two or three or four or five or six, up to nine," and He would not use this ambiguous style, because the Qur'an was revealed as an explanation of everything.

His saying ﴿two, three, or four﴾ does not mention one, because the context is one of choice and of giving the soul its share, when a person fears that he will not be just with orphans. We say: if you fear that you will not be just with the orphan girl, then before you are women, in quantity and in quality. In quantity: when does quantity begin? From two upward. In quality: He said ﴿what seems good to you﴾.

So the door is open before you regarding the women you desire, in quality and—what? —and in quantity. It is known that one has no quantity; one is one. Quantity means increase in number, from two upward.

﴿Two, three, or four. But if you fear that you will not be just﴾: ﴿fear﴾ means you think, ﴿that you will not be just, then one﴾: meaning, marry one and do not add to her.

﴿Or what your right hands possess﴾. Meaning: or marry what your right hands possess? I ask: no, because what the right hand possesses is not married. Ownership by the right hand is enjoyed through ownership, not through marriage. For this reason it is forbidden for a man to marry his slave-woman, correct? It is forbidden for a man to marry his slave-woman.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is forbidden to marry one's slave-woman, because she is lawful to him by a contract stronger than marriage, which is ownership by the right hand. The weaker does not overturn the stronger, whereas the reverse is not the case: the stronger may override the weaker.

If a man buys his wife, the marriage is annulled, and she becomes lawful to him through ownership by the right hand. Do you understand? But if he has a slave-woman, he cannot marry her, because—what? Because he owns her by a contract stronger than marriage, for the master owns both the person and the usufruct, whereas the husband owns only the usufruct.
