Therefore it is not valid to say that His saying ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾ is coordinated with ﴿one﴾, because the meaning would be disrupted. Rather, the meaning is: marry one, or enjoy what your right hands possess, or a phrase similar to that. In short, it is not coordinated with what preceded except as coordination of sentences, so a suitable verb is supposed for His saying ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾.

He said: ﴿That is closer to your not being unjust﴾. ﴿That﴾ refers to marrying one when there is fear of not being just, or refers to a man marrying two, three, or four when there is fear of not being just with orphans, or both? Both. That is, ﴿that﴾ means your marriage of two, three, or four if you fear you will not be just with orphans, or your marriage of one if you fear you will not be equitable. ﴿Closer﴾ means nearer. ﴿That you not be unjust﴾ means that you not oppress. This is the clear meaning of the verse.

As for what is reported from al-Shafi'i, that the meaning is "closer to your dependents not multiplying," that is a very weak opinion, very weak. Why? Because the multiplication of dependents is desired by God, and because dependents multiply when a person has intercourse with what his right hand possesses. God, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿one, or what your right hands possess, that is closer to your not being unjust﴾. So if a man has a hundred slave-girls and has intercourse with each one, how many children will come to him in a year? A hundred children, a hundred children in a year. If this is so, how can we say that when a person has intercourse with what his right hand possesses, it is closer to having no dependents? For this reason this opinion is considered very weak, since it contradicts the purpose of the Lawgiver regarding the multiplication of children, and because few children do not result when a man has intercourse with his possessions.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is valid, and he is the guardian (*walī*). If a man is the paternal cousin of a woman and wishes to marry her, there is no harm. He asks her: "Would you like me to marry you?" If she says yes, he marries her. But how is the contract concluded? He brings two witnesses and says: "I call you both to witness that I have married my ward (*mawlāyatī*) so-and-so," and he says: "I accept," or not? He does not say "I accept." He says: "I call you both to witness that I have married my ward so-and-so, or I have married myself to my ward so-and-so," like the Prophet's saying to Ṣafiyyah: "I have freed you and made your freedom your dowry" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (5086) and Muslim (1365/85), with the wording: he freed Ṣafiyyah and made her freedom her dowry, from the hadith of Anas].

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, because once it is distributed, we must bring something that indicates repetition.

* Student: If a man marries a slave-woman and she bears him a child, the child is a slave of the slave-woman's owner. If the man later buys the slave-woman after the child is born, does the husband buy his slave-woman?
* Shaykh: Yes, he bought his wife?
* Student: Yes, she became owned.
* Shaykh: She became owned by him.
* Student: And the child?
* Shaykh: The child is owned by the master.
* Student: The first one?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: What is your opinion, O Shaykh, of someone who derives from this verse that the basic principle is plurality?
* Shaykh: It will come to us with the benefits.

﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly toward the orphans?﴾
* Student: That you will not be just in dealing with them.
* Shaykh: That you will not be just in dealing with them.
Who are the orphans?
* Student: Someone whose father died before he reached maturity.
* Shaykh: Someone whose father died before he reached maturity.
His saying ﴿that you will not act justly toward the orphans﴾: how is "not acting justly"?
* Student: Achieving justice.
* Shaykh: That is, what is justice?
* Student: Equality is more appropriate among relatives.
* Shaykh: No, no, because He said ﴿so marry﴾; the matter is about marriage.
* Student: If the condition is certain, that he will not be just with this woman.
* Shaykh: Such as?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: For the sake of connecting the answer of the condition with the condition's verb. That is, do we want an example that links the verb of the condition with its answer?
* Student: (...), that he would not be just with her by taking her property.
* Shaykh: That is, the orphan girl is, for example, with her paternal cousin, and he fears he will not be just with her by not marrying her at the proper dowry (*mahr al-mithl*), giving her less. So God, mighty and majestic, made clear that the door is open: ﴿so marry what seems good to you of women﴾, and so on.

Why did He use *mā* (what) rather than *man* (who)?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: They are interchangeable, but whenever something departs from its original usage, there must be a benefit.
* Student: An indication that (...).
* Shaykh: Well done.

His exalted saying: ﴿But if you fear that you will not be just, then one﴾. What does it mean?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Between whom?
* Student: Between the wives.
* Shaykh: Then marry one.
In the verse there is evidence that justice among slave-women is not obligatory. From where is this derived from the verse?
* Student: From His saying: ﴿But if you fear that you will not be just, then one﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, one. We now ask: does the verse show that it is not obligatory to be just among slave-women in intercourse and in other matters as well?
* Student: ﴿Then one, or what your right hands possess﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Or what your right hands possess﴾. This indicates that justice among slave-women is not obligatory.
What is the meaning of His saying ﴿that you not be unjust﴾?
* Student: That you not oppress.
* Shaykh: That you not oppress. How is it closer that they not oppress?
* Student: That is, do not oppress among the wives.
* Shaykh: That is, if he limits himself to one, there is no one with her between whom justice is obligatory. I say: since if he limits himself to one, justice is not obligatory for him, because there is no second wife. Then there is no oppression. Likewise, regarding what the right hands possess, justice is not obligatory, so if he inclines toward one of them, there is no oppression, because justice is not obligatory.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: ﴿if you fear that you will not act justly toward the orphans﴾: it is obligatory for a person to take precaution if he fears falling into what is forbidden, because of His saying: ﴿if you fear that you will not act justly toward the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women﴾. That is, do not expose yourselves to injustice.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a person should marry a woman with whom his soul is content, because that is closer to establishing harmony (*yu'dam*) between them. For this reason it is prescribed for a person to look at the woman he proposes to, until his soul is content with her.

* Derived from this benefit: it becomes clear that the error of some Bedouin practice of forcing a man to marry his paternal cousin though he does not want her is wrong, because God says: ﴿marry what seems good to you﴾. If the man's soul is not content with this woman, how can he marry her? What some Bedouin do is undoubtedly an error and contrary to the Shariah, for if he does not marry his paternal cousin, someone else among people will marry her.

* Among the benefits of this verse: when God, mighty and majestic, closes the door to something forbidden, He opens the door to something lawful, or doors to what is lawful. Because His saying ﴿if you fear that you will not act justly toward the orphans﴾ means: then do not marry them, but rather—what? —marry what seems good to you of women.

This is from the method of the Qur'an and the method of the Sunnah: when a door is closed, they open the door of what is lawful, so that a person's work and activity are not blocked. I think similar examples have preceded this, which we covered in the explanation, including His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not say "Ra'ina" but say "Unzurna"﴾ [al-Baqarah 104], and the Prophet ﷺ's guidance on selling inferior dates for silver and then buying good dates with the silver.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the legislated nature of polygamy among wives. Consider with us: is it derived from this verse that polygamy is legislated, or that it is permissible?
* Students: Permissible.
* Shaykh: Yes, because there is a difference between saying "legislated" and saying "permissible." Apparently what is understood from it is permissibility, because the mention of numbers here is in contrast to the prohibition of marrying orphans about whom a person fears he will not act justly. It is as if He said: if you abandon marrying one of the orphans, then before you is marrying two, three, or four. This is the closer view.

However, the legislated nature of polygamy is derived from other evidences, including that the Prophet, peace be upon him, wished his community to increase in offspring, and this is achieved more through plurality than through monogamy.

Some people have shown me a newspaper clipping saying that the Shiites in al-Qatif have begun doing a good thing in reality, which is group celebrations for weddings, so that in one night, at a single banquet, they gathered over forty weddings.
* Student: Sixty-five.
* Shaykh: Sixty-five? Sixty-five weddings in one night? Do you understand the meaning now? That is, instead of going to a wedding hall for the wedding of one man only, we make it so that on this night, in the same hall, there are twenty men, or sixty-five men, or a hundred men. Without doubt this saves expenses and saves people effort, and it is a good practice, if people do it, then this is good, as far as it is feasible.
* Student: (...).
* Another student: It is not enough, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Yes, the hall is not enough, because people invite nations. But if we know that there will be forty grooms in this hall, we take forty rooms for them, and if there are none, we set up tents. We do not increase the number of guests; instead of one person inviting two hundred men, he invites twenty men.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: By God, if they intend by this the face of God, they will be rewarded for it, because this is a matter of reducing burden, and the most blessed marriage is the easiest in cost.

In any case, this is a second matter. The other matter you are pointing to, but our discussion is about the hadith: "Whoever establishes a good practice in Islam will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection" [Reported by Muslim (1017/69) from the hadith of Jarir ibn 'Abdullah, with similar wording].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is not permissible to exceed four, because of His saying ﴿two, three, or four﴾, even though the context is one of opening the door for people, multiplication, and favor. Such a door is described with the greatest favor that has nothing beyond it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of means to what is forbidden, because of His saying ﴿But if you fear that you will not be just, then one﴾. He made it obligatory to limit oneself to one wife if a person fears not being just. This principle is a great principle in the foundations of jurisprudence: means have the rulings of their ends. What the obligation cannot be completed without is itself obligatory; what the recommended act cannot be completed without is itself recommended; and what leads to the forbidden is itself forbidden.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is not obligatory to be just among slave-women in intercourse or in anything else, because of His saying ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾.

* Among its benefits: the obligation of justice among wives, because of His saying ﴿But if you fear that you will not be just, then one﴾. Injustice among wives is among the major sins, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever has two wives and inclines toward one of them will come on the Day of Resurrection with one side leaning" [Reported by Abu Dawud (2133) and al-Tirmidhi (1141); the wording is Abu Dawud's, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah].

* Among the benefits of this verse: the establishment of ownership by the right hand, because of His saying ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾. This legal ruling cannot be abolished out of fear of people's blame or their gloating. Rather, it must remain: that is, the ownership by the right hand remains when its cause exists. When the cause of ownership by the right hand exists—and what is the cause of ownership by the right hand? Disbelief. When the Muslims fight the disbelievers and take their women and offspring as captives.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment of ownership for a person. This is not the establishment of slavery; it is the establishment of ownership, that a person can own. This does not contradict our saying that ownership belongs to God. The reason is that ownership is of two kinds: complete, comprehensive ownership, in which the owner is not questioned about any disposal, and this belongs to whom? To God. And ownership that is less than that in comprehensiveness and disposal. This is established. Moreover, it has types: sometimes a person owns the person (*raqabah*), sometimes he owns only the usufruct (*manfa'ah*), and sometimes he owns both the person and the usufruct. Do you understand? Sometimes he owns only the usufruct, like a hired person; sometimes he owns only the person, like a slave bequeathed to one individual with his usufruct bequeathed to another. In that case, the owner of the person is Zayd and the owner of the usufruct is 'Ubayd. Do you understand?

Yet I can almost see some of you saying: what is the benefit of bequeathing a slave, and bequeathing his usufruct to another slave? We say: there is a benefit in it, namely manumission. If the owner of the substance frees him, he becomes free, and the owner of the usufruct has his usufruct.

The point, in any case, is this: ownership of the substance, ownership of the usufruct, and ownership of both together, like the ordinary owner who has full authority of disposal.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the right hand is superior to the left hand, since He attributed ownership to it. There is no doubt that the right hand is superior to the left; for this reason the right hand is regarded as a sign of honour and the left as a sign of humiliation. Good things are taken with the right hand, and foul things are removed with the left.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the gradation of deeds, meaning that some are higher than others in evil and lower than others in good, as indicated by His saying: ﴿That is closer to not falling into injustice﴾, because "al-adna" (the closer/lower) is a comparative form, so there must be one that is superior and one that is inferior.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 4:

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾. ﴿Give (ātū)﴾ means: bestow. The difference between (ātū) and ( utū): (ātū) means "give," and (utū) means "come." So (ātū) means "give," and ( utū) means "come."

﴿Give the women their dowries﴾. Is the address in His words ﴿give﴾ directed to the husbands or to the guardians? There are two opinions on this in the verse.

The first opinion: it is addressed to the guardians. The meaning then is that Allah commanded the guardians to give the women their dowries without taking anything from them. This is because in the Jahiliyyah, when a man married off his daughter, he would take the bride-price and give her nothing except what she wore on the night of the wedding, and he would take the rest, plundering it from her. So Allah commanded them to give the women their dowries as a gift.

The second opinion: the address is to the husbands. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded them to give the women their dowries willingly, without procrastination and without reluctance. If the verse can bear both meanings without contradiction, what is obligatory? To take it in both senses. So we say: the address is to both the husbands and the guardians.

﴿Give the women their dowries﴾. ﴿The women﴾ means: those who are married, as is shown by His words ﴿their dowries﴾. (Ṣadaqāt) is the plural of (ṣadaqah), which is the dower (mahr). It was given this name because paying it is a proof of the seriousness (ṣidq) of the one seeking the woman.

His words ﴿as a gift (niḥlah)﴾ mean: a good gift with which your souls are content. It is said: "nahalahu," meaning he gave him a good gift with which his soul was content.

On this basis, some have claimed that it is an absolute object (maf'ūl muṭlaq) of His words ﴿give the women﴾, like the speaker's saying: "I stood standing" or "I sat sitting." For (ātā) means nahala, and (ātū) means give freely, and niḥlah is a gift given with a contented soul.

﴿But if they give you of it willingly, then eat it﴾. ﴿If they give (in ṭibna)﴾ means: the women. His words ﴿willingly (nafsan)﴾ are a transferred verbal noun (maṣdar maḥwal) from the agent. A transferred verbal noun is sometimes transferred from the agent, as in this verse, and sometimes from the object, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾ [al-Qamar 12], meaning the springs of the earth.

﴿But if they give you of it (min)﴾: it is said that (min) is partitive (tab'īḍiyyah), and it is said that it is explanatory (bayāniyyah). On the first view, the meaning is: if they give you of part of it. On the second view, the meaning is: if they give you of all of it or part of it, because (min) explains the locus of the ruling, regardless of whether it is all or part.

﴿But if they give you of it willingly, then eat it﴾. He expressed it by "eating" because it is the most specific of the ways of benefiting, since eating nourishes the body and the body grows by it, unlike clothing, dwellings, and mounts, whose benefit is external. Clothing is an external covering, but eating is an internal covering. Is that correct? Eating is an internal covering? It is a benefit, yes, correct, a benefit, but it is also a covering. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, it is for you that you will not be hungry therein or be naked, and that you will not be thirsty therein or be exposed to the sun﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 118-119]. The correspondence between thirst and exposure to the sun, which is the heat of the sun, is clear, and between hunger and nakedness is clear, because being sated is a covering of the inner body. The stomach is empty, bare, and when food enters it, it covers and clothes it, so it is an inner covering.

In any case, ﴿eat it with ease and enjoyment (hanīʾan)﴾. I say: He expressed it by eating because it is the most specific of the ways of benefiting, since its benefit to the body is direct, and the body grows by it, unlike clothing, dwellings, and mounts, whose benefit is external.

His words ﴿hanīʾan﴾ mean: at the time of eating, ﴿marīʾan﴾ means: after eating. So the marīʾ is good in its outcome, and the hanīʾ is easy to swallow. Let me give you an illustrative example: if we give a person who is not from Jeddah a fish and he wants to eat it, he may choke on it ten times before it reaches his stomach, because it has bones, fins, and the like which choke him. Is this eating hanīʾ or not hanīʾ? Not hanīʾ. But you hear the crunching of its bones between his teeth and he does not mind. I have witnessed this myself, I witnessed it with my own eyes: he takes the tail, which is like a comb, and places it between his teeth and gnaws it the way we gnaw dried dates. Is this hanīʾ for him or not? It is hanīʾ for him, because he swallows it easily, but for one who is not accustomed to it, it is not hanīʾ.

﴿marīʾan﴾: we said it means good in its outcome. A person may eat food that is soft and delicious in the mouth, but when it reaches his stomach, he writhes from it. What is that? Marīʾ or not marīʾ? Not marīʾ; this is not marīʾ.

Is it among this what some people do, when the food is hot and burns their hand, then burns their mouth, then swallows it quickly, then burns their stomach? This is not good in its outcome, because it harms him. But some people, glory be to Allah, do not care about this. What a person should eat is food that is good in its outcome, which is marīʾ.

For this reason, some people said a phrase that pleased me: "Eat what is pleasant to your stomach, not what is pleasant to your mouth." Is that correct? Sometimes a person eats food that tastes good, fine and sweet, but when it reaches the stomach it causes pain in the stomach, either because the stomach was already full or for some other reason. For this reason Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: food becomes forbidden if a person fears harm or indigestion (takhmah) from it. It is forbidden to eat it if he fears harm or indigestion. Harm from what? Harm from eating: he carries a stomach that he has filled, and it tires him, to the point that if he sits he may be unable to sit except cross-legged, due to the great fullness of the stomach. We say: it is forbidden for you to eat it.

Or indigestion (al-tukhmah). Do you know what indigestion is? What is it?

* A student: Satiety.

* The Shaykh: No, it is change (al-taghayyur). We call it ghīrah or ghīrah like ṭīrah, meaning change. And change, praise be to Allah, is now very rare because of the good quality of foods, but previously, when foods were not of that quality, a person would experience indigestion; when he belched, a foul smell would come from him, and he might be afflicted with illness.

In any case, I... we have digressed a great deal. Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, says that if a person fears harm or indigestion from eating, it becomes forbidden for him, and what he said has a basis. But unfortunately we now eat a great deal, and then when we have filled our stomachs we go looking for a digestive aid, do we not? Indeed, I find that at some tables they set out Pepsi and the like so that whoever eats may drink it. We say: do not burden yourself; eat a customary amount.

A man who is a physician and was with me last week, an American doctor originally, told me: "I embraced Islam because of one hadith and one verse." We asked him: "What are they?" He said the hadith is: "The son of Adam needs only a few morsels to keep his back upright. If he must do more, then a third for his food, a third for his drink, and a third for his breath." He said: this is the foundations of medicine, and if people applied it, hardly anyone would fall ill. As for the verse, it is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe over your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles﴾ [al-Ma'idah 6].

He said: these limbs that are prominent and visible are exposed to dust and dirt, exposed to everything. When they are washed five times in the day and night, they remain clean. So Islam is a religion of cleanliness and of regimen, and these are the foundations of medicine. Then we told him: there is something else besides this: this purification purifies the immaterial impurity, which is sins, because one is forgiven with the last drop of water. But the disbelievers do not know this; the disbelievers have only the outward.

So I say: if we tried, even for one week, not to eat a great deal. But one of you may say: "If I do not eat much, I become hungry before the next meal, is that right?" What do we say? We say: eat.

Some people told me that the countries that call themselves advanced countries eat five meals in a day and night. Why? Because they do not overeat; they eat, and when they become hungry they eat, and when they become hungry they eat again. And if you try it for a week, from Wednesday night, and inform me, God willing, of the result next Wednesday night.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, regarding the Shi'ah, you say that it is praiseworthy (...) they are abundant, but these are the most hostile people toward Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah, and their solidarity is to fight Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah, so how can we say this thing is praiseworthy?

* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. This person says: the Shi'ah are known to be enemies of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah, so how can their action be praiseworthy? We say: a person may be praised for his action without being praised for his religion. That is, our praising this act of theirs does not necessitate that we praise them for their religion. Rather, we have no doubt that they follow a false religion, that they are far from the truth, and that it is obligatory for them to return to the path of Ahl al-Sunnah.

It is strange that they say: "We are Ahl al-Sunnah," that is, they say to Ahl al-Sunnah: "You are Ahl al-Sunnah," and then they oppose them. If they are Ahl al-Sunnah, do you want to (...) the Sunnah?!

This person is praised for his generosity though he is a disbeliever, and for his kindness though he is a disbeliever. The Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, said regarding the captives of Badr: "If al-Muṭ'im ibn 'Adiyy were alive and spoke to me about these foul ones, I would have released them for his sake." Why? Because he had entered under his protection. The Messenger entered under the protection of al-Muṭ'im. So it is obligatory, in justice, that we say: a praiseworthy act is praised whoever performs it.

Yes, if we feared a corruption from this, such as that this person would be pleased with himself, or that this would be propaganda for the falsehood he follows, then we would remain silent, taking the good without praising the one who did it if he is not worthy of praise.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah protect you, that justice between female slaves is not obligatory. From where is this derived from this verse?

* The Shaykh: From His words: ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾, because Allah said: ﴿But if you fear that you will not be just, then one only﴾. This is clear regarding marriage: or if you fear that you will not be just, then (take) those whom your right hands possess.

* A student: Not conjoined to ﴿what is good﴾?

* The Shaykh: No, it is not conjoined to ﴿what is good﴾, meaning it is not conjoined to (one); because whoever marries a slave-woman is obligated to be just.

* A student: When he cannot afford it?

* The Shaykh: Correct. That is, for example, if a man married two slave-women from their masters, or from their master, he would be obligated to be just. But Allah says: ﴿what your right hands possess﴾, meaning: have intercourse with, or marry, what your right hands possess, in the sense of intercourse.

* A student: A man wished to propose to a woman, and the woman's family stipulated that he not see her except after the marriage contract?

* The Shaykh: They stipulated that he not see her except after the marriage contract. We do not guarantee this; it is not a stipulation. He asked them to see her before the contract. No, he is not compelled. How could he be compelled? Indeed, in earlier times people never saw the woman at all before the proposal.

I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not give the foolish your wealth, which Allah has made for you a means of support﴾ [al-Nisa' 5]. In the verse there are two readings concerning ﴿the foolish (al-sufahā')﴾ and concerning ﴿a means of support (qiyāman)﴾.

Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾.

* Some benefits are derived from this verse. Among its benefits: the obligation of giving women their dowries, from His words: ﴿give﴾.

* Among its benefits also: it is not permissible for the guardian to take anything from the women's dowry, for two reasons. The first reason: He attributed the dowry to them, so it is their property. The second reason: He commanded us to give them their dowries: ﴿Give the women their dowries﴾.

This matter is one on which the scholars differ. Some of them said: it is permissible for the father specifically to stipulate for himself whatever he wishes from his daughter's dowry. Some scholars said: it is not permissible, neither for the father nor for others, to stipulate anything of the dowry for himself.

What the Sunnah supports is that it is not permissible for a guardian to stipulate anything of the dowry for himself, whether he is the father or someone else. But if the contract is completed and the husband wishes to give the father or other guardians, or the mother, or the maternal aunt, or the like, something as an honour, then there is no harm in it, as the Sunnah has shown. As for what is before the contract, it is all for the woman, and it is not lawful for anyone to stipulate any of it for himself.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is obligatory to give them the dowry as a niḥlah, that is, a complete gift, so that there is no obligation (minnah) in the future.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is permissible for a woman to waive part of the dowry or return it, if she has already received it, from His words: ﴿But if they give you of it willingly, then eat it, with ease and enjoyment﴾.

* Among its benefits: if she waives something out of shame or modesty, it is not lawful to accept it, from His words: ﴿But if they give you of it willingly, then eat it﴾. For this reason the scholars said: if a person gives you a gift while you know that he gave it only out of shame and embarrassment, it is not permissible for you to accept it from him, because this is like compulsion.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever possesses something with willing consent, it is lawful for him, both now and in the future, from His words: ﴿with ease and enjoyment﴾: ﴿hanīʾan﴾ at the time of eating, ﴿marīʾan﴾ after eating.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is not lawful to take anything of another's property without his willing consent, because Allah made the lawfulness of consuming it conditional on its being with willing consent. The Sunnah has also come explicitly to this: "The property of a Muslim man is not lawful except with his willing consent." And likewise the Qur'an says: ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood, except it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾ [al-Nisa' 29].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 5:

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property⁠—﴾ He said: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾. ﴿The foolish your property﴾ has two readings. The first reading is with two clear hamzas: ﴿as-sufahā'a amwālakum﴾. The second reading drops one of the two hamzas: ﴿as-sufahā amwālakum﴾. The first is the original form and the second is the eased form. Likewise His words ﴿qiyāman﴾ have two readings: ﴿qiyāman﴾ and ﴿qiyaman﴾, and the meaning is one.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾, meaning: do not give it to them. Do not give to the foolish. The foolish (as-sufahā', plural of safīh) is one who does not handle affairs well, either because of youth or because of deficiency in his intellect and sound judgment. This is the safīh. Foolishness (safah) occurs in wealth and occurs in actions, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself?﴾ [al-Baqarah 130]. So whoever turns away from the religion of Abraham, the upright and tolerant monotheism, is a fool, even if he is among the most sound-minded of people in managing his wealth.

He says: ﴿your property which Allah has made for you a means of support﴾. ﴿Your property﴾: He attributed the property to you. The scholars differed over whether the meaning is: do not give the foolish your own property, because they will waste it without benefit, so it is lost to you and lost to them. Some scholars said: rather, what is meant is their property, but He attributed it to you because of guardianship, so it is as if by our guardianship over this property we possess it. The verse is suitable for both meanings, and one of the rules of interpretation is that if a verse is suitable for two meanings that do not contradict each other, it is to be understood as both.

As for His words ﴿which Allah has made for you a means of support﴾: ﴿ja'ala﴾ means "made" or "rendered," meaning Allah made them a means of support for us. Through wealth the interests of our religion and the interests of our worldly life are upheld. How many a captive has been freed with money, how many a necessity has been removed with money, and how many an orphan's heart has been comforted with money. Wealth is in reality a support for people in the affairs of their religion and their worldly life. Indeed, Allah, glorified and exalted, mentions striving with wealth before striving with the self, because the need for wealth in jihad is greater than the need for the self. Even the one who strives with his own person needs wealth; what brings him to the battlefield except wealth? For this reason we find that Allah, glorified and exalted, mentions wealth in jihad before mentioning the lives.

﴿And provide for them from it﴾: ﴿arzuqūhum﴾ means "give them provision," and provision is giving. His words ﴿fīhā﴾ mean "from/within the property," and He did not say ﴿minhā﴾ ("from it") as an indication that the guardian must earn with the wealth of these foolish people, so that the provision is ﴿fīhā﴾ (within it, through its growth) and not ﴿minhā﴾ (out of its principal). There is a difference between provision "within it" and provision "from it," because if he does not trade with it and earn, the giving becomes, what? "from it." If we suppose it is one hundred, and he gives them ten riyals for expenses, it decreases; every time he gives them, it decreases. But when He says ﴿fīhā﴾, the meaning is that the provision comes from within it, so the property becomes larger than the provision given, and this implies that he should trade with it and then give them from the profit.

﴿And provide for them from it﴾, give them, give them what? Give them food and drink. As for clothing, He said: ﴿and clothe them and speak to them a known word﴾. ﴿Clothe them﴾: what they need of trousers, shirts and other things. There remains the bedding and housing, which fall under His words ﴿and provide for them from it﴾.

﴿And speak to them a known word﴾: that is, when you give them and clothe them, speak to them a known word, meaning a word that is gentle and mild. Do not look down upon them with your noses raised or lay obligation upon them, for that contradicts true guardianship. For example, if the foolish person comes and says, "Give me, clothe me," do not say to him a harsh word, do not say, "You never have a garment, you have no food," and similar offensive words; for the property is theirs, and even if it is yours, it is not fitting for you to reproach them for what you have given.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of giving the foolish property, whether to them or to us, on both readings, based on His words ﴿And do not give the foolish﴾. The prohibition indicates prohibition, especially when the prohibition is combined with what indicates the cause, namely foolishness, as if He said: do not give them because of their foolishness, for if you give them while they are foolish, they will waste the property.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the condemnation of foolishness, and that it is a cause of preventing a person from his property.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that foolishness necessitates restriction (hajr) upon a person regarding his property.

The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, divided restriction into two types: restriction for the right of others, and restriction for the right of the person himself.

As for the first, it is like when a person's debts exhaust his wealth. In this case he is restricted. Why? For the right of others. If a person owes debts greater than his wealth and the creditors request that he be restricted, he is restricted. If they do not request it, it is forbidden for him to dispose of his property in a way that harms the creditor, and if he does so, the transaction is not enforced. For this reason, if a person whose debts exceed his wealth endows some of his property, the endowment is not enforced. Why? Because the right of others is attached to it. This is the preferred view in this matter, and it is the opinion chosen by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him. As for the well-known position in the school, his disposal is valid so long as the creditors or some of them do not request his restriction; if they request it, he is restricted and prevented from disposing of his property.

The second type of restriction is restriction for the right of the self, which is that whose cause is foolishness, minority or insanity. The insane person is restricted regarding his property, the minor is restricted regarding his property, and the foolish person is restricted regarding property which he does not handle well. This restriction is for the right of the restricted person and not for the right of others.

So if the restricted person says, "This is my property; let me dispose of it as I wish," we say: this is not possible, because you are foolish, and if we do not restrict you, you will ruin the property.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that it is not (...) corruption, that is, by our empowering him. If someone gave a stick to a madman, we would say: this is forbidden for you, because if you give him a stick he will go out and strike people with it. And if the foolish person is forbidden from being given property, how much more so the madman?

If someone asks: what is the criterion of foolishness by which restriction is imposed? The answer: the scholars said that the foolish person is one who spends his wealth on what is forbidden or on what has no benefit. The first is like one who spends his wealth on wine, narcotics and similar things; this is a fool who is to be restricted. Or on what has no benefit, like one who spends his wealth on fireworks, firecrackers or similar things, or buys oil or gasoline and sets it on fire and merely watches it. Is this person foolish or sound-minded? This is a fool, so he is to be restricted.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, regarding the property which He gave to His servants, namely that it is a support for people in the interests of their religion and their worldly life.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that since property is a support for people in the interests of their religion and worldly life, it is forbidden to spend it on anything other than what upholds their religion and worldly life, because Allah made it a support by which the interests of religion and worldly life are established.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that it is obligatory upon the guardian of the foolish person to dispose of his property in a way that yields benefit, based on His words ﴿and provide for them from it﴾.

* And among its benefits: that it is obligatory that they be provided with what they need of food, drink and other things, because the imperative requires obligation, especially since it is connected to the right of others.

* And also among its benefits: that it is obligatory upon one whom Allah has placed over another that he not speak harshly to him, but say to him a known word, so that he combines beneficence in word and in deed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 6 (part 1 of 2):

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age﴾ [An-Nisa 6]. ﴿Test﴾ means examine. ﴿Orphans﴾ is the plural of ﴿orphan﴾ (yatim), which is anyone whose father has died before he reached maturity. Is that before the child reached maturity or before the father did? Before the child reached maturity. Whoever's father dies before he reaches maturity, that is, before the child reaches maturity. Is that not so? Yes.

As for His saying ﴿until when they reach﴾, the word ﴿until﴾ (hatta) here is inceptive (ibtida'iyya), meaning: test them and continue testing. ﴿Until when they reach marriageable age, then if you perceive in them sound judgment, hand over to them their property﴾. The word ﴿when﴾ (idha) is conditional, and His saying ﴿if you perceive﴾ is also conditional. ﴿Hand over to them their property﴾ is the response to the condition. This makes it a condition within another condition, which is permissible in the Arabic language. From it is the poet's saying:

If you call on us for help, if you are alarmed,
you will find from us strongholds of honour, adorned by generosity.

So this ﴿until when they reach marriageable age, then if you perceive in them sound judgment, hand over to them their property﴾ is a condition within a condition.

As for His saying ﴿if you perceive﴾, it means you see, as in His saying: ﴿He perceived a fire from the side of the mountain﴾ [Al-Qasas 29], meaning he saw.

As for His saying ﴿sound judgment (rushd)﴾, rushd is understood according to each context, but one word gathers all its meanings: good management. This is rushd. If it concerns property, it means that a person buys and sells repeatedly and is not cheated except by what custom allows (...), and refrains from what God has forbidden. If it concerns managing the affairs of others, it means being good at guardianship, and from it is rushd in guardianship of marriage, which means knowing what is suitable as a match and the interests of marriage. So rushd, O servants of God, is understood according to each context. What is meant here? ﴿Sound judgment﴾ means sound handling of their property.

﴿Hand over to them their property﴾ means give it to them. His saying ﴿hand over to them﴾ means deliver it to them. Do not say, "Come and take your property." You are the ones who must hand it over. It will come that this guardian is entitled to a fee, or to eat in a reasonable manner according to what his situation requires.

﴿And do not consume it﴾ means their property. ﴿Wastefully and hastily, fearing that they will grow up﴾. As for His saying ﴿wastefully﴾, it may be an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), meaning consumption that is wasteful. Israf (wastefulness) means exceeding the limit, and it too is understood according to each context.

As for His saying ﴿hastily (bidaran)﴾, it means haste, from the verb "baadara," meaning to hurry towards something. His saying ﴿fearing that they will grow up﴾ means hastily, because of their growing up, that is, racing their coming of age. When they grow up, guardianship over them ends and they become mature. So some guardians may consume their property wastefully, or moderately but hastily. For this reason no one should say that the two words are synonyms. Rather we say: wastefulness is exceeding the limit. For example, if ten suffices him, he takes fifteen. ﴿Hastily﴾ means that he consumes without wastefulness, but hurries, hurrying to consume it before they grow up.

﴿Whoever is wealthy, let him abstain﴾. Whichever guardian is wealthy and does not need the orphan's property, ﴿let him abstain﴾ means let him refrain from consuming it. ﴿Whoever is poor, let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾. The lam in His saying ﴿let him abstain﴾ is an imperative, and the second is for permissibility.

I say: the lam in His saying ﴿let him abstain﴾ is imperative, and in His saying ﴿let him eat﴾ it is permissive, because the first is required of him to abstain, while the second is permitted to him to eat.

If someone asks: what removed the lam in His saying ﴿let him eat﴾ from the imperative? We say: because it follows a prohibition, which is His saying ﴿and do not consume it wastefully and hastily﴾. An imperative after a prohibition is for lifting the prohibition. That is, either it is for permissibility according to some scholars, or for lifting the prohibition. Here, when the prohibition is lifted, it is permitted.

﴿Whoever is poor, let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾ means let him eat in a reasonable manner, that is, according to what custom has established. So he does not eat as the rich eat, but eats the amount that suits someone like him. For example, if he is poor and says, "I will eat as the rich eat, because I am his guardian," we say: this is not permitted. Eat in a reasonable manner. The reasonable manner is what custom has established, and it is well known that the poor man's eating is not like the rich man's.

He said: ﴿And when you hand over to them their property, call witnesses against them﴾. And when do we hand over their property to them? When they reach maturity and show sound judgment. ﴿When you hand over to them their property, call witnesses against them﴾ means have witnesses testify that you delivered it.

﴿And God suffices as Reckoner﴾. ("Suffices") comes from sufficiency, meaning that He, the Majestic and Exalted, suffices in place of everyone. The letter ba' in His saying ﴿by God﴾ is superfluous (za'ida) to beautify the expression, and the original is "God suffices as Reckoner." The word ﴿Reckoner (hasib)﴾ means the Watchful Observer who calls to account. So this verse, as you have seen, God concluded with this sentence as a warning to guardians of orphans not to dare to consume their property wastefully and hastily, fearing that they will grow up.

* Several benefits can be drawn from this noble verse. First: the obligation to test orphans, from His saying ﴿and test the orphans﴾.

Second: acting on experience. From where is acting on experience derived? Because testing (ibtila', meaning examination) is a form of experience.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: it is permissible for an orphan's guardian to use with him whatever will be a means of testing him. If he sees him rebelling against the test, he may discipline him until he tests him, so that what God commanded is completed.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: when the orphan reaches maturity and shows sound judgment, it is obligatory to hand his property over to him, from His saying ﴿until when they reach marriageable age, then if you perceive in them sound judgment, hand over to them their property﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: restricting orphans' control over their property does not require a judge's ruling, neither at the start nor at the end, because He entrusted the matter to whom? To their guardians.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: God's care, glorified and exalted is He, for orphans, from His saying ﴿and do not consume it wastefully and hastily, fearing that they will grow up﴾.

If someone says: what if he consumes it for a purpose other than this, to enjoy it? The answer is: no, it is not permitted. But the mention of wastefulness and haste is because these are what usually drive a person to consume it. The scholars have said that when a qualification is mentioned because it is the usual case, it has no implied meaning (mafhum). On this basis, it is not permitted to consume an orphan's property, neither wastefully nor hastily before they grow up.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation for a wealthy guardian to abstain from orphans' property, from His saying ﴿whoever is wealthy, let him abstain﴾. This is the Qur'an.

But someone may say: if the guardian says, "I cannot work with the orphan's property except in the same way others do, and how can I work without benefit?" The answer to this: if that is the case, then he must refer to the judge, who is the general guardian, because some people make this claim and say, "I cannot work except for a share of the profit, or for a wage, or something similar." We say: then you must refer to the judge.

* Student: His saying ﴿so hand over to them their property﴾ (...) in ﴿your property﴾ (...) the property of orphans?

* The Shaykh: No, the first one is about the foolish. The first verse is not about orphans.

* Student: How, O Shaykh, does it say about the poor man (...) to eat in a reasonable manner?

* The Shaykh: We have not reached it yet. Wait, wait.

* Student: Shaykh, may God be good to you, (...) to provide for them food, drink, clothing, and everything (...), even if they are young (...)?

* The Shaykh: Young children may not be given authority over property.

* Student: I give him something small, sixty riyals a month.

* The Shaykh: Yes, but he wastes it.

* Student: He wastes it on something cold, like sweets.

* The Shaykh: I fear he will waste it on something hot.

* Student: This comes down to supervision.

* The Shaykh: In any case, what custom has established is necessary. This is maintenance, this is a matter of spending. Suppose the student goes out to what they call a treat, and he is given a riyal or two riyals according to the price.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, not at all. It is better that you do not give him.

* Student: But sometimes there is need, sometimes turning away from something may (...) the soul.

* The Shaykh: Then this has a reason. If you give him out of fear that he will waste it, this has a reason. The principle is that he should not be given.

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: ﴿Do not give the foolish your property which God has made a means of support for you﴾. The first verse is general. Even if a man is forty years old, it is not given to him.

* Student: O Shaykh, the verse is general.

* The Shaykh: Which one?

* Student: The verse ﴿Do not give the foolish﴾ (...).

* The Shaykh: (...) as long as the cause is foolishness, meaning: do not give the foolish your property because of their foolishness.

* Student: Are they tested in buying and selling?

* The Shaykh: Are you asking about the first verse or the second? The second verse does not mention the foolish. The second verse mentions orphans. The orphan is tested. But a woman is not tested in buying and selling, because she is not of its people. She is tested in household needs. If she is found to manage household needs well, she is sound in judgment. If it is found that she is foolish, for example, when she kneads the dough she gives it to the cow, when she makes tea she pours it on the tiles, and so on, she is not considered sound in judgment.

* Student: O Shaykh, is the lam in ﴿let him eat﴾ permissive?

* The Shaykh: Yes. It is the lam of the imperative, and it is for permissibility.

* Student: And the lam in ﴿let him abstain﴾ is imperative. What is the difference between them, since both lams came after the prohibition, after "do not eat," ﴿and do not consume it wastefully and hastily﴾?

* The Shaykh: Did we not say that when it came after the prohibition, it became permissive? As for ﴿let him abstain﴾, it is for obligation, to protect the orphan's property. As for ﴿let him eat﴾, we do not say you must eat from the orphan's property. You are permitted. So the first, we said, is obligatory, for the protection of the orphan's property. The second, we said, is for permissibility, though its protection is also obligatory, because if we said you must eat, that would mean harm to the orphan.

* Student: His saying ﴿and God suffices﴾, the ba' here is superfluous, and the opposite of superfluous is deficient. Does this occur in the Book of God, a deficient and a superfluous?

* The Shaykh: What do you say about the brother's question? He asks: is there superfluity in the Book of God? We have mentioned this, and we said: the superfluous is superfluous, the superfluous word is superfluous.

* Student: Yes, but in the Book of God, Mighty and Majestic, is there nothing, I mean is the superfluous without...?

* The Shaykh: Yes, the superfluous in it is superfluous. A word that is superfluous in wording serves meaning. The verb "zad" is used transitively and intransitively, so the "superfluous" (za'id), which comes from the intransitive "zada," is superfluous of the transitive "zada." Is it clear?

* Student: It is not clear.

* The Shaykh: It is not clear. Look, may God bless you, everything superfluous in the Qur'an in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis) has meaning. That is, it must have come for a benefit. The benefit here, the grammarians said, is beautifying the expression.

* Student: Shaykh, we said the scholars divided restriction (hajr) into three types. We said: restriction for the benefit of the restricted person, and restriction for the benefit of others. We said that the foolish may be so because of youth, and may be so because he is foolish (...). With regard to the young, is it not before (...)?

* The Shaykh: Foolish because of youth, foolish because of madness, and foolish because of his conduct.

* Student: Yes, but the young is not included in the general category of the foolish...?

* The Shaykh: And detailed explanation is not suitable?

* Student: (...) the young (...) and for this God Most High applied it to him...

* The Shaykh: I say: is it not suitable? The foolish may be an adult who is sensible and yet foolish.

* Student: Support (qiyaman) (...)?

* The Shaykh: Support. It is not yours. Support for the interests of your religion and your worldly life. That is, the property itself is support.

* Student: Does one who uses tobacco waste property for no benefit?

* The Shaykh: He does not see it as waste. He says that when he sits and smokes, he relaxes and feels at ease, just as you eat apples and feel at ease.

* Student: Likewise one who drinks alcohol with it, and the one who...

* The Shaykh: Yes, but this clearly diminishes the intellect.

﴿And do not give the foolish your property, which God has made a means of support for you﴾ [An-Nisa 5], and so on. In this verse, ﴿the foolish, your property﴾, are there two readings?

Who are meant by "the foolish"?

﴿Reckoner (hasiban)﴾: I have not parsed it for you, but I think its parsing is clear.
