So if a woman bequeaths some of her wealth to be spent on people of musical entertainment and singing, the bequest is void and has no effect. This is because we have an important principle: legal terms are understood according to the meaning recognized by the Shari'ah. Accordingly, we say that the bequest that is recognized by the Shari'ah is one that is from one-third or less, to a non-heir, and under the known conditions among the scholars. This will come to us, Allah willing, in jurisprudence (fiqh).

His words ﴿or debt﴾. In ﴿after any bequest﴾ ﴿or debt﴾, the "or" (aw) here is "or" of permission of omission (mani'at khuluww), not "or" of exclusion (mani'at ishtirak). It is not exclusive of the two; it is the "or" of permission of omission. The difference between them is that the "or" of permission of omission means that it is required that neither of these two matters be absent, and if both occur, that is better. The "or" of exclusion (mani'at al-ishtirak) is one where the ruling applies to one of the two matters.

If you say: "Honor Zayd or 'Amr," and you mean that you should honor one of them, this is an "or" of exclusion. If you say: "Honor Zayd or 'Amr," meaning that I have given you the choice, they call this an "or" of permission of omission, meaning the situation is not free of honoring one of the two men, and honoring one of them is more fitting.

So here the "or" is of which type? It is an "or" of permission of omission. That means the debt and the bequest may both occur, or one of them may occur alone. Inheritance takes place only after the bequest and the debt. But the bequest, as you know, is from one-third or less, and the debt may consume all the wealth. If the debt consumes all the wealth, the heirs have no right. Is that right? That is, if he owed a thousand dirhams and left a thousand dirhams, the heirs get nothing, since if we pay the debt with the thousand, nothing remains for the heirs. If a woman bequeathed a thousand and left only a thousand, nothing would remain for the heirs?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: Why? Because she does not own a bequest beyond one-third or less.

In this verse, Allah, Exalted is He, placed the bequest before the debt, as He did in the first verse. The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, explained the wisdom of this: the bequest is a voluntary act of charity, while the debt is an obligation. The bequest was placed first to compensate for its deficiency, being voluntary, against the obligatory debt. This is one reason. 

The second reason: the debt has someone who demands it, unlike the bequest, which is voluntary. If the heirs wished to deny it, they could deny it. So it was placed first out of concern and attention for it.

﴿And for them is one-fourth of what you leave if you have no child; but if you have a child, then for them is one-eighth of what you leave, after any bequest you make or debt﴾. What was said about the preceding clauses applies to these clauses. The wisdom behind Allah differentiating between men and women, giving the female half of the male's share, is that this is the principle in the laws of inheritance: when a male and a female are of the same kind, the male receives twice the female's share. Except for those who inherit through the mere kinship of the womb (al-rahim al-mujarradah), where male and female are equal.

Like the children of the mother (siblings through the mother), their males and females are equal. And like the dhawu al-arham (distant blood-relatives), according to the well-known position in the school, their males and females are equal. So the son of a sister and the daughter of a sister share the estate equally. The disagreement on this will come, Allah willing. The correct view is that the inheritance of dhawu al-arham is based on the inheritance of those through whom they are related. If they are related through someone where male and female differ, they are treated accordingly.
* A student: Half of what the male has, that the female should have half of (...)?
* The Shaykh: Here the female has half of the male's share, and the male has double.

Then He said: ﴿And if a man leaves property to be inherited as kalalah, or a woman...﴾. His words ﴿if a man leaves property to be inherited﴾ may be understood with "kana" as incomplete, with the clause ﴿yurathu﴾ as the predicate of "kana". It may also be understood as complete, with ﴿rajul﴾ as its subject and ﴿yurathu﴾ as an attribute of ﴿rajul﴾. The latter is closer, because the meaning is: "if there is found a man who leaves property to be inherited as kalalah."

His words ﴿kalalah﴾ are an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). The evidence that it is an absolute object is that it is correct to supply the verbal noun before it. The meaning is: "he is inherited with the inheritance of kalalah." So it is an absolute object. The inheritance of kalalah is inheritance by someone other than ascendants and descendants, meaning the heir is from outside the ascendants and descendants, because it is like a crown (iklil) surrounding a thing. So they are the collaterals (hawashi). That is, one whose heirs are collaterals, and who has no descendant and no ascendant to inherit from him. For this reason the early scholars said: kalalah is one who has no child and no father, meaning that the collaterals inherit from him. The deceased who is kalalah is the one whom only collaterals inherit. Is that right?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: For example, a man who dies leaving brothers, we call this kalalah; leaving paternal uncles, kalalah; leaving nephews (sons of brothers), kalalah; leaving cousins (sons of paternal uncles), kalalah. So everyone who inherits without a descendant or ascendant is kalalah.

His words ﴿or a woman﴾ are conjoined to ﴿a man﴾. But the word ﴿woman﴾: do we say it is conjoined to ﴿a man﴾ with his attribute, or to ﴿a man﴾ without his attribute? With his attribute, meaning: "or a woman who leaves property to be inherited as kalalah."

The grammarians and likewise the jurists of legal theory (usuliyyun) agree that when an attribute follows a series of clauses, it returns to all of them. When it follows a series, it applies to the whole. For example, if I say: "Honor Zayd, 'Amr, Bakr, and Khalid if they work hard," it applies to all of them. But if it comes separately after an earlier group: "Honor Zayd, 'Amr, and Khalid if they work hard, and Bakr," they disagree whether honoring Bakr is absolute or is qualified by what came before, and there are two opinions on this question. The correct view is that one refers to the indicators (qara'in) in such a case.

The indicators here show that ﴿woman﴾ is conjoined to ﴿man﴾ considered as qualified by the condition of leaving property to be inherited as kalalah.

﴿or a woman, and he has a brother or a sister﴾. The pronoun in ﴿and he has﴾ refers to the man who leaves property as kalalah, and likewise the woman. It does not say "and they have a brother or sister," in consideration of the first attribute, which is the man.

His words ﴿a brother or a sister﴾ are unrestricted and include the full sibling, the paternal sibling, or the maternal sibling. But the scholars have agreed that what is meant is a brother from the mother or a sister from the mother. There is a reading attributed to some early scholars: "and he has a brother from the mother or a sister from the mother." This is very clear even if this reading were not reported, because the full and paternal siblings were addressed by Allah's ruling at the end of the surah: ﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning kalalah: if a man dies leaving no child and he has a sister...﴾ [An-Nisa 176], and so on.

﴿For each one of them is a sixth. But if they are more than that﴾, meaning more than one, ﴿they share in the third﴾. If they are two, they share in the third. If they are three, they share in the third. Four? They share in the third. A brother and a sister? They share in the third. Here the brother is not given more than the sister, because Allah said: ﴿they share﴾, and the implication of partnership, when unqualified, is equality or equal division.

﴿after any bequest that is made or debt, without harm﴾. Concerning ﴿after any bequest that is made﴾ we say what was said before: this bequest is a legal bequest within the limits the Shari'ah permits. His words ﴿or debt﴾ mean "or after a debt," and the "or" here means permission of omission, as previously explained. But here He said ﴿without harm﴾, meaning on the condition that the bequest is not intended as harm. If it is established that the bequest is intended as harm, it is void, as when we know that this deceased, who has only maternal siblings, bequeathed one-third in order to constrict the siblings. This is a bequest of harm and is not executed, because Allah stipulated for an enforceable bequest that it must not be harmful.

Similarly, if we suppose that a sick person acted foolishly and incurred a debt that harms the heirs and consumes all his wealth, then in this case it is examined. If he harmed them by it, the harm is forbidden by the Shari'ah.

Then He said: ﴿a bequest from Allah﴾. ﴿A bequest﴾ is an absolute object whose verb is necessarily omitted, because what is meant here is obligation, and "bequest" means a firm covenant.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing﴾. All-Knowing of what benefits His servants; Most Forbearing toward those who disobey Him, so He does not hasten punishment against them. The benefit of concluding this long verse, which includes the inheritance of spouses and maternal siblings, with knowledge and forbearance is that a bequest may be harmful and yet Allah does not hasten punishment against the person. For this reason He concluded this verse with these two noble names: the All-Knowing and the Most Forbearing.

* Now we return to the benefits of this noble verse, which are many. Among them:
* First: inheritance is a compulsory ownership (milk qahri) in which the person has no choice. The evidence is His words ﴿and for you﴾, that Allah has made it our possession and established it as a legal ruling. If the husband said, "I do not want my share from my wife," we would say to him: No, it enters your ownership compulsorily, and you have no option in it. If he says, "I want to give it to her as a charitable gift for a benevolent project," or, "if she has children, I will give it to her children," we would say to him: this is a fresh gift (ibtida' 'atiyyah).

Based on this: if he had a debt requiring him to spend this wealth he inherited, then his donation of this wealth is not enforceable. This is the benefit of our saying that it is compulsory ownership.

* Also derived from this: if the estate is a share of jointly held land, does the co-owner have the right of pre-emption (shuf'ah)? Do you not understand the question? The woman owns half of a plot of land, and the other half belongs to a stranger. She dies, and her heirs inherit her share of this land, which is half. Does the co-owner have the right of pre-emption?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: No. Why? Because it is compulsory ownership. But if she had sold her share during her lifetime, the co-owner would have the right of pre-emption.

* Also among the benefits of this noble verse: it is a condition of inheritance that the heir be free. From where is this derived? From the lam (of ownership, lam al-tamlik), since a slave does not own. So if a free woman's husband is a slave, when she dies he does not inherit anything from her, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sells a slave who has property, his property belongs to the one who sold him" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2379) and Muslim (1543/80) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: inheritance includes specific property, debts, and rights. Specific property such as dirhams, money, and real estate; debts owed by people; and rights, such as the right of pre-emption, the right to benefit from a permissible dog, the right to benefit from impure dung (if we say it is permissible to benefit from it), the right to benefit from impure fat (if we say it is permissible to benefit from it), and similar things. The point is that His words ﴿what he leaves﴾ are general and include all: property, debts, and rights.

* Also among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment of marriage, from His words ﴿your wives﴾, and marriage is not established except by a valid contract.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment of inheritance even if she dies before consummation. How so? Because she becomes a wife by the contract alone, whether or not consummation has occurred.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: when a wife is separated (bayn), there is no inheritance between them. From where is this derived? From His words ﴿your wives﴾, because when she is separated she is no longer a wife. So if he divorces her and her waiting period ends, and then she dies, he has no inheritance from her, because she has become a stranger to him. And if he divorced her with a final irrevocable divorce (talaq ba'in) and she died during the waiting period, he has no inheritance from her. Why? Because once she was separated from him, she was not a wife, as evidenced by the fact that she is not lawful to him except by a new contract, or after another husband if the separation was a major separation (bayniyyah kubra).

The scholars made an exception to this in one case: when he separated her during his terminal illness (marad al-mawt al-makhuf), accused of intending to deprive her. They said: in that case she inherits from him even if the waiting period has ended, so long as she has not remarried or committed something contrary to the marriage, such as apostasy (...).

[The text continues:] To separation: whenever he separates from her by three divorces or upon completion of the waiting period, inheritance is cut off, except in one situation of separation: when he separated her during his terminal illness that is fatal, accused of intending to deprive her. Three conditions: terminal illness, fatal, accused of intending deprivation. Rather, four conditions: illness, death, fatal, accused of intending deprivation. When the four conditions are fulfilled, she inherits from him. If he divorced her in health with a final irrevocable divorce and then died before the waiting period ended?

**Student:** So she does not inherit.

**Shaykh:** She does not inherit, because he divorced her while he was in good health. If he divorced her during a fatal illness (*marad makhuf*, an illness that may end in death), then recovered from it, and then a new accident befell him and he died, does she inherit?

**Student:** No.

**Shaykh:** No, she does not inherit, because he did not die from that illness. If he divorced her during an illness that was not fatal, and afterwards the illness worsened until he died, she does not inherit.

If he divorced her during his final fatal illness at her own request, she does not inherit either. Why? Because he is not suspected of intending to deprive her.

So the inheritance between spouses ends with the irrevocable separation (*baynunah*), except when he divorced her during his final fatal illness and is suspected of intending to deprive her.

**Student:** As long as she has not remarried, or...?

**Shaykh:** Yes. And if she inherits from him in this situation, her inheritance continues until she remarries or apostatizes. That is, if she inherits after the irrevocable divorce under the conditions we mentioned, she inherits as long as she does not remarry or apostatize.

* One of the benefits of this noble verse is that the husband is entitled to half, on a negative condition: the absence of a child, because of His words: ﴿If they have no child﴾.

* Another benefit: there is no difference whether the child is one or more, male or female. The proof from this verse is that the word ﴿child﴾ is indefinite in a negative context, so it includes all of them.

Is a grandchild treated like a child? The answer is yes. So if she has a son's child, the husband does not get half, because the children of sons are like the children of the loins.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: God's care for inheritance, since the verses came with this detail, as in His words: ﴿If they have a child, then for you is a quarter of what they leave﴾.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: inheritance is based on wisdom. The reasoning is that if the wife has no child, the husband gets half, and with a child he gets a quarter, so that the wealth is preserved for whom? For the child.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: there is no inheritance except after debts and bequests, because of His words: ﴿after a bequest they make or a debt﴾.

* Another benefit: the wife is free to dispose of her own property, because of His words: ﴿they make [a bequest]﴾, where the action is attributed to her. If she could not dispose of anything without her husband's permission, he might prevent her from making a bequest, and that would harm her.

Examples follow from this benefit. If a deceased person left a thousand and owed a thousand in debt, does the heirs get anything?

**Student:** No.

**Shaykh:** No, because debt takes precedence over inheritance. But how can a bequest take precedence over inheritance, given that a bequest may not exceed one third? This becomes clear through an example. If a person dies leaving a husband and a full sister, the husband gets half, because there is no child who inherits, and the full sister gets half, since she fulfills the conditions for inheriting half. If we suppose the estate is sixty thousand, the husband gets thirty thousand and the sister gets thirty thousand.

But if the deceased woman had bequeathed one third, the situation changes. We say: the bequest is one third. How much is that? Twenty thousand. The husband gets half of the remainder (...), and the full sister also gets half, twenty thousand.

Now you see: we gave the bequest its full right. How much did the legatee take? One third, twenty thousand. And you find that instead of the husband getting half, he now gets only a third, and likewise the full sister. Do you understand now? So it is clear that the bequest takes precedence over inheritance.

If we supposed that the bequest were treated like inheritance, the ruling would differ. We would say: we have a third in excess of the whole, so the problem becomes one of nine. The bequest gets three, the husband gets three, and the sister gets three.

But apparently we have erred. We say: the problem (...). The husband's half is three, and the full sister's half is three, and the third is two, which is raised (*'awl*, increase of shares) to eight. So the share of the third now becomes a quarter, does it not? Although in the first division we gave it a full third. Is that clear?

If we suppose that the bequest takes precedence over inheritance, and the deceased, a woman in the example we mentioned, bequeathed one third, with a husband and a full sister: if we say that the bequest takes precedence, we give the legatee his share from an estate of sixty thousand, that is twenty thousand. Forty thousand remains. We give the husband twenty thousand and the full sister twenty thousand. In reality, the twenty thousand that is half is now (...). So the husband's right is diminished, and the full sister's right is diminished. And was the bequest diminished or not? It was not diminished. The legatee was given his full third, and that third now equals one half.

If we said that the bequest does not take precedence, the problem would be one of six: the husband gets half, three; the full sister gets half, three; and the bequest of one third is two, which is raised to eight. So what is the share of the bequest now? (...) Just as the husband's share becomes a quarter of an eighth, and the sister's share becomes a quarter of an eighth.

The conclusion, then, is that it is clear the bequest (...) inheritance, because the legatee is given his full share, and then the remainder is divided among the heirs according to (...). You have understood that it takes precedence over inheritance, and that is clear.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: the wisdom in distributing inheritance, in that the female receives (...), of the same kind as the male, half of what the male receives. This is in the mention of whose inheritance? The inheritance of wives.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the demonstration of justice in the Islamic religion, since it did not deprive women of their share of inheritance, unlike what the people of the pre-Islamic period (*jahiliyyah*) used to do, depriving them of inheritance. Justice appears (...) in being male, or he expressed the inheritance of the wife in the same terms he used for the husband's inheritance.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: that when (...) the discussion concerns women and men, the wisdom is to mention men first, because it began with the inheritance of husbands before the inheritance of wives. This is what accords with human nature (*fitrah*), unlike those whom God has perverted in their nature and changed their disposition, so that they place women before men in mention.

In Western radio broadcasts, and in the radio of those who imitate them, they say: "Ladies and gentlemen." Someone took that and wrote on a bathroom door: "Bathroom for ladies," and beside it: "Bathroom for men," and not "for gentlemen." That is, instead of the female demanding her right, now we demand our right. They make women "ladies" and make men only men, by the attribute of manhood and not the attribute of lordship (*sayyid*).

All this indicates weakness of character, as the wise historian Ibn Khaldun said in his *Muqaddimah*, which is all philosophy, as they say. Some scholars even denied that it was his, because it is beyond his level; it is greatly lofty. He says: "It is the habit of nations that a weak nation imitates a strong nation, even in falsehood." We have now made ourselves weak and have come to imitate those whose nature God has perverted and whom He has stripped of religion in matters like these. We ask God to protect us and you.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: that the inheritance of siblings from the mother (...) one third if they are two or more, or one sixth if they are one or fewer. If he says two or more, or a sixth if they are one or fewer, is there anything less than one?

**Student:** The ambiguous hermaphrodite (*khunthā mushkil*).

**Shaykh:** The ambiguous hermaphrodite. The inheritance is the same, because the inheritance of uterine siblings is shared equally by males and females. But if it is assumed that he is partly male and partly female (*mubaʿḍ*), then he does not inherit a sixth. On this basis, our saying "a sixth for one or fewer" cannot hold at all (...): a sixth for one, and for the group of two or more, a third.

* Another benefit: for the inheritance of uterine siblings to apply, the inheritance must be *kalalah*, that is, there are no descendants or male ascendants, neither father nor son. As for female ascendants, the uterine siblings inherit along with them.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: equality between males and females in the inheritance of uterine siblings, derived from His words: ﴿they are partners in the third﴾. The principle of partnership requires equality, just as the word "between" (*bayn*) implies equality.

If you say to two men: "This is a hundred dirhams between you," each gets fifty. Likewise, when God, mighty and majestic, said of the inheritance of uterine siblings: ﴿But if they are more than that, they are partners in the third﴾, and did not mention preference of the male over the female, this shows that they are equal.

Does anyone else share with them in this equality between male and female? The answer is no, unless there is an accidental factor, such as a person who dies leaving two daughters and two parents, a mother and a father. Here the father and the mother are equal, because the two daughters take two thirds, the mother takes a sixth, and the father takes a sixth. But this equality is due to an accidental cause, since nothing remains after the fixed shares for the father to take.

Second: some scholars hold that those of the distant kin (*dhawu al-arham*) are not distinguished between male and female (...). If someone dies leaving a son of a full sister and a daughter of a full sister, they share their mother's inheritance equally.

The correct view on this matter is that if they connect through someone whose male members are preferred over female members, then the males are preferred over the females; and if they connect through someone whose male members are not preferred over female members, then the males are not preferred over the females.

An example of this: the son of a full sister and the daughter of a full sister. The full siblings: the principle of the fixed shares is that the male is preferred over the female (...). In this example we say (...) full sister and daughter of a full sister: for the male, the equivalent of the share of two females.

And in the case of a son of a uterine brother and a daughter of a uterine brother, we say: the inheritance between them is equal, because they connect through someone whose males are not preferred over females.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: God's care for bequests and debts, since whenever He mentions an inheritance He says: "after a bequest or a debt." In the section on descendants and ascendants in the previous verse (...): ﴿after a bequest one makes or a debt﴾. In the inheritance of spouses, after each husband's share He said: "after a bequest or a debt." In the case of uterine siblings here He said: ﴿after a bequest that is made or a debt﴾.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: that a bequest intended to harm is void, because of His words: ﴿without causing harm﴾. A bequest intended to harm is forbidden and carries great sin. It is even narrated from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Indeed a man or a woman may do righteous deeds for seventy years (...), then they deviate in the bequest and are punished for it."[[Recorded by Abu Dawud (2867), al-Tirmidhi (2117), and Ibn Majah (2704) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "Indeed a man or a woman may work in obedience to God for sixty years, then death comes to them and they are harmed in their bequest, and the Fire becomes due for them." The wording is that of Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi.]] This is evidence that wrongdoing in a bequest is among the major sins.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: the obligation to act upon what God has prescribed in (...), because of His words: ﴿a bequest from God﴾. God, mighty and majestic, does not prescribe except what is true. God said: ﴿And We had already enjoined those who were given the Scripture before you, and you, to fear God﴾ [An-Nisa 131].

* Another benefit of the noble verse: that this bequest is based on two matters: knowledge and forbearance, because of His words: ﴿a bequest from God, and God is Knowing, Forbearing﴾.

* Another benefit: the affirmation of these two names of God, mighty and majestic: Al-'Alim (the All-Knowing) and Al-Halim (the Forbearing).

Do they indicate two attributes? What are they?

**Student:** Al-'Alim.

**Shaykh:** No. Al-'Alim is a name, and Al-Halim is a name. Do they indicate two attributes?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** What are they? From what is Al-'Alim derived?

**Student:** From knowledge (*'ilm*).

**Shaykh:** So (...). And Al-Halim?

**Student:** From forbearance (*hilm*).

**Shaykh:** So they indicate knowledge and forbearance. And the rule we have is that every name of God includes an attribute, but not every attribute gives rise to a name. For this reason the attributes are broader than the names.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 13–14 (part 1 of 3):

(...) I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shaytan (Satan). Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾ [An-Nisa 13]. (...) This is composed of a subject and a predicate. The subject is the demonstrative ﴿These﴾, and the predicate is ﴿the limits of Allah﴾. The thing being referred to is what preceded of the inheritance shares in the verse. It is possible that the thing referred to is everything that preceded of rulings before this sentence, because the Qur'an, although it consists of distinct verses, is in reality one speech in terms of meaning and context, and our saying "one speech" means that some of it is built upon some other. For this reason some exegetes gave attention to explaining the coherence (tanasub) of the verses, just as others gave attention to explaining the coherence of the surahs, and this is a good line of inquiry.
But if someone said: the demonstrative refers to the nearest thing mentioned, according to the rule (...) that a pronoun refers to the nearest thing mentioned, and likewise a demonstrative refers to the nearest thing mentioned, then the intended referent here is what is mentioned in this verse: ﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾.
As for his saying ﴿the limits of Allah﴾: "limits" is the plural of (ḥadd), and the ḥadd is the thing that separates two things, as in the boundaries of land, one from another. The limits of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are divided into two kinds: limits of obligations and limits of prohibitions.
As for the limits of obligations, they are what Allah has made obligatory upon His servants with their conditions, pillars and obligatory elements. As for the limits of prohibitions, they are what Allah has forbidden His servants, such as fornication, sodomy, drinking intoxicants, killing a soul, and other things.
The scholars said: when Allah says ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾, it is from the limits of commands, and when He says ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them﴾, it is from the limits of prohibitions. So fornication, for example, we say: it is a limit of Allah, do not approach it; and prayer is a limit of Allah, do not transgress it, meaning do not exceed it or overstep it.
He said: ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾ — the verse here, is it from the limits of commands or prohibitions?
* Students: From the limits of commands.
* The Shaykh: From the limits of commands.
Then He said: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. This sentence is conditional. Its conditional particle is ﴿whoever﴾ (man), and its conditional verb is ﴿obeys﴾ (yuṭi'), which is jussive by sukun as is apparent. The original form of ﴿yuṭi'﴾ is (yuṭī'u), but the yā' was dropped because of the meeting of two sukūns, since the ʿayn deserved sukun by the condition and the yā' was quiescent. Ibn Malik said in al-Kafiya:
When two quiescent letters meet, make the preceding one kasra; and if the one is a soft letter, its deletion is merited.
When two quiescent letters meet, make the preceding one kasra; and if it is a soft letter — meaning one of the three soft letters — its deletion is merited. To which (...) does the verse apply?
* A student: To the second.
* The Shaykh: To the second, except in His saying ﴿yuṭi' Allah﴾ where the ʿayn is kasra, so it falls under the first. Thus the verse combined the two readings.
﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. What then is obedience? The scholars said: obedience is conformity to the command, and it is by doing the commands and avoiding the prohibitions. So one who abstains from drinking intoxicants in compliance with the prohibition of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is said to be obedient, and one who prays is said to be obedient.
This is when obedience is mentioned alone, for then it includes doing the commands and abstaining from the prohibitions. But when it is paired with disobedience, as when one says: "whoever obeys Allah and whoever disobeys Allah," then obedience is specific to the commands and disobedience to the prohibitions. Is the verse before us now of the second type or the first?
* Students: The first.
* Other students: The second.
* The Shaykh: What is the second and what is the first? It is paired with ﴿disobeys﴾ (yaʿṣi), so its meaning is the carrying out of the commands.
﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. ﴿Obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾: the mention of the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, is conjoined with the name of Allah, Exalted, because obedience to the Messenger is obedience to Allah, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [An-Nisa 80].
As for His saying ﴿and His Messenger﴾, what is meant at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an is a specific messenger, namely Muhammad, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him and his family. As for the time when the earlier laws were in force, what is meant by the messenger is whoever's law was in effect: in the time of the Messiah the messenger would be ʿĪsā, in the time of Moses the messenger would be Mūsā, and so on. But after the sending of the Messenger, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him and his family, what is meant by the messenger is Muhammad, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him and his family.
﴿He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. ﴿He will admit him﴾ is the answer of the condition, and it is jussive by sukun. Rational reasoning requires that the condition leads to the conditioned: the conditioned here is obedience, or the condition is obedience and the conditioned is the reward and recompense, so the conditioned follows from the condition by rational sequence.
So here His saying ﴿He will admit him﴾ is (...) what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has stipulated for whoever obeys Him, and it is an inevitable result, necessarily following from the truthfulness of the one who reports it, and who is he? Allah, Mighty and Majestic; for the one who reports it is Allah, and He is the most truthful of speakers, and the one who reports is able to do it. That is why you find that Allah, Exalted, says in the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾ [Aal Imran 9], because He is perfectly truthful and perfectly capable, and failure to fulfill a promise comes from one of two things: either lying, that is, the promise is false, or incapacity, lack of power; and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not fail in His promise.
﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾: (jannāt) is the plural of (jannah), and it originally means a garden with many trees, and it is so named because it conceals whoever is in it due to the abundance of its trees. This root, jīm and nūn, indicates concealment: consider (al-jinān), which is the heart, because it is hidden; (al-ajinnah), which are the foetuses in the wombs of mothers, because they are hidden; (al-jinn), because they are hidden; (al-junnah), that which the fighter is concealed by, because it conceals him. All of this material revolves around this meaning.
So the gardens are gardens with many trees, but it is not good to explain them in this place by this meaning, because if you explain them by this meaning you have, as it were, restricted their significance to what people know, and you would diminish the importance of the Paradise that is promised. For this reason we should explain them — I mean the gardens of bliss — as the abode that Allah prepared for His friends, in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human.
If you explain them with this explanation, their awe remains in souls. But if you explain them with the first meaning, a person imagines and says: this is like the garden of so-and-so son of so-and-so, with many trees and many palms and the like, whereas it is greater than what is in this world by multiples that only Allah knows. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "There is nothing in Paradise of what is in this world except the names."[[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wa'l-Nushur (332) from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas, and by Hannad ibn al-Sari in al-Zuhd (3) from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas.]] Otherwise the realities differ. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And therein is what the souls desire and the eyes delight in, and you therein will abide eternally﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 71], and He said: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes as a reward for what they used to do﴾ [As-Sajda 17]. And in the sacred hadith: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4779) and Muslim (2824) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]
His saying ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾: ﴿flow﴾ (tajrī): flowing is well known, it is the movement of water over the earth. His saying ﴿beneath which﴾ means: beneath these gardens, meaning spreading trees, shade and rivers that flow. If a person imagined this bliss, he would find it the greatest bliss. Allah, Exalted, explained these rivers in Surah Muhammad with His saying: ﴿In it are rivers of water unchanging, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to drinkers, and rivers of purified honey﴾ [Muhammad 15]. What is the honey of the bee? It is purified honey, which Allah created thus. Milk that is not the milk of cows or sheep; rivers that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created. Likewise the water never becomes stagnant, however long it remains, unlike the water of the earth, which becomes stagnant and its smell changes with long standing. The wine is a delight in which there is no harm and they are not made drunk by it.
His saying ﴿beneath which the rivers flow﴾: the scholars said: they flow beneath them without needing a structure to prevent the water from seeping away, nor digging a trench. They flow wherever you wish. Ibn al-Qayyim said in the Nuniyya:
Its rivers flow without a trench, glory be to the One who holds them back from overflowing.
So they are rivers that need no digging of channels nor establishing a ditch; they flow thus upon the earth. The scholars also said: they flow wherever the person wishes, instead of bringing building materials and direction; he wants them with his heart or commands them with his tongue. O Allah, make us among its people.
﴿Abiding therein forever; that is the great triumph﴾. ﴿Abiding﴾ (khālidīna) is a state (ḥāl). A state of whom?
* A student: Of the pronoun in ﴿He will admit him﴾.
* The Shaykh: Of the pronoun in ﴿He will admit him﴾. But there is a difficulty: a state is like an adjective, and an adjective follows what it describes in singular, dual and plural, whereas here the referent is singular and the state is plural. So what is the answer? The answer is that we say: the referent returns to (man), the conditional, and the conditional (man) may be treated according to its wording or according to its meaning. If you treat the wording, you return the pronoun to it in the singular; if you treat the meaning, you return the pronoun to it in the plural. Likewise, what resembles a pronoun, such as a state or adjective and the like, may be treated by meaning or by wording.
So here it says ﴿He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein﴾: it observed the wording in ﴿He will admit him﴾ and the meaning in ﴿abiding﴾.
It is also permissible to observe the wording and the meaning and then return a second time to observing the wording. Allah, Glorified and Exalted, said at the end of Surah At-Talaq: ﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness — He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Allah has certainly perfected for him provision﴾ [At-Talaq 11]. So He observed the wording first, then the meaning, then the wording again, and this is permissible in the Arabic language.
He says: ﴿abiding therein﴾, and His saying ﴿abiding therein﴾: the scholars said that khulūd is lasting, continuous staying, unless some evidence indicates that it is limited, in which case it means a long stay. Otherwise the basic meaning of khulūd is permanence, but if there is an indication that the intended meaning is a long stay, it is acted upon.
﴿Abiding therein; that is the great triumph﴾. ﴿That﴾ refers to what has been mentioned of this reward which Allah prepared for whoever obeys Him. ﴿The great triumph﴾: triumph (al-fawz) means profit; one says: so-and-so triumphed, meaning he profited. And great (al-ʿaẓīm) means possessing greatness, and greatness is the massiveness of a thing, its majesty, and also the abundance of a thing.
﴿That﴾ refers to what has been mentioned of this reward which Allah prepared for whoever obeys Him. ﴿The great triumph﴾: ﴿triumph﴾ (al-fawz) means: profit; one says: so-and-so triumphed, meaning he profited; and ﴿great﴾ (al-ʿaẓīm) means: possessing greatness, and greatness is: the massiveness of a thing and the majesty of a thing, and also the abundance of a thing.
It is known that the bliss of Paradise is characterized by massiveness, majesty and permanence, so it is the greatest triumph. A parallel to this is His saying, Exalted: ﴿Whoever is spared from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has triumphed﴾ [Aal Imran 185]. It is mentioned that az-Zamakhshari, who was one of the Mu'tazila, commented on this verse, ﴿Whoever is spared from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has triumphed﴾, saying: what triumph is greater than being spared from the Fire and admitted to Paradise? The interrogative here carries the sense of negation, meaning: there is no triumph greater than that.
Some annotators and critics of him said: he intended by this to negate the seeing of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because the seeing (...) and what is in it and greater triumph. Allah knows best whether he intended that. Whoever looks at the wording says there is in reality no indication in it, because among the necessary consequences of entering Paradise is — what? Looking at the face of Allah. And whoever knows the man's situation, that he was a Mu'tazili but intelligent, says: perhaps he intended that. Had such a phrase come from a person known to affirm the seeing of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, we would not explain it in this way and say that he intended to negate seeing. But one who knows his situation would not consider it unlikely that this was his intent.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the inheritance shares are among the limits of Allah.
* And among its benefits: whoever carries out these inheritance shares as Allah prescribed has this reward.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the division of inheritance is an act of worship, derived from the arrangement of the reward upon it and describing it as obedience.
* Among the benefits of this verse: the concern of the Shariʿa for delivering rights to their people, because the reality of inheritance is that rights reach their owners, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is a just judge who wants His servants to deliver rights to their owners.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: obedience to the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace and upon his family, is obedience to Allah; for this reason He joined it with (wa, "and"), which indicates togetherness and association.
If someone asks: what is the reconciliation between this verse and the saying of the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, to a man who said to him: "What Allah wills and you will": "Have you made me a rival to Allah? Rather, what Allah alone wills"?[[Narrated by Ahmad (1839) and al-Tabarani (13005) from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas.]]
The answer: there is no harm in joining the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, with the Lord, Glorified be He, with "and" in legislative matters; but in matters of creation (kawniyya) it is not permissible, because they are among the attributes of lordship, and the action of the servant must follow the action of Allah. As for the ruling, the ruling of the Messenger is the ruling of Allah; for this reason Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said in the Qur'an: ﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them﴾, and He did not say "then His Messenger," and: ﴿and said, "Sufficient for us is Allah; Allah will give us of His bounty, and His Messenger"﴾ [At-Tawba 59]; because this giving is a legislated giving, the giving of zakat and legislated wealth. As for creational matters, no, because they are among the attributes of lordship, so the action of the servant must be after the action of Allah.
"What Allah wills and you will": this is not permissible, because you made the will of the Messenger like the will of Allah, and it is not so. But obedience to the Messenger is — what? Like obedience to Allah: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [An-Nisa 80]. Allah made obedience to the Messenger obedience to Him.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of reward on the Day of Resurrection, from His saying ﴿He will admit him to gardens﴾, and its basis is that admission to gardens is not in this world but in the Hereafter.
* And among its benefits: the description of the bliss of these gardens and that rivers flow beneath them, and the types of these rivers are known from another verse.
* And among its benefits: the permanence of the bliss of these gardens, from His saying ﴿abiding therein﴾. Is the abiding here everlasting or limited? Everlasting. Allah, Glorified and Exalted, mentioned this in several verses of the Qur'an, and the Muslims agreed that the bliss of Paradise is everlasting, and no disagreement has been reported on this.
* And among its benefits: that this bliss is the great profit that nothing equals, from His saying ﴿and that is the great triumph﴾.
I forgot to parse this sentence: ﴿That is the great triumph﴾. How do we parse it?
* A student: (dhā) is a demonstrative subject, indeclinable on sukun.
* The Shaykh: No, that is not the detail; (dhā) is a demonstrative subject.
﴿The triumph﴾?
* The student: Predicate.
* The Shaykh: The predicate of the subject.
* The student: ﴿The great﴾ is an adjective.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verses 13–14 (part 2 of 3):

* The Shaykh: It is an attribute (ṣifah) of ﴿al-fawz﴾ (the triumph). If someone says: ﴿That is the great triumph﴾, could ﴿al-fawz﴾ be a substitute (badal), an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān), or an adjective (naʿt) of ﴿dhālika﴾ (that)? The meaning would then be: "That triumph is the great one." This would be acceptable, but the first grammatical analysis (iʿrab) is better.

Then God Most High says: ﴿And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire, abiding therein, and for him is a humiliating punishment﴾ [An-Nisa' 14]. Disobedience (maʿṣiyah) is opposing a command or committing a prohibited act. So whoever abandons an obligation has disobeyed, and whoever does a forbidden act has disobeyed. We say about ﴿whoever disobeys God and His Messenger﴾ what we said about ﴿whoever obeys God and His Messenger﴾, except that the grammatical analysis differs here. ﴿Yaʿṣi﴾ is the conditional verb (fiʿl al-sharṭ), in the jussive. By what is it jussive?

* The students: By the deletion of the weak letter.

* The Shaykh: By the deletion of the weak letter, which is the yāʾ.

And His saying: ﴿wa-yataʿadda ḥudūdahu﴾ (and transgresses His limits). Is ﴿yataʿadda﴾ with a fatḥah according to you?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: How is the fatḥah correct, given that it is conjoined (maʿṭūf) to the jussive ﴿yaʿṣi﴾?

* A student: It is jussive by the deletion of a letter, because it is not conjoined... (...) the conjoined element, and the fatḥah became a sign of the deleted alif.

* The Shaykh: That is, it is jussive by the deletion of the alif.

* The student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: And its root?

* The student: (yataʿadda).

* The Shaykh: (yataʿadda), yes.

And His saying: ﴿yatacadda ḥudūdahu﴾ means: he oversteps them. Does "the limits" here mean the commands or the prohibitions?

* Some students: The prohibitions.

* Other students: The commands.

* The Shaykh: There is no god but God! In ﴿yataʿadda ḥudūdahu﴾, what did we say before?

* Students: The commands.

* The Shaykh: The commands, yes. He did not say "whoever approaches His limits." He said: "whoever oversteps His limits," meaning he exceeds what has been set as a command. He did not say what has been set by commands.

﴿He will admit him to a Fire, abiding therein﴾: this is the answer of the conditional clause. The Fire is known; it is this burning, hot body. Or do we say: it is known, and that is sufficient?

* The students: It is known.

* The Shaykh: It is known and that is sufficient, just as we say: "The sky is above us and the earth is below us."

﴿Abiding therein﴾: here He said ﴿khālidan﴾ (abiding), and there, regarding the Garden, He said ﴿khālidīna﴾ (abiding, plural). Is there a subtle point here, meaning, my intention is: a benefit or a wisdom?

The answer: Yes. The people of Paradise enjoy gathering with one another, and for this reason He said ﴿khālidīna fīhā﴾. As for the people of the Fire, may God protect us, it has been reported that each one of them is in a coffin, not seeing anyone and not seen by anyone.[[Reported by Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf (36424), from the hadith of Suwayd ibn Ghaflah, as a mawquf report.]] Except as a form of rebuke. This is the secret, and God knows best, why He said of the people of Paradise ﴿khālidīna﴾ and of the people of the Fire ﴿khālidan fīhā﴾.

﴿And for him is a humiliating punishment﴾: meaning that together with his being admitted to the Fire and abiding in it, he never remains at ease at all. Rather, he is punished with a punishment of humiliation. So it is a bodily punishment and a punishment of the heart and soul, because bodily punishment is easier than the pain of the heart. For this reason the scholars said: a person should be circumcised while he is young, because the circumcision of a child involves only bodily pain. But if an adult is circumcised, there is bodily pain and pain of the heart and soul. He thinks: perhaps the wound will get worse, perhaps he will die, and so on. But a child, if he is cooled down, becomes quiet; and if the pain attacks him, he cries out. If we walk him, or walk with him if he cannot walk, he falls silent. The point is that the punishment of the people of the Fire, may God protect us, is a humiliating punishment, meaning one that involves humiliation, because they are reproached and censured.

* This noble verse contains benefits, among them: that disobedience to God, Mighty and Majestic, is a cause for entering the Fire, by His saying ﴿whoever disobeys God﴾ and ﴿He will admit him to a Fire, abiding therein﴾. We say "a cause" because it may be prevented by an obstacle, namely God's pardon, in cases other than shirk. As for shirk, its doer must certainly enter the Fire and abide in it: ﴿Indeed, whoever associates others with God, God has forbidden him Paradise, and his refuge is the Fire﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 72]. Based on this, we say: if the disobedience is less than shirk, it is a cause for entering the Fire, but entering the Fire is not necessarily required by it, since one may be pardoned. If it is shirk, it is a certain cause, and its doer must enter the Fire and abide in it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of a bequest to an heir. How is that? Because if you make a bequest to an heir, you have overstepped the limits. If a woman bequeaths a third to her husband, he would receive, according to the terms of the bequest, a third plus a half, and this is overstepping the limits. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "God has given every person with a right his right, so there is no bequest to an heir."[[Reported by Abu Dawud (2870) and al-Tirmidhi (2120), from Abu Umamah.]]

* A student: May God be good to you, O Shaykh. We have now said that major shirk is a cause for eternal abiding in the Fire. What about minor shirk?

* The Shaykh: It is not a cause for eternal abiding.

* The student: But he will enter it, O Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: This depends on His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ [An-Nisa' 48]. Is this shirk general or unrestricted? If we say it is general, then shirk, even if minor, is not forgiven. This is the view of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may God have mercy on him.

* A student: How does a person know that something is minor shirk? Can it be delimited, O Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: It can be known from the texts. Whatever the Lawgiver has called shirk, and which does not take one out of the religion, is minor shirk.

* A student: O Shaykh, the conditions of Paradise are unseen, so what is the evidence that its rivers (...)?

* The Shaykh: Yes, there is a hadith about it, indeed there are several hadiths.

* A student: Shaykh al-Islam says: doing what is prohibited counts as abandoning an obligation. O Shaykh, does it not indicate (...) ﴿Those are the limits of God﴾ (...) in the commands (...) ﴿And whoever obeys God and His Messenger﴾?

* The Shaykh: No, the limits are in the commands and they are in the prohibitions.

* The student: No, here in the verse?

* The Shaykh: ﴿Those are the limits of God﴾ [An-Nisa' 13]: these are in the commands. And doing the commands is obedience. But perhaps His saying ﴿whoever disobeys God and His Messenger and transgresses His limits﴾ indicates this. This verse indicates it.

* The student: Because He said (...).

* The Shaykh: Correct: abandoning an obligation is falling into a prohibition, and doing a prohibition is abandoning an obligation, because it is obligatory upon you to refrain.

* A student: (...) in the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas about blood, whoever abandons an obligation in the Hajj (...)?

* The Shaykh: Ibn ʿAbbas says: "Whoever abandons something of his rites, or forgets it, let him sacrifice an animal."[[Reported by al-Bayhaqi in al-Kubra (5/30), from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas.]]

* The student: (...) What does this verse indicate?

* The Shaykh: Perhaps. I say: perhaps.

* A student: ﴿After a bequest he makes or a debt﴾: is the bequest (...) or has the Sunnah restricted it: "There is no bequest to an heir"?[[Reported by Abu Dawud (2870), from the hadith of Abu Umamah.]]

* The Shaykh: No, it is derived from the verse ﴿whoever transgresses the limits of God﴾, because whoever bequeaths to an heir has given him more than God has prescribed for him, so it is a transgression of God's limits.

* A student: Some exegetes say that whoever obeys God and avoids the prohibitions will certainly enter Paradise?

* The Shaykh: He will certainly enter what?

* The student: Paradise.

* The Shaykh: Without doing an obligation?

* The student: No, if he does the obligations and abandons...

* The Shaykh: The prohibited acts.

* The student: Then he will certainly enter it. Is this statement correct?

* The Shaykh: A man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "O Messenger of God, what do you think? If I make lawful what is lawful and make unlawful what is unlawful, will I enter Paradise?" He said: "Yes."[[Reported by Muslim (1/15-16), from the hadith of Jabir.]] So if a person makes unlawful what is unlawful, makes lawful what is lawful, and does the obligations, he enters Paradise. But there are things that may prevent this. Does everyone who does the obligations do them as they should be done? There is much shortfall. For this reason the hadith says: "You receive from your prayer only what you understood of it: half of it, or a quarter, or a tenth."[[Reported by Ahmad (18894), from the hadith of ʿAmmar ibn Yasir, with similar wording.]] This indicates that a person may pray, and his prayer may be valid and discharge the obligation, but he does not obtain the reward.

* A student: The hadith of the Prophet ﷺ: "No one will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5673) and Muslim (2816/75), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] (...)?

* The Shaykh: The scholars said: regarding His saying ﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾ [As-Sajdah 17], and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "No one will enter Paradise by his deeds," the way to reconcile them is to take the bāʾ in ﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾ as causal (sababiyyah), and to take the bāʾ in "No one will enter Paradise by his deeds" as an exchange (muʿāwaḍah) and substitution. If your deed were measured against the reward, the reward would encompass the deed and would not be commensurate with it. Moreover, God's enabling a person to do righteous deeds is a blessing that requires gratitude.

* A student: His saying, Most High: ﴿He will admit him to a Fire, abiding therein﴾: is "Fire" (nāran) indefinite?

* The Shaykh: And here ﴿Gardens﴾ [jannāt] is also indefinite.

* A student: Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah says that minor shirk falls under God's saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾. Is this correct?

* The Shaykh: He says: because ﴿an yushraka bihi﴾ is a verb preceded by the verbal particle (ḥarf maṣdarī), so it is interpreted as a verbal noun. How do you interpret it?

* A student: That God does not forgive associating [others] with Him?

* The Shaykh: "Associating [others] with Him" (ishrākan bihi). And "ishrākan" is indefinite in a negative context, so it is general. But I have some reservation about this.

* A student: Is minor shirk considered among the major sins?

* The Shaykh: Minor shirk is greater than the major sins. Ibn Masʿud, may God be pleased with him, said: "That I swear by God falsely is dearer to me than that I swear by other than Him truthfully."[[Reported by ʿAbd al-Razzaq (15929), from the hadith of Ibn Masʿud or Ibn ʿUmar.]]

* A student: O Shaykh, you said in explaining ﴿khālidan﴾ that a hadith reports that each of the people of the Fire is in a coffin being punished. How do we reconcile this with the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of Paradise: "Pour water upon us"﴾ [Al-A'raf 50], which indicates that they are groups of people?

* The Shaykh: Yes, there is no contradiction. We also made an exception earlier, saying: "Except that God wills," or a similar phrase.

* A student: O Shaykh, may God be good to you. Regarding the hadith of ʿAdi ibn Hatim in Imam Muslim's Sahih: "A man stood and gave a sermon before the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'Whoever obeys them both has been guided, and whoever disobeys them both has gone astray.' The Prophet ﷺ said to him: 'What a wretched speaker you are! Rather, say: Whoever disobeys God and His Messenger has gone astray.'"[[Reported by Muslim (870/48), from the hadith of ʿAdi ibn Hatim.]] Is there a contradiction between this, O Shaykh, and the verse? And why did the Prophet ﷺ reject this speaker's words?

* The Shaykh: The best that has been said in answer to this is: the Messenger ﷺ criticized him, not because the statement is forbidden, but because the occasion did not call for it. The occasion called for detailing and elaboration, because you may address people with such a statement and they will think that misguidance only occurs when the command comes from God and His Messenger. Every occasion has its own speech. The Messenger ﷺ only criticized him for not using the sermon in its appropriate context, not because this is prohibited, since the Messenger ﷺ himself said the same.

* A student: O Shaykh, may God be good to you, what have some scholars said about this phrase?

* The Shaykh: Which one?

* The student: "Whoever obeys God and His Messenger has been guided," where he said: "Whoever obeys God," and then said: the Prophet ﷺ only rejected it because he said: "Whoever obeys God and His Messenger has been guided, and whoever disobeys both of them," and he remained silent, then said: "has gone astray." So it is as if "disobeys both of them" became conjoined to "obeys"?

* The Shaykh: By God, this is far-fetched. It requires proof that he paused. Furthermore, if a person was silent and did not speak, and said: "and whoever disobeys both of them," then said: "has gone astray," it is understood that the latter follows from what came before.

* A student: There are some framed notices in some places on which is written "God, Muhammad." Is this...?

* The Shaykh: Yes, this is a mistake and it must be removed, because whoever does not know Muhammad ﷺ may think that these two are on the same level.

* A student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: Yes. No: Paradise and Hell are not like love. Paradise and Hell are something separate.

* The student: And fear, O Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: And fear. Fear cannot be defined.

* A student: Regarding a woman continuing her studies (...) higher degrees?

* The Shaykh: A woman is like a man in the religious sciences. But in other fields, such as engineering, mathematical sciences, and the like, we do not think she should continue, because this would compel her to take a job and come tomorrow to the plots of land designated for construction to measure and map them and so on.

* A student: What about medicine, O Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: No, medicine is a necessity. There is no harm in her studying medicine, because women are half of men, indeed more than men, and they fall ill often and need women (doctors).

* A student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: That is, if people praise a person, he is pleased. No, this does not contradict good intention. A person loves to be praised by himself and loves for people to praise him. ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, when his son ʿAbdullah said, when the Prophet ﷺ presented them with the tree: "It is a tree whose likeness is that of the believer," and people disputed which tree it was, it came to his heart that it was the palm tree, but he did not speak because he was young. ʿUmar said: "If you had said it, it would have been such and such."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (131) and Muslim (2811/63), from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar.]] That is, something one is pleased with. This is not a problem. "Whoever is pleased by his good deed and saddened by his bad deed, that is a believer." This also, the praise of people for a person, is among the early glad tidings of the believer: ﴿For them are good tidings in the worldly life and in the Hereafter﴾ [Yunus 64]. The forms of glad tidings are many. Among them: good true dreams seen by a righteous man; among them: that he sees the effect of obedience on his heart as light and expansion; and among them: that people praise him and he is accepted. The forms of glad tidings are many.

* A student: May God be good to you. If a faculty member at the university says: "If the university had not forced me to research and write a thesis, I would not have researched it, knowing that its benefit is small," does this indicate soundness of intention?

* The Shaykh: Yes, because he wants to reach this degree which qualifies him for the position through which he wishes to benefit people. Much of university knowledge is not something a person would want for its own sake.

* A student: (...) in this nation, will he not think about it?

* The Shaykh: Think about what?

* The student: He thinks about a project.

* The Shaykh: A good project. This is a sincere intention.

* A student: (...) and does he intend nearness to God?

* The Shaykh: What do you say about this? A person worships God in order to attain knowledge, because God says: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ [Muhammad 17]. Is that right? We say: yes, this is a good intention. The evidence for this is that God loves righteous deeds: ﴿We will surely give him a good life﴾ [An-Nahl 97], and that He has set the legal limits (ḥudūd), the legal punishments, for the one who commits wrongdoing. Likewise, if an adulterer, for example, abandons adultery out of fear of God, but his fear of the legal punishment also influences his abstention, there is no harm.

* A student: He did not intend the face of God, especially knowledge, the attainment of knowledge?

* The Shaykh: Knowledge itself is an act of worship. Knowledge itself is an act of worship.

* * *

Shaykh Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary on Surah an-Nisa', verses 13–14 (part 3 of 3):

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. ﴿And those of your women who commit immorality, bring against them four witnesses from among you. And if they testify, then confine them to their houses until death takes them or Allah ordains for them a way.﴾ [15] ﴿And the two of you who commit it, harm them both. And if they repent and amend, then leave them alone. Indeed, Allah is ever Accepting of repentance and Merciful.﴾ [16] ﴿Indeed, the acceptance of repentance is only for those who do wrong out of ignorance and then repent soon. Those are the ones to whom Allah will return in forgiveness, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ [An-Nisa' 15–17].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those of your women who commit immorality, bring against them four witnesses from among you.﴾ ﴿Wa-allati﴾ is the plural of (allati).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits – He will admit him to a Fire, wherein he will abide eternally, and for him is a humiliating punishment.﴾

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the division of the one who opposes into one who disobeys (ʿasin) and one who transgresses the limits (mutaʿaddin lil-hudud). Disobedience here is the commission of what is forbidden, while transgressing the limits is the abandonment of an obligation or excess in it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that disobedience to the Messenger is like disobedience to Allah, since He linked it with disobedience to Allah by a particle that implies equality.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that whoever combines both matters, disobedience and transgression of the limits, will enter the Fire. But is his entry eternal or temporary? It is said: it depends on the disobedience. For Allah mentioned in the preceding verses that whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger enters the Gardens, and here He said: whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger enters the Fire. So it is said: the one whose obedience predominates enters the Garden without entering the Fire, and the one whose disobedience predominates enters it; the predominant one, if there is some obedience in him, enters the Fire (...). The one who combines obedience and disobedience enters both the Fire and the Garden, because in him are found the causes of entering both, and he is given the judgment of ﴿a recompense in accordance [with their deeds]﴾ [An-Naba' 26]. On this basis, the one who is absolutely disobedient and the one who absolutely transgresses the limits enter the Fire and do not enter the Garden, while the one who combines disobedience and obedience: if obedience prevails, he does not enter the Fire; if disobedience prevails, he enters the Fire according to the measure of his sin and comes out of it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of eternal abiding in the Fire, by His saying ﴿wherein he will abide eternally﴾. Allah the Exalted has stated that eternal abiding in the Fire is everlasting in three verses of the Qur'an: in Surah an-Nisa', in Surah al-Ahzab, and in Surah al-Jinn. In Surah an-Nisa' Allah says: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and do wrong – Allah will not forgive them, nor will He guide them to a path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever. And that is ever easy for Allah.﴾ [168–169]. In Surah al-Ahzab Allah the Blessed and Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze, abiding therein forever; they will not find any protector or helper.﴾ [64–65]. In Surah al-Jinn He says: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger – then indeed, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever.﴾ [23]. Since Allah has mentioned everlastingness in three verses, any statement that contradicts this is invalid, because eternal abiding entails the permanence of the place. If it is said: "This one abides in the Fire forever," it necessarily follows that the place in which he abides is what? Everlasting; otherwise there would be no meaning to "forever." Therefore the saying of some scholars that they abide therein forever only as long as it remains is an invalid view with no basis in reasoning, because Allah has explicitly stated everlastingness – the everlastingness of abiding – and the everlastingness of abiding necessarily entails the everlastingness of the place, otherwise there would be no benefit.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that those in the Fire – and we seek refuge in Allah – are punished with a humiliating punishment, i.e., one that involves humiliation; they are not honored.

If someone says: How do you reconcile this verse with the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then pour over his head the torment of boiling water. "Taste it; indeed, you were the mighty, the noble."﴾ [Ad-Dukhan 48–49]? The answer is one of two possibilities: either it is said to him in mockery, or it is said to recall his condition in the world, meaning: you were the mighty, the noble in the world, so that his regret increases, since he was mighty and noble in the world and is now humiliated and abased. Both of these – and we seek refuge in Allah – apply to the one to whom this address is directed: boiling water is poured over his head, and then it is said: ﴿Taste it; indeed, you were the mighty, the noble.﴾ Undoubtedly he will understand that it is said to him in mockery, and he will also recall his condition in the world, that he was honored and mighty in the world, and now he has reached this degree of humiliation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 13–14 (part 1 of 3):

(...) I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shaytan (Satan). Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾ [An-Nisa 13]. (...) This is composed of a subject and a predicate. The subject is the demonstrative ﴿These﴾, and the predicate is ﴿the limits of Allah﴾. The thing being referred to is what preceded of the inheritance shares in the verse. It is possible that the thing referred to is everything that preceded of rulings before this sentence, because the Qur'an, although it consists of distinct verses, is in reality one speech in terms of meaning and context, and our saying "one speech" means that some of it is built upon some other. For this reason some exegetes gave attention to explaining the coherence (tanasub) of the verses, just as others gave attention to explaining the coherence of the surahs, and this is a good line of inquiry.
But if someone said: the demonstrative refers to the nearest thing mentioned, according to the rule (...) that a pronoun refers to the nearest thing mentioned, and likewise a demonstrative refers to the nearest thing mentioned, then the intended referent here is what is mentioned in this verse: ﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾.
As for his saying ﴿the limits of Allah﴾: "limits" is the plural of (ḥadd), and the ḥadd is the thing that separates two things, as in the boundaries of land, one from another. The limits of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are divided into two kinds: limits of obligations and limits of prohibitions.
As for the limits of obligations, they are what Allah has made obligatory upon His servants with their conditions, pillars and obligatory elements. As for the limits of prohibitions, they are what Allah has forbidden His servants, such as fornication, sodomy, drinking intoxicants, killing a soul, and other things.
The scholars said: when Allah says ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾, it is from the limits of commands, and when He says ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them﴾, it is from the limits of prohibitions. So fornication, for example, we say: it is a limit of Allah, do not approach it; and prayer is a limit of Allah, do not transgress it, meaning do not exceed it or overstep it.
He said: ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾ — the verse here, is it from the limits of commands or prohibitions?
* Students: From the limits of commands.
* The Shaykh: From the limits of commands.
Then He said: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. This sentence is conditional. Its conditional particle is ﴿whoever﴾ (man), and its conditional verb is ﴿obeys﴾ (yuṭi'), which is jussive by sukun as is apparent. The original form of ﴿yuṭi'﴾ is (yuṭī'u), but the yā' was dropped because of the meeting of two sukūns, since the ʿayn deserved sukun by the condition and the yā' was quiescent. Ibn Malik said in al-Kafiya:
When two quiescent letters meet, make the preceding one kasra; and if the one is a soft letter, its deletion is merited.
When two quiescent letters meet, make the preceding one kasra; and if it is a soft letter — meaning one of the three soft letters — its deletion is merited. To which (...) does the verse apply?
* A student: To the second.
* The Shaykh: To the second, except in His saying ﴿yuṭi' Allah﴾ where the ʿayn is kasra, so it falls under the first. Thus the verse combined the two readings.
﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. What then is obedience? The scholars said: obedience is conformity to the command, and it is by doing the commands and avoiding the prohibitions. So one who abstains from drinking intoxicants in compliance with the prohibition of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is said to be obedient, and one who prays is said to be obedient.
This is when obedience is mentioned alone, for then it includes doing the commands and abstaining from the prohibitions. But when it is paired with disobedience, as when one says: "whoever obeys Allah and whoever disobeys Allah," then obedience is specific to the commands and disobedience to the prohibitions. Is the verse before us now of the second type or the first?
* Students: The first.
* Other students: The second.
* The Shaykh: What is the second and what is the first? It is paired with ﴿disobeys﴾ (yaʿṣi), so its meaning is the carrying out of the commands.
﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. ﴿Obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾: the mention of the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, is conjoined with the name of Allah, Exalted, because obedience to the Messenger is obedience to Allah, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [An-Nisa 80].
As for His saying ﴿and His Messenger﴾, what is meant at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an is a specific messenger, namely Muhammad, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him and his family. As for the time when the earlier laws were in force, what is meant by the messenger is whoever's law was in effect: in the time of the Messiah the messenger would be ʿĪsā, in the time of Moses the messenger would be Mūsā, and so on. But after the sending of the Messenger, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him and his family, what is meant by the messenger is Muhammad, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him and his family.
﴿He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. ﴿He will admit him﴾ is the answer of the condition, and it is jussive by sukun. Rational reasoning requires that the condition leads to the conditioned: the conditioned here is obedience, or the condition is obedience and the conditioned is the reward and recompense, so the conditioned follows from the condition by rational sequence.
So here His saying ﴿He will admit him﴾ is (...) what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has stipulated for whoever obeys Him, and it is an inevitable result, necessarily following from the truthfulness of the one who reports it, and who is he? Allah, Mighty and Majestic; for the one who reports it is Allah, and He is the most truthful of speakers, and the one who reports is able to do it. That is why you find that Allah, Exalted, says in the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾ [Aal Imran 9], because He is perfectly truthful and perfectly capable, and failure to fulfill a promise comes from one of two things: either lying, that is, the promise is false, or incapacity, lack of power; and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not fail in His promise.
﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾: (jannāt) is the plural of (jannah), and it originally means a garden with many trees, and it is so named because it conceals whoever is in it due to the abundance of its trees. This root, jīm and nūn, indicates concealment: consider (al-jinān), which is the heart, because it is hidden; (al-ajinnah), which are the foetuses in the wombs of mothers, because they are hidden; (al-jinn), because they are hidden; (al-junnah), that which the fighter is concealed by, because it conceals him. All of this material revolves around this meaning.
So the gardens are gardens with many trees, but it is not good to explain them in this place by this meaning, because if you explain them by this meaning you have, as it were, restricted their significance to what people know, and you would diminish the importance of the Paradise that is promised. For this reason we should explain them — I mean the gardens of bliss — as the abode that Allah prepared for His friends, in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human.
If you explain them with this explanation, their awe remains in souls. But if you explain them with the first meaning, a person imagines and says: this is like the garden of so-and-so son of so-and-so, with many trees and many palms and the like, whereas it is greater than what is in this world by multiples that only Allah knows. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "There is nothing in Paradise of what is in this world except the names."[[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wa'l-Nushur (332) from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas, and by Hannad ibn al-Sari in al-Zuhd (3) from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas.]] Otherwise the realities differ. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And therein is what the souls desire and the eyes delight in, and you therein will abide eternally﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 71], and He said: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes as a reward for what they used to do﴾ [As-Sajda 17]. And in the sacred hadith: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4779) and Muslim (2824) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]
His saying ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾: ﴿flow﴾ (tajrī): flowing is well known, it is the movement of water over the earth. His saying ﴿beneath which﴾ means: beneath these gardens, meaning spreading trees, shade and rivers that flow. If a person imagined this bliss, he would find it the greatest bliss. Allah, Exalted, explained these rivers in Surah Muhammad with His saying: ﴿In it are rivers of water unchanging, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to drinkers, and rivers of purified honey﴾ [Muhammad 15]. What is the honey of the bee? It is purified honey, which Allah created thus. Milk that is not the milk of cows or sheep; rivers that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created. Likewise the water never becomes stagnant, however long it remains, unlike the water of the earth, which becomes stagnant and its smell changes with long standing. The wine is a delight in which there is no harm and they are not made drunk by it.
