* Shaykh: The apparent meaning is that it was not found, because the scholars count what has passed as in the Jahiliyyah.

Yes, we say:
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of marrying those whom the fathers, near and remote, have married; due to His saying: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women﴾.
* And among its benefits: that if this contract were concluded, it would be invalid; due to His saying: ﴿except what has already passed﴾, and due to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our affair, it is rejected" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697) and Muslim (1718 / 18), the wording being his, from the hadith of ʿAʾishah.]]. Whoever marries a woman whom his father married has done an action that is not in accordance with the command of Allah and His Messenger.
* And among its benefits: the permissibility for a son of a woman whom his father fornicated with. From where is this derived?
* The students: ﴿mā nakaḥa ābāʾukum﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿mā nakaḥa ābāʾukum﴾. Fornication is not marriage, contrary to the well-known view among the Hanbalis that a woman whom the father has had intercourse with, even by fornication, is forbidden to the son. This has no evidence; rather, the evidence is against it in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾. Its analogy to marriage is not valid, because marriage is a legislated, recognized contract, whereas fornication is a vile illicit act, hateful to Allah, not legislated by Allah; so it is not valid to analogize it to marriage. More astonishing than that is that some of them said: even in sodomy, may Allah protect us; for example, if the son had sodomized a person, the ruling is that of having fornicated with his mother or his sister, the sister of that person. We will mention it, Allah willing, at the end for illustration.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of marrying the wives of fathers, even if no intercourse or seclusion has occurred; the reason being that marriage is established merely by the contract, for whoever has contracted with a woman, it is true of him that he has married her.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that the sin committed before knowledge does not burden the doer with its sin; due to His saying: ﴿except what has already passed﴾. This is a legal principle: the Sharia obligations do not bind before knowledge, as Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, established. The Sharia obligations do not bind before knowledge, neither as obligation nor as prohibition. Accordingly, if a person embraced Islam in a remote desert and did not know of the obligation of fasting Ramadan, then learned of it later, we do not oblige him to make up the fasts he missed, because the obligation did not reach him, so the proof was not established against him. Likewise with prayer: if he did not pray, or prayed while in impurity, or without wudu, or without tuma'ninah, he is not obliged to make up what he missed. The evidence for this is, in fact, numerous; among them the hadith of the one who prayed badly, where the Prophet (ﷺ) did not oblige him to make up what had passed, although he said: "You have not prayed" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (757) and Muslim (397 / 45), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]], and he only commanded him to repeat the present prayer because he was required to perform it within its time.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah's mercy precedes His wrath, in that He pardons what has passed of sins; due to His saying: ﴿except what has already passed﴾. This principle is known from His saying: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ [al-An'am 54], and from His saying, in the Book He wrote with Him beneath the Throne or above the Throne: "Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7422) and Muslim (2751 / 14), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. From this principle it follows that pardon is closer to safety than punishment. For this reason, it is reported from some of the Companions, and I think it is ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, that he said: "To err in pardon is more beloved to me than to err in punishment" [[Reported by al-Tirmidhi (1424) from the hadith of ʿAʾishah as a marfuʿ report, and by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra (8/238) and Maʿrifat al-Sunan wa al-Athar (5471) from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab as a mawquf report.]]. From this follows an important principle: if scholars dispute a matter between prohibited and permitted, and the evidences of both sides are equal, we adopt the easier and simpler view, based on this principle: that Allah's mercy precedes His wrath, and that Allah wills ease for His servants and does not will hardship for them. That is the second. And the third: that the default is the innocence of the person's liability.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that marrying within the prohibited degrees is worse than fornication; due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, it was an indecency and hatred, and an evil way﴾. Regarding marriage (to the prohibited) He said, exalted is He: ﴿And do not approach fornication; indeed, it is an indecency and an evil way﴾ [al-Isra' 32], and He did not say "and hatred." For this reason many scholars held that whoever fornicates with a woman within his prohibited degrees, or marries her, is stoned even if he is unmarried, because marrying those within the prohibited degrees is greater and more severe than fornication.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the ugliness of this course; due to His saying: ﴿and an evil way﴾.
* And among its benefits: the demonstration of Allah's blessing upon us in this Sharia, in that He has spared us from following evil, blameworthy paths; due to His saying: ﴿and an evil way﴾. From its opposite it is derived that the path of Islam, or the Islamic methodology, is the best, most excellent, and finest of paths.
As for the issue I mentioned to you, the matter of sodomy: some scholars said that sodomy takes the place of marriage, so if a man sodomized a boy, the boy's mother becomes forbidden to him, and the boy's daughter becomes forbidden to him. This is without doubt an error, a grave error. The conclusion is that the correct view on this matter is that a person is not made forbidden to someone whom his father fornicated with, nor to someone whom his son fornicated with, because that is not a legitimate marriage, so it carries no weight.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 23 (part 1 of 6):

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾. ﴿Forbidden﴾: by whom is it forbidden? By Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the agent has been omitted because it is known. The original meaning of *haram* (forbidden) in the linguistic sense is prevention, and from it comes *hareem al-bi'r* (the protected area around a well), which is what surrounds it as a protection and prevents anyone other than its owner from taking possession of it. So the original meaning of *haram* in language is prevention; that is, you are prevented from your mothers.

﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾. *Ummahat* (mothers) is the plural of *umm* or *ummah*. For the plural of *umm* referring to rational beings, one says *ummahat*, and for non-rational beings, *ummat*, with the *ha'* dropped. One says: "These sheep are *ummat*" and "These children are the young of the sheep."

His saying ﴿your mothers﴾ includes the mother in the immediate sense and the mothers of higher generations, such as the grandmother, the grandmother's mother, the father's mother, the mother's mother, the grandfather's mother, and the grandmother's mother. The point is that we say about them what we said about His saying ﴿your fathers﴾; meaning, it includes the near and the distant mothers, from the paternal side and from the maternal side.

﴿And your daughters﴾. *Banat* (daughters) is the plural of *bint* (daughter). It includes the daughter, the son's daughter, and the daughter's daughter, however far down they go. It also includes the daughter born of adultery according to the view of the majority of scholars, even though she is not legally attributed to him, since she was created from his water. So she is, according to the stronger view, included, as we will explain, Allah willing, in the benefits (*fawa'id*) section.

﴿And your sisters﴾. Who are the sisters? *Akhawat* (sisters) is the plural of *ukht* (sister), and they are the closest branches of the father.

﴿And your paternal aunts﴾. *'Ammat* is the plural of *'ammah* (paternal aunt), and they are the branches of the higher father, that is, the branches of the grandfather, the branches of the great-grandfather, and so on. Know that a man's paternal aunt is an aunt to him and to his descendants, sons and daughters. Pay attention to this: your father's paternal aunt is an aunt to you, to your children, to your daughters, to your sons' children, and to your daughters' children.

﴿And your maternal aunts﴾. Who is the *khalah* (maternal aunt)? The *khalat* are the branches of the mother's father, however high up he goes. The *'ammat* are the branches of the father's father, and the *khalat* are the branches of the mother's father; that is, the sisters of your mother.

﴿And the daughters of the brother﴾, however far down they go, and it includes the full brother, the paternal half-brother, and the maternal half-brother. What is your relation to the daughters of a brother? He is your paternal uncle (*'amm*). And to the daughters of a sister? You are their maternal uncle (*khal*). So the daughters of siblings are forbidden to a person, however far down they go.

The prohibitions by blood (*nasab*) are finished, and they are seven, as is apparent: your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, the daughters of the brother, and the daughters of the sister. These are the seven prohibitions by blood.

In the way the jurists limit them, one says: the ascendants (*usul*), the descendants (*furu'*), the descendants of the nearest ascendant however far down they go, and the descendants of the higher ascendant but not their descendants. Is it clear? The ascendants are like the mothers and grandmothers. The descendants are like the daughters, however far down they go. The descendants of the nearest ascendant, however far down they go, are these sisters, however far down they go: the daughters of the sisters. The descendants of the higher ascendant, limited to their own line (*li-sulbihim*), are the paternal aunts and maternal aunts. But limited to their own line means not extending to those further down; so the daughter of the paternal aunt, for example, is lawful, and the daughter of the maternal aunt is lawful. This is the way of the jurists.

As for the way of enumeration, which is the most eloquent thing, and it is the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, it does not need much reflection, it does not need much reflection. That is why, if you say to a layman: "It is forbidden for you to marry a mother, a daughter, a sister, a paternal aunt, a maternal aunt, a niece through a brother, and a niece through a sister," he goes away reassured and the matter is clear to him. But if you say: "The ascendants and descendants are forbidden to you," he says: "What are the ascendants and descendants?" and "the descendants of the nearest ascendant however far down they go, and the descendants of the higher ascendant limited to their own line and not those further down." He says: "This is a complicated thing," and goes looking for a translation of this thing. That is why, by the Glory of Allah the Mighty, the Qur'an is the most eloquent thing, however much anyone speaks about its eloquence; the Qur'an is more eloquent than that, clearer and more explicit.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And your mothers who have nursed you﴾. This is another category, because the prohibitions are of several categories: by blood (*nasab*), by nursing (*radha'*), and by marriage relation (*musaharah*). So here He says: ﴿And your mothers who have nursed you﴾. Nursing is well known; it is the sucking of the breast by the infant, or the infant's sucking from the breast, or giving it to him after it has been separated from the breast, as when it is placed in a cup or in an artificial breast or the like.

His saying ﴿who have nursed you﴾: the word *arda'na* (they nursed) is a verb, and the verb in its original form is unrestricted, and an unrestricted form is satisfied by a single instance. So if you say, for example, "I struck," how many times? It is satisfied by one time. Therefore ﴿they nursed you﴾ is satisfied by one time; that is, by a single feeding. So the verse indicates that nursing in general establishes the prohibition, and the Sunnah will come, Allah willing, in the benefits section, explaining that the Sunnah has restricted this.

﴿And your sisters through nursing﴾. Who are the sisters through nursing? They are the daughters of the woman who nursed you and the daughters of her husband. Correct? The sisters through nursing are the daughters of the woman who nursed you and the daughters of her husband, from him or from another. They are the daughters of the woman who nursed you, correct? And the daughters of her husband, correct, or not? Correct: the daughters of the wife who nursed you and the daughters of her husband, because the daughters of her husband are sisters through the father, and the daughters of the one who nursed you are your sisters through the father and mother, that is, full siblings, or through the mother; because she may nurse you with the milk of Zayd, and she has daughters from 'Amr, so her daughters from 'Amr are your sisters through the mother.

The point is that His saying ﴿your sisters through nursing﴾ includes full sisters, sisters through the father, and sisters through the mother. Is it clear?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, it's clear, there are no objections.
When are they full sisters? When she nursed you with milk from their father. When she nursed you with milk from their father, they become full sisters.
And when are they sisters through the father? When the husband whose milk nursed you had daughters from another woman, other than the one who nursed you, because the father is one. This is your father through nursing, and the father of these women by lineage.
And when are they sisters through the mother? When she had daughters from a husband other than the one who nursed you, while she was still married to him; they are then your sisters through the mother.
The point is that ﴿your sisters through nursing﴾ includes full sisters, or through the father, or through the mother. And does it include those who came before? For example, if you nursed with a child called Muhammad, and she had a daughter before him named Fatimah, would you marry her or not? You would not marry her, because she is your sister through nursing.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: How, with the milk of someone else?
* The student: If the wife nursed him with the milk of a man before him, then the children of this husband are not his brothers.
* The Shaykh: Known (...). They do not become siblings. Are these siblings? They are not siblings.

He says: ﴿And the mothers of your wives﴾. Who is the *umm* (mother)? As we said, when it is used without qualification it means the one who gave birth to the person. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Their mothers are none but those who gave birth to them﴾ [al-Mujadilah 2]. So the mothers of the women, meaning those who gave birth to your wives, those who gave birth to your wives. Pay attention to this point, because we will touch on it, Allah willing, the Exalted.

His saying ﴿your wives﴾ means your spouses. A woman is not a wife except through a valid contract, so the contract must be valid. And from here begins the third category: the prohibitions by what? By marriage relation (*musaharah*).

﴿The mothers of your wives﴾: who is meant by the mothers of the women? Those who gave birth to them. What is the evidence for this? His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Their mothers are none but those who gave birth to them﴾. As for "wives," we said the marriage must be valid, because if it is not valid, the woman is not one of his wives, so they are not "wives" except after the validity of the contract.

﴿And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship﴾. *Rabaib* (stepdaughters) is the plural of *rabibah*, like *sahaif* the plural of *sahifah*. ﴿And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, from your wives with whom you have consummated [the marriage]﴾. The phrase ﴿who are in your guardianship﴾ is a description of *rabaib*, and ﴿from your wives with whom you have consummated﴾ is an explanation of it; that is, the stepdaughters from these women with whom you have consummated. And ﴿from your wives﴾ means your wives whom you have contracted with a valid contract, since a woman is not one of a man's wives except through a valid contract.

﴿With whom you have consummated﴾: ﴿who﴾ here is a description of ﴿from your wives﴾. ﴿With whom you have consummated﴾: the meaning of consummation is intercourse, not mere seclusion. Here we distinguish between consummation, which is intercourse, and seclusion, and seclusion has no effect.

Allah mentioned two conditions regarding stepdaughters. The first condition: that she be in the man's guardianship; so a man marries a woman who has a daughter from another man, and he takes the daughter in with the mother so she is with him in his household. This is "in his guardianship." The second condition: that the husband has consummated the marriage with the mother, that is, has had intercourse with her. So are these two conditions binding, or is one of them the binding one?

In the verse there are two conditions. The first condition: ﴿who are in your guardianship﴾, and the second condition: ﴿from your wives with whom you have consummated﴾. Are the two conditions binding?
There are two opinions among the scholars:
The first opinion: that both are binding, and that the stepdaughter, if she is not in the man's guardianship, or if he has not consummated the marriage with her mother, is lawful; and that she is not forbidden except when both conditions are met: she is in his guardianship and he has consummated with her mother. Is this clear or not?
The second opinion, the opinion of the majority: that the binding condition is the second, which is His saying ﴿from your wives with whom you have consummated﴾, while the first condition is not binding; it was mentioned based on what is usual, or to explain the wisdom. The majority support their view by the fact that Allah, the Exalted, explicitly stated the implication (*mafhum*) of the second condition but did not state the implication of the first condition; rather He remained silent about it. He said: ﴿But if you have not consummated [the marriage] with them, there is no sin upon you﴾. Had the first condition been binding, He would have said: "If you have not consummated with them or they are not in your guardianship, there is no sin upon you." If Allah had remained silent about the implication and had not said ﴿But if you have not consummated [the marriage] with them﴾, the condition would have been binding, and the proof would be with the one who made it a requirement. So the grades are three:
The first is to say: "Your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship from your wives with whom you have consummated; but if they are not in your guardianship, or if you have not consummated with their mothers, there is no sin upon you." In this grade, both conditions are undoubtedly binding.
The second is to say: "Your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship from your wives with whom you have consummated, and the wives of your sons." Here both conditions are binding.
The third, as in the verse now, is for Him to say: ﴿And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship from your wives with whom you have consummated; but if you have not consummated with them, there is no sin upon you﴾. This indicates that the second condition is binding and the first is not, and this is the view of the majority, and it is the correct view, and Allah knows best.
* A student: (...) knowledge is better than occupation with worship. It is mentioned about Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, that he used to pray three hundred *rak'ahs* a day, and much is mentioned about others among the imams regarding the abundance of their worship. How do we reconcile this with that?
* The Shaykh: We reconcile them. First, we demand verification of the transmission that he prayed three hundred *rak'ahs* in a day; that is one point, because this is far-fetched. Second, if it is authentic, it may have been done on one of the days when he felt his heart empty of attachment to Allah and similar things, so he did it. Even a person in seeking knowledge sometimes finds hardness in his heart, especially when he enters into the disputes of the speculative theologians (*ahl al-kalam*) about the attributes, the body, the accident, the substance, and similar matters; some hardness enters him, so he turns some of his attention toward specific worship. A person is the physician of his own soul; sometimes he sees that remaining with this guest who has come is better than standing to pray or standing to learn knowledge. "That is why you find the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, sometimes fasting so much that it was said, 'He will not break his fast,' and sometimes breaking it so much that it was said, 'He will not fast'" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1969) and Muslim (1156/175), from the hadith of 'A'ishah]. And likewise regarding the night prayer.
* A student: (...) the hadith: "The feet of a servant will not move [on the Day of Judgment until he is asked about...]" [al-Tirmidhi (2416), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud]. Is the question specific to the adult, or to the adult and the child?
* The Shaykh: It is specific to the accountable person (*mukallaf*). As for children, they are asked according to one opinion only at the time of burial: "Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is your prophet?" and Allah inspires them with the right answer. However, there is a difference of opinion regarding the question for a non-accountable person after burial, whether the two angels descend to him and question him or not.
* A student: The validity of worship and the spirit of worship are valid without knowledge, because knowledge is not valid..?
* The Shaykh: A person cannot worship except with knowledge. But what is the knowledge? It is the knowledge a person acquires by devoting himself to learning, like the students of knowledge, for example. Common people now know how to pray; they understood it from the practice of people.
* A student: But, Shaykh, most worship today (...). The student of knowledge performs worship with insight, so this gives him an advantage over others.
* The Shaykh: There is no doubt. ﴿Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ [az-Zumar 9].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brother's daughters, your sister's daughters, your mothers who have nursed you, your sisters through nursing, your wives' mothers, and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship from your wives with whom you have consummated...﴾ and so on to the end.
* The Shaykh: A question: who is the one who forbids?
* A student: He is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* The Shaykh: Why was it omitted?
* The student: Because it is in the passive form.
* The Shaykh: I am asking: why was it omitted?
* The student: To specify the position.
* The Shaykh: Because it is known, as in His saying: ﴿And man was created weak﴾ [an-Nisa' 28]. Legal matters may be in the passive form, like ﴿Forbidden﴾, and likewise created matters, like ﴿was created﴾.
* The Shaykh: Who is meant by the mothers here?
* A student: The roots (*usul*) (...).
* The Shaykh: But the mothers who are like your mother in respect?
* The student: No, no, the roots (...).
* The Shaykh: But who? If he says *umm* (mother), who is she?
* The student: (...) the one who gave birth.
* The Shaykh: The one who gave birth.
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence that *umm* refers to the one who gave birth?
* A student: His saying: ﴿Their mothers are none but those who gave birth to them﴾.
* The Shaykh: Does "mother" here include the grandmother, however high up?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed, it includes her.
* The Shaykh: And does it include those who come from the father's side and the mother's side, or from the father's side only?
* The student: It includes those who come from the father's side and the mother's side.
* The Shaykh: Good, correct.
We mentioned the principle that a person's paternal aunt is an aunt to him and to his descendants until the Day of Resurrection, whether the descendants are branched through females or through males, correct?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And the maternal aunt?
* The student: The maternal aunt is also like that.
* The Shaykh: And the sister?
* The student: No, the sister is not.
* The Shaykh: How? The sister has the strongest bond with him.
* The student: And the sister.
* The Shaykh: Even if she were; what does the sister become?
* The student: The sister becomes a maternal aunt.
* The Shaykh: A maternal aunt only?
* The student: And a paternal aunt.
* The Shaykh: A paternal aunt only?
* The student: Yes, a paternal aunt and a maternal aunt.
* The Shaykh: A paternal aunt or a maternal aunt.
* The student: A paternal aunt if she is the father's sister, and a maternal aunt if she is the mother's sister.
* The Shaykh: What do you say about this, correct? He says a paternal aunt if she is the father's sister, and a maternal aunt if she is the mother's sister. Correct?
* Students: Correct.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, correct, there is no doubt.
The prohibitions by blood, based on that, how many? That is, by kinship, how many? We say: a number, not the rules.
* A student: The grandfather and the father.
* The Shaykh: How, the grandfather? The grandfather (...).
* The Shaykh: I am asking: who are the prohibitions by blood? How many are they?
* A student: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brother's daughters, and your sister's daughters﴾.
* The Shaykh: How many are they?
* The students: Seven.
* The Shaykh: Seven, excellent, these are the prohibitions by blood.
* The Shaykh: What are the rules of these seven according to the jurists? The jurists formulated the rules of these seven; they established principles for them. What did they say?
* A student: (...).
Yes, what do you say about this? Correct?
A student: The question?
Another student: Correct.
The Shaykh: He says: a paternal aunt if she is the father's sister, and a maternal aunt if she is the mother's sister, correct?
Students: Correct.

**The Shaykh:** Yes, correct. That's right now, there's no doubt. Based on that, how many are the prohibited by lineage (*al-muḥarramāt bi-l-nasab*)?

**Student:** The prohibited by lineage?

**The Shaykh:** Yes, meaning by kinship.

**Student:** By kinship, the ascendants (*al-uṣūl*).

**The Shaykh:** How many? I'm saying: count the rules (*ḍawābiṭ*).

**Student:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** I'm saying: who are the prohibited by lineage? How many are they?

**Student:** The prohibited by lineage?

**The Shaykh:** Yes, how many are they?

**Student:** Seven.

**The Shaykh:** Seven. Say them.

**Student:** The prohibited by lineage?

**The Shaykh:** Yes, you.

**Student:** Your mothers, and your daughters.

**The Shaykh:** And your sisters.

**Student:** And your paternal aunts, and your maternal aunts, and the daughters of the brother, and the daughters of the sister.

**The Shaykh:** How many are these?

**Student:** Seven.

**The Shaykh:** Seven, good. These are the prohibitions by lineage. Their governing rules (*qawā'id*) according to the jurists? The jurists formulated these seven as rules, or made them into general principles. What did they say?

**Student:** The mother, and whoever is above her.

**Another student:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** The ascendants and however high they go. And the second?

**Student:** The descendants and however far down they go.

**The Shaykh:** The descendants and however far down they go. And the third?

**Student:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** Wrong.

**Student:** (...) the ascendants.

**The Shaykh:** The ascendants however high they go, like that? I say: "however high they go"? The ascendants however high they go, you're certain? Fine?

**Student:** And the descendants.

**The Shaykh:** However far down they go, however far down they go. We're speaking of the women now. However far down they go.

**Student:** The descendants of the lower origin (*al-aṣl al-adnā*).

**The Shaykh:** The descendants of the lower origin however far down they go. One remains. Who are the descendants of the lower origin however far down they go?

**Student:** The descendants of the lower origin.

**The Shaykh:** Yes, however far down they go.

**Student:** For example..

**The Shaykh:** Who is your lower origin?

**Student:** The lower (...).

**The Shaykh:** No, who is your lower origin? Your father and your mother are the lower origin. Their descendants are who?

**Student:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** With respect to you, what do you call them? The descendants of your father?

**Student:** The siblings.

**The Shaykh:** Well done. So: the descendants of the lower origin however far down they go, such as the sisters, the daughters of the sisters, and the daughters of the brothers. One remains?

**Student:** The descendants of the higher origin, excluding their descendants.

**The Shaykh:** The descendants of the higher origin, excluding their descendants. Who are they?

**Student:** The paternal aunts and the maternal aunts.

**The Shaykh:** The paternal and maternal aunts, excluding descendants. Is the daughter of the paternal aunt permissible? The daughter of the paternal aunt is not permissible?

**Students:** She is permissible for marriage.

**The Shaykh:** Meaning, is it valid for him to marry her or not?

**Student:** It is valid.

**The Shaykh:** It is valid, good. Next are the prohibitions by fosterage (*al-muḥarramāt bi-l-raḍā'*), which is the second category. He said: ﴿And your mothers who have nursed you﴾ [al-Nisā' 23].
﴿And your foster-sisters, and the mothers of your wives﴾ [al-Nisā' 23]. We have taken that. ﴿And your stepdaughters (*rabā'ib*) who are in your guardianship, born of your wives with whom you have consummated marriage; but if you have not consummated marriage with them, there is no blame upon you﴾ [al-Nisā' 23]. All of these are prohibitions by affinity (*al-muḥarramāt bi-l-ṣihr*). He said: ﴿And the wives of your sons who are from your loins﴾ [al-Nisā' 23]. *Ḥalā'il* is the plural of *ḥalīla*, and it includes the wife and the female slave. But a wife becomes prohibited to the father of the husband by the contract alone, whereas a concubine (*surriyyah*) is not prohibited to the master's father except by intercourse. Do you understand? If he has had intercourse with her. This is because before he has intercourse with a concubine, she may be merchandise that is bought and sold; once he has intercourse with her, he has chosen her for himself. So *ḥalā'il* is the plural of *ḥalīla*, which is the wife he has made lawful through the contract, or the slave-woman he has made lawful through intercourse.

His saying: ﴿the wives of your sons who are from your loins﴾. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not mention any restriction in it, so it includes every wife, whether the son consummated the marriage with her or not. On this basis, the son's wife is prohibited to his father, even if he divorces her before consummation, and even if he divorces her before seclusion (*khalwah*), because of the generality of the verse.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿who are from your loins﴾. *Aṣlāb* is the plural of *ṣulb*, which is the back, and what is meant is the sons who were born from your water, because this is the biological son. ﴿who are from your loins﴾. This is a restriction. What does this restriction exclude?

The majority of scholars hold that it excludes adopted sons (*abnā' al-tabannī*), those whom people in the pre-Islamic period were accustomed to adopt, when a person would take a son and say: "You are my son," and make him like his own son in inheritance and other matters. So the restriction "from the loins" here is for excluding the adopted son. This is the view of the majority. However, there is no objection to saying that it includes both the adopted son and the foster son, because the foster son is not your son from your loins, yet the foster son is called a son in the Sharia. But the adopted son has been annulled by the Sharia. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And He has not made your adopted sons your sons. That is merely your saying with your mouths. And Allah says the truth, and He guides to the way﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 4]. If it has been annulled by the Sharia, there is no need for a restriction to exclude him. Why? Because he is not included in the meaning of sonship when used without qualification, neither legally nor in the physical sense. Likewise, he is not from his water. On this basis, the restriction is more evidently meant to exclude the foster son than the adopted son, because the adopted son is not recognized by the Sharia, so there is no need for a restriction to remove him from the meaning of sonship. This is the view that Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, adopted, although it is thought that he opposed the people in this. But on careful reflection, his view is the correct one: that affinity (*muṣāharah*) does not operate through fosterage, and fosterage has no connection to it, because the hadith says: "What is prohibited by lineage is prohibited by fosterage."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (3370), and Muslim (1447 / 12).]] The father of the husband and the son of the husband are prohibited by what? By affinity. So how do we include in the hadith what is not included in it? And likewise in the noble verse.

Then He said: ﴿And that you combine two sisters﴾ [al-Nisā' 23]. Here, the prohibited thing is not a person but an act, which is combining. Meaning: He has made it forbidden for us to combine two sisters. Pay attention!

Therefore it is not correct to express it by saying: "The sister of the wife is prohibited," or "The paternal aunt of the wife is prohibited," because that is not stated either in the Qur'an or in the Sunnah. In the Qur'an: ﴿And that you combine two sisters﴾. And in the Sunnah: "A woman may not be combined with her paternal aunt, nor with her maternal aunt."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (5109), and Muslim (1408 / 33).]] So the ruling is attached to an act, which is combining, and not to a specific person, namely the sister or the aunt. Therefore we say: the expression of some scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, "The sister of his wife, her paternal aunt, and her maternal aunt are prohibited," is imprecise. The correct formulation is: combining two sisters is prohibited, and combining a woman with her paternal aunt, and a woman with her maternal aunt is prohibited. This is the correct view.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that you combine two sisters﴾ includes full sisters, sisters by the father, and sisters by the mother, because the verse is unrestricted.

As for His saying: ﴿except what has already passed﴾, we say regarding it what we said regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾ [al-Nisā' 22]. That is, what has already passed is pardoned. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned it only because of the gravity of the matter, and so that a person does not preoccupy himself with an earlier act that was committed in the forbidden manner. On this basis, the child produced from a marriage that took place before the prohibition, what is its status? Is it attributed to the man who had intercourse or not? That is, if a man married his father's wife in the pre-Islamic period, she bore him a child, and then he embraced Islam, the two are separated, because the cause of prohibition remains. But the child produced from the first marriage is attributed to him legally. And this, Allah knows best, is the wisdom behind His saying: ﴿except what has already passed﴾, in order to remove completely what is in a person's heart. Because he might say: "If that was forbidden to me, what is my position before the child who was created from me at that time?"

So Allah reassured the servants by His saying: ﴿except what has already passed﴾. This is among what Allah has now opened up for us: that this is the wisdom in the exception of what came before, or the correction of what came before. Otherwise someone might say: how does what came before become subject to it? How does the prohibition apply retroactively to it, by what is called retroactive effect?

We say: the wisdom in that is the gravity of the matter. The second is that if a child was born from that marriage, the child is a legitimate child, with no concern and no worry, because he is pardoned, and so are its effects. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾. These [words] have passed over us many times, and in them is emphasis: the emphasis of two names of Allah by two emphasizers: *inna* and *kāna*, because *kāna*, as we have explained before, is stripped of time and establishes the attribute.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾. *Al-Ghafūr* (the Forgiving) is an intensive form from *al-ghafr*, which is covering sins and not holding one accountable for them. *Al-Raḥīm* (the Merciful) is likewise an intensive form from mercy. Mercy is an intrinsic attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, but it has effects, such as the descent of rain, abundance of provision, abundance of knowledge, people being directed in a sound direction, and similar things. These things are effects of Allah's mercy, and they are not the mercy itself. But they are called mercy because they are effects of Allah's mercy, as Allah said about Paradise: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whom I will."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (4850), and Muslim (2846 / 34).]] This verse contains great benefits.

The reason is that if the foster mother were included in "mother" when used absolutely, there would be no need for His saying: ﴿and your mothers who nursed you﴾, because she would be included in His saying: ﴿Prohibited to you are your mothers﴾.
* Branching from this benefit: a wife's foster mother is not included in His saying: ﴿and the mothers of your wives﴾. Why? Because "mother," when used absolutely, does not include the foster mother. So if someone says: the wife's foster mother is prohibited because she is included in the general meaning of His saying: ﴿and the mothers of your wives﴾? We say: we do not accept this, why? Because "mother," when used absolutely, does not include the foster mother, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿Prohibited to you are your mothers﴾ and ﴿and your mothers who nursed you﴾. And if "mother," when used absolutely, included the foster mother, there would be a repetition in the verse that contradicts eloquence.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment of motherhood by fosterage. On this basis, it is correct for one to say to the woman who nursed him: "my mother," but he should not say it except qualified, because Allah qualified it when He said: ﴿your mothers who nursed you﴾. So you say: "my mother through fosterage," qualifying it so that the listener does not assume she is a mother by blood.
* Branching from this benefit: what many people call a father's wife "aunt," and some call her "maternal aunt" absolutely; and likewise what some people do in calling the wife's father "uncle" or "maternal uncle." One says: "my uncle," and another says: "my maternal uncle." This is an error, because this designation is not valid linguistically or legally, and it causes confusion. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade calling the night prayer "al-ʿatamah," and said: "Let not the Bedouins overcome you regarding the name of your 'Isha' prayer, for it is in the Book of Allah 'al-ʿIsha'" [Narrated by Muslim (644/229), and its wording is: "Let not the Bedouins overcome you regarding the name of your 'Isha' prayer, for it is in the Book of Allah 'al-ʿIsha', and they delay it with the milking of camels."]. ﴿and after the prayer of ʿIsha'﴾ [al-Nur 58], as in the Qur'an. Therefore, legal terms or legal realities should not be applied contrary to their legal meanings.

Nursing applies to a single feeding, even a single suck, because whoever sucks from a woman's breast is said to have nursed. On this basis, prohibition is established by a single feeding. This was the view of the Ẓāhirites, who said that prohibition by fosterage is established by a single feeding, because it came in absolute form in the Qur'an, and the absolute applies to a single instance. But the correct view is that this absolute in the Qur'an has been qualified by the Sunnah, in what is authentically related from the Prophet (ﷺ) in his saying: "A single suck or two sucks do not prohibit, nor a single swallow or two swallows" [Narrated by Abu Dawud (2063) and al-Tirmidhi (1150) only the first part; and Ibn Hibban in full (4226)]. "A single suck or two sucks do not prohibit." Alright, and three? Three prohibit by the implication (mafhum) of this hadith: "A single suck or two sucks do not prohibit" [Abu Dawud (2063) and al-Tirmidhi (1150)]. Its implication is that a single suck and two sucks prohibit.
* Students: No, they do not prohibit.
* Shaykh: They do not prohibit. That is the explicit statement (manṭūq). Its implication (mafhum) is that what exceeds these two prohibits, and many scholars held this too, the people of analogy (qiyas), not the people of the apparent meaning (ẓāhir), the people of analogy, and they said: three prohibit by the implication of the hadith. Some scholars said: only five prohibit, because of what is authentically related in Muslim from ʿA'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "What was revealed of the Qur'an included ten known sucklings that prohibit, then they were abrogated by five known sucklings. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died while it was among what is recited of the Qur'an" [Narrated by Muslim (1452/24)]. This was the view of Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him: that what prohibits is five sucklings. He answered the hadith: "A single suck or two sucks do not prohibit" [Abu Dawud (2063) and al-Tirmidhi (1150)] by saying that the prohibition of three is by implication. When the implication and the explicit statement conflict, which is given priority? The explicit statement. Why? Because the implication is broad and applies in a single instance. For example: "A single suck does not prohibit, nor two sucks," and three, four, five, and ten are silent about by implication. If a child has five sucklings, the prohibition is established. If we say that prohibition is established by five sucklings, we have not opposed the explicit statement; its implication is that two do not prohibit, and what exceeds it applies in a single instance. Therefore we say: we give precedence to the indication of the explicit statement. But some scholars sharply criticized this hadith, saying: this hadith is not authentic even if it is in Muslim. How could the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) die while it was among what is recited of the Qur'an, and we do not find it in the Qur'an now? Because if something that existed in the Qur'an after the death of the Messenger (ﷺ) must not remain, and if this door were opened, it would be a path to validating the view of the Rafidah that the Qur'an contains something omitted. On this basis, the text is rejected, and we adopt the hadith: "A single suck or two sucks do not prohibit" [Abu Dawud (2063) and al-Tirmidhi (1150)], or we adopt the absolute. But on reflection it does not appear that this is a criticism of the hadith, because ʿA'ishah explicitly stated the abrogation, abrogation (naskh), but it remained among what was recited of the Qur'an at the death of the Messenger (ﷺ) because the one who would learn of it did not know, by the abrogation, and this is an actual matter. So the hadith indicates that the abrogation occurred late, and some people did not know of it, so they continued to recite it among what they recited of the Qur'an. When the difficulty is removed, we should not dare to criticize the narrators, because if you judge the text to be rejected, you judge that the narrators erred and were mistaken, and this is difficult. So whenever it is possible to accept the report of a trustworthy narrator, accept it. But if that is not possible, and it contradicts the Qur'an, do not accept it. But if it does not contradict and reconciliation is possible, reconcile. This is what Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, held, and it is the correct view that it is five sucklings. In the hadith: "known" [Muslim (1452/24)], which indicates that if doubt arises about their number, whether it is five or four, it is not considered. This nursing is not considered, because the hadith is qualified by "known." With doubt, the ruling is not established. This is something that reassures a person regarding what he issues as a ruling to people on this matter, because many people come and say: "the nursing is established, but we do not know how many sucklings there were." We say: praise be to Allah. As long as the hadith says five known sucklings, what is doubtful is not known, and therefore the ruling is not established by it. Is that clear? It remains for us to consider whether the absolute of the Qur'an can be qualified by the Sunnah.
  Yes, indeed, it can. The absolute of the Qur'an can be qualified by the Sunnah, just as the generality of the Qur'an is specified by the Sunnah. As for abrogating the Qur'an by the Sunnah, the correct view is that the Qur'an can be abrogated by the Sunnah if it is authentic, because all of it is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; Allah may abrogate His speech by His speech, and He may abrogate His speech by the speech of His Messenger (ﷺ). So the prohibiting number is how many? Five known sucklings. So what are the five, or what is a suckling? According to the most correct view, what is a suckling?
* Student: A satisfying suckling.
* Shaykh: Satisfying. The hadith does not say five satisfying sucklings; it says five sucklings. Some said: a suckling is a suck (maṣṣah), because of His saying: "A single suck or two sucks do not prohibit," and a suck is a suckling. It is known that when a child sucks, he has nursed, and the milk reaches him by his suck. On this basis, the five can occur in one sitting, in one breath. Can a child suck five times in one breath? He can suck five times while the breast is in his mouth, but there is some ambiguity in this, because it is difficult to determine precisely.
  Some scholars said: the meaning of a suckling is the child's latching onto the breast. As long as the infant is latched onto the breast, it is one suckling, and if he releases it for any reason, the suckling is complete, whether he released it to breathe, or because of a sound that disturbed him, or because his mother was tired of the right side so she turned him to the left, or something similar. The point is that a suckling is latching onto the breast. As long as the child is latched onto the breast, it is a suckling, and if he releases it for any reason, the suckling is complete. On this basis, the five can be completed in one sitting. These are two views.
  The third view: a suckling is a "fa'lah" (a single instance), that which counts as a suckling, i.e., a feeding in nursing, just as you say "akla" (a single meal). As in the hadith: "Allah is pleased with the servant who eats a morsel and praises Him for it" [Muslim (2734/88), in full: "Allah is pleased with the servant who eats a morsel and praises Him for it, or drinks a draught and praises Him for it."]. Does one say "praise be to Allah" every time one eats a morsel, or at the end?
  At the end. So the suckling is exactly like the morsel. There must be a separation between one suckling and another of a duration that counts as separation, such as one in the morning, one in the evening, one at night, one at dawn, and similar. This is the choice of our Shaykh ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Saʿdi, may Allah have mercy on him, that a suckling is what is clearly separated from its counterpart so as to be a complete suckling. If we assume the hadith can bear the three meanings, which are: the suck, latching onto the breast, and a feeding from nursing, then the default is permissibility until clear evidence establishes that this nursing is prohibiting. On the basis of this default, is the third view preferable, or the first, or the second?
* Students: The third.

Sheikh: The third, which is the last. We say: the indication of the hadith for the first meaning is problematic and ambiguous, and for the second meaning there is also ambiguity, while for the third meaning the opinions agree that there is no ambiguity. In that case we take this one, because the original rule is what? Permissibility (al-hill), until prohibition is established with certainty, which lifts this original rule. So the verse: ﴿the mothers who have nursed you﴾ is general, restricted by what? By the Sunnah: five sucklings. Also in the verse there is another generality: ﴿the mothers who have nursed you﴾ apparently includes nursing in infancy and nursing in adulthood. Is this intended? We say: yes, it is intended according to some scholars, the Zahiriyyah hold it is intended, that the nursing of an adult is like the nursing of an infant. They take as evidence for their view the hadith of Salim, the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfah, who was adopted by Abu Hudhayfah among the sons he had adopted in the Jahiliyyah. It is known that if he was a son he would enter the house by night and by day, and in the furthest and nearest parts of the house, just like a child entirely. So when Allah abolished adoption, "the wife of Abu Hudhayfah came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: Salim used to enter upon us; meaning, it is difficult for us to guard ourselves from him. He said: «Suckle him, and you will become unlawful to him»" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5088) and Muslim (1453/28)]. Meaning: if you become unlawful to him, it is permissible for him to look at you and to be alone with you, though he is an adult. This hadith agrees with the apparent meaning of the verse, so it serves as evidence for the generality. Do you understand?

Some scholars said: nursing counts only if it is within the two years, because His saying ﴿your mothers who have nursed you﴾ means the nursing that is legally recognized, and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And mothers nurse their children for two complete years﴾ [al-Baqarah 233]. So what is within the two years is recognized nursing, and what is after the two years has no weight, because this is the period of nursing about which Allah the Exalted said: ﴿who have nursed you﴾. This is the well-known view of most scholars and the well-known position of Imam Ahmad: the criterion is what?
* Students: (...).
* Sheikh: The two years. What is before them is recognized nursing, and what is after them is not recognized. They said: this is a clear boundary that leaves no ambiguity. Accordingly, if she nursed him three times on Saturday, the fourth in the forenoon of Sunday, and the fifth after midday on Sunday, but his birth was at the zenith of the sun, meaning he completed two years at the zenith of the sun, is the nursing recognized or not?
Students: Not recognized, according to the view of the two years.
* Sheikh: Not recognized, because the fifth occurred after the two years, so it is not counted, even though the fourth had not yet been digested from the stomach; it is in his stomach, but the two years were completed. Just as a man before completing fifteen years is not an adult, and after it he is an adult; meaning, if a person does something for which adulthood is a condition in the forenoon of the day he reached it, he is not held accountable for it, and at the end of the day he is held accountable.

Some scholars said: the criterion is weaning. What is before weaning is recognized, and what is after it is not, based on the hadith: «There is no nursing except what makes the bone grow and what is before weaning». [Narrated by Abu Dawud (2060) without the final part; it is found complete in al-Tabarani's al-Kabir (8500) but with the wording: «It does not make you unlawful; only what makes the flesh grow and strengthens the bone makes unlawful through nursing, and there is no nursing after weaning».] And this, although there is some consideration... regarding its soundness, meaning it is weak, but reason supports it, because nursing before weaning affects the child's growth, and he has no other nourishment, whereas after weaning there is no difference between the young and the old in the effect of what? Nursing. Because when he is weaned and eats only food, there is no difference between him and someone of ten years; the effect of nourishment through milk on him is like its effect on one of ten years. This view, namely that the ruling is tied to weaning, is the choice of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, that the criterion is weaning. In terms of meaning, as you have heard, this is more sound, but there is some difficulty in it, because it is not always precisely determinable, since a child is not weaned all at once but gradually, due to the difficulty of weaning for him.

If someone said: taking into account the majority of weaning or the two years, this view would not be far-fetched. Meaning: if he is weaned before two years, the ruling extends to two years; if the two years are completed before his weaning, the ruling extends to his weaning. If this were said it would be good, but tying it to weaning is more sound in meaning, because once he is weaned he is not nourished by milk. And our saying "he is not nourished by milk" does not mean he gains no benefit from it. No; a person benefits from milk even at fifty years of age; if he were fifty he would benefit from milk, but he is not nourished by it, and it does not become his food once he is weaned.

If someone asks: what is the answer regarding the generality of the verse and the story of Salim?
We say: as for the generality of the verse, we have mentioned that it is restricted by the number of five sucklings, so it should also be restricted by a time period, namely the two years. Moreover, the apparent meaning of the verse also supports the condition of weaning, because He said: ﴿who have nursed you﴾. It is known that adults are not infants who have been weaned and finished, so its apparent meaning is that ﴿have nursed you﴾ refers to the time of nursing.

As for the story of Salim, the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfah, we respond to them in one of two ways; rather, in one of three ways: either it is abrogated, or it is specific to him individually, or it is specific to him as a type. Do you understand? Abrogated, or specific to him individually, or specific to him as a type. As for the claim that it is abrogated, this is nothing, because the original is non-abrogation, and it is necessary to establish the date and the impossibility of reconciliation. As for the claim that it is specific to him individually, it is also weak, because Allah the Mighty and Majestic cannot specify anyone with a ruling except for a meaning in him. Even the Prophet ﷺ was given what was specific to him among the rulings only because he was a prophet, not because he was Muhammad son of Abdullah; because he was a prophet. So there must be a cause by which the ruling changes and is restricted to those who possess it. What is the meaning by which Salim is specified, so that we can say the ruling does not extend beyond him and that it is peculiar to him? Because if we say the ruling does not extend beyond him and is peculiar to him, its meaning becomes that the ruling was decreed for him because he was Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfah, and this has no meaning. On this basis this view is also weakened, that it is specific to him individually. What remains is that it is specific to him as a type: that is, whenever a situation like Salim's occurs, the ruling is established. This is not possible now, why? Because the adoption of sons has been abolished, so it is not possible. Therefore, as long as we have established that no one is specified individually with a ruling of Allah's Sharia, there must be a meaning extending to its type, and this is not possible. However, Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, in some of his statements considered two things. The first statement agrees with what I said: that regard must be given to adoption. The second statement: he considers need, and that whenever there is need to nurse an adult, the adult is nursed and the ruling of nursing is established. But this statement is weak, like the view of the majority; the majority holds that nursing an adult does not count. His statement here is weak, why? Because the Prophet ﷺ said: «Beware of entering upon women». They said: O Messenger of Allah, what about the brother-in-law (al-hamw)? [What is al-hamw? The husband's brother, or his paternal uncle, or maternal uncle, or the like; a relative.] He said: «The hamw is death» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5232) and Muslim (2172/20)]. It is known that the husband's brother needs to enter his brother's house, especially when they are in one house. If nursing an adult had an effect, he would have said: the wife of his relative should nurse him to remove the hardship. Since he did not say that, it is known that general need does not affect establishing the ruling of nursing for an adult, and that there must be a specific need that fits every case that occurred in the story of Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfah. If we consider that, then what is now the case? It does not exist. By this the evidences are saved from contradiction and reconciled among themselves.

Also regarding ﴿your mothers who have nursed you﴾: is it necessary that there be direct suckling, such that if milk is poured into a vessel and the child drinks it, it has no effect, or not?
The answer: No, it is not a condition that he take the breast. Rather, if it is poured into a vessel and he drinks it, and this is given to him five times, the ruling is established, because the meaning exists in this just as it exists in taking the breast. This is regarding the child's nourishment with milk. But he loses the tenderness and affection; for when an infant takes the breast, he receives from the nursing mother's tenderness and love what he does not receive if her milk is poured into a vessel and the child is given to drink. So is this taken into account, that the Law considered prohibition through nursing because the nursing mother provides the same affection and tenderness as the biological mother, and for this reason this relationship became effective? Or is the purpose only the child's nourishment with milk?
This is, I think, a point of disagreement, but the apparent view is generality; that is, there is no difference between his suckling from the breast of the nursing mother or his being given it in a vessel and drinking, because the body is nourished by both. Is it clear? And Allah knows best.

* Student: (...) on some of the texts that were transmitted either from the Prophet ﷺ or from the early scholars (...) in the saying of the brother: "None goes beyond this except one who is destroyed or a polytheist." Meaning, "or a polytheist"?
* Sheikh: This "destroyed" (al-halik) covers the polytheist and the non-polytheist, but coordinating the more specific and severe with the lighter is something that is tolerated. As long as he did not attribute it to the Messenger ﷺ, there is no harm. But if he attributed it to the Messenger, we say: it must not be exceeded.
* Student: Sheikh, may Allah have mercy on you, regarding what the two brothers mentioned: Imam al-Suyuti, may Allah have mercy on him, says that inserting [additions] into the speech of the Prophet ﷺ is absolutely forbidden.
* Sheikh: He did not attribute it to the Messenger.
* Student: But the listener's mention of it may lead him to think that...
* Sheikh: But delete the word "may" here. He did not attribute it to the Messenger.

I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And your mothers who have nursed you﴾. We have taken benefits from it and discussed nursing, which suffices without repeating it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the milk of the stallion (lahn al-fahl) creates prohibition. What is meant by "the milk of the stallion creates prohibition"? It means that the sister through the father by nursing is forbidden, by the generality of His saying: ﴿and your sisters through nursing﴾. This, and Allah knows best, is a benefit of mentioning the sisters without the daughters through nursing; the daughters through nursing were not mentioned, nor the paternal aunts, but the sisters suffice in place of the aunts, because they are collateral relatives, and they are the closest collateral relatives to a person. Thus it is derived from this verse that sisters through the father, or sisters through the mother, or full sisters through nursing, are all forbidden.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the wife's mother is forbidden without condition, by His saying: ﴿and the mothers of your wives﴾. Thus by the mere valid contract with a woman, her mother becomes forbidden, and likewise her grandmothers, however high.

* Among its benefits: that the mother of a woman who has been fornicated with is not forbidden to the fornicator, contrary to what many scholars hold; by His saying: ﴿and the mothers of your wives﴾, and the one fornicated with is not one of his wives, and her case cannot be analogized to his wives, because his wives became lawful to him through a valid legal contract, whereas the one fornicated with did not become lawful to him. How can illicit intercourse be compared to valid marriage?!

* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: the invalidity of the view of those who say that sodomy with a male, may Allah protect us, is like the marriage contract, and that whoever commits sodomy with a male becomes forbidden to the mother of the one sodomized, like the mother of a wife. This is an abominable statement! How can this great immorality be placed on the level of valid marriage?! The mother of the one sodomized is lawful, not forbidden. But indeed the one committing sodomy and the fornicator are not permitted to marry any woman until they repent.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of the stepdaughter (rabibah). But how many conditions did Allah the Exalted stipulate for the prohibition of the stepdaughter?
* Student: It is mentioned in His saying: ﴿and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship﴾. The first condition is that she be in his guardianship.
* Sheikh: The first condition: that she be in his guardianship. The second condition: that he has gone in to her mother. But the noble verse shows that the condition of her being in the guardianship is not intended as a condition for the ruling, but to describe the actual situation, and not as a condition for the judgment, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿But if you have not gone in to them, there is no blame upon you﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of sons' wives (halail al-abna'), whether wives or slave women; by His saying: ﴿the wives of your sons﴾. But a slave woman does not become a wife except through intercourse. Therefore, if a man buys a slave woman and does not have intercourse with her, and then his father acquires her, she is lawful to his father. But if he contracts marriage with a woman and does not have intercourse with her and then divorces her, she is not lawful to his father, because a slave woman does not become a wife except through intercourse, whereas a wife becomes a wife by the mere valid contract.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the wife of a foster son is not forbidden, by His saying: ﴿who are of your loins﴾.
It has been mentioned earlier in the tafsir that scholars differed over whether this qualifier excludes an adopted son or a foster son. We mentioned that the correct view is that it excludes the foster son, whereas the adopted son is not a legitimate son, so he needs no qualifier to exclude him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of combining two sisters, by His saying: ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾. Its generality includes two sisters by lineage and two sisters by nursing, so it is not permissible for a person to combine two sisters by nursing or two sisters by lineage. Whether this includes ownership by right of the right hand (milk al-yamin) or is specific to the marriage contract, the early scholars differed. The correct view is that it includes both ownership by right of the right hand and the marriage contract: if a person has two slave-women who are sisters and he has intercourse with one of them, the other becomes forbidden to him until the one he has had intercourse with is removed from his ownership, by selling her for example, or by marrying her off after istibra' (the waiting period). As long as she remains with him and he has had intercourse with her, it is not lawful for him to have intercourse with the other. As for marriage, is it a condition for the prohibition of the sister that he has had intercourse with the one he has, or is the sister forbidden by the mere contract?
* Students: The sister becomes forbidden by the mere contract.
* Sheikh: The sister becomes forbidden by the mere contract. Therefore it is permissible to combine two sisters in ownership by right of the right hand through a sale contract or otherwise, but it is not permissible to combine them by a marriage contract. The difference is that ownership by right of the right hand is intended for intercourse and for other purposes, whereas marriage is for intercourse; so the ruling is established by the mere marriage contract, whereas for slave women it is by intercourse.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that sins committed before the Sharia are not held against a person, by His saying: ﴿except what has already passed﴾. Likewise, sins committed after the Sharia but before the agent knew of it are not held against him, by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord and desists, for him is what has passed, and his affair is up to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 275]. But it has been mentioned to us before that if he was negligent in not asking, and thereby abandoned an obligation because of this negligence, then he is obligated to make it up.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 23 (part 5 of 6):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the affirmation of two of Allah's names: al-Ghafur (the Most Forgiving) and al-Rahim (the Most Merciful). Through forgiveness the disliked is removed, and through mercy the desired is attained. Forgiveness is for sins, and mercy is for good deeds, through which Allah raises people in rank. From these two names we derive two attributes: forgiveness (maghfirah) and mercy (rahmah). This is because it is the way of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah (the People of the Sunnah and the Community) that every name of Allah indicates the Essence of Allah, His attribute, and the attribute derived from it. So al-Ghafur indicates the Essence and the attribute of forgiveness, and al-Rahim indicates the Essence and the attribute of mercy.

The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, divided mercy into two types: general (ʿamm) and specific (khass). The general mercy encompasses all creation, but it is a mercy that is not connected to the mercy of the Hereafter; rather, it is connected to the justice of the Hereafter. This general mercy is for both disbelievers and believers. The specific mercy is for the believers, and it is connected to mercy in the Hereafter through mercy in this world. Thus a person is shown mercy in both this world and the Hereafter.

As an example of the first type, consider Allah's words: ﴿And your Lord is the Most Forgiving, Possessor of mercy﴾ [Al-Kahf 58], meaning general mercy. And His words: ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [Al-Fatihah 3]. As an example of the second type, consider His words: ﴿And ever is He, toward the believers, Merciful﴾ [Al-Ahzab 43].

Then Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And [prohibited to you are] married women, except those your right hands possess﴾ [An-Nisa 24], meaning: "And prohibited to you are the married women, except those your right hands possess." The word ﴿al-muhsanat﴾ (married women/chaste women) is the passive participle of the quadriliteral verb (uhsina), because the passive participle is derived from a verb in the passive form. The root ihsan (chastity, protection, marriage) is used with several meanings. It is used for free women, for chaste women, and for married women, and all of this occurs in the Qur'an. Allah, the Exalted, says in the first sense: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women, then [he may marry] from what your right hands possess of believing maidens﴾ [An-Nisa 25]. The intended meaning of al-muhsanat here is free women.

As an example of the second sense, Allah says: ﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unaware, believing women are cursed in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [An-Nur 23]. Here ﴿al-muhsanat﴾ means women who are chaste, chaste from fornication.

As an example of the third sense, which is married women, this verse: ﴿And [prohibited to you are] married women, except those your right hands possess﴾.

If someone says: "How do we determine the specific intended meaning among these meanings of such homonymous words (mushtarak) that have several meanings?"

We say: We know it by context. If there is no context that specifies it, then the correct view is that it is permissible to use the homonymous term in all of its meanings, and it encompasses them all, just as a general term (lafz 'amm) encompasses all of its individual instances. Therefore, a word shared between two or more meanings is general for those meanings if no indicator specifies one of them. Pay attention to this benefit.

Just as a general term includes all its individuals, a homonymous term includes all its meanings. Now let us look at the three examples.

Example one: that the intended meaning of al-muhsanat is free women. What context specifies that? His words: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women, then [he may marry] from what your right hands possess of believing maidens﴾. The phrase ﴿from what your right hands possess﴾ indicates that the ﴿al-muhsanat﴾ are those who are not owned. Therefore they are free women.

The second: ﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unaware, believing women are cursed in this world and the Hereafter﴾. The context specifying it is His words: ﴿unaware, believing women﴾, meaning unaware of fornication, and it never occurred to them. So they are chaste women.

The third: married women. There is nothing in the wording of the noble verse that specifies the intended meaning, but the Sunnah has come with it. So what are the ﴿al-muhsanat﴾, and what is the meaning of His words: ﴿except those your right hands possess﴾? Does it mean that if a man has a married slave-woman, it is permissible for him to have intercourse with her? No. Rather, the matter concerns a specific case: a captive woman taken in battle against the disbelievers who was married. Then the Muslims took possession of her, and she becomes lawful to them because her first marriage is annulled by her capture. So the ﴿al-muhsanat﴾, meaning married women, who are taken captive, by what? By jihad. When they are taken captive through jihad, they become what? Property of the captor, and at that point they become lawful to him. Therefore ﴿al-muhsanat﴾ means married women, ﴿from among women﴾ means captive women, from among captive women. And this is in fighting against whom?

* Students: The disbelievers.
* Shaykh: The disbelievers. As for fighting against believers, there is no taking of women as captives, even if that fighting is prohibited, such as fighting the rebels (ahl al-baghy), for example. Their women are not taken captive. But the intended meaning is the women of the disbelievers. ﴿except those your right hands possess﴾, meaning they are lawful. But we must be mindful that what is lawful must not be among the prohibited persons, such as one's sister, paternal aunt, or the like.

﴿except those your right hands possess—the decree of Allah upon you﴾. Regarding ﴿kitab﴾ (decree), it has been said that it is an object of a verb that is omitted, meaning: "Adhere to the decree of Allah upon you," that is, "Adhere to the obligation of Allah upon you," because the word kitab here means "maktub" (prescribed), that is, obligatory. The root kateb can mean obligation, as in His words: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [Al-Baqarah 183]. "Adhere to the decree of Allah upon you," that is, "Adhere to the obligation of Allah upon you, do not transgress it." Allah emphasized this because of its importance. It is also possible that ﴿kitab Allah﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) of an omitted verb, meaning: "Allah has prescribed the decree of Allah upon you," so it is a verbal noun of an omitted verb indicated by the context. However, the first meaning seems clearer. ﴿The decree of Allah upon you﴾, meaning its obligation is imposed upon you.

﴿And lawful to you is what is beyond that﴾ [An-Nisa 24]. ﴿Uhilla﴾ (is made lawful) is in the passive. In one of the seven canonical readings, it is ﴿Ahalla﴾ (He has made lawful). The seven-reading ﴿Ahalla﴾ is more appropriate to the context of His words: ﴿the decree of Allah upon you﴾. The other seven-reading ﴿Uhilla﴾ is more appropriate to the context of His words: ﴿Prohibited to you are your mothers﴾, meaning ﴿hurrimat﴾ (was prohibited) in the passive. ﴿Uhilla﴾ is passive, so there is a correspondence between the two wordings that indicate these two rulings. In any case, in the reading with the passive voice, the agent is omitted because it is known. When creation or legislation is put in the passive, that is only because the agent is known, since there is no creator except Allah, and no lawgiver except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

And His words: ﴿lawful to you is what is beyond that﴾. ﴿Ma wara'a﴾ (what is beyond) here means "other than" or "besides," meaning: whatever is besides that is lawful. This is a general term, ﴿ma wara'a dhalikum﴾, because ﴿ma﴾ is a relative pronoun that indicates generality, so it includes everything besides that. Now we return to the verse and see what results. Is the paternal aunt through nursing lawful?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Was she mentioned?
* Student: No, the paternal aunt through nursing was not mentioned.
* Shaykh: Your sisters through nursing? We say: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: «Whatever is forbidden by blood ties is forbidden by suckling» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3370) and Muslim (1447/12)]. So this ruling is one that the Sunnah added to, and what comes from the Messenger of Allah is like what comes from Allah. "Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah, and whoever disobeys the Messenger has disobeyed Allah." So the prohibition of the paternal aunt through nursing and the maternal aunt through nursing is derived from where?
* Students: From the Sunnah.
* Shaykh: From the Sunnah. Therefore ﴿lawful to you is what is beyond that﴾ has been qualified by specification. What is it?
* Students: The paternal aunt through nursing, and the maternal aunt.
* Shaykh: The paternal aunt through nursing and the maternal aunt through nursing, and ﴿and to join two sisters in marriage﴾. Now, if a man combines a woman and her paternal aunt, what then?
* Students: It is not permissible.
* Shaykh: It is not permissible? No. Allah said: ﴿two sisters in marriage﴾, and there is no doubt that between two sisters there are bonds that do not exist between others.
* Students: The Sunnah.
* Shaykh: We say: the Sunnah has come with it: «A woman may not be married together with her paternal aunt, nor with her maternal aunt» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5109) and Muslim (1408/33)]. So now we have four: the paternal aunt through nursing, the maternal aunt through nursing, combining a woman with her paternal aunt, and combining a woman with her maternal aunt. All of this has come in the Sunnah, so it specifies the generality of His words: ﴿And lawful to you is what is beyond that﴾. Here we ask about the prohibition of joining two sisters: until when does it end?
* Student: When there is a divorce.
* Shaykh: Until she dies?
* Student: Or a divorce... or she is divorced.
* Shaykh: Or she is divorced.
* Student: Or the contract is annulled.
* Shaykh: Alright. If she is divorced, is there a detail or not? We say: If she is divorced with a revocable divorce (talaq raj'i), it is obligatory to wait until the waiting period ('iddah) ends. That is, if a man divorces his wife who has a sister with a revocable divorce, and you have known revocable divorce before, then it is obligatory to wait until the waiting period ends, by consensus. If the separation is irrevocable (ba'in), indeed, if the separation is irrevocable through a triple divorce, or a divorce for compensation, or annulment, is it obligatory to wait until the waiting period ends, or may he marry her sister?

The well-known view in the school of the Hanbalis is that it is obligatory to wait until the waiting period ends, because she is still bound by a right of the husband, so waiting is obligatory. Some scholars said: If the separation is irrevocable by annulment, or divorce for compensation, or triple divorce, then it is valid for him to marry her sister, because she is no longer a wife, and Allah said: ﴿to join two sisters in marriage﴾ [An-Nisa 23], and now there is no joining, since she has separated from him.

If someone said that there should be a distinction between the major irrevocability (al-baynunah al-kubra) and the minor irrevocability (al-baynunah al-sughra), there would be a basis for it: it may be said that if the irrevocable separation is by triple divorce or by a separation through li'an (mutual oath-cursing), then it is permissible for him to marry her sister immediately upon the separation, because he cannot return to her. But if the irrevocability is by other means, such as divorce for compensation or annulment, then he may not marry her sister, because in this case he can still take her back by a new contract.

If someone held this view, it would have some merit, and it would be somewhat like the view of the one who says it is permissible absolutely. But permissibility absolutely is closer to the principles: that is, if the divorce is irrevocable, whether or not it is possible to return to her, she becomes lawful, and it is permissible for him to marry her sister, because he has not combined two sisters.
