Now, if he combines two women who are paternal aunts, what if one is the paternal aunt of the other's niece? Two women who are paternal aunts?

* Student: Sisters.
* Shaykh: One may not combine a woman with her paternal aunt.
* Students: Two paternal aunts are sisters.
* Shaykh: How? Two paternal aunts are sisters?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: How are two paternal aunts sisters?
* Student: It may be.
* Shaykh: It does not work. If (...) sisters (...) sisters, sisters in Islam, that is?
The question now: is it permissible to combine two paternal aunts?
* Student: It is not permissible.
* Shaykh: Because if it is forbidden to combine a woman with her paternal aunt, then combining two paternal aunts is even more so. Is it permissible to combine two maternal aunts?
* Student: It may be, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: I am saying: Is it permissible to combine them in marriage, to marry two maternal aunts, each one being a maternal aunt to the other?
* Student: Each one a maternal aunt to the other?
* Shaykh: This is our discussion. Essentially, one does not marry his paternal aunt, even individually, so that he combines two paternal aunts, meaning each one is a paternal aunt to the other. Is that permissible or not? Give me the ruling.
* Students: It is not permissible.
* Shaykh: Is it permissible to combine two maternal aunts?
* Students: It is not permissible.
* Shaykh: It is not permissible? (...) It is not difficult, it is very easy. I thought you would picture it. Two women who are paternal aunts: each one is a paternal aunt to the other. Two women who are maternal aunts: each one is a maternal aunt to the other?
* Students: It is not permissible.
* Shaykh: It is not permissible?
* Students: It is not permissible.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Alright, what are they?
* Student: Her paternal aunt from her mother's side, and her paternal aunt from her father's side.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, by lineage.
Leave them as a riddle for you until next week, God willing, on the condition that you do not review anything from the books of tafsir (...). Picture them. It is very easy, (...) easier than that.
* Student: (...) invalid marriage.
* Shaykh: No, a valid marriage, a valid marriage from the outset, all of them valid marriages.
The main point, in any case, is to leave it as a riddle: how can it be imagined that there are two women, each of whom is a paternal aunt to the other, or each of whom is a maternal aunt to the other?
In any case, combining them is forbidden.
* Student: The evidence?
* Shaykh: His words: ﴿and to join two sisters in marriage﴾, and: «A woman may not be married together with her paternal aunt» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5109) and Muslim (1408/33), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. If it is not permissible to combine a woman with her niece, then likewise combining a woman with her aunt, meaning each one is an aunt to the other, there is no difficulty in this. The ruling has no difficulty, but the picturing of it is what a person may find unlikely. Yet it is closer than the strap of one's sandal.
* Student: A question, Shaykh: a man and his son marry a mother and her daughter.
* Shaykh: No, that is another matter.
If two men each marry the mother of the other, then their two daughters become paternal aunts to each other, and if each marries the daughter of the other, then they become maternal aunts to each other.
* Student: May Allah be good to you. If a man's sister through nursing is a Christian (kitabiyyah), is she lawful?
* Shaykh: His sister through nursing is not lawful, whether she is a Christian or a Muslim, it is all the same. These rulings are established. A person's mother is forbidden to him even if she is a Christian. Even if she is a disbeliever, a polytheist, she is forbidden to him.
* Student: We said that the ﴿muhsanat﴾, the married women, except the captives. Then the ruling on captives came down as though they were the ﴿muhsanat﴾, to the point that I stopped writing.
* Shaykh: Yes, they are the ﴿muhsanat﴾, but when they are taken captive, they become owned. That is, a married woman...
* Student: So the ﴿muhsanat﴾, are they not the married free women? Or does it include both?
Shaykh: No, this and that do not matter. But even free women among the disbelievers, if we take them captive, they become our property. So the meaning is: if a woman was married among the disbelievers, her husband a disbeliever, and she was taken captive and the Muslims took possession of her, then she is lawful.
* Student: A man married a woman but did not consummate the marriage, and he had children. This woman was nursing, and she nursed a boy. Are this man's children lawful to the woman's son?
* Shaykh: That is, would he be a brother to his children from another wife? Alright, whose milk is it?
* Student: The first husband's.
* Shaykh: So he is not part of the household.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but the milk is not his, the milk belongs to the first husband.
* Student: May Allah be good to you. If in His words ﴿except those your right hands possess﴾ the exception means not (...), then what is the benefit of His words: ﴿And lawful to you is what is beyond that﴾?
* Shaykh: Who said this?
* Student: (...) the ﴿muhsanat﴾ when they are taken captive (...). What is the benefit of His words: ﴿And lawful to you is what is beyond that﴾?
* Shaykh: That is, all that preceded it. Who says the matter is only specific? ﴿lawful to you is what is beyond that﴾, meaning other than all those mentioned from His words: ﴿Prohibited to you are your mothers﴾ to the end.
* Student: Does it not refer back to the exception in His words: ﴿except what your right hands possess﴾?
* Shaykh: It does not refer back to the exception in His words: ﴿except what your right hands possess﴾; it refers back to what preceded, because what your right hands possess is lawful.
* Student: What is the criterion for prohibition through nursing?
* Shaykh: The criterion: «Whatever is forbidden by blood ties is forbidden by suckling» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2645) and Muslim (1447/12), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas].
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The prohibited persons by blood are likewise. That is, the rules the jurists mentioned say: it is forbidden for a person by nursing: his ancestors however high they go, and his descendants however low they go, and likewise the descendants of the nearest ancestor however low they go, and the descendants of the higher ancestor only, specifically the descendants of their loins. The same thing: whatever is forbidden by lineage is forbidden by nursing.
* Student: For the nursling?

* Shaykh: As for the suckling child and his descendants, yes. But as for his ascendants and collateral relatives, they have no bearing on the matter. This is a point that should be noticed: fosterage has no connection to the kinship of the suckling child except his offspring only, his descendants. For this reason, his blood brother may marry the one whom his mother nursed (in fosterage), and he may marry his foster sister, and his blood brother may [also] do so, because fosterage has no connection to anyone other than the suckling child except his descendants alone.

* Student: And ﴿مَا وَرَاءَ ذَلِكُمْ﴾ means what is other than that (...), and the intended meaning is not the verse (...) ﴿وَلَا تَنْكِحُوا مَا نَكَحَ آبَاؤُكُمْ﴾?

* Shaykh: It is included in this; that is, "Lawful for you is whatever is other than what We have forbidden to you."

* Student: (...) ﴿أَخَوَاتُكُمْ مِنَ الرَّضَاعَةِ﴾ (...).

* Shaykh: We mentioned the benefit a little while ago. The benefit is to make clear that the milk of the stallion (the father) is also forbidding, that is, lest someone say: the forbidden relations come only through the mother, as some scholars have said. For example, your half-sister on the father's side, whose mother you did not nurse: your half-sister from fosterage, that is, for example, she came from another wife other than the one you were nursed by. Someone might say, as if he had said: "your mothers through fosterage" (only), that there is no effect in fosterage except for the mother and those who branch from her. So when He said "your sisters through fosterage," there is a benefit: that a paternal half-sister through fosterage is forbidden.

* Student: (...) "What is forbidden through fosterage is what is forbidden through lineage."

* Shaykh: Yes, correct. This is the evidence for its lawfulness... The wife of your son, is she forbidden to you through lineage or not?

* Student: Forbidden to me.

* Shaykh: From where?

* Student: From lineage (...).

* Shaykh: No, there is no lineage between you and her. She is forbidden through affinity (ṣihr): the wife of your son. A man has a son, and the son has a wife; the son's wife is forbidden to him. What is the relationship between him and her?

* Student: Affinity.

* Shaykh: Or lineage?

* Student: Between me and her is affinity.

* Shaykh: Affinity. And the hadith: "What is forbidden through fosterage..."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2645) and Muslim (1447/12) from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas.]]

* Students: "...what is forbidden through lineage."

* Shaykh: For this reason, glory be to God the Mighty, some scholars have claimed consensus that the wife of a son through fosterage is like the wife of a son through lineage, and they all cite this hadith as evidence. Yet this hadith, if you reflect upon it, is a proof against them, because there is no lineage between a person and his son's wife, nor between him and his father's wife.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, I am saying: the matter is that saying "it is permissible for you to marry her" or "you may not marry her."

* Student: And likewise she is veiled from him?

* Shaykh: She is veiled according to the view of the majority. The majority hold that she is not veiled from him, while Shaykh al-Islam holds that she is veiled from him. The majority hold that she is not lawful to him, while Shaykh al-Islam holds that she is lawful to him. We now say: we take up both opinions on the basis of caution, or rather, on what is cautious now.

But if someone asked us, saying: "So may I marry the wife of my father through fosterage if he divorces her?"

We say: Yes, if no one remains in the world except her, marrying her is not prohibited. But as long as there are many women other than her, and your marrying someone else avoids the disagreement of the majority of scholars, that is better and more cautious. The matter is not trivial.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, and this gives a sense of hesitation; this gives the sense that he was hesitant.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, and its prohibition. This gives a sense of hesitation, but in reality there is no basis for hesitation, because we say: His saying ﴿وَأَنْ تَجْمَعُوا بَيْنَ الْأُخْتَيْنِ﴾ ("and that you combine two sisters") if one owns two sisters, it enters the verse; just as ﴿حُرِّمَتْ عَلَيْكُمْ أُمَّهَاتُكُمْ﴾ ("your mothers are forbidden to you") includes a slave-woman owned. He, may God be pleased with him, hesitated, but the matter is clear. Indeed, "some people said to Ibn Masʿud" regarding ﴿إِلَّا مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُكُمْ﴾ ("except what your right hands possess"), he said: "Fine, and your camel, of what your right hand possesses, would you marry it?"[[Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Kabir (9667) from the hadith of Ibn Masʿud with the wording: "your camel of what your right hand possesses."]]

* Student: And Ibn Taymiyyah (...) this view?

* Shaykh: By God, I do not know that it is correct. But he, may God have mercy on him, must have had a predecessor, because if he had not found a predecessor, he would have restricted it. When he said regarding a woman divorced three times that she must wait one menstrual cycle, he said: this is what the text requires, unless there is a consensus to the contrary. Here he made no exception.

* Student: (...) one of the brothers said: "How can you say this, since this would mean that (...) remains written (...)."

* Shaykh: No, it is not written. Where is it written? Let him establish for me one single hadith from the Companions that they said: the wife of a son through fosterage is like the wife of a son through lineage. He cannot establish it.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Who among our predecessors said this? Were they not the Companions? Let him establish this. Perhaps the Companions understood it as Shaykh al-Islam understood it and proceeded upon it without concern; then those after them came and the matter became as it is.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: But who says that it has not become clear now?

* Student: Meaning the general body of scholars (...) "Guide us to the straight path." You find the general body of scholars (...) the reality of causes and what God commanded, then clarified.

* Shaykh: No, he does not say so; he does not say that. Shaykh al-Islam's custom was not to speak these words about opponents.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Meaning he says these words with the opponent.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: In any case, we demand from you the soundness of the transmission, may God bless you. But in any case, this matter cannot be (...) from the Rightly Guided Caliphs, or from the jurists among the Companions, that they said the wife of a son through fosterage or the father through fosterage is like his wife through lineage, and then?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, check. What people say is only that the truth is not established except by the hand of Shaykh al-Islam. We say: Fine, it is no problem. Like someone who says, for example, "He settled upon the Throne": bring us one authentic word from the Companions that means "He rose above the Throne." Is this needed? It is not needed. What is understood does not require that we know it was acted upon or said; it proceeds on the original principle. And if you reflect on the Qur'an: ﴿حَلَائِلُ أَبْنَائِكُمُ الَّذِينَ مِنْ أَصْلَابِكُمْ﴾ [an-Nisa' 23], and "What is forbidden through fosterage is what is forbidden through lineage"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2645) and Muslim (1447/12) from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas.]], then the relationship between filial lineage and paternal lineage in reverence and respect toward their women is not like the relationship through fosterage.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes indeed, personally I have had a fosterage relation.

* Student: (...).

* * *

* Shaykh: In any case, if you advise them: the best and noblest thing we study, by God, is the science of tafsir. It is the capital and everything. In it, if we wished, are all the disciplines: if you wish, we parse grammatically; if you wish, we bring rhetorical points; if we wish, we bring the usul and jurisprudence. But we will not lengthen. We now, perhaps, study for two years and have not reached the women, beginning with tafsir. Yes, two years or more. In any case, we did not wish to lengthen repeatedly. But I wish you would advise your brothers: be eager for tafsir, because it is the foundation. "The Companions would not go beyond ten verses until they had learned what is in them of knowledge and action"[[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (23482) from some of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ.]]. God is the One sought for help. We have lengthened. For example, the matters that need lengthening, we lengthened in them, and the matters whose like recurs, [we passed over]; because the Qur'an, as you know, has verses whose like recurs, so a person need not dwell on them much.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Praise be to God; our answer is sufficient in the reply of the brothers.

Student: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And [prohibited to you are] married women, except those your right hands possess. [This is] the decree of Allah upon you. And lawful to you are [all] those beyond that, provided you seek [them] with your properties, desiring chastity, not unlawful intercourse. So for whatever you have enjoyed from them, give them their compensation as an obligation. And there is no blame upon you for what you mutually agree to beyond the obligation. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ [An-Nisa 24].

Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And married women, except those your right hands possess﴾. The waw is a conjunction particle, so where is the element being conjoined?

Student: The element being conjoined is ﴿the women﴾ (al-nisa').

Shaykh: Meaning which women?

Student: ﴿And married women of the women﴾.

Shaykh: ﴿And married women, except those your right hands possess﴾.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: How is it conjoined? Conjoined to what?

Student: The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Prohibited to you are your mothers﴾ [An-Nisa 23] is conjoined to the forbidden women.

Shaykh: It is conjoined to ("mothers"), meaning: and [also] forbidden are the married women among the women. Good. Now, what is meant by "al-muhsanat" (married women) here in the verse?

Student: Married slave women.

Shaykh: Married slave women?

Student: Married women taken captive.

Shaykh: Married women taken captive, [those] captured from among the married women. What is obligatory when a woman is taken captive and is owned by one of the soldiers who owns her?

Student: She must undergo istibra' (a period of waiting to ensure she is not pregnant) by one menstrual cycle.

Shaykh: That he must not have intercourse with her until he has done istibra' by one menstrual cycle, meaning until she menstruates; except if she is pregnant, then until she gives birth. Well done.

A man combined two sisters through nursing. Is that permissible?

Student: It is not permissible.

Shaykh: It is not permissible. The evidence?

Student: The evidence is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And that you combine two sisters﴾.

Shaykh: "Between the two sisters." If someone claimed that what is meant is two sisters by lineage?

Student: And likewise the hadith of the Prophet ﷺ: "What is forbidden by lineage is forbidden by nursing" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2645) and Muslim (1447/12) from Ibn 'Abbas].

Shaykh: Yes. If combining two sisters by lineage is forbidden, then combining two sisters by nursing is forbidden.

The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Kitaba Allah 'alaykum﴾ is in the accusative. What governs it, and what is the meaning?

Student: "Hold fast to the Book of Allah upon you."

Shaykh: "Hold fast to the Book of Allah upon you." Kitab carries the meaning of... is the meaning of the verse this?

Student: "Hold fast to what Allah has obligated upon you."

Shaykh: "What Allah has decreed upon you." And kitab here means the maktub (that which is written), i.e., what?

Student: The obligated.

Shaykh: I.e., the obligated?

Student: I.e., the prescribed.

Shaykh: I.e., the prescribed. What is your evidence that kataba comes with the meaning of "prescribe"?

Student: The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Prescribed for you is retaliation for the murdered, the free for the free﴾ [Al-Baqarah 178].

Shaykh: No, is that "prescribed"?

Student: ﴿O you who have believed, fasting is prescribed for you﴾ [Al-Baqarah 183], i.e., obligated.

Shaykh: I.e., obligated. ﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at specified times﴾ [An-Nisa 103].

Then the Exalted said, at the beginning of tonight's lesson: ﴿And lawful to you are [all] those beyond that﴾. Regarding ﴿uhilla﴾ there are two authentic seven canonical readings: the first is ﴿ahalla﴾, and the second is ﴿uhilla﴾. Each has a rationale. As for the reading in the passive form, it is for the sake of its harmony with His saying ﴿Prohibited to you are your mothers﴾ [An-Nisa 23]; and as for the active form ﴿wa-ahalla lakum﴾, it is for the harmony with His saying ﴿the Book of Allah upon you﴾. So each of the two readings has a rationale.

﴿And lawful to you﴾: (ahalla) means permitted, and no sin will attach to you. ﴿Beyond that﴾ means beyond these mentioned [prohibitions]; the demonstrative refers to what preceded.

As for His saying ﴿dhalikum﴾, this is the eloquent (standard) dialect: when the demonstrative is accompanied by the second-person kaf, it must agree with the addressee. If it is singular masculine, it is "dhalika" with fatha; if singular feminine, "dhalika" with kasra; if dual, it takes the dual form, as in ﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me﴾ [Yusuf 37]; if it is for a group of males, it is "dhalikum"; if for a group of females, it is "dhalikunna," as in ﴿She said, "That is the one you blamed me for"﴾ [Yusuf 32].

Here, ﴿beyond that [dhalikum]﴾: the address is to whom? To a group of males. This is the eloquent dialect. There is another dialect, with singular form and fatha for the masculine in all cases (singular, dual or plural), and kasra for the feminine in all cases; and there is a third dialect with fatha in all cases. The rationale for the last is that the addressee is a person, so it is correct to use the singular and masculine form. As for the second, its rationale is to observe the meaning rather than the addressee: the masculine takes fatha and the feminine takes kasra. As for the eloquent dialect, the matter there is clear.

He said: ﴿And lawful to you is what is beyond that, that you seek [them] with your properties﴾. ("An") here is a verbal-source particle (masdariyya), and for this the verb after it is put in the subjunctive, ﴿an tabtaghu﴾, so the nun is dropped. The meaning: it is made lawful on this condition, namely that you seek [them] with your properties, i.e., that you seek marriage with your wealth. Mal (wealth) is everything that is valued, whether tangible goods or benefits; everything that is valued, whether tangible goods or benefits, is wealth.

﴿That you seek with your properties, [being] chaste, not unlawful﴾: ﴿muhsinin﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of ﴿tabtaghu﴾, meaning while you are chaste, i.e., preserving your private parts, preserving the private parts of your wives. Ihsan in the linguistic sense means prevention, and from it comes the word hisn (fortress) for an impregnable castle, because it protects what is within it. Lawful marriage is a means of preventing fornication. The Prophet ﷺ said: "O assembly of youth, whoever among you is able to marry, let him marry, for it lowers the gaze and better guards the private parts" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1905) and Muslim (1400/1) from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud].

As for His saying ﴿not unlawful﴾: musafaha is from safh, which is fornication. Fornication was called safh because its intent is the pouring out of water, i.e., attaining desire. The fornicator does not want children or companionship; he wants to pour out this water that has constricted upon him until his desire cools. Safh originally means pouring and expelling. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Except that it be carrion or flowing blood﴾ [Al-An'am 145].

﴿Not unlawful﴾. Then He said: ﴿So for whatever you have enjoyed from them, give them their compensation as an obligation﴾: meaning whatever enjoyment you have had, through the contract. ﴿From them, give them their compensation﴾: i.e., give them their ujur. Ujur here is the plural of ajr, which is the dower, i.e., the wealth by which you sought them. ﴿That you seek with your properties﴾: meaning, when you seek with your wealth and contract the marriage, then give them their compensation. The dower is called ajr because it is in exchange for a benefit; it is like a man who hires a worker to build him a house and gives him his wage. Likewise the husband with his wife. The subtle point regarding His saying ﴿ujurahunna﴾ will come, God willing, when we mention the benefits.

﴿So give them their compensation as an obligation﴾: i.e., while they—the compensations—are obligatory (mafrudha), meaning what you have made obligatory, so give them the dowers. ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you mutually agree to beyond the obligation﴾: meaning there is no sin upon you for what you mutually agree upon beyond the obligation, by an increase or a decrease. That is, if the dower has been specified and fixed and the wife knows her share, there is no blame on him or on her for what they mutually agree upon beyond the obligation, by increase or decrease. A woman may forgo part of what was fixed for her, or all of it, and she may ask for an increase and the husband may give it. All of this is not objectionable, since He said: ﴿for what you mutually agree upon beyond the obligation. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ As you can see, this sentence is emphasized with ("inna") and ("kana"), because ("kana") here is stripped of time and so conveys establishment and certainty. The knowledge is the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, which is vast and complete, not preceded by ignorance and not subject to forgetfulness; nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Him, neither in the present, nor the past, nor the future.

﴿Hakiman﴾: i.e., possessing wisdom. Hikma is placing a thing in its proper place, whether it relates to decree or to legislation, for Allah's decrees and His legislations are all wisdom. But the meaning of (hakim) is broader than what I have just mentioned; that is, broader than merely indicating wisdom. Rather it indicates wisdom and what?

Students: And ihkam (perfection).

Shaykh: Ihkam, from hikma and hukm: it indicates wisdom and judgment. So the meaning of (hakim) is: a judge who is perfected, i.e., a judge from judgment, one made firm from ihkam, which is wisdom.

Furthermore, the judgment of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is divided into two kinds: cosmic (kawni) and legislative (shar'i). Moreover, wisdom and perfection are wisdom in the form of a thing and wisdom in the ultimate purpose of a thing; all of this is established by His saying ﴿Hakiman﴾. On this basis there are four categories: cosmic judgment, legislative judgment, perfection in the form of a thing, and perfection in the ultimate purpose of a thing.

The reason the verse is concluded with this is that these are great rulings.

(...)

These two noble names indicate that these rulings proceed from complete knowledge of what benefits creation and from complete perfection (...).

Now let us return to the benefits of this noble verse: ﴿And married women, except those your right hands possess﴾, and so on to its end.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: captured women become slaves merely by capture, and this is so; the Muslims' practice follows this. If she was captured together with her husband, she remains with him, but without him she becomes a slave.

* Also among its benefits: the husband's marriage is annulled, her marriage to her husband is dissolved, because the Muslims have taken possession of her.

* If someone says: Can this be analogized to the case where her ownership is transferred while she is with a husband, so that she is divorced by this transfer?

The answer: On this the scholars have two opinions:
The first: the sale of a slave woman is her divorce.
The second: No, she is not divorced; she remains in her marriage, and the buyer, if he did not know she was married, has the option. Why does he have the option? Because he loses the enjoyment of her. The evidence for this correct view is that when Barirah was freed, the Prophet ﷺ gave her the choice to remain with her husband or to annul the marriage [Muslim (2234) from 'A'isha]. Had the sale been a cause of divorce or annulment, the marriage would have been annulled without any option. Therefore the sale of a slave woman cannot be analogized to her capture, even though her ownership has been transferred.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment of slavery, as in His saying ﴿except those your right hands possess﴾. This is a matter on which the Muslims agree, namely the existence of slavery, and no one can deny it, since it is in the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the Muslims. But the question remains regarding the cause of slavery: can a person be enslaved for any cause, or is a legitimate cause required?

The answer: the second. On this basis, many of the slaves who existed were not truly enslaved, because they were sold—that is, their family sold them for need or for no need—and the buyer purchased them and enslaved them. This is not a legitimate cause of slavery. But when a legitimate cause is established, the effect is established and slavery is established, and it is not permissible to abolish it, since it is a legislated ruling, so it is not permissible to abolish it under any circumstances.

But if someone says: these existing slaves, by what were they enslaved? Then we abolish slavery here because its cause is invalid. However, one must not express it as "abolishing slavery" in that way, since that contradicts the text and the consensus. Rather it should be said: the slavery existing now is not on a legitimate cause, so it may not be relied upon; this is how it should be stated, to clarify the wisdom or to clarify the cause, so that the legislated ruling—namely enslavement—remains.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of applying a part to the whole, from where? ﴿Aymanukum﴾; because (aymān) is the plural of (yamin), which is the hand, whereas ownership in reality belongs to the whole person. But it was expressed by the right hand because, usually, taking and giving are done with it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to adhere to what Allah has imposed upon us; from His saying ﴿the Book of Allah upon you﴾.

The Book of Allah, glorified and exalted, is divided into two kinds: a legislative book, as in this verse and in His saying ﴿Fasting is prescribed for you﴾, and a cosmic book, as in His saying ﴿And We have enumerated everything in a Book﴾ [An-Naba' 29], i.e., the book of decree; and as in His saying: ﴿And We had already written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 105].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the lawful women are more numerous than the forbidden. The lawful women are more than the forbidden ones. Its basis? Yes, it is derived from His saying ﴿And lawful to you is what is beyond that﴾, but the reason for this restriction is that He restricted the forbidden and generalized the lawful.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that whoever claims a woman is forbidden must provide evidence. That is, if a man proposes to a woman and some people say to him, "This woman is forbidden to you, one of the prohibited women," the answer is that he must establish proof for that, because the forbidden women are enumerated, whereas for the lawful women the matter is general.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that if we doubt the cause of prohibition, the default is non-prohibition, i.e., the default is permissibility. An example of this: if we doubt whether this infant suckled five times or four times, the default is four. So if this woman had nursed from a man's mother and we doubt whether she nursed five times or four, the default is permissibility, and she is not forbidden to him until the cause of prohibition is established.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah's mercy is broader than His wrath and precedes it. As for its precedence, there is the authentic hadith: "Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7422) and Muslim (3194) from Abu Hurayra]; and as for its breadth, it is because what Allah has made lawful to His servants is more than what He has forbidden them.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to expend wealth in marriage, and that there is no marriage without wealth; from His saying ﴿that you seek with your properties﴾.

On this basis, marriage necessarily involves wealth, and there are three situations:

* The first situation: he stipulates a specific amount, saying, "The dower is one thousand riyals." Is this permissible or not? It is permissible; there is no problem with it.

* The second situation: he stipulates its absence, saying, "I marry you my daughter," and the husband accepts, saying, "On condition there is no dower," and she is married to him on condition of no dower. On this the scholars have two opinions:
* The first opinion: the marriage is valid and she has the customary dower (mahr al-mithl). This is the school's position.
* The second opinion: the marriage is not valid. This is the choice of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya, who says: because Allah made the lawfulness conditional upon wealth, and if its absence is stipulated, the conditioned thing is negated, which is the lawfulness. His view is strong; the view of Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, is strong. Perhaps the basis of shighar marriage (exchange marriage without dower) is from here, that there is no wealth in it, and if wealth is mentioned in it, it is mentioned but not intended.

* The third situation: he remains silent about it, neither stipulating a specific amount nor stipulating its absence, saying, "I marry you my daughter," and he says, "I accept." In this situation the marriage is valid and she has the customary dower, as came in the Qur'an and the Sunnah: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women before you have touched them or specified for them an obligation; but provide for them﴾ [Al-Baqarah 236]. This is if she is divorced before consummation. If she is divorced after consummation, she has the customary dower, as is authentically established in the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him [Abu Dawud (2114) and al-Tirmidhi (1145) from Ibn Mas'ud].

* One of the benefits of this verse: the seeker of marriage is the husband, ﴿that you seek [wives]﴾. Can a wife seek a husband? We say: it is possible for a woman to propose herself to a man.
* A student: That is rare.
* The Shaykh: Rare? Yes, in any case it is rare in relation to the second case, but it does happen. A woman gave herself to the Prophet (ﷺ) [[Narrated by al-Bukhari (5029) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd.]], and 'Umar offered his daughter Hafsah to Abu Bakr and 'Uthman [[Narrated by al-Bukhari (5122) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar.]]. There is nothing wrong with it, but the usual case is that the seeker is the husband.
* Another benefit of the noble verse: if the dowry (mahr) is usurped, it is not counted. From where is this taken?
* Students: ﴿with your wealth﴾.
* The Shaykh: From His saying ﴿with your wealth﴾. It is wealth, but it is not his, and Allah attributed the wealth to him.
* Another benefit of the verse: what our brother pointed to, that if the dowry is wine, it is not valid. Why? Because it is not wealth.
* Another benefit of the noble verse: it is permissible to make a benefit (manfa'ah) the dowry. From where is this taken?
* A student: From (wealth, māl).
* The Shaykh: Perhaps we take it from (māl), if we consider māl to be the physical item and the benefit, or from ujūr (wages), if we say māl is the physical item. We say: Allah called them ujūr, and wages are paid for benefits and for physical items. In any case, the dowry may be a benefit. If the benefit returns to the wife, the matter is clear. If it returns to someone else with her permission, there is nothing wrong with it, as in the story of Musa with the man of Madyan, because the dowry was that he would pasture his sheep for eight years. So the benefit belongs to whom? To her father, but with her consent. If she consents, the right is hers; otherwise the dowry belongs to the woman.
Is it valid for the husband to make his service to her the dowry, such as, for example, he washes her clothes, spreads her bedding, and lays out the prayer mat for her to pray on (...)? Is it valid or not? It is valid, as the brother said, since it is a benefit. But some scholars said it is not valid, because this would make the husband a slave. The opposite is correct, for the Messenger (ﷺ) said: «Women are captives (ʿawān) with you» [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (1163) and Ibn Majah (1851) from the hadith of 'Amr ibn al-Ahwas.]], meaning like prisoners with us. So how can she serve her husband? She says: "Come on, boy, bring (...)!" That is a problem.
In any case, if the benefit is the husband's service to the wife, there is a difference of opinion among the scholars, since her making him serve her is a kind of humiliation and the opposite of what the Sharia intends, namely that men are the guardians (qawwamun) over women.
* A student: And what is the correct view?
* The Shaykh: By Allah, the correct view is that if there is a need, there is nothing wrong with it. That is, if a man cannot find a woman to marry except on this condition. But if she makes the dowry the grazing of her sheep or the upkeep of her garden, which is not direct service, then there is no doubt about its permissibility.
* Another benefit of this noble verse: the prohibition of mut'ah (temporary marriage), from His saying ﴿chaste, not fornicating﴾.
The one who seeks mut'ah does not want chastity; he wants fornication (sifah), because whoever wants chastity, chastity is not attained except through continuity. As for staying with her for two or three days or a week, this does not increase chastity; rather it only increases the matter in intensity, because a person who restrains himself and makes himself despair may be somewhat protected, but if he enjoys her for two or three days he becomes more inflamed, and chastity is not attained. Allah, glory be to Him, made chastity a condition. Mut'ah marriage is only for fornication, to pour out this water that was constrained. For this reason no rulings of marriage are established by it: there is no divorce, no lineage, no waiting period ('iddah), and no chastity. None of the rulings of marriage apply to it, even according to those who permit it. This indicates that it is fornication, as the Sunnah shows. In the hadith of Sabrah ibn Ma'bad al-Juhani, that the Messenger (ﷺ), at the Farewell Pilgrimage or at the Conquest, declared that mut'ah is forbidden until the Day of Resurrection [[Narrated by al-Bazzar (658) from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.]]. This prohibition is a perpetual statement: forbidden until the Day of Resurrection. We only say that it is a perpetual statement so that no claimant can assert that it was abrogated (naskh), since making its end the Day of Resurrection means that abrogating it is impossible. If it could be abrogated, it would be possible to deny the Messenger (ﷺ), and that is impossible.
Some scholars permitted mut'ah in cases of necessity (darurah). They said: if a person fears for himself adultery, because he has intense desire and adultery is easily available, as is found in lands of disbelief, and he fears for himself adultery, then there is no blame if he enjoys mut'ah. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said it is like carrion: if a person is compelled to it, he may do it, otherwise not [[Narrated by 'Abd al-Razzaq (14021) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]]. Their argument is that it involves committing the lesser of two harms to avert the greater. What is the greater? Adultery, by which a person feels like a billy-goat that found a she-goat on the road and mounted her and went on. That is adultery. But mut'ah involves some kind of bond between the man and the woman, namely a bond for the term they agreed on, so there is some relationship that no one doubts. But adultery is otherwise.
However, the preponderant view is that it is never permissible, based on Allah's saying: ﴿And let those who cannot find marriage keep chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾ [al-Nur 33]. This is the correct view. 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, strongly denounced Ibn 'Abbas on this issue, and this is the place of denouncing this view, because the Prophet (ﷺ) generalized when he said: «It is forbidden until the Day of Resurrection» [[Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Awsat (938) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah al-Ansari.]], and he stated it without restriction. Also, the reality of mut'ah is hiring a woman to commit adultery with her for a specific term. That is its reality. When the term ends, she leaves by the same door she entered, without any waiting period or anything at all. Is adultery anything other than this?
As for necessity, the Lawgiver has provided a solution for it. He (ﷺ) said: «Whoever is not able, let him fast, for it is a shield for him» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1905) and Muslim (1400/1) from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]]. As for committing the lesser of two harms, it is said: this is a harm like the first, like adultery; there is no difference between them. The relationship that arises is like someone who agrees with a woman to commit adultery with her on certain nights, in which a relationship arises between them during those nights. So the correct view is absolute prohibition.
* A student: It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he retracted his view on permissibility. Is this correct?
* The Shaykh: No, he did not retract. He retracted from what was attributed to him, that it is permitted absolutely.
* A student: What about marriage with the intention of divorce?
* The Shaykh: Marriage with the intention of divorce is not mut'ah, because there is no stipulation in it. But it involves the prohibition of deception (ghish). Deception toward whom? Toward the wife and her family, because if the wife and her family knew that this man wants to divorce her when he travels, for example, or when his wife becomes pure from postnatal bleeding, they would not marry her to him.
* A student: The way out?
* The Shaykh: The way out is not to do it.
* A student: All right, Shaykh, if he cannot (...).
* The Shaykh: He does not fast at night?
* The student: He prays.
* The Shaykh: He prays. Then there is something lighter than this. There is something lighter. First, there are now medicines that reduce desire, though they do not eliminate it; as for those that eliminate it, that is not permissible. Second, he may masturbate, for example, because masturbation is less severe than mut'ah and marriage with the intention of divorce.
* A student: They say mint (na'na') reduces it.
* Another student: Masturbation by hand!
* The Shaykh: Yes, in case of necessity. Masturbation is less grave than adultery. What you told us needs verification.
* A student: If he takes these medicines, do they affect the future?
* Another student: But mint, Shaykh.
* Another student: Some vegetables, Shaykh.
* Another student: In general, mint calms the nerves, and when the nerves are calm, desire calms.
* The Shaykh: People always serve us mint in gatherings. What do we do? Do we not drink it?
* A student: We bring a study.
* The Shaykh: Bring a study. You are a doctor.
* A student: If the husband of a captive woman returns as a Muslim, is she returned to him?
* The Shaykh: She is not returned, because we have taken ownership of her. It is not possible. She is returned.
* Student: But in some of the battles (...), did the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, return the women and offspring they had taken captive?
* The Shaykh: Perhaps they enslaved them. But by captivity alone she becomes a slave (raqiqah).
* A student: (...) informed the woman that he would divorce her...
* The Shaykh: This is not mut'ah, as long as they did not stipulate a condition.
(...)
* A student: If in the contract they agreed that he would divorce her...
* The Shaykh: Yes, I answered that it is not mut'ah.
* The student: So it is permissible for him to do that?
* The Shaykh: That is, he will divorce her. All people have the option; people divorce their wives.
* A student: What if he sets a term?
* The Shaykh: If he specified, saying "I marry her to you, and when next month comes, I divorce her," then this is mut'ah.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The deceiver conceals and does not declare.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: In this case, she should protect herself. If she wishes, she says: "When a term is set, we say this is mut'ah (...)."
* A student: You told us that masturbation is less grave than mut'ah. Shaykh, you mentioned that some books say masturbation is forbidden...
* The Shaykh: We will mention it now. We say: it is forbidden.
* The student: But Shaykh, our saying "in case of necessity" opens a great door. Everyone who is compelled, meaning (...), says: "I am compelled."
* The Shaykh: No, that is not correct. That is, if the matter is between going to a place of prostitution and committing adultery, or masturbating, which is less grave?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Perhaps in our country, thank God, it is a conservative country, and adultery is not easily found. But in other countries, nothing is available.
* A student: Shaykh, we know that the circumstances of many young men (...) for the slightest desire?
* The Shaykh: No, we say: in case of necessity. We cannot lock people up one by one.
* A student: Is he sinful?
* The Shaykh: Be quiet, meaning, in response to your saying that it is permissible, because some scholars permitted it.
* A student: Is he sinful in case of necessity?
* The Shaykh: No, he is not sinful, because this is averting the greater of the two harms. It is permissible for him.
(...)
We have stopped at His saying: ﴿So for what you enjoy from them, give them their wages (ujur)﴾.
* One of the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of mut'ah. It has already been mentioned that all the scholars of the Sunnah say it is forbidden, but the Rafidah (Rafidites) disagreed. It is astonishing that they disagree on this, since their own imam states its prohibition and declares it. But this is not strange for one who follows his desires. Here is 'Ali, who narrated, or was among those who narrated, wiping over the leather socks (khuff), yet the Rafidah do not hold to wiping over the socks. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, was among those who narrated the prohibition of mut'ah, yet they do not hold to its prohibition. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, says from the pulpit of Kufa, declaring that the best of this Ummah are Abu Bakr and 'Umar [[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (833) from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.]], but they say: No, they are not the best of this Ummah. Some of them say they died as hypocrites, and some say they were disbelievers, and similar things that show that the foundation of their creed is not guidance but desire. Otherwise, if they truly followed the family of the Prophet, they would not oppose 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who is the most virtuous of the family of the Prophet.
So mut'ah is forbidden. But is it considered mut'ah if a person marries with the intention of divorce after a specific term?
It has been said before that it is not mut'ah, but it contains deception and trickery. After I spoke with you on this, I saw a statement by Shaykh Muhammad Rashid Rida that supports this and says it casts a stain on the Muslims, so people know about them that they are manipulative in their marriages. Furthermore, it closes the door to marriage, because everyone knows that these people marry and then divorce when they travel, so he does not trust them and does not feel safe that they might do the same to him, and in that case it closes the door of marriage.
For this reason, when a benefit appears to us, we should not hasten to act on it until we see what follows from it. Harms greater than the benefit may result from it. Those who said it is permissible argue that every person whose wife does not suit him divorces her. But we say: there is a difference between a man who entered only intending to divorce her on a specific day and a man who entered intending her to be his wife, but an obstacle arose that prevents the continuation of the marriage. That is a great difference.
Then we say: do you not say that if a man marries a woman with the intention of making her lawful (tahlil) for the first husband, with the intention of tahlil but not as a condition, the marriage is invalid? This is similar: the first intended to divorce after a certain time, and this one intended to divorce after a certain time, and "actions are by intentions, and every person will have what he intended."
If they say: "This may be desired, and he may remain," we say: "The muhallil may also desire and remain."
In any case, I do not see that it is permissible for a person to marry with the intention of divorcing when he travels. But the question remains: is the marriage valid or not? The position of the Hanbalis is that the marriage is invalid, because the intention of mut'ah is like its condition, just as the intention of tahlil is like its condition.
* Another benefit of this noble verse: the dowry is established by the husband's enjoyment of his wife, from His saying: ﴿So for what you enjoy from them, give them their wages﴾. Accordingly, the dowry is established by intercourse and by enjoying the woman in a manner that is only possible from a husband with his wife, such as kissing and embracing and the like. It is also established by seclusion (khalwah), as was reported from the Rightly-Guided Caliphs.
* Another benefit of this noble verse: calling the dowry a wage (ajr). Its reason is that it is a compensation in exchange for a benefit, not for a physical item. If it were in exchange for a physical item, it would be called a sale, but it is in exchange for a benefit, namely the husband's enjoyment of the wife, so it becomes like a hiring contract (ijarah).
* Another benefit of the verse: the dowry is obligatory, like the obligation of a wage upon the one who hires. But if the one entitled to it forgives it, does it fall away?
The answer: Yes, based on Allah's saying: ﴿Then half of what you have specified, unless they (the women) forgo it or he in whose hand is the marriage tie forgoes it﴾ [al-Baqarah 237].
Here is an important question: since Allah called the dowry a wage, does the husband treat his wife as if she were a hired worker, or is the husband's companionship and treatment of his wife loftier and higher than that?
The second, because if he feels she is like a hired worker whom he has hired to enjoy, the purpose of marriage is not achieved, which is affection and mercy. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from yourselves that you may find tranquility in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy﴾ [al-Rum 21]. And if he felt this way, he would become angry whenever she refused him, for a reason or for no reason, and might even divorce her. But if he feels that the matter is higher and loftier than that, he says: "Yes, the dowry is a wage, because it is in exchange for a benefit, but the one to whom the dowry is given is not like a hired worker." Although the compensation is called a wage, the one who receives the compensation is not like a hired worker.
* Another benefit of this noble verse: the obligation of giving women their dowries, from His saying: ﴿an obligation (fariḍah)﴾, meaning it is obligatory upon you to give them their wages.
* Another benefit of it, that is, of the noble verse: if the husband and wife agree on an increase, a decrease, or a waiver, there is no blame, from His saying: ﴿And there is no blame upon you in what you agree upon after the obligation﴾.
* Another benefit: we take an important principle, namely: whatever Allah, mighty and majestic, made obligatory for a person's right and then waived his right, there is no sin upon the one who does not perform it. If Allah makes a right obligatory for a person and then waives that right, there is no sin upon us if we do not perform it. This principle will have many branches. Among them: accepting an invitation to a wedding feast (walimah). Accepting the invitation to a wedding feast is obligatory for whose sake? For the sake of the one who invites. If he waives it, there is no sin on you if he invites you. If he invites me and I say, "Brother, I have work, I cannot, and so on," and he says, "Then you are excused," there is no sin on you, because the right belongs to him, and something that Allah made obligatory as a right among people, one toward another, falls away if the one entitled to it waives it.

Among the benefits of this noble verse, and this is a benefit that may seem remote, is that whoever reviles the Messenger (ﷺ) must be killed, even if he repents. Whoever reviles Allah, however, is not killed if he repents. Do you understand? Which is greater: reviling Allah or reviling the Messenger? Reviling Allah is greater. But Allah has told us about Himself that whoever turns to Him in repentance, He turns to him in forgiveness. As for the right of the Messenger (ﷺ), we do not know that He has waived it. It is a right of a human being (haqq adami), so he is killed for the right of the Messenger, but his repentance is accepted. He is killed while his repentance is accepted. How?

We say: we accept his repentance. If we kill him, we wash him, shroud him, pray over him, and bury him among the Muslims, because he has repented. But the killing is unavoidable.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: it affirms two of Allah's names, al-'Alim (the All-Knowing) and al-Hakim (the All-Wise), whose explanation has already been given in a thorough commentary.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free, believing women, then [he may marry] from what your right hands possess of believing maidens﴾ [An-Nisa 25].

**Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary on Tafsir al-Qur'an al-Karim, Surah 4, verse 25 (part 1 of 4)**

His saying: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford﴾. ﴿Man﴾ here is a conditional noun (ism shart jazim, a conditional particle that jazms the verb). ﴿Then from what your right hands possess﴾ is the response (jawab) of the condition. Here we ask: two elements that cause jazm (apocopation) have combined in this sentence, the first being (man) and the second being (lam). Is the verb apocopated by (man) or by (lam)?

We say: by (lam), because it is the immediate one. On this basis, we say: ﴿yastati'[1]﴾ is an imperfect verb apocopated by (lam), and it is the verb of the condition.

[1] *Jazm* (apocopation): the grammatical process by which the final vowel of an imperfect verb is dropped, here under the influence of the particle *lam*.

His saying: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford ṭawlan﴾. The ṭawl is wealth, meaning: whoever among you does not have sufficient wealth to pay the dower of free women ﴿to marry the chaste women﴾, that is, the free women, ﴿the believing women﴾, as opposed to the disbelieving women. ﴿Then from what your right hands possess﴾, meaning: then marry from what your right hands possess, that is, from those whom your right hands possess, and they are the female slaves. So a person marries another's slave-woman, not his own. If he were to marry his own slave-woman, the marriage would not be valid, because ownership of the private parts by ownership (milk) is stronger than ownership by marriage, and it is not possible for the weaker to be returned to the stronger.

So ﴿from what your right hands possess﴾ means: what the right hands of others possess, such as a man who wishes to marry the slave-woman of Zayd. This is what Allah intends in this verse: ﴿from what your right hands possess of your believing young women﴾. The (min) here explains the (ma) in His saying ﴿from what your right hands possess﴾. The fatayat (young women) is the plural of fatah, and it means the slave-woman. The word fatah is applied to a young woman when it is attached to a free woman, and to a female slave when it is attached to a servant.

He says: ﴿from what your right hands possess of your believing young women﴾. The believing women are the opposite of the disbelieving women, even if they are from the People of the Book. So the slave-woman must be a believer. A disbelieving woman in this position, even a Jewish or Christian one, is not valid.

He said: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your faith﴾. Allah is most knowing of your faith, meaning: you only have the outward appearance, while the inward is known to Allah. So if a person says: "This is a slave-woman, and we do not know whether she is truly Muslim or Muslim out of fear," we say: Allah knows her faith; you have only the outward appearance.

﴿You are one from another﴾. He brought this emphatic sentence to affirm equality in humanity, because the Arabs had a great aversion to a free man marrying a slave-woman. So Allah lightened this for them and said: ﴿You are one from another.﴾ You are only marrying a human being, so you are, with her, one from another.

﴿So marry them with the permission of their people﴾. ﴿Marry them﴾: is the hamzah here a hamzat wasl or a hamzat qat'? It is hamzat wasl, because it is from the triliteral root (n-k-ḥ).

﴿So marry them﴾, that is, the believing young women. ﴿With the permission of their people﴾, that is, their masters. Here He said ﴿with the permission of their people﴾ and did not say "with the permission of their guardians," because there is no guardianship over a slave-woman except by her master, since her master owns her in both person and benefit. He is the one who marries her, even if she has a father; he does not marry her when her master is present.

﴿And give them their wages in a fair manner﴾. Give them (ātū, with the meaning of "give"), unlike (atū), which means "came." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿until, when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾ [an-Naml 18], where atū means "came."

﴿Their wages﴾, that is, their dowers. ﴿In a fair manner﴾, that is, in accordance with what people customarily recognize and what the Sharia has approved, without procrastination and without reproach. Do not say, "She is a slave-woman," so that you delay her dower or reproach her for it.

* Student: Insulting the Messenger ﷺ: is the one who insults the Messenger ﷺ killed by consensus? I say: is there consensus on this matter?
* Shaykh: I do not know whether there is consensus or not, but the evidences indicate this. Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) composed a comprehensive book on the subject, which he named *al-Sarim al-Maslul fi Tahatum Qatl Sabb al-Rasul* (The Drawn Sword on the Obligation of Killing One Who Insults the Messenger).
* Student: (...) The benefit of the verse (...) killing the one who insults the Messenger?
* Shaykh: What is it? We said that this is a benefit that may be remote, but what brings it closer? What brings it closer is that we said: the right of a human being, if he pardons it, is dropped, even if Allah had made it obligatory for him. Among the rights of people is the right of the Messenger, peace be upon him. If someone insults the Messenger of Allah in front of the Messenger of Allah and he pardons him, it is dropped. But it becomes obligatory for him to repent from apostasy if it is apostasy.
Student: Why is the female People of the Book not analogized to the free woman in marriage?
* Shaykh: This will be derived among the benefits, God willing.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah preserve you, the right of invitation (ḥaqq al-da'wa), the right of obligation: is it only for the husband, or for whoever invites, whether the wife's father or the husband's father?
* Shaykh: No, only the husband, because the wedding feast (walimah) is legislated only in regard to the husband.
* Student: Shaykh, we said: ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾, meaning (...) the faith of others. Shaykh, we take the Qur'an according to its apparent meaning, and this is an inference, that we say: the stronger (...) and it returns to the text (...) how do we give precedence to understanding over the apparent meaning? This comes at us, O Shaykh.
* Shaykh: This will be among the benefits, God willing.
(...)
* Student: O Shaykh, is it possible that a person is upright and then is envied and deviates?
* Shaykh: In any case, everything that the decree touches, the evil eye touches. Even the upright may be struck by the evil eye and deviate.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: This is a calamity he has caused. It is one of the calamities, just as a person who seeks the truth but is not guided to anyone who explains it to him will be punished.
* Student: (...) ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah 286]. Is this an act within his capacity?
* Shaykh: Yes. If we suppose that the man wants to worship, and performs ablution to pray, but is unable, then what he would have done correctly is written for him, and the reward is not withheld.
* Student: What if he deviates?
* Shaykh: But if he deviates by his own choice, saying: "O so-and-so, pray!"
* Student: Is it possible that he is upright and then is envied and deviates?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is possible. This is something observed. He deviates, but it may not be a deviation of will. He may, for example, be afflicted with a fracture or an illness and similar things, which keep him from work.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: In any case, the saying of the Messenger: «If anything could precede the decree, the evil eye would have preceded it»[2] indicates that the evil eye occurs in everything the decree touches. We ask Allah for safety.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Perhaps.

[2] Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2059) and Ahmad (27470), from the hadith of Asma' bint 'Umays.

* * *

* Shaykh: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford ṭawlan to marry the chaste believing women, then from what your right hands possess﴾. The discussion of this part of the verse has already preceded. We said that what is meant by ṭawl is wealth and ample means, and what is meant by the chaste women is the free women, as is evident from its contrast with His saying ﴿then from what your right hands possess﴾. The preceding phrase is ﴿and the married women from among women﴾, meaning the married women. ﴿Then from what your right hands possess﴾, meaning: marry from what your right hands possess. The address here is to all of you collectively, not to each individual. He addresses all of you in terms of the group, not in terms of each individual. We said this because the owner may not marry his own slave-woman. A master cannot marry his slave-woman; he may only take her as a concubine (yatasarraha tasariyyan). This is because Allah made ownership by the right hand equivalent to a wife, or to marital status, saying: ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun 6]. This shows that what the right hand possesses is other than wives.

The people of knowledge said: a master cannot marry his slave-woman, because his taking her private part by a contract is stronger than a marriage contract. The contract of ownership confers ownership of her for all kinds of enjoyment, while the marriage contract confers only ownership of enjoyment of her. The slave-woman owns all her benefits: she may be made to serve, and she may be hired out. She has no property; the property is yours. And you own enjoyment of her. A wife is not like that.

﴿Then from what your right hands possess﴾ [an-Nisa' 25], meaning: marry from what your right hands possess. The address here is to all collectively, not to each individual. He addresses all of you in terms of the group, not in terms of each individual. We said this because the owner may not marry his slave-woman. A master cannot marry his slave-woman; he may only take her as a concubine, because Allah made ownership by the right hand equivalent to marital status, saying: ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun 6]. This shows that what the right hand possesses is other than wives.

The people of knowledge said: a master cannot marry his slave-woman, because his taking her private part by a contract is stronger than a marriage contract. The contract of ownership confers ownership of her for all kinds of enjoyment, and the marriage contract confers only ownership of enjoyment of her. So the slave-woman owns all her benefits: she may be made to serve, and she may be hired out. She has no property; the property is yours, and you own enjoyment of her. A wife is not like that. Thus, ownership of the enjoyment of the private part by the right hand is stronger than ownership by a marriage contract, so the stronger is not returned to the weaker. This is the reasoning. As for the textual evidence?

* Student: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾.
* Shaykh: What is the point of inference?
* Student: That ownership by the right hand is other than marriage.
* Shaykh: That Allah made ownership by the right hand a counterpart to marital status: ﴿then from what your right hands possess﴾.

So, regarding ﴿from what your right hands possess﴾: is the address to all collectively or to each individual? To the group, not each individual. So whoever owns a slave-woman may not contract marriage with her.

﴿of your believing young women﴾. The fatayat are the plural of fatah, and it means the female slave. Allah, glorified and exalted, made faith a condition for her, saying ﴿the believing women﴾, meaning: she must be a believer. If she is a People of the Book, she is not lawful, even if one cannot afford the free woman's dower.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your faith﴾. This sentence is a parenthetical sentence (jumlah i'tiradiyyah), meaning that Allah, glorified and exalted, is most knowing of faith. So when Allah has made faith a condition, we have only the outward appearance. As for the inward, whose knowledge is it? It is Allah's. That is why accountability in this world is based on the outward and in the Hereafter on the inward.

﴿You are one from another﴾. The "oneness" here is human oneness, meaning that Allah permitted us to have slave-women because they are of us, human beings like us. So some of us are from others, even if the free person is nobler and higher.

﴿So marry them with the permission of their people﴾. The hamzah here, ﴿fa-nkiḥūhunna﴾, is a hamzat wasl, because it is from (n-k-ḥ). As for His saying, ﴿And marry the single ones among you﴾ [an-Nur 32], the hamzah is a hamzat qat', because it is from the quadriliteral (ankaḥa).

As for His saying ﴿fa-nkiḥūhunna﴾: the origin of nikah is gathering, because by its contract there is a gathering of the husband and the wife, and likewise a gathering of in-laws toward one another. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And He it is who created from water a human being and made him [a line of] lineage and marriage relations; and your Lord is ever Competent﴾ [al-Furqan 54].

﴿So marry them with the permission of their people﴾, meaning: with consent. Permission (idhn) means allowance and consent. What is meant by "their people" is their masters. That is because the slave-woman does not own herself, and her guardian by kinship does not own her; rather, her guardian owns her by cause, that is, her owner. That is why the master marries off the slave-woman, and her father does not marry her off, because the master's guardianship is stronger than the father's. So He said: ﴿with the permission of their people﴾, and they are their masters.

﴿And give them their wages in a fair manner﴾. ﴿Give them﴾, that is, give them, because it is from the quadriliteral, and ātā (the quadriliteral) means "gave," as Allah said: ﴿and gave wealth in spite of love for it﴾ [al-Baqarah 177], meaning he gave the wealth.

﴿And give them their wages in a fair manner﴾. ﴿Their wages﴾, that is, their dowers. It is called ajr (wage) because it is compensation for a benefit. Its attribution here, ﴿their wages﴾, is an attribution of specification (idafat ikhtisas), not an attribution of ownership, because the slave-woman does not own. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Whoever sells a slave who has property, his property belongs to the one who sold him»[3]. So the attribution here is one of specification, like the attribution of a saddle to a riding animal. You say "the saddle of the horse," not because the horse owns it, but because it is specific to it.

[3] Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (2379) and Muslim (1543/80), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.

His saying: ﴿in a fair manner﴾, meaning in a manner recognized by the Sharia and by custom. What is recognized by the Sharia is that the dower be something of value in the Sharia, whether gold, silver, iron, lead, clothing, bedding, doors, or other things. What is recognized by custom is that one not procrastinate, but give the slave-woman her dower as one gives the free woman. Allah mentioned this because a man may look down on the slave-woman and not give her her right as he should. That is why He said: ﴿give them their wages in a fair manner﴾.

﴿Chaste, not fornicators, nor taking secret lovers﴾. ﴿Chaste﴾ (muḥṣanāt) is a circumstantial state from the pronoun in His saying ﴿so marry them﴾, meaning: marry them while they are chaste. Or it is from the object pronoun in ﴿give them﴾, meaning: give them their wages while they are chaste, not giving them wages for fornication but wages for chastity.

His saying: ﴿muḥṣanāt﴾ here means married, that is, not fornicators. It is an emphasis on what came before, because His saying ﴿so marry them with the permission of their people﴾ already suffices for it: their lawful marriage with the permission of their people makes the contract with them a contract of chastity, not fornication. But because of the gravity of this matter, Allah, glorified and exalted, emphasized it with His saying ﴿chaste, not fornicators﴾. The musāfiḥ is the fornicator, and we seek refuge in Allah. He is called musāfiḥ because his only concern is to pour out water in the private part. He wants no children, no companionship, and no affection; he is like a male goat that wants only to satisfy its lust.

﴿Nor taking secret lovers﴾. Akhdān is the plural of khidn or khadan, and what is meant by it is what is known among the disbelievers as a friend or companion. In the lands of disbelief, a woman takes a male friend and companion who does with her what a husband does with his wife, except intercourse, and sometimes the situation reaches intercourse. Since the slave-women did not concern themselves with this matter, Allah restricted it by His saying: ﴿nor taking secret lovers﴾. As for free women, fornication is unlikely among them, so much so that it was said: "Hind bint 'Utbah, when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, took the pledge from women that they would not steal nor commit fornication, said: O Messenger of Allah, does a free woman commit fornication?"[4] This report is weak, but some scholars mentioned it. Fornication among free women is rare, and it is common among slave-women. That is why it was restricted by His saying: ﴿not fornicators, nor taking secret lovers﴾.

[4] Narrated by Abu Ya'la in his Musnad (4754), from the hadith of 'A'ishah.

﴿And when they are chaste﴾. In another reading: ﴿aḥṣanna﴾, meaning: when they make themselves chaste. The exegetes differed about the meaning of ihsan (chastity). ﴿Fa-idha uḥṣinna﴾, meaning: when someone makes them chaste. On the reading ﴿fa-idha aḥṣanna﴾, meaning: when they make themselves chaste. The exegetes differed about the meaning of ihsan. Some scholars said: on the reading with the fatḥah, ﴿aḥṣanna﴾ means "they became Muslim," and ﴿uḥṣinna﴾ means "they were married."

Some scholars said: both have the same meaning, and the meaning of ﴿aḥṣanna﴾ is that they became possessors of chastity, as one says "anjada," meaning he entered Najd, so "aḥṣana" means he became one possessing chastity.

﴿Uḥṣinna﴾, meaning they became possessors of chastity. As for the reading with the ḍammah, ﴿uḥṣinna﴾, the matter is clear that the meaning is ﴿uḥṣinna﴾, that is, they were married, and so they guarded their private parts by this marriage. The correct view is that both have the same meaning, and that the two words have one meaning. That it means "they became Muslim" is far-fetched, because the context here concerns the believing young women, ﴿of your believing young women﴾, and the believing woman is a Muslim.

This is part 2 of Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary on Surah an-Nisa' (4), verse 25.

﴿So when they are chaste, if they commit immorality, then for them is half the punishment of free chaste women﴾. This is a conditional within a conditional. ﴿When they are chaste﴾ is the first condition. ﴿If they commit immorality﴾ is the second condition. ﴿Then for them﴾ is the answer to the second condition. So it is a condition within a condition, meaning: if the slave woman becomes chaste and then commits immorality, then for her is half of the punishment of free chaste women. Here "the chaste women" means the free women. It is not valid to say: "When they are chaste, then for them is half the punishment of the chaste slave women." That does not work. The meaning is ﴿half of what is upon the chaste women﴾, i.e., the free women, ﴿of the punishment﴾. The punishment of free women is that a virgin is flogged one hundred lashes and a married woman is stoned. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿and it averts from her the punishment that she bear witness﴾ [An-Nur 8]. The "punishment" here is the prescribed penalty (hadd), as in His saying: ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator, flog each one of them a hundred lashes, and let not pity for them take you in the religion of Allah, if you should believe in Allah and the Last Day. And let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾ [An-Nur 2]. So the "punishment" here means the hadd.

What is the hadd? For a free married woman, if she is "muhsana" in the sense of being married, the hadd is stoning, "because the Prophet (ﷺ) stoned al-Ghamidiyyah"[[Narrated by Muslim (1695/23) from the hadith of Buraydah ibn al-Husayb.]]. If she is not married, the hadd is flogging, by the saying of Allah: ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator, flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾. So what is the prescribed penalty for a married free woman that can be halved for a slave woman?

*Students:* Flogging.

*Shaykh:* Flogging? And stoning?

*Students:* It cannot be halved.

*Shaykh:* Can we stone her by half a stoning? No, because stoning results in death, and death cannot be halved. Therefore the meaning of ﴿half of what is upon the chaste women of the punishment﴾ is fifty lashes. The free woman is punished by another penalty as well, which is exile (taghrib). Exile has come in authentic Sunnah: the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abu al-'Asif: "Upon your son is a hundred lashes and a year's exile"[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (2696) and Muslim (1698/25) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani.]]. The Messenger (ﷺ) also said: "For a virgin with a virgin, a hundred lashes and a year's exile"[[Narrated by Muslim (1690/12) from the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit.]]. However, the scholars differed about the exile of a free woman: is she exiled or not? Some of them said she is not exiled, because exile is only to protect a person from fornication, and if a woman is exiled her fornication may increase, especially if she has no mahram with her. So the woman is not exiled. If she is not exiled, we say that the slave woman's punishment is fifty lashes without exile, because the free woman is not exiled. But if we take the second view, that she is exiled, then is the slave woman exiled as the free woman is?

Some scholars said: she is exiled for half a year. Other scholars said: she is not exiled, because exiling her harms her owner, and Allah said: ﴿and no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ [Al-An'am 164]. But this reasoning is weak, because we say: if we hold that exile is a hadd, then just as it harms the master, so flogging also harms the master. Is that not so? Yes, it harms the master, because her health may be affected by it, her reputation will be affected by it, and her value will decrease. Now, if we say that exile for a free woman is left to the judgment of the ruler and is not an obligatory hadd, then we say that exile for the slave woman is also left to the judgment of the ruler. The correct view is that she bears half of what the free woman bears of punishment, in flogging and exile.

And if she is not chaste? ﴿So when they are chaste, if they commit immorality, then for them is half the punishment of free chaste women﴾. If she is not chaste, what is upon her?

Some scholars said: nothing is upon her. Do you understand? Because the implication of the noble verse is that if she is not chaste, there is no punishment upon her, and the implication is clear. When Allah is silent about something, it is among what He has pardoned. There is no doubt that the fornication of a woman who is chaste is worse than that of a woman who is not chaste, meaning one who is not married.

Other scholars said: if she is chaste, then upon her is half the punishment of the free woman, and if she is not chaste, then upon her is the full punishment. If she is chaste, upon her is half the punishment of the free woman; if she is not chaste, upon her is the full punishment. They said: we take both verses. ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator, flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾ is general for free and slave women. What was excluded from it is the slave woman who is chaste, for whom half the punishment of the free woman applies. The slave woman who is not chaste, meaning not married, remains under the general ruling, like the virgin free woman who has not married. And the virgin free woman who has not married receives how many? A hundred lashes. On this basis, if a chaste slave woman commits fornication, upon her is fifty lashes; and if she is not chaste, upon her is a hundred lashes. Who has the most right to this view? The Zahiriyyah. Yes, and so it is, for the Zahiriyyah held this view. They said: we have only the apparent meaning. Among the scholars is one who said: if she is chaste, upon her is half of what is upon the free woman; and if she is not chaste, it is obligatory to punish her with flogging without a specified limit (hadd), based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "If a slave woman of one of you commits fornication, let him flog her. If she commits it again, let him flog her. If she commits it again, let him flog her. Then if she commits it again, let him sell her even for a rope of hair"[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (6839) and Muslim (1703/30) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, in similar wording.]]. That is, even for a rope. He said "let him flog her" and gave it no limit. So, on this view, if she commits fornication before becoming chaste, her punishment is due by flogging that is not a prescribed hadd. This view is the correct one: that if she is married, upon her is half of what is upon the free woman, which is fifty lashes.

We cannot say: upon her is half of stoning, because it cannot be divided. And if she is not chaste, it is obligatory to flog her as a discretionary punishment (ta'zir), because if we leave her alone that too is problematic. As for the view that if she commits fornication before becoming chaste she is stoned, or that she receives the full prescribed penalty, because stoning does not apply when she has not been made chaste by marriage, but rather that she must receive the full flogging: this view is weak without doubt, because the cause of halving is chastity, meaning marriage. When the cause is removed, the ruling is removed.

* * *

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and blessings and peace upon our Prophet Muhammad, and upon his family and companions and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.

Allah, the Exalted, said, explaining the conditions for marrying a slave woman: ﴿This is for whoever among you fears falling into sin﴾. ﴿This﴾ refers to the ruling mentioned, which is the permissibility of marrying slave women.
