This is the preponderant view: that the unauthorized transaction, or the unauthorized disposal (express it with this or that), if its owner authorizes it, is permissible and effective. This is because the generality of His saying: ﴿except that it be a trade by mutual consent from you﴾ includes this case. But some scholars said: it is not valid in any case, whether he authorizes it or not, whether it concerns his liability or the specific property, whether in buying or selling. Some scholars made a distinction between buying and selling, saying: if he buys for him in his liability without naming him in the contract, and he consents, there is no harm; otherwise there is. But the preponderant view is that whenever the owner consents, even after the contract, the contract takes effect as valid.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of killing, the killing of a person himself, from His saying: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾.
* And according to the second interpretation of its benefits: the believers are like a single soul, and a person killing another is as if he had killed himself.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that God, mighty and majestic, is more merciful to a person than he is to himself, because He forbade him from killing himself, so He became more merciful to him than he is to himself.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the attribute of mercy for God, from His saying: ﴿indeed, God is ever Merciful to you﴾. Mercy, according to the Salaf, is a real attribute established for God, mighty and majestic. The negators (al-mu'attila) denied it, denying it by way of interpretation (ta'wil), not by way of denying its reality. They did not say that God has no mercy. Rather, they said: what is meant by His mercy is such and such, arguing that mercy involves some softness and tenderness, and God, mighty and majestic, is not described by this. So we say to them: how do you interpret mercy?

They said: We interpret it as the will to bestow favour and goodness, or we interpret it as goodness. But to say that there is a mercy in Him by which He wills goodness and so does good, this is not permissible. There is no doubt that by this interpretation they have contradicted the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and contradicted the consensus (ijma') of the early generations (salaf). Someone may say: Where is the consensus of the salaf? We say: The Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language, and they understood it according to the requirements of the Arabic language. So when Allah affirms mercy for Himself, they affirm mercy for Him, because this is the basic principle. And to the one who says there is no consensus we say: Bring one single report from the salaf interpreting mercy in a way contrary to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. This is an important benefit by which one who casts doubt and confuses is refuted, and who says: Where is the consensus of the salaf? We say: The Qur'an was before them, and they did not interpret it contrary to its apparent meaning. The basic principle is that they understood it according to what? According to its apparent meaning, in accordance with the Arabic tongue. Then we say to them: You interpret it as will, fleeing from resemblance to the created, in your claim, but the created has a will: ﴿Among you are those who desire the world, and among you are those who desire the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran 152]; ﴿You desire the goods of this world, but Allah desires the Hereafter﴾ [Al-Anfal 67]; "Actions are only by intentions" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1) and Muslim (1907 / 155) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.]] and no one doubts that the created has a will. If they say: The will of the created befits it and the will of the Creator befits Him, we say to them: Mercy of the Creator befits Him and mercy of the created befits it. Likewise, if you interpret mercy as bestowal, which is created, or as blessing, which is created, we say: Blessing does not exist except by will, and will does not exist except by mercy; whoever has no mercy does not will blessing and does not bestow it. And by this the falsity of their distortion becomes clear, and we call it distortion (tahrif), not interpretation (ta'wil), in every case. If we were to ask you now: Which is greater, that the Qur'an and the Sunnah be distorted concerning the attributes of Allah, or concerning the legal rulings related to the actions of servants?
* Students: The first.
* The Shaykh: The first is more severe, because in the first there is no room for the intellect, so it is obligatory to keep it upon its apparent meaning. As for the second, these are legal rulings in which the intellect has room, through analogy for example, so distortion in them is lighter. You will find these Mu'attilah denying most vehemently those who distort texts concerning the actions of the mukallaf, yet they do not object to their own distortion of texts concerning the attributes of the Lord, glorified and exalted.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of trade and commerce, because Allah approved it by His saying: ﴿except that it be a trade﴾. The apparent generality of the verse is that commerce is permissible for people of rank and nobility, for common people, and for those below them. There is no fault in a person trading and seeking provision. For this reason Allah directed the believers to strive toward the Friday prayer when it is called, and said: ﴿And when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty, and remember Allah much that you may succeed﴾ [Al-Jumu'ah 10]. When He commanded us to seek provision after leaving the Friday prayer, He reminded us not to forget the remembrance of Allah: He said: ﴿seek of Allah's bounty and remember Allah﴾, lest you forget; ﴿and remember Allah much that you may succeed﴾.
In any case, trade is permissible, and there is no fault in a person engaging in it. It is mentioned in history that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), when he was appointed caliph over the Muslims, went down to the market to sell and buy. They said to him: How can you sell and buy while you are a responsible caliph?! He said: It must be so. So they set aside for him a specific portion from the public treasury (bayt al-mal) sufficient for his needs, may Allah be pleased with him.
What is blameworthy trade? Blameworthy trade is that which diverts from the remembrance of Allah. For this reason Allah praised the men whom neither trade nor sale diverts from the remembrance of Allah, the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakah. Some scholars said: Trade that is intended for accumulation of worldly wealth is also blameworthy, because it is generally the case that whoever has this intention is diverted by trade from the remembrance of Allah. So if you perceive in yourself greed, covetousness and stinginess in trade, then refrain; refrain, because it is feared that this may be at the expense of religion. Then Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And whoever does that in transgression and injustice, We will drive him to a Fire﴾. His saying: ﴿that﴾ refers only to what was mentioned in the previous verse, unlike some scholars who said: ﴿whoever does that﴾ means everything prohibited from the beginning of the surah. This has no basis; rather we say: ﴿whoever does that﴾ the reference returns to the nearest mentioned thing, i.e., whoever consumes wealth falsely, except what is excepted, and whoever kills a soul in transgression and injustice.
﴿'Udwanan﴾ means: aggression, by doing it deliberately. ﴿Zulman﴾ it was said: it is of the type of coordinating a synonym with its synonym, since injustice is transgression and transgression is injustice. And it was said: rather there is a difference between them: transgression is what is done deliberately, and injustice returns to the doer himself. So if he violates what was mentioned, or does what was mentioned as prohibited, he has transgressed against another, consuming his wealth or killing him, and he has wronged himself. So it is transgression with regard to the other and injustice with regard to what? The self. And which of these is more correct?
* Student: The second.
* The Shaykh: The second is undoubtedly more correct, because interpreting speech as conveying a distinct meaning (ta'sis) is preferable to interpreting it as synonymy (taradif), since if you make them synonyms it becomes repetition. But if you say: each of these has a meaning, that is the basic principle. Accordingly we say: ﴿'udwanan﴾ means: deliberately and intentionally, and it is transgression against others. ﴿zulman﴾ means: against the self, because all sins are injustice to the self.
He said: ﴿So We will drive him to a Fire﴾, meaning We will make him enter a Fire that burns him. This ﴿nusliihi naran﴾ is in the accusative with two objects whose original structure is not subject and predicate, so it is of the category of?
* Students: (kasa wa a'ta, "clothed and gave").
* The Shaykh: (kasa wa a'ta), yes. ﴿So We will drive him to a Fire﴾, meaning We will make him enter a Fire that he will burn in, so it burns him. ﴿And that was ever, for Allah, easy﴾: ﴿that﴾ refers to making him enter the Fire he will burn in; it is easy for Allah, meaning simple, because no one can prevent Him in His dominion. Punishment by fire may be difficult for some worldly kings, for example, but for Allah it is easy and simple: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82].
The grammar in this verse: (man), what is it? Conditional. The condition verb? ﴿yaf'al﴾. Its response: ﴿fasawfa nusliihi naran﴾. The response clause is linked by the fa' because of what requires it, which is sawfa. The response that requires linking with fa' is gathered in the poet's saying:
Nominal, imperative, and what is with ...
[The verse is quoted as given in the source, and is not reproduced beyond this, as it is a source-text quotation.]

Where is sawfa?
* Students: With the tanfis (future particle).
* The Shaykh: The tanfis, yes, you enter it in his saying: "and with the tanfis."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: warning against committing these prohibited acts, by the threat of Fire for them.
* And among its benefits: that committing these prohibited acts is among the major sins, because a threat of Fire is attached to it, and every sin threatened with Fire is a major sin.
* And among its benefits: showing the greatness of Allah and the completeness of His authority and power, by His saying: ﴿And that was ever, for Allah, easy﴾.
* And among the benefits of the verse: the glorification of Allah by Himself, by His saying: ﴿nusliihi naran﴾; because the pronoun here is estimated as "We" (nahnu), which is the pronoun of majesty. It is not ambiguous except to one whose heart Allah has sealed, like the Christian who says that the plural pronoun indicates plurality, forgetting the clear verses that show that Allah is one God; because Allah has sealed his heart, and whoever Allah seals, the truth is not made clear to him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verses 29–30 (part 1 of 2):

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who believe, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾. The address (al-nida'), as has already been explained, indicates that the message that follows is to be given special attention. The reason is that the address alerts the one being addressed. A divine speech that opens with an address is distinguished from one that comes without it. Addressing the believers with ﴿O you who believe﴾ conveys an urging (al-igra') to adhere to this address, or to adhere to what it implies. The reason is that describing a person as a believer moves him to comply. It also indicates that complying with this matter is one of the requirements of faith, and that opposing it is a deficiency in faith. He, may He be glorified and exalted, says: ﴿O you who believe﴾. We must give this address our full attention and wait to see what God directs us to, as was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "When God says, 'O you who believe,' prick up your ears, for it is either good that you are commanded or evil that you are forbidden."[[Narrated by Sa'id ibn Mansur in his Tafsir (50).]]

Then He said: ﴿O you who believe, do not consume your wealth﴾. The prohibition came: ﴿do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾. Here "la" is a prohibitive particle, which is why the verb after it is in the jussive mood with the nun dropped.

﴿Do not consume your wealth﴾ means: whatever you hold as property, whether little or much, whether goods or cash, whether debts or specific items. It covers all wealth in general.

His words ﴿between you﴾ mean: in dealings, because consuming wealth must necessarily occur between two or more parties. If it is from one person to another person, then that person has consumed his own wealth.

﴿Between you﴾ means: during your dealings with one another.

His words ﴿unjustly﴾: al-batil (the unjust or falsehood) in the lexicon means that which is lost in vain, that which perishes and contains no good. The intended meaning of "unjustly" here is that which contradicts the Sharia, because the Sharia is truth, and whatever contradicts it is falsehood. The meaning on this basis is: do not consume your wealth among yourselves in a manner that contradicts the Sharia, such as usury (riba), fraud, lying, deception, and the like.

﴿Except that it be﴾: "illa" (except) is a particle of exception, but what is intended by it is istidrak (a correction or contrast), meaning "but." That is: but if there is a trade, or a trade (tijara) among you by mutual consent from you, then this is permissible. We say that the exception here is disconnected (al-istithna' al-munqati'), because His words ﴿except that it be a trade by mutual consent from you﴾ are not of the same kind as consuming wealth unjustly. Rather, it is consuming by what? By right. The disconnected exception is when the excluded item (al-mustathna) is of a different kind from the item it is excluded from. Here it must be disconnected, because trade by mutual consent is not consuming unjustly, but consuming rightfully. For this reason we say that the exception in this verse is disconnected.

﴿Except that it be a trade﴾ has two canonical readings: ﴿tijaratun﴾ with the damma, and ﴿tijaratan﴾ with the fatha. With the reading of the damma there is no difficulty; that is, "except that a trade occurs among you." Here "kana" is complete, not incomplete. With the reading of the fatha, "kana" is incomplete, and ﴿tijaratan﴾ is its predicate, and its subject is a hidden pronoun. In this case a problem arises: would the subject be a hidden pronoun, understood as "it" (huwa), even though the word "consuming" (ta'kulu) that it would refer to is masculine? Can we say "except that the consuming be a trade"? That is not correct. But here there is a useful point: when a pronoun or demonstrative falls between two things, and the second is masculine while the first is feminine, or the reverse, it is permissible to take into account either the first or the second. Do you understand?

When a pronoun or demonstrative falls between two things, and the first is masculine while the second is feminine, or the reverse, it is permissible to make it masculine or feminine. It may be masculine in consideration of its earlier referent, and feminine in consideration of its later referent. Here it has been made feminine in consideration of its second, later referent. That is: except that the trade by which you consume wealth be a trade by mutual consent from you. Trade (tijara) is exchange, or the exchange among people for the sake of profit. This is trade, and from it comes the jurists' expression "trade goods" ('urud al-tijara). As for what is given as a gift, pledged, or lent, this is not trade. Likewise, what is bought to meet a need, such as buying bread to eat, is not trade, because a person does not intend profit by it.

At this point a difficulty remains in the meaning of the verse: if transactions are more numerous than trade, why were they not mentioned? It has been said that they were not mentioned, meaning dealings without the intention of trade, because the most common form of people's dealings is trade, and it is in trade that disputes over bargaining arise. As for other transactions, gifts come from the giver's good will, and likewise loans and pledges. What is bought for need usually does not lead to dispute, because a person intends by it to meet a need, not to obtain profit. Therefore trade was mentioned. Otherwise, it is well known that contracts made by mutual consent are more numerous than trade contracts.

﴿By mutual consent from you﴾: the prepositional phrase ﴿by mutual consent﴾ is attached to an omitted element whose assumed form is: "proceeding from mutual consent from you," or "resulting from it." And ﴿tarad̄in﴾ here is in the form of mutual action (tafā'ul), which shows that what is intended is mutual consent from both parties, the taker and the giver.

His words ﴿by mutual consent from you﴾ mean: proceeding from you yourselves, who are the parties to the transaction, not from others. So if a father agrees to sell his son's property while the son has not agreed, and the property belongs to the son, then the father's consent carries no weight.

Then he said:
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, yes. If a father agrees to sell his son's property without the son's agreement, his consent carries no weight.

He said: ﴿And do not kill yourselves; indeed, God is ever Merciful to you﴾. ﴿Do not kill yourselves﴾: killing is well known as taking a soul's life. But does ﴿yourselves﴾ mean the killer's own soul, so that it refers to suicide, or does it mean "your fellow believers," as in His words: ﴿And do not defame one another﴾ [al-Hujurat 11], since a person does not defame himself but defames others? Which of these is intended?

We say: it is inclusive. It is not restricted to one who kills himself, nor to one who kills others. Rather, the verse includes both. If the meaning is "do not kill yourselves," meaning you yourselves, there is no difficulty in the verse. If the meaning is "do not kill others," then why was the others expressed as "yourselves"? We say: others were expressed as "yourselves" because the believer with his brother is like one body, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, gave this as an example: "When one of its limbs complains, the rest of the body responds to it with fever and sleeplessness."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6011), Muslim (2586/66), from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir.]] Also, expressing one's brother as one's self carries urging and exhortation, as if he were yourself. This contains an incitement for a person to avoid killing others, and a summons for a person to show compassion toward his brother, or to move him to compassion toward his brother.

His words ﴿indeed, God is ever Merciful to you﴾: this clause is a reason (ta'lil) for what precedes it, giving the reason for both rulings: consuming wealth and killing souls. God, glorified and exalted, is merciful to us. Among His mercy is the prohibition of consuming one another's wealth unjustly, or the prohibition against consuming one another's wealth unjustly. The second is the prohibition against killing ourselves, for this is from God's mercy toward us. The reasoning for the first is that consuming wealth unjustly leads to disputes and conflict, and perhaps to armed clashes, and the killing of people is evident.

His words ﴿indeed, God is ever Merciful to you﴾: to whom does the address ﴿you﴾ return? To the believers, because He is addressing the believers with ﴿O you who believe﴾. This is confirmed by His saying: ﴿And He is ever Merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab 43]. Nowhere in the Quran is mercy attributed to God in relation to the disbelievers, in the general sense. The mercy by which God is described appears in the Quran either in a general form or in a particular form directed at whom? At the believers. As for a particular form directed at the disbelievers, it does not appear.

* Student: May God be gracious to you. It appears in another place, O Shaykh, His saying: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqara 195]. Shaykh, can we say that this falls under this category (...) some of you?
* Shaykh: What?
* Student: (...) some of you.
* Shaykh: Which ones? His words ﴿with your own hands﴾. Yes. Regarding the verse ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾, it has been said that what is intended is: do not abandon spending in the way of God, lest you perish. What is intended is not throwing oneself into what destroys, such as killing or exposing oneself to it. But the correct view is that the verse is general: ﴿do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ applies to this and to that.
* Student: Can this wording, O Shaykh, be taken in its apparent sense: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾, in its apparent sense?
* Shaykh: And what is that?
* Student: The soul, meaning the agreed sense, as we said: killing others without an indicator (...). So we have abandoned the original meaning and not the meaning (...) without an indicator?
* Shaykh: No. May God bless you. The indicator is that aggression against another is like aggression against oneself, because the Messenger made the punishment of one who aggresses against himself the same as the punishment of one who aggresses against others: that he is eternally abiding in the fire of Hell and is tormented therein. Do you understand?
* Student: Is it not the case that if he kills a soul, he is killed?
* Shaykh: Do you understand?
* Student: O Shaykh, where is the indicator?
* Shaykh: The indicator is that God expresses believers toward one another as "souls." That is the indicator. That the word may bear two meanings, and carrying it on both is better than limiting it to one. But if we say that what is meant by souls here is others, not the person's own soul, that is an error. He says: why do you take it this way and not that without an indicator? But if we say it is general, there is no difficulty.
* Student: Does His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿God intends to lighten for you﴾ [al-Nisa' 28] benefit? The character of the Prophet, peace be upon him, in the hadith of 'A'isha: "He was never given a choice between two matters without choosing the easier of them"?[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6786), Muslim (2327/77), from 'A'isha.]]
* Shaykh: Yes, yes. From it we learn that the Messenger loves what God loves. But this is not in the verse for us to mention it among its benefits.
* Student: May God be gracious to you. Can we interpret the verse ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ as meaning that consuming wealth may be (...) is that correct or not?
* Shaykh: That is not correct, because this "wa" (and) is a conjunction, and conjunction requires difference. Say: do not kill yourselves by consuming wealth. Rather, it is said that God, mighty and majestic, mentioned the prohibition regarding wealth and regarding souls.
* Student: (...) wealth?
* Shaykh: (...) Wealth: not spending in the way of God. It is not consuming another's wealth.
* Student: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾. Is it not the case that if a person kills a soul, he is killed for it?
* Shaykh: No. He is killed if the conditions are fulfilled, so it is a cause. (...)

He asks about the Salafi methodology. The Salafi methodology in what? It was eager for knowledge. The methodology of the People of the Sunna is in what? Read the commentary on al-Tahawiyya, or the commentary on al-'Aqida al-Wasitiyya.

* Student: In da'wa.
* Shaykh: In calling to God? They call to God, exalted is He, with wisdom and good admonition, and they argue with them in the best manner. They argue with the People of the Book in the best manner, except those of them who commit wrong. They do not condemn anyone for exercising independent reasoning (ijtihad) provided it does not oppose the consensus (ijma') of the Salaf, or an explicit text of the Quran or the Sunna.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in God from Satan the accursed. ﴿And whoever does that, in aggression and injustice, We will drive him into a Fire, and that is ever easy for God. (30) If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you to an honorable entrance. (31) And do not wish for that by which God has made some of you exceed others. For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned. And ask God of His bounty. Indeed, God is ever Knowing of all things. (32) And for each We have appointed heirs to what is left by parents and close relatives, and those with whom your oaths have bound you, so give them their share. Indeed, God is ever Witness over all things. (33)﴾ [al-Nisa' 30–33].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in God from Satan the accursed. God, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿O you who believe, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾. The discussion of the beginning of this verse has already been given, and I believe there is nothing in it that requires further discussion.
* In this verse, among its benefits: the concern for preserving wealth and avoiding aggression, from His saying: ﴿do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾.
* And in it: the prohibition of taking a person's property without his consent, from His saying: ﴿except that it be a trade by mutual consent from you﴾.
* And in it also: the prohibition of forbidden transactions, even if they are by mutual consent of both parties, because a forbidden transaction is consuming wealth unjustly. On this basis, if the two parties agree to a usurious transaction, that is forbidden.
* Among its benefits: that it is a requirement of faith to avoid consuming wealth unjustly, because He directed the address to whom? To the believers.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the condition of mutual consent in contracts, from His saying: ﴿except that it be a trade by mutual consent from you﴾. If consent precedes the contract, there is no difficulty in the permissibility and validity of the contract. But if it comes afterward, does the contract take effect or not? This is the matter called by the scholars the unauthorized transaction (al-tasarruf al-fudooli), meaning: if I sell a person's property without his permission and consent, but he later grants permission and consents, is the earlier contract valid or void? If we look at the generality of His saying: ﴿except that it be a trade by mutual consent from you﴾, we say that it is valid, because this trade has come to result in mutual consent. This is the preponderant view: that the unauthorized transaction, or the unauthorized disposal (express it with this or that), if its owner authorizes it, is permissible and effective. This is because the generality of His saying: ﴿except that it be a trade by mutual consent from you﴾ includes this case. But some scholars said: it is not valid in any case, whether he authorizes it or not, whether it concerns his liability or the specific property, whether in buying or selling. Some scholars made a distinction between buying and selling, saying: if he buys for him in his liability without naming him in the contract, and he consents, there is no harm; otherwise there is. But the preponderant view is that whenever the owner consents, even after the contract, the contract takes effect as valid.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of killing, the killing of a person himself, from His saying: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾.
* And according to the second interpretation of its benefits: the believers are like a single soul, and a person killing another is as if he had killed himself.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that God, mighty and majestic, is more merciful to a person than he is to himself, because He forbade him from killing himself, so He became more merciful to him than he is to himself.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the attribute of mercy for God, from His saying: ﴿indeed, God is ever Merciful to you﴾. Mercy, according to the Salaf, is a real attribute established for God, mighty and majestic. The negators (al-mu'attila) denied it, denying it by way of interpretation (ta'wil), not by way of denying its reality. They did not say that God has no mercy. Rather, they said: what is meant by His mercy is such and such, arguing that mercy involves some softness and tenderness, and God, mighty and majestic, is not described by this. So we say to them: how do you interpret mercy?

They said: We interpret it as the will to bestow favour and goodness, or we interpret it as goodness. But to say that there is a mercy in Him by which He wills goodness and so does good, this is not permissible. There is no doubt that by this interpretation they have contradicted the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and contradicted the consensus (ijma') of the early generations (salaf). Someone may say: Where is the consensus of the salaf? We say: The Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language, and they understood it according to the requirements of the Arabic language. So when Allah affirms mercy for Himself, they affirm mercy for Him, because this is the basic principle. And to the one who says there is no consensus we say: Bring one single report from the salaf interpreting mercy in a way contrary to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. This is an important benefit by which one who casts doubt and confuses is refuted, and who says: Where is the consensus of the salaf? We say: The Qur'an was before them, and they did not interpret it contrary to its apparent meaning. The basic principle is that they understood it according to what? According to its apparent meaning, in accordance with the Arabic tongue. Then we say to them: You interpret it as will, fleeing from resemblance to the created, in your claim, but the created has a will: ﴿Among you are those who desire the world, and among you are those who desire the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran 152]; ﴿You desire the goods of this world, but Allah desires the Hereafter﴾ [Al-Anfal 67]; "Actions are only by intentions" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1) and Muslim (1907 / 155) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.]] and no one doubts that the created has a will. If they say: The will of the created befits it and the will of the Creator befits Him, we say to them: Mercy of the Creator befits Him and mercy of the created befits it. Likewise, if you interpret mercy as bestowal, which is created, or as blessing, which is created, we say: Blessing does not exist except by will, and will does not exist except by mercy; whoever has no mercy does not will blessing and does not bestow it. And by this the falsity of their distortion becomes clear, and we call it distortion (tahrif), not interpretation (ta'wil), in every case. If we were to ask you now: Which is greater, that the Qur'an and the Sunnah be distorted concerning the attributes of Allah, or concerning the legal rulings related to the actions of servants?
* Students: The first.
* The Shaykh: The first is more severe, because in the first there is no room for the intellect, so it is obligatory to keep it upon its apparent meaning. As for the second, these are legal rulings in which the intellect has room, through analogy for example, so distortion in them is lighter. You will find these Mu'attilah denying most vehemently those who distort texts concerning the actions of the mukallaf, yet they do not object to their own distortion of texts concerning the attributes of the Lord, glorified and exalted.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of trade and commerce, because Allah approved it by His saying: ﴿except that it be a trade﴾. The apparent generality of the verse is that commerce is permissible for people of rank and nobility, for common people, and for those below them. There is no fault in a person trading and seeking provision. For this reason Allah directed the believers to strive toward the Friday prayer when it is called, and said: ﴿And when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty, and remember Allah much that you may succeed﴾ [Al-Jumu'ah 10]. When He commanded us to seek provision after leaving the Friday prayer, He reminded us not to forget the remembrance of Allah: He said: ﴿seek of Allah's bounty and remember Allah﴾, lest you forget; ﴿and remember Allah much that you may succeed﴾.
In any case, trade is permissible, and there is no fault in a person engaging in it. It is mentioned in history that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), when he was appointed caliph over the Muslims, went down to the market to sell and buy. They said to him: How can you sell and buy while you are a responsible caliph?! He said: It must be so. So they set aside for him a specific portion from the public treasury (bayt al-mal) sufficient for his needs, may Allah be pleased with him.
What is blameworthy trade? Blameworthy trade is that which diverts from the remembrance of Allah. For this reason Allah praised the men whom neither trade nor sale diverts from the remembrance of Allah, the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakah. Some scholars said: Trade that is intended for accumulation of worldly wealth is also blameworthy, because it is generally the case that whoever has this intention is diverted by trade from the remembrance of Allah. So if you perceive in yourself greed, covetousness and stinginess in trade, then refrain; refrain, because it is feared that this may be at the expense of religion. Then Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And whoever does that in transgression and injustice, We will drive him to a Fire﴾. His saying: ﴿that﴾ refers only to what was mentioned in the previous verse, unlike some scholars who said: ﴿whoever does that﴾ means everything prohibited from the beginning of the surah. This has no basis; rather we say: ﴿whoever does that﴾ the reference returns to the nearest mentioned thing, i.e., whoever consumes wealth falsely, except what is excepted, and whoever kills a soul in transgression and injustice.
﴿'Udwanan﴾ means: aggression, by doing it deliberately. ﴿Zulman﴾ it was said: it is of the type of coordinating a synonym with its synonym, since injustice is transgression and transgression is injustice. And it was said: rather there is a difference between them: transgression is what is done deliberately, and injustice returns to the doer himself. So if he violates what was mentioned, or does what was mentioned as prohibited, he has transgressed against another, consuming his wealth or killing him, and he has wronged himself. So it is transgression with regard to the other and injustice with regard to what? The self. And which of these is more correct?
* Student: The second.
* The Shaykh: The second is undoubtedly more correct, because interpreting speech as conveying a distinct meaning (ta'sis) is preferable to interpreting it as synonymy (taradif), since if you make them synonyms it becomes repetition. But if you say: each of these has a meaning, that is the basic principle. Accordingly we say: ﴿'udwanan﴾ means: deliberately and intentionally, and it is transgression against others. ﴿zulman﴾ means: against the self, because all sins are injustice to the self.
He said: ﴿So We will drive him to a Fire﴾, meaning We will make him enter a Fire that burns him. This ﴿nusliihi naran﴾ is in the accusative with two objects whose original structure is not subject and predicate, so it is of the category of?
* Students: (kasa wa a'ta, "clothed and gave").
* The Shaykh: (kasa wa a'ta), yes. ﴿So We will drive him to a Fire﴾, meaning We will make him enter a Fire that he will burn in, so it burns him. ﴿And that was ever, for Allah, easy﴾: ﴿that﴾ refers to making him enter the Fire he will burn in; it is easy for Allah, meaning simple, because no one can prevent Him in His dominion. Punishment by fire may be difficult for some worldly kings, for example, but for Allah it is easy and simple: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82].
The grammar in this verse: (man), what is it? Conditional. The condition verb? ﴿yaf'al﴾. Its response: ﴿fasawfa nusliihi naran﴾. The response clause is linked by the fa' because of what requires it, which is sawfa. The response that requires linking with fa' is gathered in the poet's saying:
Nominal, imperative, and what is with ...
[The verse is quoted as given in the source, and is not reproduced beyond this, as it is a source-text quotation.]

Where is sawfa?
* Students: With the tanfis (future particle).
* The Shaykh: The tanfis, yes, you enter it in his saying: "and with the tanfis."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: warning against committing these prohibited acts, by the threat of Fire for them.
* And among its benefits: that committing these prohibited acts is among the major sins, because a threat of Fire is attached to it, and every sin threatened with Fire is a major sin.
* And among its benefits: showing the greatness of Allah and the completeness of His authority and power, by His saying: ﴿And that was ever, for Allah, easy﴾.
* And among the benefits of the verse: the glorification of Allah by Himself, by His saying: ﴿nusliihi naran﴾; because the pronoun here is estimated as "We" (nahnu), which is the pronoun of majesty. It is not ambiguous except to one whose heart Allah has sealed, like the Christian who says that the plural pronoun indicates plurality, forgetting the clear verses that show that Allah is one God; because Allah has sealed his heart, and whoever Allah seals, the truth is not made clear to him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 31 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your bad deeds and admit you to an honourable entrance.﴾ The phrase ﴿If you avoid﴾ here is a shift from the third person (ghayba) to the second person (khitab). Where is the third person? The verse before it said, "And whoever does that," which is third person, "We shall burn him." As for ﴿If you avoid﴾, it is the second person: Allah, glorified and exalted is He, addresses the servants with His words ﴿If you avoid﴾, meaning: if you keep away from ﴿the major sins that you are forbidden﴾. ﴿Major sins﴾ is the plural of (kabira, major sin). ﴿That you are forbidden﴾: al-nahy (prohibition) is the demand to refrain made from a position of superiority. That is, what Allah has forbidden you. ﴿We will remove from you your bad deeds﴾, meaning your minor sins. ﴿Remove﴾ (nukaffir) is derived from (al-kafr), which means covering, so takfir (expiation) means covering over bad deeds, and that is by pardoning them.

His words, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿bad deeds﴾ (sayyi'at) is the plural of (sayyi'a), and what is meant here is the minor sin. The evidence that what is meant is the minor sin is that it is placed in contrast to the major sins: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your bad deeds﴾. Otherwise, the basic meaning of sayyi'a is general, covering both major and minor sins. It is one of the eloquent features of the Qur'an that the meaning of a word is known by mentioning its opposite. Among examples of this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So go forth in separate groups or go forth all together﴾ [al-Nisa' 71]. If someone asked: what is the meaning of thubat?
* A student: Separately (furada).
* The Shaykh: Separately? What is your evidence?
* The student: ﴿all together﴾.
* The Shaykh: That it is contrasted with His words ﴿or go forth all together﴾. Although if you went to check it in the dictionary or other lexical works, it would take you some time. But when you know that Allah, mighty and majestic is He, mentions a thing together with its opposite, as in this verse, you know that thubat is meant to mean separately.

As for His words ﴿We will remove from you your bad deeds and admit you to an honourable entrance﴾: the honourable entrance (al-mudkhal al-karim) is Paradise, because it is the abode of the honourable, the abode of grace, the abode of kindness, the abode of peace. Here He said ﴿mud'alan﴾ and did not say ﴿mad'alan﴾, because it comes from the quadriliteral form, and the noun of place or time, and the mimi verbal noun (masdar mimi), when derived from the quadriliteral, follow the pattern (mufa'al) and not (mafa'al). That is why you say: "The man stayed (aqama) with us as a muqam (a stay)," or "a maqam"?
* Students: Muqaman.
* The Shaykh: Muqaman. And you say: "The man stood (qama) among us in a maqam (standing position)," because it is from the triliteral form. Accordingly, ﴿nudkhilakum mud'alan﴾ has its meem vowelled with a dammah, because it is from the quadriliteral of (adkhala, yudkhilu, to cause to enter). ﴿And admit you to an honourable entrance﴾, meaning: We will admit you into an honourable place of entry, on the basis that mud'al here is a noun of place. It may also be a mimi verbal noun, meaning: We will admit you with an honourable admission. It is also possible that both meanings are intended, that is, honour is an attribute both of the admission and of the place of entry.

If someone says: what are the major sins? We say: al-kaba'ir is the plural of (kabira), and hadiths have come counting them as three, four, seven, nine, and the hadiths differ on this. Hence the scholars disagreed. It was said: the major sins are those explicitly stated to be major, and whatever is other than that is minor. In the hadith of Abu Bakra, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins?" We said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Associating partners with Allah, and disobedience to one's parents." He had been reclining, then he sat up and said: "Beware, and false testimony, and false speech."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5976) and Muslim (87/143), from the hadith of Abu Bakra al-Thaqafi.]] It is also reported from him: "Avoid the seven destructive sins,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2766) and Muslim (89/145), from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.]] and he listed them. He was asked about the major sins and said: "Nine,"[[Reported by Abu Dawud (2875), from the hadith of Umayr ibn Qatada.]] and he listed them. Hence the scholars differed. Some of them said: whatever is reported to be a major sin is major, and whatever is not is minor. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, was asked whether the major sins were seven, and he said: "They are nearer to seventy than to seven."[[Reported by Ma'mar in al-Jami' (19702).]] In another narration he said: "They are nearer to seven hundred than to seven, but there is no major sin with seeking forgiveness, and no minor sin with persistence."[[Reported by al-Lalika'i in Sharh Usul I'tiqad Ahl al-Sunna wa'l-Jama'a (1919).]]

Imam Ahmad said: the major sin is defined (mahdudah), not counted (ma'dudah). It is that which carries a prescribed penalty (hadd) in this world or a threat (wa'id) in the Hereafter. Whatever carries a prescribed penalty in this world or a threat in the Hereafter is a major sin, and whatever does not is not. Thus adultery is a major sin, theft is a major sin, slander is a major sin, and whoever drags his garment out of arrogance, Allah will not look at him, is a major sin. Whatever carries a prescribed penalty in this world or a threat in the Hereafter is among the major sins.

Ibn 'Abd al-Qawi said in his long rhymed poem (al-Daliyya), which contains about fourteen thousand verses on jurisprudence, he said:
"Whatever has a prescribed penalty in this world..."
That is, in this world.
"...or a threat in the Hereafter, then mark it as major, according to Ahmad's text."
"Sim" means "sammahu" (name it) or "a'lamahu" (mark it), since it may be from the sima (mark) or 'alama (sign). So "fasim kubra" means: describe it as one of the major sins, according to the text of Ahmad.
"Hafid al-Majd added, or whose threat was that: a negation of faith, or a perpetual curse."

Who is Hafid al-Majd?
* Students: Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya.
* The Shaykh: Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya. Hafid al-Majd added, or whose threat, is a negation of faith, such as: "He does not believe who does such and such," "He is not of us who does such and such," or a perpetual curse, meaning whatever mentions a curse, such as: "Allah curses whoever curses his parents"[[Reported by Muslim (1987/44), from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.]] and the like. So how many did he add?
* Students: Four, O Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: He added. How many did he add?
* Students: Two.
* The Shaykh: He added two. With the first two, that makes four. Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, has another statement in which he said: whatever has a specific religious or worldly punishment ordained for it is a major sin, and whatever carries merely a prohibition or merely a forbidding is a minor sin. The reasoning behind this is that singling out a sin with a punishment indicates its gravity; otherwise general punishments for sins would have sufficed. Since a specific punishment is stipulated for it, this indicates its gravity. This criterion mentioned by Shaykh al-Islam is an acceptable criterion, but many sins will fall under it. Nonetheless, we have found no distinguishing feature separating major from minor sins except something like this. So if a specific worldly, religious or otherwise-worldly punishment is ordained, it is a major sin. A religious one is like saying: "By Allah, he does not believe whose neighbour is not safe from his harms,"[[Reported by al-Bukhari (6016), from the hadith of Abu Shurayh al-Khuza'i.]] this is religious: a negation of faith. A worldly one is like the prescribed penalty (hadd). An otherworldly one is like the threat: "Three whom Allah will not speak to on the Day of Resurrection, nor look at, nor purify, and for them is a painful punishment."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2672) and Muslim (108/173), from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.]] Is this a definition of the major sin by counting or by definition?
* Students: By definition.
* The Shaykh: By definition, yes.
* A student: Shaykh, may Allah pardon you. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, says: ﴿And whoever does that by transgression and wrongdoing﴾. Could this refer to killing a soul and consuming wealth by falsehood?
* The Shaykh: Yes, consuming wealth by falsehood.
* The student: Consuming wealth by falsehood. Now, Shaykh, if a person has someone killed, for example, and he knows the killer, then goes to kill that killer, does this not fall under transgression and wrongdoing, especially if the ruler does not establish the prescribed punishments? How (...)?
* The Shaykh: So the meaning is that whoever has the right to kill takes retribution himself?
* The student: Yes, but is this transgression and wrongdoing?
* The Shaykh: Well, let us ask: is this transgression and wrongdoing?
* A student: No, no, no, it is his right.
* The Shaykh: It is his right, it is his right. But regarding killing, the scholars said: it is not to be carried out except in the presence of the ruler or his deputy, lest the one taking retribution be overcome by zeal and mutilate the killer or something similar.
* A student: Shaykh, what is your view on the saying of some who say that the major sins are those in which there are wrongs between you and the servants, and the minor sins are those in which there are wrongs between you and Allah, and he said that all the major sins mentioned in the texts are mostly wrongs between you and people, such as severing kinship ties?
* The Shaykh: That is not correct. I say: this is incorrect. He says: if the wrongs are between you and people, they are major sins, and whatever is between you and Allah is minor.
* A student: Trailing garments, Shaykh. Does trailing garments fall under this ruling?
* The Shaykh: I say: this is incorrect, because "Whoever drags his garment out of arrogance, Allah will not look at him"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3665) and Muslim (2085/44), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar.]] has not wronged anyone.
* A student: Shaykh, the minor sins are mentioned in contrast to the major sins: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your bad deeds﴾. What is the basis of the contrast?
* The Shaykh: How, what (...)?
* The student: That is, the expiation of bad deeds in general.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but the major sins and bad deeds were mentioned. He did not say: We will expiate their major sins for you or expiate them for you. He said: If you avoid, We will expiate the bad deeds; that is, We will expiate the minor sins.
* A student: Does (...) include both major and minor sins?
* The Shaykh: No, no. Now, how can we say: one who avoids major sins while committing them?! Is that clear?
* A student: Shaykh, the third line from the bottom of the benefits of His saying, exalted is He, is written: ﴿And whoever does that by transgression and wrongdoing, We will burn him in a Fire﴾.
* The Shaykh: From the benefits of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever does that by transgression and wrongdoing﴾.
* * *
* A student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your bad deeds and admit you to an honourable entrance (31). And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others. For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned. And ask Allah of His bounty. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing of all things (32). And for all We have made heirs to what is left by parents and close relatives, and those with whom your oaths have been made, give them their share. Indeed, Allah is ever Witness over all things (33)﴾ [al-Nisa' 31-33].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever does that by transgression and wrongdoing, We will burn him in a Fire.﴾ Is transgression (udwan) the same as wrongdoing (zulm), or something else?
* A student: It has been said that they are synonymous.
* The Shaykh: It has been said that they are synonymous. And what else has been said?
* A student: That transgression occurs deliberately and intentionally, and is directed at others, whereas wrongdoing is against oneself, such as sins.
* The Shaykh: So it has been said that they are distinct: transgression refers to wronging others intentionally and deliberately, and wrongdoing refers to wronging oneself. Which is more correct?
* A student: What is the question, Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: Are they distinct or synonymous?
* The student: No (...), Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: Which is more correct?
* A student: Distinct.
* The Shaykh: Distinct on what basis?
* The student: In the sense of this?
* The Shaykh: In the sense of: on what basis did you judge that they are distinct?
* A student: That the basic principle in speech is establishing a new meaning and difference.
* The Shaykh: Yes, on the basis that the basic principle in speech is establishing a new meaning and difference, that is, not emphasis and synonymy.

I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted is He, said: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your bad deeds and admit you to an honourable entrance.﴾
* From the benefits of this noble verse: what is forbidden is divided into major and minor sins, as His saying indicates: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your bad deeds.﴾
* Among its benefits: people differ in their faith. The reasoning is that faith increases with increased action, in quantity, quality or type. Here Allah divided sins into two categories, and the more a person is engaged in a greater sin, the more deficient and lesser his faith becomes. From this it is derived that faith increases and decreases, and this is the position of the majority of the People of the Sunna: that faith increases and decreases, based on the Book, the Sunna and observed reality. Do you understand? From the Book, Allah, blessed and exalted is He, said: ﴿As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith﴾ [al-Tawba 124], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So that those given the Scripture may be certain, and those who believed may increase in faith﴾ [al-Muddaththir 31]. Is there evidence of decrease in the two verses? Yes, because increase cannot be conceived except over something that falls short of it; there must be a deficiency. From the Sunna, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "I have not seen anyone more deficient in intellect and religion (he meant women) who takes away the intellect of a resolute man more than one of you."[[Reported by al-Bukhari (304), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]]

As for observed reality, it is evident. According to the People of the Sunna, deeds are part of faith, and deeds vary by increase. Is that not so? The one who prays ten rak'ahs is not equal to the one who prays six. This is apparent and perceptible. Likewise in the heart: faith increases and decreases in the heart. The proof is that Abraham said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. He said: Have you not believed? He said: Yes, but so my heart may be at rest﴾ [al-Baqara 260], in order to increase firmness and faith. You yourself feel that your faith in a matter increases in the heart. If a reporter comes to you with a report, and he is trustworthy in your view, you believe his report. If another like him comes and reports the same report, your faith undoubtedly increases; and if he reports the opposite, your earlier faith in what the trustworthy one told you weakens. Is that not so? This is something observed. Likewise regarding watchfulness of Allah, mighty and majestic is He. A person sometimes finds in himself that his heart is present before his Lord, and that he is at his sweetest and most delightful, and that he has tasted the flavour of faith, to the point that he wishes he could be only in this joy, and wants neither this world nor the Hereafter. He sees nothing better or more pleasant than the hour he is in, whether he is in prayer, or reciting the Qur'an, or reflecting on the biography of the Prophet, peace be upon him.
The proof is that Abraham said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. He said: Have you not believed? He said: Yes, but so my heart may be at rest﴾ [al-Baqara 260], in order to increase firmness and faith. You yourself feel that your faith in a matter increases in the heart. If a reporter comes to you with a report, and he is trustworthy in your view, you believe his report. If another like him comes and reports the same report, your faith undoubtedly increases; and if he reports the opposite, your earlier faith in what the trustworthy one told you weakens. Is that not so? This is something observed.
Likewise regarding watchfulness of Allah: a person sometimes finds that his heart is present before his Lord, and that he is at his sweetest and most delightful, and that he has tasted the flavour of faith, to the point that he wishes he could be only in this joy, and wants neither this world nor the Hereafter. He sees nothing better or more pleasant than the hour he is in, whether he is in prayer, or in recitation of the Qur'an, or in reflection on the biography of the Prophet, peace be upon him.
Sometimes heedlessness overtakes him, and he prays with the same recitation he recited yesterday, but his heart is stone and does not soften, while the time is the same time, the place is the same place, and the action is the same action.

A person prays in the last part of the night, one night finding great sweetness in this prayer and feeling close to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and another night finding the opposite, feeling that he has nothing of the meaning of worship. Which is stronger in faith: yesterday or today? Yesterday is far stronger. Even the Companions said: "O Messenger of Allah, when we are with you and hear what you say, it is as if we see it with our own eyes, but when we go away and busy ourselves with wives and children, we forget." So he (ﷺ) said: «If you were always in the state you are in when with me, the angels would shake hands with you, but (it is) an hour and an hour»[[Narrated by Muslim (12 / 2750) from the hadith of Handhalah al-Usaydi, with a similar wording.]]. An hour and an hour.

So faith increases in feeling. It increases in feeling, without doubt. But obedience undoubtedly increases faith, on the condition that it is accompanied by the work of the heart. As for the work of the limbs when it is not accompanied by the work of the heart, it does not increase faith, and may diminish faith, may Allah protect us, because it becomes mere futility. But when the works of the limbs are accompanied by the works of the heart, such as fear, hope, and seeking reward from Allah, then without doubt the heart increases through obedience. Therefore this matter must be considered.

Who are those who said: it neither increases nor decreases? There are two groups, or rather three groups. The Murji'ah said: it neither increases nor decreases, because good and bad deeds have no bearing on faith. People are, in their view, equal in faith, like a comb, as Ibn al-Qayyim said in his Nuniyyah:

"People in faith are one single thing, like a comb when its teeth are equal."

The teeth of the comb are equal, so people are the same in their view. And what is faith in their view? Merely affirmation and acknowledgment. Even Satan is a believer in their view, because he affirms. For this reason Ibn al-Qayyim said:

"Ask the father of the accursed jinn: do you know the Creator, or have you become one who denies?"

Does the father of the accursed jinn know the Creator or not? He knows Him and calls upon Him, saying: "My Lord, give me respite." Yet he is the greatest disbeliever of Allah's creation.

The second group that opposed: the Khawarij. And what will make you know what the Khawarij are! They are people of apparent deeds and ruined inner hearts. The Khawarij say: if a person commits a major sin, he leaves faith and his blood and property become lawful, because he is a disbelieving apostate. So in their view faith does not increase; it either exists entirely or is entirely absent. If a person is free from major sins and from persistence in minor sins, and performs the obligations and duties, then he has what? The complete faith. But if he commits one major sin, all his faith is destroyed. Who are these? The Khawarij.

The third group: the Mu'tazilah resembled the Khawarij in that faith neither increases nor decreases. But they do not say that the perpetrator of a major sin is a disbeliever. They say: faith neither increases nor decreases; either one is a complete believer, or otherwise one is neither a believer nor a disbeliever. In their view the perpetrator of a major sin is neither a believer nor a disbeliever, because they looked with a blind eye. They looked at the fact that he still has the root of faith, and said: faith has left him through the major sin, but he still has the root of faith, so we do not say he is a disbeliever, and we do not say he is a believer. We say: he is in an intermediate position between two positions. And where is that position? Where is it in the Qur'an and the Sunnah? They invented it. They said: it is like a man who leaves Makkah heading for Madinah and stops midway on the road. What is he? He is neither in Makkah nor in Madinah; he is in a position between two positions. But they agreed with the Khawarij that he will be eternal in the Fire, so his rulings in the Hereafter are like his rulings according to the Khawarij.

As for the People of the Sunnah and the Congregation, may Allah make us and you steadfast upon their saying until death, they said: no. Faith increases and decreases, disbelief has degrees, and a person may have characteristics of faith and characteristics of disbelief. The perpetrator of a major sin does not leave faith. Rather, describe him as: a believer by his faith, a sinner by his major sin; or say that he is a believer with deficient faith. Do not give him the unqualified name, and do not strip him of the name entirely. Say: he has deficient faith, or: he is a believer by his faith and a sinner by his major sin. This is justice and balance: that a person be described by what his deeds require, whether faith or disbelief.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: minor sins are expiated by avoiding major sins, based on His saying: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your evil deeds﴾ [An-Nisa' 31]. So if one does not avoid major sins, is he held accountable for minor sins?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, he is held accountable for minor sins, but major and minor sins are subject to Allah's will, so long as they are not disbelief.

So what is the benefit of our saying that he is held accountable for them? The benefit is that when he avoids major sins, we are certain that Allah has expiated his minor sins; and when he does not avoid major sins, he is under Allah's will and in danger.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others. For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned. And ask Allah of His bounty. Indeed, Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing (32). And for all We have made heirs to what is left by parents and close relatives. And to those whom your oaths have bound, give them their share. Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, Witness (33)﴾ [An-Nisa' 32-33].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. From the benefits of the verse: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾.
* From its benefits: affirmation of the greatness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, based on His saying: ﴿We will remove﴾ and ﴿and We will admit you﴾, because the "nun" here indicates magnification. The vile Christian has said: this indicates a plurality of gods, because the pronoun here is plural, so we are more entitled to the truth than you, O monotheists. We say to him: this is a matter of magnification, and you have had your heart sealed by Allah and have neglected the saying of Allah the Most High: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no deity except Him, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ [Al-Baqarah 163].
* From the benefits of this noble verse: the vastness of Allah's bounty, the Glorified and Exalted. This is seen in the expiation of evil deeds by avoiding major sins. Otherwise, if He repaid people with strict justice, He would punish them for minor sins and for major sins, each according to its measure. The punishment for major sins is severe, and for minor sins less. But by His bounty, the Mighty and Majestic, He made minor sins expiated by avoiding major sins. This is from the effect of His saying, the Glorified and Exalted, in the sacred hadith: «Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7422) and Muslim (15 / 2751) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, and the wording is al-Bukhari's.]].
* From the benefits of this noble verse: whoever Allah expiates his evil deeds for is among the people of Paradise, based on His saying: ﴿and We will admit you to an honorable entrance﴾.
* From its benefits: clarification that Paradise is the highest of what there is, and indeed it is one of the honorable entrances. And the honorable is according to each thing: the finest kinds of wealth are the best of them, and the finest kinds of dwellings are the best of them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Mu'adh ibn Jabal: «Beware of the choicest of their wealth»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1496) and Muslim (29 / 19) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal.]].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 32:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others.﴾ ﴿Do not wish﴾: (lā) is a prohibitive particle, and the verb is put in the jussive by dropping the nūn. ﴿That by which He has favoured﴾ is the object of ﴿wish﴾. So what is tamannī (wishing)? Tamannī is longing for something that is difficult or impossible to attain. This is tamannī: longing for something that is difficult or impossible to attain, like the words of the poet:

Oh, would that youth would return one day, so that I could tell it what old age has done!

This is longing for something that is impossible to attain. And the words of the poor man: "Would that I had wealth so that I could give charity from it." This is longing for something that is difficult to attain. Tamannī may also be used to mean rajā' (hope), the general sense of hoping, where a person longs for a matter that is easy to attain, even if he does not actually obtain it, but it would be easy to attain if Allah willed.

So His words ﴿do not wish﴾ mean: do not long for the matter by which Allah has favoured some of you over others. His words ﴿by which Allah has favoured﴾ mean: has increased. ﴿Some of you over others﴾ applies whether that is in knowledge, in wealth, in children, in standing, in dominion, or in anything else. Do not wish for that by which Allah has favoured another over you. For favour is in whose hand? It is in the hand of Allah: He gives it to whom He wills.

Then He said: ﴿For men there is a share of what they have earned, and for women there is a share of what they have earned.﴾ ﴿For men there is a share of what they have earned﴾: that share is what Allah gives them of reward for righteous deeds. ﴿And for women there is a share of what they have earned﴾: meaning, for women there is a share of righteous deeds, each according to what Allah has decreed for them. Men have jihad, and women have the keeping of the homes. There is a difference between jihad and keeping the homes. But who has favoured these with this and those with that, or who has singled out these with this and those with that? It is Allah. Since the matter belongs to Allah, Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is the Just Judge who gives each of the two sexes what befits it.

The explanation of what Allah has favoured men with will also come in His words: ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ [an-Nisa' 34].

The main point is that what Allah has favoured some people with over others, whether because of maleness, wealth, knowledge, health, money, or anything else, is from the favour of Allah. Do not wish for that by which Allah has favoured another over you.

Then He said: ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty.﴾ ﴿Ask﴾ (is'alū), and there is a reading ﴿salū Allāh﴾; both are recognised seven readings. ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty﴾ means: ask Him from that by which He has favoured some of you over others. When you ask Allah of His bounty, He gives you. For example, if you see a person who has been favoured over you in wealth, do not wish for the wealth that Allah has given that man, but ask Allah of His bounty. If you find a man favoured over you in knowledge, do not wish for the knowledge that Allah has given someone else, but ask Allah of His bounty, and leave his knowledge with him, and his wealth with him in the first case.

﴿And ask Allah of His bounty﴾: is the asking here a request for giving, or a request for knowledge?

* Students: What is "asking for giving"?

* The Shaykh: Asking for giving means that you ask Him, i.e., you request from Him that He give you wealth, as in His words: ﴿for the beggar and the deprived﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 19]. And sa'ala also means istakhbara (to inquire), that is, asking for knowledge, meaning one wants to be informed. So is this asking for wealth or asking for knowledge?

* Students: Asking for giving... asking for wealth.

* The Shaykh: Asking for giving, i.e., asking for wealth; meaning: ask Allah to give you. So it is asking for giving. We turned away from saying "asking for wealth" because a person may ask Allah for other than wealth, such as knowledge, standing, intelligence, reason, and the like.

﴿And ask Allah of His bounty. Indeed, Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing.﴾ This sentence is resumptive (isti'nāfiyyah), and the evidence that it is resumptive is that the hamza of (inna) is kasra'd, and the hamza of (inna) is kasra'd at the beginning of a sentence. Accordingly, it is a resumptive sentence explaining the cutting off of wishing, i.e., a person's wishing for what Allah has favoured another with over him. That is, what Allah has favoured another with is issued from knowledge that this one favoured is fit for favour. Men are fit for jihad, fit to protect the homelands, fit to protect the religion, and the like, unlike women, who are deficient.

* This verse contains many benefits. Among them: the prohibition on a person wishing for what Allah has favoured another with over him, from His words: ﴿And do not wish﴾. Is the prohibition for prohibition (taḥrīm)? The answer: yes, it is for prohibition, because this kind of wishing is envy (ḥasad), envy itself; for He said: ﴿that by which Allah has favoured﴾ and did not say: "like what Allah has favoured." Had He said "do not wish for the like," the matter would have been problematic, and the beginning of the verse would contradict its end in His words: ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty.﴾ Rather, the meaning of "do not wish" is that what Allah has favoured another with should become yours while that other is deprived of it. Accordingly we say: the prohibition here is for prohibition, and this kind is envy.

However, it should be known that wishing for what Allah has given another divides into three categories. The first: that one wishes for its removal from someone in general. The second: that one wishes for its removal from another person, not from the one wishing. The third: that one wishes for its removal to himself. Which of these is in the verse here? The first, the second, or the third?

* Students: The second.

* The Shaykh: No, ﴿And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others.﴾

* Students: The third.

* The Shaykh: The third. There is no doubt it is the third: wishing for the favour that Allah has given another. But the first and second are known from other evidences: it is forbidden for a person to wish for the removal of Allah's blessing from another, whether he wishes it to pass to a specific person or to pass altogether. This is envy according to the majority of scholars. Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: envy is disliking what Allah has given this man of His bounty, whether one wishes its removal or does not wish its removal. So if you dislike what Allah bestows on another, this is envy.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, in giving and bestowing, in that He favours some over others. There is no doubt that this issues from wisdom and is not mere choice, contrary to those who deny Allah's wisdom and say that His action is merely by choice. Rather, the choice is a choice issuing from wisdom.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment that rulings revolve with their causes (`ilal), from His words: ﴿For men there is a share of what they have earned, and for women there is a share of what they have earned﴾. The share of men befits them, and the share of women befits them.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of a person wishing for the like of what Allah has favoured another with over him, its basis being His words: ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty.﴾ So we do not say to you: do not wish that Allah give you the like of what He gave so-and-so. We say: there is no harm, but do not wish for what Allah has given so-and-so. There is a difference between the two.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the distinction between the two sexes, men and women. It has been said that the verse was revealed because some women said, when Allah revealed: ﴿To the male, the like of the share of two females﴾ [an-Nisa' 11], "Would that we were men, so that we would have the like of the male and not be deficient compared to him." [Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir (9249) from the hadith of Qatadah.] Whether or not this cause is authentic, the verse indicates that there is a difference between the two sexes, contrary to those who try to place the two sexes under one ruling, or who try to favour women over men.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the vastness of Allah's bounty and generosity, from His words: ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty.﴾ He, glorified and exalted is He, did not command us to ask except that He would give us. For had He commanded us to ask without giving us, this would be what? Vain, without benefit. But He, mighty and majestic, is the Generous who presents Himself to His servants, saying: "Ask Me." ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty.﴾

In asking, one should observe the proper etiquette, which is that you ask Allah, glorified and exalted is He, as one who is in need, not as one who is self-sufficient. This is the first. You ask Allah, glorified and exalted is He, as one who trusts in his Lord and that He is able, not as a trial. You ask as one who trusts in Allah and that He is able to give, as one who trusts in the promise of Allah and that He gives the asker what he asked.

A person should choose the times, places, and states that are a cause of answer. Examples of times: the last part of the night, and the period between the adhān and the iqāmah. Examples of places: what? 

* Students: Prostration.

* The Shaykh: No.

* Students: Makkah and the virtuous places.

* The Shaykh: Yes, that one is in virtuous places.

Examples of states: the state of prostration, the state of travel, the state of rain falling. A person should choose what is closest to being answered.

Fifthly: that he should avoid what is unlawful, for eating what is unlawful is a barrier that prevents the acceptance of supplication. The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed Allah is Good and accepts only what is good, and Allah has commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things We have provided for you and be grateful to Allah﴾" and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and act righteously﴾. Then he mentioned a man who prolongs travel, dishevelled and dusty, who raises his hands to the sky saying: "O Lord, O Lord," while his food is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he is nourished with the unlawful. He said: "How could he be answered?" [Narrated by Muslim (65/1015), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] Here "how" (anná) is an interrogative of astonishment, meaning: it is far-fetched that this man should be answered.

Sixthly: that he should not transgress in supplication. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly. Indeed, He does not like transgressors﴾ [al-A'raf 55]. If one transgresses in supplication by asking for what is not lawful for him, or rather by asking for what is impossible legally or by decree, then it will not be granted.

If he asks for sin, by saying, may Allah protect us, "O Allah, make a woman available to him so he may commit adultery with her, or a cup of wine for him to drink," this will not be granted to him. It is transgression and mockery of Allah, mighty and majestic is He. This is impossible legally; it cannot be accepted, because it is legally impossible.

Impossible by decree, such as saying, "O Allah, make me a prophet." This is impossible by decree through the report of Allah, not because it is impossible in its essence; it is not impossible in itself, but by the report of Allah it has become impossible, as in His words: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any one of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets﴾ [al-Ahzab 40]. All of these are etiquettes which a person should observe in supplication.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment of the comprehensiveness of Allah's knowledge, from His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing.﴾

* Among its benefits: conviction in what Allah has decreed, legally or by decree. How so? Because when I know that it issues from knowledge, I am convinced. I say: had it not been that there is benefit in the existence of this thing, Allah would not have made it, for Allah, glorified and exalted is He, does not act except with knowledge. This increases my conviction in what Allah has decreed, legally or by decree.

* Among its benefits: the obligation of vigilance, vigilance toward Allah. For the intelligent person, when he knows that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, knows him, he will be vigilant toward his Lord with his tongue, his heart, and his limbs. With his tongue, how does he remain vigilant toward Allah with his tongue?

* Student: He does not say what Allah has forbidden.

* The Shaykh: He does not say what Allah has forbidden. And with his heart?

* Student: With his heart he does not believe in anything Allah has forbidden.

* The Shaykh: That is, he does not hold as permissible anything Allah has forbidden, or he says in his heart something Allah has forbidden, because the speech of the heart is its movement and its action. With his limbs: meaning his bodily parts.

We ask Allah to grant us and you faith, for when a person truly believes in this, he will be vigilant toward Allah, because Allah knows him. Indeed, Allah said: ﴿And know that Allah knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him﴾ [al-Baqarah 235].

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And to each We have made heirs (mawali) of that which is left by parents and close relatives.﴾ ﴿To each﴾ is a prepositional phrase (jar wa-majrur) attached to ﴿We have made﴾ (ja'alna), with it as the second object placed first, and ﴿mawali﴾ as the first object.

The word ﴿li-kull﴾ ("to each") is one of those words that are never used except when they are annexed (mudaf), either explicitly or implicitly. Explicitly, as in much usage: ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾ [al-Hijr 30]. Implicitly, one supposes an appropriate annexed noun for the context. So which is appropriate here? The estimate is: "And to every person We have made heirs, to every male and female."

﴿We have made mawali﴾ means: We have appointed. ﴿Mawali﴾ is the plural of (mawla), and mawla is used with several meanings, among them the helper (nasir). The word mawla is used for the helper, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you two back each other against him, then indeed Allah is his protector (mawla), and Jibril﴾ [al-Tahrim 4], meaning: his helper. It is also used for one who takes charge of another, meaning one who exercises authority over another, as in: ﴿Know that Allah is your protector (mawlakum), an excellent protector and an excellent helper﴾ [al-Anfal 40].

Mawla is also used for the one who frees (mu'tiq) and for the one who is freed (ʿatiq), right? It is used for the one who frees, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Loyalty (al-wala') belongs only to the one who frees"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2155), and Muslim (5/1504) from the hadith of ʿAʾishah.]], and it is used for the one who is freed, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The mawla of a people is from among them"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6761) from the hadith of Anas.]], meaning: their freed slave.
