It is also used for one who manages affairs, such as a king, a commander, a minister, or what is similar to that, and he is also called "the one in charge of affairs" (waliy al-amr).

What remains is the last meaning, which is the one in this verse: mawla, meaning the one who takes over your property after you, and that is the heir. Its evidence is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Give the shares of inheritance to their people; then whatever remains belongs to the nearest male relative"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6737), and Muslim (3/1615) from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas.]], and from it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And blood relatives are more entitled to one another﴾ [al-Anfal 75].

﴿We have made mawali﴾ means: they take charge of his estate after him; therefore He said: ﴿mawali of that which he left﴾.

And His saying: ﴿the parents and the close relatives﴾. ﴿The parents﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and ﴿and the close relatives﴾ is conjoined to it, and it is an explanation of the mawali. This is one of the two interpretations of the verse. On this view, the pause falls after His saying: ﴿And to each We have made mawali of that which is left﴾, and then ﴿the parents and the close relatives﴾.

The second opinion: that ﴿the parents﴾ is the agent (fa'il) of ﴿left﴾. So ﴿And to each We have made mawali of that which is left by the parents and the close relatives﴾, meaning: We have made heirs of what was left by the parents and close relatives.

The two meanings are mutually linked, but which of them is closer to the wording? Some scholars hold that the second is closer, namely that ﴿the parents﴾ is the agent of ﴿left﴾, with ﴿the close relatives﴾ conjoined to it, and the meaning is: to every person among mankind We have made mawali, that is heirs, of what the parents and close relatives left. On this view, are the parents inheritors or inherited from? On the latter, they are those inherited from; on the former, they are heirs. As I told you: the two meanings are mutually linked, because there is no heir except that he has someone he inherits from. So whether you say ﴿We have made mawali of that which is left﴾, meaning they take charge of it from what was left, namely the parents and close relatives, who are the heirs; or of what the parents and close relatives left, who are the ones inherited from.

As for His saying ﴿the close relatives (al-aqrabun)﴾: it came in the form of the superlative and not (al-qaribun), because in the case of relatives one begins with the nearest, then the nearest.

* Student: Is the word "mawliyyah" used for shaykhs?
* The Shaykh: It may be used; it is valid, because they take charge of people's affairs through knowledge.
* Student: ﴿And ask Allah for His bounty﴾ — does it refer to the beginning of the verse, or to the preference of men over women?
* The Shaykh: It is general.
* Student: There is no difficulty?
* The Shaykh: There is no difficulty, because something else may compensate the woman if she falls short of the man.
* Student: May Allah reward you, Shaykh: His saying ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾ — is there evidence in it that killing a soul is among the major sins?
* The Shaykh: I said the verse did not specify any particular major sin, any major sin; and it is known that killing a soul is a major sin.
* Student: Shaykh, is it reported that wishing for the removal of another's blessing is envy?
* The Shaykh: There is no doubt.
* Student: Then, Shaykh, how do we oppose Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed; because the words of Shaykh al-Islam, the dislike of God's favouring another with this, contain a kind of objection to the decree of Allah the Exalted.
* Student: Shaykh, I read in a treatise by the Shaykh mentioning this meaning.
* The Shaykh: Which one?
* Student: He said: it is wishing for the removal of the blessing.
* The Shaykh: No, he said: it is dislike, and he said: this is better than the definition of (...).
* Student: If a slave frees a slave, then buys another slave and frees him, so that now he is a higher mawla (...) and has lower mawali, and he said: I bequeathed (...)?
* The Shaykh: Do we take mawali to mean the first, direct one? The first. Good. We mentioned the mawla from below, and we are not concerned here with mentioning inheritance: does the lower mawla inherit or not? The well-known view is that he does not inherit, and Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, chose that he inherits when the three causes of inheritance are absent.
* Student: What is your view of someone who asks Allah, Glorified and Exalted, but is not confident of being answered, not out of bad opinion of Allah but out of accusing himself?
* The Shaykh: No, this is not appropriate; it should not come from him; rather he should be certain. That is why the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "None of you should say: O Allah, forgive me if You wish"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6339), and Muslim (8/2679) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].
* Student: May Allah protect you, if such a verse passes during prayer, should the person supplicate? And should he begin with praise and blessings upon the Prophet, as mentioned in the hadith?
* The Shaykh: What do you say? He asks: if it passes in prayer, ﴿and ask Allah for His bounty﴾, should one ask Allah from His bounty? Or is this restricted to a particular situation, namely when it arises in a person's heart to wish for what Allah has favoured another with? In any case, asking from His bounty is without doubt legislated at all times. But if we say that Allah said ﴿and ask Allah for His bounty﴾ meaning: when it falls into your hearts to wish for what Allah has favoured some of you over others — if we say this, then it is not prescribed for a person to ask from His bounty while reciting it.
* Student: Grammar, Shaykh: ﴿al-walidan﴾ as a subject in the nominative?
* The Shaykh: We said: in its grammatical analysis there are two possibilities. The first is that it is the predicate of an omitted subject; the second is that it is the agent of ﴿left﴾, and the meaning differs.
* Student: Shaykh, the definition of Shaykh al-Islam, that it is the dislike of what Allah has favoured another with — does sin follow from it, given that it is merely an inner conversation of the soul?
* The Shaykh: And if he dislikes it, then dislike is not mere inner talk; dislike is an act of the heart, just as love is an act of the heart. When he settles into dislike, it becomes an action. But if this dislike occurs in his heart and he then repels it, saying to himself: Why are you envying your fellow? Envy is a characteristic of the Jews, and envy brings nothing but misery — if he drives it away, there is no harm; it is like a passing thought that comes to a person and he expels it, like showing off (riya'), for example. But if he settles into it and his heart remains disliking this thing, and whenever Allah bestows a blessing on His servant, his heart is wrung with intense dislike — this is an action.
* Student: ﴿Men have a share of what they have earned﴾ — does the particle "min" here imply partiality, so that the meaning is that it is part of this thing?
* The Shaykh: What do you say? He says: "min" is partitive in ﴿a share of what they have earned﴾, and likewise in ﴿what they have earned﴾ for women; and the bounty with Allah is not lost?
* Student: "Min" could be causal, because of this.
* The Shaykh: Good, that is not it.
* Student: "Min" is never partitive absolutely.
* The Shaykh: It is explanatory, to explain the kind: a share of this.
But what may cause difficulty is His saying ﴿a share﴾: why would they not have all that they earned? So is the difficulty in the word ﴿a share﴾?
* Student: No, Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: Do you have an answer?
* Student: ﴿A share of what they have earned﴾ may be good and may not be good.
* The Shaykh: If Allah says: a share of their earnings, then this share has been specified by Allah.
* Student: The wish in the verse, Shaykh, is specific to the believers. May I wish for the removal of a disbeliever's blessing?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, but not out of envy; rather out of retribution. That is not objectionable.
* Student: Some exegetes, regarding His saying ﴿And ask Allah for His bounty﴾, restricted it to this world, and some to the Hereafter. Is this correct?
* The Shaykh: What do you want? What do you wish: that the statement be correct or incorrect? The verse is general.

* * *

* Student: ﴿Over them a way. Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted and Grand﴾.
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And to each We have made mawali of that which is left by the parents and close relatives, and those with whom your oaths have been made — give them their share. Indeed Allah is ever, over all things, Witness﴾. When Allah the Exalted mentioned — rather, when He forbade wishing for what He has favoured some of us over others, and among it the favouring of men over women in inheritance — He stated, Mighty and Majestic, that He has made for each, male or female, mawali. And (mawali) is the plural of (mawla), and mawla is used with several meanings, among them: the one in charge of affairs, the helper, the one who frees, and the one who is freed. It has several meanings, and a single word whose meanings are multiple is called, among the scholars, a homonym (mushtarak).

Some people, especially the heretics (zanadiqah), have criticised the Arabic language, saying that Arabic is poor because of its homonyms, one word having multiple meanings, and that the Arabs were unable to give each meaning its own independent word. This speaker is unjust in his judgment, because if he claims that homonymy is poverty and deficiency in the language and an inability to give each meaning its own specific word, he has overlooked its opposite, namely synonymy (taraduf). Synonymy is an enrichment and breadth of the Arabic language, in that two or more words are used for one meaning. The fair-minded person considers both sides.

Moreover, homonyms are evidence of the Arabs' shrewdness, intelligence and acuity, in that they interpret each word by what suits it in context. The word "ayn," for example, comes in one context and is meant in one sense, and in another context is meant in another sense. This is evidence that the Arabs had strong acuity and insight, such that the meaning of a single word with multiple meanings is determined according to the context.

It also opens the door to reflection and contemplation: a person pauses, saying: this word is used with several meanings, so what is its meaning in this context? It requires that the person exert himself, reflect and consider. But some people are biased or superficial, and they charge the Arabic language with what it is innocent of.

So "mawla" has several meanings; what determines the meaning? Context and circumstantial indicators. This is what determines the meaning: context is verbal indication, and circumstances are situational indication that clarifies what is intended.

As for His saying: ﴿We have made mawali of that which is left by the parents and close relatives﴾: ﴿mawali of that which he left﴾, the phrase ﴿of that which he left﴾ is attached to an omitted element, and the meaning does not stand if we attach it to ﴿mawali﴾. The omitted element is estimated according to what suits the context; ﴿left﴾ is suited by (inheritance, irth).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, the equivalent of the share of two females﴾ [al-Nisa' 11], and in the next verse He said: ﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾ [al-Nisa' 12]. So when He said ﴿of what the parents left﴾, we understand that the omitted element is: they inherit of what the parents and close relatives left. This estimate is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Give the shares of inheritance to their people; then whatever remains belongs to the nearest male relative"[[Previously cited.]].

So ﴿of that which he left﴾: "min" is explanatory or partitive, and the attached element is omitted, estimated as "they inherit": ﴿of that which the parents left﴾, namely the father and mother; ﴿and the close relatives﴾, namely all besides the two parents. We explained "close relatives" as those other than the two parents even though the parents are the closest of people, because conjunction requires difference. So Allah made the mawali inherit of what the parents left.

And who are these mawali who inherit of what the parents left? They are the descendants (furu'), namely the offspring; so the heir is the one born, and they are the descendants. Allah the Exalted has explained in His Book how they inherit: if only males remain, or only females, or both. If only females remain, their inheritance is only by fixed shares (fard). If only males remain, their inheritance is only by residuary entitlement (ta'sib). If both remain, their inheritance is by residuary entitlement, but its basis differs: males are residuary in their own right (asabah bi-al-nafs), and females are residuary through others (asabah bi-al-ghayr), meaning through the males; they become residuaries because of others.

As for His saying ﴿and the close relatives﴾: this is a broad word, and He did not say "the relatives (al-qarabat)" but said ﴿the close relatives (al-aqrabun)﴾, because inheritance goes to the nearest then the nearest. Even among those with fixed shares, the nearer is preferred over the more distant: a daughter with a son's daughter: she has one half, and the son's daughter has one sixth; two daughters exclude the son's daughters; a full sister with a half-sister: she has one half, and two full sisters exclude the half-sisters; and so on. That is why He said ﴿the close relatives﴾, meaning: the nearest then the nearest.

﴿And those with whom your oaths have been made﴾: it has two seven-fold readings: ﴿'aqadat﴾ and ﴿'aqadat﴾... from (mu'aqadah), which is mutual covenanting, and the covenant was called "aqd" because it is the binding of an agreement between the contracting parties. In the pre-Islamic period they used to contract with one another regarding loyalty and inheritance, according to conditions between them: one would say, "For you is a sixth of what I leave, or a third, or a quarter," according to what they agreed upon.

﴿And those with whom your oaths have been made — give them their share﴾: "give" (ataw) means give them. In the Arabic language: "ata" with the long vowel means to give, and "ata" with the short vowel means to come. The form with the long vowel means giving, and it governs two objects, both of which are complements (fudlah), not core elements (umdah), meaning their original structure is not subject and predicate.

﴿Give them their share﴾: this governs two objects, neither of which originally forms a subject and predicate. "Give": give them their share. What is their share? Their share is estimated according to what the contracting parties agreed upon, because this is part of fulfilling the covenant, and fulfilling covenants is something the Sharia has brought. The Prophet (ﷺ) warned strongly against breaking promises and stated that it is a trait of whom?

* Students: The hypocrites.
* The Shaykh: The hypocrites.

﴿Give them their share. Indeed Allah is ever, over all things, Witness﴾: the sentence, as we know, is declarative, emphasized with "inna," and "kana" is a past-tense verb that conveys the attribution of its subject to its predicate in a continuous and enduring manner; it is stripped of time, meaning it does not indicate a past time as is the case with the past tense, but rather indicates the established attribution of this quality from eternity to eternity.

﴿Witness﴾ means: an observer, one who oversees everything. This sentence is a resumptive statement (isti'nafiyyah) conveying a warning: a warning to whoever conceals any part of what is due to the parents, close relatives and those with whom your oaths have been made; for if he conceals it, it will not be hidden from Allah the Exalted, rather He is Witness over all things.

This verse was abrogated by the verses of inheritance. Is this abrogation restricted (muqayyad) or absolute (mutlaq)? On this there are two opinions among the scholars. Some said: it is a restricted abrogation, applying only when there are relatives by blood (dhawu al-arham); if none exist, the contracting parties inherit according to what they agreed upon. Others said: it is an absolute abrogation, so there is no inheritance by mutual alliance at all. The second is the view of the majority of scholars, and the first is the view of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him.

The apparent meaning is that the verse presents no difficulty from the standpoint of i'rab (Arabic grammatical analysis).

* A student: ﴿al-walidani wa-l-aqrabun﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿al-walidani wa-l-aqrabun﴾. Is there a difficulty in it? I do not think there is any difficulty.
* A student: The stronger view?
* The Shaykh: The stronger view is the one supported by evidence. That is the stronger view.
* Among the benefits of the verse: affirming that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, makes (ja'l). This is among the attributes of action (sifat fi'liyyah), because it is connected to His will.
Then the ja'l that Allah attributes to Himself, the Mighty and Majestic, is divided into two kinds: legislative ja'l (shar'i) and cosmic ja'l (kawni). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We made you more numerous in manpower﴾ [al-Isra' 6] is cosmic ja'l. His saying ﴿And We made the night as clothing, and We made the day for livelihood﴾ [al-Naba' 10-11] and what is similar to them are all cosmic ja'l. His saying here, ﴿For every one We have made heirs﴾, is legislative ja'l. Likewise His saying ﴿Allah has not instituted any bahirah or sa'ibah or wasilah﴾ [al-Ma'idah 103] is legislative ja'l, and it cannot be cosmic ja'l. Why? ﴿Allah has not instituted any bahirah﴾, why can it not be cosmic ja'l?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It cannot be cosmic ja'l, because it exists in one case and is negated in the other. So Allah did not legislate it, but He did decree it. The difference between legislative ja'l and decreed (qadari) ja'l is like the difference between legislative will and cosmic will. Legislative ja'l is loved by Allah, and it may or may not occur from the servants. Cosmic ja'l is not connected to what Allah loves; it occurs in what He loves and in what He does not love, and it certainly happens.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirming inheritance by lineage (nasab) and by cause (sabab). By lineage, from His saying ﴿from what the parents and the close relatives leave﴾. By cause, from His saying ﴿and those whom your oaths have bound﴾, since this cause is the person's own act. Marriage is a cause and not a lineage, and manumission is a cause and not a lineage.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the indication that the nearer has precedence over the more distant in the matter of inheritance. We derived this from His saying ﴿and the close relatives﴾, and we mentioned in the explanation what clarifies this matter.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the perfection of the Islamic Shari'ah in requiring the fulfilment of covenants and contracts, from His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and those whom your oaths have bound﴾.
* Among its benefits: the occurrence of naskh (abrogation) in the Shari'ah, because this verse is abrogated, either absolutely or with a restricted abrogation. The scholars of the religion have differed about abrogation. Most of the Ummah hold that abrogation is established in the Shari'ah, from His saying ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring forth one better than it or similar to it﴾ [al-Baqarah 106]; and from His saying ﴿So now (al-an), have relations with them and seek what Allah has decreed for you, and eat and drink﴾ [al-Baqarah 187], where "now" (al-an) refers to what was previously forbidden; and from His saying ﴿Now Allah has lightened your burden, and He knows that there is weakness in you﴾ [al-Anfal 66], which is explicit in affirming abrogation; and from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I had forbidden you to visit graves, so visit them." [Recorded by Muslim (106/977) and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (1385), from Buraydah.]
Some scholars, among them Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, said: there is no abrogation in the Shari'ah. They interpreted abrogation as specification (takhsis), and said: the implication of the first ruling is that it continues until the Day of Resurrection. So when it is cancelled, this is a specification by time, meaning that it was once inclusive of all time and has become specific to the period before the abrogation. But this is an artificial interpretation. What makes us shy away from the word "naskh", when it is present in the Qur'an in its wording, present in the Qur'an in its meaning, and present in the Sunnah in its meaning as well? What makes us shy away?
The Jews denied abrogation and said: it is impossible for Allah to abrogate one ruling with another, because if the benefit lies in the second ruling, why was the first ruling given? And if the benefit lies in the first ruling, why was the second ruling given? And if the benefit of the first was hidden from Allah, then the first implies ascribing to Allah the attribute of foolishness, may Allah protect us, because He did something contrary to wisdom; and the second implies ascribing to Allah the attribute of ignorance. Is that clear?
It is said to them: benefit varies according to time, place and community. Is that not so? Yes. And if that is so, then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, establishes a ruling as long as it has benefit for the community, and abrogates it when it no longer has benefit. This is the utmost wisdom. And you, O Children of Israel, were permitted meat, but because of your wrongdoing Allah forbade you good things that had been made lawful for you. He forbade them to you after they had been lawful. Then your Shari'ah abrogates the Shari'ah that came before it. If you say "there is no abrogation", you nullify your own Shari'ah, because it abrogates what came before it.
So in the noble verse ﴿and those whom your oaths have bound﴾, there is an affirmation of abrogation.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation to fulfil the covenant, from His saying ﴿so give them their share﴾.
If someone says: how do we give them their share when the agreement, this covenant, is void? We say: it was not nullified except after what? After the abrogation, after the revelation of the verse. As for what was established before that, it is obligatory that they be given their share.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of the witnessing of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, over everything, and that everything, however distant and however hidden, is witnessed by Allah.
* It follows from this: a warning against opposing Allah, exalted is He. Why? Because when a person knows that Allah is witness over him, he refrains from everything that angers Allah and performs what is due to Allah. These names with which verses are concluded require that a person not remain rigid, understanding only the literal meaning from them. Rather, he should be educated by them, and his conduct should accord with what these names require. For example: when you know that Allah is "the Knower of the unseen" (`Allam al-Ghuyub), this does not mean merely that you realize Allah knows everything. This realization is shared by the disbeliever and the believer alike; even disbelievers who know Arabic know such a word. What matters is being shaped by the requirement of this attribute, which is knowledge of the unseen. This is an important matter that many people do not notice.
So it is said, for example: among the benefits of the noble verse is that when a person believes that Allah is witness over everything, what does he do? He becomes cautious, fears, and guards himself before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
And is al-Shahid (the Witness) one of Allah's names or one of His attributes?
* A student: One of His names.
* The Shaykh: One of Allah's names. Al-Shahid is one of Allah's names.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 34–35 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Men are in charge of women by [right of] what Allah has given one over the other and what they spend [for maintenance] from their wealth. So righteous women are devoutly obedient, guarding in [the husband's] absence what Allah would have them guard.﴾ To the end of the verse.

﴿Men﴾ is the plural of (rajul), which is a broken plural. A rajul is an adult male of the children of Adam; an adult male of the children of Adam is called a rajul, while the word (dhakar, male) applies to both adult and non-adult males. For this reason, the hadith reads: «And what remains goes to the nearest male man (rajul dhakar)» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6737) and Muslim (3/1615), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]], although had he said, "to the nearest male (dhakar)," it would have sufficed; and had he said, "to the nearest man (rajul)," it would have excluded the young boy, so that he would not be an 'asib (residuary heir). But the word (dhakar) was used to make clear that maturity is not a condition for entitlement to residuary inheritance, rather even one who has not reached manhood qualifies.

If someone says: then is the word (rajul) with (dhakar) redundant, a redundancy with no meaning? The answer: No, it has a meaning, which is to indicate that the male—i.e., the dhakar—is more entitled to residuary inheritance, because he is a rajul upon whom responsibilities fall that do not fall upon a woman.

﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ ﴿qawwamun﴾ is the plural of (qawwam), and (qawwam) is an intensive form (sigha mubalaghah) of (qa'im). Had it been said outside the Qur'an, "men are standing over women (qa'imun)," the meaning would have been weaker than the word (qawwamun), because (qawwamun) is an intensive form that implies authority over women in every situation.

As for His saying ﴿over women﴾ (ʿala al-nisa'): it is the plural of what? It is the plural of (niswah), and if you wish you may say it is the plural of (imra'ah, woman), but it is a plural not derived from the same root as the singular, since sometimes the meaning is pluralized in a form different from the singular, as (ibil, camels) is a plural with no singular from its own root; its singular is (ba'ir).

He says: ﴿by [right of] what Allah has given one over the other﴾. The (ba') here indicates causation, and (ma) may be either a verbal-masdar (maṣdariyyah) or a relative pronoun (mawsulah). If you make it a relative pronoun, the sense becomes: "by that which Allah has given some of them over others," and then we need a returning pronoun (a'id) that refers back to the relative pronoun; the returning pronoun is then omitted, its sense being: "by that with which Allah has given some of them over others." The omission of a returning pronoun governed by a preposition is well known in the language, and among its examples is His saying: ﴿He eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink﴾ [al-Mu'minun 33], meaning: "of it."

He says: ﴿by what Allah has given one over the other﴾. (fadhdhala) means "he gave more," and (al-fadl) is excess, i.e., some of them exceeded others. Who is the one given excess and who is the one over whom excess is given? The men are the ones given excess, and the women are the ones over whom it is given. So (ba'dahum) here refers to the men, and (ʿala ba'd) refers to the women. Then what is it with which Allah has given the men excess over the women?

* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What follows should be: ﴿and what they spend from their wealth﴾.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: He gave them excess over them.
* The Shaykh: That is, in apparent and inner strength. Apparent strength is physical strength; for this reason you find that the male, even among creatures other than the children of Adam, is stronger than the female, with larger and firmer muscles. These are apparent strengths. Inner strengths are endurance, patience, intelligence, reason, and what is similar to these.
* A student: And courage.
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed, and courage and determination. The point is that Allah has given men excess over women in apparent and inner strengths.

The second cause: He said: ﴿and what they spend from their wealth﴾, and this is an external preference. ﴿And what they spend﴾ refers to the men, ﴿from their wealth﴾ means on the women. The man is responsible for maintaining the woman, and the woman is weak and cannot earn; so the man is the one responsible.

As for His saying ﴿from their wealth﴾, it means the wealth of the men. Thus, by reason of physical preference (apparent and inner strength), and by reason of external preference, which is spending from one's wealth, the man has become superior to the woman.

* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, the bequest is independent; he may bequeath to these and to others according to what he sees as beneficial.
* A student: Prophethood and messengership (...)?
* The Shaykh: That is the apparent view, because a man's readiness for prophethood and messengership is more complete than a woman's readiness.
* * *
* A student: ﴿by what Allah has given one over the other and what they spend from their wealth. So righteous women are devoutly obedient, guarding in [the husband's] absence what Allah would have them guard. And those from whom you fear arrogance, admonish them, forsake them in bed, and strike them. But if they obey you, seek no means against them. Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted and Grand (34). And if you fear dissension between the two, appoint an arbiter from his people and an arbiter from her people. If they both desire reconciliation, Allah will cause it between them. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Acquainted (35).﴾ [al-Nisa' 34–35].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Men are in charge of women by [right of] what Allah has given one over the other﴾.

This is the beginning of tonight's lesson. Before beginning, we congratulate you on what Allah has bestowed upon us all: completing this blessed month of Ramadan in fasting and night prayer. We ask Allah the Exalted to accept from us and from you righteous deeds and to overlook our negligence and neglect. Among the wisdom and mercy of Allah the Mighty and Majestic toward His servants is that this noble month—whose fasting and night prayer cause the expiation of sins and forgiveness of wrongdoings—had no sooner ended than it was immediately followed by the months of Hajj to the House of Allah, concerning which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: «Whoever performs Hajj without obscenity or wickedness returns as on the day his mother bore him» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1521) and Muslim (438/1350), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah; the wording is al-Bukhari's.]]. Thus the seasons of goodness—praise be to Allah—are many and numerous, because Allah the Exalted has written a writ with Him that His mercy precedes His wrath. For this reason, the causes of mercy are far more numerous than the causes of punishment and seizure. All of this is from the mercy of Allah the Exalted toward the servant.

When the Muslim performs an act of obedience, he should be closer to hope than to fear. If we hope that Allah, who has blessed us with the deed, will accept it from us so that we attain this great virtue, then we should not return after it to evil deeds, negligence, and neglect. Rather, this should be a motivation for us to strive and exert ourselves in righteous deeds: in performing the specific acts of worship, and in benefiting the servants in general by all that we can, even with a good word, by enjoining good, forbidding evil, teaching, and even by giving the greeting of peace. The Prophet ﷺ said that giving the greeting of peace is among the causes of entering Paradise: «By Him in whose hand is my soul, you will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love one another. Shall I not inform you of something which, if you do it, you will love one another? Spread the greeting of peace among you» [[Narrated by Muslim (93/54) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. So spreading the greeting of peace is among the causes of love, love is among the perfection of faith, and faith is among the causes of entering Paradise; they are links of a chain, each following the other.

Regrettably, many people, and especially the distinguished students, we find do not spread the greeting of peace among themselves. A person passes by his brother without offering him the greeting of peace. This is without doubt an error and contrary to the legal etiquette which is among the fruits of seeking knowledge. And knowledge, if it is not beneficial, then ignorance is better than it, because the ignorant person knows his own state and may learn, and the ignorant is excused, unlike the scholar.

Likewise, it is incumbent upon us to cultivate affection among ourselves, especially among relatives, for «The likeness of the believers in their mutual love, their mercy, and their compassion is like the likeness of one body: when one of its limbs complains, the whole body responds to it with wakefulness and fever» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6011), and narrated by Muslim (66/2586) from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, and the wording is his.]].

And what is to be desired—indeed, what is obligatory—for the seeker of knowledge, if he truly wants knowledge, is that he be eager to acquire knowledge to the extent of his ability, by night and by day, in secret and in public, because the attainment of knowledge is lofty and elevated. It has been said: "Give knowledge all of yourself and it will give you a part of itself; if you give it only part of yourself, you will miss all of it." Therefore there must be eagerness and gathering: gathering of benefits, controls, and principles, because this is more beneficial to the seeker of knowledge than knowing isolated issues. Knowing isolated issues is shared by the layman and the seeker of knowledge, but gathering similar cases and gathering principles and controls is beneficial to the seeker of knowledge. For example, we find in the books of the jurists constant explanations (ta'lilat) of the legal rulings.

If the seeker of knowledge were to record these explanations, they would become controls upon which many issues are built. And if he finds that a given control does not hold universally and is broken in some issues, he may ask and investigate with one greater than himself in knowledge, and say: "Why do we give this explanation, and then the explanation is broken?" For the seeker of knowledge may think that the explanation is broken when in reality it is not broken; the matter is confused for him and he supposes it is broken, but it is not broken, because the case in which it appears broken differs from what this principle and control requires by a difference the young seeker of knowledge does not perceive. Therefore the seeker of knowledge should gather controls, principles, and similar issues until he comprehends knowledge fully.

As for superficial knowledge that a person picks up as a locust picks up grain, grain by grain, this is about to fly away and its possessor will not benefit from it. But firmly rooted knowledge, by which a person is able to apply issues to their foundations, is what I have mentioned here. I emphasize it: by knowing the controls and principles, gathering and classifying, until a person attains knowledge.

Then it is well known, especially in our present age because of the large number of students of knowledge—praise be to Allah—and because of the deficiency of some students from another angle, that differences arise, differences arise between your teachers at the college, for example, or between those you hear from outside, and confusion comes upon the seeker of knowledge. This is because some people are eager for knowledge and love to benefit others, so they hasten to spread among people what they consider to be knowledge so that people may benefit from it, but there is a flaw in it, and so it confuses the seeker of knowledge. For this reason, when a person sees among people a difference over some issues, it is good for him to discuss them with those between whom the difference exists until the matter becomes clear, because some people look at issues or evidences with one eye, and thereby much error results. Perhaps such a person has limited knowledge or limited understanding, so the matter becomes confused for him; and being a lover of spreading knowledge, he spreads what has become clear to him or what has appeared to him, even if it is contrary to the truth, because he loves to spread knowledge.

As for the abundance of pamphlets now, or the leaflets that are distributed and even pasted on the doors of mosques and on walls, some of these leaflets are certainly wrong, and the seeker of knowledge has no doubt that they are erroneous, whether they contain fabricated or weak hadiths or erroneous rulings. All of this comes from the love of some people for spreading their knowledge, but without a foundation. Such matters must be guarded against, and a person should investigate and discuss until he is upon clear proof.

We wished to say this word at the opening of the lesson after the blessed month of Ramadan—may Allah return it to us and to you and to the Muslims with goodness, blessing, and abundance—because at this time a person is energetic and finds in himself vigor to receive his time in seeking knowledge. We ask Allah for help for us and for you.

As for the verse you have just recited, we have explained it, I think, or we have explained most of it, have we not? Yes.

﴿Men are in charge of women by [right of] what Allah has given one over the other and what they spend from their wealth﴾. ﴿Qawwamun﴾ here is an intensive form or a relative form (nisbah), and what is meant by standing here is not standing on two feet, but the standing of guardianship: ﴿qawwamun﴾ means in guardianship and authority. It may therefore be a relative form, it may be an intensive form, and it may bear both meanings together, both relative and intensive. So the man is qawwam over the woman: ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾, and for this reason they hold guardianship, judgeship, leadership, and other positions involving authority, to the exclusion of women.

As for His saying ﴿over women by [right of] what Allah has given one over the other﴾: the (ba') here indicates causation, and (ma) may be a verbal-masdar or a relative pronoun. If it is a masdar, it needs no returning pronoun; if it is a relative pronoun, it needs one: ﴿by what Allah has given one over the other﴾. So on the view that it is a masdar, the sense is: "by Allah's giving preference to some of them over others"; and on the view that it is a relative pronoun, the sense is: "by that with which Allah has given some of them over others," the returning pronoun being omitted together with the preposition, as in His saying: ﴿He eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink﴾ [al-Mu'minun 33], meaning "of it," "of what you drink from it." The omission of a returning pronoun governed by a preposition is permissible when the two prepositions agree in form and meaning.

As for His saying ﴿by what Allah has given one over the other﴾, preference here means excess: by that with which Allah has given some of them excess over others. The preference between men and women is evident, in intellect, thought, body, courage, and everything; in all qualities and characteristics we find men preferred over women. This preference is considered on the basis of the category (jins), so it is not objected to that there exist some women better than many men; for when we speak of preference of a category, the consideration is the general case, not the particular. As we say, for example: the Successors (tabi'un) are better than the Successors of the Successors (taba' al-tabi'in), but this does not mean that every single Successor is better than every single Successor of the Successors; for among the Successors of the Successors there are those better than many of the Successors.

Thus His saying ﴿by what Allah has given one over the other﴾ means in general terms, not with regard to each individual. For this reason, no objection is to be raised of the kind: "We find a foolish man who knows nothing, and he is opposed by an intelligent, understanding woman who knows?" We say: this carries no weight, for what is the consideration? It is the category: ﴿by what Allah has given one over the other and what they spend from their wealth﴾.

﴿And what they spend from their wealth﴾ [al-Nisa' 34] is a coordination with His saying ﴿by what He has preferred﴾, meaning: and by that which they spend from their wealth; for the ones who spend on women are the men. Men spend on women because they are the ones who earn. A husband spends on his wife even if she is wealthy, and a father spends on his household. He is the source of expenditure. For this reason the men have guardianship, by Allah's preferring them in creation, character, intellect, and thought, and by their excelling over women in what? In spending. So they are qawwamun by Allah's preference of them and by their own excellence over women: ﴿and what they spend from their wealth﴾.

Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic divided women into two categories, saying: ﴿So righteous women are devoutly obedient, guarding in [the husband's] absence what Allah would have them guard﴾. ﴿Righteous women are devoutly obedient﴾: ﴿al-salihat﴾ is the subject, ﴿qanitat﴾ its predicate, and ﴿hafizat﴾ a second predicate.

﴿Al-salihat﴾ means those characterized by righteousness. Here we may say that ﴿al-salihat﴾ is an adjective of an omitted noun, the sense being: "So the righteous women." And who is the righteous one? The righteous one is the opposite of the corrupt; she is the one who fulfils the right of Allah and the right of her husband. This is the righteous woman.

As for His saying ﴿qanitat﴾: that is, persistent in righteousness, for qunut is meant in the sense of constancy, and this is the meaning intended here. It is also possible that what is meant by ﴿qanitat﴾ here is "obedient to Allah," as an emphasis: ﴿righteous women are devoutly obedient﴾, meaning obedient to Allah; and by their obedience to Allah they are also obedient to their husbands.

﴿So the righteous women are devoutly obedient and guard in secret what Allah has commanded them to guard﴾. This means they guard what is hidden from people, namely the secret affairs that take place in the husband's house and between her and her husband. You will find that a righteous woman does not allow anyone to see into her home. If she is asked about what happens in her house, she says, "We are fine." Consider the two wives of Isma'il. When Ibrahim asked one of them about their condition, she complained and showed her dissatisfaction, so he said to her, "When your husband comes, tell him to change the threshold of his door." The other one praised them well, and he said, "When the husband comes, tell him to keep the threshold of his door." Some women are complainers who expose and disclose to people everything that happens in their homes. Some of them, may Allah protect us, go even further and speak about what passes between them and their husbands, including private matters that only the husband should know. Such a woman is not among the righteous in any way. She has lost as much righteousness as she has lost of guarding.

﴿guarding in secret what Allah has guarded﴾. That is, by Allah's protection, or: by that which Allah has guarded, meaning He has commanded that it be guarded and not disclosed. So they guard the unseen, not revealing it, by Allah's protection of them and His favour upon them in preserving them. Or it means "by what Allah has guarded," i.e., what He has commanded to be guarded. The two meanings are mutually connected.

The second category is the opposite of this. He says: ﴿And those (wives) from whom you fear defiance, admonish them, forsake them in the beds, and strike them﴾. ﴿Those (wives)﴾ means: and the women from whom you fear defiance. How do we fear a wife's defiance? We fear it when its signs appear. Nushuz (defiance, disobedience) literally means elevation, as in the Arabic phrase al-ard al-nashiz, "the raised land." What is meant by nushuz is the wife's raising herself above her husband, such that she does not render what is obligatory upon her of his rights. Or she renders them but grudgingly and resentfully, so that he finds no comfort in her and does not feel at ease with her. Thus nushuz means raising oneself above what is owed to the husband. This happens when she does not obey him in what she is obliged to obey him, or she obeys but in a sulking, resentful, and weary manner, not giving him what is proper. This is nushuz. When a wife commits nushuz, the rights she has, such as maintenance and others, fall away, because maintenance is an exchange (mu'awadah), and if the countervalue is not present, it lapses.

﴿And those from whom you fear defiance﴾. So nushuz is a disease. Nushuz is a disease. Does it have a cure? Yes. Allah has mentioned a cure for it in three stages. The first, He says: ﴿admonish them﴾. The second: ﴿forsake them in the beds﴾. The third: ﴿strike them﴾. The fourth He did not mention because it is disliked by Him: divorce them. Unfortunately, this last one is the first stage for many people. Many people, if their wife opposes them in the slightest matter, divorce her. But the three stages Allah mentioned are the legislated stages. First: admonition. You admonish her by reminding her of what softens her heart. This is admonition: you remind her of her husband's right and of the reward she has if she fulfils it, and the punishment if she opposes it. You say to her, for example: "If you are obedient and fulfil what is due to me from you, I will reciprocate with its like or with something better." You promise her the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter, and you warn her of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, if she commits nushuz. If she complies, this is what is required. If not, He says: ﴿forsake them in the beds﴾. Hajr (forsaking) means leaving, and from it comes hijrah (emigration), which is a person leaving the land of disbelief for the land of Islam. Forsake them in the beds: that is, do not lie with them. You are in one bed and she is in another, or you are in one room and she is in another. This is the forsaking of the beds. If she mends her ways, this is what is required. If not, we move to the third stage, which is His saying: ﴿strike them﴾. This is the benefit of the qiwamah (guardianship) He mentioned: ﴿Men are the protectors and maintainers of women﴾. ﴿Strike them﴾. But with what?

The purpose of striking is discipline. You strike in a manner that achieves her discipline without causing her injury, that is, without wounding her. So you strike her with a strike that is not severe, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said in his Farewell Sermon: "And you have a right over them that they do not allow anyone you dislike to tread upon your bedding. If they do that, then strike them with a strike that is not severe."[[Recorded by Muslim (1218 / 147) from the hadith of Jabir.]] So she is struck, but with a strike that is not severe. It is obligatory to avoid, when striking her, what one has been commanded to avoid, such as the face, for example, for she is not to be struck there. This will come, Allah willing, in the explanation of the benefits.

﴿And strike them. Then if they obey you﴾. That is: they fulfil what is obligatory upon them of obedience.
﴿then do not seek a way against them﴾. The word tabghu (seek) means: seek a means against them. That is: leave the past. His saying ﴿then do not seek a way against them﴾ is not only for the future, but also for the past. Leave it, forget it, do not bring up investigation or stirring up of it, because reminding oneself of the past leads to the continuation of defiance and disobedience. ﴿Do not seek a way against them﴾, as if nothing had happened.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Most High, Most Great﴾. The sentence here is a resumptive statement (isti'nafiyyah) to warn against haughtiness and pride over women. For when a man feels that he is in charge of the woman and has authority over her, to the extent that the Shari'ah has empowered him to strike her in the third stage, he may become arrogant and proud over her. So the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Most High, Most Great﴾. That is: know that your superiority over women is beneath that which is higher than it, namely the loftiness and greatness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So do not be haughty over them and do not be proud over them, for above you is One who is higher and greater, namely Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Then He said: ﴿And if you fear a breach between the two, send an arbiter from his family and an arbiter from her family﴾ [An-Nisa 35]. This is the fourth stage after the three stages. The fourth stage after the three stages is what? 
* Students: Admonition.
* Shaykh: Admonition.
* Students: Forsaking.
* Shaykh: Forsaking in the beds.
* Students: Striking.
* Shaykh: Striking. If they fear a breach, meaning that these three stages have not borne fruit, then the address is directed to the community: ﴿send an arbiter﴾. He did not say, "Let the two of them send an arbiter." Here the two spouses are removed, and the matter becomes the domain of others. Whose domain? The domain of the legitimate ruler who represents the community. Accordingly, ﴿send﴾ is an address to the community, but it does not mean that everyone in the market, the mosque, or the shop sends. The legitimate ruler acts on behalf of the community. So the address here is to the community, meaning those who represent it, namely the legitimate ruler.
﴿send﴾ means: dispatch. Al-ba'th means sending.
﴿send an arbiter from his family and an arbiter from her family﴾. (ḥakam) The ḥakam is one who holds an enforceable judgment, that is, the one who is appointed to judge. So he is more specific than the ḥākim (judge). The ḥakam is more specific than the ḥākim, because he holds an enforceable judgment, so he is one who is delegated (muḥakkam). ﴿from his family and an arbiter from her family﴾. The ḥakam must have knowledge and insight into the reality. It is well known that he must be adult, sane, mature, and knowledgeable of the legal ruling, and knowledgeable of the reality of the spouses' situation, what the problems are, and what caused these problems, because the ḥakam must have these qualities. As for a common or foolish person coming and wanting to be an arbiter between spouses, this is not valid. The arbiter must know the Shari'ah and know the circumstances of the spouses, and be thoughtful, patient, and insightful. When the two arbiters meet, intention comes into play and they have a role. Either the arbiter from the husband's family wants the husband to prevail and the arbiter from the wife's family wants the wife to prevail, and in this case the two men will not be granted success, because their intention is not sound. Or the purpose of the arbiter from the husband's family and the arbiter from the wife's family is reconciliation between them. Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who is Able and truthful in His word, says: ﴿If they both intend reconciliation, Allah will bring about agreement between them﴾. The pronoun in His saying ﴿if they both intend reconciliation﴾ refers to the two arbiters, because they are the ones who wish to judge, and the intention of reconciliation comes from them, not from the spouses, because between the spouses there is a breach, and each one of them wants to prevail for himself. So most likely they do not want reconciliation, but the ones who want reconciliation are the two arbiters.
And His saying ﴿Allah will bring about agreement between them﴾. Does the pronoun in "between them" refer to the spouses who feared a breach between them, or does it refer to the two arbiters, each of whom presents what he considers to be proof? There are two possibilities. The first possibility: it refers to the spouses, because the matter concerns them, namely the matter of breach. But the arbiters examine the affairs of the spouses, so the pronoun refers to whom? To the spouses. It may also refer to the two arbiters, meaning that each arbiter will bring what counters the other, so the meaning of ﴿Allah will bring about agreement between them﴾ is that their statements will harmonize and no dispute will arise between them, so the arbiter from the husband's family does not prevail for the husband, nor the arbiter from the wife's family for the wife.
So if it is said: why do we not say it is general to both of these?
The answer: we say this too. The answer is that we say this, ﴿Allah will bring about agreement between them﴾, between the two arbiters. If they agree, Allah, Exalted is He, also in His bounty and generosity brings agreement between the spouses.
﴿Allah will bring about agreement between them. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing, Acquainted﴾. That is, All-Knowing, All-Aware. Khibrah (awareness) is knowledge of the inner realities of matters. Knowledge of the inner realities of matters is khibrah, and knowledge of the outward and inward is 'ilm. Accordingly, mentioning "Acquainted" after "Knowing" is the mention of the specific after the general. The sentence is a resumptive statement explaining the kindness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in what happens through the two arbiters, that He, the Mighty and Majestic, is All-Knowing and Acquainted with what takes place between them regarding judgment between the spouses.

* In these two verses there are many benefits.
* First: the superiority of men over women, its basis being that Allah made men maintainers over women.
* Second: the clarification that Allah's legislative and cosmic rulings are based on causes. From where do we take this?
* Student: ﴿with that by which Allah has preferred some of them over others﴾.
* Shaykh: The causative link, meaning the mention of causation. So the acts of Allah are based on causes, correct? Good.
It follows from the fact that the acts of Allah, or His legislative and cosmic rulings, are based on causes, the affirmation of wisdom and that Allah, Exalted is He, is Wise.
* And among the benefits of these two noble verses: the preference among human beings.
* Student: ﴿with that by which Allah has preferred some of them over others﴾.
* Shaykh: Good, ﴿with that by which Allah has preferred some of them over others﴾.
If someone says: Does the one who is preferred over another have the right to argue with Allah, saying: "O Lord, why did You prefer this one over me?"
* Student: He does not have that right.
* Shaykh: He does not have that right. Why?
* Student: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic (...).
* Shaykh: That is not clear.
* Student: ﴿That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills, and Allah is the Owner of great bounty﴾ [Al-Hadid 21].
* Shaykh: Yes. It is said to the one who was preferred over another: "Has Allah withheld your right from you? If that is the case, then you have an argument. Otherwise, the bounty of Allah He gives to whom He wills." For this reason, when "the Prophet (ﷺ) struck a parable for the Jews, the Christians, and this community, with a man who hired workers from morning until noon, and from noon until the afternoon prayer, and gave each one a qirat, and from the afternoon prayer until sunset he gave them two qirats each. The first group said: Why are we given a dinar while we have done more work? He said: Have I wronged you of any of your wages? They said: No. He said: That is My bounty; I give it to whom I will."[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (2268) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.]] Do you understand? So the one who was preferred over another has no argument against Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, regarding the preference. But what does the one who was preferred over another do?
Allah pointed to this in a previous verse, when He said: ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty﴾ [An-Nisa 32]. Ask Allah for His bounty.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that the one who spends has a superiority over the one on whom he spends. From where is this taken?
* Student: ﴿and from what they have spent﴾.
* Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿and from what they have spent of their wealth﴾.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the disliking of asking, the disliking of asking people.
* Student: ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty﴾.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: That Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, explained the cause of preference: the cause of preference is spending, which is the opposite of asking.
* Another student: Shaykh, His saying ﴿of their wealth﴾ means (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and from what they have spent of their wealth﴾. They spent on the women and did not ask them for maintenance.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...) and did not ask.
* Shaykh: That the spender has a superiority over the one spent upon means that your asking him is humiliation, because when you ask him, you have affirmed for him a superiority over you. If you ask him and he gives you, you have affirmed for him a superiority over you, and this is humiliation. For this reason, "the Prophet (ﷺ) took a pledge from his companions that they would not ask people for anything, that they would not ask people for anything at all. Even if one of them dropped his whip from the back of his camel, he would dismount, take it, and mount again without saying to the people, 'Give it to me.'"[[Recorded by Muslim (1043 / 108) from the hadith of Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i.]] Because asking people is humiliation.
Good. Allah gave men a superiority over women through the spending of wealth. So the one who spends on you has a superiority over you. If you ask him, he has a superiority, does he not?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: He has a superiority. Thus you have humbled yourself before him by making him superior to you.
* Student: If spending is an obligation, is there humiliation in it? That is, if it is for a wife's maintenance and it is a binding obligation, is there humiliation in it? I mean, what humiliation?
* Shaykh: There is no doubt that his spending on her gives him control over her by this spending. He has a superiority over her, without doubt, even if it is obligatory.
* Student: Spending on a father is obligatory if the father is unable to...
* Shaykh: Now, the one who spends on women, even if the maintenance is obligatory, the one spent upon sees that he has a superiority over him.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. You said at the beginning that the principles (ḍawābiṭ) benefit the student of knowledge. How do we know the principles and gather them?
* Shaykh: Yes, I pointed to this. I told you: the reasonings (ta'ālīl) of the jurists, may Allah have mercy on them, are all principles. You will find the reasoning in Ar-Rawḍ al-Murbi' for example, or in Ash-Sharḥ al-Mumti', al-Iqna', or al-Majmu' of al-Nawawi, or others. All these reasonings are principles. I told you when we began the lesson on Zad al-Mustaqni': if one of you were to set himself to gather these principles or reasonings by which they are justified, he would benefit us and benefit himself.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that women have no guardianship over men, neither in judgeship, nor in leadership, nor in anything else, because of His saying: ﴿Men are the protectors and maintainers of women﴾. So whoever reverses this has opposed the sunnah of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Whoever gives a woman guardianship has opposed the sunnah of Allah.
If someone says: Is not a mother a guardian over her children and their property?
We say: This is a specific guardianship and a temporary guardianship, unlike general guardianship. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A people will never prosper who entrust their affairs to a woman."[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (4425) from the hadith of Abu Bakrah.]]
If someone says: We find some women who are prime ministers, presidents, or queens.
We say: But look at the condition of those under their rule. If this woman had not governed them, they would certainly have been in a better state, more successful and more prosperous. But they lagged behind to the extent that this woman took charge over them. Look, for example, at Britain. Britain was the greatest of the colonial powers in colonisation, to the point that it was said: the sun never sets on its colonies. Now it has shrunk until it is in third place. All of that is because it is ruled by women.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 34–35 (part 3 of 3):

We reached His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and from what they spend of their wealth﴾, and we said: from it is derived the dislike of asking (for wealth), since Allah made the giver superior to the one given to. And there is witness to this in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): «The upper hand is better than the lower hand; the upper hand is the hand of the giver, and the lower hand is the hand of the taker»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1429) and Muslim (1033/94) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.]].
* Among the benefits of these two verses is His saying: ﴿from their wealth﴾. Wealth, as is well known, is everything that is considered valuable, whether tangible goods, benefits or other things; everything that is regarded as property. From this it is derived that these people spend only from what they are certain is theirs, and that they do not transgress against the property of anyone.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that women are divided into two categories.
* Student: Women are divided into two categories: those who are guarding (their husbands' rights), and those who are not.
* Another student: Righteous and obedient to her husband, and disobedient (nashiz).
* The Shaykh: Yes, righteous and obedient to her husband, and disobedient.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: praise for guarding what is unseen; that is, what is secret between you and your spouse. From where is this taken?
* Student: ﴿guarding in the absence (of their husbands)﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿guarding in the absence by what Allah has guarded﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the husband has authority over his wife. From where is this taken?
* Student: Shaykh, ﴿And those from whom you fear disobedience, admonish them, forsake them in the beds, and strike them. But if they obey you, do not seek a way against them﴾.
* The Shaykh: Good.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: gradualness in discipline.
* Student: The gradualness: ﴿admonish them﴾, then ﴿forsake them﴾, then ﴿strike them﴾.
* The Shaykh: Good.
* Among its benefits: an indication that Allah restrains by authority what He does not restrain by the Qur'an.
* Student: In His command to discipline, O Shaykh, He said..
* The Shaykh: He restrains by authority what He does not restrain by the Qur'an.
* The student: Since admonition may not always be effective, so one moves on to forsaking in the bed or striking, because it may be more effective.
* The Shaykh: Yes, good.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that if discipline can be achieved through legislated religious address, one does not resort to physical discipline.
* Student: "Do not seek a way against them; ﴿but if they obey you﴾."
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: Because Allah, glory be to Him, made forsaking and striking come after admonition.
* The Shaykh: He began with admonition, which softens the heart through the Shari'ah; if that is not possible, then with punishment.
* Among the benefits of these verses: an indication that the bed of the husband and the wife is one.
* Student: From His saying: ﴿and forsake them in the beds﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿and forsake them in the beds﴾, which indicates that a person's forsaking his wife's bed is only at the time of disobedience (nushuz).
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the prohibition of a wife's disobedience to her husband.
* Student: The ordering of this punishment indicates that disobedience is forbidden.
* The Shaykh: Yes; since this disobedience is met with admonition, then forsaking, then striking.
* Among the benefits of the verse: an indication that forsaking by speech is not permitted.
* Student: ﴿But if they obey you, do not seek a way against them﴾.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: When He followed His saying: ﴿and forsake them in the beds﴾, He followed it with: ﴿in the beds﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿in the beds﴾. And is forsaking in speech permitted?
Answer: It is permitted only within three days, due to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): «It is not lawful for a believer to forsake his brother for more than three days; when they meet, one turns away from the other and the other turns away from him, and the better of them is the one who begins with the greeting»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6077) and Muslim (2560/25) from the hadith of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari with the wording: «who begins with the salam».]].
* Among the benefits of the verses: the invalidity of the saying of some contemporary educationists who say that discipline is not achieved by striking; from His saying: ﴿and strike them﴾.
Is there also evidence for this in the Sunnah?
Yes, it is His saying (ﷺ): «And strike them for it at ten»[[Narrated by Abu Dawud in his Sunan (495) and Ahmad in his Musnad (6756) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As.]], and by this the saying of those educationists who claim that striking does not benefit and only hardens the heart is refuted.
* Among the benefits of the verses: reciprocation in kind.
* Student: When they obey; ﴿but if they obey you, do not seek a way against them﴾.
* The Shaykh: That when they obey, it is not permissible for a person to seek a way against them.
* Among its benefits: overlooking what has passed.
* Student: From His saying: ﴿do not seek a way against them﴾.
* The Shaykh: How is that?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Because ﴿do not seek a way against them﴾ includes the past and the future.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication that the one who possesses absolute highness is Allah, so do not exalt yourself over others.
* Student: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Most High, Great﴾.
* The Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Most High, Great﴾. «The Prophet (ﷺ) saw a man striking his slave, so he said to him, peace be upon him: The man, this Companion, heard a voice: "O so-and-so, O so-and-so, Allah is more capable over you than you are over this slave." So he turned, and behold, it was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he freed the slave»[[Narrated by Muslim (1659/34) from the hadith of Abu Mas'ud al-Badri.]]. In this there is an indication... every person who exalts himself should remember the highness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of these two names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, namely: Al-'Ali (the Most High), Al-Kabir (the Great).
Is Allah's highness figurative or literal?
* Student: Literal and figurative.
* The Shaykh: Literal and figurative, which includes?
* Student: It includes the highness of His essence and the highness of His rank.
* The Shaykh: And the highness of His attributes; the highness of essence, and the highness of attributes includes rank and dominance.
What is the position of the people of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah on this question, and the position of those who oppose them?
* Student: (...) They affirm for Allah (...) with His majesty and greatness (...).
* The Shaykh: They affirm for Allah both meanings: the highness of essence and the highness of attributes. Who opposes them?
* Student: They said: Allah is immanent among the servants.
* The Shaykh: Everywhere; this is one. Another group?
* Student: The Ittihadiyya (monists).
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: The Mu'tazila and the Ash'ari.
* The Shaykh: Those who said what?
* Student: The highness of attributes without the highness of essence.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but what do they say? Even those who said that He is in His essence everywhere deny the highness of essence.
* Student: They say: Allah, glory be to Him, is neither above, nor below, nor in a direction.
* The Shaykh: Correct. So there are two extremist groups: one group affirmed that Allah is everywhere, and another group negated that Allah is in any place. Do you understand? One group said: We say that Allah is neither above the world nor below it, nor within it, nor outside it, nor connected nor separated, nor distinct from it, nor in a direction, and we do not describe Him with anything of this. In reality, these, as Mahmud ibn Sebuktigin said to Ibn Furak, said: Explain to me the difference between your god and nothingness. Indeed this is nothingness. And those who said Allah is everywhere also did not measure Allah with His true measure, because they placed Him in places of filth, places of honor, places of vanity and in every place. So we believe that Allah, glory be to Him, is high in His essence above all creation, and that all creation in relation to Him is nothing but what? Like a mustard seed in the palm of one of us, and is nothing in relation to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
What is meant by "Al-Kabir" here in ﴿'Aliyyan Kabira﴾: is it pride, or something more general?
* Student: Something more general.
* The Shaykh: Not more general; meaning the pride which is the inner greatness, as Allah said: ﴿And to Him belongs the majesty in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Jathiyah 37], and He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿the Compeller, the Majestic﴾ [al-Hashr 23]; and likewise that everything in relation to His essence is nothing.
* Among the benefits of the second noble verse: the obligation of rulers to attend to the community.
* Student: From His saying: ﴿And if you fear a breach between the two﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿then send an arbiter﴾, and the address here, we said, is to the rulers.
* Among the benefits of the second noble verse: that the ones sent are two arbiters (hakamayn), not agents (wakil), as some scholars said.
* Student: From His saying: ﴿then send an arbiter from his people﴾.
* The Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿then send an arbiter﴾. Is the arbiter independent or an agent?
* Student: Independent.
* The Shaykh: Independent? Good.
* * *
* Student: ﴿Then send an arbiter from his people and an arbiter from her people. If they both intend reconciliation, Allah will cause harmony between them. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Acquainted﴾ (35). ﴿And worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents and to relatives and orphans and the needy and the neighbor who is near and the neighbor who is far and the companion by your side and the traveler and those whom your right hands possess. Indeed, Allah does not like those who are self-deluding and boastful﴾ [an-Nisa 35, 36].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan.
We are in the process of deriving the benefits and rulings from the verse that the brother recited, which is His saying: ﴿And if you fear a breach between the two, send an arbiter from his people and an arbiter from her people﴾. We mentioned benefits, how many?
* Student: Twenty-one.
* The Shaykh: Twenty-one benefits.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: it is necessary that the two arbiters have knowledge of the Shari'ah, since an arbiter cannot judge except after knowledge, and it is necessary that they have trustworthiness and religious reliability, since one who is not trustworthy is not relied upon. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿O you who have believed, if a deviator brings you a report, verify it﴾ [al-Hujurat 6].
The judge is an informer, an obligator and a decider: he informs of the ruling of Allah, obligates by what he rules, and decides between the two disputants, so he must be just in his religion.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication that the judge should be knowledgeable about the circumstances of those he judges, from His saying: ﴿from his people﴾ and ﴿from her people﴾, since one from their own people is closer to knowing their conditions than a stranger. On this basis, one should not appoint a judge over a people whose natures he does not know, whose language he does not know, or whose conditions he does not know, for much of judgment would be lost by that.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of a relative judging for or against his relative. As for judging against him, there is no problem, since suspicion is absent; as for judging for him, there may be suspicion. A relative judging for a relative: what is the matter that may involve suspicion preventing the enforcement of the ruling?
Some scholars said: a person does not judge for his ancestor, his descendant, or his spouse, because he is suspect due to the strength of the connection; his descendant is part of him, based on the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ): «Fatimah is only a part of me»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3714) and Muslim (2449/94) from the hadith of al-Miswar ibn Makhramah.]], and his ancestor is also part of him. On this basis, he does not judge for his ancestor or his descendant.
The correct view is that he may judge for his ancestor and descendant when trust is strong, and in this we require more certainty regarding trust than with a stranger or a distant relative.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication of good intention in judging, based on His saying: ﴿If they both intend reconciliation, Allah will cause harmony between them﴾, and that a person appointed as arbiter must have as his aim reconciliation alone, not pleasing this person or that person: reconciliation.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that good intention is a cause for the soundness of action.
* Student: Based on His saying: ﴿If they both intend reconciliation, Allah will cause harmony between them﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿If they both intend reconciliation, Allah will cause harmony between them﴾. Accordingly we derive two opposite benefits: the prohibition of bad intention in judging, and that bad intention leads to the corruption of the matter, since what is achieved by something is lost with its loss.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that affairs are in the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, even minor matters, based on His saying: ﴿Allah will cause harmony between them﴾. In this there is a refutation of the Mu'tazila, who hold that servants create their own actions with no connection to Allah in them; they are the Qadariyya, the Mu'tazila are Qadariyya.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the reward is of the same kind as the deed. Its meaning: since they intended reconciliation, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, rewarded them with success, based on His saying: ﴿If they both intend reconciliation, Allah will cause harmony between them﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of the two attributes of knowledge and expertise, from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Acquainted﴾. Expertise (khibrah) is more specific than knowledge, since it is knowledge of the inner realities of matters.
Can it be inferred from His saying ﴿was Knowing and Acquainted﴾ that He is not so now?
* Student: No, He was and still is.
* The Shaykh: How do we understand "was and still is" when ﴿kana﴾ is a past-tense verb?
* Student: Because it is not on its original meaning.
* The Shaykh: It is not on its original meaning; what is meant by it?
* Student: What is meant by it is affirmation.
* The Shaykh: Affirmation of the attribute, correct; so it is stripped of time.
I think we mentioned that the two arbiters have the right to separate and to join, with or without compensation.
* So it is derived from the noble verse that these two arbiters have the authority to separate and to reconcile between the spouses between whom discord is feared, whether with compensation or without compensation.
* Also among the benefits: their ruling is binding, because Allah named them arbiters (hakamayn), and the ruling of an arbiter is binding and his decision is final.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 34–35 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Men are in charge of women by [right of] what Allah has given one over the other and what they spend [for maintenance] from their wealth. So righteous women are devoutly obedient, guarding in [the husband's] absence what Allah would have them guard.﴾ To the end of the verse.

﴿Men﴾ is the plural of (rajul), which is a broken plural. A rajul is an adult male of the children of Adam; an adult male of the children of Adam is called a rajul, while the word (dhakar, male) applies to both adult and non-adult males. For this reason, the hadith reads: «And what remains goes to the nearest male man (rajul dhakar)» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6737) and Muslim (3/1615), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]], although had he said, "to the nearest male (dhakar)," it would have sufficed; and had he said, "to the nearest man (rajul)," it would have excluded the young boy, so that he would not be an 'asib (residuary heir). But the word (dhakar) was used to make clear that maturity is not a condition for entitlement to residuary inheritance, rather even one who has not reached manhood qualifies.

If someone says: then is the word (rajul) with (dhakar) redundant, a redundancy with no meaning? The answer: No, it has a meaning, which is to indicate that the male—i.e., the dhakar—is more entitled to residuary inheritance, because he is a rajul upon whom responsibilities fall that do not fall upon a woman.

﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ ﴿qawwamun﴾ is the plural of (qawwam), and (qawwam) is an intensive form (sigha mubalaghah) of (qa'im). Had it been said outside the Qur'an, "men are standing over women (qa'imun)," the meaning would have been weaker than the word (qawwamun), because (qawwamun) is an intensive form that implies authority over women in every situation.

As for His saying ﴿over women﴾ (ʿala al-nisa'): it is the plural of what? It is the plural of (niswah), and if you wish you may say it is the plural of (imra'ah, woman), but it is a plural not derived from the same root as the singular, since sometimes the meaning is pluralized in a form different from the singular, as (ibil, camels) is a plural with no singular from its own root; its singular is (ba'ir).

He says: ﴿by [right of] what Allah has given one over the other﴾. The (ba') here indicates causation, and (ma) may be either a verbal-masdar (maṣdariyyah) or a relative pronoun (mawsulah). If you make it a relative pronoun, the sense becomes: "by that which Allah has given some of them over others," and then we need a returning pronoun (a'id) that refers back to the relative pronoun; the returning pronoun is then omitted, its sense being: "by that with which Allah has given some of them over others." The omission of a returning pronoun governed by a preposition is well known in the language, and among its examples is His saying: ﴿He eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink﴾ [al-Mu'minun 33], meaning: "of it."

He says: ﴿by what Allah has given one over the other﴾. (fadhdhala) means "he gave more," and (al-fadl) is excess, i.e., some of them exceeded others. Who is the one given excess and who is the one over whom excess is given? The men are the ones given excess, and the women are the ones over whom it is given. So (ba'dahum) here refers to the men, and (ʿala ba'd) refers to the women. Then what is it with which Allah has given the men excess over the women?

* A student: (...).
