﴿And sufficient is Allah as protector﴾: i.e., as one who manages affairs. ﴿And sufficient is Allah as helper﴾: i.e., as one who defends and supports.

* There are benefits in these two verses. First: among people is one who is given the Scripture and granted knowledge, but does not benefit from it. Such people were given a portion of the Scripture, yet they did not benefit from it; they purchased error in exchange for guidance.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever does not benefit from his knowledge resembles these people. Whoever Allah has given knowledge but who does not benefit from it resembles them. For this reason Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Whoever among our scholars is corrupt has a resemblance to the Jews, and whoever among our worshippers is corrupt has a resemblance to the Christians."[[See al-Fatawa of Ibn Taymiyyah (2/142) from the narration of Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah.]] And this is sound.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: it bears witness to the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The Qur'an is a proof for you or against you."[[Recorded by Muslim (1/223) from the hadith of Abu Malik al-Ash'ari.]] So the books of Allah which people carry are either for them or against them.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the love of these people for error and evil, from His words ﴿they purchase error﴾.

* Among its benefits: caution regarding these people, and that however they act with us, they do not wish us any good at all, from His words ﴿and they wish that you would lose the way﴾. They may lavish upon us wealth, factories, and everything else, but what do they want? They want to mislead us; they want us to lose the way. Conquest through worldly means is conquest with a deadly weapon; that is, lavishing worldly goods and comfort upon a person is conquest with a deadly weapon, because man, as Allah said of him: ﴿And you love wealth with immense love﴾ [Al-Fajr 20]. So when wealth he loves is lavished upon him, the nature of human circumstances requires that he become soft toward the one who provided and lavished that wealth upon him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: praise of the Muslims for being upon the path, because His words ﴿that you would lose the way﴾ imply that, had they not been upon the path, they would not have tried to mislead them; for the one who is astray is astray, so what would he try to do?

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: warning against these Jews or Christians or others, because if Allah warns us against those who were given a portion of the Scripture, then our caution against those who are blind, deaf and dumb is all the more appropriate.

* Among the benefits of the second verse: affirmation of Allah's knowledge, from His words ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your enemies﴾.

* Among its benefits: the perfection of Allah's knowledge.

* Student: Because it was expressed in the comparative form.

* The Shaykh: Yes, because it was expressed in the comparative form ﴿most knowing of your enemies﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: consolation of the believers and strengthening of their resolve, because He is most knowing of our enemies, and He is our helper and our protector.

* Among its benefits: a threat and warning to the polytheists, from His words ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your enemies﴾. For if we supposed (and to Allah belongs the highest likeness) that your father said to your enemy: "I know you and your enmity," he would fear and be wary.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Muslims must have an enemy; rather, enemies. As we mentioned earlier in commenting on the word: every non-Muslim, of whatever creed, is an enemy of the Muslims.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: praise of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, for complete sufficiency in protection and what else? And support; from His words ﴿And sufficient is Allah as protector and sufficient is Allah as helper﴾. ﴿Protector﴾ (waliyyan) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), transferred from the subject, because what suffices is Allah's protection and support, so it is a specification transferred from the subject. The "bā'" in His words ﴿bi-Allah﴾ — they said it is superfluous, and that the original is: "Allah suffices as protector, and Allah suffices as helper." (...)

* Student: May Allah bless you. ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your enemies﴾: ﴿most knowing﴾ came in the form of a comparative. In the language it is known that comparison occurs only between two, so how is it explained? And it has already been mentioned, O Shaykh, that some people say "a'lam" means "'alim" (knowing)?

* The Shaykh: We have explained the falsity of this, and we said that "a'lam" is more emphatic than "'alim", because "'alim" does not prevent sharing: Allah is knowing, and so-and-so is knowing, and so-and-so is knowing.

* Student: What is the benefit of this interpretation? Why did they resort to it (...)?

* The Shaykh: Out of their assumption that if the Creator and the created share in knowledge, this would indicate resemblance; or it is in the sense of the poet's saying:

Have you not seen that the sword diminishes in worth when it is said that the sword is more cutting than the staff?
But this is an error. We say: even the life, knowledge, hearing and sight of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, share with those of the created in origin, a sharing in origin; but the Creator is more perfect than the created in this.

* Student: So comparison is permissible, then?

* The Shaykh: It is permissible; indeed Allah said: ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate?﴾ [An-Naml 59].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 46 (part 1 of 3):

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿Among those who are Jews, they distort words from their places and say, "We hear and we disobey," and "Hear without being heard," and "Ra'ina," twisting their tongues and attacking the religion. And if they had said, "We hear and we obey, and hear, and look at us," it would have been better for them and more upright. But Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so they do not believe, except a few.﴾ (46) ﴿O you who were given the Scripture, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you, before We obliterate faces and turn them back upon their backs, or curse them as We cursed the companions of the Sabbath. And the command of Allah is always executed.﴾ [An-Nisa' 46-47].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. We have already discussed the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾ and so on to the end. Who is meant by "those who were given a portion of the Scripture"?
* Student: The Jews and the Christians.
* The Shaykh: The Jews and the Christians. Good. Why did He express it with His words ﴿they purchase﴾ instead of saying "they go astray"?
* Student: To indicate their desire for misguidance.
* The Shaykh: To indicate their desire for misguidance, as if it were a commodity they seek and are eager for. Good. Has Allah mentioned a parallel to this verse from what preceded?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: How?
* Student: The verse that follows it.
* The Shaykh: No. ﴿Showing off to people﴾: people who purchased misguidance in exchange for guidance?
* Student: But (...).
* The Shaykh: Allah mentioned that in the description of the hypocrites, and on this basis the disbelievers and the hypocrites are each alike. Is there a witness in the verse that they love for us to go astray? Here He says: ﴿They wish that you would go astray from the way.﴾ So is there a parallel to this verse?
* Student: Yes. ﴿And the Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion﴾ [Al-Baqarah 120], and from it the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved﴾ [An-Nisa' 89].
* The Shaykh: And from it the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved.﴾ Did they agree with Satan in this wish?
* Student: Yes, they agreed with Satan, and the evidence is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And Satan wishes to lead them far astray﴾ [An-Nisa' 60].
* The Shaykh: So they wish to misguide creation, and Satan also wishes to misguide creation.
What is the benefit of His saying: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your enemies﴾?
* Student: It was (...) the knowledge of Allah (...).
* The Shaykh: And others, but what is the benefit? Why did He say: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your enemies﴾?
* Student: It contains encouragement and warning.
* The Shaykh: Correct. How is that?
* Student: As for encouragement, because He knows better than the believers their enemies, so they (...) ﴿And Allah is sufficient as Reckoner﴾ [An-Nisa' 6]. As for warning, He knows the state of the disbelievers, so He plots against them a plot greater than theirs.
* The Shaykh: Did you hear what he said? He says: it contains a threat and a support: support for the believers, that Allah knows their enemies better and will suffice them against them, as Allah said: ﴿Indeed, Allah defends those who believe﴾ [Al-Hajj 38], and a threat to the disbelievers that He will return their plot upon their own necks and grant victory to His allies over them. For this He said: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as a Protector, and sufficient is Allah as a Helper.﴾ Good. Are "al-Wali" (the Protector) and "al-Nasir" (the Helper) among the names of Allah?
* Student: "Al-Wali" is among the names of Allah.
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence?
* Student: The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿He is the Protector﴾ in Surat ash-Shura.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: At the end of the verse, ﴿He is the Protector﴾ (...).
* Another student: ﴿Or have they taken protectors besides Him? But Allah is the Protector﴾ [Ash-Shura 9].
* The Shaykh: ﴿Or have they taken protectors besides Him? But Allah is the Protector﴾, and likewise: ﴿And He is the Protector, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Ash-Shura 28]. Is "al-Nasir" (the Helper) among the names of Allah?
* Student: Indeed Allah gives victory to those who believe.
* The Shaykh: I am saying, is "al-Nasir" among the names of Allah?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence?
* Student: The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿An excellent Protector and an excellent Helper﴾ [Al-Anfal 40].
* The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿an excellent Protector and an excellent Helper.﴾ Well done.
* * *
* The Shaykh: Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Among those who are Jews, they distort words from their places.﴾ The "min" here is for partitioning (tab'id).

﴿Those who are Jews⦆ means: those who returned (hadu), and they are the Jews, who returned from worshipping the calf, so they were named ﴿those who are Jews⦆ due to the saying of Allah: ﴿Indeed, we have returned to You﴾ [Al-A'raf 156], meaning: we have returned to You.

As for His saying: ﴿they distort words⦆, this clause cannot be a subject (mubtada'), because a verb is not used as a subject. And if it cannot be a subject, how do we parse it? We say: it is an adjective (sifah) of a deleted noun which is the subject, and the implied meaning is: from those who are Jews are a people who distort words from their places.

Some grammarians said: the partitive "min" is a noun, so it is parsed as a subject, because the implied meaning of partitive "min" is: some of those who are Jews distort words from their places. On this view, "min" takes the form of a particle but is a noun, and it is the subject, and the clause ﴿they distort⦆ is the predicate, and no implied element is needed.

It has parallels in the Qur'an, such as the saying of Allah: ﴿And among the people of Madinah are those who have become obstinate in hypocrisy﴾ [At-Tawbah 101]. The implied meaning: and among the people of Madinah are a people who have become obstinate in hypocrisy. Each of the two opinions has a basis. As for those who said the partitive "min" is a noun, their view is strengthened by the fact that we do not need an implied element in the verse, and when speech falls between an implied element and none, not implying is preferable, because the original state is non-deletion. As for the second view, it is strengthened by the fact that the partitive "min" is a particle, and using it as a noun removes it from its original function, so by estimating it as a noun we have committed a figurative usage, and the estimate of a noun is more preferable. This is called brevity by deletion (ijaz bil-hadhf), because brevity is of two kinds: brevity by deletion and brevity by restriction. That is: a short sentence that carries a large meaning is brevity by restriction; a sentence in which things are deleted is brevity by deletion.

His saying: ﴿they distort words from their places⦆ means: they turn them away, and tahrif is taṣrif (turning). From it: "harafa al-dabbah" means he turned the animal away from the direction of its travel.

﴿Al-Kalim⦆ is a noun, its plural whose singular is kalimah. Ibn Malik said in the Alfiyyah:
"...and noun and verb and particle, al-kalim..., its singular is kalimah..."

The intended meaning of "al-kalim" here is what Allah sent down to His messengers of revelation.

His saying: ﴿from their places⦆ means: they turn it away from what Allah, mighty and majestic, intended by it, because what Allah intended by His speech is its place.

The scholars said: tahrif is of two kinds: verbal distortion (tahrif lafzi) and meaningful distortion (tahrif ma'nawi). Each may occur alone or they may combine. Verbal distortion may change the meaning, or it may not change the meaning.

Let us give an example of each. Verbal distortion that changes meaning: like some people's distortion of the saying of Allah: ﴿And Allah spoke to Musa with speech﴾ [An-Nisa' 164], changing it to "wa kallama Allaha Musa taklimā" (making Allah the one spoken to, not the speaker), so this is verbal and meaningful distortion: verbal because he made the word Allah in the accusative after it was nominative, and meaningful because the meaning changed, since it now indicates that the one who speaks is Musa.

An example of verbal distortion that does not change meaning: a reader says "al-hamdu lillahi rabba al-'alamin" where it should be ﴿Rabbi al-'alamin﴾ [Al-Fatihah 2]. Here the distortion is verbal, and the meaning does not change.

An example of meaningful distortion while keeping the wording as it is: the distortion of the Mu'attilah (deniers of divine attributes) of the saying of Allah: ﴿The Most Merciful, above the Throne, istawa﴾ [Taha 5], reading "istawla" (seized). They did not change the wording, leaving it as it is, but they said: the intended meaning of istiwa' is istila' (dominion), and this is meaningful distortion.

Then these followers of this meaningful distortion called it ta'wil, and they said: ta'wil is turning speech from its apparent meaning to a meaning contrary to the apparent one for a proof. So they named this distortion ta'wil. But we say: this naming is a deception upon the listener, because ta'wil is turning speech from its apparent meaning on account of a sound proof, whereas the proof they cite is an imaginary proof with no basis in soundness. Accordingly we say: if a person interprets speech away from its apparent meaning to a meaning contrary to the apparent one, then if there is a proof from the Book or the Sunnah it is accepted, and if there is no proof it is not accepted.

So if someone says: the intended meaning of the saying of Allah: ﴿When you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ [An-Nahl 98] is: when you want to recite the Qur'an, we say: this is not accepted until you bring us a proof. He says: yes, I have a proof, which is that the Prophet ﷺ "used to seek refuge when he intended to recite," [narrated by Abu Dawud (775) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri], not at the end of recitation. We say: this is accepted and welcome. The proof? The action of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him.

And if someone says: ﴿The Most Merciful, above the Throne, istawa⦆ means istawla (seized), we say: this is turning speech from its apparent meaning and it is not accepted, because there is no proof for it. Thus ta'wil, which is turning the wording from its apparent meaning, if a proof indicates it, is accepted, and we call it tafsir; and if no proof indicates it, it is rejected, and we call it tahrif.

Those Jews, or some of those Jews, distorted words from their places, neither concerning 'Isa nor concerning Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.

As for 'Isa, they attributed to him what Allah had cleared him of: that he was the son of an adulteress, and that he could not be a messenger, since messengers are pure and purified, and this one is the son of an adulteress, so he is not a messenger. And they killed him by judgment, not in reality. How by judgment? Because they said: ﴿Indeed, we killed the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam, the messenger of Allah﴾, so they acknowledged against themselves that they killed him, and thus they have the ruling of those who killed him. As for reality, Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them﴾ [An-Nisa' 157].

They also distorted words regarding Muhammad ﷺ and said: this is not the awaited messenger. Before he was sent, they used to seek victory over those who disbelieved, saying: a prophet will be sent and we will follow him and defeat you. But when he was sent from the sons of Isma'il, and the sons of Isma'il were their paternal cousins, they envied them, because they knew his description in the Torah and the Gospel and knew that he was the best prophet. They had thought he would be from the Children of Israel, without basis, because if they had returned to the source they would have found that the Torah and the Gospel explicitly stated that he would be sent from Umm al-Qura. Historians say that the gathering of the Jews in Madinah at the time of the Messenger's mission, peace and blessings be upon him, was based on their knowledge that his place of migration would be Madinah, so they said: we will welcome him and believe in him.

So the Jews distorted words from their places regarding the message of 'Isa and regarding the message of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.

﴿And they say, "We hear and we disobey"⦆ openly, and Allah forbid, this is the utmost of opposition to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and to His messengers, that a human says: "We hear and we disobey." And disobedience is opposing a command, that is, leaving the realm of obedience: if it is a command, by abandoning it, and if it is a prohibition, by committing it. This is disobedience.

﴿And hear without being heard⦆: they say to the Messenger ﷺ: ﴿hear without being heard⦆, meaning: hear, may Allah make you deaf so that you do not hear. This is the meaning of ﴿without being heard⦆: hear our words while you are unheard. And who is unheard? The deaf. So they say: hear without being heard, meaning they invoke deafness upon him, and they mock him, because if they invoke deafness upon him, how do they say "hear"?

It was also said: the meaning is hear without hearing what you dislike. But this is far from the context of the verse and far from the condition of the Jews. It may also mean: hear without hearing what pleases you, meaning: we will say to you what displeases you, as they said: ﴿We hear and we disobey.﴾ But this requires evidence, because it requires an implied element: unheard of what? Unheard of what you dislike. The first meaning is sufficient for their disgrace, and Allah forbid, that they say to the Messenger: hear, may Allah not let you hear.

﴿Ra'ina⦆: whoever hears this word takes it to be an imperative verb to which an object pronoun is attached, with a hidden obligatory subject whose implied form is "you": "ra'ina", you (watch over) us. From what? From care (ri'ayah) or from consideration (muraa'ah), and both are good meanings. But they do not intend either care or consideration; they intend ru'unah, which is cowardice, weakness, and the like. In the Hebrew language this word has this meaning, so they say "ra'ina", meaning: may Allah afflict you with ru'unah. For this reason Allah forbade the believers to say this word, because the Jews said it intending evil by it. So He, the Exalted, said: ﴿O you who believe, do not say "ra'ina," but say﴾ instead ﴿"unzurna" (look at us)⦆.

﴿And ra'ina, distorting with their tongues and attacking the religion⦆: meaning they say these words "distorting with their tongues," by showing a correct, acceptable meaning while not intending the correct meaning. So "ghayra musma'" may mean "without hearing what displeases you," as previously mentioned, and "ra'ina" may mean from consideration or from care, while they intend the opposite: they intend invoking against him that he not hear, and invoking against him with ru'unah. This is distortion with the tongue, is it not? It is distortion with the tongue: distortion with the tongue means intending by the wording something other than its apparent meaning, because one twists it, speaks but twists this wording toward another meaning other than what is understood from the wording. For this He said: ﴿distorting with their tongues⦆.

﴿Layyan⦆: its origin is "lawiyyan," but waw and ya' came together in one word and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the waw was changed to ya' according to the morphological rule. Now, that this is distortion with their tongues is clear, but He said: ﴿and attacking the religion⦆. Attacking the religion? How is it an attack on the religion? We say: yes, it is clear.

﴿They say "We hear and we disobey"⦆: why did they disobey? Because they did not approve of this religion, and not approving of the religion entails attacking the religion, that is, entails faulting the religion. They wish to invoke against him with ru'unah, and this is distortion with the tongue, is it not? Distortion with the tongue: intending by the wording something contrary to its apparent meaning, because one twists it; one speaks, but twists this wording toward another meaning other than what is understood from the wording.

For this He said: ﴿distorting with their tongues⦆ [An-Nisa' 46]. ﴿Layyan⦆: its origin is "lawiyyan," but waw and ya' came together in one word, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the waw was changed to ya' according to the morphological rule. Now, that this is distortion with their tongues is clear. But they said: ﴿and attacking the religion⦆. Attacking the religion? How is it an attack on the religion? We say: yes, it is clear. ﴿They say "We hear and we disobey"⦆: why did they disobey? Because they did not approve of this religion, and not approving of the religion entails attacking it, that is, its defect, entails faulting the religion and disparaging it. For whoever approves of something cannot, when commanded to it, say "We hear and we disobey" ever. Also, ﴿attacking the religion⦆: if they say ﴿hear without being heard⦆, this is an attack on the religion, because it is an attack on the Messenger who brought the religion, and attacking the Messenger is attacking what he was sent with.

Likewise their saying ﴿ra'ina⦆: if it is from ru'unah, it is also an attack on the religion. So the attack on the religion occurs through all the preceding phrases: ﴿We hear and we disobey⦆.

The second [matter]: "Hear, but may you not be made to hear."
The third: "Pay attention to us (ra'ina)."
All of this is a slander against the religion.

For this reason Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And if only they had said, "We hear and we obey"﴾, instead of their saying: ﴿"We hear and we disobey," and "Hear"﴾. They omitted ﴿"but may you not be made to hear"﴾ and said only "Hear." And instead of ﴿"Pay attention to us"﴾ they should have said ﴿"and look upon us"﴾, because this is the expression Allah commanded the believers to say in place of their saying ﴿"Pay attention to us"﴾. ﴿If they had said that, it would have been better for them and more upright.﴾ The "better" includes the goodness of the religion and of the worldly life, and the goodness of the reward in the Hereafter. ﴿"More upright"﴾ means in their religion and in their lives, because this Qur'an, as Allah the Exalted said, ﴿guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra' 9]. But they turned away from this statement, which was better, because Allah cursed them for their disbelief: ﴿But Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾, meaning He expelled them and removed them from His mercy because of their disbelief. They are the ones who wronged themselves. The Lord, Mighty and Majestic, did not withhold His bounty from them; rather, they were the cause of that, so they disbelieved.

﴿So they do not believe, except a few.﴾ "They do not believe" refers to those who said what they said. ﴿They do not believe, except a few.﴾ Does the word ﴿"a few"﴾ refer back to the subject (the waw of the verb) or to the belief?

Some exegetes said: It is valid for it to refer to the belief and valid for it to refer to the subject. The difference between them: if we say it refers to the belief, the meaning becomes: "They do not believe except with a little belief." If we say it refers to the subject, the meaning becomes: "They do not believe except a few of them." So whoever among them is a disbeliever is a disbeliever with no belief in him, and the believer among them is few.

Some of them preferred the first view and said: If we say "they do not believe except a few of them," the sentence does not stand properly, because the whole sentence has been brought to describe these people. But on this preference there remains the phrase ﴿"except a few"﴾, meaning "except a little belief." What is this little belief when they say "We hear and we disobey"? They said: "few" comes to mean "none," so the meaning is: "they do not believe except with a belief that is little, which does not benefit them," so it is as if it were nonexistent, since what has no benefit in it is entirely like what does not exist.

* Student: The preferred view?

* Shaykh: Some scholars denied clearly that the exception applies to the pronoun in ﴿they do not believe﴾. But what appears to me is that the verse is open to meaning, and that among them there are people who believe. These believers may be understood from His saying ﴿of those who are Jews﴾, meaning: some of those who are Jews do not say this, so they are believers. There is no doubt that some Jews believed, and whose belief was good, whose Islam was good, and whose faith was upright, such as Abdullah ibn Salam.

* We return to the benefits of the verse:

﴿Among those who are Jews, they distort words from their places.﴾

* Several benefits are derived from it:

* First: that among the Jews there are those who were upright and did not distort words from their places. From where is this derived? From the partitive (the word "among"), since He made some of them distort words from their places.

* Another benefit of this verse: that those who distort words from their places resemble the Jews in their way of handling revelation.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the justice of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, since He spoke of the Jews with equity. He mentioned those described with the defect, and it is taken from this that some of them were not described with that, from His saying ﴿of those who are Jews﴾, and He did not say "all those who are Jews." Likewise, when a person speaks of a people in the context of evaluation, he should mention both the good-doer and the wrongdoer. But in the context of warning, he does not mention the good, because the good does not fit with the presentation of a warning.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the severity of the obstinacy of the Jews who distort words from their places, from His saying ﴿They say, "We hear and we disobey."﴾ If they had said, "We did not hear," or "We heard but did not understand," someone might say that this is an excuse. But they say, "We hear and we disobey," so nothing prevented them from obedience except mere disobedience.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: whoever from this nation becomes rebellious and says, "I know that congregational prayer is obligatory, but I do not pray in congregation," we say: whoever says that resembles whom? The Jews who said, "We hear and we disobey."

* Another benefit of this verse: the intensity of the Jews' hatred for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since they confronted him with this evil word ﴿"Hear, but may you not be made to hear."﴾

* Another of its benefits: the arrogance of these Jews, their haughtiness, even toward the Messenger. This is shown by their saying ﴿"Hear"﴾, because the word "hear" is usually used in address from the higher to the lower: "Hear, boy! Listen!" For this reason some people are offended when someone says to an elder: "Listen" to his father, or says to his mother: "Listen." This indicates the arrogance of the Jews, and we seek refuge in Allah.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: a person is held accountable for what he intends. This is shown by His saying ﴿twisting their tongues﴾, while as for what is in their hearts, He said: ﴿If only they had said, "We hear and we obey"﴾ ﴿it would have been better for them and more upright.﴾

If someone asks: Is one held outwardly accountable for what he intends in matters of judgment and disputes between people?

The answer: No, one is judged by the outward, because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: «I only judge according to what I hear» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6967) and Muslim (1713/4) from Umm Salamah]], and his saying: «Your oath is upon what your companion accepts as true from you» [[Narrated by Muslim (1653/20) from Abu Hurayrah]], not upon what is in your heart. There is a difference between a ruling on a matter connected with worship and a ruling on a matter connected with dealings between people.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: slander against the religion can be explicit, and it can be by necessary implication. The explicit form is that a person says: "This religion causes its adherents to fall behind, to regress, and to become rigid," and similar things. This is explicit. The second form is when it is not explicit, but is a necessary consequence of the statement. In this case, when you look at their speech, you do not perceive slander in an explicit manner, but it follows necessarily from what they say.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: slander against the religion is a characteristic of whom? A characteristic of the Jews. So whoever slanders the religion resembles the Jews, and we seek refuge in Allah.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the prohibition of slandering the religion, and that the religion must be a subject of respect and veneration, not a subject of mockery and disparagement.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: presenting the truth to one who is arrogant toward the truth, from Allah's saying ﴿If only they had said, "We hear and we obey..."﴾ to the end. Similar to this is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who tormented the believing men and believing women and then did not repent will have the punishment of Hell﴾ [al-Buruj 10]. Look: they killed His friends and burned them with fire, and what was offered to them? Repentance. He said: ﴿Then they did not repent, so for them is the punishment of Hell, and for them is the punishment of the Burning﴾ [al-Buruj 10].

* Another benefit of the noble verse: when something objectionable is objected to, the one objecting should put in its place something that is not objectionable. Do you understand this point? That when the objectionable is objected to, one should put in its place what is not objectionable. This is from His saying ﴿If only they had said, "We hear and we obey"﴾ instead of ﴿"and we disobey,"﴾ ﴿"Hear"﴾ without ﴿"but may you not be made to hear,"﴾ ﴿"look upon us"﴾ instead of ﴿"Pay attention to us,"﴾ as He said, Exalted, in addressing the believers with this: ﴿Do not say "Pay attention to us," but say "look upon us"﴾ [al-Baqarah 104].

* Another benefit of the noble verse: it is permissible, or it is valid, to use the elative form (ism al-tafdil) between two things where there is nothing of the quality in the other party. The statement that the elative between two things requires that both share the basic meaning is not absolute, but it is so in most cases; it may depart from this rule. Do you understand? Is this clear, whether in Arabic or English? If you say, "So-and-so is better than so-and-so," then both have virtue and the one preferred exceeds the other. This is the basic principle: in the elative, the preferred and the one it is preferred over share the basic meaning. But sometimes the elative comes while the other party has nothing of it at all. Here He said: ﴿If only they had said, "We hear and we obey," "Hear" and "look upon us," it would have been better for them and more upright.﴾ Was there any goodness in their earlier statement? No. Was there any uprightness in their earlier statement? No. Yet He said: ﴿better for them and more upright.﴾ Is the call to prayer at dawn, "Prayer is better than sleep," similar to this?

* Students: No.

* Shaykh: As for the one who does not love sleep, he will say it is like that, because sleep has no good in it. But the one who loves sleep will say it is not like that, because sleep is good. So what do you say?

* Student: (...) Sleep is restricted at this time and is not absolute, so it is like the verse.

* Shaykh: We say: sleep that prevents one from an obligation has no good in it, although a person may be excused for it. Is a verse like this His saying, Exalted: ﴿The companions of Paradise on that Day are better in residence and finer in resting place﴾ [al-Furqan 24]? Yes, why? Because the companions of the Fire have no good in their dwelling and no fineness in their resting place, and they wish they were not among the people of the Fire.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the affirmation of the basic principle of preference among deeds and statements, because Allah said: ﴿better for them and more upright.﴾ There is no doubt that preference between bad and good statements, and bad and good deeds, is established. No one denies this. But do good deeds differ in virtue? And do bad deeds differ? (...) We say: deeds do differ in virtue. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked: "Which deed is most beloved to Allah?" He said: «Prayer at its appointed time.» He said: "Then which?" He said: «Kindness to one's parents.» He said: "Then which?" He said: «Jihad in the way of Allah.» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (527), Muslim (85/139)]]. The questioner was Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him.

Likewise Allah, the Exalted, said in a sacred hadith: «My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him» [[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6502) from Abu Hurayrah]]. So righteous deeds differ in virtue, just as bad deeds differ, some being minor sins and some major sins, and among the major sins some are greater and some lesser, and likewise the minor sins.

* If someone asks: Does it follow from this that faith increases and decreases?

* We say: Yes. According to the basic position of the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jama'ah), the increase and decrease of faith follows from this, because faith increases with obedience and decreases with disobedience.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: whoever is cursed, and we seek refuge in Allah, and is expelled from the mercy of Allah, the truth is turned into falsehood for him and falsehood into truth. For this reason they did not take the better and good course in their speech, because Allah cursed them.

* A corollary of this principle: the sensible person does not expose himself to what brings Allah's curse, because when a person exposes himself to what brings Allah's curse, he is cursed, expelled, and forsaken. In the authentic hadith the Prophet (ﷺ) said: «Allah curses the one who curses his parents.» They said: "O Messenger of Allah, how does a man curse his parents?" He said: «He insults the father of a man, so he insults his father, and he insults his mother, so he insults his mother» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5973), Muslim (90/146) from Abdullah ibn 'Amr]]. Accordingly, do not expose yourself to insulting your parents, because if you expose yourself you will be cursed, and when you are cursed you are expelled and removed from the mercy of Allah.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: disbelief is a cause of cursing, from His saying ﴿But Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾. If a person has characteristics of disbelief, does he receive from the curse in proportion to the characteristics of disbelief he has?

The answer: Apparently yes. But it may also be said: No. It may be said: the curse is a great punishment and is only for a great deed. It may also be said: a ruling attached to a deed means that if the deed is found complete, the ruling is complete, and if part of it is found, then part of the ruling applies.

Based on this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: «Two things among people are disbelief: slandering lineage and wailing over the dead» [[Narrated by Muslim (67/121) from Abu Hurayrah]]. Do we say that whoever slanders lineage or wails over the dead has a share of the curse, because he has a share of disbelief? It is possible. It may be said that the curse is divided just as disbelief is divided. And it may be said that the curse applies only to major disbelief. But when we return to the Messenger's (ﷺ) saying: «Allah curses the one who curses his parents» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5973), Muslim (90/146) from Abdullah ibn 'Amr]], and cursing one's parents does not take a person out of the religion, it becomes clear to us that whoever does a deed to which the term disbelief is applied receives from the curse in proportion to the share of this description that he has.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the affirmation of causes, from His saying ﴿because of their disbelief﴾.

* Another benefit of the verse: a refutation of the Jabriyyah (those who hold that man is compelled in his acts) and a refutation of the Qadariyyah (those who deny that Allah's decree encompasses human acts). Both are misguided groups regarding divine decree and predestination. The Jabriyyah say that man is compelled in his deeds, and the Qadariyyah say that man is independent in his deeds, and Allah has no governance over them. The verse refutes both. As for the Jahmiyyah, who are the Jabriyyah, the proof is His saying ﴿because of their disbelief﴾, where He attributed the deed to them. They say the deed is attributed to the doer only figuratively; in reality it is not his act, because it is not by his choice. As for the Qadariyyah, the proof is the affirmation of causes ﴿because of their disbelief.﴾ They say that a person's act is independent, with no involvement of Allah in it at all. You act, recite, stand, sit, go, and come, and Allah, Exalted, has no connection to you at all. The People of the Sunnah and the Community say: a person's deed is by his choice, without doubt. But who made it his choice? Allah. So it results from Allah's will and Allah's creation, and the one who creates a complete cause creates what it causes.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: that faith is lacking among these Jews. If you wish, say: faith decreases among the believers, or faith decreases among all of them, according to what we said about the exception, whether it refers to the subject or to the verb. There is no doubt that among the Jews, despite the strength of the revelation that came to them, there are the obstinate. Otherwise, the Messenger (ﷺ) saw in a dream that the largest of the nations is the nation of Musa after this nation, because he said: «I looked, and there was a great dark mass, and I thought they were my nation. It was said to me: This is Musa and his people» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5705), Muslim (220/374) from Abdullah ibn 'Abbas]]. And here the benefits end.

But it does occur, as in the hadith that has passed: «Indeed, among the worst of people in standing with Allah on the Day of Resurrection...» [[Narrated by Muslim (1437/123) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri; the wording there is: «Indeed, among the worst of people in standing with Allah on the Day of Resurrection...»]].

**The Shaykh:** Yes, indeed. We understood the arrogance (ta'ālī) when they said ﴿Listen, but may you not be made to hear﴾, that they were being arrogant. **Student:** Regarding the words of Allah the Exalted ﴿among those who are Jews﴾ (...). Is the name "Jews" (al-Yahud) derived from the verb ﴿hādū﴾ (they repented/turned back), or are the Jews attributed to their forefather Yahudha (Judah)?

**The Shaykh:** This is a matter of difference of opinion. Is the word "Jews" (al-Yahud) a relative noun (nisba) to Yahudha, or a relative noun to the verb, because they ﴿hādū﴾ (repented/turned), and so they were named Jews (Yahud)? If we say both, that is not far-fetched: it is attributed to this and to that.

**Student:** Who are the categories of people mentioned in the Qur'an as being under the curse of Allah?

**The Shaykh:** Yes indeed: the hypocrites and the disbelievers, and the Jews are among the disbelievers.

**Student:** May Allah bless you, Shaykh. Our saying regarding ﴿qalīlan﴾ (a little) that it is (...) for faith. Does this not favour the view that Allah, glorified and exalted, said ﴿among those who are Jews﴾, so that whoever believed completely is excluded, and what remains is the one who did not believe, so that the meaning of "little" is "none", and this meaning is thereby determined?

**The Shaykh:** In any case, each has its own direction. Some of them said as you said, but others said that taking the word ﴿qalīlan﴾ out of its original meaning is also open to question, because using "little" to mean "none" requires a qarīna (contextual indicator).

**Student:** (...). And faith is not applied except to one who professes it, and they never professed it at all.

**The Shaykh:** No. Among those who are Jews there are those who believed.

**The Student:** But it excluded ﴿among those who﴾.

**The Shaykh:** For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians, whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:62], and He said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Book﴾ [al-Bayyinah 98:6], and He did not say "Indeed, the People of the Book."

**Student:** Shaykh, sometimes Allah says ﴿they distort words from their places﴾, and sometimes ﴿from after their places﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:41]. What is the difference between the two expressions?

**The Shaykh:** The difference between them is that ﴿ʿan﴾ (from/away from) indicates transgression, that is, they transfer it from its original meaning to another meaning. As for ﴿min baʿdi mawāḍiʿihi﴾ (from after its places), it indicates that their distortion occurred after reflection and after consideration, but they uprooted it from its origin to the other meaning.

**Student:** Regarding His words ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:85]: does this indicate that ﴿qalīlan﴾ does not refer back to the waw (the plural subject)?

**The Shaykh:** Yes indeed. But those who believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part, what is their ruling with Allah? What is their ruling with Allah? They are disbelievers. ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers, and wish to make distinction between Allah and His messengers, and say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others," and desire to adopt a way between that. Those are the disbelievers in truth﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:150-151]. Because the one who believes in part and disbelieves in part means that he believes only in what agrees with his desire, so he becomes a non-believer in reality.

**Student:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** What do you say? He says: one who pursues dispensations (rukhas), shall we say that he is among those who believe in part and disbelieve in part? Yes, without doubt, because he takes whatever agrees with him, and whatever does not agree with him he seeks someone who will issue a fatwa in accordance with his opinion. But this is lesser, because he does not disbelieve by the second statement; rather he considers the first statement preponderant on the basis of the saying of the one who issued the fatwa to him. So it is lesser. Nevertheless, the scholars said that pursuing dispensations is forbidden, to the extent that some of them went to excess and said: whoever pursues dispensations has become a zindiq (heretic).

**Student:** (...)?

**The Shaykh:** It depends on the pursuit. What may motivate him may be dislike of the hardship that the Sharia indicates, which he claims is hardship, and he may have another excuse, according to what (...) of the person.

**Student:** Someone might cite the end of the verse as evidence that ordinary people are disbelievers, from the causal bā' in ﴿but Allah cursed them for their disbelief﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:46]. So the Jews say: they were cursed because of their disbelief, so they must take the authentic evidences. Likewise, whoever takes a rival to Allah, because they take rivals besides Allah, this is a cause for him (...) from accepting the truth. How is one to respond to them?

**The Shaykh:** Do these people say: "We hear and we disobey"?

**The Student:** The causal bā' in ﴿but Allah cursed them for their disbelief﴾: because of their disbelief...

**The Shaykh:** Manifest disbelief, this is manifest disbelief. After they knew, they said "We hear and we disobey"; they did not say "We hear and did not understand."

**Student:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** (...).

**Student:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** Disbelief, yes, without doubt.

**The Student:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** If it is so, does every sin that Allah called disbelief fall under his statement regarding a sin to which the name of disbelief is applied but which does not take one out of the religion? Do you understand?

**The Student:** Shaykh, ﴿ghayra musmaʿin﴾ does not suit; its meaning would be "not obeyed."

**The Shaykh:** You mean "not heard"?

**The Student:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** No. It does not fit the morphological pattern (bunya) of the word. If he had said ghayra musmiʿ (with kasra on the mīm) it would be correct; what you mentioned is correct for that form. But if it is with the fatḥa, the context refuses it.

**Student:** Shaykh, you mentioned, may Allah preserve you, that when a munkar (wrong) is denounced by the one who denounces it, that is, he brings something in place of that wrong. Now, for example, in our country people gather for condolence, the ta'ziya, and at this gathering they have what we call a reciter (muqri'). If this committed person comes and sits, and this practice is abstained from, so he speaks with a talk instead, but this is repeated for seven days, is it permissible?

**The Shaykh:** No. In any case, confronting people with matters they have become accustomed to, until it has become a belief for them, is difficult to denounce head-on. But the better way is gradually.

**The Student:** Should he attend all the days, Shaykh, or attend one day and denounce?

**The Shaykh:** That is, he begins, for example, by sitting with them and then says: "Why are you sitting? Why, when the Messenger (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed the dead person is punished for what is wailed over him' [Bukhari (1292), Muslim (927/17), from Umar ibn al-Khattab], 'and indeed he is punished for the weeping of his family' [Bukhari (1286), Muslim (927/23), from Umar ibn al-Khattab]. Would you be content for your father, or your brother, or your son to be punished?!"

**Student:** We deduced from the words of Allah, from the statement of the Jews ﴿and listen, but may you not be made to hear﴾, we deduced that it is from their arrogance, and that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, corrected their expression, ﴿And if they had said, "We hear and we obey"﴾. And you said, Shaykh, may Allah preserve you, that this is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as a permission (tajawwuz) for them, meaning on the basis that it is permissible for them; otherwise "Listen" alone.

**The Shaykh:** Yes indeed. It is a custom that is only said from a higher to a lower. This is the custom. Even now, in speech among us, if one said "Listen, so-and-so," there is some lack of courtesy in it.

**The Student:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** Yes, but these are disobedient people; it is permissible for us to condescend to them for the sake of winning their hearts (ta'lif).

**Student:** Is the definition of disbelief (kufr) derived from this, Shaykh?

**The Shaykh:** You mentioned that alladhān and alladhatān (the dual relative pronouns) are inflected (mu'rabatān) and are inflected with the dual ending. But can we not say that their construction (binā') is closer to correct, because of their resemblance to a particle in a dependent-type resemblance (shabah iftiqārī)? We mentioned that this is the view of the majority of grammarians. But the correct view is that they are inflected, and this resemblance, its manifestation, is their change with the change of governing factors, and this is one of the characteristics of nouns.

This person says: he was preceded by one or two rak'ahs (the imam had missed some of the prayer). A late man came and wished to follow this latecomer as imam. Is his prayer valid behind an imam who was preceded? The correct view is that it is valid, but it is better to avoid it. There are two views of the scholars: some said it is valid, and some said it is not. But the correct view is that it is valid, though it is not appropriate (...).

**Student:** What is the evidence for this?

**The Shaykh:** For what?

**The Student:** For its being valid.

**The Shaykh:** The evidence is that it is permissible for a person to intend to follow an imam during the prayer, as Ibn 'Abbas did with the Messenger (ﷺ) [Bukhari (117), Muslim (763/181), from Ibn 'Abbas].

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you, before We obliterate faces and turn them back upon their hindquarters, or curse them as We cursed the people of the Sabbath. And the command of Allah is always executed.﴾ (47) ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills. And whoever associates with Allah has certainly fabricated a tremendous sin.﴾ [An-Nisa' 47, 48].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you.﴾ The address in His words ﴿O you who were given the Book﴾ is intended to refer primarily to the Jews, and likewise the Christians, since they were given the Book. The Book given to the Jews is the Torah which Allah sent down to Musa (Moses), which He wrote with His own hand, glory be to Him, and sent down upon Musa, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. As for the Book that was sent down to Isa (Jesus), it is the Injil (Gospel).

﴿Believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you﴾, which is the Qur'an. He said ﴿sent down﴾ (nazzalna) because it was revealed piece by piece, according to what the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, requires. The scholars said: the difference between (nazzalna) and (anzalna) is that when (nazzalna) is used together with (anzalna), the meaning of (nazzalna) becomes gradual revelation. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And the Book which He sent down before﴾ [An-Nisa' 136], and He says: ﴿And a Qur'an We have separated so that you may recite it to the people over time, and We have sent it down in stages﴾ [Al-Isra' 106]. So the Qur'an was sent down gradually, according to what the wisdom of Allah requires; whether it be an event Allah speaks about, or a problem on which Allah gives a ruling, or otherwise.

As for His words ﴿confirming what is with you﴾, meaning confirming what is with you, and what is with them is the Torah with respect to whom? 

* Students: With respect to the Jews.

* The Shaykh: And the Injil with respect to the Christians. And how is this confirmation?

Confirmation of it has two aspects. The first aspect is that it confirms them, i.e., it bears witness to what they brought, bears witness to what they brought and that they are true, and the Qur'an is full of this, that the previous books revealed upon the messengers are all true. The second of the two aspects is that it confirms them in that it came in accordance with what they reported; for this noble Qur'an and the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, were both mentioned in the Torah and the Injil, as Allah says: ﴿Those who find him written down with them in the Torah and the Gospel, who enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong and makes lawful for them the good things﴾ [Al-A'raf 157]. So confirmation has two aspects: the first aspect?

* Student: The first aspect is that the Qur'an contains verses that indicate and establish the soundness of the previous books, the Torah and the Injil.

* The Shaykh: So it confirms them, i.e., it bears witness to their soundness. And the second aspect?

* Student: That it bears witness to what they brought.

* The Shaykh: That is the first.

* Student: That it confirms them, in that it came with what they reported.

* The Shaykh: That it came in agreement with what they reported; this Qur'an came in agreement with what they reported. This aspect is different from the first.

﴿Before We obliterate faces and turn them back upon their hindquarters, or curse them﴾. This is a warning and a threat: if they hold back from faith, this will happen to them, ﴿before We obliterate faces and turn them back upon their hindquarters﴾. The scholars differed regarding this obliteration: is it a figurative obliteration or a literal one? It was said that it is figurative, meaning they will not see the truth, will not hear it, and will not benefit from it, and Allah will turn them back upon their heels so that they plunge into disbelief.

It was also said: rather it is literal, namely that the faces are obliterated until they become like the sole of a camel's foot, with no eye, no nose, no lip, no brow, but are entirely like the back of the head; just as the back of the head has none of these, so their faces are likewise obliterated until their faces are like their backs, and then they are turned back upon their hindquarters.

It was also said: the intended obliteration is literal, but it is that the necks are twisted so that the faces are at the back; and this is the meaning of His words ﴿and turn them back upon their hindquarters﴾. And as we told you earlier in the interpretive principle: if a verse can bear two meanings that do not contradict each other, it is to be understood as both together, because the speech of Allah has broad meaning. If the wording admits this and that with no contradiction between them, then it is obligatory to take it in both senses. So here we say: Allah threatened them with both literal obliteration and figurative obliteration.

He said: ﴿or curse them as We cursed the people of the Sabbath﴾. ﴿Curse them﴾ means We will expel them from Our mercy and inflict upon them the punishment that befell the people of the Sabbath. What befell the people of the Sabbath is that they were told: ﴿Be apes, despised and driven away﴾ [Al-Baqarah 65], so they became despised apes, and we seek refuge in Allah.

The difference between the two threats is that the first, if we say it is literal, pertains specifically to one part of the body, which is what? The face. As for the second, it is general: the whole form is transformed, and we seek refuge in Allah, into the form of apes.

It is mentioned that 'Abdullah ibn Salam, may Allah be pleased with him, when he heard this verse, came hastening with his hand on his face, fearing that it would be obliterated, out of his faith and affirmation, until he came to the Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, and believed in him [[Mentioned by al-Baghawi in his Tafsir (2/231).]]. Likewise it is mentioned about Ka'b al-Ahbar in the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him [[Mentioned by al-Baghawi in his Tafsir (2/231).]]; and Allah knows best, but there is no doubt that believers among them would fear this matter.

* If someone says: They did not believe, and this threat did not befall them. They did not believe, but this threat did not befall them. What is the answer?

* The answer: When some of them believed, this threat was lifted, because this threat is conditional upon what, if? If none of them believes. It was also said: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, threatened them with this, and the threat remains until the Day of Resurrection; so if it is supposed that it did not happen in the past, it is still anticipated, because Allah, glory be to Him, threatened them with it: ﴿before We obliterate faces and turn them back upon their hindquarters, or curse them as We cursed the people of the Sabbath﴾.

The first explanation may be closer to the truth, because threatening the People of the Book in the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him, with a matter that will not occur except near the Hour has no meaning or basis. So it is said: when some of them believed, this threat was lifted from them, and the proof was established upon the rest, since those among them who believed and acknowledged the truth.

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿And the command of Allah is always executed﴾. Indeed, by Allah, the command of Allah is executed; who can reverse the command of Allah? No one can reverse it, so the command of Allah must come to pass. The word "command" here means "that which is commanded," i.e., what Allah commanded is executed. It may also be that "command" means the universal command, i.e., decree, and "executed" here means "that which occurs." Whichever it is, whether we say "command" means "that which is commanded," which is not far-fetched, since "command" is a verbal noun, and a verbal noun sometimes carries the sense of the passive participle, as in His words: ﴿and for those with loads, their term is that they lay down their burden﴾ [At-Talaq 4], meaning "those with burdens"; since "ahmal" is the plural of "haml," and "haml" is the fetus in the womb. And as in the Prophet's, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, saying: "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our affair, it is rejected" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697) and Muslim (1718/18), and the wording is his, from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]]; i.e., rejected. ﴿And the command of Allah is always executed﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse:

* First: the obligation upon the People of the Book to believe in the noble Qur'an, by His words: ﴿O you who were given the Book, believe﴾.

* Among its benefits: the establishment of proof against those who were given the Book and disbelieved in Muhammad, that they have no excuse. How so? Because they were given the Book, so they have knowledge, and because what was sent down upon Muhammad, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, confirms what is with them. So they have no excuse: their Book is before them, and it is the means of knowledge; then the coming of this Qur'an confirming what is with them establishes that Muhammad, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, is true, so it is obligatory upon them to believe in him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah. What is its aspect? ﴿What We have sent down﴾.

* If someone says: Sending down attributed to Allah may be concerning created things, such as His words: ﴿And We sent down iron, in which is great might﴾ [Al-Hadid 25], and ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [Az-Zumar 6]?

* The answer to that comes through the following detailed explanation: that what is sent down from Allah divides into two kinds: entities and attributes.

Entities are separate and detached from Allah, so they are what? They are created, such as: ﴿And We sent down iron, in which is great might﴾, ﴿And We sent down from the sky pure water﴾ [Al-Furqan 48], ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾. These are entities, separate and detached from Allah, so they are created.

The second kind: attributes that subsist only in a subject, such as speech. Speech is an attribute that subsists only in a described subject. So when Allah attributes the sending down of speech to Himself, it is one of His attributes, and it is uncreated. On this basis, the Qur'an is uncreated.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment of Allah's being above, what is its aspect? ﴿We sent down﴾, since sending down only occurs from above, and so it is. The proofs for the highness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, have preceded us many times, and we said that the highness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, divides into two kinds: a sensory kind and an abstract kind.

The abstract kind is agreed upon among the people of the faith; even the people of ta'til (denial of attributes) claim that they deny them out of glorifying Allah above imperfection. So the abstract highness is denied by no one among the people of the faith; all people of the qibla affirm it. The essential sensory highness is what those other than Ahl as-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah denied, saying: Allah is not high in His essence, with a false argument.

We have already explained earlier that the essential highness is indicated by five kinds of evidence: the Book, the Sunnah, consensus, reason, and innate nature (fitrah), and we explained how; this is known to most of you, and whoever lacks knowledge should return to it in the recordings.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that the noble Qur'an confirms the previous books, bearing witness to their truthfulness, and that it confirms them in that it came in agreement with what they reported. It does not conflict with them nor diverge from them. However, the laws differ according to the nations and even according to circumstances; even in the Islamic law the rulings differ according to circumstances, is that not so? The poor person has no zakat obligation, and the wealthy person has zakat obligation; this is a difference. How can it be said: this man whose name is Zayd owes zakat, and this man whose name is 'Amr owes no zakat?

We say: yes, because the first is wealthy and the second is poor. The laws differ, as Allah says: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 48], but the foundations, the foundations of the religions, are one and the same; this noble Book confirms what is before it.

In Surat al-Ma'idah Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, explained that it is muhaymin over what preceded it, and the meaning of muhaymin is what? That is, dominant; dominance over a thing means authority and control, and if that is so, it necessarily follows that it abrogates what preceded it.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the threat to those people, meaning the People of the Book, if they do not believe in this Qur'an, with these two warnings: the obliteration of faces and turning them back upon their hindquarters, and the second, that they be cursed as the people of the Sabbath were cursed.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: avoiding direct address when taking someone to account. Here He said: ﴿before We obliterate faces﴾, and did not say "your faces", though the context would have required: before We obliterate your faces, since they are the ones threatened. Yet it was expressed in the indefinite form, avoiding what? Avoiding direct confrontation in accountability. This is one aspect. Another aspect: it may be said that the indefiniteness here conveys glorification, meaning faces held in esteem among you, so they will be obliterated; they are the faces of their leaders who turned them away from the path of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that reference to what is known is valid even with a vague wording. From where is this derived?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, reference to what is known is valid even with a vague wording.

* Students: His words: ﴿as We cursed the people of the Sabbath﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿As We cursed the people of the Sabbath﴾; because if someone asks: what was the curse that befell the people of the Sabbath? And who were the people of the Sabbath? We say: they are mentioned here in summary, since their matter is known. This resembles what the grammarians say about the "al-" that denotes a mentally known referent.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, glory be to Him, mentions Himself with the wording of greatness: ﴿We obliterate﴾, (We turn them back), (We curse), ﴿as We cursed﴾. Why? Because the context requires it; the context is one of threat, and the threatener must necessarily make his greatness manifest before the one threatened. This is the height of eloquence: observing the state of the addressee. This is eloquence.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility, indeed the recommendation or preferability, of changing the style when the need calls for it; from His words: ﴿And the command of Allah is always executed﴾, where He did not say "And Our command is executed". So the verse shifts from second-person address to what? To the third person; because ﴿the command of Allah﴾ speaks of an absent party, whereas "We obliterate", "We curse" and the like speak in the first person. So there is a shift from the first person to the third person for glorification, since the saying of a great one, "So-and-so did such-and-such," meaning himself, is more eloquent than saying "I did such-and-such."

Student: "And whoever associates others with Allah has fabricated a tremendous sin. Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves?" [An-Nisa 4:48-49].

The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾. What is meant by His saying: ﴿confirming that which is with you﴾? The People of the Sabbath are well known to us, those who transgressed regarding the Sabbath, so they devised a stratagem to hunt fish on the Sabbath, when it had been forbidden to them, and the fish used to come to them openly. ﴿And on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come to them﴾ [Al-A'raf 7:163]. They devised by setting nets on Friday and taking the fish on Sunday; so they were transformed into apes, despised.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive﴾: He, glory be to Him, speaks of Himself in the third person, out of magnification of Himself, as a king says: "Indeed the king commands you to go to such-and-such a place." This is a form of magnification; the speaker referring to himself in the third person is considered a mark of honour.

As for His saying: ﴿He does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾: forgiveness (maghfirah) is concealment together with overlooking. This meaning, that it is composed of concealment and overlooking, is supported by the derivation of the word, for maghfirah is derived from maghfar, which is what is placed upon the head, called the helmet (bayda), by which arrows are warded off. When it is placed upon the head and used to ward off arrows, it has in it concealment of what? And protection.

So: ﴿He does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ means He does not overlook nor conceal association with Him. As for His saying: ﴿that partners be associated with Him﴾, the "an" here is a verbal-source particle (an masdariyyah). The masdariyyah "an" is among the particles that... connect (mawsulah)? Thus it is joined with what follows to form a verbal noun, and the estimate would be: Indeed Allah does not forgive a partner ascribed to Him, or associating with Him. Do you understand? He does not forgive association with Him. When we convert this verb together with "an" into a verbal noun, it becomes an indefinite noun in a negative context, and an indefinite noun in a negative context denotes generality.

His saying, exalted be He: ﴿that partners be associated with Him﴾ includes association in lordship (rububiyyah), association in divinity (uluhiyyah), which is association in worship, and third, association in the names and attributes. Allah does not forgive it, because the aspect of tawhid is the greatest of aspects in that it must be upheld; so if a person neglects it, Allah, glory be to Him, does not forgive it. Unlike the other sins that are less than it, or other than shirk, which Allah forgives. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾. Whoever believes that there is with Allah a creator or a helper is a polytheist; or that any of the creation has something he holds independently apart from Allah is a polytheist. That is, whoever says: the heavens are Allah's and the earth belongs to other than Allah, is a polytheist; whoever says: the heavens and earth are shared between Allah and others, is a polytheist; whoever says: Allah has a helper in creating the heavens and earth, is a polytheist. All of this Allah does not forgive. In worship: whoever prostrates to other than Allah, or vows to other than Allah, or slaughters to other than Allah, is a polytheist. Whoever associates others with Allah in worship through showing off (riya') is a polytheist; showing off is shirk according to the text of the hadith[[Recorded by Ibn Majah (3989) from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Indeed, the slightest showing off is shirk." Ahmad (11252) and Ibn Majah (4204) also recorded from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "... the hidden shirk: that a man stands to pray and beautifies his prayer because of the gaze of a man upon him." And other hadiths.]].

So showing off is not forgiven. Likewise whoever claims that Allah has a likeness in His attributes, or that Allah's istiwa' upon the Throne is like a man's sitting upon a couch, or that Allah's descent to the lowest heaven is like a man's descent from a roof to the lowest step, and similar things, is a polytheist. All of this Allah does not forgive.

﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾. Regarding His saying ﴿what is less than that﴾: is what is meant "what is other than that," or "what is lesser than that"? Is it the "dun" meaning lesser, or the "dun" meaning other than?

Students: (...).

The Shaykh: Let us see. If we say "other than that," it would follow that Allah forgives the denial of disbelief (kufr al-juhud), since it is other than shirk. If a person said: Allah did not send Muhammad ﷺ, this is not shirk; it is other than shirk without doubt. Is this forgiven? Answer me.

Students: No.

The Shaykh: Then it is necessary that the meaning of "what is less than that" is what is lesser, not the "dun" meaning "other than," because if we interpreted it as "other than that," the denial of disbelief would be included in the verse, and it is not so.

﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾: His saying ﴿for whom He wills﴾ means for whomever He wills. Accordingly, shirk and what is in its position, such as denial of disbelief and the like, is not forgiven, while what is less than that is under His will: it is neither forgiven nor necessarily punished, but under His will.

Furthermore, we say: everything Allah has restricted by will is joined with wisdom; if wisdom requires it He wills it, and if it does not require it He does not will it, because the loss of wisdom is folly, and Allah is exalted above it.

What supports this restriction, that everything Allah restricts by His will is joined with wisdom, is His saying in Surat al-Insan: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills; indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [Al-Insan 76:30]. He said: ﴿indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾, following it with: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾, showing that Allah's will follows His knowledge and wisdom.

Then He said: ﴿And whoever associates others with Allah has fabricated a tremendous sin﴾. Our Lord has spoken truly. Whoever associates others with Allah is the greatest fabricator, that is, whoever associates others with Allah in His lordship, or in His worship, or in His names and attributes, has fabricated a tremendous sin, meaning he has lied a great lie, or lied in a way that deserves a great sin. For the greatest sin, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4477) and Muslim (86/141) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]]. This is the greatest sin: that you set up a rival to Allah when He created you. How can you set up a rival to Allah when He is the One who created you? This is the greatest thing: ﴿Indeed, association [with Allah] is a tremendous injustice﴾ [Luqman 31:13]. This is the meaning of the verse; its benefits are many.

Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you, does "sawa" (other than) not include (...) so that disbelief is not part of shirk?

The Shaykh: Yes.

Student: Is disbelief not shirk?

The Shaykh: No, but it is not called shirk.

Student: But in magnitude, Shaykh?

The Shaykh: Yes indeed, and for this reason we said "what is less than that," meaning what is lesser. Is it clear? If we say "what is other than that," He forgives what is other than that. Is disbelief shirk or not?

Student: Disbelief is shirk, Shaykh.

The Shaykh: If one denies what the Messenger brought, has he associated or denied?

Student: (...).

The Shaykh: Leave aside shirk in the general sense; even one who backbites people is a polytheist in the general sense. Shirk is making a rival to Allah. Does this make a rival to Allah?

Student: No.

The Shaykh: Then "what is less than that" is better than "what is other than that."

* * *

Student: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves? Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills, and they will not be wronged a bit (fatil). See how they fabricate lies against Allah, and that is sufficient as a manifest sin﴾ [An-Nisa 4:49-50]. ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, who believe in jibt and taghut, and say of those who disbelieved: "These are better guided than those who believed in the way"﴾ [An-Nisa 4:51].

The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah says: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾.

In this verse there are benefits, among them: the greatness of shirk, and that Allah, glory be to Him, does not forgive it, because it is the greatest sin. The Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, was asked: "Which sin is greatest?" He said: "That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4477) and Muslim (86/141) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]].

Another benefit: the affirmation of Allah's voluntary acts, Mighty and Majestic. You know that many of the muattilah, the Ash'arites, the Mu'tazilites and their like, deny that an act connected to His will subsists in Allah, because they say: acts connected to will are originated, and the originated subsists only in something originated. There is no doubt that this is false, a false conception; for an originated thing can subsist in the eternal, just as an originated thing that happened today can subsist in a creature created fifty years ago. The occurrence of an act does not necessitate that the agent be originated.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: that what is less than shirk is under His will, by His saying: ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾, and it is not decisively known that it will be forgiven nor decisively known that one will be taken to account for it, since it is under His will.

It follows from this benefit: the refutation of the words of those who delay repentance, who commit sins and then say: Allah forgives what is less than shirk for whom He wills. We say to him: what made you know that you are among those whom Allah wills to forgive? Do you know? So you are gambling. Even if we suppose your sinful act could be forgiven, it is not certain; sin is a manifest corruption that has occurred, and its forgiveness is a benefit but is under will: it may occur and it may not.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of tawhid of Allah, since shirk is not forgiven; and it follows that Allah's tawhid is obligatory. Indeed it is the most obligatory of obligations in His essence, names, attributes and acts; Allah, Mighty and Majestic, must be singled out in all of this.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the polytheist is one who fabricates against Allah, by His saying: ﴿whoever associates others with Allah has fabricated a tremendous sin﴾.

And among its benefits too: that this lie is among the greatest lies, by His saying: ﴿a tremendous sin﴾. In another verse: ﴿whoever associates others with Allah has certainly strayed far astray﴾ [An-Nisa 4:116]. So he is astray in his religion, and he is also a fabricator in His saying: ﴿has fabricated a tremendous sin﴾.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's will; by His saying: ﴿for whom He wills﴾. We have already alerted in the commentary that everything Allah has linked to will is joined with wisdom, and we cited as evidence His saying: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills; indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [Al-Insan 76:30].

The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿He does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ is that it includes minor shirk and major shirk, and Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, stated this clearly in the book al-Ikhtiyarat: that Allah does not forgive shirk even if it is minor. But we must know that our saying that minor shirk is not forgiven does not mean its perpetrator will remain forever in the Fire; rather he will be punished according to the measure of his deed and then enter Paradise. As for major shirk, it is not forgiven, and its perpetrator is eternal in the Fire, by His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Indeed, whoever associates others with Allah, Allah has forbidden him Paradise, and his refuge is the Fire, and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 5:72].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 49 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you not seen those who ascribe purity to themselves?﴾ [An-Nisa' 49] The interrogative here is for amazement and affirmation; that is, "Are you not amazed at the state of these people?"

The address in His words ﴿Have you not seen﴾ is either to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the address directed to him is directed to the Ummah through the branch, because the Ummah is a branch. It has also been said that the address is directed to everyone to whom address can be directed, that is, to everyone to whom it is valid to direct the address. Which of the two is more general? The second is more general.
