But the two opinions do not contradict each other, because even if we say that the original address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), the address to the leader is an address to him and to those who follow him.

His words ﴿Have you not seen those who ascribe purity to themselves﴾ mean that the answer to the interrogative is omitted: "Will purity be attained by them?" This is the meaning, because when such a statement comes, there must be an interrogative sentence, either mentioned or omitted.

His words ﴿ascribe purity to themselves﴾ mean that they attribute purity (zakah) to themselves. Zakah is the opposite of wretchedness. Who is meant by "these people"? It means everyone who purifies himself, and the first to enter this are the Jews and the Christians, because the Jews and the Christians said: ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 18], and this is self-purification. And ﴿They said: None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ [Al-Baqarah 111], and ﴿They said: The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ [Al-'Imran 24]. So they purified themselves in deed and in the reward for it: they purified themselves in deed when they said ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾, and they purified themselves with the reward for it when they said ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾. And they also purified themselves from another angle, regarding the punishment, when they said ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾.

Whoever is like them, that is, whoever purifies himself, takes a share of resemblance to them. Whoever says "I am a saint (wali)," or "I am pious," or the like, has purified himself. This is especially so with what occurs from some Sufi shaykhs who deceive people; they say: "We are saints, we are the chosen ones," and the like. They purify themselves so that people will be deceived by them.

His words ﴿But Allah purifies whom He wills﴾: is "bal" (but/rather) here for idrab ibtali (refutational transition) or idrab intiqali (transitional shift)?
* Some students: Intiqali.
* Other students: Ibtali.
* The Shaykh: Ibtali, because the implied meaning is: ﴿Have you not seen those who ascribe purity to themselves?﴾ Will purity be attained by them?
The answer: No, purity will not be attained by them. Had everyone who purified himself attained purity, the most wicked of people would purify himself. Now, those who worship idols, who worship cows, who worship trees, who worship whatever they worship, say: "We are the ones upon the truth," and so they purify themselves. But to whom does purification return? To Allah.

For this reason Allah, glorified and exalted, refuted all these claims of purity and said: ﴿But Allah purifies whom He wills﴾. So "bal" here is for idrab what? The ibtali. And "bal" comes for idrab ibtali and comes for idrab intiqali. Look at His words: ﴿Rather, their knowledge has failed concerning the Hereafter. Rather, they are in doubt about it. Rather, they are blind to it﴾ [An-Naml 66]. Is this idrab intiqali or ibtali?
* Students: Intiqali.
* The Shaykh: Intiqali. It moves from one thing to another, and the first thing remains, but it is a transition; their states move them until they reach this limit.

So the summary is that idrab can be ibtali and can be intiqali.

﴿But Allah purifies whom He wills﴾: He is the One who purifies, glorified and exalted; He is the One who praises. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest. Those are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterward. But to each Allah has promised the best﴾ [Al-Hadid 10]. So Allah the Exalted gave purification to these, each according to his state. ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest, and those are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterward﴾: He gave these their share and those their share, then He purified all of them in a general way, saying: ﴿But to each Allah has promised the best﴾; this is the purification. And He said: ﴿Not equal are those who sit [at home] among the believers, other than those who have a disability, and those who strive in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives. Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their lives over those who sit at home by a degree. But to each Allah has promised the best﴾ [An-Nisa' 95].

So Allah the Exalted is the One who purifies. Likewise His Messenger (ﷺ) also purifies: "The best of people are my generation, then those who follow them, then those who follow them" [Agreed upon; Bukhari (2652) and Muslim (2533/212), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud]. Whoever the Messenger (ﷺ) has purified is pure, because the Prophet (ﷺ) in matters like these does not speak except by revelation. ﴿But Allah purifies whom He wills﴾.

His words ﴿whom He wills﴾: this also follows wisdom. Every act that is tied to will follows wisdom. So Allah, glorified and exalted, purifies whoever is worthy of purification, whether the purification is after the deed or before the deed. Purification after the deed is as you have heard from the verses, and purification before the deed is that Allah grants a person righteous deeds. He is, as He knows where to place His message, also knowing where to place the effect of this message, which is faith and righteous deeds. So Allah's purification is purification before the deed and purification after it. He, glorified and exalted, purifies whom He wills before and after the deed. If we say that will follows wisdom, then He will not purify except one who is what? Worthy of purification.

He said: ﴿But Allah purifies whom He wills, and they will not be wronged the extent of a fatil﴾. ﴿They will not be wronged﴾: the waw is the plural marker. And ﴿whom He wills﴾: "man" is a relative pronoun whose wording is singular, so here the pronoun returns to "man" according to meaning. ﴿They will not be wronged﴾ means: whoever Allah, glorified and exalted, purified, or ﴿they will not be wronged﴾ means those who purified themselves. They will not be punished except in accordance with their evil deeds. Whether this or that, Allah does not wrong anyone; He does not increase their bad deeds nor decrease their good deeds.

He says: ﴿They will not be wronged the extent of a fatil﴾. The fatil is said to be the thread that is inside the pit of a date stone. The date stone contains three things, all mentioned in the Qur'an: the qitmir, the naqir and the fatil. The qitmir is the thin skin upon it, the naqir is the small pit on its back, and the fatil is the thread inside it. It has also been said that the fatil is what you twist between your fingers when you rub something; when a person rolls it between his fingers like this, something comes out, and likewise when he scratches his chest or back, the fatil appears. But the first is the well-known one: the fatil is what is in the inside of the date stone, the thread that is in its inside, and it is used as a proverb for something very little.

* * *

(...) A man was in the mosque to fetch something and then returned. Does he pray the greeting of the mosque (tahiyyat al-masjid)?
The answer: No, he does not pray the greeting of the mosque as long as he stood up intending to return. But if he stood up, for example, intending to leave, then something appeared to him so he returned, then he prays the greeting of the mosque, even if he took only one step.

He says: One of the brothers found at the door of the great central mosque a sum of money. What should he do with it? And if we say he should announce it, should we write an announcement on the door of the mosque or not? Advise us.
Yes, write an announcement on the door of the mosque, and there is no harm.

And this one says: If several causes combine for a ruling, is it not established except when all the causes are present?
Yes, if it is not established except by two causes, then it is not established except by both, and one of them is called juz' al-'illah (part of the cause).

* Student: Shaykh, how long is the announcement period?
* The Shaykh: A full year.
* Student: A year?
* The Shaykh: Yes.
Student: Shaykh, does he not take it with the intention of its owner?
* The Shaykh: No, unless the owner has lost hope of it, like what is found on the roads. On the roads you cannot... Perhaps the one who lost it is from the desert far away, or perhaps from the town in front or behind, and one does not know. But this must be announced.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿Have you not seen those who ascribe purity to themselves? But Allah purifies whom He wills, and they will not be wronged the extent of a fatil. (49) Look how they invent lies against Allah, and that is sufficient as a manifest sin. (50) Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, who believe in jibt and taghut and say to those who disbelieve, "These are better guided than those who believe in the way"? (51) Those are the ones Allah has cursed, and whomever Allah curses, you will not find for him a helper. (52) Or do they have a share in dominion? If so, they would not give the people even a speck. (53) Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty? But We had already given the family of Abraham the Scripture and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom. (54) Among them were those who believed in it and among them were those who averted from it, and sufficient is Hellfire as a blaze.﴾ [An-Nisa' 49-55].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. We have already discussed His words ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with﴾, and I think we discussed it too? So let us begin with the verse after it: ﴿Have you not seen those who ascribe purity to themselves?﴾ First, to whom is the address?
﴿Have you not seen those who ascribe purity to themselves?﴾ To whom is the address?
* Student: The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it has been said: to whoever the address can be directed.
* The Shaykh: To whom it is valid to direct the address.
* Student: And the second is more general (...).
* The Shaykh: The second is general, so it is preferable. But do they differ in the meaning conveyed?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: They do not differ.
* Student: The address to the Prophet (ﷺ) is an address to the Ummah.
* The Shaykh: Who is meant by "those"?
* Student: What is meant by them are the Jews and the Christians.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
How was their self-purification? With what?
* Student: They said: ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 18], and they said: ﴿None will enter Paradise﴾ [Al-Baqarah 111], by deed and by reward.
* The Shaykh: Yes. They said: ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾, and they said: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾.
Did Allah approve of them in that?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: No?! How?!
* Student: Those who purify themselves, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, did not approve of them; rather He placed the matter in His hands, the purification.
* The Shaykh: The evidence?
* Student: ﴿But Allah purifies whom He wills﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿But Allah purifies whom He wills﴾. Good. And this "bal", is it for idrab ibtali or intiqali?
* Student: For ibtali.
* The Shaykh: For ibtali. Good, correct.
His words ﴿and they will not be wronged the extent of a fatil﴾: what is meant by the fatil?
* Student: (...).
* Another student: The fatil is what is twisted in the hand.
* The Shaykh: Well done. It has been said: it is the thread of the date stone that is inside it, and it has been said: what is twisted in the hand of dirt or the like. The first is more famous.
In the Qur'an, concerning the date stone, there are three things. Say them.
* Student: The fatil, the naqir and the qitmir.
* The Shaykh: What is the difference? What is the fatil? What is the qitmir? What is the naqir?
* Student: The fatil is the white thread that is in the stone itself...
* Another student: The membrane on the stone is a thin membrane, and the naqir is the hollow that is on the back of the stone.
* The Shaykh: The small pit on the back of the stone. And for what is it used as a proverb?
* Student: For paucity.
* The Shaykh: It is used as a proverb for paucity.
Among the benefits of this noble verse: the denunciation of one who purifies himself. The reason for this is that His words ﴿Have you not seen﴾ [An-Nisa' 49] are a rhetorical interrogative of denunciation.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of self-purification, because Allah, the Exalted, denounced it, as He stated in His words: ﴿He knows you best when He produced you from the earth and when you were fetuses in the wombs of your mothers. So do not ascribe purity to yourselves; He is most knowing of who fears Him﴾ [An-Najm 32].
Among the branches of this is a person's saying: "I am a believer." Is it permissible for a person to say "I am a believer," or must he say "I am a believer, if Allah wills"?
On this there are two opinions among the scholars. Some said: it is not permissible to say "I am a believer" except with an exception, because a person does not know how he will die, and what counts is the end. A person may be a believer today and a disbeliever tomorrow, and it is not permissible to affirm something in the future.
Others said: it is not permissible to say "I am a believer," not for this reason, but because this statement entails self-purification and testifying to oneself that one is in Paradise. Because if he says "I am a believer," then every believer is in Paradise, so it follows that he must affirm that he is among the people of Paradise, and this is not permissible.
Others gave a third reason and said: faith in its absolute sense is intended as complete faith, which includes performing the obligations, abstaining from the prohibitions, performing the recommended acts and abstaining from the disliked acts. A servant cannot affirm this. How many recommended acts do we not perform, and even obligatory acts! And how many disliked acts do we perform, and even prohibited acts! So on this basis one must say: "I am a believer, if Allah wills."
Others said: it is not permissible to say "I am a believer, if Allah wills," because this is doubt; "I am a believer, if Allah wills" is doubt, and doubt in faith is disbelief, since what is obligatory in faith is certainty, and hesitation in it is disbelief.
But the preferred opinion on this question is that one should say: what prompts a person to say "I am a believer"? On this the ruling depends. If what prompts him is self-purification, then this statement is forbidden, because Allah says what? ﴿Do not ascribe purity to yourselves﴾ [An-Najm 32]. Furthermore, this involves presumption before Allah, the Exalted, and claiming favor over Him. Allah the Exalted said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿They consider it a favor to you that they have embraced Islam. Say: Do not consider your Islam a favor to me. Rather, Allah has conferred favor upon you that He guided you to faith, if you are truthful﴾ [Al-Hujurat 17].
So if his saying "I am a believer" is to express self-admiration, this is not permissible, because it is self-purification and is forbidden, so it is unlawful.
But if what is intended by it is information, meaning by saying "I am a believer" that he is not a disbeliever, then there is no harm in it. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to the people he met on his way to Hajj: "Who are the people?" They said: "The Muslims" [Muslim (1336/409), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas], and the Prophet (ﷺ) approved them in that, because they intended by it what? Information. So if a person says "I am a believer," meaning "I am not a disbeliever," then there is no harm, and the consequences he mentioned from forbidding the saying "I am a believer" do not follow from it.
As for if he says "if Allah wills," meaning if he ties his faith to will, this must be examined, and again there is detail: if he intends by it hesitation, then it is what? Disbelief. For example, if someone said to him: "Are you a believer?" and he said: "If Allah wills," meaning he is hesitant, this is disbelief, because there is no faith with doubt; certainty is necessary.

If the motive for that was that his faith is by the will of Allah and not by His power and might, then there is no harm in it. Why? Because a certain matter may be linked to the will (of Allah) as a sign that it will occur by the will of Allah. Among this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security﴾ [al-Fath 27]. That is, you will enter it by His will, because the statement here is a definite report emphasized with three emphatics: ﴿you will surely enter﴾. And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when Umar said to him, "Did you not say that we would come to the House and circumambulate it?", the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Did I tell you that it would be this year?" He said: "No." He said: "Indeed you will come to it and circumambulate it." [Related by al-Bukhari (2732) from the hadith of al-Miswar and Marwan.] He said that in the exchange between him and Umar concerning the matter of the treaty, the treaty of al-Hudaybiyah.

Among this also is the saying of the visitor to the graveyard: "And we, if Allah wills, will certainly join you." The joining with them is certain, for no one denies death. But what is meant by "if Allah wills" is: we will join you by the will of Allah; whenever Allah wills that we join you, we will join you.

Third: if his intention in saying "if Allah wills" is to ward off self-praise (tazkiyah), that is, to ward off the praising of the self, and he fears for himself that if he does not say "if Allah wills," something of self-praise will arise in his soul, then here his saying "if Allah wills" is—what?—obligatory; it is obligatory.

So we now have, may Allah bless you, that a person's saying "I am a believer" is either conjoined with the will or not conjoined. If it is not conjoined with the will, then there are two states:
The first state: self-praise, and this is forbidden.
The second state: merely reporting that he is a believer and not a disbeliever, and this is permissible.

If he conjoins it with the will, then there are three states:
Either the motive for that is doubt, and this is disbelief.
Or the motive for that is to clarify that his faith is by the will of Allah, and this is permissible, because it is true.
Or the motive for that is what?
* The students: Warding off self-praise.
* The Shaykh: Yes, warding off self-praise, the praising of the self; this is obligatory. And this distinction is the one by which the evidences are reconciled.

* Among the benefits of the verse: ﴿Have you not seen those who justify themselves?﴾ [an-Nisa' 49]: that praising others is not objectionable, because the prohibition or censure is directed at what? At the praising of the self. As for if one praises another, there is no harm in that.

Here we ask: can one praise another merely on the basis of appearance, or is experience necessary? The second: experience is necessary. It is not sufficient for you to see a person's appearance and say, "He is just and trustworthy." Rather, experience is necessary. Why? Because he may not be just; he may be a show-off, a hypocrite, a deceiver. And perhaps he is just in his religion but has poor memory. So if you vouch for him in matters relating to reports, such as testimony for example, without having tested him, that becomes testimony to what you do not know. Is that not so? Is it clear or not clear?
* The students: Clear.
* The Shaykh: Clear. That is, a man comes and says: "Vouch for so-and-so; so-and-so testified to me about something; will you vouch for him?" I may vouch for him in terms of his religion, and know that he is an upright man in religion who prays, gives zakat, and fasts, who keeps all the works of religion. But as for memory, and the matter is one of testimony and report, then I must have knowledge of his inner state and examination. So vouching in matters of reports is not permissible unless you know that the man has a good memory.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the matter of vouching for a person and withdrawing such vouching from him rests with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. From where is this taken?
* The students: ﴿Rather, Allah﴾.
* The Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills﴾. So the judgment of purification, whether affirmation or negation, belongs to Allah alone; it is He who purifies whom He wills.

If someone says: How do we reconcile this with the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it (9), and he has failed who corrupts it﴾ [ash-Shams 9, 10]?

The answer: if the doer in His saying ﴿who purifies it﴾ is Allah, then there is no difficulty, correct?
* The students: Correct.
* The Shaykh: Correct, because the one who purifies is Allah in this and in that. And if the pronoun that is the doer refers to the human being, meaning: he has succeeded who purifies himself, and ﴿he has failed who corrupts it﴾ [ash-Shams 10], that is, corrupts himself. So the reconciliation is that the attribution of purification to the human being here is the attribution of a thing to its cause, not to its occurrence. The human being performs the obedience and thus becomes pure; and who is the doer? The human being. So the meaning of purification is the performance of its cause, and on this basis there is no difficulty either.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: it is recommended, rather obligatory, for a person to seek purification from whom? From Allah; by His saying: ﴿Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills﴾. So when you know that Allah is the One who purifies, ask Allah. For this reason, among the transmitted supplications is: "O Allah, grant my soul its piety, and purify it; You are the best of those who purify it. You are its Guardian and its Master." [Related by Muslim (2722/73) from the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam, with the wording: "O Allah, grant..."]

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: a refutation of the Qadariyyah who claim that a person is independent in his deeds. From where is this taken?
* The students: ﴿Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills﴾.

* And among its benefits: the affirmation of will for Allah, the Exalted, by His saying ﴿whom He wills﴾, and that Allah, glorified and exalted, has a will by which He directs affairs. But is this will an absolute will, meaning He wills whatever He wills, for wisdom or without wisdom? No, rather it is a will conjoined with wisdom.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the negation of injustice from Allah, by His saying: ﴿and they will not be wronged even a thread﴾. And injustice is forbidden for Allah, or not forbidden?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Forbidden for Allah?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Who forbade it for Himself?
* The students: He Himself.
* The Shaykh: He Himself, glorified and exalted. In the sacred hadith: "O My servants, I have forbidden injustice for Myself and made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another." [Related by Muslim (2577/55) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]

In this there is a fine point: that Allah imposes upon Himself and forbids upon Himself, because Allah is the One who directs the affair. ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy: whoever of you does evil out of ignorance and then repents after that and corrects himself, indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-An'am 54]. (Kataba) means what?
* The students: Imposed it.
* The Shaykh: Imposed. He has imposed it upon Himself, and here in the sacred hadith: "I have forbidden injustice for Myself."

If someone says: Is there among Allah's attributes something that is pure negation, or is every negation in Allah's attributes necessarily implying an affirmation?
* The students: The second.
* The Shaykh: The second. Every negation in Allah's attributes necessarily implies an affirmation. So His saying ﴿and they will not be wronged even a thread﴾ is for what? Because Allah is perfect in justice, and whoever is perfect in justice does not wrong even a thread.

The scholars said: It is impossible that there be among Allah's attributes a pure negation that does not imply praise. It is impossible for there to be a pure negation that does not imply praise. They gave the reason: a negation, if it does not imply a perfection, may be a deficiency, or may be neither a deficiency nor a perfection. The categories are three: deficiency, perfection, and what? Neither this nor that. Deficiency and what is neither this nor that are impossible for Allah, by the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest description﴾ [an-Nahl 60].

If someone says: We want an example of negating injustice that contains neither praise nor blame? The answer: if you say, "The wall does not wrong, the piece of wood does not wrong, the car does not wrong," this implies neither perfection nor deficiency, why? Because it is not capable of being described with injustice or its absence, since the wall has no will so as to wrong or not wrong.

And if you say: give us an example in which the negation of injustice is a deficiency, we say: the saying of the poet:

A tribe that does not betray a covenant,
and does not wrong people even a mustard seed's weight,

This means: they do not betray a covenant, i.e., they have fidelity, and they do not wrong people even a mustard seed's weight, i.e., they have justice. It is said: the poet did not intend that, but rather intended to show their weakness and incapacity, as evidenced by his saying "a tribe" in diminutive form. Likewise the saying of the Hamasi:

But my people, though they are numerous,
are not in any way evil, even if they were ...

That is, they are not (...) evil, even if it were minor.

They repay the injustice of the unjust with forgiveness,
and the evil of the wicked with kindness.

If someone wrongs them, they endure and forgive and say, "May Allah forgive you." And the evil of the wicked they repay with kindness: if someone harms them, they treat him well; if he ruins their farm, they send him sacks of grain. So they repay the evil of the wicked with what? Kindness. Whoever hears these words says: these people are good. But read what follows:

Would that I had among them a people who, when they ride,
launch a raid, horsemen and riders.

That is: would that I had in their place others; so they are weak and cannot do that. This is a deficiency.

So when Allah negates injustice from Himself, it cannot be of this kind nor of the previous kind, but rather it is the negation of injustice that implies the perfection of justice.

[Translation begins]

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Look how they invent lies against Allah﴾ [An-Nisa 4:50]. ﴿Look﴾: to whom is the address directed?

* Student: There are two opinions.

* The Shaykh: Either it is addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to everyone to whom address is validly directed. By way of relevance, let us recall what was mentioned earlier: that address directed to the Messenger (ﷺ) is divided into three categories.

The first category: that which evidence shows is specific to him. This is specific to him, such as ﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear victory. That Allah may forgive you your sins of the past and those to come﴾ [Al-Fath 48:1-2]. ﴿You﴾ is addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ). Does it include the Ummah?

* The students: No.

* The Shaykh: Yes? No. ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [Ash-Sharh 94:1] Does it include the Ummah?

* The students: No.

* The Shaykh: ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾ [Ad-Duha 93:6]?

* The students: It does not include them.

* The Shaykh: It does not include them. ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾ [An-Nisa 4:79] does not include them. This is clear; this is specific to the Messenger (ﷺ) without dispute or difficulty.

The second category: that which evidence shows is general, such as the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them at their waiting period﴾ to the end [At-Talaq 65:1]. Here, evidence shows that the address ﴿O Prophet﴾ is not specific to him. What is the basis of this indication?

* The students: ﴿When you divorce﴾.

* The Shaykh: He said ﴿When you divorce﴾ and did not say "When you (singular) divorce", ﴿When you divorce women﴾ to the end.

The third category: that for which there is no evidence, either of specificity or of generality. The scholars differed concerning it into two opinions.

The first opinion: that it is general, addressed to everyone to whom address is validly directed.

The second opinion: that it is specific to the Messenger, and its inclusion of the Ummah is by way of general meaning, not general wording; because the ruling established regarding the Messenger (ﷺ) is a ruling for him and for the Ummah, by the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly you have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example﴾ [Al-Ahzab 33:21].

﴿Look﴾: from which of the categories is it?

* Students: The third.

* The Shaykh: The third, for which there is no evidence either way. The meaning of looking here, ﴿Look how﴾, is intellectual looking, not visual looking; because inventing lies against Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is not something seen with the eye, but something seen with what? With the intellect and the eye of insight. ﴿Look how they invent lies against Allah﴾ by their saying: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:24], and by their saying: ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 5:18], and by their saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:111]. So look how they invent lies against Allah, and how bold they are against Allah! We seek refuge in Allah.

﴿And sufficient is it as a manifest sin﴾: meaning, by the inventing. This sentence carries the meaning of wonder: how great is this sin, which is inventing against Allah; because inventing against Allah is a greater invention than against one who is invented against. And if the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat in the Fire"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (107) and Muslim (3/3) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]], then lying against Allah is more severe and greater.

As for His saying ﴿sufficient is it as a manifest sin﴾: ﴿manifest﴾ here means clear. We have mentioned earlier, and repeat now, that the quadriliteral (abana) comes intransitive and comes transitive. If transitive, its meaning is making manifest ("abana" means: he made manifest). If intransitive, its meaning is clarity: you say "abana al-fajr" (the dawn became clear). Is this intransitive or transitive?

* Student: Intransitive.

* The Shaykh: Intransitive; its meaning: became clear and evident.

And you say: the Qur'an made clear that lying is forbidden, meaning it clarified and made evident.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Clear Book﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 43:2]: which of the two types is it?

* Student: Of both types.

* The Shaykh: It includes this and that; it is clear in itself and makes clear to others.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: calling a person to marvel at what is worthy of marvel, and that this is among the methods of the Qur'an; by His saying: ﴿Look how they invent lies against Allah﴾.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: magnifying the lie against Allah, since He only commanded marvel at it because it is a great matter. Lying against Allah includes lying about Him in His essence, in His names, in His attributes, in His acts, and in His rulings. If you wish, say: in His rulings, both the cosmic (kawniyyah) and the legislative (shar'iyyah), in His essence, His names and His attributes, and His cosmic and legislative rulings.

So lying against Allah regarding His essence is like a person speaking about the essence of Allah, Mighty and Majestic without knowledge; any person who speaks of the essence of Allah without knowledge is a liar against Allah.

Lying against Allah regarding His names is like what the Mu'attilah did in saying that the names of Allah are mere labels with no meaning. They say: al-Ghafur, al-Rahim, as-Sami', al-Basir, al-'Aziz, al-Hakim have no meaning; they are merely labels indicating the one named and carry no meaning. This is a lie against Allah. How can you say they are mere labels, when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says in the Qur'an that it is in a clear Arabic tongue? The requirement of this clear Arabic tongue is that the active participle indicates the root meaning and the establishment of that meaning. One cannot say of someone who has not struck: he is ... what? He is a striker; nor of someone who has not heard: he is hearing. Moreover, Allah has shown that this meaning is intended in His saying: ﴿Allah has indeed heard the speech of the one who disputes with you﴾ and ﴿Allah hears your mutual dialogue﴾ [Al-Mujadilah 58:1], ﴿Do they think We do not hear their secret and their private talk?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 43:80], and the like. So those who say that Allah intended by His names mere naming without meaning are liars against Allah, are they not? They are liars against Allah.

Likewise regarding His attributes: whoever distorts the attributes of Allah and says the meaning of istiwa' is istila' (domination), this is a lie against Allah. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says about Himself: ﴿The Most Merciful, established above the Throne﴾ [Al-A'raf 7:54], and the Qur'an is in a clear Arabic tongue; and "istawa 'ala" in the Arabic tongue means what? It means he rose above it and settled upon it. So if they say istawa means istawla, they have lied against Allah. Did Allah intend this? Never. We are certain that Allah did not intend it. Why are we certain? Because Allah said in the Noble Qur'an that it is in a clear Arabic tongue, and the clear Arabic tongue requires nothing other than that He rose above it and settled upon it. ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 43:3], meaning: We made it in the Arabic tongue; why? ﴿So that you may understand﴾, meaning: that you may comprehend its meaning according to the requirement of this Arabic tongue.

As for those who say: this is forbidden and this is permitted, without knowledge? They have lied against Allah. They have invented lies against Allah, because what informed them that Allah forbade this or made it obligatory?

This is why, from the scrupulousness (wara') of Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, as transmitted from him by Shaykh al-Islam, he would not say "this is forbidden" except for what was explicitly stated as forbidden. For carrion he says it is forbidden, because it is explicitly stated; for marrying one's mother he says it is forbidden, because it is explicitly stated. But for what is merely disapproved, you find him saying: "I dislike this," "it does not please me," "I find it repugnant," and the like.

Yet despite this, Allah preserved for him this path: his companions, the companions of Imam Ahmad, said: when Imam Ahmad says "it does not please me," it means prohibition; and when he says "I dislike this," it means prohibition. Allah, glorified and exalted, preserved him regarding the rulings he intended, along with his scrupulousness in not applying "forbidden" except to what was explicitly declared.

So what about one who now says: "Islam says such and such," and yet you find him among the most ignorant of people regarding Islamic rulings, then attributes to Islam this statement he made, which is an error! And when it becomes clear to people that it is an error, they will blame Islam.

The summary: inventing lies against Allah includes lying about Him in His essence, His names, His attributes, and His rulings, both cosmic and legislative. The legislative: have you understood them? He says: this is forbidden, this is permitted.

The cosmic: that he says the punishment for this sin is such and such punishments, without knowledge; for example, saying: if a person disobeys his parents, the Throne shakes. The Throne shakes? Who says this? The common people say it: "whoever disobeys his parents, the Throne of the Merciful shakes because of him"; "if a male mounts a male, the Throne trembles." Who says this? Whoever rules a specific punishment for a sin without knowledge has invented a lie against Allah.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: magnifying the lie against Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿And sufficient is it as a manifest sin﴾, meaning: how great and how immense is it, when one invents lies against Allah, that he incurs this sin!

We have a grammatical analysis of this sentence, ﴿sufficient is it as a manifest sin﴾, which occurs frequently in the Qur'an: ﴿Sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 13:43]. Here, ﴿sufficient is it as a manifest sin﴾. Where is the subject of ﴿sufficient﴾?

* Student: A pronoun.

* The Shaykh: Its subject is always, or usually, in the genitive case, so the noun following the bi (preposition) is the subject with the added bi. After it comes the noun in the accusative, and they say it is a tamyiz (specification). Some parse it as a hal (circumstantial accusative): ﴿Sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 13:43], meaning: in the state of being a witness. Others hold it is a tamyiz of sufficiency, since sufficiency occurs in anything, and so it is specified. ﴿Sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾, and the like.

* Student: We said that a person's saying "I am a believer" may admit of self-praise and other things. So if someone speaking about innovators or deviant groups says: "they claim to be the People of the Sunnah and the Community; rather we are the People of the Sunnah and the Community." Is this self-praise?

* The Shaykh: We do not know what was in his heart.

* The Student: Merely the report.

* The Shaykh: Does he intend to inform that he is among the People of the Sunnah and the Community, or does he want to boast over the innovators?

* The Student: No, merely informing, so that people accept his words.

* The Shaykh: No, this is a report, a report and nothing wrong with it.

* The Student: O Shaykh, we mentioned that the preferred view regarding a person's saying "I am a believer, God willing" or "I am a believer" returns to what he intends in himself, what he wants, whether he intended self-praise or other things. And it is well known that we were not commanded to split open the heart of a person, or (...) what he conceals, apart from that...?

* The Shaykh: No, we are speaking of a person's own saying, not our judgment on him. It is the person's own statement. There is a difference between (...) one who says "I am a believer," and I judge him. No, he himself says it. May I say, "I am a believer", or not (...)?

Then al-Nawawi, may Allah have mercy on him, said in the book al-Adhkar: that if the imam, upon rising from bowing, says "Sami' Allahu liman hamidah," and that the Shafi'i mentioned this statement and permitted it. What is your opinion, may Allah preserve you, on this view?

My view is that it is not correct, and that a person should say what the Sunnah has brought.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, who believe in idols and false deities and say of those who disbelieve, "These are better guided than those who believe in the way"? (51) Those are the ones Allah has cursed. And whomever Allah curses, you will not find for him a helper. (52) Or do they have a share in the kingdom? And if so, they would not give the people as much as a speck. (53) Or do they envy the people over what Allah has given them of His bounty? But We had already given the family of Abraham the Scripture and wisdom and given them a great kingdom. (54) And among them is he who believed in it, and among them is he who averted from it. And sufficient is Hellfire as a blaze. (55)﴾ [An-Nisa 4:51-55].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, who believe in idols and false deities﴾. The discussion of His saying ﴿Look how they invent lies against Allah, and sufficient is it as a manifest sin﴾ has already passed, and we explained that this shows the gravity of speaking against Allah, Mighty and Majestic. I think we have taken the benefits?

* From the benefits of this noble verse, ﴿Look how they invent lies against Allah﴾: alerting the addressee to what the speech of the people of falsehood entails of deviation and misguidance, by His saying: ﴿Look how﴾.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: magnifying the lie against Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Included in this are matters:

* Among them: lying against Allah regarding His names and attributes, such as saying that the names of Allah are merely designations without indicating a description, as the Mu'tazilah said. They say: Allah is Hearing without hearing, and Seeing without sight, and so on.

Also among it: speaking about Allah without knowledge: distorting the words from their places by negating their apparent meaning and affirming what contradicts their apparent meaning, such as the distortion by the people of negation (ta'til) of the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Then He istawa over the Throne﴾ [Al-A'raf 7:54] into "istawla over the Throne" (took possession of), and the distortion of "hand" into "blessing" and "power" and the like.

Also among it: speaking about Allah without knowledge in His legislative rulings, such as saying: this is permitted and this is forbidden, while Allah did not permit it nor forbid it. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely, "This is lawful and this is unlawful," to invent lies against Allah. Indeed, those who invent lies against Allah will not succeed. (116) [They will have] brief enjoyment, and for them is a painful punishment﴾ [An-Nahl 16:116-117].

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: showing the magnitude of the sin that befalls these people; by His saying: ﴿And sufficient is it as a manifest sin﴾.

* And among its benefits: that the sin of these people is clear and evident. The manner of its being evident and manifest is that if a person, by the indication of reason, cannot possibly fabricate something against another of his own kind, then fabricating against Allah is of a far greater and more severe kind. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, said concerning His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut from him the aorta. And not one of you could have prevented Us from him﴾ [Al-Haqqah 69:44-47]. Not all sayings, but some.

[Translation ends]

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 51–52:

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾ What is said about ﴿Have you not seen﴾ is the same as what was said about the verse before it: the interrogative is for denunciation and astonishment, meaning that He expresses wonder at the condition of these people. ﴿Those who were given a portion﴾ means: who were given a portion, and (ātā, "to give") takes two objects. Here it has taken two objects: the first of them is the deputy of the subject, which is the wāw (of "ūtū"), and the second is ﴿a portion﴾.

His saying: ﴿those who were given a portion﴾ means: who were given a portion, that is, a share, ﴿of the Scripture﴾, that is, the Scripture revealed to the messengers, peace be upon them, ﴿a portion﴾, meaning: a share of the Scripture, the Scripture revealed to the messengers. Who is meant by these people? The ones meant by these are the Jews, because Allah gave them a portion of the Scripture, which is the Torah, and did not give them knowledge of everything.

﴿They believe in jibt and ṭāghūt﴾. This is the point of wonder: that they were given a portion of the Scripture and the proof was established against them, yet they still believe in jibt and believe in ṭāghūt. Jibt (idolatry, sorcery, superstition): everything that has no benefit in it; everything in religion that has no benefit is jibt, and among it are sorcery, soothsaying, augury by roads, bird-omens and the like, for all of these are jibt.

As for ṭāghūt (tyrant, false object of worship): ṭāghūt is everything by which a person transgresses his limit, so ﴿those who disbelieve, their protectors are ṭāghūt﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:257]. The leaders of disbelief and the callers to disbelief are ṭawāghīt, and Satan is a ṭāghūt. For this reason ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Jibt is sorcery, and ṭāghūt is Satan"[[Narrated by Saʿid ibn Manṣūr (649), and al-Ṭabarī (7/135).]], meaning that sorcery is one individual instance of jibt, and Satan is one individual instance of ṭāghūt. Otherwise, the general definition of ṭāghūt is what Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned: everything by which the servant exceeds his limit, whether an object of worship, one who is followed, or one who is obeyed.

﴿They believe in jibt and ṭāghūt﴾. Their belief in it means their acknowledging it and not denying it.

﴿And they say to those who disbelieve, "These are better guided than those who believe in the way."﴾ ﴿They say to those who disbelieve﴾: some exegetes said that the lām here means "concerning", i.e., they say concerning them, ﴿these﴾, that is, those who disbelieve, ﴿are better guided than those who believe in the way﴾. It was also said that the lām is like your saying "I said to so-and-so", i.e., it is the lām that makes the verb transitive, and that His saying ﴿these﴾ means "you" (plural), i.e., these people say to those who disbelieve: "You are better guided than those who believe in the way." On this reading the demonstrative takes the place of the second-person pronoun, because when you say "I said to so-and-so such-and-such", so-and-so becomes the addressee, so a second-person pronoun must be used; "these" (hā'ulā') is a demonstrative and not a second-person pronoun, but they said it means "you", and this is the view followed by the Jalalayn.

﴿They say to those who disbelieve﴾: the ones meant by "those who disbelieve" are the people of Makkah. A group of Jews met the people of Makkah, and the people of Makkah said to them: "This is Muhammad, who has divided us from our sons, our servants and our wives, and has divided us from the Arabs, and reviled our gods and belittled our minds. As for us, we are the People of the House, we give drink to the pilgrims, and we do such-and-such," and they mentioned other things, and asked: "Which of us is better guided, we or Muhammad?" The Jews seized this opportunity and said: "You are better guided than Muhammad", because they did not want anything good to come to the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, and they envied him. So they seized the opportunity when a people who were the followers and kinsmen of Muhammad, peace be upon him, asked them, and they said this statement.

﴿These are better guided than those who believe in the way﴾: that is, a path. ﴿In the way﴾ here is a specification (tamyīz), because it occurs after the comparative noun (ism al-tafḍīl), and the accusative after the comparative noun is a specification.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed﴾. ﴿Those﴾: the one referred to is these people who were given a portion and who said to the disbelievers: "You are better guided than those who believe in the way." ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed﴾. This sentence conveys exclusivity (ḥaṣr) because both of its parts are definite, the subject and the predicate: the subject ("ulā'ika") is a definite demonstrative, and the predicate ("alladhīna") is a definite relative pronoun. ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed﴾, that is, He has expelled them and removed them far from His mercy, and we seek refuge with Allah.

﴿And whoever Allah curses, you will not find for him a helper﴾. ﴿Man﴾ here is a conditional noun, and ﴿yalʿan﴾ is the conditional verb, jussed, but it was given a kasrah because of the meeting of two sukūns. ﴿And whoever Allah curses, you will not find for him a helper﴾: that is, you will not find anyone to help him, to bring him near to the mercy of Allah and admit him into the mercy of Allah; for when Allah, glorified and exalted, intends evil for a people, there is no turning it back.

From this verse and the one before it, several benefits are derived:

* First: the wonder, or the causing of wonder, at the condition of those who were given a portion of the Scripture and yet deny what the Scripture indicates.

* Among its benefits: showing the ugliness of their conduct, since Allah had given them a portion of the Scripture, yet they said to the disbelievers that they were better guided than the believers. It is well known that one who judges contrary to what he knows is worse than one who judges without knowledge, and both are ugly, but the first is more severe.

* Among the benefits of this verse: showing the envy of the Jews toward the believers.

* Among its benefits: that they believe in jibt and believe in ṭāghūt, so they neither deny jibt nor ṭāghūt, but affirm them.

* Among its benefits: an indication that the origin of sorcery is taken from whom? From the Jews; for this reason they bewitched the Prophet, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him and his family, "for Labīd ibn al-A'ṣam bewitched the Prophet, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him and his family, with a great sorcery"[[Narrated by Muslim (2189/43) from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah.]], but Allah protected His Prophet, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him and his family, from being affected by it to the degree they had intended.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Jews are people of envy, for they know in the depths of their souls that Muhammad is better guided than the polytheists, since they recognize him as they recognize their own sons; but when their hearts were filled with envy of him, they came to prefer the disbelievers over him and over those who followed him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the effect of propaganda in mixing truth with falsehood; for it is well known that the disbeliever, in what he aims at or what he pursues, has no guidance whatsoever, yet they said that they were better guided than those who believe in the way.

* Following from this benefit: what some people today say, that the disbelievers are more faithful to covenants than the believers, that they are more sincere than the believers, more sincere in advice than the believers, and similar things. Whoever says this about the Muslims has in him a resemblance to the Jews. We do not deny that among the Muslims there are those who deviate from the way of Islam by not being truthful in speech, not fulfilling covenants, not keeping promises, and not sincerely advising in action; but all these traits were warned against by the Prophet, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him and his family, in the strongest terms[[From that is his saying ﷺ: "The sign of the hypocrite is three: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, and when he is entrusted he betrays," agreed upon; al-Bukhari (33) and Muslim (107/59), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]], and they are alien traits upon the Muslim community, and their cause is the deficiency in knowledge and the deficiency in faith found among such people.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of preferring the disbelievers over the believers, since Allah denounced it with His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾ and so on to the end.

* Among the benefits of the second verse: showing that everyone who says a statement like this deserves the curse, based on His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed﴾; and Allah's legislative and retributive rulings are never tied to specific individuals. So if these people deserved the curse for believing in jibt and ṭāghūt and for saying to those who disbelieve, "These are better guided than those who believe in the way," then whoever follows their course deserves what they deserve of punishment.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that whomever Allah curses has no helper, based on His saying: ﴿And whoever Allah curses, you will not find for him a helper﴾.

* Among its benefits: a warning against exposing oneself to the curse of Allah, because when a person exposes himself to the curse of Allah and it is decreed upon him, he will find no one to help him.
