* Among its benefits: the prohibition of referring disputed matters to man-made laws or to the judgment of disbelievers and atheists, based on His saying: ﴿to Allah and the Messenger﴾.
* Among its benefits: the prohibition of taqlid (blind following) when the evidence is clear, based on His saying: ﴿refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾. We said "when the evidence is clear" because taqlid is permissible out of necessity when a person does not know, based on the Most High's saying: ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know﴾ [an-Nahl 43]. Allah, glorified and exalted, only commanded asking the people of remembrance in order to return to what they say; otherwise there would be no benefit in asking them.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that returning to Allah and the Messenger is a requirement of faith, based on His saying: ﴿if you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [an-Nisa' 59].
* Among its benefits: that whoever claims to believe in Allah and the Last Day, but does not refer matters of dispute to Allah and His Messenger, is a liar, because His saying ﴿if you [truly] are﴾ is in the sense of a challenge, so he is lying in what he claims. Allah, blessed and exalted, has said: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe until they make you judge concerning that over which they dispute among themselves, and then find within themselves no resistance to what you have decided and submit completely﴾ [an-Nisa' 65]. Look at the emphatic oath: ﴿No, by your Lord, they will not believe﴾; this oath is emphasised by (la), which is used for alerting.
﴿until they make you judge﴾: this is the first level, the judgment of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. If they take someone other than you as judge, they are not believers.
Second: ﴿then find within themselves no resistance (haraj) to what you have decided﴾, that is, no constriction or tightness. Even the one against whom judgment is given: if he finds within himself resistance and tightness, he is not a believer. This is the second level: the absence of resistance and tightness, meaning that your heart is expanded by what the Messenger judges, peace and blessings be upon him and his family.
The third level: ﴿and submit﴾, that is, yield, ﴿completely﴾. This is an emphatic verbal noun: they submit and yield complete submission to what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, decides. Thus it negates both inner and outer opposition. Inner opposition is tightness and resistance in the breast; outer opposition is not submitting fully but procrastinating. Your affair should not be one of mere reluctant compliance. Here He says: ﴿refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [an-Nisa' 59].
Among the benefits of this noble verse: whenever a person's faith in Allah and the Last Day increases, his returning to the Book and the Sunnah increases. This is because a ruling conditioned on a condition that includes an attribute grows stronger with the strength of that attribute and weakens with its weakness: ﴿if you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the Last Day, and that there will be a resurrection in which people will be recompensed for their deeds. Whoever denies it, or doubts it, may Allah protect us, is a disbeliever, even if he believes in Allah.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that returning to the Book and the Sunnah is good in the present and in the future, based on the Most High's saying: ﴿That is best﴾, meaning in the present, ﴿and best in outcome﴾, meaning best in consequence in the future.
* Among its benefits: the refutation of the illusion of one who makes man-made laws the judge and thinks that the community is reformed by them. We say: whatever in these man-made laws is sound and agrees with the Book and the Sunnah, its soundness and its reforming quality do not lie in itself, but in its agreement with the Book and the Sunnah. It is also not correct to regard this ruling as a man-made legal ruling. Rather, this ruling is the ruling of the Book and the Sunnah. In other words, when we find beneficial things in the laws attributed to human formulation, this counts as theft from the Sharia, theft from the divine ruling, because everything that benefits creation is based on the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, upon the Sharia.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that whoever takes his disputes to other than Allah and His Messenger is a disbeliever. But is it disbelief that takes one out of the religion or not? We say: this has detail according to the state of the one who seeks judgment. If he sees that the ruling issued by these laws is better than the ruling of Allah and His Messenger, or equal to it, then he is a disbeliever, because he denies the Most High's saying: ﴿And who is better in judgment than Allah for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 50], and His saying: ﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ [at-Tin 8]. But if he does not hold that belief, and merely follows the scholar's path, then he is not a disbeliever, because many people, especially the common folk, do not perceive this distinction, and such a person is not a disbeliever.
It remains to be said: if you are in a country that rules only by laws, like the countries of the disbelievers and those who adopt their laws, and you are now between two matters: either your right is lost, or necessity compels you to seek judgment before these people. Is it permissible for you to seek judgment before them? At first glance it may appear to a person that it is not permissible to seek judgment, because this is seeking judgment before the taghut. But we say: you may seek judgment, not with the belief that this is a binding ruling, but in order to reach your right, which you cannot reach except by this path. Then, if they rule in your favour in accordance with the Sharia, take it, because it is the Sharia of Allah. If they rule against that, do not accept it. This is what preserves people's rights, because it is a difficulty if you are in a country that rules only by law. Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, pointed to this at the beginning of his book at-Turuq al-Hukmiyyah.
If someone says: the expression in the verse ﴿if you dispute﴾ (fa-in), and "in" does not indicate that the condition occurs, unlike "idha" (when), which indicates that the condition occurs but specifies its time. This is why you find the difference between saying, "When Zayd stands, honour him," and saying, "If Zayd stands, honour him." The first indicates that he will stand, but honouring him is conditioned on his standing; the second does not indicate that he will stand: if he stands. Here, ﴿fa-in tanazi'tum﴾ means that dispute is originally something removed among us, and that the default is the absence of dispute. But if a dispute arises, then refer it to Allah and the Messenger.
* And to this we add a benefit to the preceding benefits: an indication that there should be no dispute among us, and that, whenever it is possible to avert such a dispute, that is the better course.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verses 60–63 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you?﴾ [An-Nisa 60]. The interrogative here (al-istifham) is for expressing wonder. It means: Are you not amazed at these people?

The address in His words ﴿you (tara)﴾ may be directed to the Messenger (ﷺ), and it may be directed to every addressee of this Mighty Book. If the matter is between this and that, which is preferable, the second or the first? The second is preferable: that it be taken in its general sense. On the first view, that the one addressed is the Messenger (ﷺ), this does not mean that the Ummah is not addressed by it, because whatever was addressed to the Messenger is also an address to the Ummah, either through emulation (al-uswah) or because he is the leader, and an address to the leader is an address to him and to those who follow him in his leadership.

Here there are three matters:
First: Is the address general, to the Messenger and to the Ummah? We say: if there is no obstacle, this is the default, and it is the more correct view.
Second: If we say it is specific to the Messenger, is it specific to him, with the rest of the Ummah following him by way of emulation? Or was the address directed to the Messenger as a ruling, in the sense that since he is the leader and imam of this Ummah, the address was directed to it, and an address directed to the leader is an address to him and to those behind him?
There are two possibilities. In either case the address is clear. We say it is general, meaning: Have you not seen, O addressee, those who claim...

Now, this whole assessment is undone by His words ﴿who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾, which leads us to say that the correct view is that it is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). But our first statement remains based on the principle that if there is no obstacle, the default is to take it in its general sense. Here an obstacle exists, namely His words ﴿those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you﴾. It is known that no revelation was sent down to each one of us, so this is an address to the Messenger (peace be upon him), and the Ummah follows him, either through emulation or because he is the leader, and an address to the leader is an address to those who follow him. ﴿Those who claim that they believe﴾: ﴿claim (yazAmUna)﴾ means "they say," and this statement is to be examined to see whether it is correct or not. ﴿Those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾, such as the Jews, for example, who say: "We believe in what has been revealed to you, O Muhammad, and we believe in the Torah." The Christians say: "We believe in what has been revealed to you and we believe in the Gospel and the Torah." But ﴿they desire to take their disputes to the Taghut﴾. This is the point of wonder: they claim, while they desire to take their disputes to the taghut. The taghut (idol or false authority, here whatever opposes the Sharia) is everything that contradicts the Sharia, because whatever contradicts the Sharia is transgression (tughyan). So they desire to take their disputes to the taghut. ﴿And they were commanded to reject it﴾, meaning to reject the taghut. And who is the one who commanded them? The one who commanded them is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, but He used the form of the passive participle, so that this command, although its origin is from Allah, is also issued by the Messenger and by every believer. Every believer commands that disputes be referred to Allah and His Messenger, and that a person reject the taghut. ﴿And they were commanded﴾ means by Allah and by the friends of Allah ﴿to reject it﴾, meaning to reject the taghut.

We say that it is from Allah and from His friends because it is parallel to His words: ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have evoked anger﴾ [al-Fatiha 7]. He did not say "not of those You have been angry with," because the way of those people angers Allah and angers the friends of Allah. ﴿And they were commanded to reject it, and Satan intends to lead them far astray﴾. So they are followers of Satan, who prompts them to take their disputes to the taghut. Satan intends to lead them far astray, that is, far from the truth, because taking disputes to the taghut necessitates that a person move away from the truth and attach his heart to this taghut.

If someone says: give an example?
We say: an example is that someone is invited to the noble Qur'an, but says: "No, we will take our disputes to the Torah, to the Gospel, to such-and-such law." We say: how can you claim that you believe in Allah? Or, for example, he says: "We will take our disputes to commercial courts and commercial laws," and he is invited to take disputes to Allah and His Messenger, and he says: "No, we will return to the customs of trade even if they contradict the Sharia." This falls under this verse.

Then He said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion﴾ [An-Nisa 61]. ﴿When it is said to them﴾: who is the speaker? Any one of the people, any one of the people who says: ﴿"Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger"﴾. Here He said ﴿what Allah has revealed﴾, meaning the Qur'an, and ﴿to the Messenger﴾, meaning to his Sunnah. ﴿You see the hypocrites﴾, and the seeing here is visual sight, the sight of the eye. On this basis ﴿the hypocrites﴾ is the object, and ﴿turning away﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). Here He said ﴿you see the hypocrites﴾ and did not say "you see them." He made the noun explicit in a place where a pronoun was expected. Making the noun explicit in place of a pronoun has benefits:
The first benefit: the ruling against these people as hypocrites, because if He had said "you see them," it would not have become clear that they are hypocrites.
* A student: (...)
* The Shaykh: This is what is required. Who gave me (...)? You understood? In your case, you say: "the Creator" is a name, and "the creating" is an attribute, and he excluded the attribute that he creates. Then afterward, they were under the indication of correspondence (dalalat al-mutabaqah), inclusion (tadammun) and implication (luzum). Why did you not mention the indication of implication? The indication of implication is its indication of knowledge and power.
* The student: I knew (...).
* The Shaykh: We heard. I think it is ﴿Have you not seen those who claim﴾.
* * *
* A student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion (61). So how will it be when a disaster strikes them for what their hands have put forth? Then they come to you swearing by Allah, "We intended nothing but good and reconciliation" (62). Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts, so turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them about themselves a far-reaching word﴾ [An-Nisa 60–63].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you?﴾ What do you derive from His words ﴿claim (yazAmUna)﴾?
* A student: Do you mean its meaning, O Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: No, what do you derive from it?
* A student: The invalidity of what they claim...
* The Shaykh: That their belief is not real. ﴿They claim that they believe﴾. The clause ﴿they desire to take their disputes to the taghut﴾: what is its place in grammar?
* A student: A circumstantial clause (hal).
* The Shaykh: A circumstantial clause from whom?
* The student: From the waw in ﴿claim (yazAmUna)﴾.
* The Shaykh: From the waw in ﴿yazAmUna﴾. What is meant by the taghut here? The meaning of taghut here, because in every place it is according to its context?
* A student: Whoever rules by other than what Allah has revealed.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
No, here, the taghut here, because in every place it is according to its context?
* A student: Whoever rules by other than what Allah has revealed.
* The Shaykh: Yes. And His words ﴿that He intends to lead them far astray﴾ [An-Nisa 60]: what is the wisdom in His making ﴿astray (dalalan)﴾ indefinite and describing it as far?
* A student: (...) that they have reached a great degree of error.
* The Shaykh: In error. Good.
* * *
﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger"﴾ [An-Nisa 61]. The pronoun in ﴿it is said to them﴾ refers to those who claim that they believe in what was revealed to the Messenger (peace be upon him) and what was revealed before him, namely the hypocrites among the People of the Book who were hypocritical. ﴿Come (ta'alaw)﴾: come forward. ﴿To what Allah has revealed﴾, meaning the Qur'an. He did not say "to the Qur'an," as an indication of its status and the height of its rank, that it was sent down from Allah, because what descends from Allah establishes proof against every person.
﴿And to the Messenger﴾. He did not say "to the words of the Messenger," because they are called to come into the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), to come to him so that he may debate with them and explain to them. The (al) in His words ﴿and to the Messenger﴾ is the mental reference (al-ahd al-dhihni). This is because references are of three kinds: mental, mentioned, and present. If the (al) points to something already mentioned, the reference is mentioned (al-ahd al-dhikri), as in His words: ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger (15). But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ [Al-Muzzammil 15–16]. Who is the messenger here? Moses, who was sent to Pharaoh.
It is mental when the thing is known in the mind, as when a speaker says to his opponent: "Let us go to the judge," meaning which judge? The known judge of the city. This verse and its examples are many.
It is present (al-ahd al-hudури) as in His words: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 3], meaning the present day. One of the rules for this is that it comes after a demonstrative noun, such as: "this man," "this day," "this week." So when it comes after a demonstrative, what is it? It is the present reference, because the demonstrative indicates a present, pointed-to thing, so the (al) following it is the present reference.
So ﴿the Messenger (al-Rasul)﴾ means Muhammad (peace be upon him). He was called a messenger (rasul) because Allah sent him and made him an intermediary between Himself and His servants in conveying His law. Allah's sending him is the greatest proof of his purification and that he is worthy to bear the message, as Allah said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [Al-An'am 124]. The Prophet (peace be upon him) combined trustworthiness with strength in conveying the message, and therefore no one is more trustworthy than he, and no one is more patient than he in what he endures in conveying the message of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
﴿You see the hypocrites﴾: the clause ﴿you see (ra'aytа)﴾ is the answer to the condition in His words ﴿when it is said to them, "Come"﴾. ﴿You see the hypocrites﴾. The taa in ﴿ra'ayta﴾ is for address. Who is addressed? Either the Messenger, because of His words ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you﴾, since the whole context is an address to the Messenger. It may also be general, but its being addressed to the Messenger is closer to the context.
﴿You see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion﴾. ﴿The hypocrites (al-munafiqin)﴾ is the active participle of (nafaqa), derived from nafiqa' al-yarbu', meaning its burrow. The burrow of the jerboa (yarbu') is built on deception, because the jerboa is clever: it makes a door in its burrow through which it enters, and makes another door of earth's crust at the far end of the burrow. When someone confronts it at the known open door, it leaves through the hidden door and deceives him. For this reason the word "hypocrite (munafiq)" was taken from it.
It has been said that this word is a newly coined Islamic term, meaning that its meaning is not known in the language in this sense, because the pre-Islamic period was unbelief with no faith in it, and a believer would be a believer by what remained of the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him), or he would be a Christian like Waraqah ibn Nawfal, or similar. But after the corruption of these people became apparent, in that they showed people that they were believers while they were unbelievers, this word came into use.
In His words ﴿you see the hypocrites﴾ there is a rhetorical point. What is it?
* A student: (...) it could have been made implicit.
* The Shaykh: Making the noun explicit in place of the pronoun, this is the rhetorical point. This is because the context requires that He say: "And when it is said to them, 'Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger,' you see them." This is what the context requires. But He said ﴿you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion﴾. When the explicit noun comes in place of the pronoun, it has three benefits:
The first benefit: the causation of the ruling (illiyyat al-hukm), because this explicit noun indicates that the cause of this ruling is this thing. So the cause of their aversion is what? Hypocrisy.
The second benefit: the marking of the referent of the pronoun with this attribute. That is, if the referent of the pronoun is described by this attribute, which is hypocrisy, but if He had said "you see them," we would not know that they were hypocrites.
The third benefit: generality, meaning that it includes these people and other hypocrites. If He had said only "you see them," it would not include others. So making the noun explicit in place of the pronoun has three benefits.
* A student: Marking and generality..
* Another student: The causation of the ruling.
* The Shaykh: And generality. Khalid mentioned this.
* The student: The referent of the pronoun.
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: Marking them with the attribute.
* The Shaykh: Correct. That is, marking them with the attribute, meaning this attribute applies to them, that is, to the one to whom the pronoun refers.
﴿You see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion﴾. Here ﴿yaSudduna (turn away)﴾: the same verb can be transitive or intransitive. It is said: "sadda bi-nafsihi" (he turned away by himself), and "sadda ghayrahu" (he turned another away). Here, is it the first or the second, ﴿yaSudduna 'anka sududa﴾?
* Students: The second.
* A student: It includes both.
* The Shaykh: O my brothers, ﴿when it is said to them, "Come"﴾ ﴿you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion﴾: it is from the first, which is intransitive, meaning: they turn away from you.
His words ﴿sududa﴾ is an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid), and it may also be a specifying infinitive (masdar nawʿi). The emphatic infinitive is the one that emphasizes its verb so that metaphor is excluded, because the verb may be used metaphorically, that is, it is ascribed to the agent figuratively. When it is emphasized, the possibility of metaphor is removed. It may also be a specifying infinitive, meaning that it is great aversion, so it is qualified by a deleted adjective, and the estimate is: "aversion great." Which of the two is more eloquent? The second is more eloquent, because it includes the first and not vice versa.
So these people, may Allah protect us, when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed, to the Qur'an, so that we may take our disputes to it, and to the Messenger, so that we may take our disputes to him," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion. That is, you see them in their hypocrisy and immersion in hypocrisy turning away from you with aversion.
Here He said ﴿turn away from you﴾ and did not say "turn away from the one who said it to them," because what concerns them is not who said it to them. What concerns them is the Messenger (peace be upon him). They may turn away from the Messenger and not come, but they do not turn away from the one who invited them. Perhaps they meet him with a cheerful and pleasant face, but they turn away from the Messenger. For this reason He did not say "turn away from him," meaning from the speaker, but said ﴿turn away from you﴾, because this is what they intend.
﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them for what their hands have put forth﴾ [An-Nisa 62]. ﴿How (kayfa)﴾ here is for wonder, meaning: be amazed at their condition when a disaster strikes them for what their hands have put forth. This disaster is that their hypocrisy and their aversion and turning away become known. When it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed, come to the Messenger," and they turn away and avert, and then this is discovered, this is the disaster. It is a disaster for them because they do not want their defects and their unbelief to be exposed. They are hypocrites who conceal themselves to the utmost degree because of the unbelief they hide. When they are discovered, this discovery is what? A great disaster. When this disaster strikes them ﴿for what their hands have put forth﴾, that is, because of what their hands have put forward of unbelief and hypocrisy.
﴿Then they come to you﴾: that is, they come to the Messenger (peace be upon him), ﴿swearing by Allah, "We intended nothing but good and reconciliation"﴾. The clause ﴿swearing (yahlifuna)﴾ is a circumstantial clause, the agent of the waw in ﴿came to you (ja'uka)﴾: they came to you while wearing this oath.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 4, verses 60–63 (part 2 of 3):**

﴿They swear by Allah, "We intended nothing but good and reconciliation."﴾ Here "in" (إن) is a negating particle. What is the evidence that it is a negator? The exception particle (إلا) that follows it. ﴿Nothing but good﴾ means: we intended nothing but good. Now, "in" (إن) can also be a conditional particle. Can one of you brothers give an example?

* Student: إن تقم أقم (*in taqum aqum*, "If you stand, I will stand").
* Shaykh: "In taqum aqum." Good. It can also come as a lightened form of the heavy (*mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah*). Go ahead and answer.
* Student: إنْ زيدًا قائمٌ (*in Zaydan qa'imun*).
* Shaykh: What?
* Student: إن الزيدانُ قائمٌ (*in al-Zaydani qa'imun*).
* Shaykh: إن الزيدانِ?
* Student: إن الزيدانُ قائمٌ.
* Shaykh: إنِ الزيدان? Like that? More eloquently, more eloquently, my brother. There is no problem with it.
* Student: إن الزيدانُ قائمٌ.
* Shaykh: What does he say?
* Students: إن زيدًا قائم (*in Zaydan qa'im*).
* Shaykh: إن زيدًا قائم? No.
* Student: ﴿And indeed they were, before that, in manifest error﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:164].
* Shaykh: ﴿And indeed they were, before that, in manifest error﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:164]. That is: *wa-innahum kanu min qablu fi dalalin mubin* ("indeed they were, before that, in manifest error"). And the poet's words:

  ......................... ∗∗∗ And indeed Malik was of noble origin...

  It also comes as an extra (*za'idah*, "superfluous") particle.

* Student: The poet's words:

  Banu Ghudanah, you are not gold, ∗∗∗ nor pure silver, but you are mere potsherds.

* Shaykh: "Banu Ghudanah, you are not gold, nor pure silver, but you are mere potsherds." That makes three uses. The fourth is the negating use, as in this verse: ﴿We intended nothing but good and reconciliation﴾.

As for His words, ﴿nothing but good and reconciliation﴾: what is "good" (*ihsan*)? The good is that they be cordial with the believers, ﴿when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:14], and with the disbelievers, when they meet those who disbelieved, they say, "We are with you." They intend good, meaning they walk the path without hostility toward either of them.

﴿And reconciliation﴾ means among the people: they show these people that they are with them and agree with them, and they show those people that they are with them and agree with them too. This, and Allah's refuge is sought, is the utmost hypocrisy. In other words: "We intended nothing but good, that there be no conflict between us and others, because the hypocrites cannot tolerate it." As for reconciling between people (*tawfiq*), we reconcile them. The explanation of this will come, Allah willing, in the lessons (*fawa'id*).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah knows﴾ [an-Nisa' 4:63]. ﴿Those﴾ refers to those who claim that they believe in what was revealed to you and what was revealed before you. Did He use the demonstrative indicating distance because of their high rank, or because of their low rank?

* Students: Low rank.
* Shaykh: Because of their low rank. The distant demonstrative may indicate physical distance, as when you say, "That man over there is far away." It may also indicate figurative distance, distance in rank, either high or low, according to what the context requires. Here ﴿those who﴾ indicates lowness. His words, ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds — those are the best of creation﴾ [al-Bayyinah 98:7], indicate height. ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell, abiding eternally therein. Those are the worst of creation﴾ [al-Bayyinah 98:6], indicates lowness. So the two verses combine height and lowness.

﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah knows.﴾ He said ﴿knows﴾ (*ya'lamu*, present tense) and did not say "knew" (*'alima*, past tense), because Allah's knowledge is continuous, past, present, and future. For this reason He used the present tense, which indicates continuity.

His words, ﴿what is in their hearts﴾, mean what they conceal of hypocrisy and disbelief. In other words: as for you, you do not know what is in their hearts, because we have only the outward. But we know them by indicators. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if We willed, We would have shown them to you, and you would have recognized them by their marks﴾ [Muhammad 47:30]. And then? ﴿And you will surely know them by the tone of their speech﴾ [Muhammad 47:30], that is, by its allusion and implication. This belongs to people of discernment (*firasah*). The stronger a person's faith in Allah, the sharper his discernment. Indeed, some people can read what is in a person's heart from the features of his face. Therefore we say: the hypocrites are known only to Allah, this is the principle. But sometimes we recognize them through the tone of their speech, or through discernment that Allah grants to whomever He wills of His servants.

﴿So turn away from them﴾ means: do not wear yourself out with them, and do not treat them as you would treat disbelievers, fighting them, because they did not openly declare enmity. For this reason, when the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked for permission to kill some of them, he said, "No. Lest people say that Muhammad kills his companions" [agreed upon; reported by al-Bukhari (3518) and Muslim (2584/63), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah]. This is the very essence of wisdom, because if we unsheathed our swords against such people we would kill a world of people, and they may be believers.

And when the man who polytheized, whom Usamah caught up with and struck with the sword, was addressed by the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Did you kill him after he had said, 'There is no god but Allah'?" [agreed upon; reported by al-Bukhari (4269) and Muslim (96/159), from the hadith of Usamah ibn Zayd], even though it is apparent that he said it out of fear. If this man's blood was protected by this word, how much more so these hypocrites who mention Allah, come with us, pray, and give charity! Therefore, refraining from them is the very essence of wisdom.

﴿And admonish them﴾. Admonition (*maw'izah*) is reminder combined with encouragement and warning. The admonition is to remind a person of what he must do or refrain from, together with what? Encouragement or warning: encouragement regarding what you command, and warning regarding what you forbid.

﴿And speak to them concerning themselves a far-reaching word﴾ means: say to them a word that reaches the depths of their souls. For this reason He made the soul the container of the speech. It may also be understood to mean: ﴿speak to them concerning themselves﴾, that is, concerning their affair and their condition.

﴿A far-reaching word﴾ reaches their hearts. The two meanings are not contradictory, and so both are true. In other words: speak to them about their affair and about themselves, that "you did such and such, and you did such and such, and you did such and such." Or: speak to them a word within the soul that reaches the souls and the innermost hearts. ﴿A far-reaching word﴾ means eloquent, or it means "reaching its utmost aim." Both are correct, because the more eloquent the speech, the greater its effect. For this reason it came in a hadith: "Indeed, there is magic in eloquence, and indeed there is wisdom in poetry" [reported by Abu Dawud (5011), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas].

How many a person expresses a meaning in an eloquent phrase, extremely clear and eloquent, and it has an effect; then another person comes and expresses the same meaning, but it has no effect because he lacks eloquence. For this reason it is one of Allah's blessings upon the servant that He grants him eloquence and fluency, so that he can express what is in himself and have an effect on others. The opposite of this is one who is not eloquent.

Eloquence (*balaghah*) has become an independent discipline, and the scholars wrote books on it. It is a very delightful discipline. I wish it were easy for us to read from it, because it is beneficial in one respect and has a fine taste in another. We ask Allah to make it easy.

These verses, as you have heard, were revealed concerning a group of hypocrites who claim that they believe in Allah and His Messenger, but they are not so.

Now we return to deriving lessons from these verses. Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim﴾.

* From this verse many benefits are derived. Among them: wonder at this strange state. Wonder at this strange state. From where do we know that? From the interrogative ﴿Have you not seen﴾, because the intent is to express wonder, that we should marvel at their condition.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: a person may claim what he is not truthful about, as in His words: ﴿they claim that they believe in what was revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾.

* And among its benefits: the obligation to believe in what was revealed to the Messenger and what was revealed before him, as in His words: ﴿that they believe in what was revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾. This indicates that belief in what was revealed before him is equivalent to belief in what was revealed to him, although it differs in method and law (*shir'ah* and *minhaj*), as Allah said: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a method﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:48]. Otherwise, the origin of the religions is one in terms of faith and beliefs, but it differs in law and method, because Allah is All-Wise, legislating for each nation what suits it, and what its condition requires of righteousness and reform.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the perfection of Islam and of those who adhere to it, because Islam commands people to believe in everything Allah has revealed, and those who adhere to it likewise believe in everything Allah has revealed. Those who have adopted other than Islam, such as the Jews and Christians, do not believe in everything Allah has revealed, do they? As for the earlier ones among them, they believe in it only in a general, implicit way (*iman hukmi*), meaning they believe in what came after their laws in a general way, because they did not encounter it. The believers in Moses in his time and the believers in Jesus in his time believe in the Qur'an, because they find that the Messenger is written in their Torah and Gospel. But it is implicit belief. As for the belief of Muslims in the Qur'an and in the earlier laws, it is true belief, because the religion of Islam is the latest.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's elevation (*'uluw*). From where is this derived?

* Students: From the fact of sending down.

* Shaykh: From the fact of sending down? If someone says: the sender is not mentioned in ﴿what was revealed to you﴾. Did He not say "what We revealed"?

* Students: It is known.

* Shaykh: Because it is known, and what is known is like what is mentioned. For this reason Allah said: ﴿and man was created weak﴾ [an-Nisa' 4:28]. If someone asks: who created man? We say: what? Allah. The verse does not say "Allah created man." We say: because it is known that there is no creator except Allah. This is known by the created order (*kawnan*). ﴿Man was created weak﴾. And the sending down of revelation is known by the law (*shar'an*), because the one who sends down revelation is Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Therefore, from this we derive the elevation of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. This is what the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus (*ijma'*) of the early generations, sound reason, and fifthly, innate nature (*fitrah*) indicate. This is a known matter, and praise be to Allah.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that seeking judgment from other than Allah and His Messenger is seeking judgment from the false deity (*taghut*, false authority or transgressor). As in His words: ﴿they desire to seek judgment before the false deity﴾.

* And among its benefits: that seeking judgment from other than Allah and His Messenger is disbelief. From where is this derived? From their being declared liars in their claim of faith, in His words: ﴿they claim﴾, because if they were believers they would have desired to seek judgment before Allah and His Messenger.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: if desiring to seek judgment before the false deity removes one from Islam, then actually seeking judgment before it is all the more so. Whoever loves and desires that judgment be sought before the false deity, even if he does not actually seek it, is not a believer. How much more so is one who fulfills this desire and actually seeks judgment before the false deity! For this reason Allah the Exalted said in another verse: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe until they make you judge concerning that over which they dispute among themselves, and then find within themselves no discomfort from what you have decided, and submit in full submission﴾ [an-Nisa' 4:65]. These are great, emphatic conditions. ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe﴾ is a sentence emphasized by an oath and by an extra particle in form: the oath is ﴿by your Lord﴾, and the extra particle is ﴿no﴾, because this "no" is not a negator.

﴿Until they make you judge concerning that over which they dispute among themselves.﴾ This is the act. ﴿Then find within themselves no discomfort from what you have decided.﴾ That is: they do not find constriction regarding what you have decided. The third: ﴿and submit in full submission﴾, that is, complete submission without hesitation. A person may find within himself discomfort with a legal ruling, or may not find it, but he does not submit and hasten to comply. But he does not believe until the discomfort is removed from him and until he submits in full.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: we are commanded to disbelieve in the false deity: ﴿and they have been commanded to reject it﴾. Our faith is not complete except by disbelieving in the false deity, as His words indicate: ﴿So whoever disbelieves in the false deity and believes in Allah has grasped the most reliable handhold﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:256]. There must be disbelief in the false deity, or else faith in Allah is not valid.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that Satan has a will. From where is this derived? ﴿And Satan intends﴾. Yes, he has a will, and indeed he has a command. From where is this derived? From His words: ﴿Satan threatens you with poverty and orders you toward immorality﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:268]. He wills and he commands. Alright, can we, or is it possible for us, to repel this will and this command? By what? By seeking refuge in Allah from him, because Allah, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿And if an evil suggestion from Satan should tempt you, then seek refuge in Allah﴾ [al-A'raf 7:200]. When the Companions complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) about the evil thoughts they found in their souls, he said: "Whoever finds that, let him seek refuge in Allah," and [let him] "desist" [agreed upon; reported by al-Bukhari (3276) and Muslim (134/214), from the hadith of Abu Hurairah]. This is the protection from it.

* And among the benefits of this verse: that Satan wants the children of Adam to go astray a far-off straying, not a near straying. As in His words: ﴿and Satan intends to lead them far astray﴾. But do you think that Satan orders far-off straying right from the start? What does he do?

* Students: Gradually.

* Shaykh: Gradually. He first commands immorality and minor sins, then major sins, then disbelief, may Allah protect us and you from it. For this reason the scholars said: sins are the postal route to disbelief. Do you know what a postal route (*bareed*) is? A postal route is a fixed distance of three farsakh (about 18 km). In the past they had no airplanes or telephones, so how did they deliver messages in a short time? They divided the distance into postal stages. A rider takes the messages from one station and gallops with his horse to the end of the stage. Then another rider is waiting, takes the message, and proceeds with it to the next station, and so on until they reach the destination. This is the reason it is called a postal route. The point is that the scholars say: sins are the postal route to disbelief. Satan leads a person step by step until he destroys him.

* Student: O Shaykh, may Allah bless you. Regarding those who judge by other than what Allah has revealed, there are lawyers, O Shaykh. That is, is the lawyer included in His words: ﴿They desire to seek judgment before the false deity, and they have been commanded to reject it﴾?

* Shaykh: This question is very important. In other words, if we are in a country that does not rule by the Shari'ah but by civil law, may we seek judgment before it? We say: first, if there is no necessity, we do not seek judgment before it. That is, if reform is possible, we do not seek judgment. If reform is not possible, we look to see whether there is someone we can choose to be an arbitrator between us. If we find one, it is not permissible for us to seek judgment before these courts. If we do not find one, then we seek judgment, not with the intention of accepting everything they rule, but with the intention of accepting only what agrees with the Shari'ah, because this is a necessity. Otherwise, rights would be lost. Rights are not ten riyals or twenty riyals, which does not matter, but may be property and real estate. If a person does not seek judgment before these courts, he loses his right.

So here we say: it is permissible to seek judgment, not with the intention of accepting their ruling, but with the intention of accepting what agrees with the Shari'ah. But after two preliminaries: the first is attempting reform, and the second is seeking judgment before a man who rules by the law of Allah. If that is not possible, then rights are not lost.

As for the lawyer now: this lawyer who wishes to seek judgment before a non-Shari'ah court, we say: if his intention is that, were they to rule by other than the Shari'ah, he would not accept it, then there is no harm. But if his intention is that they rule in his favor according to what he wants, whether or not it agrees with the Shari'ah, then this is forbidden, even if it is in Shari'ah courts.

Suppose a person is an excellent advocate, eloquent in pleading and argument, and he wishes to represent someone even before a Sharia court, while intending to reach his own objective rather than the objective of Allah and His Messenger. Is this forbidden or permissible? It is forbidden, and there is no doubt about this. Some people have a powerful ability to persuade in argument or in pleading. When such a person sits before the judge with a quiet, gentle opponent, he may devour him with his words, and the judge rules by what?

* Student: By what he hears.
* Shaykh: By what he hears, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said. This is the principle of every advocate who pleads while wishing to reach his own goal rather than the goal of Allah and His Messenger. Such people are not permitted to follow this method.
* Student: (...) because they come and take their in-laws, they take...
* Shaykh: That is not correct. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They are the enemy, so beware of them﴾ [al-Munafiqun 4].
* Student: If they are the in-laws of the Muslims, they take them...

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by Allah's permission. And if, when they wronged themselves, they had come to you and asked Allah's forgiveness, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance, Merciful. But no, by your Lord, they do not believe until they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves, then find within themselves no resistance to what you decide and submit in full submission. And if We had prescribed for them, "Kill yourselves or leave your homes," only a few of them would have done it. But if they had done what they were admonished, it would have been better for them and firmer in strengthening [their faith]. And then We would have given them from Us a great reward. And We would have guided them to a straight path.﴾ [al-Nisa' 64–68].
* Shaykh: Enough, praise be to Allah. I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by Allah's permission﴾. The benefits remaining from...
* Student: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows﴾.
* Shaykh: Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾.
* From this noble verse it is derived that nothing that is in the breasts is hidden from Allah the Exalted, by His saying: ﴿Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾.
* Among its benefits: a person is held accountable for what the heart earns. This is not contradicted by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah has overlooked for my nation what their souls whisper about, as long as they do not act on it or speak of it."[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (5269) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] This is because the whisper of the soul (hadith al-nafs) is not settled. That is, a person may whisper to himself but it does not take hold. If it takes hold, it becomes an act.
For this reason the scholars said: the heart has an act, and the soul has a whisper. The act of the heart is to settle upon a thing and adopt it. So what is it that Allah threatened in His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾? The answer: it is the act of the heart, that a person acts with his heart, meaning he becomes content with the thing his soul has whispered to him.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to turn away where speech is of no benefit, by His saying: ﴿So turn away from them﴾. Some scholars held that this verse was abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later text) by the verses on jihad. That is not so. Rather, the verses on jihad concern one matter and this verse concerns another. This verse concerns disputing with the hypocrites, and the hypocrites cannot be fought with weapons, because they show that they are Muslims. They can only be struggled against with knowledge and clear explanation. So when we have explained to them and yet they persist in dispute, we turn away from them.
For this reason Imam Malik may Allah have mercy on him said: If a disputer comes to you, explain the Sunnah (the prophetic way) to him and do not dispute with him. For when you explain the Sunnah to him, you place the proof before him. If he disputes, then whom is he disputing with? He is disputing with Allah, not with you. Explain the Sunnah and do not argue about it with a disputer, because the obligation of one to whom the Sunnah has been made clear is to accept it without dispute.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: when a person turns away from these hypocrites and their like, he does not leave them without admonition. Rather he admonishes them, perhaps they will benefit, by His saying: ﴿And admonish them﴾. We have already discussed the meaning of admonition (mawiza). What is it?
* Student: Reminding of Allah combined with encouragement and warning.
* Shaykh: Reminding combined with encouragement and warning, yes.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: when a person speaks, he should speak with eloquent speech that reaches the soul, by His saying: ﴿And speak to them concerning themselves a far-reaching word﴾.
* Among its benefits also: it is part of the etiquette of the speaker to face the one he addresses, by His saying: ﴿And speak to them﴾. The word (lahum, "to them") means that the speaker should turn toward the one he addresses. So he should not speak while turning away, or speak while facing another direction. Rather, when he wants to speak with a person in admonition, his face should be turned toward that man, by His saying: ﴿And speak to them﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verses 60–63 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you?﴾ [An-Nisa 60]. The interrogative here (al-istifham) is for expressing wonder. It means: Are you not amazed at these people?

The address in His words ﴿you (tara)﴾ may be directed to the Messenger (ﷺ), and it may be directed to every addressee of this Mighty Book. If the matter is between this and that, which is preferable, the second or the first? The second is preferable: that it be taken in its general sense. On the first view, that the one addressed is the Messenger (ﷺ), this does not mean that the Ummah is not addressed by it, because whatever was addressed to the Messenger is also an address to the Ummah, either through emulation (al-uswah) or because he is the leader, and an address to the leader is an address to him and to those who follow him in his leadership.

Here there are three matters:
First: Is the address general, to the Messenger and to the Ummah? We say: if there is no obstacle, this is the default, and it is the more correct view.
Second: If we say it is specific to the Messenger, is it specific to him, with the rest of the Ummah following him by way of emulation? Or was the address directed to the Messenger as a ruling, in the sense that since he is the leader and imam of this Ummah, the address was directed to it, and an address directed to the leader is an address to him and to those behind him?
There are two possibilities. In either case the address is clear. We say it is general, meaning: Have you not seen, O addressee, those who claim...

Now, this whole assessment is undone by His words ﴿who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾, which leads us to say that the correct view is that it is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). But our first statement remains based on the principle that if there is no obstacle, the default is to take it in its general sense. Here an obstacle exists, namely His words ﴿those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you﴾. It is known that no revelation was sent down to each one of us, so this is an address to the Messenger (peace be upon him), and the Ummah follows him, either through emulation or because he is the leader, and an address to the leader is an address to those who follow him. ﴿Those who claim that they believe﴾: ﴿claim (yazAmUna)﴾ means "they say," and this statement is to be examined to see whether it is correct or not. ﴿Those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾, such as the Jews, for example, who say: "We believe in what has been revealed to you, O Muhammad, and we believe in the Torah." The Christians say: "We believe in what has been revealed to you and we believe in the Gospel and the Torah." But ﴿they desire to take their disputes to the Taghut﴾. This is the point of wonder: they claim, while they desire to take their disputes to the taghut. The taghut (idol or false authority, here whatever opposes the Sharia) is everything that contradicts the Sharia, because whatever contradicts the Sharia is transgression (tughyan). So they desire to take their disputes to the taghut. ﴿And they were commanded to reject it﴾, meaning to reject the taghut. And who is the one who commanded them? The one who commanded them is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, but He used the form of the passive participle, so that this command, although its origin is from Allah, is also issued by the Messenger and by every believer. Every believer commands that disputes be referred to Allah and His Messenger, and that a person reject the taghut. ﴿And they were commanded﴾ means by Allah and by the friends of Allah ﴿to reject it﴾, meaning to reject the taghut.

We say that it is from Allah and from His friends because it is parallel to His words: ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have evoked anger﴾ [al-Fatiha 7]. He did not say "not of those You have been angry with," because the way of those people angers Allah and angers the friends of Allah. ﴿And they were commanded to reject it, and Satan intends to lead them far astray﴾. So they are followers of Satan, who prompts them to take their disputes to the taghut. Satan intends to lead them far astray, that is, far from the truth, because taking disputes to the taghut necessitates that a person move away from the truth and attach his heart to this taghut.

If someone says: give an example?
We say: an example is that someone is invited to the noble Qur'an, but says: "No, we will take our disputes to the Torah, to the Gospel, to such-and-such law." We say: how can you claim that you believe in Allah? Or, for example, he says: "We will take our disputes to commercial courts and commercial laws," and he is invited to take disputes to Allah and His Messenger, and he says: "No, we will return to the customs of trade even if they contradict the Sharia." This falls under this verse.

Then He said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion﴾ [An-Nisa 61]. ﴿When it is said to them﴾: who is the speaker? Any one of the people, any one of the people who says: ﴿"Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger"﴾. Here He said ﴿what Allah has revealed﴾, meaning the Qur'an, and ﴿to the Messenger﴾, meaning to his Sunnah. ﴿You see the hypocrites﴾, and the seeing here is visual sight, the sight of the eye. On this basis ﴿the hypocrites﴾ is the object, and ﴿turning away﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). Here He said ﴿you see the hypocrites﴾ and did not say "you see them." He made the noun explicit in a place where a pronoun was expected. Making the noun explicit in place of a pronoun has benefits:
The first benefit: the ruling against these people as hypocrites, because if He had said "you see them," it would not have become clear that they are hypocrites.
* A student: (...)
* The Shaykh: This is what is required. Who gave me (...)? You understood? In your case, you say: "the Creator" is a name, and "the creating" is an attribute, and he excluded the attribute that he creates. Then afterward, they were under the indication of correspondence (dalalat al-mutabaqah), inclusion (tadammun) and implication (luzum). Why did you not mention the indication of implication? The indication of implication is its indication of knowledge and power.
* The student: I knew (...).
* The Shaykh: We heard. I think it is ﴿Have you not seen those who claim﴾.
* * *
* A student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion (61). So how will it be when a disaster strikes them for what their hands have put forth? Then they come to you swearing by Allah, "We intended nothing but good and reconciliation" (62). Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts, so turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them about themselves a far-reaching word﴾ [An-Nisa 60–63].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you?﴾ What do you derive from His words ﴿claim (yazAmUna)﴾?
* A student: Do you mean its meaning, O Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: No, what do you derive from it?
* A student: The invalidity of what they claim...
* The Shaykh: That their belief is not real. ﴿They claim that they believe﴾. The clause ﴿they desire to take their disputes to the taghut﴾: what is its place in grammar?
* A student: A circumstantial clause (hal).
* The Shaykh: A circumstantial clause from whom?
* The student: From the waw in ﴿claim (yazAmUna)﴾.
* The Shaykh: From the waw in ﴿yazAmUna﴾. What is meant by the taghut here? The meaning of taghut here, because in every place it is according to its context?
* A student: Whoever rules by other than what Allah has revealed.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
No, here, the taghut here, because in every place it is according to its context?
* A student: Whoever rules by other than what Allah has revealed.
* The Shaykh: Yes. And His words ﴿that He intends to lead them far astray﴾ [An-Nisa 60]: what is the wisdom in His making ﴿astray (dalalan)﴾ indefinite and describing it as far?
* A student: (...) that they have reached a great degree of error.
* The Shaykh: In error. Good.
* * *
﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger"﴾ [An-Nisa 61]. The pronoun in ﴿it is said to them﴾ refers to those who claim that they believe in what was revealed to the Messenger (peace be upon him) and what was revealed before him, namely the hypocrites among the People of the Book who were hypocritical. ﴿Come (ta'alaw)﴾: come forward. ﴿To what Allah has revealed﴾, meaning the Qur'an. He did not say "to the Qur'an," as an indication of its status and the height of its rank, that it was sent down from Allah, because what descends from Allah establishes proof against every person.
﴿And to the Messenger﴾. He did not say "to the words of the Messenger," because they are called to come into the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), to come to him so that he may debate with them and explain to them. The (al) in His words ﴿and to the Messenger﴾ is the mental reference (al-ahd al-dhihni). This is because references are of three kinds: mental, mentioned, and present. If the (al) points to something already mentioned, the reference is mentioned (al-ahd al-dhikri), as in His words: ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger (15). But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ [Al-Muzzammil 15–16]. Who is the messenger here? Moses, who was sent to Pharaoh.
It is mental when the thing is known in the mind, as when a speaker says to his opponent: "Let us go to the judge," meaning which judge? The known judge of the city. This verse and its examples are many.
It is present (al-ahd al-hudури) as in His words: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 3], meaning the present day. One of the rules for this is that it comes after a demonstrative noun, such as: "this man," "this day," "this week." So when it comes after a demonstrative, what is it? It is the present reference, because the demonstrative indicates a present, pointed-to thing, so the (al) following it is the present reference.
So ﴿the Messenger (al-Rasul)﴾ means Muhammad (peace be upon him). He was called a messenger (rasul) because Allah sent him and made him an intermediary between Himself and His servants in conveying His law. Allah's sending him is the greatest proof of his purification and that he is worthy to bear the message, as Allah said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [Al-An'am 124]. The Prophet (peace be upon him) combined trustworthiness with strength in conveying the message, and therefore no one is more trustworthy than he, and no one is more patient than he in what he endures in conveying the message of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
﴿You see the hypocrites﴾: the clause ﴿you see (ra'aytа)﴾ is the answer to the condition in His words ﴿when it is said to them, "Come"﴾. ﴿You see the hypocrites﴾. The taa in ﴿ra'ayta﴾ is for address. Who is addressed? Either the Messenger, because of His words ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you﴾, since the whole context is an address to the Messenger. It may also be general, but its being addressed to the Messenger is closer to the context.
﴿You see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion﴾. ﴿The hypocrites (al-munafiqin)﴾ is the active participle of (nafaqa), derived from nafiqa' al-yarbu', meaning its burrow. The burrow of the jerboa (yarbu') is built on deception, because the jerboa is clever: it makes a door in its burrow through which it enters, and makes another door of earth's crust at the far end of the burrow. When someone confronts it at the known open door, it leaves through the hidden door and deceives him. For this reason the word "hypocrite (munafiq)" was taken from it.
It has been said that this word is a newly coined Islamic term, meaning that its meaning is not known in the language in this sense, because the pre-Islamic period was unbelief with no faith in it, and a believer would be a believer by what remained of the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him), or he would be a Christian like Waraqah ibn Nawfal, or similar. But after the corruption of these people became apparent, in that they showed people that they were believers while they were unbelievers, this word came into use.
In His words ﴿you see the hypocrites﴾ there is a rhetorical point. What is it?
* A student: (...) it could have been made implicit.
* The Shaykh: Making the noun explicit in place of the pronoun, this is the rhetorical point. This is because the context requires that He say: "And when it is said to them, 'Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger,' you see them." This is what the context requires. But He said ﴿you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion﴾. When the explicit noun comes in place of the pronoun, it has three benefits:
The first benefit: the causation of the ruling (illiyyat al-hukm), because this explicit noun indicates that the cause of this ruling is this thing. So the cause of their aversion is what? Hypocrisy.
The second benefit: the marking of the referent of the pronoun with this attribute. That is, if the referent of the pronoun is described by this attribute, which is hypocrisy, but if He had said "you see them," we would not know that they were hypocrites.
The third benefit: generality, meaning that it includes these people and other hypocrites. If He had said only "you see them," it would not include others. So making the noun explicit in place of the pronoun has three benefits.
* A student: Marking and generality..
* Another student: The causation of the ruling.
* The Shaykh: And generality. Khalid mentioned this.
* The student: The referent of the pronoun.
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: Marking them with the attribute.
* The Shaykh: Correct. That is, marking them with the attribute, meaning this attribute applies to them, that is, to the one to whom the pronoun refers.
﴿You see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion﴾. Here ﴿yaSudduna (turn away)﴾: the same verb can be transitive or intransitive. It is said: "sadda bi-nafsihi" (he turned away by himself), and "sadda ghayrahu" (he turned another away). Here, is it the first or the second, ﴿yaSudduna 'anka sududa﴾?
* Students: The second.
* A student: It includes both.
* The Shaykh: O my brothers, ﴿when it is said to them, "Come"﴾ ﴿you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion﴾: it is from the first, which is intransitive, meaning: they turn away from you.
His words ﴿sududa﴾ is an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid), and it may also be a specifying infinitive (masdar nawʿi). The emphatic infinitive is the one that emphasizes its verb so that metaphor is excluded, because the verb may be used metaphorically, that is, it is ascribed to the agent figuratively. When it is emphasized, the possibility of metaphor is removed. It may also be a specifying infinitive, meaning that it is great aversion, so it is qualified by a deleted adjective, and the estimate is: "aversion great." Which of the two is more eloquent? The second is more eloquent, because it includes the first and not vice versa.
So these people, may Allah protect us, when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed, to the Qur'an, so that we may take our disputes to it, and to the Messenger, so that we may take our disputes to him," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion. That is, you see them in their hypocrisy and immersion in hypocrisy turning away from you with aversion.
Here He said ﴿turn away from you﴾ and did not say "turn away from the one who said it to them," because what concerns them is not who said it to them. What concerns them is the Messenger (peace be upon him). They may turn away from the Messenger and not come, but they do not turn away from the one who invited them. Perhaps they meet him with a cheerful and pleasant face, but they turn away from the Messenger. For this reason He did not say "turn away from him," meaning from the speaker, but said ﴿turn away from you﴾, because this is what they intend.
﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them for what their hands have put forth﴾ [An-Nisa 62]. ﴿How (kayfa)﴾ here is for wonder, meaning: be amazed at their condition when a disaster strikes them for what their hands have put forth. This disaster is that their hypocrisy and their aversion and turning away become known. When it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed, come to the Messenger," and they turn away and avert, and then this is discovered, this is the disaster. It is a disaster for them because they do not want their defects and their unbelief to be exposed. They are hypocrites who conceal themselves to the utmost degree because of the unbelief they hide. When they are discovered, this discovery is what? A great disaster. When this disaster strikes them ﴿for what their hands have put forth﴾, that is, because of what their hands have put forward of unbelief and hypocrisy.
﴿Then they come to you﴾: that is, they come to the Messenger (peace be upon him), ﴿swearing by Allah, "We intended nothing but good and reconciliation"﴾. The clause ﴿swearing (yahlifuna)﴾ is a circumstantial clause, the agent of the waw in ﴿came to you (ja'uka)﴾: they came to you while wearing this oath.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 4, verses 60–63 (part 2 of 3):**

﴿They swear by Allah, "We intended nothing but good and reconciliation."﴾ Here "in" (إن) is a negating particle. What is the evidence that it is a negator? The exception particle (إلا) that follows it. ﴿Nothing but good﴾ means: we intended nothing but good. Now, "in" (إن) can also be a conditional particle. Can one of you brothers give an example?

* Student: إن تقم أقم (*in taqum aqum*, "If you stand, I will stand").
* Shaykh: "In taqum aqum." Good. It can also come as a lightened form of the heavy (*mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah*). Go ahead and answer.
* Student: إنْ زيدًا قائمٌ (*in Zaydan qa'imun*).
* Shaykh: What?
* Student: إن الزيدانُ قائمٌ (*in al-Zaydani qa'imun*).
* Shaykh: إن الزيدانِ?
* Student: إن الزيدانُ قائمٌ.
* Shaykh: إنِ الزيدان? Like that? More eloquently, more eloquently, my brother. There is no problem with it.
* Student: إن الزيدانُ قائمٌ.
* Shaykh: What does he say?
* Students: إن زيدًا قائم (*in Zaydan qa'im*).
* Shaykh: إن زيدًا قائم? No.
* Student: ﴿And indeed they were, before that, in manifest error﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:164].
* Shaykh: ﴿And indeed they were, before that, in manifest error﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:164]. That is: *wa-innahum kanu min qablu fi dalalin mubin* ("indeed they were, before that, in manifest error"). And the poet's words:

  ......................... ∗∗∗ And indeed Malik was of noble origin...

  It also comes as an extra (*za'idah*, "superfluous") particle.

* Student: The poet's words:

  Banu Ghudanah, you are not gold, ∗∗∗ nor pure silver, but you are mere potsherds.

* Shaykh: "Banu Ghudanah, you are not gold, nor pure silver, but you are mere potsherds." That makes three uses. The fourth is the negating use, as in this verse: ﴿We intended nothing but good and reconciliation﴾.

As for His words, ﴿nothing but good and reconciliation﴾: what is "good" (*ihsan*)? The good is that they be cordial with the believers, ﴿when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:14], and with the disbelievers, when they meet those who disbelieved, they say, "We are with you." They intend good, meaning they walk the path without hostility toward either of them.

﴿And reconciliation﴾ means among the people: they show these people that they are with them and agree with them, and they show those people that they are with them and agree with them too. This, and Allah's refuge is sought, is the utmost hypocrisy. In other words: "We intended nothing but good, that there be no conflict between us and others, because the hypocrites cannot tolerate it." As for reconciling between people (*tawfiq*), we reconcile them. The explanation of this will come, Allah willing, in the lessons (*fawa'id*).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah knows﴾ [an-Nisa' 4:63]. ﴿Those﴾ refers to those who claim that they believe in what was revealed to you and what was revealed before you. Did He use the demonstrative indicating distance because of their high rank, or because of their low rank?

* Students: Low rank.
* Shaykh: Because of their low rank. The distant demonstrative may indicate physical distance, as when you say, "That man over there is far away." It may also indicate figurative distance, distance in rank, either high or low, according to what the context requires. Here ﴿those who﴾ indicates lowness. His words, ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds — those are the best of creation﴾ [al-Bayyinah 98:7], indicate height. ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell, abiding eternally therein. Those are the worst of creation﴾ [al-Bayyinah 98:6], indicates lowness. So the two verses combine height and lowness.

﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah knows.﴾ He said ﴿knows﴾ (*ya'lamu*, present tense) and did not say "knew" (*'alima*, past tense), because Allah's knowledge is continuous, past, present, and future. For this reason He used the present tense, which indicates continuity.

His words, ﴿what is in their hearts﴾, mean what they conceal of hypocrisy and disbelief. In other words: as for you, you do not know what is in their hearts, because we have only the outward. But we know them by indicators. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if We willed, We would have shown them to you, and you would have recognized them by their marks﴾ [Muhammad 47:30]. And then? ﴿And you will surely know them by the tone of their speech﴾ [Muhammad 47:30], that is, by its allusion and implication. This belongs to people of discernment (*firasah*). The stronger a person's faith in Allah, the sharper his discernment. Indeed, some people can read what is in a person's heart from the features of his face. Therefore we say: the hypocrites are known only to Allah, this is the principle. But sometimes we recognize them through the tone of their speech, or through discernment that Allah grants to whomever He wills of His servants.

﴿So turn away from them﴾ means: do not wear yourself out with them, and do not treat them as you would treat disbelievers, fighting them, because they did not openly declare enmity. For this reason, when the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked for permission to kill some of them, he said, "No. Lest people say that Muhammad kills his companions" [agreed upon; reported by al-Bukhari (3518) and Muslim (2584/63), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah]. This is the very essence of wisdom, because if we unsheathed our swords against such people we would kill a world of people, and they may be believers.

And when the man who polytheized, whom Usamah caught up with and struck with the sword, was addressed by the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Did you kill him after he had said, 'There is no god but Allah'?" [agreed upon; reported by al-Bukhari (4269) and Muslim (96/159), from the hadith of Usamah ibn Zayd], even though it is apparent that he said it out of fear. If this man's blood was protected by this word, how much more so these hypocrites who mention Allah, come with us, pray, and give charity! Therefore, refraining from them is the very essence of wisdom.

﴿And admonish them﴾. Admonition (*maw'izah*) is reminder combined with encouragement and warning. The admonition is to remind a person of what he must do or refrain from, together with what? Encouragement or warning: encouragement regarding what you command, and warning regarding what you forbid.

﴿And speak to them concerning themselves a far-reaching word﴾ means: say to them a word that reaches the depths of their souls. For this reason He made the soul the container of the speech. It may also be understood to mean: ﴿speak to them concerning themselves﴾, that is, concerning their affair and their condition.

﴿A far-reaching word﴾ reaches their hearts. The two meanings are not contradictory, and so both are true. In other words: speak to them about their affair and about themselves, that "you did such and such, and you did such and such, and you did such and such." Or: speak to them a word within the soul that reaches the souls and the innermost hearts. ﴿A far-reaching word﴾ means eloquent, or it means "reaching its utmost aim." Both are correct, because the more eloquent the speech, the greater its effect. For this reason it came in a hadith: "Indeed, there is magic in eloquence, and indeed there is wisdom in poetry" [reported by Abu Dawud (5011), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas].

How many a person expresses a meaning in an eloquent phrase, extremely clear and eloquent, and it has an effect; then another person comes and expresses the same meaning, but it has no effect because he lacks eloquence. For this reason it is one of Allah's blessings upon the servant that He grants him eloquence and fluency, so that he can express what is in himself and have an effect on others. The opposite of this is one who is not eloquent.

Eloquence (*balaghah*) has become an independent discipline, and the scholars wrote books on it. It is a very delightful discipline. I wish it were easy for us to read from it, because it is beneficial in one respect and has a fine taste in another. We ask Allah to make it easy.

These verses, as you have heard, were revealed concerning a group of hypocrites who claim that they believe in Allah and His Messenger, but they are not so.

Now we return to deriving lessons from these verses. Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim﴾.

* From this verse many benefits are derived. Among them: wonder at this strange state. Wonder at this strange state. From where do we know that? From the interrogative ﴿Have you not seen﴾, because the intent is to express wonder, that we should marvel at their condition.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: a person may claim what he is not truthful about, as in His words: ﴿they claim that they believe in what was revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾.

* And among its benefits: the obligation to believe in what was revealed to the Messenger and what was revealed before him, as in His words: ﴿that they believe in what was revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾. This indicates that belief in what was revealed before him is equivalent to belief in what was revealed to him, although it differs in method and law (*shir'ah* and *minhaj*), as Allah said: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a method﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:48]. Otherwise, the origin of the religions is one in terms of faith and beliefs, but it differs in law and method, because Allah is All-Wise, legislating for each nation what suits it, and what its condition requires of righteousness and reform.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the perfection of Islam and of those who adhere to it, because Islam commands people to believe in everything Allah has revealed, and those who adhere to it likewise believe in everything Allah has revealed. Those who have adopted other than Islam, such as the Jews and Christians, do not believe in everything Allah has revealed, do they? As for the earlier ones among them, they believe in it only in a general, implicit way (*iman hukmi*), meaning they believe in what came after their laws in a general way, because they did not encounter it. The believers in Moses in his time and the believers in Jesus in his time believe in the Qur'an, because they find that the Messenger is written in their Torah and Gospel. But it is implicit belief. As for the belief of Muslims in the Qur'an and in the earlier laws, it is true belief, because the religion of Islam is the latest.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's elevation (*'uluw*). From where is this derived?

* Students: From the fact of sending down.

* Shaykh: From the fact of sending down? If someone says: the sender is not mentioned in ﴿what was revealed to you﴾. Did He not say "what We revealed"?

* Students: It is known.

* Shaykh: Because it is known, and what is known is like what is mentioned. For this reason Allah said: ﴿and man was created weak﴾ [an-Nisa' 4:28]. If someone asks: who created man? We say: what? Allah. The verse does not say "Allah created man." We say: because it is known that there is no creator except Allah. This is known by the created order (*kawnan*). ﴿Man was created weak﴾. And the sending down of revelation is known by the law (*shar'an*), because the one who sends down revelation is Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Therefore, from this we derive the elevation of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. This is what the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus (*ijma'*) of the early generations, sound reason, and fifthly, innate nature (*fitrah*) indicate. This is a known matter, and praise be to Allah.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that seeking judgment from other than Allah and His Messenger is seeking judgment from the false deity (*taghut*, false authority or transgressor). As in His words: ﴿they desire to seek judgment before the false deity﴾.

* And among its benefits: that seeking judgment from other than Allah and His Messenger is disbelief. From where is this derived? From their being declared liars in their claim of faith, in His words: ﴿they claim﴾, because if they were believers they would have desired to seek judgment before Allah and His Messenger.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: if desiring to seek judgment before the false deity removes one from Islam, then actually seeking judgment before it is all the more so. Whoever loves and desires that judgment be sought before the false deity, even if he does not actually seek it, is not a believer. How much more so is one who fulfills this desire and actually seeks judgment before the false deity!
