For this reason we find people now have made armored vehicles and fortified buildings, and have protected themselves against the enemy with the strongest protection possible.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the deception by enemies of the messengers upon the common people, through what Allah the Exalted decrees of trial and testing, such as the decree of drought, poverty, and sickness when the messengers are sent. This is not constant, but it may occur. Allah has wisdom in what He decrees, so that He may test His servants as to whether they will accept or not. But the enemies of the messengers take advantage of this—they take from it what? A pretext for repelling people from the messengers.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation by those who denied the Messenger, peace be upon him, of the Oneness of Lordship (tawhid al-rububiyyah). From where is this derived? From their saying: ﴿from Allah﴾. They affirm Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and they affirm that whatever happens in the universe is from Allah, that Allah is the Provider, the Giver of life and death; they affirm all of this, but they do not affirm its necessary consequence, which is the Oneness of Divinity (tawhid al-uluhiyyah).
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that good deeds and evil are all from Allah; by His saying: ﴿Say: All is from Allah﴾.

If someone says: What is the reconciliation between this verse and the one that follows it, which is His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾?

We say: The difference... The reconciliation between them is that each address has its place. Here we are addressing those people who argued with the calamities that befell them, using them as an argument against the validity of what the messengers brought; so Allah the Exalted wanted to respond to them by saying that all is from Allah. As for the second verse, it explains that what befell the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, of good is from Allah, and what befell him of evil is from himself. Similar to this is that Allah refuted the saying of those who said: ﴿If Allah had willed, we would not have associated [others with Him]﴾ [al-An'am 148], because they used predestination as an argument for their sins and their polytheism. And He said in another verse: ﴿Had Allah willed, they would not have associated﴾ [al-An'am 107]. Because the address in the second verse is directed to whom? To the Messenger ﷺ: ﴿Had Allah willed, they would not have associated; We did not make you a guardian over them, nor are you a manager over them﴾. The address was directed to him in a matter that was refuted when it came from another direction, in order that the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, be reassured that their association was by the decree of Allah, so that he would be content and submit to the decree of Allah; yet that does not prevent him from carrying out what is obligatory of conveying the message. And this is similar to it. We say: when the polytheists wanted to argue that good is from Allah as a mere favor from Him, and that evil is from the messengers, Allah refuted that. So in what way would the coming of the messengers be a cause of drought, barrenness, poverty, and sickness?

Rather, what befalls a person of good is from Allah, and what befalls him of evil is from himself, because he is the cause; so attributing it to himself is attributing things to their causes, and attributing it to Allah is attributing what is decreed to its Decreer, who is Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the censure of one who has no understanding; by His saying: ﴿What is wrong with these people that they can hardly understand any statement?﴾
* And it follows from this: the praise of one whom Allah has granted success in understanding the religion of Allah. For this reason the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever Allah intends good for, He gives him understanding in the religion."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (71), and Muslim (1037 / 98), from the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan.]]

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾. ﴿Mā﴾ here is conditional, and its response is His saying ﴿from Allah﴾. The same is said about His saying ﴿and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾.

﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah﴾: the good here means what a person obtains of health, provision, and other things; it is pure favor from Allah, like His saying: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾. Were it not for Allah's bounty and favor, this good in which we live would not have come to us.

﴿And whatever evil befalls you﴾: which is the opposite of good, i.e., what distresses you of the decree of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿is from yourself﴾, meaning you are the cause.

The address in His saying ﴿whatever befalls you﴾ is said to be to the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, because Allah said to him: ﴿Say: All is from Allah﴾, then said: ﴿whatever befalls you﴾. And it is said that the address is to others; it is directed to everyone who can be addressed. The argument of the first view is that the context requires it: ﴿Say: All is from Allah﴾.

Then He said: ﴿whatever befalls you﴾, and the context follows one pattern. The argument of the others is that the Prophet ﷺ does not commit an offense for which the calamities that befall him would come from him. But the better course is to adopt the apparent context, that the address is to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him; and if this is addressed to the Messenger, then those below him are all the more so, without doubt. For this reason He said: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾. So the view we have preferred becomes supported by what precedes it and what follows it: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾.

If someone says: "﴿We have sent you to mankind﴾: would it not suffice without His saying ﴿as a messenger﴾?"

We say: Yes, but the word ﴿messenger﴾ is more eloquent than if it were limited to the verb. This is one aspect. Another aspect is that mentioning it indicates that he is fit for the messengership, just as you say to a person: "I have appointed you as an agent (wakkaltuka fi al-bay' bā'i'an)" — meaning, because you are qualified for agency, being knowledgeable of sale and capable of it. So mentioning "messenger" here is for emphasis and to clarify that he is fit for the messengership, peace and blessings be upon him.

﴿And Allah suffices as a witness﴾: (kafā) is a past-tense verb, and (bi) is a prepositional particle, extra in wording but not extra in meaning; the meaning is: Allah the Exalted suffices as a witness over every thing.

* In this noble verse there are benefits. First: the clarification that what good befalls us is purely a favor from Allah; by His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah﴾. What supports this is that the good that befalls us is either initial (ibtida') or a reward (thawab). If it is initial, then its being a favor is clear; and if it is a reward for a deed, then our success in that deed, for which this good is a reward—from where is it? From Allah the Mighty and Majestic. So it is from Allah, whether it is initial or a reward.
* Among the benefits of this verse: the attribution of a thing to its cause; the permissibility of attributing a thing to its cause, by His saying: ﴿and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾.
* Among the benefits of this verse: that when good befalls a person, he must render thanks to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, since it is from Him as bounty and kindness; and when evil befalls him, he should look into himself, so that he may call himself to account and seek to make amends, and the evil is thereby lifted.

If someone says: If the address is to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, does the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, commit an act for which he is punished?

The answer: that the Prophet ﷺ..
When good befalls him, he must render thanks to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, since it is from Him as bounty and kindness; and when evil befalls him, he should look into himself, so that he may call himself to account and seek to make amends, and the evil is thereby lifted. If someone says: If the address is to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, does the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, commit an act for which he is punished?

Answer: The Prophet ﷺ was commanded by Allah to seek forgiveness for his sin and for the believers, and Allah said: ﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest, that Allah may forgive you your past sins and those to come﴾ [al-Fath 1, 2]. He is a son of Adam, and the sons of Adam are sinners, and the best of sinners are those who repent. So the Prophet ﷺ may err; for this reason he said: "O Allah, forgive me my earnestness and my jest, my errors and my deliberate faults" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (6399) and Muslim (2719/69) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari].

But the difference between him and the rest of mankind to whom he was sent is that he is necessarily granted success in seeking forgiveness and repentance, whereas others may or may not be granted it. Through this we know that something may occur from the Prophet ﷺ that becomes a cause of his committing an evil deed, but by it he increases in elevation and rank with Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the generality of the Prophet's ﷺ message to all of mankind; for His saying: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind﴾ [an-Nisa 79]. From this follows a refutation of the Christians who claim that Muhammad ﷺ was a messenger to the Arabs alone; for we say to them: You now believe that he is a messenger, and that he is from Allah, and Allah said of him: ﴿We have sent you to mankind﴾. Your acknowledgment that he is a messenger obliges you to acknowledge that his message is general; otherwise you have denied him. Once you acknowledge that he is a messenger—even if only to the Arabs—you are bound to acknowledge that he is a messenger to all people.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that the Prophet ﷺ is fit for the message, suited to it, and carries it out; for His saying: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾. He is fit for it from the outset, and in the end he fully carried it out.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah's testimony to him as a messenger suffices as every testimony, but for those who fear Him. So what is the form of Allah's testimony to him?
Allah bore witness to His Prophet ﷺ that he is truly a messenger, by two testimonies: a verbal testimony and an actual testimony. As for the verbal testimony: it is in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you; He sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness, and Allah suffices as a witness﴾ [an-Nisa 166].
As for the actual testimony: it is His establishing him in conveying the message and His granting him victory over his enemies. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if he had invented some of the sayings concerning Us﴾ [al-Haqqah 44]—"some," not all the sayings—﴿We would have seized him by the right hand. Then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ [al-Haqqah 45, 46]; meaning: We would have destroyed him. So the Prophet ﷺ has been witnessed by Allah as a messenger by a verbal and an actual testimony. The verbal one?
* Student: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind﴾ [an-Nisa 79].
* Shaykh: No, we want the word "testimony."
* Student: ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you﴾ [an-Nisa 166].
* Shaykh: ﴿He sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness﴾. The actual one?
* Student: The actual one: that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, established His religion until..
* Shaykh: Established it for him and supported him.
* Student: Established for him..
* Shaykh: And supported him.
* Student: And supported him against his enemies, and if he were, meaning..
* Shaykh: Not a messenger.
* Student: Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, would not have established him; for He says: ﴿And if he had invented some of the sayings concerning Us﴾ [al-Haqqah 44], and not all the sayings, We would have seized him..
* Shaykh: ﴿We would have seized﴾.
* Student: ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ [al-Haqqah 45], meaning: We would not have left him in his state.
* Shaykh: Well done, may Allah bless you. Nevertheless, with all of this, Allah the Exalted strengthened him with clear signs, manifest miracles, sensory and immaterial.
It is excellent to review what Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) wrote on this point in his book al-Jawab al-Sahih liman Baddala Din al-Masih, for at the end of the book he mentioned the Prophet's ﷺ sensory and immaterial signs in a way I have not seen from anyone else, to the extent that Ibn Kathir (may Allah have mercy on him) in his book al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah transmitted it, either verbatim or in meaning. So it is excellent to review this research that Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) wrote on this subject.
* Among the benefits of the verses: the first of these verses, this one: the prohibition of tiyarah (superstitious omen-taking); for His saying: ﴿Say: all is from Allah﴾ [an-Nisa 78]. If you wish, we will postpone discussion of it, as it is important.
* Student: Shaykh, could the context of these verses be about the hypocrites, up to His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who were told: restrain your hands﴾ [an-Nisa 77]? All this context comes later about the hypocrites; they are not a people of the Companions who emigrated.
* Shaykh: No, ﴿those who were told: restrain your hands﴾ are not all of them ﴿they said: Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us?﴾ [an-Nisa 77], ﴿then a party of them﴾: a party, not all of them.
* Student: Shaykh, the verses after it are their saying: ﴿And if a good befalls them, they say: this is from Allah﴾ [an-Nisa 78], then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And they say: obedience; but when they go out from your presence, a party of them plots by night other than what you say﴾ [an-Nisa 81]. Speech about the hypocrites: ﴿And when there comes to them a matter of security or fear, they spread it; and if they had referred it to the Messenger﴾ [an-Nisa 83]. They are not disbelievers.
* Shaykh: He does not rule it out, and it has been said, but as I told you during the tafsir: most exegetes hold that it concerns a people in Makkah who were oppressed and asked the Messenger ﷺ to fight, so they were told: restrain your hands. Also, did the hypocrites ever say at any time: let us fight?
* Student: Some of them, Shaykh..
* Shaykh: Not at all. Rather, even at the Battle of Uhud, when they set out, they turned back midway along the road.
* Student: But the first ones used to promise the Messenger that they would remain with him and support him.
* Shaykh: No, the Jews. These Jews are the ones who used to seek victory over those who disbelieved.
* Student: Shaykh, some newspapers and magazines (...) the zodiac signs: Aries, Scorpio, Aquarius and similar, so is there a basis for this?
* Shaykh: There is no harm; the calendar is built on this. The written calendars that are published every year, are they not written? They built their timekeeping on the zodiac.

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah; and whoever turns away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them (80). And they say: obedience; but when they go out from your presence, a party of them plots by night other than what you say; and Allah records what they plot by night. So turn away from them and rely upon Allah; and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs (81). Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an? Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [an-Nisa 80–82].
* Shaykh: We seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. It has already passed that the enemies of the messengers used to take omens from the messengers, and Allah, glorified and exalted, made clear that everything that occurs is from Allah. In another verse He made clear that their omen is with them; that is, if there is ill omen, the ill omen is from you upon yourselves. It has also passed that whatever good befalls a person is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls him is from himself.
It has also passed that we reconciled between this verse and the preceding one: that evil and good are from Allah in creation and decree, and evil from the human is by way of cause, meaning he is the cause, not the one who brought it into existence; and by this the two verses are reconciled.
It has also passed our explanation of the generality of the Prophet's ﷺ message to all people from His saying: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾ [an-Nisa 79], and this is one of many verses indicating his message and its generality.
It has also passed that Allah bore witness to the truthfulness of His Messenger ﷺ in two ways: verbal, and actual.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you are in fortified towers.﴾ Let us begin first with the grammar. (ʾAyna) here is a conditional noun of unconditional sense (ism shart jazim), and (mā) is an extra particle for emphasis (zā'ida lil-tawkīd). The conditional verb is ﴿takūnū﴾ and ﴿yudrikkumu﴾ is the response of the condition (jawab al-shart).

﴿And even if you were in fortified towers﴾: (law) here is a conditional particle, and its conditional verb is ﴿kuntum﴾. We do not find a response of the condition for (law), so it was said: the response of the condition is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, and the sense is: "And even if you were in fortified towers, death would overtake you." It was also said that in this context it does not need a response. This is the view of Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, in his book Aqsam al-Qur'an: that in such a context it does not need a response, and that if a response were supplied the speech would be awkward and not eloquent. This occurs frequently in the Qur'an: you find a conditional clause referring back to what came before, meaning its response is understood from what preceded it; in that case we say it needs no response, and supplying a response makes the speech clumsy.

As for the rest of the verse, there is apparently no difficulty in it, except that His saying ﴿lā yakādūna yafqahūna ḥadīthan﴾ (yakād) is one of the verbs of approximation (af'al al-muqarabah), and it works like (kāna and its sisters): it raises the noun and puts the predicate in the accusative.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says in response to those who said: ﴿Why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You had delayed us to a near term﴾. He says: if you say this for the sake of enjoying a little in this world, then you will not escape death: ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you﴾, whether you are in the air, or in the sea, or on the earth, or in fortified towers, or in crumbling houses, or in a barren wilderness. ﴿Wherever you may be﴾, and (ʾayna) is well known to indicate place.

His saying ﴿death will overtake you﴾ means: it will not miss you, and you cannot escape it. Rather, in another verse there is something stronger and more eloquent, where He the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Say: Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 8]. He did not say "it will reach you (lāḥiqukum)"; He said ﴿meet you (mulāqīkum)﴾. And what do you think of a thing from which you flee, and which meets you? Without doubt you will be quicker to reach it than if it were merely pursuing you! Because your fleeing and your meeting combine, and so that is swifter. Thus He the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you are in fortified towers.﴾ And what comes after death? After death is meeting Allah the Mighty and Majestic, with good or with evil. And when does it occur? We do not know when death will come, or in which land. We do not know. ﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾ [Luqman 34]. So let us prepare, and let us always be vigilant, so that when death overtakes us we are in the state with which our Lord is pleased, the Mighty and Majestic.

His saying ﴿in fortified towers﴾: (burūj) is the plural of (burj), which is a high building, and from it come the burūj in the sky, which are twelve zodiacal signs, to which Allah alluded in His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky zodiacal signs﴾ [al-Furqan 61]. The seasons of the year revolve through these burūj: spring, summer, autumn, and winter; each season has three of them. The best and most beneficial of the burūj for the body is the sign of Aries (al-Hamal), which occurs at the beginning of spring, for bodies are at their healthiest then. This is from the standpoint of it being a sign; but there are matters that befall a person in which his body is healthy or sick, according to circumstances. Yet in terms of time, the best season is spring.

So what is meant by burūj here? High buildings, since they resemble the zodiacal signs in their height and elevation. As for one who said that what is meant is the celestial burūj, he has strayed far and erred, because Allah said ﴿fortified (mushayyadah)﴾, and this description never applies to celestial burūj; it applies only to lofty palaces.

His saying ﴿mushayyadah﴾ means: well-fortified and firmly built. To this is added that they are plastered with (shīd), which is (gypsum), i.e., whitewashed; because whiteness is loved by the soul and protects from the heat of the sun, which is why palaces are built with it. ﴿And even if you were in fortified towers﴾.

﴿And if good befalls them, they say: "This is from Allah"; and if evil befalls them, they say: "This is from you [O Muhammad]."﴾ The pronoun in His saying ﴿if it befalls them﴾ refers to those who denied the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. By evil (sayyi'ah) here is meant what distresses, not evil deeds; rather, what distresses a person, such as drought, sickness, poverty, and the like. Drought from the sky, when it does not rain, and barrenness from the earth, when it does not grow; poverty and sickness. If evil befell them, they said: "This is from you." And if good befell them—its opposite: fertility, rain, wealth, health—when these befell them, they said: "This is from Allah," meaning you have no merit in it. And in the case of evil they said: "This is from Muhammad; he is the one who brought it. May Allah not bring him near us," thereby taking omen from him, peace and blessings be upon him. This is like the saying of the Children of Israel to Musa: ﴿We have taken an omen from you and those with you. He said: Your omen is with Allah; rather, you are a people being tested﴾ [al-Naml 47].

Likewise the peoples said to their messengers: ﴿We take an omen from you. If you do not desist, we will surely stone you, and a painful punishment will surely touch you from us﴾ [Ya-Sin 18]. Thus taking omens was a habit of those who denied the messengers: they said that whatever drought, barrenness, sickness, or poverty befell them was from you; and if the opposite befell them, which was pleasing to them, they said: "This is from Allah."

Allah the Mighty and Majestic responded to them: ﴿Say﴾, i.e., O Muhammad: ﴿All is from Allah﴾. Good and evil are from Allah, because Allah is the One who decrees them, not from the coming of the messengers. Rather, the coming of the messengers brings nothing but good; but they use these doubts as an argument against the messengers in order that people will deny them and shun them.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: All is from Allah﴾. It is He who decrees good and decrees evil. This answer is a sound answer, because none can bring rain except Allah, none can withhold rain except Allah, none can bring health except Allah, and none can bring sickness except Allah the Mighty and Majestic; so all is from Allah.

﴿What is wrong with these people that they can hardly understand any statement?﴾ (mā) is an interrogative of wonder: that is, how strange these people are. ﴿They can hardly﴾, i.e., they do not come close to. ﴿Understand any statement﴾, i.e., they do not come close to understanding the statement, knowing the rulings and the wisdom, since they said this false statement.

His saying ﴿lā yakādūna﴾ means "they do not come close," and it is known that negating coming close is a negation of the act itself, and more so. So if they can hardly understand, then all the more so are they—what?—not understanding at all and not even near to understanding. And ﴿ḥadīthan﴾ means: what is related/spoken to them.

* This noble verse contains several benefits.
* The first benefit: there is no escape from death, however strong a person may be in his authority and in his fortresses; he has no escape from it. This is drawn from His saying: ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you﴾.
* Among the benefits of this verse: it is obligatory for a person to prepare for death, since there is no escape from it; and since there is no escape, let us prepare for it so that we may act.
* Among the benefits of this verse: the attribution of overtaking to death.
* And it follows from this: that it is valid to attribute a thing to causes, but on condition that one believes these causes do not act by themselves, and that they are only from Allah the Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: fortresses do not avail against the decree of Allah; by His saying: ﴿even if you were in fortified towers﴾.
* Among its benefits: the use of hyperbole in speech, and that this is one of the methods of the Arabic language; by His saying: ﴿even if you were in fortified towers﴾.
* Among its benefits: the permissibility of omitting what is known, and that this does not count as a defect in speech; by His saying: ﴿even if you were in fortified towers﴾.
* And this branches from this benefit: what occurs in contracts—contracts of sale, hire, pledge, endowment (waqf), and the like. For example, if someone says: "I have endowed this for so-and-so even if he is rich," the meaning is: even if he is rich, it is an endowment for him; and accordingly the endowment is valid for this beneficiary under every circumstance.
* Among the benefits of this verse: it is the custom of people to protect themselves against death with what? With lofty, well-built palaces. If there were an enemy who wanted to attack you, would you seek refuge from him in a tent of cloth? In a building of wood? No, in towers: lofty, strong towers, so that nothing from him reaches you. For this reason we find people now have made armored vehicles and fortified buildings, and have protected themselves against the enemy with the strongest protection possible.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the deception by enemies of the messengers upon the common people, through what Allah the Exalted decrees of trial and testing, such as the decree of drought, poverty, and sickness when the messengers are sent. This is not constant, but it may occur. Allah has wisdom in what He decrees, so that He may test His servants as to whether they will accept or not. But the enemies of the messengers take advantage of this—they take from it what? A pretext for repelling people from the messengers.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation by those who denied the Messenger, peace be upon him, of the Oneness of Lordship (tawhid al-rububiyyah). From where is this derived? From their saying: ﴿from Allah﴾. They affirm Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and they affirm that whatever happens in the universe is from Allah, that Allah is the Provider, the Giver of life and death; they affirm all of this, but they do not affirm its necessary consequence, which is the Oneness of Divinity (tawhid al-uluhiyyah).
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that good deeds and evil are all from Allah; by His saying: ﴿Say: All is from Allah﴾.

If someone says: What is the reconciliation between this verse and the one that follows it, which is His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾?

We say: The difference... The reconciliation between them is that each address has its place. Here we are addressing those people who argued with the calamities that befell them, using them as an argument against the validity of what the messengers brought; so Allah the Exalted wanted to respond to them by saying that all is from Allah. As for the second verse, it explains that what befell the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, of good is from Allah, and what befell him of evil is from himself. Similar to this is that Allah refuted the saying of those who said: ﴿If Allah had willed, we would not have associated [others with Him]﴾ [al-An'am 148], because they used predestination as an argument for their sins and their polytheism. And He said in another verse: ﴿Had Allah willed, they would not have associated﴾ [al-An'am 107]. Because the address in the second verse is directed to whom? To the Messenger ﷺ: ﴿Had Allah willed, they would not have associated; We did not make you a guardian over them, nor are you a manager over them﴾. The address was directed to him in a matter that was refuted when it came from another direction, in order that the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, be reassured that their association was by the decree of Allah, so that he would be content and submit to the decree of Allah; yet that does not prevent him from carrying out what is obligatory of conveying the message. And this is similar to it. We say: when the polytheists wanted to argue that good is from Allah as a mere favor from Him, and that evil is from the messengers, Allah refuted that. So in what way would the coming of the messengers be a cause of drought, barrenness, poverty, and sickness?

Rather, what befalls a person of good is from Allah, and what befalls him of evil is from himself, because he is the cause; so attributing it to himself is attributing things to their causes, and attributing it to Allah is attributing what is decreed to its Decreer, who is Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the censure of one who has no understanding; by His saying: ﴿What is wrong with these people that they can hardly understand any statement?﴾
* And it follows from this: the praise of one whom Allah has granted success in understanding the religion of Allah. For this reason the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever Allah intends good for, He gives him understanding in the religion."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (71), and Muslim (1037 / 98), from the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan.]]

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾. ﴿Mā﴾ here is conditional, and its response is His saying ﴿from Allah﴾. The same is said about His saying ﴿and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾.

﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah﴾: the good here means what a person obtains of health, provision, and other things; it is pure favor from Allah, like His saying: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾. Were it not for Allah's bounty and favor, this good in which we live would not have come to us.

﴿And whatever evil befalls you﴾: which is the opposite of good, i.e., what distresses you of the decree of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿is from yourself﴾, meaning you are the cause.

The address in His saying ﴿whatever befalls you﴾ is said to be to the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, because Allah said to him: ﴿Say: All is from Allah﴾, then said: ﴿whatever befalls you﴾. And it is said that the address is to others; it is directed to everyone who can be addressed. The argument of the first view is that the context requires it: ﴿Say: All is from Allah﴾.

Then He said: ﴿whatever befalls you﴾, and the context follows one pattern. The argument of the others is that the Prophet ﷺ does not commit an offense for which the calamities that befall him would come from him. But the better course is to adopt the apparent context, that the address is to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him; and if this is addressed to the Messenger, then those below him are all the more so, without doubt. For this reason He said: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾. So the view we have preferred becomes supported by what precedes it and what follows it: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾.

If someone says: "﴿We have sent you to mankind﴾: would it not suffice without His saying ﴿as a messenger﴾?"

We say: Yes, but the word ﴿messenger﴾ is more eloquent than if it were limited to the verb. This is one aspect. Another aspect is that mentioning it indicates that he is fit for the messengership, just as you say to a person: "I have appointed you as an agent (wakkaltuka fi al-bay' bā'i'an)" — meaning, because you are qualified for agency, being knowledgeable of sale and capable of it. So mentioning "messenger" here is for emphasis and to clarify that he is fit for the messengership, peace and blessings be upon him.

﴿And Allah suffices as a witness﴾: (kafā) is a past-tense verb, and (bi) is a prepositional particle, extra in wording but not extra in meaning; the meaning is: Allah the Exalted suffices as a witness over every thing.

* In this noble verse there are benefits. First: the clarification that what good befalls us is purely a favor from Allah; by His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah﴾. What supports this is that the good that befalls us is either initial (ibtida') or a reward (thawab). If it is initial, then its being a favor is clear; and if it is a reward for a deed, then our success in that deed, for which this good is a reward—from where is it? From Allah the Mighty and Majestic. So it is from Allah, whether it is initial or a reward.
* Among the benefits of this verse: the attribution of a thing to its cause; the permissibility of attributing a thing to its cause, by His saying: ﴿and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾.
* Among the benefits of this verse: that when good befalls a person, he must render thanks to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, since it is from Him as bounty and kindness; and when evil befalls him, he should look into himself, so that he may call himself to account and seek to make amends, and the evil is thereby lifted.

If someone says: If the address is to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, does the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, commit an act for which he is punished?

The answer: that the Prophet ﷺ..
When good befalls him, he must render thanks to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, since it is from Him as bounty and kindness; and when evil befalls him, he should look into himself, so that he may call himself to account and seek to make amends, and the evil is thereby lifted. If someone says: If the address is to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, does the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, commit an act for which he is punished?

Answer: The Prophet ﷺ was commanded by Allah to seek forgiveness for his sin and for the believers, and Allah said: ﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest, that Allah may forgive you your past sins and those to come﴾ [al-Fath 1, 2]. He is a son of Adam, and the sons of Adam are sinners, and the best of sinners are those who repent. So the Prophet ﷺ may err; for this reason he said: "O Allah, forgive me my earnestness and my jest, my errors and my deliberate faults" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (6399) and Muslim (2719/69) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari].

But the difference between him and the rest of mankind to whom he was sent is that he is necessarily granted success in seeking forgiveness and repentance, whereas others may or may not be granted it. Through this we know that something may occur from the Prophet ﷺ that becomes a cause of his committing an evil deed, but by it he increases in elevation and rank with Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the generality of the Prophet's ﷺ message to all of mankind; for His saying: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind﴾ [an-Nisa 79]. From this follows a refutation of the Christians who claim that Muhammad ﷺ was a messenger to the Arabs alone; for we say to them: You now believe that he is a messenger, and that he is from Allah, and Allah said of him: ﴿We have sent you to mankind﴾. Your acknowledgment that he is a messenger obliges you to acknowledge that his message is general; otherwise you have denied him. Once you acknowledge that he is a messenger—even if only to the Arabs—you are bound to acknowledge that he is a messenger to all people.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that the Prophet ﷺ is fit for the message, suited to it, and carries it out; for His saying: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾. He is fit for it from the outset, and in the end he fully carried it out.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah's testimony to him as a messenger suffices as every testimony, but for those who fear Him. So what is the form of Allah's testimony to him?
Allah bore witness to His Prophet ﷺ that he is truly a messenger, by two testimonies: a verbal testimony and an actual testimony. As for the verbal testimony: it is in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you; He sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness, and Allah suffices as a witness﴾ [an-Nisa 166].
As for the actual testimony: it is His establishing him in conveying the message and His granting him victory over his enemies. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if he had invented some of the sayings concerning Us﴾ [al-Haqqah 44]—"some," not all the sayings—﴿We would have seized him by the right hand. Then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ [al-Haqqah 45, 46]; meaning: We would have destroyed him. So the Prophet ﷺ has been witnessed by Allah as a messenger by a verbal and an actual testimony. The verbal one?

It is excellent to review what Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) wrote on this point in his book al-Jawab al-Sahih liman Baddala Din al-Masih, for at the end of the book he mentioned the Prophet's ﷺ sensory and immaterial signs in a way I have not seen from anyone else, to the extent that Ibn Kathir (may Allah have mercy on him) in his book al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah transmitted it, either verbatim or in meaning. So it is excellent to review this research that Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) wrote on this subject.
* Among the benefits of the verses: the first of these verses, this one: the prohibition of tiyarah (superstitious omen-taking); for His saying: ﴿Say: all is from Allah﴾ [an-Nisa 78]. If you wish, we will postpone discussion of it, as it is important.

* Student: Shaykh, some newspapers and magazines (...) the zodiac signs: Aries, Scorpio, Aquarius and similar, so is there a basis for this?

* Shaykh: But a group of them, not all of them, a group of them. Perhaps this group are those who, when they emigrated, hypocrisy arose among them; when they emigrated to Madinah, hypocrisy arose among them, although most hypocrisy was among the Khazraj and the Aws.

They emigrated; a group of them, not all of them, deviated from their original principle, and when fighting was prescribed for them they backed off and became hypocrites. This is not unlikely: the first of them were believers, then they became hypocrites.

* Shaykh: Like al-birr and al-taqwa.

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah; and whoever turns away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them (80). And they say: obedience; but when they go out from your presence, a party of them plots by night other than what you say; and Allah records what they plot by night. So turn away from them and rely upon Allah; and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs (81). Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an? Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [an-Nisa 80–82].
* Shaykh: We seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. It has already passed that the enemies of the messengers used to take omens from the messengers, and Allah, glorified and exalted, made clear that everything that occurs is from Allah. In another verse He made clear that their omen is with them; that is, if there is ill omen, the ill omen is from you upon yourselves. It has also passed that whatever good befalls a person is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls him is from himself.
It has also passed that we reconciled between this verse and the preceding one: that evil and good are from Allah in creation and decree, and evil from the human is by way of cause, meaning he is the cause, not the one who brought it into existence; and by this the two verses are reconciled.
It has also passed our explanation of the generality of the Prophet's ﷺ message to all people from His saying: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾ [an-Nisa 79], and this is one of many verses indicating his message and its generality.
It has also passed that Allah bore witness to the truthfulness of His Messenger ﷺ in two ways: verbal, and actual.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah, and whoever turns away — We have not sent you as a guardian over them.﴾ In it there are two conditional sentences.

The first: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾. Here "man" (مَن, whoever) is conditional, and the conditional verb is ﴿yuṭi'[1]﴾. In this there are two difficulties. The first difficulty: where has the root letter of the word gone? The second difficulty: why is it vowelled with a kasra, given that "man" governs the jussive (jazm)?

The answer to the first difficulty: the middle radical of the word has been elided, because its final radical was jussive and its middle radical was quiescent. Ibn Malik said:

"If two quiescent letters meet, vowel the first; and if the first is a soft letter, its deletion is required."

So the yā' is quiescent and the 'ayn is quiescent, so the soft letter, the yā', is deleted. As for the kasra on the 'ayn, while it is jussive, it is due to the meeting of two quiescent letters. Examples of this are numerous, such as the Exalted's saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved were not [going to be] ...﴾ [al-Bayyinah 1]. Where is the response of the condition in ﴿man yuṭi'[1]﴾? Its response is His saying: ﴿then has obeyed Allah﴾.

The second sentence: ﴿And whoever turns away, then We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾. In the second sentence, the conditional verb is (...), and the response clause is a nominal sentence! ﴿fa-mā arsalnāka ʿalayhim ḥafīẓan﴾ is a nominal sentence! Like (...), it is a verbal sentence, because "mā" is a negation particle and ﴿arsalnāka﴾ is a past-tense verb.

As for the reason the response is prefixed with "fa" in both sentences, it is because the response cannot validly be a condition itself; and when the response cannot validly be a condition, it must be prefixed with "fa", as Ibn Malik said in his Alfiyya:

"Bind with 'fa' necessarily a response that, if it were made a condition for 'in' or others, would not be valid as one."

This has been mentioned in a line of poetry, which is?
* Student: (...)

* The Shaykh:

"Nominal, imperative, and with a fixed noun, and with mā, qad, lan, and with the future particles."

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾. The "al" in "al-rasūl" is for mental (specific) reference, namely Muhammad ﷺ, since the Qur'an was revealed during his prophetic mission. It is also valid to say that it is general, covering every messenger; on this view "al" is for generality and not for reference. However, this possibility is weakened by His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away — then We have not sent you﴾, because this address is to the Prophet ﷺ; accordingly the intended "Messenger" is Muhammad ﷺ, and "al" is for mental reference, what?, mental.

﴿Then has obeyed Allah﴾. So obedience to the Messenger is obedience to Allah the Mighty and Majestic. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commands us with a matter and we obey him, we have obeyed Allah.

﴿And whoever turns away﴾, meaning: does not obey the Messenger, ﴿then We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾, because upon you is only the delivery, and you have delivered; and the preservation of people and their deeds belongs to Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

* Several benefits are derived from this noble verse, among them: that the default regarding what the Messenger ﷺ said or did is that it is legislation (sharʿ), by the generality of His saying: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾. Upon this it follows that if we doubt whether what the Messenger ﷺ did or said was legislation or forgetfulness, we interpret it as legislation. Among examples: "He recited Surat al-Zalzalah in the two units of the dawn prayer. The narrator said: I do not know whether he forgot — meaning — or was acting with knowledge."[1] So we say: is this possibility valid or not valid?

* Students: Valid.

* The Shaykh: No. If we say that the default is that what he did is legislation, this possibility is not valid; and if it is valid rationally, it is weak legally. We say: the default is that what he did is legislation, not forgetfulness.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the use of the Sunnah as evidence, and that it is like the Qur'an in the obligation to act upon it. But for the Sunnah we need to establish its authenticity or establish its attribution to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; we need this, because as long as it is not established, it is not the words of the Messenger.

* And it is derived from this verse: the permissibility of abrogating the Qur'an by the Sunnah, and the permissibility of specifying the Qur'an by the Sunnah. As for the second, there is consensus that the Sunnah specifies the Qur'an. As for the first, it is disputed. It was said that the Sunnah (i.e., it) does not abrogate the Qur'an, for two reasons:

The first reason: the authenticity of the Qur'an is certain, because it was transmitted by mass transmission (tawātur) both verbally and in meaning, whereas the Sunnah, what?, is not like that.

The second: the Qur'an is the speech of Allah transmitted to us by mass transmission both verbally and in meaning, whereas the Sunnah — narrators may alter it, transmitting it by meaning, and this is common. Therefore they said: the Qur'an is not abrogated by the Sunnah. The correct view is that the Qur'an is abrogated by the Sunnah if it is authentically established from the Prophet ﷺ; that is, the Qur'an is indeed abrogated by the Sunnah. However, until now we have not found an evidence or example that is free from opposition; but from the standpoint of reasoning, we say: its abrogation (i.e., abrogation of the Qur'an by the Sunnah) is established.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that disobedience to the Messenger is disobedience to Allah, derived by implication (mafhūm), since if his obedience is obedience to Allah, then his disobedience is disobedience to Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

* And among its benefits: the establishment of the Prophet ﷺ's prophethood in two ways: first, describing him as "the Messenger"; second, making his obedience like the obedience of Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

Here is an issue: may the Prophet ﷺ exercise ijtihad? The answer: yes, and his Sunnah is of two kinds: ijtihadi (independent judgment) and revelation (waḥy). From revelation is when he was asked about martyrdom and said: "It expiates everything," then Jibril came to him and said: "Except debt." So his saying "except debt" is by revelation.

As for what he ﷺ said without attributing it to Allah, it is revelation in the sense of Allah's approval of it, as we say: when the Prophet ﷺ approved someone's saying or action, it becomes part of his Sunnah; and his Sunnah is saying, action, and tacit approval.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the warning to whoever turns away and turns from obedience to the Prophet ﷺ, due to His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away — then We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾, as if He were saying: We shall preserve him, preserve his deeds against him, and leave him to himself.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Prophet ﷺ is not asked about the turning away of his ummah, and that whoever of his ummah turns away, his sin is upon himself, due to His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away — then We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾.

* And among the benefits of this verse: the establishment of Allah's majesty, in that He used the plural pronoun in His saying: ﴿fa-mā arsalnāka ʿalayhim ḥafīẓan﴾. Some scholars mentioned that Christians use pronouns of this kind to argue for a plurality of gods, saying: these indicate plurality. It is said: there is no surprise, no surprise that the Christians argue with this ambiguous verse for their falsehood, because deviation is in their hearts, and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 7].

The answer to this is easy: we say, what is wrong with you that you cling to this ambiguous verse and abandon the clear, decisive verses that plainly state that Allah is one God? As in His saying: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no deity except Him, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [al-Baqarah 163].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 81 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿They say, "Obedience," but when they go out from your presence, a group of them plan by night other than what you say. And Allah records what they plan. So turn away from them, and rely upon Allah. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾
They say: these are from the hypocrites, or a mixture of hypocrites and believers. ﴿They say, "Obedience"﴾ meaning: when you order them, they say, "Obedience," and do not oppose him. But when they go out from the Messenger (ﷺ), a group plans ﴿when they go out﴾. Al-Buruz (going out) means appearing, meaning: when they leave the gathering and their departure from him becomes apparent, and instead of being in the room they are in the market. The purpose of this is to show that when they leave the place completely, ﴿a group of them plan other than what you say.﴾
﴿Bayyata﴾ means: they did at night. Their action was at night because the night is the place of concealment and secrecy. So you find them saying to the Prophet (ﷺ), "Obedience," but when they go to their homes, they plan other than what they say.
﴿A group of them plan﴾, not all of them, a group of them, ﴿other than what you say.﴾ Here "other than" (ghayr) means opposition. So when he says, "Do such-and-such," they say, "Obedience," but when they return to their homes they say, "No obedience," meaning they plan opposition to what the Messenger (ﷺ) says.
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah records what they plan.﴾ This sentence is informative and conveys two matters. First, a threat to those who plan other than what the Messenger (ﷺ) says. Second, consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ), and that their affair is not hidden from Allah. He may hasten their punishment or delay it. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, turn away from them, meaning: do not concern yourself with them, and do not preoccupy your mind with them.
﴿And rely upon Allah﴾, depend upon Him, and know that even if they plan what they plan, they will not harm you, even if they plan to assault the Messenger (ﷺ), or to repel his call with false propaganda or the like. So rely upon Allah.
The scholars said that tawakkul (reliance) upon Allah is the sincere dependence upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, together with trust in Him and performing the means He has commanded. It consists of three meanings. First, sincere dependence upon Allah. Second, trust in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because reliance benefits no one if he is not confident in Allah's promise, and Allah said: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him﴾ [at-Talaq 3].
The third: performing the means He has commanded. Whoever does not perform the means is not one who relies upon Allah, but one who neglects, and performing the means is necessary. This is tawakkul upon Allah: sincere dependence upon Allah, together with trust in Him, and performing the means He has commanded.
Our saying "which He has commanded" excludes performing means that have no reality or basis, as sorcerers and those who use unlawful amulets do, and the like.
He says: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾ The grammatical analysis of such a sentence was previously given at His saying: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as witness﴾; and we said that the "ba" is an extra preposition, that the word Allah is in the nominative case as the subject, and that ﴿wakilan﴾ is either a specification (tamyiz) or a circumstantial accusative (hal).
* In this noble verse, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, shows His Messenger (ﷺ) that among people are those who believe outwardly and disbelieve inwardly; as in His saying: ﴿They say, "Obedience," but when they go out from your presence, a group of them plan other than what you say.﴾
* Among the benefits of this verse: a warning against hypocrisy, and that a person must be clear and manifest, not appearing to people in one way and, when hidden from them, showing them another face. For this reason you will not find anyone better than the truthful person who does not care, does not dispute, and is not deterred in Allah's cause by the blame of any blamer. This is what every Muslim must do: that his outward and inward be the same.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the invalidity of taqiyya (dissimulation) which the Rafidah take as a religion. From where is this derived? From Allah's threat to those who display obedience and plan contrary to obedience, in His saying: ﴿And Allah records what they plan.﴾
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of an act for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as in His saying: ﴿Allah records﴾. But is the meaning that He records it Himself directly, or that He commands its recording? The second is intended. Yet what is done by the command of one who commands is attributed to him; otherwise, those who record the deeds of servants are the angels, as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿No! Rather, you deny the Recompense. But indeed, over you are guardians, noble and recording﴾ [al-Infitar 9-11].
It is valid for an act to be attributed to the one who commands it, legally and by custom. For this reason it is said: "Amr ibn al-'As built the city of al-Fustat." It is well known that Amr ibn al-'As did not personally do the work, but commanded it.
It is said: "The Amir built his palace." Did he bring the bricks and clay himself? No, but he commanded it.
Among this is His saying: ﴿And the heaven We built with strength﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 47], ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is the heaven? He built it﴾ [an-Nazi'at 27]. He did not directly build it with His hand, as He created Adam with His hand; rather He said "Be," and it is. As in His saying: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth, "Come willingly or by compulsion." They said, "We come willingly"﴾ [Fussilat 11].
* Student: May Allah be good to you. If a person announces obedience, then privately harbours the opposite of obedience, but does not resolve upon it, does he not get held accountable? A passing thought...
The Shaykh: But?
* The student: That is, his self spoke of the opposite of obedience. Will Allah forgive this thought which his self utters?
* The Shaykh: No, he is not held accountable for it, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah has overlooked for my nation what their souls whisper, so long as they do not act upon it or speak of it"[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (5269) and Muslim (127 / 201) from Abu Hurayrah.]].
* Student: Shaykh, do we say that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, creates with His hand?
* The Shaykh: Yes. The scholars, the early scholars (salaf) in their creeds, said: He wrote the Torah with His hand.
* Student: The hadith, "Seek help in fulfilling your needs by secrecy" [[Related by al-Ruyani in his Musnad (1449), and al-Tabarani in his Mu'jams: al-Kabir (183), al-Awsat (2455), al-Saghir (1186), and in Musnad al-Shamiyyin (408), and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman (6228); the wording in al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi is "Seek help in accomplishing needs by concealment," all from Mu'adh ibn Jabal.]]. What contradicts this?
* The Shaykh: First, authenticate this hadith for me before anything else. If you authenticate it and bring it to me as authenticated, I will answer you.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, this is not a valid objection. Rather, this is evidence that the Sunnah is accepted just as the Qur'an is accepted, and that it may bring details and explanation not present in the Qur'an. This is the reality: there are verses in the Qur'an that are general, whose meaning we only understand through the Sunnah.
* Student: May Allah pardon you. The polytheists of Makkah, with their strength and their might (...) the Messenger (ﷺ) (...) but frankly we cannot in such a matter, for example (...).
* The Shaykh: What is the request?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿And among the people of Madinah are those who have become accustomed to hypocrisy﴾ [at-Tawbah 101]. The reason is that when the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madinah and his affair became manifest at the battle of Badr, the hypocrites began to fear. They began to be hypocritical. Indeed, at his arrival he did not even know hypocrisy, nor did it rise until the Messenger (ﷺ) became manifest at Badr.
* Student: Shaykh, you said that the word "bayyata" in His saying ﴿a group plans﴾ has a broader meaning of intention (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes. Linguistically, "bayyata" denotes intention, and this is the most common usage, but nothing prevents it from being an intention a person hides, like a statement he concealed at night.
* Student: Shaykh, we said: the paths are taking the means. If someone says: from His saying, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you should be in towers built up﴾ [an-Nisa' 78], one understands that we take the means.
* The Shaykh: Death is unavoidable.
* Student: So all...
* The Shaykh: There is no escape from it.
* Student: And even if... it is the head of (...) other things.
* The Shaykh: If a person says: I rely upon Allah, and I will build a fortified palace, and place guards and soldiers around me, and rely upon Allah so that death does not reach me, does it happen? It does not happen; death is unavoidable.
* Student: If the battle arrives, how should (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, when the battle arrives he must wear armour and must take cover.
* Student: What is the benefit?
* The Shaykh: The benefit is that in front of me is an enemy from whom I can escape. But death that comes from Allah, a person cannot escape from it.
* Student: If death is decreed, one cannot prevent it.
* The Shaykh: But as long as I have means by which to repel death, that too is decreed. Just as a person who goes hungry and eats does not die, but if he left eating he would die.
But if someone says: what do we do about a man who was killed, when we think that if he had not been killed he would have lived?
The answer: the matter cannot change from what has occurred. What is written in the Preserved Tablet is that this man dies by this killing at that time and in that place. Our supposition that if he had not been killed he would have lived is a supposition with no reality; it is an invalid assumption. What has occurred cannot change at all, however much a person acts.
* Student: You said, Shaykh: sincere dependence upon Allah. First, sincere dependence upon Allah; second, trust in Allah; third...
* The Shaykh: Performing the means commanded.
* Student: So whether a man comes or does not come, if his son falls ill, do you treat him with Prophetic medicine or with modern medicine?
* The Shaykh: Treat him with whatever is most beneficial; combine the two.
* Student: Meaning, first we try...
* The Shaykh: No, we do not say "try." The word "try" does not belong in legal matters. In matters made by people it is fine: try.
* Student: But Prophetic medicine, as you said yesterday, Shaykh, we take it, and the person is certain about it.
* The Shaykh: Yes, yes, that is known in legal matters, because Allah informed about them, so you must take them while certain. As for man-made matters, do you have certainty that what these people made is correct?
* Student: Do we understand from the verse the turning away (...)?
* The Shaykh: Turning away, no. What is meant by turning away is not to concern oneself with them. Otherwise, the falsehood must be clarified, but instead of troubling himself, he turns away from it, just as we say: turn away from whisperings and the like.
* Student: In Allah's saying ﴿And the heaven We built with strength﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 47], the verse resembles: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke, and said to it﴾ [Fussilat 11].
* The Shaykh: ﴿bi-aydin﴾ means: with strength.
* Student: Would this be an entry point for the Ash'aris?
* The Shaykh: An entry point, yes. But whoever tries to enter will find the door closed.
* Student: But he (...).
* The Shaykh: Did Allah attribute the hands to Himself?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Did Allah attribute the hands to Himself? Did He say: "with Our hands"?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: Then if we say "bi-aydin" meaning "with the hands of Allah," we would be saying about Allah what He did not say. Do you understand? In the Arabic language, "aydi" means strength. Look at His saying: ﴿And We built above you seven strong ones﴾ [an-Naba' 12], meaning strong and mighty.
* Student: If someone says their saying, may we attribute to Him its necessary implication?
* The Shaykh: As for the saying of Allah and His Messenger, its correct necessary implication is true, because Allah is knowing of what follows from His speech. But it is required that the implication be correct, lest someone come and say: this is from the implication of Allah's speech, and it is not so.
As for other than Allah and His Messenger, the necessary implication of his saying is not a saying of his unless he commits to it, because he may not acknowledge it as a implication of his words, and it may not have been in his mind when he spoke. So if this implication is mentioned to him and it is false, he retracts.

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿They say, "Obedience," but when they go out from your presence, a group of them plan by night other than what you say. And Allah records what they plan. So turn away from them, and rely upon Allah. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾ (81) ﴿Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an? If it had been from other than Allah, they would have found within it much contradiction.﴾ (82) ﴿And when there comes to them a matter of security or fear, they spread it. But if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those of authority among them, those who [can] draw correct conclusions would have known it. And if not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except for a few.﴾ (83) ﴿So fight in the cause of Allah; you are not held responsible except for yourself. And urge the believers. Perhaps Allah will restrain the aggression of those who disbelieve, and Allah is stronger in might and stronger in punishment.﴾ [an-Nisa' 81-84].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿They say, "Obedience," but when they go out from your presence, a group of them plan other than what you say. And Allah records what they plan. So turn away from them, and rely upon Allah. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾
From the benefits of this verse that you mentioned, recite them to us so they are not repeated. Read.
* Student:
* First benefit: that among people are those who conceal what is contrary to what they display.
* Second: a warning against hypocrisy.
* Third: the invalidity of taqiyya.
* The Shaykh: Taqiyya?
* Student: The invalidity of the taqiyya which the Rafidah take as a religion, and this is derived from Allah's threat to them in His saying: ﴿And Allah records what they plan.﴾
* Fourth: Is the meaning that He records directly, or that He commands recording? The second is intended, but what is done by Allah's command is attributed to Him (...), and among it His saying: ﴿And the heaven We built with strength﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 47], ﴿And the heaven and He who built it﴾ [ash-Shams 5] (...).
* The Shaykh: * Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the hypocrites are eager to hide their deeds, and for this reason they carry them out at night; as in His saying: ﴿a group of them plan other than what you say.﴾
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) is like the saying of Allah regarding the obligation to obey him and abandon what he forbids; its basis is that he warned those who plan other than what the Messenger (ﷺ) says.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of voluntary acts that proceed from Allah; as in His saying: ﴿And Allah records.﴾
If someone says: you have explained the recording here as the recording of the angels?
We say: but the recording of the angels occurred by His command, and command is among the voluntary attributes. This is what the verse indicates, the position of the People of the Sunnah and the Community, that Allah's acts are voluntary acts.
The Mu'attilah (deniers of divine attributes) held that Allah does not have voluntary acts subsisting in Him, and that no new act can occur to Him, because they claim that a originated thing subsists only in an originated thing. This is false.

Rather, we say to them the opposite of what they intended: whoever does not act is deficient, and whoever acts is what? Perfect. There is no doubt that the one who acts is more complete than the one who does not. So the voluntary attributes, which are the active attributes (al-sifat al-fi'liyyah), are undoubtedly among the perfections of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Accomplisher of what He intends﴾ [Hud 107].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's knowledge, based on His saying: ﴿He records﴾, for there is no recording except after knowledge.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: turning away from those whom we have despaired of reforming, based on His saying: ﴿So turn away from them and rely upon Allah﴾ [An-Nisa 81]. But does this mean absolute turning away, such that we never return to them a second time? The answer is no; we only turn away from them as long as we have despaired of their rectification.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of relying upon Allah, based on His saying: ﴿and rely upon Allah﴾. That is, depend upon Him in bringing about benefits and warding off harms, meaning that you do not hope for the attainment of benefits except from Him, nor for the averting of harms except from Him, glory be to Him and exalted be He. Relying upon Allah (al-tawakkul) means entrusting the matter to Him, sincerely depending upon Him, and placing trust in Him, glory be to Him and exalted be He.

Is it permissible to use this term of a created being, saying: "I relied upon so-and-so in buying a car for me"? Yes, it is permissible. The difference between this and relying upon Allah is that relying upon Allah is an absolute entrustment, in which the one relying believes he is in need of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. As for this, it is a restricted entrustment. Moreover, the one who entrusts or the one who relies sees that the one relied upon is of a lower rank than himself. This is the difference. However, if a person avoids this expression ("I relied upon so-and-so") and replaces it with his saying ("I appointed so-and-so as my agent" — wakkaltu fulanan), it is better.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the sufficiency of Allah, glory be to Him and exalted be He, for whoever relies upon Him, based on His saying: ﴿And Allah is sufficient as Disposer of affairs﴾ (wa kafa billahi wakilan), and this is like His saying: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him﴾ [At-Talaq 3].

Some exegetes mentioned, concerning Allah's statement, blessed and exalted, about Yusuf, that he said to the one of the two who would be saved: ﴿Mention me to your lord﴾, but ﴿Satan made him forget the mention of his lord, so he remained in prison several years﴾ [Yusuf 42], that Allah the Exalted decreed that this man be made to forget, because when Yusuf said "Mention me to your lord," there was in it a kind of reliance upon this lord, so he thought, and Allah knows best.

It may also be said: Allah, glory be to Him and exalted be He, decreed that this man forget in order to test Yusuf, so that his patience would be perfected in its three types.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 82:

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ [An-Nisa 82].

First: The grammatical analysis (i'rab). ﴿Afala﴾: the hamzah here is for interrogation, and the fa' is conjunctive (fa' al-'atf). So where is the element it conjoins to?

* The student: There are two opinions. The first is that the element conjoined to is omitted. The second is that there is no element conjoined to; rather, the original order is that the conjunction precedes the interrogative particle.

* The Shaykh: There is no element conjoined to?

* The student: Yes indeed.

* The Shaykh: So the fa' is a conjunction?!

* The student: The interrogative has priority (al-istifham lahu al-sadarah).

* The Shaykh: If the fa' is a conjunction, where is the element conjoined to?

* A student: He says: it is conjoined to what precedes it, so "afa-la".

* The Shaykh: "Afa-la," good. There are two opinions on it. The first: the hamzah enters upon an omitted element whose estimate is: "Have they been heedless, so they do not reflect upon the Qur'an?" Or it is what precedes. On this view, the position of the hamzah is after the fa', but it was moved forward because it has priority. The first is more grounded in the rules, as there is something estimated as the element conjoined to; the second is easier, because it needs no estimation. Sometimes it is very difficult for you to identify that omitted element.

And His saying: ﴿And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [An-Nisa 82]. In it is the conditional "law" (lau). What is its protasis (fi'l al-shart)? It is His saying: ﴿had been from other than Allah﴾, and its apodosis (jawab al-shart) is: ﴿they would have found﴾, ﴿they would have found in it much contradiction﴾.

Know that when the apodosis of "law" is affirmative, it is always or usually accompanied by the lam, as in this verse: ﴿And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾, and as in His saying: ﴿Were We to will, We would have made it crumbled debris﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah 65].

The lam may be omitted, as in His saying: ﴿Were We to will, We would have made it salty﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah 70], but this is rare. When its predicate is negated, the lam is usually omitted, and the reason is that the lam conveys emphasis, and negation contradicts emphasis. So you say: "Law jaa Zayd ma jaa 'Amr" (If Zayd had come, 'Amr would not have come), and you do not say "lama jaa 'Amr." Do you understand?

However, the lam may sometimes accompany a negation with "ma," as in the poet's words:

"Wa law nu'ta al-khiyara lama iftaraqna * wa lakin la khiyara ma'a al-layali"
"Had we been given the choice, we would not have parted, but there is no choice with the nights."
The eloquent form is "ma iftaraqna."

Allah, may He be exalted, rebukes these people: ﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ The hamzah here is for reproach; it is an interrogation carrying the sense of reproach.

﴿Yatadabbarun﴾ means: they contemplate and reflect; it is derived from a person taking a thing by turning it back and forth, i.e., they ponder its meanings and comprehend them.

﴿Al-Qur'an﴾ is on the pattern "fu'lan." Is it in the sense of "maf'ul" (object), or is it a verbal noun (masdar)?

It has been said: it is a verbal noun, like "shukran" and "ghufran." It has also been said: it is in the sense of the passive participle. Even if we say it is a verbal noun, it is in meaning the passive participle, because the Qur'an means "the recited," and "the recited": does its meaning denote "that which is recited," or "that which is gathered"?

Is it from "qara, yaqra," meaning "to gather," from which comes "qaryah" (village), because it gathers people, or from "qara'a, yaqra'u," meaning "to recite"?

Regarding this too the linguists have two opinions, and the correct view is that it is from both: the Qur'an is recited and gathered, its letters gathered one to another.

By "the Qur'an" is meant the speech of Allah, may He be exalted, which He sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ), the one whose recitation is an act of worship, and which is inimitable in its style and meaning.

﴿And if it had been from other than Allah﴾: the noun of "kana" (was) refers to the Qur'an; i.e., if the Qur'an had been from other than Allah, that is, from someone other than Allah.

﴿They would have found in it much contradiction﴾: i.e., they would have found in it contradiction, either in meaning or in style or otherwise. But "much contradiction" is not "little contradiction." And if it is from Allah, would they find in it a little contradiction? No. Rather, the phrase "much contradiction" describes the actual state of what is from other than Allah; it is not a condition implying that if it were from Allah they would find a little contradiction, since there is no contradiction in the Book of Allah, may He be exalted.

* This noble verse contains benefits. Among them: the exhortation to reflect upon the Qur'an. What is the basis for this?

* Students: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, what is the basis for this?

* A student: The rebuke of one who does not listen.

* The Shaykh: The rebuke of one who does not reflect. And if one who does not reflect upon the Qur'an is rebuked, then one who reflects upon it is praised and commended. So there is in it an exhortation to reflect upon the Qur'an.

* Among its benefits: a refutation of those who say that the verses of the Divine Attributes have unknown meanings. These are the people of tafwid (delegation of meaning), who say: our duty regarding the verses of attributes is only to recite them and not to speak about their meaning, because their meaning is unknown.

It is said to them: the word "the Qur'an" is general and includes the verses of attributes and others, and Allah rebuked those who did not reflect upon it. The necessary implication is that the verses have a meaning, for exhorting reflection upon something whose meaning cannot be reached is an exhortation to something impossible or difficult, and on this basis the exhortation would be vain speech, from which the speech of Allah, may He be exalted, is free. If someone says: if you say the verses of attributes are not of unknown meaning, and that their meaning is known, does affirming the meaning necessarily entail resemblance to creation?

The answer is: no, it does not necessarily follow, because Allah says: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [Ash-Shura 11]. The verse contains both affirmation and negation of likeness. So if affirmation were impossible without affirming likeness, the verse would contain, what?

* Students: Contradiction.

* The Shaykh: Contradiction, a clear contradiction. So the verses of attributes have known meaning, but without modality (tamthil).

If someone says: is it possible to affirm a meaning without modality?

The answer is: yes. Let us give an example of His saying: ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched; He spends as He wills﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 64]. The people of tafwid say: we do not know what is meant by His saying: ﴿Rather, both His hands﴾.

The people of ta'wil say: its meaning is blessing and power.

The people of the Sunnah and the Community say: its meaning is the literal hand, whose named reality has parts and components like ours. The hand, for example, is a part of us, but it is not possible to apply the word "part" to any of Allah's attributes, because a part is that which can be separated from the whole; for Allah's hand, Allah's foot, and Allah's eye, this meaning is not possible.

So we say: Allah has a true hand, who folds the heavens with His right hand, and the earth entire will be His grip on the Day of Resurrection. How can we conceive of a hand without resemblance? We say: this is an easy matter. Do you not now see that "the camel has a hand" and you see that "the cat has a hand"? That is, do you witness the content of this sentence?

The answer: Yes, we witness it. Does affirming a hand for the camel or the cat necessitate that the two hands be alike? No, it does not necessitate that; rather, we witness that they differ.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Qur'an contains no discrepancy or contradiction, by His saying: ﴿And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾.

If someone says: we find in the Book of Allah what appears to be contradictory; how does that agree with this verse? We say: if you see in the Book of Allah something that appears contradictory, this is either due to deficiency in your understanding, or deficiency in your knowledge, or bad intention in you. How many possibilities are there?

* The students: Three.

* The Shaykh: Three. We say: there is no contradiction. But if you think there is contradiction, it is either because your understanding is deficient, meaning your comprehension is poor and inadequate; or because your knowledge is deficient, meaning there is knowledge that shows how to reconcile them but it has not reached you; or because of bad intention in you, since when a person's intention is bad he is not granted success. How would his intention be bad? He wants to show that the Qur'an is contradictory; he does not want to reach a sound conclusion, which is reconciling the apparent differences. For this reason, you find that the one afflicted with this sees clear verses as confusing, because he searches and investigates, hoping that some verse may conflict with another, and you find him, and Allah forbid, confusing clear verses. Is it clear, everyone?

We may add a fourth possibility: neglect in seeking, whose result is lack of knowledge. If we add it as a fourth cause, it is good, and on this basis the causes of failing to understand the Qur'an are four.

There are verses that appear contradictory but in reality do not contradict, and there are many such verses, which many scholars have mentioned and written about, including Shaykh al-Shinqiti, may Allah have mercy on him, in his book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab fi Ayat al-Kitab," a moderate book but a useful one.
