Student: It would be (...).

Shaykh: What?

Student: (...) the described entity (al-mawsuf).

Shaykh: No, that is not valid. The attribute (sifa) is other than the described entity, but it subsists in it. So, for example, "length" (al-tul) is not the "long thing" (al-tawil), but it subsists in the long thing; and "knowledge" (al-'ilm) is not the "knowing one" (al-'alim), but it subsists in him.

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿So what is wrong with you that you are divided into two groups concerning the hypocrites? Allah has overturned them for what they have earned. Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray? And whomever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way.﴾ (88) ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so that you would be equal. So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the cause of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them an ally or a helper,﴾ (89) ﴿except for those who reach a people between whom and you there is a treaty, or who come to you with their breasts constricted from fighting you or fighting their own people. And if Allah had willed, He would have given them power over you, and they would have fought you. So if they remove themselves from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you a way against them.﴾ (90) [An-Nisa' 88-90].

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿So what is wrong with you that you are divided into two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾ The address in His words ﴿So what is wrong with you﴾ is to the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. The word (ma) is an interrogative noun serving as the subject (mubtada'), and the interrogation here is meant as a rebuke directed at them. (Lakum) is a prepositional phrase serving as the predicate of the subject. The meaning is: what is the matter with you regarding the hypocrites, that you differ and become two groups? This is because the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, after those who withdrew from the hypocrites at Uhud returned, and you know that about a third of the army withdrew from the army at Uhud, all of them hypocrites, the Companions later differed. Some of them said: we should kill them, because they betrayed and their apostasy became clear. Others said: we should not kill them, because they display Islam. So they differed and disputed, and the Muslims became two groups. On this basis, His words ﴿two groups﴾ are the predicate of an omitted (sara), and the estimate is: so what is wrong with you regarding the hypocrites, that you have become two groups, or you were two groups. Both are correct. What did the first group say? "We should kill them." The second group said: "We should not kill them." Another group said: "These are Muslims." Another group said: "These are disbelieving hypocrites."

Then Allah clarified the ruling between the two groups, saying: ﴿Allah has overturned them for what they have earned.﴾ ﴿Allah has overturned them﴾: (al-irkas) means returning and sending back, but in a blameworthy manner. So the meaning of ﴿arkasahum﴾ is that He returned them and sent them back in a blameworthy manner. ﴿For what they have earned﴾: the (ba') is causal, and (ma) may be parsed either as a verbal-infinitive (masdariyyah), so the estimate is: He overturned them for their earning, or as a relative pronoun, so the estimate is: for what they earned. If Allah overturned them for what they earned, then the correct view is with those who say they are disbelievers and apostates. As for the matter of fighting them, the detailed explanation will come in the verses.

﴿Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray?﴾ This interrogation is a rebuke, and "wishing" here means either love or will; both are correct. That is: do you will to guide those whom Allah has sent astray? Or do you love to guide those whom Allah has sent astray?

The answer: this is not for you, because whoever Allah wills to send astray, for him there is no protector or helper from Allah.

﴿Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray?﴾ The noble name (Allah) is in the nominative as the agent (fa'il), and on this basis the word ﴿adalla﴾ contains an omitted pronoun which is the return pronoun of the relative clause, and the estimate is: whom Allah has sent astray.

﴿And whomever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way.﴾ (man) here is conditional, and the evidence that it is conditional is that the verb after it is in the jussive mood, but it was given a kasra vowel because of the meeting of two sukuns: ﴿man yudlil Allah﴾. Ibn Malik said in al-Kafiyah:

"If two sakins meet, put a kasra on what precedes; and if it is a soft letter, its deletion is deserved."

Meaning: if it is a letter of prolongation, delete it; if it is quiescent, give it a kasra.

As for His words ﴿fa-lan tajida lahu sabilan﴾: (lan) here is the apodosis (jawab al-shart), and why is it joined with the fa'? Because the apodosis cannot validly be a verb of the condition, and whenever the apodosis cannot be a verb of the condition, it must be joined with the fa'. The places where the apodosis is joined with the fa' have been collected in a verse, which someone recited to us. Who recites it?

* Student: (...)

* Shaykh:

"A nominal sentence, an imperative, a jamid (non-derived noun), (ma), (qad), (la), (lan), and the negation (tanfis)."

Of these seven, which is (lan)? ﴿fa-lan tajida lahu sabilan﴾.

Someone may ask: how is ﴿fa-lan tajida lahu sabilan﴾ singular while the address before it is plural: ﴿Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray, and whomever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way﴾?

We say: it seems, and Allah knows best, that this sentence was separated from what precedes it, and its intended addressee became the one addressed; that is: then you, O addressee, will never find for him a way. The meaning of ﴿sabilan﴾ is a path to guidance.

* In this verse: a rebuke of the believers for their disagreement about the hypocrites, by His words ﴿So what is wrong with you that you are divided into two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾

* A consequence of this benefit: this indicates the blameworthiness of disagreement, and the blameworthiness of disagreement is an established matter, because this nation was enjoined to establish the religion and not to split over it, and disagreement is division. Indeed Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not be like those who became divided and differed after clear proofs had come to them; those will have a great punishment.﴾ [Al 'Imran 105].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a person is overturned and returned in a blameworthy manner because of his deeds. From where is this taken? From His words: ﴿Allah has overturned them for what they have earned.﴾

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of causes. From where is this taken? From His words ﴿for what they have earned﴾, where the (ba') is causal. People regarding causes are of two extremes and a middle. Among people are those who entirely denied the influence of causes and said: there is no effect of a cause on what it causes, to the extent that they contradicted reason and the senses, and said: if you throw a glass with a stone and it breaks, the stone did not break it; rather the glass broke at it, not by it. Why? They said: because if we affirm the influence of causes, we would be affirming a creator alongside Allah. Glory be to Allah! If this view is attributed to Islam, it will be a cause of disparagement of Islam, because non-Muslims observe that causes have effects.

* The second extreme: those who say causes have influence by their own nature, not because Allah, glorified and exalted, placed in them the effective power. These have gone astray and associated partners with Allah; they too are in error.

* The third group said: causes have influence by what Allah deposited in them of effective powers, and they do not act by themselves. These are the people of truth and correctness. Allah, the Exalted, is the One who made burning in fire, so it burns, and made breaking in a stone fall on the glass, so it breaks. The evidence for this is that Allah said about Abraham's fire: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 69]. And what is the nature of fire? Heat, and burning, which is destruction. But He said to it: ﴿Be coolness and safety upon Abraham,﴾ and it became coolness and safety for him. Therefore causes do not act by their own essence, but by what Allah deposited in them of effective powers.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: deeds may be a cause of a person's apostasy and the multiplication of his sins. Evil draws evil; minor sins are a path to major sins, and major sins are a path to disbelief. This is clear: ﴿He overturned them for what they earned.﴾ So if you see in yourself an overturning, may Allah protect us, then pull yourself out by repentance, seeking forgiveness from Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and asking Allah for steadfastness. Do not be negligent. Do not say: "God willing, my faith will strengthen later." From now, from the moment you feel the sickness, you must take the medicine.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a refutation of the Jabriyyah. From where is this taken? From His words ﴿for what they have earned﴾; He affirmed for them an earning, whereas the Jabriyyah say that a person has no earning and his deeds are compelled upon him.

* Among its benefits: a refutation of the Qadariyyah as well. From where is this taken? From His words ﴿Allah has overturned them﴾. The Qadariyyah say that the actions of servants have no connection whatsoever to the decree of Allah the Exalted. So the verse refutes both deviant, innovating groups. The people of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah say: a person has an action that is truly attributed to him, and the one who decreed this action is Allah the Mighty and Majestic. This is what agrees with transmitted texts, reason, and the senses.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a rebuke of those believers who wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray, by His words ﴿Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray?﴾

If someone says: a great difficulty arises here, namely the call to Allah the Mighty and Majestic and the attempt to reform creation, for the caller wants what? That Muslims be guided, that those being called be guided?

It is said in reply: Allah rebuked those who observe that Allah has sent these people astray through hypocrisy, may Allah protect us, and yet try to rule on their Islam, saying that they are Muslims, as the second group did.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: guidance and misguidance are in whose hand? In the hand of Allah.

* A branch of this benefit: you should ask for guidance from misguidance only from Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and when you ask some people "how do I become guided?", make your question about the cause and the way; but the One who holds the reins of affairs is Allah the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason Allah said to His Prophet: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [Al-Qasas 56].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever Allah has decreed to send astray, no one can guide him; because of His words ﴿And whomever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way.﴾

If it is said: this implies that the disobedient person has a proof for his disobedience, saying: "whomever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way." What is the answer?

The answer is that there is no proof in this for the disobedient person whatsoever. This is because a person does not know that Allah has sent him astray except after he has gone astray himself, and his going astray proceeds from his will, the will and power of the person. He is the doer, and he is the one who misguided himself. But he does not know that Allah decreed misguidance upon him except after what? After its occurrence. So how can one argue with a proof he only learns of after the thing has happened? This is false.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration that affairs are in the hand of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray?﴾ And if you believe this, you will ask for guidance only from whom? Only from Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They wish you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike.﴾ ﴿They wish﴾: the subject is the hypocrites, because the context concerns them. His words ﴿that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved﴾: here (*law*) is a verbal particle (*masdariyyah*), meaning that it introduces a verbal noun. The sense is: they wish for your disbelief. It is thus equivalent to (*an*), meaning "that," so the sense is: they wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved. We have seen many times that (*law*) comes with several meanings. Will you explain them to us?

* Student: It comes for wishing (*tamanni*), and it comes for the impossibility of one thing due to the impossibility of another.

* Shaykh: It comes as a verbal particle, as it does here, and it comes for wishing.

* Student: And it comes as a conditional.

* Shaykh: And it comes as a conditional. It is a particle indicating the impossibility of one thing because of the impossibility of another. If you want to know the meanings of particles, then refer to the book *al-Mughni* by Ibn Hisham, may Allah have mercy on him.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They wish you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike﴾ [An-Nisa 89]. ﴿They wish﴾: the subject is the hypocrites, because the context concerns them. His words ﴿that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved﴾: here (*law*) is a verbal particle, meaning: they wish for your disbelief. It is equivalent to (*an*), meaning: they wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved. We have seen many times that (*law*) comes with several meanings?

* Student: It comes for wishing, and it comes (...).

* Shaykh: It comes as a verbal particle, as it does here, and it comes for wishing.

* Student: And it comes as a conditional.

* Shaykh: And it comes as a conditional. It is a particle indicating the impossibility of one thing because of the impossibility of another. If you want to know the meanings of particles, then refer to the book *al-Mughni* by Ibn Hisham, may Allah have mercy on him, for it presents a word and explains its meanings. We have abridged its important parts in a booklet that is not very long.

He, the Majestic and Mighty, says: ﴿They wish you would disbelieve as they disbelieved﴾, meaning: like their disbelief. On this basis, (*ma*) here is a verbal particle, and it cannot be a relative pronoun, because the intended meaning is: they wish you would disbelieve like their disbelief. What is the nature of the hypocrites' disbelief? The disbelief of the hypocrites is a strange kind of disbelief: ﴿When they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; but when they are alone with their devils, they say, "We are with you"﴾ [Al-Baqarah 14]. It is a hidden disbelief, whose outward appearance contains mercy and whose inward reality, from their side, is punishment. They wish that all people would act this way with the Prophet, peace be upon him, believing outwardly and disbelieving inwardly. For this reason Allah, the Majestic and Mighty, said: ﴿until, when the messengers despaired and thought they had been denied, Our help came to them﴾ [Yusuf 110].

What is the meaning of ﴿that they had been denied﴾? It means that their people denied them in their claim of believing in them. That is, their people said, "We believe," but they had not believed. This is the meaning of His words ﴿and thought they had been denied﴾. There is also a canonical reading (*qira'ah sab'iyyah*): ﴿and thought they had been denied﴾ (with a doubled letter), meaning: they became certain that they were being rejected, and Our help came to them.

He said: ﴿so that you would be alike﴾. Here the (*fa'*) is conjunctive and not a response to (*law*), because (*law*) is not conditional here. ﴿So that you would be alike﴾ means: so that you would be with them, alike, with no superiority of yours over them. This accords with human nature: when a person follows a course, he wishes that people would follow it with him. Every person, whether one of goodness or one of evil, when he follows a course, wishes that people would follow it too. These people wished that the believers would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike.

Allah, the Exalted, said, warning against them and against allying with them: ﴿So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah﴾. ﴿Do not take from among them allies﴾: are they (the allies) those who ally with you, or those with whom you ally, or both?

* The students: Both.

* Shaykh: Yes, both. That is: do not take them as allies, because they are enemies, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [Al-Mumtahanah 1]. Likewise, do not take them as allies with whom you ally, because allegiance to the disbelievers is disbelief.

﴿Until they emigrate in the way of Allah﴾: is (*hatta*) here a limit (*ghayah*) or a cause (*'illah*)? It is a limit. That is: continue in your enmity toward them until they emigrate in the way of Allah. Know that (*hatta*) can be a limit and can be a cause. In His words ﴿They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse"﴾ [Al-Munafiqun 7], it is definitely a cause. In His words ﴿We will not cease to remain devoted to it until Moses returns to us﴾ [Ta-Ha 91], it is a limit.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿They wish you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike. So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them an ally or a helper﴾ (89). ﴿Except for those who reach a people between whom and you there is a treaty, or who come to you with hearts constricted at fighting you or fighting their own people. And had Allah willed, He would have given them power over you, and they would have fought you. So if they keep away from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you a way against them﴾ (90) [An-Nisa 89–90].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, said: ﴿What is the matter with you regarding the hypocrites, two groups?﴾ Who is the hypocrite?

* Student: The hypocrite is the one who displays the opposite of what he conceals.

* Shaykh: Wrong.

* Student: The one who displays good and conceals evil.

* Shaykh: He is the one who displays good and conceals evil. Among them is the one who conceals disbelief and displays belief.

And who is meant by the hypocrites in the verse?

* Student: The disbelievers who returned from Badr.

* Shaykh: Returned from where? From Uhud.

His words ﴿two groups﴾: what is its grammatical analysis (*i'rab*)?

* Student: Object of a verb.

* Shaykh: An object? There is no preceding verb, nor anything functioning as a verb.

* Student: The predicate of (*kana*, "was") or of (*sara*, "became").

* Shaykh: The predicate of (*kana*) or of the omitted (*sara*). That is: you became two groups.

Is there another possibility?

* Student: It is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*).

* Shaykh: A circumstantial accusative from where?

* Student: From (...) ﴿What is the matter with you﴾.

* Shaykh: From ﴿What is the matter with you﴾. Yes, this is acceptable, but the first is more evident, because the verse speaks of an actual event.

His words ﴿Allah has overturned them for what they earned﴾: what is the meaning of ﴿overturned them﴾?

* Student: Returned them and turned them back.

* Shaykh: But a return that is praiseworthy, or?

* Student: A return in a manner that is not pleasing.

* Shaykh: In the manner of overturning. The root (*raks*) means a filthy thing.

What is meant by the interrogative in His words ﴿Do you want to guide those whom Allah has sent astray?﴾?

* Student: (...)

* Shaykh: And what is the meaning of His words ﴿whom Allah has sent astray﴾?

* Student: That is, those who (...)

* Shaykh: And the meaning of ﴿you guide﴾: guidance?

* Student: Guidance of success (*tawfiq*).

* Shaykh: His words ﴿you will not find for him a way﴾ up to ﴿Do you want to guide those whom Allah has sent astray? And whoever Allah sends astray, you will not find for him a way.﴾

* Student: A path to guidance.

* Shaykh: To guidance. Well done.

Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, said: ﴿They wish you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike﴾. ﴿They wish﴾: *wudd* is pure love. The meaning is that they wish with all their hearts ﴿that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved﴾. (*Law*) here is a verbal particle with the sense of (*an*): they wish that you would disbelieve. His words ﴿as they disbelieved﴾: the (*ka*) is for comparison, and (*ma*) may be a verbal particle, meaning: like their disbelief, or it may be a relative pronoun, meaning: like the disbelief they committed. The meaning is one and the same, but it differs in terms of grammatical analysis (*i'rab*).

﴿So you would be alike﴾: that is, you would be with them alike. In disbelief or in belief? In disbelief. ﴿So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah﴾: that is, do not take as allies those with whom you ally, or who ally with you. As for your not allying with them, that is clear, because they have not fulfilled the emigration required of them. As for your not taking them as allies whom you hope will be allies to you, that is because one who is not on your religion cannot aid you or help you.

His words ﴿until they emigrate in the way of Allah﴾: scholars differ about the intended meaning of emigration here. It has been said: it means until they emigrate from the lands of disbelief to the lands of Islam. If they are in the desert, they are obligated to emigrate to Medina, and if they are in Mecca, the same applies. It has also been said: the intended emigration is going out with the Prophet, peace be upon him, to fight in jihad, because whoever goes out for jihad has emigrated, meaning he has left his land for the field of what? The battle, the field of battle.

His words ﴿in the way of Allah﴾: that is, on the path that leads to Him, which is His religion. Know that Allah, glorified and exalted, attributed the way to Himself in several verses like this one, and there are many such. Like His words ﴿So forgive those who repent and follow Your way﴾ [Ghafir 7], that is, Your path. It is called the way of Allah because Allah is the one who laid it down for His servants, and it leads to Allah. Its establisher is Allah, and it leads to Allah, the Majestic and Mighty.

He has attributed it to the believers in His words ﴿and follows other than the way of the believers﴾ [An-Nisa 115]. Its attribution to the believers is because they are the ones who travel it. Thus the way is attributed either to Allah or to the believers. Its attribution to Allah has two reasons: first, that Allah is the one who laid it down for His servants to walk upon, and second, that it leads to Allah, the Majestic and Mighty. Its attribution to the believers is because they travel it.

The same applies to the path (*sirat*). Allah attributed it to Himself in His words ﴿the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [Ash-Shura 53], and ﴿And indeed, this is My path, straight﴾ [Al-An'am 153]. He also attributed it to those upon whom He bestowed favor, in His words ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾ [Al-Fatihah 7]. Its explanation is the same as the explanation of "the way."

﴿If they turn away﴾: that is, if they turn away from emigrating in the way of Allah. ﴿Then seize them﴾: that is, if you find them, seize them as captives, as evidenced by His words ﴿and kill them﴾. So seizing means taking captive, and killing means taking life.

﴿Wherever you find them﴾: that is, in whatever place you find them, whether you find them in the open country, in their lands, or elsewhere, as long as they have not emigrated in the way of Allah and have turned away from the way of Allah.

﴿And do not take from among them an ally or a helper﴾: He repeated this once more, either as a preparation for His words ﴿or a helper﴾, or for emphasis, or for both. His words ﴿do not take from among them an ally﴾ are like His words ﴿So do not take from among them allies﴾, but here He added ﴿or a helper﴾.

The difference between an ally (*wali*) and a helper (*nasir*) is that a helper is one who defends you, who stands up for you against one who attacks you. As for the ally, he is one who takes care of you by securing what you seek and warding off what you fear.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the disbelievers wish with all love that the believers would disbelieve as they disbelieved, as His words show: ﴿They wish you would disbelieve as they disbelieved﴾.

* A consequence of this benefit: if this is their wish, they will strive for it by every means, whether the means is destroying the economy, or by weapons, or by spreading vile and base morals, because when base immoral conduct spreads among a nation, farewell to it.

In short, since we know that they wish that we would disbelieve as they disbelieved, they must strive for that by every way: by threat at times, by enticement at times, by adorning falsehood at times. As we now witness, the states of disbelief play a game with the states of the Muslims that should not be taken lightly.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: human beings by nature find consolation in one another and strengthen one another. This is evident in His words ﴿as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike﴾. There is no doubt that when someone shares with you in what has befallen you, it is encouragement for you. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you have wronged, that you are sharing in the punishment﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 39]. Meanwhile, in this world, when criminals share in the punishment, it becomes easier for them. Al-Khansa', in lamenting her brother Sakhr, said:

Were it not for the abundance of those weeping
over their brothers, I would have killed myself.
They do not weep like my brother,
but I console myself for him with consolation.

So the conclusion is that sharing in a punishment lightens it. Here, sharing in disbelief makes disbelief easier for its adherents.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the disbelievers take pride in whoever enters their religion, as shown in His words ﴿They wish you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of taking disbelievers as allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah, as His words show: ﴿So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever does not emigrate in the way of Allah is evidence that he is not truthful in his faith, because when a person is truthful in his faith, he will abandon both the precious and the cheap to preserve that faith.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication of sincerity, and from where is it taken? From His words ﴿in the way of Allah﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever turns away from emigrating in the way of Allah is not our ally, and it is obligatory for us to fight him, as His words show: ﴿But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them﴾. This is because they have no faith and no covenant, since they have turned away from the religion of Allah and have not emigrated in the way of Allah.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: emphasis on the prohibition of taking disbelievers as allies, as His words show: ﴿And do not take from among them an ally or a helper﴾.

If someone says: how can we reconcile this verse with the Prophet's, peace be upon him and his family, alliance with the tribe of Khuza'ah after the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah? The answer: what is meant by taking allies is that a person supports them and aids them against those who fight and wage war against him, whether they are Muslims or disbelievers. As for merely making an alliance with them, by which one gains strength and wards off many evils, there is no harm in this when there is need for it, because the Prophet, peace be upon him and his family, approved of that in the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah.

Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary on Surah an-Nisa', verse 90:

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Except those who reach a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾. This is an exception from what came before, in His words: ﴿So seize them and kill them﴾ and ﴿do not take from them a friend or a helper﴾. He said: ﴿Except those who reach a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾, meaning: except a people who reached a people between whom and you there is a covenant, sought their protection, and made alliances with them. These people do not have the ruling of those before them. That is why He said: ﴿or who come to you﴾, and so on.

﴿Except those who reach a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾. The mithaq (covenant, from the word withaq, meaning the tie with which a thing is bound) is a firm agreement.

﴿or who come to you﴾ is coordinated with ﴿reach﴾, meaning: or those who come to you, that is, they did not take refuge with a people between whom and you there is a covenant, but came to you instead.

﴿Their breasts constricted from fighting you or fighting their own people﴾. Ḥaṣirat (constricted) means "became narrow and could not bear fighting." The clause beginning with ﴿constricted﴾ is said to be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), with the particle qad implied, meaning: "their breasts have constricted from fighting you."

﴿or fighting their own people﴾. These people have now come to the Muslims so that they will not fight the Muslims alongside their people. But they will not fight their own people alongside whom? Alongside the Muslims. That is why He said: ﴿from fighting you﴾, meaning: alongside their people, ﴿or fighting their own people﴾, meaning: alongside you. These are a peaceful people.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says about these people: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have empowered them over you, and they would have fought you﴾, meaning: if Allah had willed, He would have empowered these who came to you over you, and they would have fought you. Pay attention! Is the particle law (لو) conditional or verbal? It is conditional. Its protasis is shā'a (willed), and its apodosis is ﴿lasallaṭahum﴾ (He would have empowered them).

His words ﴿falaqātalūkum﴾ (and they would have fought you) are coordinated with the apodosis of law, with the connecting lām repeated. That is why, if you removed it and said "lasallaṭahum ʿalaykum fa-qātalūkum" (He would have empowered them over you, and they would have fought you), the sentence would be sound. So the first lām was repeated for emphasis.

His words ﴿lasallaṭahum ʿalaykum﴾ mean: He would have given them authority over you in fighting. Did Allah will this? No, because they did not fight the Muslims.

﴿So if they withdraw from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, Allah has not made for you a way against them.﴾ He explained ﴿if they withdraw from you﴾ with His words ﴿and do not fight you and offer you peace﴾: they withdrew from you, were not with you, and did not fight you. ﴿And offer you peace﴾ means salām (peace). ﴿Allah has not made for you a way against them﴾, because they are a peaceful people who did not fight you or fight their own people. These are peaceful people.

﴿Allah has not made for you a way against them﴾. His words ﴿fa-mā jaʿala﴾ (then He has not made) are the answer to the condition in ﴿fa-in iʿtazalūkum﴾ (so if they withdraw from you). The meaning of ﴿sabīlan﴾ (a way) is a path that permits you to fight them.

Benefits of this noble verse:

* The exemption of this category of people from those whom we were commanded to fight. They are of two groups: a group who reached a people between us and whom there is a covenant, and entered among them; and a second group who came to us, and did not fight us alongside their people, nor did they fight their people alongside us. These are peaceful people.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the perfection of Islam's fulfilment of covenants, since it protected the covenant of the one who made the covenant with us and of the one who sought refuge with them. From where is this derived? From His words: ﴿Except those who reach a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾, and so on.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever makes peace with us, we make peace with them, based on His words: ﴿their breasts constricted from fighting you or fighting their own people﴾. Earlier we discussed, in the chapter on jihad, when a truce (hudnah) may be made, and whether it may exceed ten years. We explained that the correct view is that an unrestricted truce based on our weakness is valid, and when we become strong, we may repudiate it toward them.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirming the will of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, based on His words: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have empowered them over you﴾.

* Among its benefits: the actions of servants occur by the will of Allah. From His words ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have empowered them﴾, the verse is used to refute a deviant, astray sect. Who are they?

* The students: The Jabriyyah (determinists)?

* The Shaykh: No, the Qadariyyah (who deny divine decree), who say that a person's action is independent of him, with no connection to Allah. The proof of this is: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have empowered them over you﴾.

* Among the benefits of His words ﴿falaqātalūkum﴾ (and they would have fought you): a refutation of the Jabriyyah, since He attributed the fighting to the human being. They attribute actions to the human being only figuratively. Thus one says, "The man prayed," and he prayed only figuratively, whereas in reality he was compelled to pray.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: if someone who came to us under safe-conduct withdraws from us, does not fight us, and offers peace, it becomes obligatory to refrain from him, based on His words: ﴿So if they withdraw from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, Allah has not made for you a way against them.﴾

* Among the benefits of the noble verse, derived by implication: if they took a covenant from us but then betrayed it and fought, the covenant is broken. It is broken, and there is no covenant between us and them. This is derived from the implication of His words: ﴿If they withdraw from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, Allah has not made for you a way against them.﴾

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: whoever lays down his weapons, it is obligatory to refrain from him, based on His words: ﴿Allah has not made for you a way against them.﴾ However, if it is feared that laying down his weapons is treachery and deception, then his laying them down carries no weight, because the enemy may lay down weapons as treachery and betrayal, and may also flee before our armies in treachery and betrayal. So vigilance is obligatory.

If someone says: Is not what happened with Usamah ibn Zayd, when he killed a polytheist after he had said "There is no god but Allah," and the Prophet (ﷺ) rebuked and reprimanded him and said: "Did you kill him after he had said, 'There is no god but Allah'?!"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4269) and Muslim (96/159), from the hadith of Usamah ibn Zayd.]] while what appears is that he said it seeking refuge from being killed?

We say: there must be a strong indication that shows he is feared to be treacherous and deceitful. Mere suspicion is not sufficient, because the basic principle is that a covenant protects a person's blood, so this principle is upheld until something opposing it appears.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that legislation, whether prohibiting, repelling, or permitting, belongs entirely to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, based on His words: ﴿Allah has not made for you a way against them.﴾ This shows that the command is in the hand of Allah, who decides whatever He wills of what is lawful, unlawful, obligatory, and otherwise.

* * *

* Student: ﴿Every time they are returned to temptation, they are plunged back into it. So if they do not withdraw from you, offer you peace, and restrain their hands, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them. Those—We have given you clear authority over them. (91) It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake. And whoever kills a believer by mistake—then the freeing of a believing slave and a compensation payment delivered to his family, unless they forgo it. But if he was from a people hostile to you and he was a believer, then the freeing of a believing slave. And if he was from a people between you and them is a covenant, then a compensation payment delivered to his family and the freeing of a believing slave. And whoever does not find [one], then fasting for two consecutive months as a repentance from Allah. And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise. (92) And whoever kills a believer intentionally—his recompense is Hell, abiding eternally therein; and Allah will be angry with him and curse him and prepare for him a great punishment. (93)﴾ [An-Nisa' 91–93].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. We have already discussed the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Except those who reach a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾. What is the meaning of the verse?

* Student: (...) of the people now, those we fight, are divided into two types: (...) for fighting there are two types. The first type are those who have a covenant, and the second type are those who emigrated from their people to the Muslims and did not fight alongside the Muslims against their people.

* Shaykh: Do you agree with this?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: I mean ﴿Except those who reach﴾. What is the meaning of the verse: ﴿Except those who reach a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾?

* Student: To a people (...).

* Shaykh: What is the meaning of ﴿reach a people﴾?

* Student: (...) to the disbelievers (...) who have a covenant with them (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, excellent, correct. The second category, also those we do not fight?

* Student: The second people came to the Muslims. They are from the disbelievers, and they withdrew from the Muslims, so they did not fight them, nor did they fight their people.

* Shaykh: Yes, well done. This second category is derived from His words: ﴿or who come to you, their breasts constricted from fighting you or fighting their own people﴾.

* Student: What is the meaning of His words: ﴿So if they withdraw from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, Allah has not made for you a way against them﴾?

* Student: Those who did not fight us and withdrew (...) and did not fight them. Allah the Exalted has not made for the Muslims a way over them.

* Shaykh: And offered them peace.

* Student: They offered them peace too. Allah the Exalted has not made a path for fighting these disbelievers.

* Shaykh: Excellent. In this verse there is a refutation of two deviant sects: the Jabriyyah and the Qadariyyah?

* Student: A refutation of the Qadariyyah from His words, Exalted is He: (...).

* Shaykh: Well done.

* Student: And of the Jabriyyah by His words: ﴿falaqātalūkum﴾.

* Shaykh: Yes, correct.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You will find others who wish to be secure from you and secure from their own people.﴾ (The sin) here is for future (istiqbal, "an-tanfis"), and its sister (sawfa) is for postponement (at-taswif). The difference between them is that taswif is delayed, while tanfis is near. Both affirm assertion, certainty and confirmation. For example, if you say, "You will find Zayd" (anta tajidu Zaydan) and "You will surely find Zayd" (anta sa-tajidu Zaydan), which of them is more emphatic? The second is more emphatic, yet both convey emphasis and affirmation. However, sawfa indicates distance in time, and sin indicates nearness.

﴿You will find others﴾: these are a fourth category. ﴿who wish to be secure from you and secure from their own people﴾: this is not possible except through hypocrisy. ﴿Secure from you﴾: when they come to you they say, "We believe," so that they are secure from you; and when they go back to their devils they say, "We are with you," so that they are secure from them. They wish to please these and those, and this is impossible. It is not possible to please the friends of Allah and the enemies of Allah at the same time, because the friends of Allah and the enemies of Allah are all enemies to one another. It is not possible for an enemy of Allah to be a friend of a friend of Allah, or the reverse. These people are not with these nor with those, because they are not with the Muslims outwardly and inwardly, nor with the disbelievers outwardly and inwardly. Or not? They are not with the Muslims outwardly and inwardly, nor with the disbelievers outwardly, but inwardly they are with them.

﴿Every time they are returned to temptation, they are plunged back into it.﴾ That is: their final destination is temptation, and misguidance—we seek refuge with Allah—and what is meant by temptation here is leaving Islam.

﴿They are plunged back into it﴾: that is, they increase in reversal and depth in it and in distance from guidance. Likewise, every person who desires temptation increases in evil and in plunging deeper into temptation.

﴿So if they do not withdraw from you, offer you peace, and restrain their hands, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them.﴾ That is: if their enmity toward you becomes apparent, and they do not withdraw from you until they become clear and manifest. ﴿Offer you peace (as-salam)﴾: that is, submission or peace-making? Apparently both meanings are intended.

﴿Offer you peace and restrain their hands﴾ from harming you. ﴿Then seize them and kill them wherever you find them﴾: seize them means take them as captives, and kill them means put them to death. ﴿Wherever you find them﴾ means wherever you encounter them, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If they overcome you, they will be enemies to you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 2], meaning: if they find you.

﴿And We have given you, against them, a clear authority.﴾ ﴿Those (ulaʼika)﴾: the demonstrative here is the one used for the distant, despite the nearness of the mention, because of the lowliness and degradation of their rank; for the near may be pointed to with the demonstrative of the distant, either because of its distance in descent or its distance in height, according to what the context requires.

﴿And We have given you, against them, a clear authority﴾: that is, a manifest right and authority to fight them and seize them, since they did not withdraw from you, offer you peace, and restrain their hands.

All these verses concern the hypocrites and those like the hypocrites, because they begin with them and end with them. Their summary in general meaning is: people are divided into categories: Muslims, those under treaty (mu'ahadun), protected non-Muslims (dhimmis), and hypocrites, and each has a ruling from these categories, a ruling suited to it.

* The noble verse contains benefits, among them: the knowledge of Allah the Mighty and Majestic of the unseen, from His saying: ﴿You will find others who wish to be secure from you and secure from their own people.﴾

* Among them: the affirmation of will for the servant. From where is this derived?

* A student: It is derived from the saying of the Exalted: ﴿who wish to be secure from you﴾.

* The Shaykh: How? We said: does this verse affirm will for the human being?

* A student: ﴿who wish to be secure from you﴾.

* The Shaykh: Correct, ﴿who wish to be secure from you and secure from their own people﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is not possible to combine loyalty and enmity, that a person be a friend of the friends of Allah and a friend of the enemies of Allah. This is impossible, from His saying: ﴿who wish to be secure from you and secure from their own people﴾, and this was said in the context of blame, not praise.

If someone says: Is it possible to combine enmity and loyalty in one specific person? Yes, it is possible: if this person brings faith and piety on one side, and has some disbelief and wickedness on another side, he becomes a friend from one side and an enemy from another side. This is what the people of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah hold: that faith and disbelief may be combined, but not absolute faith nor absolute disbelief, because absolute faith and absolute disbelief cannot be combined; yet absolute-in-kind faith and absolute-in-kind disbelief can be combined.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: warning against falling into temptations, and that a person, whenever he falls into temptation, is plunged back into it.

* * *

* A student: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake. And whoever kills a believer by mistake, then [he must free] a believing slave and pay blood-money to his family, unless they forgo it as charity. And if he was from a people hostile to you and he is a believer, then [he must free] a believing slave. And if he was from a people between you and them is a treaty, then blood-money must be paid to his family and [he must free] a believing slave. And whoever does not find [the means], then fasting two consecutive months as repentance from Allah. And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise. (92) And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever, and Allah will be angry with him and curse him and prepare for him a great punishment. (93)﴾ [an-Nisa' 92, 93].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan.

Among the benefits of the previous noble verse, ﴿You will find others who wish to be secure from you and secure from their own people﴾, we have taken, as you said, four benefits:

* The first: the knowledge of Allah the Exalted of the unseen, from His saying: ﴿You will find others﴾.

* Among them: the refutation of the Jabriyyah (determinists), from His saying: ﴿who wish to be secure from you and secure from their own people﴾.

* Among its benefits: that these people, since they were not truthful in faith, ﴿every time they are returned to temptation, they are plunged back into it﴾, and likewise every person who is not truthful in his faith, whenever he is returned to temptation, increases in evil and reversal.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is permissible to fight such people if they do not withdraw from the Muslims, that is, do not refrain from them and offer them peace (as-salam), meaning: salam.

* Among them: the excellence of eloquence of the Qur'an, where it says here: ﴿seize them and kill them wherever you find them﴾, and there in the first verse: ﴿wherever you find them (wajadtumuhum)﴾; because variation in wording leads to vigor, and sameness generally leads to tedium.

* Among its benefits: that Allah the Exalted has given the believers against these people a clear authority, that is, a legitimate authority, and perhaps also a manifest, evident authority of destiny (qadariyyah).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 92 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake.﴾ Grammar (i'rab): ﴿مَا كَانَ﴾ (ma kana) is a negated defective verb (kana naqisa), its predicate is ﴿لِمُؤْمِنٍ﴾ (li-mu'minin), and its subject is ﴿أَنْ يَقْتُلَ﴾ (an yaqtula), taken as a verbal noun (mu'awwal bil-masdar), meaning: it is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake. As for ﴿إِلَّا﴾ (illa), it is a particle of exception. ﴿خَطَأً﴾ (khata'an) may be an adjective of a omitted noun, meaning: except a mistaken killing (qatlan khata'an), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿أَنِ اعْمَلْ سَابِغَاتٍ﴾ [Saba' 11], meaning: make coats of mail that are full-length. Omitting the modified noun while retaining the adjective is common in the Arabic language and in the Noble Qur'an.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake.﴾ The believer (mu'min) is one in whose heart faith (iman) has settled. Faith in the sharia sense is more specific than faith in the linguistic sense, since faith in the sharia sense is the affirmation by the heart that includes acceptance and submission, i.e., accepting the report, accepting the command, submitting to it, complying with it, and not being arrogant.

His saying: ﴿أَنْ يَقْتُلَ﴾ (an yaqtula). Killing (al-qatl) is: taking away the soul by any means, whether by sword, arrow, burning, drowning, or any kind of killing.

His saying: ﴿إِلَّا خَطَأً﴾ means that he cannot kill him while being a sinner (khati'an) but only as one who errs (mukhti'an). The difference between the khati' and the mukhti' is: the khati' is one who commits the error deliberately, while the mukhti' is one who commits it without intention or purpose. The error may be either in the intention or in the instrument. As for error in intention, it is like one who shoots at a game animal with a fatal shot and it hits a person he did not intend. This is an error in what? In intention. As for error in the instrument, it is like one who deliberately strikes a person with a whip that does not usually kill someone like him; this is an error in the instrument, because he did not think it would kill him, and therefore he did not intend to kill him. It is a stick with which a person is customarily disciplined, but Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, decreed that this injury would spread until the one struck dies.

Then He said: ﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake, then the freeing of a believing slave and a compensation (diyah) paid to his family, unless they forgo it as charity.﴾ ﴿مِن﴾ (man) here is conditional, its condition is ﴿قَتَلَ﴾ (qatala), and ﴿فَتَحْرِيرُ﴾ (fa-tahriru) is the response of the condition, and it is joined with the fa' because it is a nominal sentence. The word (tahrir) is the subject, and the predicate is omitted; the estimate is: upon him is the freeing of a slave. Tahrir of a thing is its release. The intended tahrir here is the release of the neck from slavery specifically, not its release from destruction; therefore one who saves a person is not called a liberator of him, rather one who frees him from slavery and releases him from it is the liberator. The intended meaning of "neck" (raqabah) here is the whole soul, but it is expressed by the neck because the body cannot function without a neck; therefore when the neck is severed, one perishes.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿believing﴾ (mu'minah). The intended faith here includes Islam, and it is not intended as complete faith in the absolute sense, rather it is absolute faith; therefore if one frees a wicked (fasiq) slave, it suffices for him.

﴿And compensation (diyah)﴾ is conjoined to (tahrir), meaning: and upon him is a compensation paid to its family. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, did not specify who pays it, rather He said: ﴿paid (musallamah)﴾ in the passive form.

His saying: ﴿unless they forgo it as charity﴾ is an exception from His saying: ﴿compensation﴾, meaning: upon him is a compensation paid to his family, unless they forgo it, i.e., they give charity to the one upon whom the compensation is due by waiving it and pardoning him, so it falls. The intended meaning of "giving as charity" here is pardon and remission, because it is not a matter of giving but of waiving.

His saying: ﴿unless they forgo it as charity﴾: its original form is: unless they tasaddaqu (give charity), but the taa' was assimilated into the saad, so it became: unless they yassaddaqu.

﴿And if he was from a people hostile to you and he is a believer, then the freeing of a believing slave﴾: ﴿فَإِنْ كَانَ﴾ (fa-in kana) — the pronoun refers to the slain person, and it is the subject of (kana).

His saying: ﴿وَهُوَ مُؤْمِنٌ﴾ (wa huwa mu'min) is a clause in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (hal) from the hidden pronoun in ﴿كَانَ﴾, meaning: while he is a believer. ﴿فَتَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ مُؤْمِنَةٍ﴾ (fa-tahriru raqabatin mu'minah) means: upon the killer is the freeing of a believing slave; accordingly, (tahrir) is the subject and the predicate is — what? — omitted, and the estimate is: upon him.

﴿And if he was from a people between you and them there is a covenant, then a compensation paid to his family and the freeing of a believing slave﴾: He says: ﴿إِنْ كَانَ﴾ — the pronoun refers to whom? To the slain person. ﴿مِنْ قَوْمٍ بَيْنَكُمْ وَبَيْنَهُمْ مِيثَاقٌ﴾ means: a covenant (ahd). The covenant was called a mithaq because it is like the rope by which a captive is bound, since a covenant is a bond between the contracting parties such that neither dares against the other and neither transgresses against the other.

His saying: ﴿from a people between you and them is a covenant﴾ means: are they disbelievers or Muslims? They are disbelievers, because the believers were mentioned in the first case.

﴿then a compensation paid to his family﴾, i.e., upon him, i.e., upon the killer, ﴿a compensation paid to his family﴾, i.e., the family of the slain. Who is meant by "family" in both places? The intended "family" is the heirs, because the heirs are those who inherit what the deceased left, and the compensation is among what the deceased leaves behind.

﴿and the freeing of a believing slave﴾: we say about it what we said about the first.

His saying: ﴿Then whoever does not find (a slave), then fasting two consecutive months﴾: whoever does not find what? The compensation? No, whoever does not find the neck. Either the slaves are unavailable, or their price is unavailable; therefore in the noble verse it came as ﴿فَمَنْ لَمْ يَجِدْ﴾ without mentioning the object, so that this is more comprehensive and general, i.e., whoever does not find a slave or does not find its price.

﴿then fasting two consecutive months﴾, i.e., upon him is fasting. Accordingly, (siyam) is the subject and the predicate is omitted; the estimate is: upon him is fasting two consecutive months, meaning one follows the other such that he does not break the fast between them.

His saying: ﴿as a repentance from Allah﴾: this is a verbal noun for an omitted verb, i.e., he repents thereby a repentance to Allah. Repentance to Allah is returning to Him from disobedience to obedience, and it will come that it has conditions.

His saying: ﴿from Allah﴾ means: what Allah legislated of these rulings is a repentance from Him toward His servant; otherwise, had He willed, it would have been burdensome for us, and the obligation for accidental killing would have been greater than that.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing, Wise﴾: (kana) here is a past-tense sister verb (fi'l madi nasikh), the name of Allah is its subject, ﴿عَلِيمًا﴾ (alimán) is its predicate, and ﴿حَكِيمًا﴾ (hakiman) is a second predicate. It is not valid for it to be an adjective, because a pronoun is not described, a pronoun is not described nor is it used as a description; therefore it is necessary to parse it as a second predicate. Knowledge (al-'ilm) is perceiving a thing as it is with certainty. This is knowledge: if I perceive, for example, that this is a paper, it is called knowledge because I perceive it as it is with certainty. If I say: it seems likely to me that it is paper, this is not knowledge because it is not certain; and if I say: I do not know what it is, this is also not knowledge because I have not perceived it.

As for (hakim), the hakim is derived from hukm (judgment) and ihkam (perfecting). He is hakim in the sense of hakim (judge) and in the sense of muhkim (one who perfects). The judge among His servants and the judge over His servants is Allah. Note how I said: judge over His servants and among His servants. The judge among His servants means He settles disputes among them; the judge over them means the one who has authority over the servants and judges them as He wills.

It is also derived from hikmah (wisdom), and the scholars said: hikmah is placing a thing in its fitting place. Thus His name al-Hakim includes both judgment and perfection.

Judgment has two kinds, and wisdom has two kinds as well, and if you multiply two by two the result is four; this will come, God willing, in the explanation of the benefits.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: first, the prohibition of a believer killing a believer intentionally. It is derived from His saying: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾. When (ma kana), (lam yakun), (la yanbaghi), or (ma yanbaghi) appear, they indicate prohibition; but is this prohibition legislative or decreed? 
* A student: Legislative.
* Another student: Decreed.
* The Shaykh: The apparent view is that it is legislative, indeed it is necessarily so; because decreed-wise he could kill him — intentionally, not by mistake. Therefore, legislatively it is impossible; hence whoever kills a believer by mistake is considered deficient in faith to a great degree, so much so that we may negate faith from him, saying: this is not a believer, i.e., not a believer of complete faith; because if theft is forbidden... "A person does not seize plunder of honour which people raise their eyes to when they raise them, while he is a believer" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5578) and Muslim (57/100) from Abu Hurayrah, with the wording: "when he seizes it"], so what of one who kills?

* From the benefits of the noble verse: a believer may intentionally kill a non-believer; from His saying: ﴿an yaqtula mu'minan﴾. But is this permissible? The answer: no; there is detail: if he is a combatant (muharib), killing him is permissible, and then it may be obligatory or not depending on what the situation requires; but if he is a covenanted person (mu'ahad), a protected person (musta'man), or a dhimmi, killing him is haram; we say: it was not for him to kill him.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the wisdom of the sharia in distinguishing between mistake and intention, because mistake does not occur by intention, while intention occurs by intention; the one who errs is deserving of leniency, and the intentional killer is not deserving of it, and there is no doubt this is from the wisdom of the sharia; had this wisdom not existed, the intentional and the mistaken would be equal.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the division of killing into mistaken and non-mistaken; because the exception in His saying: ﴿except by mistake﴾ indicates there is intentional killing, and that is so; the mention of intention will come in the following verse.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: that mistaken killing in both its forms — according to what we explained earlier — requires two things: first, manumission; second, diyah. This is derived from His saying: ﴿then the freeing of a believing slave and a compensation paid to his family﴾. If it is asked: what is required of one who kills a non-believer? We say: Allah has explained it later in the same verse.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the virtue of manumission and its high rank, because it becomes an expiation for this sin, killing a believer, and this indicates its virtue and high standing, and that it is great; and so it is.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the sharia's concern for freeing necks from slavery.

* A consequence of this benefit: the refutation of one who objects to Muslims enslaving people; it is said: enslavement came as a result of a necessary matter, and nevertheless there are many encouragements to liberation.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the requirement of faith in the manumitted slave in killing; from His exalted saying: ﴿then the freeing of a believing slave﴾.
Does this extend to every slave freed as expiation for a sin? On this the scholars have two opinions. Some say faith is required in every slave freed as expiation; in His saying concerning the expiation of oaths: ﴿feeding ten needy persons, from the middle of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave﴾ [al-Ma'idah 89], the slave here is unqualified; is faith required in it? Some scholars hold that it is required, and others hold that it is not, and this is based on specifying the text by another text.

We have explained that if the cause and the ruling agree, it is specified; if the ruling differs, it is not specified when the cause agrees; and if the ruling agrees while the cause differs, most scholars hold that it is specified. The cause of freeing a slave here is killing, and in the expiation of oaths it is swearing; the cause differs but the ruling is one, which is freeing a slave; and most scholars hold that the unqualified in the expiation of oaths is qualified by the qualified in the expiation of killing.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of freeing a male or female slave in the expiation of killing. From where is this derived? From the unqualified: ﴿freeing a slave﴾; it did not say male or female, so it remains unqualified.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: that if one frees a non-believing slave, such as one who frees a slave who does not pray, it does not suffice for the expiation of killing.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation of diyah for accidental killing.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the magnification of killing; therefore Allah made expiation obligatory for it, although the legal principle is that the mistaken person bears no expiation and that the pen is lifted from him: "My Ummah is pardoned for error, forgetfulness, and what they are compelled to do" [Ibn Majah (2043), from Abu Dhar al-Ghifari]; but out of magnification of the matter of killing, whoever commits killing, even by mistake, is required to make expiation.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: that whoever frees a non-believing slave, it does not suffice for him. Must this slave also be free of bodily defects, as freedom from legal defect is required? On this there is disagreement. Some scholars hold that the slave must be free of defects harmful to work, because freeing one with harmful defects that impair work leads to his becoming a burden on society. For example, if this man had had his hands cut off while a slave, then on the view requiring soundness he does not suffice, and on the view not requiring it he suffices; and most scholars, as I think, hold that soundness from defects harmful to work is required, because freeing such a slave makes him a burden on others.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation of diyah in killing by mistake; from His saying: ﴿and a compensation paid to his family﴾.

* From its benefits: that whoever is obligated to pay the diyah must send it to the family of the dead person; from His saying: ﴿paid to his family﴾. Is it deferred, or is it immediate? On this the scholars differ. Some say it is not deferred unless the judge sees benefit in deferring it, because the principle regarding the obligation of a debt is that its payment is immediate; if the judge sees deferral, he defers it, and it is deferred for three years.

Is the diyah obligatory on the killer originally and on the 'aqilah (paternal kin) secondarily, or is it obligatory on the 'aqilah originally? On this too there is disagreement.

Some scholars say: it is obligatory on the killer originally and on others secondarily, because the killer is the direct perpetrator of the killing, and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am 164]; and imposing it on the 'aqilah is only for assisting and aiding him. So if we assume this man who killed by mistake has millions of dirhams while the 'aqilah are of ordinary means, it may not be wise to burden the 'aqilah and constrain their livelihood while leaving this killer, in whose case the offense occurred, with his wealth and abundance.

Others say: it is obligatory on the 'aqilah originally, and accordingly nothing is required of the killer, even if he is among the richest of people and the 'aqilah are poor; he is not required to pay any part of the diyah, because it is obligatory on whom? On the 'aqilah.

What appears to me is to take the middle view: if the 'aqilah have capacity, we require them, meaning that if the 'aqilah are of wide means, we require them, because of the cooperation in that and the sense of kinship that some are support to others; but if the 'aqilah cannot bear the diyah except with hardship and difficulty and the loss of some needs, while the killer is wealthy, then we require him, because he is the original party.

If someone asks: what is the diyah? We say: the Sunnah has explained it: one hundred camels for a free male, and fifty camels for a free female. This is the correct view: that camels are the original basis of the diyah; as for cows, sheep, gold, silver, and garments, they are valuations; otherwise the original is camels. This is the correct view.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: that the diyah is delivered to the family of the deceased; from His saying: ﴿to his family﴾. Who is his family? His family are the heirs. (...)

* A student: ﴿And Allah became angry with him and cursed him and prepared for him a great punishment﴾.

* The Shaykh: In the previous verse Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿unless they forgo it as charity﴾; this is an exception from His saying: ﴿and a compensation paid to his family﴾.

Among the benefits of this verse: forgiveness of the blood-money (diyah) is a form of charity (sadaqah). It is drawn from the noble verse that forgiveness is a form of charity, since charity is either giving or releasing. Giving is obvious; releasing means that a person absolves a debtor of his debt and drops it from him. However, this does not suffice for the obligatory zakat on property (zakat al-'ayn). That is, if a person owes zakat and he has a debt owed to him by a poor man, and he releases the poor man from the debt and counts it toward his zakat, this does not suffice. In other words, a debt does not suffice in place of zakat on property.

Another benefit of this noble verse: permissibility of pardoning the perpetrator. However, this is restricted to cases where the pardon brings about reconciliation (islah), based on the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿But whoever forgives and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾ [ash-Shura 40]. If there is no reconciliation in it, then leaving pardon is better, and indeed it may be obligatory to take the right and leave pardon, because reconciliation is more important than private interest. Forgiving the blood-money is a private interest, but reconciliation is a public interest. So if this one who killed by mistake is a reckless man, and if we pardoned him he would go on doing it a second time, a third time and a fourth time, then pardoning him is not reconciliation, and so it should not be pardoned.

Another benefit of the noble verse: the killing of a mu'ahad (one under covenant) is forbidden. The indication is that Allah made obligatory, for the killing of one between us and whom there is a covenant, the blood-money and the expiation.

Another benefit of the noble verse: the blood-money of a covenanted disbeliever is not like the blood-money of a Muslim, because He said: ﴿And if he was from a people between you and them is a covenant, then blood-money﴾, and this is indefinite (nakirah), and repeating the word in indefinite form indicates that the second is other than the first, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, with hardship is ease (5). Indeed, with hardship is ease﴾ [ash-Sharh 5-6]. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "One hardship will not overcome two eases."[[Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari (8/712): Al-Farra' narrated it with a weak chain from Ibn 'Abbas as his own statement; 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated it in his Tafsir (2/309), and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak (2/528), from the hadith of al-Hasan al-Basri, from the Prophet ﷺ, as a mursal report.]] And if the blood-money of a covenanted person were like that of a believer, He would have said: "then the blood-money delivered to his family", meaning the blood-money already mentioned; but this is another blood-money. 

If someone asks: then what is it? We say: the scholars differed about it. Some said its blood-money is a third of the blood-money of a Muslim, and some said it is half the blood-money of a Muslim, and this is the correct view. For example, if the blood-money of a Muslim is one hundred camels, the blood-money of one between us and whom there is a covenant from among the People of the Book is fifty camels, at half.

Another benefit of the noble verse: the Islamic religion's respect for covenants and agreements; therefore the right of the covenanted person between us and whom there is a covenant was not nullified, but rather the blood-money was made obligatory for his family.

Another benefit of the noble verse also: the obligation of expiation for killing one between us and whom there is a covenant, even if they are not Muslims; based on the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿then blood-money delivered to his family and the freeing of a believing slave﴾.

Another of its benefits: the obligation of delivering the blood-money to its rightful recipient. So if he says: "Your blood-money is with me in the house; come and take it," he is not bound by this, because the one obligated must deliver it to the one it belongs to.

Another benefit of the noble verse: an indication that in manslaughter by mistake the blood-money is not obligatory on the killer, because He did not say "he shall deliver it," but said ﴿delivered﴾. Upon whom then is it obligatory? It is obligatory upon the 'aqilah, who are the wealthy male agnatic relatives ('asabah), and the imam or judge strives to impose on each of them what suits his condition. The nearer is charged more than the more distant, the wealthy is charged more than the average, and the poor has nothing upon him because he is poor.

Another benefit of the noble verse: whoever does not find a slave or the price of one, then upon him is fasting for two consecutive months; based on the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿but whoever does not find [it], then fasting for two months consecutively﴾.

Another of its benefits: whoever is unable to fast, there is nothing upon him: neither freeing a slave, because he cannot find one, nor fasting, because he is unable to; is that so? Nor feeding, because it is not mentioned in the verse. For this reason, when Allah the Mighty and Majestic wanted feeding to be a substitute for fasting, He mentioned it, as in the verses about zihar.

If someone says: Should this not be analogized to zihar? We say: It is not valid, because the cause differs. The cause of expiation in zihar is zihar, and the cause of expiation in killing is killing, and there is a difference between them. Zihar, Allah the Exalted called it "a dishonourable word and a falsehood," whereas manslaughter by mistake, Allah the Exalted did not describe its doer with anything that implies the ugliness of his act.

Another benefit of this noble verse: that the killer by mistake, in addition to the expiation, must repent, based on the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿a repentance from Allah﴾. At this point a difficulty arises: how is repentance obligatory upon him along with expiation, given that his act was a mistake? We say: because a mistake may be the result of negligence in not exercising care. For example, it is a mistake for one to shoot at game and hit a human being; we say: had this man been patient until the matter was verified, he would have been spared this mistake. Therefore, since souls are great and transgression against them is great, and a person may fall short at times, Allah made expiation obligatory and made repentance obligatory.

If someone asks: Is expiation obligatory in deliberate killing? We say: No, it is not obligatory in deliberate killing, because deliberate killing is too grave to be expiated by freeing a slave or by fasting, and whoever analogizes it to manslaughter has erred, because of the difference between the offence and the requirements of the offence. For the requirement of deliberate killing is that the killer be killed; and manslaughter—?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Or is he killed? No, he is not killed.
Likewise, in deliberate killing the blood-money is upon the killer's property and is aggravated, while in manslaughter it is upon his 'aqilah and is also lightened. So this cannot be analogized to that, given the difference in cause and requirement.

Another benefit of this noble verse: the affirmation of two of Allah's names, the first: al-'Alim (the All-Knowing), and the second: al-Hakim (the All-Wise). As you know, Allah the Exalted often pairs al-'Alim with al-Hakim, to show that what He judges, whether legislated rulings or cosmic decrees, proceeds from knowledge and wisdom, not from ignorance and folly. The root of error in a ruling is either ignorance or folly: if it is without knowledge it is from ignorance, and if it is without wisdom it is from folly. For this reason Allah often concludes verses that contain rulings with these two names: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾.

If someone asks: If the heirs of the blood-money pardon it, does the expiation fall away? The answer: No, because expiation is a right of Allah and the blood-money is a right of the human being.

Likewise, if a person is unable to perform the kinds of expiation, meaning he is unable to free a slave and unable to fast two consecutive months, does the blood-money fall away? The answer: No, because the blood-money is a right of the human being, so it does not fall away when the right of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, falls away.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 93 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally - his recompense is Hell, abiding eternally therein; and Allah is angry with him and has cursed him and has prepared for him a great punishment﴾. This is among the most severe of the verses containing warning. ﴿Whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell﴾. The word "believer" here is meant as "Muslim," meaning it is meant in a sense broader than the believer, so "believer" includes one whose faith is deficient and one whose faith is complete.

And His saying: ﴿intentionally﴾ means: intending to kill, that is, aiming at it. This is not realized except by deliberately doing an act that usually kills, meaning that he intends the killing by means that usually kill, such as the sword, bullets, a large stone, poison, sorcery, and what is similar to these. Accordingly: if he did not intend the act, it is not deliberate; and if he intended the act by means that do not usually kill, it is not deliberate either. But the first is called error (khata'), and the second is called quasi-deliberate (shibh 'amd). It is called quasi-deliberate because he deliberately did the act but with an instrument that does not usually kill, so the scholars named it quasi-deliberate. It has already passed for us that error may be in the intention and may be in the instrument.

He says: ﴿his recompense is Hell﴾. This clause is the response of the conditional in His saying: ﴿And whoever kills﴾. ﴿Recompense﴾ means: his punishment by which he is requited. ﴿Hell﴾ is one of the names of the Fire; it was so named for its depth and its darkness. May Allah protect us and you from it.

﴿Abiding eternally therein﴾. ﴿Abiding eternally﴾: the khuluud (abiding) means remaining, but it is among the blessings of Allah that He did not describe it as "forever," rather He said: ﴿abiding eternally therein﴾.

﴿And Allah is angry with him﴾. Anger is more intense than punishment, because when Allah is angry, He does not speak to the one with whom He is angry, and He does not show mercy to him as He shows mercy to others, and He takes vengeance upon him according to what his sin requires. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them﴾ [az-Zukhruf 55], meaning: when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them.

﴿And has cursed him﴾: that is, He expelled him and removed him from His mercy.

﴿And has prepared for him a great punishment﴾. (A'adda) means: He prepared it; He prepared for him a great punishment.

* In this noble verse there is evidence that intentionally killing a believer is one of the major sins, because the warning is attached to it, and every sin for which a warning and punishment are prescribed is among the major sins.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: intention is necessary, by His saying: ﴿intentionally﴾. But is it a condition of intention that he knows he is a believer, or if he intentionally kills this man while doubting whether he is a believer or a mu'ahad (one under covenant), is it deliberate? This is a matter of disagreement among the scholars. Some said: if he intentionally does what is not permitted and hits a believer, it is deliberate, such as one who shoots a mu'ahad, and a mu'ahad may not be shot, but he hits a believer. Indeed they said: if he shoots a camel whose shooting is forbidden to him and then hits a person, it is considered deliberate.

But the correct position in this matter is that if he intentionally kills a person and hits one who is like him, it is deliberate, meaning: he intended to kill Zayd and hit 'Amr, this is deliberate. But if he intended to kill a camel and hit a man, it is not deliberate; this is because of the clear difference between the human and the beast, and it cannot be said that intending to kill an animal is like intending to kill a believer. So the correct position in this matter is to say: deliberateness includes the case where he intended this believer specifically, or intended one who fits the description of believers, in which case it is considered deliberate.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: whoever kills a believer without intent, there is no punishment upon him, that is, he is not punished with this punishment, because the qualification ("intentionally") is considered a condition for the consequence attached to it.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the one who intentionally kills a believer abides eternally in the Fire, by His saying: ﴿abiding eternally therein﴾.

The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, differed concerning the meaning of this word. Some said: khuluud is a long stay, and it is not required that it be permanent; for this reason the verse was not qualified by "forever." According to this view, there is no difficulty in the verse at all.

Some scholars say: khuluud is a lasting stay, and according to this view there arises a difficulty with this verse: the one who intentionally kills a soul does not leave the faith, by the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, prescribed for you is retribution for the murdered﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And whoever is pardoned by his brother [i.e., the victim's heir] for anything﴾ [al-Baqarah 178].
