As for His saying: ﴿and He is with them when they plot by night what He does not approve of in speech﴾. His saying ﴿and He is with them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah hal). It is a circumstantial clause of what? Of the waw in ﴿they hide﴾, or of ﴿from Allah﴾? It is closer to the word Allah (lafz al-jalalah). That is, "and they do not hide from Allah while He is with them."

As for His saying ﴿and He is with them﴾: al-mi'iyyah (being with) means companionship (al-musahabah). But the companionship of each thing is according to its nature. The basic meaning of this word is companionship, but it varies, and its implications vary according to what it is attached to. It is said, for example: "The woman is with her husband," "The commander is with his soldiers," "The goods are with the one carrying them," and "The moon is with us." There are many things in which the sense of being with varies from one context to another, but all these meanings are gathered under companionship, pure companionship, and its implications vary according to what it is attached to. So Allah, the Exalted, is with those who plotted what He does not approve of in speech, and He is "with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good" [An-Nahl 128]. The two kinds of being with differ according to their implications and requirements. Allah, the Exalted, was with Muhammad (ﷺ) in the cave, and with Musa and Harun in the mission. This being with differs from His being with the believers and the God-fearing, and the like, according to what it is attached to.

So what does this being with necessitate in this verse? It necessitates a warning (tahdid). It necessitates a warning in addition to encompassment (al-ihatah), because the specific meanings, in addition to the general meaning which is complete encompassment of creation. Then, is this being with a literal reality, or is what is meant its implication?

The correct view is that what is meant is literal being with, and that He, glory be to Him, is with us while He is above (on His throne). There is no contradiction between the two meanings. There is no contradiction, for three reasons.

The first reason: Allah, the Exalted, combined these two meanings in the Quran, indeed in a single verse: ﴿He it is who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself on the Throne. He knows what enters into the earth and what comes out of it, what descends from the sky and what ascends into it, and He is with you wherever you are﴾ [Al-Hadid 4]. He mentioned that He is established on the Throne, and it is impossible for Allah to combine for Himself two contradictory attributes, ever.

The second reason: there is no contradiction between being high (al-'uluww) and being with. This is established for created things, as the Arabs say: "We kept traveling while the moon was with us," even though the moon is one of the smallest celestial bodies. Yet it is with the traveler and with the non-traveler, and it is in the sky. If the combining of the two, I mean the combining of the literal reality of being with and being high, is permissible regarding the created, then their combining regarding the Creator is more fitting.

The third reason: even if it were assumed that their combining is impossible regarding the created, that does not necessitate their being impossible to combine regarding the Creator, because Allah, the Exalted, "there is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing" [Ash-Shura 11]. If the seven heavens and the seven earths are in His hand, glory be to Him and exalted, like a mustard seed in the hand of one of us, can He be compared to creation? It is impossible.

Therefore, we believe that Allah is with us literally, and He is in the sky. He knows what is in our hearts, hears what we say, sees what we do, and He has complete authority over us and complete power. All of these are among the requirements of being with. The early generations (al-salaf), or many of them, explained it by these requirements, and they said: "He is with us by His knowledge." This does not contradict that what is meant is the literal reality, because they sometimes explain it by its necessary implication, as Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on him) said in the introduction to tafsir (muqaddimat al-tafsir): that the explanations transmitted from the early generations may be an explanation by a necessary implication, not a denial of the literal meaning.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that these people plotted what He does not approve of in speech, meaning they fabricated it and gathered together over it. When? At night, because al-bayat (plotting) only happens at night. For this reason, some narrators say that they came to the Messenger (ﷺ) at night after they had cooked up their opinions, and they came to the Messenger (ﷺ).

* It is derived from this: the intense concealment of these people, and that they do not like anyone to find out about them. Can it be taken from this that if we want to hide something, we should do it at night? Yes, perhaps it can be taken from it. For this reason, there is the well-known proverb: "A matter decided at night."

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of approval (al-ridha) for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿what He does not approve of in speech﴾. What is the wisdom of this?
The negation of approval from these people indicates its affirmation for others, for if it were negated from all, it would not be good to negate it from these people specifically. So what is approval?
The approval that is established for Allah is a true approval, and it is not a metaphor for rewarding them, as the people of distortion (ahl al-tahrif, those who alter the meanings of the attributes) say. Rather, it is an approval that Allah truly has, but it is not like our approval. It is a greater and more majestic approval, and we cannot encompass it.
Did Allah affirm approval for Himself? That is, did He mention it for Himself and attribute it to Himself in the form of affirmation? Yes, like His saying: ﴿Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 119]. Allah, the Exalted, is pleased with speech, deeds, and persons. That is, the object of His approval is either deeds, or speech, or persons. But His approval of persons is only because of their deeds and words that please Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah's encompassment of everything, by His saying: ﴿and Allah is ever encompassing of what they do﴾.

If someone says: the object (al-muta'allaq) has been placed before the verb's complement (al-muta'allaq), and this indicates restriction (al-ikhtisas)?
The answer to that is what we pointed out earlier: that placing it first does not mean restriction, but it means intensity of warning and the attachment of the ruling to this preposed element. It is as if Allah, the Exalted, were saying: "Even if He did not know anything, He would know their deed." So what is meant from this (i.e., what is derived from it) is the intensity of the warning against these people, and that it is impossible for them to be hidden from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Student: May Allah bless you. Does the intensive form (sighat al-mubalaghah) come, as we said in our topic, for attribution (lil-nisbah)?
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: Is this always so, or is it by context?
* The Shaykh: No, no. By context. The basic rule is that it is for intensity, the basic rule is that it is for intensity, meaning frequency of the act. That is the basic rule.
* The student: "Zawwarat al-qubur" (women who frequently visit graves). How is it used? In the explanation, we said it is for attribution, or was it added?
* The Shaykh: Yes, because in it there is (...).
* Student: We said: The correct view is that the Messenger (ﷺ) may do such a thing, but...?
* The Shaykh: He is not left to persist in it.
* The student: He is not left to persist in it. But as for what contradicts the message, it does not occur from him.
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed.
* The student: Like what?
* The Shaykh: Like lying. It is impossible for him to lie, and impossible for him to betray. We mentioned this. Didn't we mention it to you?
* The students: No.
* The student: Major sins cannot occur from him?
* The Shaykh: Musa (peace be upon him) killed a soul without right. The point is that everything that contradicts the message is impossible. As for the Messenger (peace be upon him), we do not know that he committed any major sin. He did matters of ijtihad (independent judgment) in which he acted hastily, such as his permission to the hypocrites, and his prohibiting what Allah had made lawful for him. And the most serious thing that happened from him was in the matter of Zayd ibn Harithah.
* Student: Is the defense of those who betray themselves among the major sins?
* The Shaykh: How?
* The student: The defense of those who betray themselves among the major sins?
* The Shaykh: What do you say? Is defending those who betray themselves a major sin?
* The students: No, it is not a major sin.
* The Shaykh: I have doubt about this. That is, whoever helps a person to commit a major sin without participating in it, the person hesitates as to whether his act is a major sin. Someone may say it is a major sin, because the Messenger (ﷺ) "cursed the one who consumes usury, the one who feeds it, its two witnesses, and its scribe, and he said: 'They are all alike'" [Narrated by Muslim (1598/106) from the hadith of Jabir]. And it may be said that it cannot be like the doer of a major sin, because he did not commit the sin himself but only assisted in it. So he is at risk. In my opinion, he is at risk.
* Student: May Allah pardon you. Regarding His saying: ﴿They plot by night what He does not approve of in speech﴾, does this indicate that betrayal is a greater sin than theft? Because theft is an act, and Allah did not attach to it... (...) The whole speech is about betrayal. Can this be said?
* The Shaykh: Because this is more severe in relation to making light of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and of the Messenger (peace be upon him). And it will come, if Allah wills, that they intended to lead the Messenger (peace be upon him) astray.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. Regarding His saying: ﴿They hide from the people, but they do not hide from Allah﴾, do we say that this is general, that everyone who commits a sin hides from people in that act and does not hide from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?
* The Shaykh: Yes. There is no doubt that this applies to them and to others. Every person for whom the creature is greater than the Creator hides from the creature and does not hide from Allah. There is no doubt that he has some resemblance to these people.
* Student: Regarding the ruling on those people who said that sins (...), but sometimes a person relies on Allah, yet fear of a tyrannical person enters his heart, who may cause harm to him.
* The Shaykh: No, this is not from that angle. But a person, for example, wants to commit a sin and conceals it from people, but does not conceal it from Allah.
* The student: Does the second statement contradict the reality of reliance upon Allah (tawakkul)?
* The Shaykh: Which of them?
* The student: That a person may be approached by a tyrannical man who oppresses him or harms him?
* The Shaykh: And he does what would deliver him from him?
* The student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: There is nothing wrong with that.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. If we say that betrayal is among the major sins, the Messenger of Allah mentioned a punishment for it. Shaykh, is it one act of betrayal, or many...?
* The Shaykh: One, because persisting in betrayal is problematic. Even minor sins, if a person persists in them, become major sins.
* Student: Shaykh, those who deny the active attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, meaning they have doubts. They say that the active attributes which imply perfection for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, were never there before (...)?
* The Shaykh: Have we not answered this, O brothers? He says: the voluntary active attributes contain a doubt, because if they were perfection, He would have been characterized by them eternally and forever, and if they were deficiency, He could not be characterized by them while they are a deficiency. We have examined this and answered it. We said: in the presence of their causes they are perfection, and in the absence of their causes they are deficiency. If Allah became angry without there being any cause for anger, that would be deficiency. And if He became angry in the presence of the requirement of anger, that would be perfection.
* The student: (...) Shaykh, the statement, meaning, is it...
* The Shaykh: This is if we argue with them by reason. As for by revelation (al-sam'), we say: Allah affirmed that for Himself, so we must affirm it.
* The student: They do not accept (...).
* The Shaykh: He affirmed for Himself being established on the Throne, and the Messenger affirmed that He descends to the lowest heaven. That is enough. But even by reason we argue with them, there is no obstacle. (...)
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself, then seeks forgiveness from Allah, will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful. And whoever earns a sin, he earns it only against himself, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise. And whoever earns a fault or a sin and then throws it onto an innocent person has certainly borne a slander and a clear sin. And if not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, a group of them would have resolved to mislead you, but they do not mislead except themselves, and they cannot harm you at all. And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom and taught you what you did not know. And the bounty of Allah upon you has ever been great﴾ [An-Nisa' 110-113].
* The Shaykh: Well done. I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself, then seeks forgiveness from Allah, will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾.
* We will take the remaining benefits of His saying: ﴿They hide from the people, but they do not hide from Allah, and He is with them﴾, and so on to the end.
The being with of Allah, glory be to Him, is divided into kinds. There is a being with intended to show encompassment, meaning to show Allah's encompassment of everything. Among it is His saying: ﴿There is no secret conversation among three but that He is their fourth, nor among five but that He is their sixth, nor less than that nor more but that He is with them wherever they are﴾ [Al-Mujadilah 7].
And sometimes it is intended as a warning, as in this verse: ﴿They hide from the people, but they do not hide from Allah, and He is with them when they plot what He does not approve of in speech﴾.
And sometimes it is intended as support and assistance, attached either to a quality or to a person:
An example of the one attached to a quality is His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿And your large number will not avail you at all, and Allah is with the believers﴾ [Al-Anfal 19]. ﴿Be patient, for Allah is with the patient﴾ [Al-Anfal 46]. ﴿Indeed Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾ [An-Nahl 128]. This is a being with that entails support and assistance, but it is restricted to what? To a quality.
And a being with that entails support and assistance, restricted to a person, like His saying to Musa and Harun: ﴿Do not fear. Indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ [Ta-Ha 46], and the saying of the Prophet (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family) to Abu Bakr: ﴿Do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us﴾ [At-Tawbah 40]. This being with entails support, assistance, protection, and safeguarding, but it is restricted to a person.
And here we ask: is what is meant by being with its literal reality or its implication?
We say: what is meant by it is its literal reality, but the early generations always explain it by its implication. As they said: being with is knowledge, so He is with them by His knowledge. But this is an explanation of it by some of its requirements, for the requirement of being with is knowledge, hearing, sight, encompassment, authority, power, and other things. But its real meaning is literal, and what the early generations explained it by is an explanation by an implication. As Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) said in the introduction to tafsir: the early generations may explain a thing by its implication.
So if we say that it is literal, does this mean we have gone along with what the proponents of incarnation (ahl al-hulul), who say that Allah is with us in His essence in our places, went along with?
The answer is no. Rather, we utterly deny this, and we say it is misguidance, indeed it is disbelief. We only say that He is with us literally while He is in the sky, because the proofs, both revelational and rational, all indicate that Allah is in the sky, and that does not prevent Him from being with us, for three reasons:
The first: Allah combined the two in His description of Himself, and Allah does not combine two contradictories.
Second: being high and being with are both possible regarding the created, as they say: "We kept traveling while the moon was with us," or "that star is with us," and even sometimes "that mountain is with us," yet it is in its place. The moon is in the sky, the star is in the sky, the mountain is far, and similar things.

Third: Even if it were supposed that the true meaning of "being with" (al-ma'iyyah) and "being above" (al-'uluww) were in conflict in the case of created beings, this would not hold true with respect to the Creator, because the Creator is not like anything in all of His attributes. As Shaykh al-Islam (rahimahu Allah) said in al-'Aqidah al-Wasitiyyah: "He is High in His nearness, Near in His highness."

* I also mentioned among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of Allah's pleasure (al-rida). Is that not so?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: We have discussed it.
* I also mentioned: the encompassing of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, over everything. And I mentioned why ﴿بِمَا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ was placed first. It is well known that fronting an object of a verb (taqdim al-ma'mul) indicates restriction (al-hasr). Allah encompasses everything, so why did He single out ﴿بِمَا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ("what they do")? It is by way of warning (al-tahdid), and that what you did is not hidden from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Then He said: ﴿Here you are, you who argued on their behalf in the life of this world﴾ [An-Nisa 109]. (Ha) is for drawing attention. (An) is the subject (mubtada'). ﴿Ha'ulaa'﴾ is either a vocative with the particle omitted, the implied meaning being "O you," in which case His saying ﴿argued﴾ is the predicate of the subject; or ﴿Ha'ulaa'﴾ is the predicate, so that ﴿Ha antum ha'ulaa'﴾, and the clause ﴿argued﴾ is in the position of an accusative of circumstance (hal), meaning: "Here you are, arguing on their behalf in the life of this world." The reference in His saying ﴿Here you are﴾ is to the people of the man who stole a shield and blamed it on a man from the Jews, as we mentioned in the explanation of the verses.

﴿You argued on their behalf﴾, though they argued on behalf of one man only. But this argument on behalf of that one man is in reality an argument on behalf of all of them, because branding one man of the tribe as a thief is branding the whole tribe, since they are reproached for it and it is said, "Among you are thieves, such as so-and-so," for example. This is why He said ﴿you argued on their behalf﴾, although the argument was on behalf of one individual. ﴿In the life of this world﴾: argument may achieve victory, even through falsehood, in the life of this world, because a person may argue with falsehood, bringing eloquent and clear speech by which he mixes truth with falsehood and succeeds.

But ﴿who then will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection﴾? Here (man) is an interrogative used in the sense of negation, meaning: no one will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection. When interrogation comes in the place of negation, it is more emphatic than plain negation, because it becomes a negation tinged with challenge, as if the speaker is saying, "If this matter is possible, then bring it to me." So the interrogative in the place of negation is stronger in negating, because it carries the meaning of challenge: ﴿who then will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection?﴾

The answer: no one. No one is able to argue on their behalf. Even if we suppose that someone did argue, his own limbs will testify against him: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will bear witness against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [An-Nur 24]. ﴿Or who will be a guardian over them?﴾ meaning: who has agency, authority, who can defend, prevent and help? The answer: no one.

* In this noble verse there are benefits:

* Among them: that disputing and contending for falsehood, even if it benefits in this world, will not benefit in the Hereafter. Is this to be taken?

* Student: ﴿Here you are, you who argued on their behalf in the life of this world﴾...

* The Shaykh: ﴿Who then will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: people may support one another in falsehood, because these people argued with falsehood while knowing that their companion had stolen, as shown by His saying ﴿Here you are, you who argued on their behalf in the life of this world﴾.

* Among its benefits: the prohibition of advocacy when the advocate knows that his client is in the wrong. The reason is that Allah denounced these people for arguing on behalf of their companion. As for when the advocate wishes to defend the truth so as to establish it, this is permissible, and may even be obligatory, as when a person who does not know, and can hardly express himself, appoints you to defend him; this is not objectionable.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the Last Day, which is the Day of Resurrection, by His saying ﴿who then will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that arguing with falsehood on the Day of Resurrection is of no avail, and its practitioner is an adversary; therefore one must beware of what the Prophet (ﷺ) said in the hadith qudsi that Allah said: "There are three whose adversary I will be on the Day of Resurrection: a man who gave a pledge in My name and then betrayed it; a man who sold a free person and consumed his price; and a man who employed a worker, took full work from him, and did not give him his wage." [Related by al-Bukhari (2227) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] For we know that whoever has Allah as his adversary is defeated in every case.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, glorified and exalted, hides nothing from Him, and that whoever tries to hide something from Allah has harbored an evil opinion of his Lord; yet this opinion will not benefit him, by His saying ﴿who then will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection, or who will be a guardian over them?﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 110 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself, then seeks forgiveness from Allah, will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ All praise is due to Allah.

﴿Whoever does evil﴾ means: to others. That is, what harms others. This is shown by the fact that all the verses are in the context of one specific story, so the meaning of "evil" here is what harms others, such as accusing that Jew of theft.

﴿or wrongs himself﴾ means: through sins, because sins are a wronging of the self. The self is an trust (amanah) entrusted to you, and you must look after it with proper care. So when you disobey Allah, you have wronged it. For this reason Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they declined to bear it and feared it, and man bore it﴾ [al-Ahzab 72]. Why? ﴿Indeed, he was a wrongdoer, ignorant﴾ [al-Ahzab 72]. So he wrongs himself through the sins between him and his Lord, and he does evil that harms others.

﴿then seeks forgiveness from Allah﴾. Here there is a grammatical difficulty: ﴿yastaghfiru﴾ (seeks forgiveness) is kasra-ended. Why is it kasra-ended though it is a verb, when kasra is well known as a mark of nouns?

* Student: Perhaps because of the meeting of two sukun (liltiqa' al-sakinayn).
* The Shaykh: Perhaps. Fine. And the less likely? Because "perhaps" indicates that this is the more likely view. And the less likely? Do you not know?
* Student: It is so.
* The Shaykh: That means "expected."
* Student: No, it is...
* The Shaykh: It is. You said "it is so," and "so" (kadha) indicates equality. You did not say what he said.
* Student: I said it is certain.
* The Shaykh: Yes, certainly. Fine. Another difficulty arises for us: how is it conjoined to ﴿ya'mal﴾, when ﴿ya'mal﴾ is jussive and ﴿yastaghfiru﴾ is kasra-ended?
* Student: It is not kasra-ended, O Shaykh, but it was given a vowel because of the meeting of two sukun. It is jussive.
* The Shaykh: It is jussive, and the vowel here is incidental.

﴿Whoever does evil or wrongs himself, then seeks forgiveness from Allah﴾ means: he asks Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for forgiveness through his state and his speech. As for speech, it is obvious: he says, "O Allah, forgive me," or "I seek Allah's forgiveness." As for state, it is to be fulfilling the five conditions of repentance (tawbah). What are they? Begin with them one by one.

* Student: To resolve not to return to it.
* The Shaykh: There is something before that. First, state the condition upon which the action is built.
* Student: Sincerity (ikhlas).
* The Shaykh: Well done, may Allah bless you. Sincerity, meaning that concern for any person does not move him to repent. Second?
* Student: To give up the sin.
* The Shaykh: No, before that.
* Student: Ceasing the action.
* The Shaykh: He gives up the sin and ceases the action. May Allah reward you with good!
* Student: To feel remorse.
* The Shaykh: To feel remorse, and to feel grief in his soul over having committed the sin. The third?
* Student: To give up the sin.
* The Shaykh: To give up the sin. The fourth?
* Student: The resolve not to return.
* The Shaykh: The resolve not to return. And the fifth?
* Student: That it be at the time of repentance.
* The Shaykh: That it be at the time of repentance, meaning at the time when repentance is accepted.

So ﴿yastaghfiru Allah﴾ means: he seeks forgiveness, by what? By his state and his speech. He says, "O Allah, forgive me." So what is forgiveness?

Forgiveness is the covering of the sin and passing over it, not merely covering. This is because the derivation indicates that there must be both covering and protection, since it is derived from al-mighfar, which is the iron cover of steel or similar material worn over the head to protect against arrows, so that covering and protection are achieved by it.

I tell you that it is derived from al-mighfar, because the principle is that abstract meanings are derived from concrete things. For this reason you find the scholars of language returning meanings to their concrete origins. They say: it is derived from such-and-such. The origin of this, as it has been said, is that man began to speak by imitating what he heard around him: the sound of the winds, the rustling of trees, and the like. So it has been said, along with what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, taught Adam of the names.

So forgiveness is the covering of the sin and passing over it.

﴿then seeks forgiveness from Allah﴾ says: "O Allah, forgive me," or "I seek Allah's forgiveness."

﴿will find Allah﴾: this is the answer of the conditional, the answer of "whoever" (man). For this reason it is jussive, and it was given a kasra because of the meeting of two sukun. The meaning of ﴿will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is that Allah forgives him. The Forgiving (al-Ghafur) is the One possessing forgiveness, as Allah said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Ra'd 6].

The Merciful (al-Rahim) is the One possessing mercy, as Allah said: ﴿Your Lord is the Forgiving, Possessor of mercy﴾ [al-Kahf 58]. So if you seek forgiveness from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and repent to Him in the manner He is pleased with, you will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful. I think there is no need to discuss the divisions of mercy, because they have been mentioned again and again. Have you understood this? There is no god but Allah!

Mercy is applied to the attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and to the effects of the attribute, meaning to the created thing. It is applied to the mercy that is His attribute, and to the effects of mercy that are His creation. The first is the origin: mercy is an attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As for the second, from it is His saying to Paradise: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whomever I will" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4850) and Muslim (2846/34), from Abu Hurayrah]. The meaning is not the mercy that is His attribute. That is, mercy here is a separate created thing. From this also, according to the view of some scholars, is His saying: ﴿And He is the One who sends down rain after they had despaired, and spreads His mercy﴾ [al-Shura 28]. ﴿Spreads His mercy﴾ means the plants and the provision that comes through the water descending from the sky.

As for the mercy that is His attribute, scholars divide it into two kinds: general and specific.

The general is that which encompasses every creature, and the specific is that which is particular to the believers, and with which the happiness of this world and the Hereafter is connected. The general mercy is mercy to all people, or to all creation, in this world. For this reason we find that for the disbelievers there is mercy from Allah: He provided for them, gave them sustenance, and gave them minds, that is, minds with which they perceive, though not minds of right guidance and right conduct. This is in general. Whatever mention of the name al-Rahim passes by you, its meaning is the general, and the specific is included (...). When it is restricted, it is the specific, as in His saying: ﴿And He is ever Merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab 43]. This is mercy specific to the believers.

It is strange that the Ash'aris denied that Allah is described with mercy, and affirmed for Him will. They said: it is not permissible to affirm mercy for Allah, because mercy is tenderness and softness, which is not fitting for the Creator. This is based on their corrupt principle, which is that they take what they believe about their Lord from their own corrupt intellects as well, because sound evidence does not contradict clear reason. They say: do not describe Allah with mercy. So the meaning of "the Merciful" for them is "the Bestower of favor" or "the One who wills to bestow favor": the Bestower, because blessing is separate, distinct and created; or the One who wills to bestow favor, because they affirm will. Glory be to Allah! Look at the contradictory intellect. They say: will is indicated by reason through the mechanism of specification. That is, the specification of some creatures in some matters indicates will. That a human has this attribute and a horse has that attribute: what made this one have one attribute and that one another? The will of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

They said: the specification of creatures by what is particular to them indicates the will of Allah. The inference of will from this is a hidden inference that only students of knowledge grasp, after they have read as well. Yet they do not affirm mercy, whose effects both the elite and the common people recognize: the night, the day, the rain, the trees, the rivers, the seas. Everyone knows these are from the mercy of Allah. For this reason you find that when the sky rains, the common person says, "We have been rained on by the grace and mercy of Allah," and he has no doubt about it. But whomever Allah has not given light, for him there is no light.

* In this noble verse there are benefits. First: whoever harms another and then seeks forgiveness from Allah, Allah forgives him. At this point a difficulty arises for us, because the scholars have said that there are three registers (dawawin), one of which is the register of creation, meaning dealings with people. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not forgive this. But the apparent texts indicate that if repentance is valid, Allah forgives it. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah any other deity, and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, and do not commit unlawful sexual intercourse; and whoever does that will meet a penalty. The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein in humiliation, except for those who repent﴾ [al-Furqan 68-70]. Although murder is mentioned, if a person repents from murder with a repentance whose conditions are fulfilled, Allah forgives him.

Among the conditions of repentance for murder is that he surrender himself to the heirs of the one murdered. If he surrenders himself to the heirs of the one murdered, and they kill him or pardon him, while he feels remorse for what he did and seeks forgiveness from his Lord, then Allah bears the right of the murdered person on his behalf on the Day of Resurrection. Do you understand? This is because the fulfilling of the murdered person's right in this case is transferred. The murderer whose repentance is valid says to himself: if I could make the dead person content, I would do it, but I now cannot do more than surrender myself to the heirs of the murdered person. So Allah bears this on his behalf.

Now, if someone steals property from a person, this is doing evil to another. If he repents from that, will Allah accept his repentance?

Yes, if the conditions of repentance are fulfilled. Among the conditions of repentance is returning the property to its owner. If he returns the property to its owner, he has repented. On this basis we say: the apparent meaning of this verse and of other texts is that whenever repentance is valid, even regarding the rights of people that one cannot free oneself from, Allah accepts his repentance.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a person's repentance from sin can be valid even if it is repeated. From where is this derived?

* Student: From the present tense in ﴿ya'mal﴾ and ﴿yajid﴾. Being in the present form indicates continuity. So if he seeks forgiveness and then repents...
* The Shaykh: The generality of ﴿whoever does evil﴾ and ﴿then seeks forgiveness from Allah﴾. This is general for one who repeats it and one who does not repeat it. The authentic hadith from the Prophet, peace be upon him, supports this: "A man committed a sin and sought forgiveness from Allah. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: My servant knows that he has a Lord who forgives sins and seizes for them. I have forgiven My servant. Then he returned a second time, then a third time, until Allah said to him: Let him do what he wills" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7507), Muslim (2758/29), Ahmad (7948), and this wording is his, from Abu Hurayrah]. This indicates that repentance is established and accepted by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, even if the sin is repeated. For this reason the scholars said: among the conditions of repentance is the resolve not to return. Not that one must never return, but if he resolves not to return, his repentance is valid. If he returns, his earlier repentance is not nullified. Rather, his earlier repentance is valid, and he must renew a second repentance for the second sin.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: sins are a wronging of the self, from His saying ﴿or wrongs himself﴾. This is a fixed matter repeated in the Qur'an. Allah said: ﴿And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 57]. ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves﴾ [Hud 101]. And there are other texts indicating that a person is himself the wrongdoer to his own soul when he disobeys Allah.

* Among its benefits: a person may be an enemy to himself. From where is this derived?

* Student: That he wrongs himself, and whoever wrongs himself is an enemy to himself.
* The Shaykh: Yes, that he wrongs himself. The one who wrongs you is your enemy. So a person is an enemy to himself, just as the closest people to a person may be his enemies: ﴿Indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them﴾ [al-Taghabun 14]. So beware of yourself, for it is your enemy.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah accepts from His servant seeking forgiveness when its conditions are fulfilled, that is, through his state and his speech. This is from His saying ﴿will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾. You, seek forgiveness. Be sincere in your seeking forgiveness, and you will find Allah, Mighty and Majestic, Forgiving and Merciful.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And whoever earns a sin, he earns it only against himself. And ever is Allah Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Nisa' 111].

* Student: May Allah be good to you, O Shaykh. Regarding disputation (jidal), O Shaykh, is it blameworthy in every case, or is there a distinction?
* The Shaykh: Disputation is not blameworthy in every case. The disputation that is in His saying: ﴿And they disputed with falsehood to refute thereby the truth﴾ [Ghafir 5] is blameworthy and false. The disputation intended to establish the truth is praiseworthy and obligatory. Allah said: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best﴾ [al-Nahl 125].

* Student: O Shaykh, there is a hadith: the words of the Messenger, peace be upon him: "I am a guarantor of a house on the outskirts of Paradise for whoever abandons mira' (contentious argument), even if he is..." [narrated by Abu Dawud (4800) from Abu Umamah al-Bahili].
* The Shaykh: This is other than mira' in religion. Then note that mira' is other than jidal. Mira' is when the disputant intends to twist the opponent, whether by right or by wrong.
* Student: May Allah bless you, O Shaykh. From what has preceded: the lesson is in the generality of the wording, not the specific cause. We said, in explaining His saying ﴿Here you are, those who argued on their behalf in the worldly life﴾, that what is meant is the people for whom the disgrace would fall upon the tribe. Could any obstacle prevent us from saying that this verse is general for the whole Ummah, so that it forbids the Ummah from arguing on behalf of others?
* The Shaykh: No, that is not correct. ﴿Here you are﴾ points to specific people...
* Student: The lesson is in the generality.
* The Shaykh: There is no generality here, may Allah bless you. ﴿Here you are, those who argued on their behalf in the worldly life﴾.
* Student: What prevents it if the wording admits it?
* The Shaykh: It does not admit it at all. Are we pointing to specific people and then saying it admits generality? ﴿Here you are﴾.
* Student: Then the demonstrative has specified them.
* The Shaykh: There is no doubt it has specified them. But in any case, others are like them. If someone argues on behalf of a person for falsehood, we say to him: you have argued for him now, and perhaps you will succeed. But who will argue with Allah on the Day of Resurrection? For this reason: "Whoever seizes a span of land (unjustly)..." [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2452), Muslim (1610/137), wording his, from Sa'id ibn Zayd].

Be sincere in your seeking forgiveness, and you will find Allah, Mighty and Majestic, Forgiving and Merciful.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And whoever earns a sin, he earns it only against himself. And ever is Allah Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Nisa' 111].

* Student: May Allah be good to you, O Shaykh. Regarding disputation, O Shaykh, is it blameworthy in every case, or is there a distinction?
* The Shaykh: Disputation is not blameworthy in every case. The disputation in His saying: ﴿And they disputed with falsehood to refute thereby the truth﴾ [Ghafir 5] is blameworthy and false. The disputation intended to establish the truth is praiseworthy and obligatory. Allah said: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best﴾ [al-Nahl 125].
* Student: There is a hadith, O Shaykh: "I am a guarantor of a house in the outskirts of Paradise for whoever abandons mira', even if he is right" [narrated by Abu Dawud (4800) from Abu Umamah].
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is other than mira' in religion. Note that mira' is other than jidal. Mira' is when the disputant intends to twist the opponent.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 110 (part 2 of 2):**

* **Student:** May Allah bless you, Shaykh. Earlier we said that the ruling follows the general wording of a text (al-'ibrah bi-'umum al-lafz, the general wording), not the specific cause of its revelation (khusus al-sabab). We said that in His words ﴿Here you are, you argued on their behalf in the life of this world﴾, the intended people are the tribe to whom the shame would attach. Is there anything preventing us from saying that this verse is general to the whole Ummah? It would then be a prohibition for the Ummah from arguing; that is, arguing on behalf of others?
* **Shaykh:** No, that does not hold, it does not hold. ﴿Here you are﴾ points to specific people.
* **Student:** The ruling follows the general wording.
* **Shaykh:** There is no generality in it, may Allah bless you. ﴿Here you are, you argued on their behalf in the life of this world﴾.
* **Student:** What is the objection if the wording allows it?
* **Shaykh:** It does not allow it at all. We are pointing to specific people, and you say it allows generality? ﴿Here you are﴾.
* **Student:** So there is an indication here?
* **Shaykh:** There is nothing that specifies it. But in any case, whoever is like them is included. If someone argues on behalf of a person in falsehood, we say to him: you have argued for him now, and perhaps you will succeed. But who will argue on his behalf before Allah on the Day of Resurrection? And for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever usurps a span of land unjustly, Allah will encircle him with it from seven earths." [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3198), and Muslim (1610/137) with his wording, from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd.]]
* **Student:** What is the meaning of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Beware of injustice, for it is darkness on the Day of Resurrection"? [[Related by Muslim (2578/56) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.]] What does he mean by "darkness"?
* **Shaykh:** It is clear. It means that light is withheld from the person on the Day of Resurrection. On the Day of Resurrection, those who are not believers have no light. ﴿The Day you see the believing men and believing women, their light running before them and on their right hands﴾ [al-Hadid 12]. So this person is punished by having light withheld from him on the Day of Resurrection.
* **Student:** Someone stole money from another person, then this money was stolen from him, and he wanted to repent, so...?
* **Shaykh:** The first one has his hand cut off, and the second one does not have his hand cut off.
* **Student:** No, that is not what we mean... I mean, if it is not enforced against them?
* **Shaykh:** This is adding to the answer. What is it that you want?
* **Student:** I mean, setting aside the ruling: for him, he wanted to repent, he was not seized and was not caught. That is, he wanted to repent, but this money that he stole was stolen from him?
* **Shaykh:** He goes to its owner and says to him: "I stole such-and-such from you, and what I stole from you was stolen from me." He compensates him with its equivalent if it is a fungible item (mithli), or with its value if it is a valued item (mutaqawwam).
* **Student:** If it is impossible for him to go to him, that is, if he has died, does he go to his heirs?
* **Shaykh:** Yes indeed. If the one from whom it was stolen has died, he returns to his heirs.
* **Student:** Shaykh, we said that one of the conditions of repentance from killing is that he surrender himself. But in the law of those before us, Musa (peace be upon him), when he killed a soul, did not surrender himself. He fled, and said: "My Lord, forgive me," when he went out... Should we say that the law of those before us is not our law?
* **Shaykh:** But Musa was acting on an interpretation (mu'awwil)...
* **Student:** (...)
* **Shaykh:** No, he was acting on an interpretation. This Egyptian who assaulted the Israelite interpreted that he wanted to rescue the Israelite from him, because he had called for help, so he wanted to defend him. And for this reason he said: "Indeed I killed a soul, and I was not commanded to kill it." [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4712), and Muslim (194/327), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]
* **Student:** (...) In our law, if someone acts on an interpretation and kills, does he flee?
* **Shaykh:** No, that is not permissible, except if it was in self-defense (mudafa'ah).
* **Student:** Yes, self-defense.
* **Shaykh:** Yes, he flees. If it was self-defense, he flees.
* **Student:** May Allah bless you. This man who stole the money, then felt reluctant to go to the owner of the money and inform him that he had stolen from him, does he give this money in charity?
* **Shaykh:** That is not valid. It must reach its owner, either directly or through an intermediary.
* **Student:** Perhaps he gives it to him without...
* **Shaykh:** Through an intermediary whom he trusts. He says: "O so-and-so, I stole from so-and-so, and I want, may Allah reward you with good, that you take it and deliver it to him."
* **Student:** (...) He gives it in charity on his behalf?
* **Shaykh:** No, he may not dispose of another person's property.
* **Student:** May Allah bless you all. We have mentioned the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ) (...).

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. "Whoever earns a sin, he earns it only against himself, and Allah is ever All-Knowing, All-Wise" (4:111). "And whoever earns a fault or a sin and then throws it onto an innocent person has certainly borne a slander and a manifest sin" (4:112). "And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, a group of them would have intended to mislead you, but they mislead none except themselves, and they do not harm you at all. And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom and has taught you that which you did not know. And ever has the bounty of Allah been upon you tremendous" (4:113).

* The Shaykh: Well done. I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: "Whoever earns a sin..."

He, may He be exalted, says: "Whoever earns a sin, he earns it only against himself." This is a conditional sentence. Its condition (fiʿl al-sharṭ) is "yaksib," and its response (jawab al-sharṭ) is "fa-innamā." The question here is: why is the "fa" attached to the response?

* Student: Because it is a verbal sentence preceded by (qad)?

* The Shaykh: How?

* Student: Fa-qad.

* The Shaykh: No.

* Student: The response is attached to (innamā), a verbal sentence preceded by (innamā).

* The Shaykh: Good.

* Student: A nominal sentence.

* The Shaykh: How is it a nominal sentence?

* Student: If (inna) was (...).

* The Shaykh: But is the sentence now nominal or verbal? This is a particle of restriction (adat ḥaṣr), and "yaksib"?

* Student: Verbal.

* The Shaykh: The answer: it is verbal.

* Student: I say: because in the sentence here the response is preceded... preceded, meaning the "fa" by the one who...

* The Shaykh: And where is the "fa"?

* Student: "Fa-innamā yaksibuhu ʿalā nafsihi."

* The Shaykh: No.

* Student: Except that the response of the condition is with the "fa," innamā yaksib.

* The Shaykh: The answer is to say: this resembles the nominal sentence, because it is attached to (innamā). The origin of (innamā) is: (inna), a particle of emphasis, to which (mā) the restrictive (kāffa) was attached, so it became (innamā).

His saying: "Innamā yaksibuhu ʿalā nafsihi" means: no, against another, "and Allah is ever All-Knowing, All-Wise."

In this verse Allah, mighty and majestic, informs that whoever earns a sin, he harms only himself. Why? Because he earns it against himself and not against another.

His saying: "ithman" is an indefinite noun in a conditional context, so it encompasses all sins: the major and the minor, and it encompasses direct sins and sins by causation, because a person may commit a sin himself, or he may be one who points to it or helps in it, and that too is a sin.

His saying: "And Allah is ever All-Knowing, All-Wise." We have already explained that such an expression does not indicate occurrence, and that Allah was All-Knowing, All-Wise in the past. Rather, the verb here is stripped of what? Time. Its purpose is to affirm that He is named by these two names and characterized by what they indicate.

In the noble verse Allah, mighty and majestic, establishes that when a person earns a sin, he earns it only against himself, because these verses, as we have passed over before, were revealed concerning the story of the man who stole a coat of mail and then threw it onto a Jew. They wanted to accuse this Jew, and they came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the innocence of the Jew became clear. So He, mighty and majestic, says: when a person earns a sin, he earns it against himself.

* From this several benefits are derived. The first: that when a person earns sin, he earns it against himself, and no one else bears it for him. This is confirmed by the saying of the Most High: "And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another" (6:164).

If someone says: Has it not been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "Whoever initiates in Islam a bad practice, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection"[[Recorded by Muslim (1017/69) from the hadith of Jarir ibn ʿAbd Allah.]]?

The answer: Yes. Then how can it be upon him when he did not himself perform the act? We say: because he is the one who initiated this evil innovation. For this reason, no soul is killed unjustly except that upon the first son of Adam is a share of it, because he was the first to initiate killing. On this basis it is said: whoever initiates an innovation and people follow him in it, his initiating it is from his own deeds.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: Allah the Exalted does not wrong anyone by placing another's sin upon him except with right. It has been stated many times that whoever wrongs people, the people take from his good deeds until they are exhausted, then their sins are taken and cast upon him and he is cast into the Fire. This is not the bearing of another's sin, but is by way of retribution and recompense. So if this person has no good deeds to return the injustice to others, then their sins are taken from them and placed upon him, and he is cast into the Fire.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of these two names among the names of Allah: Al-ʿAlim (the All-Knowing) and Al-Hakim (the All-Wise), by His saying: "And Allah is ever All-Knowing, All-Wise."

* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of the attributes contained in these two names. Al-ʿAlim contains the attribute of knowledge, and Al-Hakim contains wisdom and judgment, because we have passed over that al-Hakim is derived from (al-ḥukm) and (al-iḥkām), which is wisdom. There is no need to repeat that wisdom has four states, since that has already passed, and repetition takes up time.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that from the knowledge and wisdom of Allah is that whoever earns a sin, he earns it only against himself, and this is from consummate wisdom.

Then He says: ﴿And whoever earns a fault or a sin and then throws it onto an innocent person has certainly borne a slander and a manifest sin.﴾ The words khatiah (فالخطيئة, "fault") and ithm (الإثم, "sin") are among those words which, when they are combined, become distinct, and when they are distinct, become combined. So khatiah, ithm, and sau' (السوء, "evil") and the like have one meaning when each word stands alone apart from the other. But when one of them is paired with the other, we must give each one a meaning, lest there be repetition without benefit. The basic principle in conjunction (عطف, 'atf) is that it implies difference.

So what is khatiah, and what is ithm?

Some scholars said: khatiah is what a person commits without intention, and ithm is what he commits intentionally.

But this requires consideration, because a fault committed without intention is one for which Allah has lifted blame and sin, so it would not be a khatiah. It was answered that there is no obstacle to a person earning a khatiah while there is an obstacle to being punished for it. Otherwise, the basic rule is that whoever commits a fault is punished for it, but here there is an obstacle, namely the pardon of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It was also said: khatiah is what transgresses to others, and ithm is what is specific to the person himself. And it was said: the reverse. All these opinions are attempts to avoid repetition in the verse.

His saying: ﴿then throws it onto an innocent person﴾ — the verb cannot take a kasrah, so why is this verb in the kasrah form?

* Student: (...) upon the conditional verb (...).

* The Shaykh: And this?

* The student: It is a deleted weak letter.

* The Shaykh: This is jussive by what?

* The student: By the weak letter, the yā'.

* The Shaykh: By deleting the weak letter, which is the yā'.

﴿then throws it onto an innocent person﴾ means: innocent of this sin, such as the throwing of that group's accusation onto the Jew that he was the thief.

﴿has certainly borne a slander﴾ means: a lie.

﴿and a manifest sin﴾ means: a clear punishment. The word (mubīn) means clear, because mubīn may come in the sense of bayyin (clear), and may come in the sense of making something clear, since abāna and bāna are both used intransitively, just as abāna is used transitively. For example, you say: abāna lī al-ḥujjah (he made the proof clear to me), which is transitive, and it is said: abāna al-fajr (the dawn appeared), which is intransitive. Accordingly, the word mubīn here means bayyin (clear).

His saying: ﴿has borne a slander﴾ is because it is a lie against another.

﴿and a manifest sin﴾ is because he combined the fault or sin with throwing it onto someone else, so he combined two evils, and therefore it is a manifest sin.

* In the noble verse: the prohibition of throwing onto others what a person himself has done of fault. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿has certainly borne a slander and a manifest sin﴾. If someone accuses another of a fault or sin that was not previously attributed to him, does this fall under it? That is, a man accused a person of committing a fault or sin and said: he committed the fault or sin. Do we say that he has borne a slander and a manifest sin?

Yes, we say so, but the verse specifically addresses one who committed the act and then threw it onto another, because it narrates an actual incident, and narrating an actual incident does not carry an implied restriction so long as the meaning holds in this and its like. There is no doubt that whoever accuses another of committing a fault while knowing he is lying has borne sin and slander.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that evil deeds multiply with the multiplicity of their attributes, as shown by His saying: ﴿slander and a manifest sin﴾. This is the reality and it is justice. Consider one who slanders a relative and one who slanders a stranger: both are qadhf (slander), but added to slandering a relative is, what? Severing of kinship ties. So this evil is multiplied, and its sin is necessarily multiplied, because rulings are structured according to their attributes. Likewise, one who gives charity to a distant person and one who gives charity to a close relative: his act is all charity, but his charity to the distant one is charity only, while to the relative it is charity and maintaining kinship. Thus evil deeds multiply with the multiplication of attributes, and likewise good deeds multiply with the multiplication of attributes.

* Among the benefits of this verse: a warning against throwing faults and sins onto others, as shown by His saying: ﴿has certainly borne a slander and a manifest sin﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 113 (part 1 of 2):

Then He says: ﴿And were it not for Allah's grace upon you and His mercy, a group of them would have resolved to mislead you.﴾

﴿Lawla﴾ is a conditional particle. Its grammatical description is usually given as: a particle of prohibition for prohibition? Correct? A particle of prohibition due to existence (imtina' li-wujud)? What exists and what is prohibited here? What exists is ﴿Allah's grace﴾, and what is prohibited is ﴿a group would have resolved﴾. There is a sister particle, or a cousin, namely (law), which is described as: a particle of prohibition for prohibition, as in His saying: ﴿And if they had, when they wronged themselves, come to you and asked Allah's forgiveness﴾ [An-Nisa 64]. This is a particle of prohibition for prohibition. You say: "If Zayd had come, I would have honored him." And they have a more distant cousin, which is what?
* Students: Lamma (لولا)?
* The Shaykh: No, law is not lawla. (Lamma) (لَمَّا). It is described as: a particle of existence for existence, like His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [Al-Baqarah 89]. This is a particle of existence for existence: disbelief existed because the coming existed. You say: "When Zayd came, 'Amr came." The coming of 'Amr existed because the coming of Zayd existed. On this basis, these three particles have distributed existence and non-existence. (Lamma) is a particle of what?
* Students: Existence for existence.
* The Shaykh: And (law)?
* The Students: A particle of prohibition for prohibition.
* The Shaykh: And (lawla)?
* The Students: A particle of prohibition for existence.
* The Shaykh: Prohibition for existence. Here He says: ﴿And were it not for Allah's grace upon you and His mercy﴾. Grace (fadl) is surplus bounty, while mercy is more general, because mercy involves warding off what is disliked and attaining what is desired, whereas grace is the attaining of what is desired.
And His saying: ﴿a group would have resolved﴾ is the response (jawab) of (lawla).
﴿A group of them would have resolved to mislead you.﴾ Who is this group? They are those who claimed that the thief was the Jew, and they gathered around this and confused the Prophet ﷺ, and they resolved to mislead him. Here there is a difficulty, for the apparent meaning of the noble verse is that they did not resolve to mislead him. If we look at the story, we find that they did resolve; that is, they all came to the Messenger, denied that their companion was the thief, and accused the Jew of theft. So they resolved and acted.
The answer to this is to say: they resolved in a way by which he would be misled, but they did not reach their aim. So it is correct that His saying ﴿would have resolved﴾ is the response to His saying ﴿And were it not for Allah's grace upon you and His mercy﴾.
﴿A group of them would have resolved to mislead you.﴾ (An) here is a verbal (masdariyya) particle from which the preposition has been dropped; its estimate is: "bi-an yudillukum" (with them misleading you). Dropping the preposition before (an) and (anna) is regular. When the preposition is dropped, the following noun is put in the accusative. This is a regular rule, but it is regular only with (anna) and (an), as Ibn Malik said:
"...and with (anna) and (an) it is regular, when there is no ambiguity, like (I wondered that they should return)."
With other than (anna) and (an), it is heard from the Arabs and is not used as a basis for analogy. Among examples is the poet's verse:
"You pass by the abodes and you do not turn aside; your speech to me is then forbidden."
The evidence lies in his saying (al-diyar), and the original is: "You pass by the abodes (bi-l-diyar)" and "you did not turn aside," but the ba' was dropped, so the noun became accusative by removal of the preposition. However, it is not regular except with (anna) and (an).
﴿That they should mislead you﴾: (al-idlal) originally means: "dalla al-tariq", meaning he wandered and his journey was not upon clear evidence. The intended sense of misleading the Messenger ﷺ here is what these people resolved upon, but the grace and mercy of Allah forestalled the Prophet ﷺ from judging that the thief was the Jews.
This verse is like His saying: ﴿And had We not made you firm, you would nearly have inclined toward them a little﴾ [Al-Isra 74]. So it means: if you had inclined to them, even a little. ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death; then you would not find for yourself any helper against Us﴾ [Al-Isra 75]. Reflect upon this verse, my brother, and it will become clear to you the greatness of opposing the Shari'ah for the sake of Allah's servants: ﴿Had We not made you firm, you would nearly have inclined toward them a little.﴾
This is the Messenger ﷺ: were it not that Allah made him firm, he would have inclined toward them a little. So what about us? It is obligatory upon a person to be alert to verses like this, and to always ask Allah for steadfastness, that the blame of any blamer not seize him in the matter of Allah. If he were to do so, Allah would make him taste double life and double death, because the sin of the Messenger ﷺ is not like the sin of anyone else.
He says: ﴿And they do not mislead except themselves﴾: that is, by their scheming, their accusing of others, and their desire to mislead the Messenger ﷺ, they cannot mislead him; rather, what results from this is only the misguidance of themselves.
﴿And they cannot harm you at all﴾: (min) here is redundant, redundant. ﴿Min shay'in﴾ is redundant, redundant. How is it redundant twice? A contradiction! Redundant in grammar, what? Redundant in meaning. The first redundancy: is it from an intransitive verb or from a transitive verb? Pay attention! Redundant, redundant: is the first from the intransitive or the transitive?
* Student: Intransitive.
* The Shaykh: From the intransitive. The second?
* The Student: From the transitive.
* The Shaykh: From the transitive, because the meaning is that it is redundant in itself, redundant in meaning, i.e., it increases the meaning. Clear?
* The Student: The first, we said: redundant in grammar.
* The Shaykh: Yes, redundant in grammar, redundant in meaning. But we say: redundant in grammar. Is the verb (zada) transitive or intransitive?
* The Student: In grammar.
* The Shaykh: No, not in grammar; redundant, this is redundant, i.e., by itself. Clear? This is redundant for the meaning, so it is transitive. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety﴾ [Muhammad 17]. So it may be transitive and it may be intransitive.
In any case, ﴿min shay'in﴾: this (min) is redundant in grammar, what? And redundant for the meaning. So what is the redundancy in grammar?
It is that if it were removed, the sentence would still be correct. If it were in other than the Qur'an and one said "wa ma yadurrunaka shay'an," the sentence would be correct. It is redundant in terms of meaning, i.e., it increases the meaning, because the superfluous particles are among the emphasis particles; they emphasize the meaning. For this reason we say that (shay'an) here is an indefinite noun in a negative context, so it conveys generality; when (min) enters upon it, it becomes explicit in generality, like (la) of generic negation.
﴿And they cannot harm you at all﴾: that is, it is impossible that they harm you with anything at all, because Allah, glorified and exalted, has bestowed upon you His grace and mercy.
﴿And Allah sent down to you the Book and wisdom﴾: the Book is the Qur'an, and regarding the meaning of wisdom two views have been stated.
The first view: what is meant is the secrets of the Shari'ah, that is, the secrets of its rulings, for the Messenger's Shari'ah as a whole comprises secrets and great wisdoms.
It is said, and this is the second view: wisdom means the Sunnah. So Allah sent down to him the Qur'an and the Sunnah. The two meanings do not in reality contradict each other: Allah sent down the Book to the Messenger ﷺ and sent down the Sunnah to him, and likewise both the Book and the Sunnah include rulings and profound wisdoms, some of which the intellects attain and some of which they do not.
﴿And taught you that which you did not know﴾: yes, Allah taught His Prophet what he did not know. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And you did not recite before it any book, nor did you write it with your right hand﴾ [Al-Ankabut 48]. And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you an inspiration of Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor [what] faith [was]﴾ [Ash-Shura 52]. This does not diminish the Prophet ﷺ in any way; rather, it adds evidence that he is truly the Messenger of Allah. From where did this knowledge come to him? From Allah, Mighty and Majestic. For this reason Allah described Muhammad ﷺ as "ummi" (unlettered), a description of praise, not of censure, because his being unlettered, and then bringing this great Book which has defeated humankind, shows that he is what? That he is truly the Messenger of Allah.
﴿And taught you that which you did not know, and the grace of Allah upon you has been great﴾: this is like an emphasis of His saying: ﴿And were it not for Allah's grace upon you and His mercy﴾.
And what do you think of describing grace with greatness, from the Great One who has no greater? This greatness will be exceedingly great, because describing a thing as great by the Great One indicates what? A great magnitude. For this reason you will find that a poor man, for example, considers it a great thing to have a thousand riyals, while the rich man belittles it and does not regard it as anything. So describing it with greatness, coming from Allah who is greater than everything, indicates the greatness of the grace which the Messenger, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, was given.

* This noble verse contains many benefits. Among them: the demonstration of Allah's grace upon His Messenger.
* Among them: the affirmation of special mercy, for His saying ﴿and His mercy﴾ is a special mercy that was not for anyone other than the Messenger ﷺ. Mercy is of two kinds: general and special. General mercy is that which encompasses all servants; and what else?
* Student: General mercy.
* The Shaykh: What I asked you?
* Student: General mercy that encompasses all servants.
* The Shaykh: Yes, and what else?
* Student: ﴿My mercy encompasses all things﴾ [Al-A'raf 156].
* The Shaykh: The saying of Allah: ﴿My mercy encompasses﴾. Good. And ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [Al-Baqarah 163]?
* Student: And ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾.
* The Shaykh: As for special mercy, it is for the believers specifically, by His saying: ﴿And ever is He, toward the believers, Merciful﴾ [Al-Ahzab 43].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Prophet ﷺ is in need of Allah's grace and mercy, and were it not for Allah's grace and mercy upon him, he would have suffered what others suffer; by His saying: ﴿And were it not for Allah's grace upon you and His mercy, a group of them would have resolved﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that when a person is prevented from going astray, whether by a cause or without a cause, that is from Allah's grace upon him. This becomes manifest in that a person sometimes holds an opinion on some question, that it is forbidden or permitted, and then Allah brings someone to debate him on this question until the truth becomes clear to him and he returns. This is from Allah's blessing upon him and from His grace upon him. Sometimes the truth flashes to him without debate, either by reflection and contemplation, or by looking, for example, at other matters to which he analogizes, or otherwise.
The main point is that whenever the truth becomes clear to a person by any cause, that is from Allah's blessing upon him, so let him praise Allah for it.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: caution against people of evil, and that a person should not be deceived by outward appearance. But if there is nothing but outward appearance, he must judge accordingly, based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "I only judge according to what I hear"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6967) and Muslim (1713/4), from the hadith of Umm Salamah.]], yet he must be cautious, for a person may mislead others by his condition, as in His saying: ﴿A group of them would have resolved to mislead you.﴾
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that whoever wishes to mislead people harms none but himself; by His saying: ﴿And they do not mislead except themselves﴾; because they were in fact blind to the truth and called people to falsehood, so they earned sin upon their sins, and thus misled themselves.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the protection of the Messenger ﷺ from the harm of these people, or from their causing him harm; by His saying: ﴿And they cannot harm you at all﴾.
* Among its benefits: that the Noble Qur'an is sent down from Allah; by His saying: ﴿And Allah sent down to you the Book and wisdom﴾.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of Allah's elevation; by His saying: ﴿sent down﴾, and descent occurs from above. The elevation of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is of two kinds: elevation of attributes (al-'uluww al-ma'nawi) and elevation of essence (al-'uluww al-dhati). As for elevation of attributes, it is the perfection of His attributes, mighty and majestic, and no one who claims to be Muslim denies this; everyone who claims Islam acknowledges Allah's elevation in this sense. The second is elevation of essence, which the Salaf and the Imams of the Ummah affirm, and which the Jahmiyya, the Mu'tazila and the Ash'ariyya deny; they deny essential elevation. So what do they say?
They divided into two groups. One group says: Allah is with us everywhere; He has no higher place. If we are in the mosque, He is with us; if we are in the house, He is with us; in the market, He is with us; in any place, He is with us, and with so-and-so and so-and-so in any place. There is no doubt that this is manifest misguidance. Is the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, one?
* The students: One.
* The Shaykh: One. How could He be essentially present everywhere? This entails either multiplicity or divisibility, and it also entails that Allah be inside places while He is greater than everything: "the heavens are folded up in His right hand, and the earth entire is His handful." As for the others, they said: Allah the Exalted is not described as above the world nor below the world, nor to the right of the world nor to its left, nor connected to the world nor separate from the world, and where does He go? Nothingness. For this reason Mahmud ibn Sabuktakin, may Allah have mercy on him, said to Muhammad ibn Fawrak when he described Allah, Mighty and Majestic, with this attribute: "Distinguish for us between the Lord you worship and the non-existent lord?" That is nothingness. If a person were asked to describe nothingness more eloquently than this description, he would find no way to do so. As for the people of truth, they say: Allah the Exalted is, in His essence, above everything, and He cannot be everywhere, nor can we describe Him as nothingness as these people did.
Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah. Its basis is that Allah said: ﴿And Allah sent down to you the Book﴾, and it is known that the Qur'an is speech, and speech is an attribute of the speaker. So if sending down indicates the elevation of the One from whom it is sent down, that is evidence that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, for the Qur'an is an attribute that cannot subsist by itself, so it must be the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk, except for one who enjoins charity or what is right or reconciliation between people. And whoever does that seeking the pleasure of Allah, We will give him a great reward (114). And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows other than the way of the believers, We will give him what he has taken and drive him into Hell, and evil it is as a destination (115)﴾ [An-Nisa 114, 115].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk, except for one who enjoins charity or what is right or reconciliation between people.﴾
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah sent down to you the Book and wisdom and taught you that which you did not know.﴾
* Among the benefits of this part of the noble verse: that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah; by His saying: ﴿And Allah sent down to you the Book﴾, since Allah sent it down from Himself.
If someone says: there is a problem with this inference, for Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We sent down iron, wherein is great might﴾ [Al-Hadid 25], and He said: ﴿And He sent down for you eight kinds of livestock﴾ [Az-Zumar 6], and He said: ﴿And We sent down from the sky pure water﴾ [Al-Furqan 48]. There is no doubt that these three things are not the speech of Allah. So is there a problem with the inference?

The answer to that is: these things are entities that subsist by themselves, so they are created. The Qur'an, however, is an attribute that does not subsist by itself, because it is speech. It follows that it is an attribute of Allah and is not created. This is the position of the People of the Sunnah and the Congregation (Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah). As for the Ash'ariyyah (a theological school), they said: this Qur'an that is in our hands is created, and the speech of Allah is uncreated, because they hold that speech is the meaning subsisting in the soul. The reality of their position is that they have defined speech as what? As knowledge, not speech, because the meaning subsisting in the soul is not speech. Indeed, the Jahmiyyah (another theological sect) are better than them in this matter, because the Jahmiyyah say: the speech of Allah is created, and it is this that is in our hands. They say: this that is in our hands is created and is not the speech of Allah, but rather it is an expression of the speech of Allah, and it is not the speech itself. Thus the Jahmiyyah are better than them in this respect.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of the Messenger (ﷺ), in that he was the place where the Book was sent down upon him. Allah, blessed and exalted, has said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am 124].

* Among its benefits: that the Qur'an is *kitab* in the form *fi'al* with the meaning of *maf'ul* (written), and it is written in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), written in the scrolls in the hands of the noble, obedient angels, and written in the mushafs that are in our hands.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Prophet (ﷺ) was given wisdom (hikmah). So what is the wisdom? It has been said: it is the Sunnah, because the Sunnah is wisdom. But this view, although many scholars have held it, leaves something troubling in the soul, because the wisdom contained in the Qur'an is like the wisdom contained in the Sunnah, or greater.

Accordingly, we say: the intended meaning of wisdom is the secrets that the law of the Prophet (ﷺ) and what this Qur'an brought comprise. Allah, exalted, has sent down to His Messenger rulings and wisdoms. This view, in my opinion, is the more preponderant, because describing the Sunnah as sent down from Allah is also problematic, since not all of the Sunnah is revelation. Some of it is revelation, and some of it is Allah's approval of the Messenger (ﷺ). Whatever Allah approved for His Messenger (ﷺ) is from Him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of knowledge, since Allah bestowed it as a favour upon His Messenger, saying: ﴿and taught you what you did not know﴾. There is no doubt that knowledge is the most noble thing a person can be given after Islam. It is better than wealth, better than children, better than spouses, and better than the whole world. Look at the scholars whose knowledge illuminates us today, and look at the kings, nobles, dignitaries, and notables of their times and others: where is their remembrance? Gone. But the scholars' remembrance remains, and they continue to teach people while they are in their graves. This is a great virtue of knowledge. A person has been given nothing better after Islam than knowledge. The wonder is that knowledge, as the poet said:

*It increases with the spending of it,*
*and diminishes if you clench your palm upon it.*

Whenever you teach, your knowledge increases; whenever you withhold knowledge, your knowledge decreases. Wealth is the reverse. Were it not that Allah sends down blessing upon whoever gives charity, so that charity does not diminish it, wealth would soon come to an end.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knows only what Allah tells him, and he has no knowledge of anything except from Allah, based on His saying: ﴿and taught you what you did not know﴾.

If someone says: this implies that the Messenger (ﷺ) was ignorant before, and that is a belittling of him?

We say: No, it is not a belittling. Rather it is a perfection for him, because bestowing perfection after deficiency in this regard is itself a perfection. There is no doubt that before the Book was sent down to him, the Messenger (ﷺ) had no knowledge, as Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿You did not recite any book before it, nor did you write it with your right hand﴾ [al-Ankabut 48], and as He, exalted, says: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit of Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was﴾ [al-Shura 52]. Had Allah, exalted, not bestowed knowledge upon him as a favour... We ask Allah to bestow upon us and you beneficial knowledge.

﴿and taught you what you did not know﴾: from what thing did He teach him what he did not know?

Of course, not from everything. Even this verse does not indicate that He taught him everything. He taught him what he had not known before. It may be a thousand issues, or a million issues, or how many? Ten issues. For He said: ﴿taught you what you did not know﴾, and He did not say: taught you everything. With this we refute those liars who say: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knows the unseen. We say: You have lied, by the Lord of the Throne. He does not know the unseen. If, when some of his companions slipped away from him, he did not know where they had gone, even though they were in one place, how can you say he knows the unseen? And if he would enter his house and not know what was in the house, saying: "Do you have anything?"
