And those who believe in Allah and His messengers and do not distinguish between any of them, those – We will give them their rewards, and Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful. The People of the Scripture ask you to bring down to them a book from heaven. But they had asked Moses for greater than that and said, "Show us Allah outright," so the thunderbolt seized them for their injustice. Then they took the calf after the clear proofs had come to them, but We pardoned that, and We gave Moses clear authority. And We raised over them the mount for their covenant and said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating," and We said to them, "Do not transgress in the Sabbath," and We took from them a solid covenant. So for their breaking of their covenant and their disbelief in the signs of Allah and their killing of the prophets without right and their saying, "Our hearts are closed," – rather, Allah has sealed them for their disbelief, so they believe not, except a few﴾ [al-Nisa' 150–155].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers, and intend to make distinction between Allah and His messengers, and say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others," and intend to adopt a way between that. Those are the disbelievers in truth.﴾

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that disbelief in some messengers is disbelief in all of them, by His saying: ﴿Those are the disbelievers in truth.﴾

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the dominance of desire over many people, because those who make distinction between Allah and His messengers, or believe in some messengers and not others, are moved to that only by desire. The Jews say: "We do not believe in anyone other than Moses," and the Christians say: "We do not believe in anyone other than Jesus," purely out of desire.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: that disbelief in some messengers is disbelief in all of them. This is also shown by His saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 105], although Noah was the first of the messengers, yet He made his people's denial of him a denial of all the messengers, because disbelief in a messenger is as if it were disbelief in the category, that is, in the category of messengership. Otherwise, what is the difference between Muhammad, Jesus, Moses, Idris, Noah, and so on?

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: that these distinguishers say: "We are adopting a way between that," meaning: to please both sides. This does not save them from the punishment of Allah, nor does it save them from disbelief.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the censure of that method, that is, believing in some and not others, and that this is an ugly approach.

* From this follows: the censure of the people of kalam who wanted to combine the textual (sam') and rational ('aql) evidence regarding the attributes of Allah, saying: "We have taken this and that in order to reconcile the evidences." In fact they opposed all the evidences. They wanted to combine textual and rational evidence, but in reality they opposed both the text and reason, as is well known from their debates and the refutations against them.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the warning to the disbelievers of a humiliating punishment.

* And from its benefits: that the recompense is of the same kind as the deed, because they only distinguished between the messengers out of arrogance and desire, so there was prepared for them a punishment that humiliates and disgraces them. For this reason He said: ﴿We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾

* And from its benefits: that the use of an explicit noun in place of a pronoun is not considered needless prolixity without benefit. The reason for this is that the pronoun is more concise than what? Than the explicit noun. So no speaker should say that using the explicit noun in place of a pronoun is redundant and useless. We say: rather, it has a benefit. We mentioned earlier that among the benefits of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is what? Intending generality, and applying the description to those to whom the pronoun would refer had it been present. There is a third benefit, but we said "among the benefits," and there is indeed a third benefit: explaining the causal reason for the ruling. For example, ﴿We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾: had he said "We have prepared for them," it would not have been clear why this humiliating punishment was prepared for them. But when he says ﴿for the disbelievers﴾, this description implies causation, meaning that the reason for preparing the humiliating punishment for them is disbelief.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who believe in God and His messengers and do not make any distinction between any of them﴾.

When God, mighty and majestic, mentioned the state of those who believe in some and disbelieve in others, He mentioned the state of those who unite all of them in faith. The Qur'an is like this: when it mentions one state, it mentions its opposite. When it mentions punishment, it mentions reward. This is because it is *mathani* (oft-repeated, a text in which meanings are doubled), so one thing is presented and then its counterpart. Also, variety draws the soul and mind to what is being recited or heard. And so that a person's journey to God, mighty and majestic, lies between two extremes: excess and negligence. If a person inclines too far toward hope, he becomes secure from the plotting of God. If he inclines too far toward fear, he falls into despair and hopelessness regarding the mercy of God.

He, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿And those who believe in God and His messengers﴾. Belief in God has been explained several times already, and so has belief in the messengers. Belief in the messengers, peace be upon them, means believing that they are truthful in what they conveyed from God, mighty and majestic. As for belief in their *shara'i'* (laws), the Islamic law brought by Muhammad, may God's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, abrogated (*nasakha*, i.e. annulled through later revelation) all the previous laws. Nevertheless, we believe that their laws were from God, mighty and majestic.

﴿and do not make any distinction between any of them﴾ in the foundation of faith, not in practice. In the foundation of faith, we believe in all of them, and that they are all true, and that their messages are true and from God. As for practice, God, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿For each of you We have appointed a law and a way﴾ [al-Ma'idah 48].

The reason for this is that the foundation of faith is one thing, which is belief in the One, the Subduer, mighty and majestic. As for the laws, they differ according to the differences in people and their circumstances, and in generality and specificity. Therefore God made for each a law and a way. Even the Islamic law at the beginning of its revelation was not like the Islamic law at its end. At the beginning there was no fasting, no zakah, and no hajj. Then prayer, fasting, hajj and zakah were prescribed. This is because God, mighty and majestic, legislates laws according to what suits the circumstances of people.

His saying ﴿and do not make any distinction between any of them﴾ means in the foundation of faith. They say: "Our faith in Muhammad and our faith in Noah are on an equal footing," meaning that we believe that these two noble messengers, and likewise all the messengers between them, are upon the truth and from God. This is in the foundation of faith, as I told you. As for the laws, they differ.

﴿Those—He will give them their rewards﴾. The demonstrative ﴿those﴾ is used here to honour them. And it came in the form of the distant (*al-ba'id*) to indicate the loftiness of their rank.

His saying ﴿He will give them﴾: *sawfa* (will) and *sin* (the prefix of future) alternate frequently with the imperfect verb, but there is a difference between them. *Sin* is for certainty and nearness, while *sawfa* is for certainty with distance. This is the difference between them. Both indicate certainty, but *sin* is for what is near and *sawfa* for what is distant.

So is the giving of their rewards distant?

The answer: it is both distant and near. As for its extension, in that God rewards them little by little and then the full reward comes on the Day of Resurrection, it is without doubt distant. But as for every coming thing being near, it is near, as God, exalted, said: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Shura 17].

His saying ﴿He will give them their rewards﴾ means the reward for their deeds. God called the reward of deeds *ujur* (wages) out of His generosity and grace, mighty and majestic, as if He hired these people for a work they did, and then gave them their wages, like a person who hires people to build for him a building, and when they build it, he gives them their wages. This means that God, mighty and majestic, has committed Himself and obligated Himself, glory be to Him, to reward these people. There is no objection to God obligating Himself to whatever He wills, as He, exalted, said: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ [al-An'am 54]. And the earlier poet said:

The servants have no binding right over Him, by no means,
nor is any deed of theirs lost in His sight.
If they are punished, it is by His justice;
if they are blessed, it is by His grace, and He is the Generous, the All-Encompassing.

This is what the earlier poet said, but Ibn al-Qayyim, may God have mercy on him, qualified this, saying:

The servants have a binding right over Him:
He made obligatory upon Himself the great reward.
So He made a binding right upon Himself, but it is He who obligated it.

If they are punished, it is by His justice; if they are blessed, it is by His grace, and grace is for the Most Bountiful.
Or he said: "for the Benefactor" (*lil-mannan*).

The conclusion is that God, exalted, called the reward *ajr* (wage) out of His generosity and grace, as if those who worked for themselves were working for Him, and when their work ends, He pays them their wages in full.

His saying ﴿He will give them their rewards﴾ does not specify the amount here, but He specified it in many places in the Qur'an, and likewise in the Sunnah: a good deed is rewarded tenfold, up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples.

﴿And God is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾. Since these believers in God and His messengers, who make no distinction between any of them, may err, God concluded this verse with His saying: ﴿And God is ever Forgiving﴾. And since this correct faith is from His grace and mercy, He followed forgiveness with what? With mercy. These people must fall short, and no one does not fall short. So He concluded the verse with forgiveness. Then this faith that they attained is not by the earning of their hands, nor by the work of their hands, but it is from the mercy of God, mighty and majestic. Therefore it was fitting that the verse end with *al-Ghafur al-Rahim* (the Forgiving, the Merciful).

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: first, the noble Qur'an is *mathani*. When it mentions something, it mentions its opposite, for the reasons we mentioned in the explanation.

* Also among the benefits of this noble verse: it is necessary for us to believe in God and all the messengers. But how is faith, and in whom do we believe? As for faith, its manner is that we believe in the foundation of the message, and that they are messengers of truth from God, mighty and majestic. As for the laws, what? They differ; each of them has a law and a way. As for whom we believe in, it is obligatory for us to believe in everyone whom God mentioned in the Qur'an by name and identity, because they have been specified for us. And whoever is not specified, we believe in him in general terms, because we believe that among the messengers are some whom God has not related to us, so we believe in them in general terms.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is not permissible to make a distinction between any of them, and that is in the foundation of faith. Now, may we distinguish between them in excellence, saying: "This messenger is better than that messenger"? Yes, it is obligatory for us to prefer some over others, because God informed of this in His Book. He, exalted, said: ﴿Those messengers—We preferred some of them over others﴾ [al-Baqarah 253]. Based on this, what is the cause of preference? Is it *tawqifi* (revealed, based on textual evidence) or *nazari 'aqli* (rational speculation)? The cause of preference is what God granted them of virtues and excellences, the large number of followers, and similar things. As for whether it is *tawqifi* or rational speculation, we say: it is *tawqifi*. But when we know that God preferred this messenger over that one, either we know the cause and it becomes clear, or we do not know it.

For this reason the scholars said: the messengers of *ulu al-'azm* (the resolute messengers) are five, the first of whom is Muhammad ﷺ. God preferred him over others because of his great virtues that no one else attained, the excellences with which God particularly honoured him, and the followers who have no equal among the followers of all the messengers. Indeed, they are double the followers of all the messengers, because the Messenger ﷺ informed that Paradise has one hundred and twenty rows, eighty of which are from this *ummah*. This means that this *ummah* equals all the nations and exceeds them, and exceeds them by what? By double. Then Ibrahim, peace be upon him, after Muhammad, may God's peace and blessings be upon him and his family. These two noble messengers are the two intimate friends (*khalilan*) of the Most Merciful, and friendship (*khullah*), as far as we know, has not been established for anyone other than them. Then Musa, because he, peace be upon him, endured hardship with Pharaoh and with the Children of Israel, the like of which is not known to us for any other messenger.

Remaining with us are Isa and Nuh. Which of them is better? Some said that Nuh is better, because Nuh, peace be upon him, remained calling his people for nine hundred and fifty years, and they mocked and ridiculed him, as is known from the Qur'an and Sunnah. Isa endured the Children of Israel, and the Children of Israel are the most arrogant and tyrannical of people, as is evident to whoever reflects on the Qur'an and Sunnah. Hardship reached him to the point that the Children of Israel accused his mother of fornication, and claimed that Isa was the son of adultery, God forbid, may God curse them. He, peace be upon him, faced such distresses, and attained virtues and miracles that we do not know Nuh attained.

If someone said: "Either we make them equal, or we suspend judgment," that would be better, because there are no clear indications that distinguish definitively which of them is better.

The point is that our faith in the messengers includes faith in what God granted them of excellences, and that we prefer some of them over others. This does no harm. But if this preference leads to dispute, contention, and belittling our Messenger, when we prefer him over the messengers of others, then it is obligatory to hold back and be silent. Indeed the Messenger, peace be upon him, said: "Do not prefer me over Yunus ibn Matta"[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (4631) and Muslim (2376/166) from Abu Hurayrah, with the wording: "It is not befitting for a servant to say: I am better than Yunus ibn Matta." As for the Shaykh's wording: Ibn Abi al-'Izz said in his commentary on al-Tahawiyyah (1/244): this wording was not narrated by anyone from the books relied upon.]], even though Yunus, peace be upon him, left his people in anger before he was given permission to leave. That is why they were saved when they believed when the punishment came to them, because their prophet was no longer among them, so God saved them.

The point is that if we supposed that we wanted to compare Muhammad with Musa, and we had Jews present, then if we preferred Muhammad, they would go on preferring Musa and belittling Muhammad. In that case, restraint is obligatory.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven. Indeed they asked Musa for greater than that, when they said: "Show us God openly," so the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing. Then they took the calf after the clear proofs had come to them, but We pardoned that, and gave Musa clear authority. And We raised the mount above them for their covenant, and We said to them: "Enter the gate prostrating," and We said to them: "Do not transgress in the Sabbath," and We took from them a solemn covenant. So, for their breaking of their covenant, their disbelief in the signs of God, their killing of the prophets without right, and their saying: "Our hearts are uncovered," rather God has sealed them for their disbelief, so they believe only a little﴾ [al-Nisa' 153–155].
* The Shaykh: ﴿And those who believe in God and His messengers and do not make any distinction between any of them﴾ [al-Nisa' 152]. * Among the benefits of this noble verse: God promised those who believe in God and His messengers and do not make a distinction between any of them that He would give them rewards: ﴿Those—He will give them their rewards﴾.

* Among its benefits: the completeness of God's favour upon the servants, in that He called the reward *ajr* (wage). It is well known that a wage is binding on the one who hires. Who obligated this wage? God obligated it upon Himself. This shows the completeness of God's grace and favour, mighty and majestic. As for how these rewards are, God explained them in His Book and likewise in the Sunnah: a good deed is rewarded tenfold, up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples. The reward differs according to the differences in persons, differences in intentions, and differences in following.

As for its difference according to persons, the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, said: "Do not revile my Companions. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of you were to spend gold equal to Uhud, it would not reach the *mudd* (a measure) of one of them, nor half of it."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3673) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]] This is because they are his Companions. This is in terms of persons.

Likewise, the Prophet, peace be upon him, informed about the days of patience: "For the one who acts in them is the reward of fifty of the Companions."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4343) and al-Tirmidhi (3058) from Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani.]] One person is equal to fifty of the Companions. The meaning is that the hardship that befalls him in the work equals fifty times the work of the Companions, because the Companions were all believers, all upright. But in the days of patience, all people are contrary to this man who stands in obedience to God. He is a stranger among them, and it is well known that when one is a stranger among them, worship will be hard for him. For this reason the doer in those days has the reward of fifty of the Companions. This does not mean absolute superiority over the Companions, because those people surpassed the Companions only in hardship, in the difficulty of the work for them. But absolute superiority belongs to the Companions.

It is also according to sincerity. The reward is according to sincerity, so whoever was more sincere to God had greater reward. Indeed God said in the Hadith Qudsi: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in being associated. Whoever does a deed in which he associates others with Me, I leave him and his association."[[Narrated by Muslim (2985/46) from Abu Hurayrah.]]

Likewise it differs according to following. Whoever followed the Messenger ﷺ more closely, his reward was greater. Indeed the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Beware of novel matters, for every novelty is an innovation, and every innovation is misguidance."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4609) and al-Tirmidhi (2676) from al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah.]]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirming two of God's names: *al-Ghafur* (the Forgiving) and *al-Rahim* (the Merciful). *al-Ghafur* corresponds to sins, and *al-Rahim* corresponds to reward and good deeds.

Indeed God said in the Hadith Qudsi: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in being associated. Whoever does a deed in which he associates others with Me, I leave him and his association."[[Narrated by Muslim (2985/46) from Abu Hurayrah.]]

Likewise it differs according to following. Whoever followed the Messenger ﷺ more closely, his reward was greater. Indeed the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Beware of novel matters, for every novelty is an innovation, and every innovation is misguidance."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4607) and Ahmad (17144) from al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah.]]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirming two names of God: *al-Ghafur* and *al-Rahim*. *al-Ghafur* corresponds to sins, and *al-Rahim* corresponds to the reward and good deeds, because forgiveness relates to the sin, and mercy relates to attaining what is sought of reward and wages.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 153 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven.﴾ In another recitation it is read ﴿أَنْ تُنْزِلَ﴾ (an tunzila). Both have the same meaning.

The address in His words ﴿يَسْأَلُكَ﴾ (yas'aluka, "they ask you") is directed to the Messenger (ﷺ) specifically, and it is one of the addresses directed to him in particular. ﴿يَسْأَلُكَ﴾ does not therefore extend to his ummah.

An address directed to the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) is of three kinds. Either evidence shows that it applies to him and to the ummah, and this is clear, so it applies to him and to the ummah. Or evidence shows that it is specific to him, and this too is clear, so it is specific to him. Or there is no indication either way, and then the basic rule is that it applies to him and his ummah follows him.

As for His words, may He be exalted: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ لِمَ تُحَرِّمُ مَا أَحَلَّ اللَّهُ لَكَ تَبْتَغِي مَرْضَاتَ أَزْوَاجِكَ وَاللَّهُ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ (١) قَدْ فَرَضَ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ تَحِلَّةَ أَيْمَانِكُمْ﴾ [At-Tahrim 1-2]: here the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause. This is why He said ﴿قَدْ فَرَضَ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ﴾ ("Allah has already ordained for you") and did not say "for you" in the singular.

And ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ إِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّسَاءَ فَطَلِّقُوهُنَّ﴾ [At-Talaq 1] and ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ إِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ﴾ [At-Talaq 1]: this indicates that it applies to him and to the ummah.

Similar to this verse, ﴿يَسْأَلُكَ﴾ is for him alone; ﴿أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ لَكَ صَدْرَكَ﴾ [Ash-Sharh 1] is for him alone; ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ إِنَّا أَرْسَلْنَاكَ﴾ [Al-Ahzab 45] is for him alone; ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الرَّسُولُ بَلِّغْ مَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكَ مِنْ رَبِّكَ﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 67] is for him alone.

﴿يَسْأَلُكَ أَهْلُ الْكِتَابِ﴾: Who are the People of the Book? They are the Jews and the Christians. But the Jews in Medina were far more numerous than the Christians; there were Christians, without doubt, but the Jews were more. The reason for their large number in Medina is that they read in the Torah that a prophet would be sent, the seal of the prophets, whose law would be the most perfect of laws, and that his place of migration would be Medina. So they came from Palestine, because the Children of Israel had their home in Palestine, and they came from Palestine to Medina, awaiting the mission of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him). Allah has indicated this in His words: ﴿وَكَانُوا مِنْ قَبْلُ يَسْتَفْتِحُونَ عَلَى الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ [Al-Baqarah 89], "they used to seek victory over those who disbelieved" — they would say to the polytheists: a prophet will be sent, and we will be his followers and will overcome them. ﴿فَلَمَّا جَاءَهُمْ مَا عَرَفُوا كَفَرُوا بِهِ﴾ [Al-Baqarah 89] — "but when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it." This is the reason that three tribes of Jews were found in Medina.

So the People of the Book here, in origin, include the Jews and the Christians, but what is most common in Medina is the Jews.

﴿أَنْ تُنَزِّلَ عَلَيْهِمْ كِتَابًا مِنَ السَّمَاءِ﴾ ("that you bring down to them a Book from heaven"): is this request for a challenge, or for establishing proof, as they claim that he is not a messenger? Because the earlier books used to be sent down from heaven, especially the Torah, since Allah wrote for Moses on the tablets concerning everything and sent them down to him?

It is as though they are saying: either you bring a book from heaven and we will believe you, or you be like Moses, to whom a book is sent down from heaven, so that you become a prophet. The verse admits of both this and that.

As for the Quraysh, they said: ﴿لَوْلَا أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْهِ مَلَكٌ﴾ [Al-An'am 8] ("Why was an angel not sent down to him?"). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَلَوْ أَنْزَلْنَا مَلَكًا لَقُضِيَ الْأَمْرُ ثُمَّ لَا يُنْظَرُونَ (٨) وَلَوْ جَعَلْنَاهُ مَلَكًا لَجَعَلْنَاهُ رَجُلًا﴾ [Al-An'am 8-9]: "Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided and they would not be reprieved. And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man." That is, in the form of a man, because it is not possible for an angel in the form of an angel to address mankind; if Allah sent an angel to mankind, He would make him in the form of a human being.

﴿أَنْ تُنَزِّلَ عَلَيْهِمْ كِتَابًا مِنَ السَّمَاءِ فَقَدْ سَأَلُوا مُوسَى أَكْبَرَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ﴾: meaning, do not be surprised. Do not be astonished that they ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven. ﴿فَقَدْ سَأَلُوا مُوسَى أَكْبَرَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ﴾ ("for they asked Moses for something greater than that"). On this reading, the فَ in فَقَدْ is a conjunction linking to an implied clause indicated by what? By the context. The meaning: if they ask this, do not be amazed or consider this question great, for they asked Moses for something greater than that.

What did they ask? They said: ﴿أَرِنَا اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً﴾ ("Show us Allah plainly"), and we seek refuge in Allah. These were the seventy men whom Moses chose. Moses chose seventy men from his people for his appointed time. They came to Allah's appointment and heard Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, speaking to Moses. They heard Him with their own ears speaking to Moses, and still they did not believe, and said: ﴿أَرِنَا اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً﴾, meaning: otherwise you are not truthful, and what we hear is not the speech of Allah.

What happened to them? The thunderbolt seized them; they died at the same instant, the thunderbolt took them. But Moses, peace be upon him, asked his Lord to revive them, and ﴿قَالَ رَبِّ لَوْ شِئْتَ أَهْلَكْتَهُمْ مِنْ قَبْلُ وَإِيَّايَ﴾ [Al-A'raf 155] ("He said: My Lord, had You willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me"). Allah revived them, and they then remained among the Children of Israel.

In summary, these people said a saying greater than what they asked of the Messenger. They said: ﴿أَرِنَا اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً﴾, meaning: let us see with our eyes. This is an impossible thing. Who among them sees Allah, the Exalted, in this world? The prophets, peace be upon them, do not see Allah in this world. How, then, could these stubborn, obstinate people? So He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿فَقَالُوا أَرِنَا اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً فَأَخَذَتْهُمُ الصَّاعِقَةُ بِظُلْمِهِمْ﴾ ("They said: Show us Allah plainly, and the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing"), meaning they were struck and perished.

﴿بِظُلْمِهِمْ﴾ means "because of their wrongdoing"; the bāʾ here indicates cause. What, then, is the wrongdoing? That they transgressed in supplication: they said ﴿أَرِنَا اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً﴾, and this is a great transgression, both with respect to Moses and with respect to the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, for such a thing is never possible. Whoever supplicates for what is impossible has transgressed in supplication. ﴿فَقَالُوا أَرِنَا اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً فَأَخَذَتْهُمُ الصَّاعِقَةُ بِظُلْمِهِمْ﴾: what is the wrongdoing intended here? Their saying ﴿أَرِنَا اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً﴾.

﴿ثُمَّ اتَّخَذُوا الْعِجْلَ مِنْ بَعْدِ مَا جَاءَتْهُمُ الْبَيِّنَاتُ﴾ ("Then they took the calf after clear proofs had come to them"). In ﴿ثُمَّ اتَّخَذُوا الْعِجْلَ﴾ there is an ellipsis: the second object is omitted, meaning "as a god". The "then" marks sequence: add to this evil act another evil, their taking the calf as a god.

Was this calf an animal calf? No, it was a calf of inanimate material. They borrowed ornaments and fashioned them into the form of a calf-bull, and made a hollow within it, with an opening in its head and a hole at its rear. They would face it toward the wind, so the wind entered the hollow through a wide opening and exited through a narrow one, and naturally it produced a sound, a lowing like the lowing of a bull. The people of the calf were calves. As-Samiri said to them: ﴿هَذَا إِلَهُكُمْ وَإِلَهُ مُوسَى فَنَسِيَ﴾ [Taha 88] ("This is your god and the god of Moses, but he has forgotten"), meaning that Moses went astray and lost the god, because he had promised his Lord thirty nights, which Allah completed with ten, making them forty. He said: Moses is lost, searching for the god, and this is the god. So they took this calf they had made with their own hands and took it as a god to worship. Harun advised them and said: ﴿يَا قَوْمِ إِنَّمَا فُتِنْتُمْ بِهِ وَإِنَّ رَبَّكُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ فَاتَّبِعُونِي وَأَطِيعُوا أَمْرِي﴾ [Taha 90] ("O my people, you are only being tested by it; your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command"). What was their answer?

﴿قَالُوا لَنْ نَبْرَحَ عَلَيْهِ عَاكِفِينَ حَتَّى يَرْجِعَ إِلَيْنَا مُوسَى﴾ [Taha 91] ("They said: We will not cease being devoted to it until Moses returns to us"). They knew that Moses had not lost his god and that he had a god other than this, yet they remained worshipping the calf. This too is a great evil, for they placed with Allah another god which they had made with their own hands. Then they became like children: the wind enters from the rear and exits from the mouth, and they think this is its lowing. Well, if it lows, is it a god that lows? What benefit is there in it? But this shows the foolishness of their minds, and that they were at an extreme of folly.

﴿ثُمَّ اتَّخَذُوا الْعِجْلَ﴾, meaning as a god, ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِ مَا جَاءَتْهُمُ الْبَيِّنَاتُ﴾ ("after the clear signs had come to them"). ﴿الْبَيِّنَاتُ﴾ means the clear signs.

﴿الْبَيِّنَاتُ﴾ means the manifest ones that have no ambiguity, for Allah gave Moses nine clear signs, nine manifest and evident signs, of which one would suffice. He would throw down his staff, and it was a staff, an inanimate thing, a staff with which he herded his sheep, leaned upon, and which had other uses for him, such as defending himself and so on. When he threw it, it immediately turned into a manifest serpent, a great snake. This is among the greatest signs. Moreover, it was not an imaginary, illusory snake as the sorcerers' tricks were; it was a real snake that moved, ate, and swallowed, by the permission of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The sorcerers, I mean, filled the world with ropes and staffs, and it seemed to Moses that they were moving, until he felt fear within himself. He threw down this staff, and it began to devour these ropes and staffs. Glory be to Allah, in an instant these ropes and staffs dissolved, and then it swallowed the rest in an instant, contrary to the usual course, for normally food enters the belly, remains for a time, turns into blood, and then the waste is expelled. But this, by the permission of Allah, was swallowed, and apparently, Allah knows best, it came out at once, melted and pure. This is one of the signs of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Yet despite this, the clear signs came to them and they witnessed them, but they took the calf as a god.

﴿فَعَفَوْنَا عَنْ ذَلِكَ﴾ ("Yet We pardoned that"). Indeed, the Lord, our Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, pardoned them, Allah pardoned them, because they were commanded to repent, but it was a severe repentance. Allah bestowed grace upon us, the community of this Muhammadan Islamic ummah, by lifting it. They were commanded to kill themselves, meaning that each would kill himself. No, it means some of them would kill others.

The one community is like a single soul. Darkness was cast upon them, and they took daggers and knives, and each one would kill whoever was closest to him, even his father or his mother. When Allah knew from them the sincerity of their return to Him and their compliance with the command, since for a person to be commanded to kill his own people is among the hardest things for souls to bear, when they submitted and humbled themselves to this kind of repentance, Allah lifted that from them and pardoned them.

﴿فَعَفَوْنَا عَنْ ذَلِكَ وَآتَيْنَا مُوسَى سُلْطَانًا مُبِينًا﴾ [An-Nisa 153] ("Yet We pardoned that, and We gave Moses a manifest authority"): We gave him manifest authority. Authority (sultan) is according to each context; the authority of the prophets is their signs, because they are a strong proof by which they prevail over whoever denies them.

This authority given to Moses was the proofs and evidences, to the extent that Allah, glory be to Him, wrote for them in the Torah concerning everything ﴿مَوْعِظَةً وَتَفْصِيلًا لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [Al-A'raf 145] ("an admonition and a detailed explanation of all things"). The generality here, "all things," means what the Children of Israel needed. As in His words: ﴿وَفَضَّلْنَاهُمْ عَلَى الْعَالَمِينَ﴾ [Al-Jathiyah 16] ("and We preferred them over the worlds"), meaning over the worlds of their time, not over all the worlds, including this ummah.

So His words about the Torah, ﴿تَفْصِيلًا لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [Al-An'am 154] ("a detailed explanation of all things"), refer to what the Children of Israel needed in their era. But this Clear Book, of which Allah said ﴿تِبْيَانًا لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [An-Nahl 89] ("an explanation of all things"), encompasses everything, because it is a book for the ummah until the Day of Resurrection, so it must have brought what the ummah needs until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿وَآتَيْنَا مُوسَى سُلْطَانًا مُبِينًا﴾ [An-Nisa 153]. His word ﴿مُبِينًا﴾ ("manifest") derives from (abāna). But is it (abāna) intransitive or (abāna) transitive, or suitable for both?

* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: The third, yes. Good. Because the word (abāna) is quadriliteral; it is intransitive, as one says: "abāna al-subh" (the dawn became clear), meaning it became evident. And it is transitive, as you say: "abāna lī hādhā al-rajul mā ushkila ʿalayya" (this man made clear to me what had been unclear to me). Is this transitive or intransitive?
* Students: Transitive.
* The Shaykh: Transitive. So is this authority given to Moses manifest, making the truth apparent, or is it clear in itself? We say both, and this is based on the preponderant view, which is the permissibility of using a homonym in two meanings. Do you know the homonym (mushtarak)?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: It is a word whose meanings are multiple while its form is one. Did we not explain once that the divisions of words with their meanings are four? The homonym now is what has multiple meanings but a single form: one word that is suitable for two or more meanings, such as the word ʿayn. ʿAyn is for the eye that sees, it is used for gold, it is called ʿayn, it is used for the sun, it is called ʿayn, and it is used for flowing water, it is called ʿayn. This is the homonym.

Can a homonym be used in all the meanings it is suitable for? We say yes, it can, but there must be an indication, and the two meanings must not be contradictory. Allah the Exalted's words: ﴿وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا عَسْعَسَ﴾ [At-Takwir 17] ("By the night when it departs"): the scholars said ʿas-ʿasa is a word suitable for both approach and withdrawal, that is, when it approaches or when it withdraws. Can we say that ʿas-ʿasa here means both approached and withdrew?
* A student: No.
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: No, it is valid, it is valid, because the two do not contradict each other. Allah swears by the night as it approaches, which is at sunset, and swears by the night as it withdraws, which is at the break of dawn or sunrise.

So here, regarding ﴿مُبِينًا﴾, we say: since it is suitable for both transitive and intransitive, it belongs to the homonyms, and it is permissible to use it in both meanings, since they do not contradict each other.

Let us return to the benefits. We say: * In this verse there is evidence of the obstinacy of the Children of Israel, or, to put it more accurately, of the obstinacy of the People of the Book. I said "more accurately" because this is the wording that matches the Qur'an, and whenever you can use the wording that is the Qur'an's own and that corresponds to it, that is preferable.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah's defense of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), for He consoled him with His words: ﴿فَقَدْ سَأَلُوا مُوسَى أَكْبَرَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ﴾. Otherwise, it is well known that when the People of the Book asked the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) to bring down to them a Book from heaven, and he did not do it, it would surely have caused distress in his heart, because the People of the Book were known among the pagans for their knowledge from the books in their hands. So when they said: "Bring down to us a Book from heaven," and he did not, there must have been something in his heart, and he would have been afflicted with grief and sorrow. So Allah defended him and said: do not be amazed, do not consider this question great, for they asked Moses for something greater than it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: just as the Children of Israel harmed Moses, they harmed Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him), meaning the People of the Book, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لَا تَكُونُوا كَالَّذِينَ آذَوْا مُوسَى فَبَرَّأَهُ اللَّهُ مِمَّا قَالُوا﴾ [Al-Ahzab 69] ("O you who believe, do not be like those who harmed Moses, but Allah cleared him of what they said"). And the People of the Book harmed the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ). They intended to kill him, as in the story of the Banu al-Nadir. Likewise they actually killed him: they sent him a sheep with poison in it at Khaybar, and he tasted it but spat it out, yet it affected his palate (ﷺ), causing him pain, until in his final illness he said: «مَا زَالَتْ أُكْلَةُ خَيْبَرَ تُعَاوِدُنِي، وَهَذَا أَوَانُ انْقِطَاعِ الْأَبْهَرِ مِنِّي» ("The morsel of Khaybar has continued to trouble me, and now is the time of the cutting of my aorta")[[Reported by al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-Nubuwwah (1684) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah.]]. For this reason, some of the Successors, and I think it was al-Zuhri, held that Muhammad (ﷺ) is among the prophets whom the Children of Israel killed.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that a person asking to see Allah plainly is among the greatest transgressions, according to His words: ﴿فَقَدْ سَأَلُوا مُوسَى أَكْبَرَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ﴾. And is it deduced from this that it is impossible for anyone to see his Lord in this world?

Yes, it appears that this is deduced, because Allah said: ﴿فَقَدْ سَأَلُوا مُوسَى أَكْبَرَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ﴾, for if it were possible, their request would not be so monstrous. But it is not possible: it is not possible for Allah to be seen in this world. What supports this is that Moses (ﷺ) said: ﴿رَبِّ أَرِنِي أَنْظُرْ إِلَيْكَ﴾ [Al-A'raf 143] ("My Lord, show me that I may look at You"). But his words ﴿رَبِّ أَرِنِي أَنْظُرْ إِلَيْكَ﴾ are not like the words of these people, ﴿أَرِنَا اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً﴾; there is a difference between them. They asked Moses for vision out of longing for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and love of seeing Him (O Allah, do not deprive us of it), longing for Allah and love of seeing Him. But the Children of Israel said that as a challenge, in obstinacy and arrogance. Allah said to him: ﴿لَنْ تَرَانِي﴾ [Al-A'raf 143] ("You will not see Me"), it is not possible.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 153 (part 2 of 2):

Then Allah struck a parable for him, saying: ﴿But look at the mountain; if it remains firm in its place﴾ [al-A'raf 143] as it is, ﴿then you will see Me﴾. ﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾ [al-A'raf 143], what became of it? ﴿He made it crumble to dust﴾ [al-A'raf 143], it was leveled at once and became like sand, and it did not flee as people might expect. ﴿It remained firm in its place, [so] you will see Me﴾ [al-A'raf 143]. Does this mean that even if it had fled, you still would not see Me? No. It is as if the mountain could not contain itself until it was crushed, and it could not flee, so He made it crumble.

When Musa saw this tremendous matter, Musa fell down unconscious, he swooned. ﴿When he regained consciousness, he said: Glory be to You! I repent to You, and I am the first of the believers﴾ [al-A'raf 143]. That is: I did not ask this out of denial or disbelief, for I am the first of the believers, but I repent to You for what I asked, because this request is not permissible. And did Muhammad (ﷺ) see Allah?
* A student: According to one opinion.
* Another student: No.
* The Shaykh: No, he did not see Allah according to all opinions, because the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked: "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw light"[[Narrated by Muslim (178 / 292) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]] And in another narration he said: "Light, how could I see Him?"[[Narrated by Muslim (178 / 291) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]] That is, how could I see Him with these veils of light? Great veils of light. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "His veil is light; had He removed it, the glories of His Face would have burned away whatever His sight reached of His creation."[[Narrated by Muslim (179 / 293) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]] The meaning is: the glories of the Face of everything would have been burned, because His sight reaches everything. So what is this greatness? How could anyone in this world see Allah? It is impossible.

The Messenger (ﷺ) did not see his Lord according to all opinions. First, from his own words: he said, "Light, how could I see Him?" and in another wording he said, "I saw light," meaning light that prevented the seeing.

ʿĀʾisha denied this and said: "Whoever claims that Muhammad saw his Lord has committed a great slander against Allah."[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (4855) and Muslim (177 / 287) from ʿĀʾisha.]] This is evidence.

Ibn ʿAbbas: Shaykh al-Islam says that he did not say that Muhammad saw his Lord with his eyes; we do not say that his statement contradicts ʿĀʾisha's. The seeing that Ibn ʿAbbas affirmed is the seeing of the heart, which became so strong that it was like witnessing. This is the closer reading regarding Ibn ʿAbbas, because Ibn ʿAbbas was too learned to think that Muhammad saw Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in this world. The summary is that this verse contains an indication that seeing Allah in this world is impossible, and the other verse in Surat al-A'raf is explicit.
* A student: Shaykh, is it not the case that he saw Him in a dream, so the dream is absolute (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, no, in wakefulness. We negate it now; we tell you: in wakefulness.
* A student: May Allah bless you. Some scholars mentioned that a believer may see his Lord according to the measure of his faith.
* The Shaykh: In a dream?
* The student: Yes, the vision is not in a dream but a vision in wakefulness according to the measure of faith?
* The Shaykh: Not at all.
* The student: That is, with his heart (...)?
* The Shaykh: This is not called seeing with the eye. Our discussion is about seeing with the eye. Otherwise the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him; but if you do not see Him, He sees you."[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9 / 5) from Abu Hurayra.]] And the reality is that a person sometimes reaches a degree where it is as if he is witnessing Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, but this is not what we mean. We mean seeing with the eye in wakefulness, and this is impossible.
* A student: How do you call this seeing, Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: As I mentioned earlier, it is from the strength of certainty, as if he is witnessing. So it is seeing in terms of certainty, because when a person sees something he becomes certain. If he sees it with his heart and reaches this level, it becomes as the Messenger said: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him."[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9 / 5) from Abu Hurayra.]]
* A student: The two meanings in His saying: ﴿that You send down upon them a Book from heaven﴾ [al-Nisa' 153] have not become clear to me.
* The Shaykh: We said: it is possible that they said that as a challenge, just as the polytheists said: ﴿Why has not an angel been sent down to him?﴾ [al-An'am 8], ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ [al-Furqan 32]. It is a challenge; their intent was not to compare his message with the message of Musa, meaning that at that time it was not in their minds that his book would be like the Torah. And it is possible the meaning is: send down to us a Book as was sent down to Musa, so that we may know you are a prophet.
* A student: Shaykh, what do you say about the statement of some scholars who say: al-Samiri took dust from the footprint of the Messenger, and then when the calf was fashioned and he placed this dust in its mouth, it became at that time, at the time of lowing, alive?
* The Shaykh: No. As for his taking it, yes, because Allah said of him: ﴿So I took a handful from the footprint of the Messenger and threw it, and thus my soul enticed me﴾ [Ta-Ha 96]. But as for his placing it in its mouth and then it lowing, no.
* The student: It became alive at that time.
* The Shaykh: No, no. The correct view is what we mentioned first.
* A student: Shaykh, (...) in a dream.
* The Shaykh: (...) Shaykh al-Islam?
* A student: Shaykh al-Islam?
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is well known from Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, that he says: the believer sees Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in a dream, he sees Him according to his deeds, his faith in Him, and his following of the Messenger. But I have some reservation about this. It may be said that Allah shows this person an angel or something similar, according to the measure of his following and adherence. And it is mentioned that Imam Ahmad also saw his Lord. And Allah knows best.
* A student: Shaykh, regarding the statements of Ibn al-Qayyim, is he the closest to the truth?
* The Shaykh: Which one?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It is not Ibn al-Qayyim. We said: some of the Successors, and I think it is al-Zuhri.
* A student: Is he the closest to the truth?
* The Shaykh: Apparently it has not been made clear, but since he said: "The meal of Khaybar has continued to afflict me, and this is the time of the severing of my aorta,"[[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-Nubuwwa (1684) from the hadith of Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah.]] he points to this. But it is not clear whether they took a knife or a spear and killed him.
* A student: Shaykh, may Allah pardon you, is it derived from the verse the prohibition of transgression in supplication, and that it is counted among the major sins?
* The Shaykh: What?
* The student: Is transgression in supplication (...)?
* The Shaykh: Transgression in supplication, may Allah bless you, is that a person asks for what is impossible. It depends on the one being asked. It may be among the major sins and it may be among the minor sins, according to the one being asked.
* * *
* A student: ﴿And We raised over them the mountain by their covenant, and We said to them: Enter the gate prostrating, and We said to them: Do not transgress in the Sabbath; and We took from them a firm covenant. So because of their breaking their covenant, and their disbelief in the signs of Allah, and their killing of the prophets without right, and their saying: Our hearts are wrapped up. Rather, Allah has sealed them for their disbelief, so they believe not, except a few. And because of their disbelief and their saying against Maryam a tremendous slander﴾ [al-Nisa' 154–156].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan.
* Among the lessons of this noble verse, namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They had asked Musa for something greater than that, and said: Show us Allah plainly; so the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing. Then they took the calf after clear proofs had come to them, and We pardoned that, and We gave Musa a manifest authority﴾.
First: We have told you the reading. They said: ﴿Arina Allah﴾, and there is another reading, ﴿Arna Allah﴾, that is with a sukun on the ra', because it is lighter on the tongue; otherwise the meaning is the same.
* Among its lessons: the obstinacy and stubbornness of the Children of Israel, for they heard the speech of Allah, yet they said to their prophet: ﴿We will not believe you until we see Allah plainly﴾ [al-Baqarah 55].
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the greater the sin, the swifter the punishment; for His saying: ﴿so the thunderbolt seized them﴾, and the fa' indicates sequence and immediacy; therefore the thunderbolt seized them at once and they all died.
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's power, for He destroyed them all, and He is over all things capable. At the establishment of the Hour, He will blow into the Horn, and whoever is in the heavens and the earth will swoon except whom Allah wills, in a single instant, and He will blow into it again and people will rise from their graves in a single instant.
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the affirmation of causes, and that they have an effect in bringing about their results; for His saying: ﴿because of their wrongdoing﴾, for the bāʾ indicates causation. Some scholars have mentioned that on this matter there are a thousand proofs in the Book of Allah for affirming causes, explaining rulings, and clarifying wisdoms.
* Among its lessons: that Allah, Exalted, does not wrong people in anything; for His saying: ﴿because of their wrongdoing﴾. The seizing of them was not mere will; rather, they were the ones who wronged themselves, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿They did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 57].
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the demonstration of the foolishness of the Children of Israel, and that despite their obstinacy and arrogance they were a foolish people, by their worship of the calf and taking it as a god; for His saying: ﴿Then they took the calf﴾.
* Among its lessons: that they took it knowingly, so they have no excuse; for His saying: ﴿after clear proofs had come to them﴾. It is known that the sinner after knowledge is worse than the sinner without knowledge; indeed, the sin of one without knowledge has no effect according to the preponderant view absolutely.
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: that what the messengers brought is a manifest proof, hidden from none except those whose hearts Allah has blinded; for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿after clear proofs had come to them﴾.
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the demonstration of the comprehensiveness of Allah's pardon, for He said: ﴿and We pardoned that﴾.
* Among its lessons: the greatness of the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, shown by the return of the pronoun to Allah, Exalted, in the plural form; for His saying: ﴿We pardoned﴾ is without doubt for exaltation and not for plurality, as the wicked Christian claims. The Christian says: the deities are many. This occurs in the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, We give life to the dead﴾ [Ya-Sin 12], ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder﴾ [al-Hijr 9], and similar.
So it is said to him: this is for exaltation, and you are among those in whose hearts is deviation, following what is ambiguous. Otherwise you have clear, decisive verses: ﴿Your God is one God; there is no god but He, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [al-Baqarah 163]. But this one whose heart has deviation is the one who follows the ambiguous.
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: that Allah, Exalted, gave Musa clear proofs that are hidden from no one; for His saying: ﴿and We gave Musa a manifest authority﴾ [al-Nisa' 153]. This is the apparent meaning of the verse, though some have said it means dominance over the Children of Israel. But the correct view is what we mentioned. ﴿A manifest authority﴾, that is, by clear, evident proofs. It has passed us that Allah gave him nine clear signs.
Then the Exalted said: ﴿And We raised over them the mountain by their covenant﴾.
* A student: Shaykh, what is the connection of the ending of the verse ﴿and We gave Musa a manifest authority﴾ with what precedes it?
* The Shaykh: Its connection is clear: the worship of the calf by these people was not in obscurity, but after clear signs, as in His saying: ﴿after clear proofs had come to them﴾.
* A student: If it were so, would it have sufficed with that?
* The Shaykh: Is there not repetition of meanings? Much of the Qur'an repeats meanings for emphasis.
* A student: You mentioned the nine clear signs of Musa, and you did not mention (...) and you did not mention the staff?
* The Shaykh: How? In the Qur'an, explicitly in the Qur'an: ﴿And We indeed gave Musa nine clear signs﴾ [al-Isra' 101].
* The student: From among them?
* The Shaykh: That is, what are they?
* The student: Yes indeed.
* The Shaykh: Recite ﴿So We sent upon them the flood and the locusts and the lice and the frogs and the blood, as distinct signs﴾ [al-A'raf 133]. Recite it.
* The student: I do not memorize it.
* The Shaykh: Glory be to Allah.
* A student: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood and the locusts and the lice and the frogs and the blood, as distinct signs﴾ [al-A'raf 133].
* The Shaykh: These are five. After them? The staff, and the hand. How many are these?
* Students: Seven.
* The Shaykh: Seven. After it: ﴿And We indeed seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and shortage of fruits﴾ [al-A'raf 130]. How many are these?
* Students: Nine.
* A student: Eight.
* The Shaykh: Nine.
* Students: And the sea, Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: No, these that he mentioned are explicit signs. These signs are a clear authority and proof. But ﴿We sent upon them the flood﴾ means what? Drowning. He drowned the crops before they came out. ﴿And the locusts﴾ ate them after they came out. ﴿And the lice﴾ spoiled them after they were stored. Is that right?
﴿And the frogs﴾ spoiled the water.
﴿And the blood﴾: the correct view is that it is the bleeding, by which the benefit of nourishment is lost.
So consider now the chain from when they sowed until it reached the nourishment of the body, which is blood; and all of them were afflicted by it, and Allah forbid: the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood.
* A student: May Allah reward you, Shaykh. The saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿after clear proofs had come to them﴾, can it be derived from this, may Allah protect you, that ignorance is an excuse absolutely?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed.
* The student: Even the grave-worshippers who...
* The Shaykh: Yes, even the grave-worshippers. The correct view is that there is no difference, and that the religion is all one.
Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And We raised over them the mountain by their covenant﴾. The pronoun in ﴿We raised﴾ returns to the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, but it came in the plural form as exaltation.
﴿Over them﴾: that is, over the Children of Israel.
And (al-Tur): the well-known mountain, a great and large mountain, which Allah, Exalted, raised when they held back from carrying out the commands. The mountain became above them as if it were a canopy, until they thought it was about to fall on them. It was said to them: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ [al-Baqarah 63], so they believed with the belief of compulsion in reality, because they were threatened with what?
* A student: With death.
* The Shaykh: With death and destruction. So their belief was belief of necessity, and Allah forbid. For this reason, when they prostrated, the exegetes said: when they prostrated, they were like this, looking at the mountain leaning. And to this day they say that the Jews prostrate on the edge of the forehead, not straight, on the edge of the forehead, as if looking at something they fear will fall upon them.
And His saying: ﴿with their covenant﴾ (...).

**Commentary of Ibn ʿUthaymin (Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-Karīm) on Sūrat an-Nisāʾ, verses 154–155 (part 1 of 2):**

**Student:** I seek refuge in God from Satan the accursed. ﴿So, for their breaking of their covenant, and their disbelief in the signs of God, and their killing of the prophets without right, and their saying, "Our hearts are uncircumcised." Rather, God has sealed them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except a little (155). And for their disbelief and their uttering against Mary a tremendous slander (156). And for their saying, "We killed the Messiah, ʿĪsā son of Maryam, the Messenger of God," — but they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them. Indeed, those who differ concerning him are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption, and they did not kill him for certain (157). Rather, God raised him up to Himself, and God is ever Mighty, Wise (158). And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death, and on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them (159)﴾ [an-Nisāʾ 155–159].

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge in God from Satan the accursed. God, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And We raised the mount above them﴾. God Most High says: ﴿And We raised the mount above them by their covenant, and We said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating"﴾.

﴿We raised above them﴾ means above their heads. ﴿The mount﴾ is the well-known mountain, which God, Mighty and Majestic, uprooted until it was above their heads, so that they would take the Book with strength, meaning that they would act by the Torah with determination.

His saying ﴿by their covenant﴾ means a raising accompanied by a covenant, because God commanded them, at the time of its raising, to take the Book with strength. A covenant (mīthāq) is a firm pledge.

﴿And We said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating"﴾ means the gate of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

﴿Enter the gate prostrating﴾ means prostrating to God, Mighty and Majestic, in gratitude to God Most High for the blessing, because God had commanded them to go to this town and fight its people. But they said: ﴿Indeed, in it are a people of giants﴾ [al-Māʾidah 22]. The story is set out in Sūrat al-Māʾidah. After they had been made to wander in the desert for forty years, God permitted them to enter the town, and it was said to them: ﴿Enter the gate prostrating﴾, meaning while you are prostrating, that is, prostrating to God, Mighty and Majestic.

Is the intended meaning of prostration its literal reality, or is the intended meaning of prostration humility and submission, as in His saying: ﴿And to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly, and their shadows in the mornings and the evenings﴾ [ar-Raʿd 15]?

The apparent meaning is the first, because they entered on their *astāhihim* (buttocks), and God says: ﴿And We said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating"﴾ [an-Nisāʾ 154], but they did not do it. What did they do? They entered on their *astāhihim*. The *ist* is the *dubur* (rear). The meaning is that they entered crawling, seeking refuge in God, out of arrogance. It was also said that they entered on their *aqfāʾihim* (the back of their necks). And it was said to them: "Say *ḥiṭṭah*" (a request for forgiveness), but they did not do it; they did not say *ḥiṭṭah*. Rather, they said *ḥinṭah* (wheat). It is as if these people wanted nothing but to eat and drink, like cattle.

﴿And We said to them, "Do not transgress in the Sabbath"﴾. In another reading it is ﴿lā taʿaddaw (not transgress)﴾ with a shadda, and *al-taʿaddī* and *al-ʿadw* have the same meaning; it is only a verbal difference. The meaning is: do not transgress in the Sabbath by hunting fish, when they had been forbidden to you. God had forbidden the Jews to hunt fish on the Sabbath as a trial and a test. The fish would come on the Sabbath *shurraʿan*, meaning openly, floating on the surface of the water, and in great numbers. The Jews, as is well known from their conduct, were people of greed and avarice, and this angered them. They said: "What is the way to take these fish that come on the Sabbath *shurraʿan*, when nothing comes on other days?" So they devised a trick for this: they placed nets on Friday, the fish came and fell into them, and then they came on Sunday and took them. The act here, outwardly, is permissible, because they did not transgress on the Sabbath itself; but its real intent was violating the sanctity of hunting on the Sabbath. For this reason it was said to them: ﴿Be apes, despised﴾ [al-Baqarah 65], and they became apes, because the ape is the most similar of creatures to a human. By this act of theirs it seemed lawful, because they had not hunted directly on the Sabbath.

When it was said to them: ﴿Do not transgress in the Sabbath﴾, did they comply? No. Rather they transgressed on the Sabbath by way of trickery, deceit and cunning. Whoever deems the forbidden lawful through a trick is more sinful than one who deems it lawful openly, because when he deems it lawful by a trick he combines two corruptions: the first is deeming the forbidden lawful, and the second is deceit and outwitting the Lord of the worlds, who knows the treachery of the eyes and what the chests conceal.

For this reason, those who devise tricks to get around *ribā* (usury) are more sinful than those who practise *ribā* openly, because those who devise tricks deceive God, so they combine the corruption of *ribā* with the corruption of deception. Also, those who devise tricks think they are right, so they hardly ever desist from it, whereas the one who does a thing openly knows that he has erred, and perhaps his soul will blame him one day until he refrains.

﴿And We said to them, "Do not transgress in the Sabbath," and We took from them a firm covenant﴾ [an-Nisāʾ 154], meaning a strong pledge to carry out what they were commanded. But they did not carry it out. They broke the covenant and did not care, and they were ungrateful for God's blessing. For this reason He said: ﴿So, for their breaking of their covenant, and their disbelief in the signs of God, and their killing of the prophets without right, and their saying, "Our hearts are uncircumcised." Rather, God has sealed them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except a little (155). And for their disbelief and their uttering against Mary a tremendous slander﴾, and so on to the end.

﴿So, for their breaking of their covenant﴾: the *fā'* is conjunctive, the *bi-* is a prepositional particle, and *mā* is *zāʾidah* (superfluous) in its grammatical function (iʿrāb), but it is not superfluous in meaning, because every particle that is superfluous in iʿrāb gives emphasis, and emphasis is undoubtedly an addition to meaning. On this basis we parse *mā* as *zāʾidah*, and *naqḍ* (breaking) is a noun in the genitive after the *bi-*, because if *mā* were removed the construction would be *fa-binaqḍihim mīthāqahum*.

Where is the complement of the prepositional phrase ﴿*bi-mā naqḍihim mīthāqahum*﴾?

The speech of God explains itself in Sūrat al-Māʾidah: ﴿So, for their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts hard﴾ [al-Māʾidah 13]. On this basis the prepositional phrase is attached to an omitted element that is explained by what is stated in the Noble Qur'an itself.

His saying ﴿*fa-bi-mā naqḍihim*﴾ means *fa-bi-naqḍihim mīthāqahum* (so for their breaking their covenant). And what is the breaking of a covenant?

Breaking a covenant is to oppose it: that there is a covenant between you and another and then you oppose it. This is the breaking of a covenant.

These people opposed what they had been commanded and did not carry it out, so they broke the covenant. ﴿And their disbelief in the signs of God﴾: are these the cosmic signs or the legislated signs? The apparent meaning is generality: that is, and for their disbelief in the signs of God, when they disbelieved in Mūsā and made demands of him, and said: ﴿Make for us a god as they have gods﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 138], and other things known from the history of this people, a wrathful nation. Whoever wants to know something of their history should return to the book *Ighāthat al-Lahfān* by Ibn al-Qayyim, may God have mercy on him, for he explained their faults and disgraceful acts. We seek refuge in God.

﴿And their killing of the prophets without right﴾: the word ﴿*qatlihim*﴾ has three readings: ﴿*qatluhum*﴾ (with a *ḍamma* on the *hāʾ* and the *mīm*); the second reading: a *kasra* on the *hāʾ* and a *ḍamma* on the *mīm*, ﴿*qatlihum*﴾; the third reading: a *kasra* on the *hāʾ* and the *mīm*, ﴿*qatlihim*﴾. All of these are Sabʿī (canonical seven) readings which the reciter may recite.

But this is fitting only for the student of knowledge. As for the common person, do not let him hear a reading other than the one in his own copy of the Qur'an, because if you let him hear another reading, the Qur'an would become light in his heart, or he would consider you mistaken and say that you are playing with the Book of God, Mighty and Majestic. Just as ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, objected to whom? To Hishām ibn al-Ḥakam, when he recited the verse in Sūrat al-Furqān in a way different from how ʿUmar recited it, until they took their dispute to the Prophet ﷺ.

So if the common people hear a reading different from what is in their hands, without doubt they will object to you vehemently, even if you are right. Then, even if we assume they trust you, the Qur'an would become less significant in their souls, and a person must make the veneration of the Qur'an in people's hearts higher than anything else that is venerated besides God, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And their killing of the prophets without right﴾: *al-anbiyāʾ* is the plural of *nabī*. If *nabī* is with a hamza it is said *al-anbiʾāʾ*, and if it is with a *yāʾ* it is said *al-anbiyāʾ*. Both are readings: ﴿*al-anbiʾāʾ*﴾ and ﴿*al-anbiyāʾ*﴾.

His saying ﴿without right﴾ is a statement of the actual situation, not a restrictive qualifier, because it is impossible for the killing of a prophet to be rightful. Rather, it is a statement of fact that the killing of a prophet is not rightful. A qualifier that states the actual situation indicates causation, as if he had said: "And their killing of the prophets, because the killing of the prophets is without right." The right in the matter will come, God willing, in the explanation of the benefits.

﴿And their saying, "Our hearts are uncircumcised"﴾: may God grant us well-being. When they are called to the truth they say: "Our hearts are uncircumcised." *Ghulf* is the plural of *aghlaf*, and *aghlaf* is one that is wrapped, that has a covering to which nothing can reach. They speak in this way: ﴿Our hearts are uncircumcised﴾. This is like the saying of Quraysh: ﴿And they said, "Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a barrier"﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 5]. Quraysh were the greater.

﴿Our hearts are in coverings﴾ was said by Quraysh, and the Children of Israel said: ﴿Our hearts are uncircumcised﴾, ﴿and in our ears is deafness﴾, meaning we do not hear, ﴿and between us and you is a barrier﴾, meaning we do not see. Thus they blocked all the avenues, I mean Quraysh. They said: the hearts do not understand, and the ears—

**Students:** They do not hear.

**Shaykh:** And the eyes.

**Students:** They do not see.

**Shaykh:** They do not see. We seek refuge in God, even though the truth is at its clearest and most evident. But we ask God for guidance.

God Most High says: ﴿Rather, God has sealed them for their disbelief﴾. Here *bal* is for *iḍrāb ibṭālī* (a retraction that negates what preceded): meaning, rather, there is no covering in their hearts, and their hearts are not uncircumcised, but God has sealed them for their disbelief. Why? Because the origin is *fiṭrah* (the natural disposition), and the *fiṭrah* is the religion of Islam. Whatever reaches it that does not bring the truth to the heart is an incoming matter, an incoming matter, and not something original in it. So God declared them liars, saying that the hearts are not uncircumcised, but rather, what? But rather He sealed them, after they had been upon the *fiṭrah*, because of their disbelief.

His saying ﴿God has sealed them for their disbelief﴾ means He placed a seal upon them, and a sealed thing has a seal placed upon it; it is sealed, meaning in the sense of stamping.

His saying ﴿for their disbelief﴾: the *bāʾ* is causal, meaning because of their disbelief their hearts were sealed, so good does not reach them. For this reason He said: ﴿so they do not believe except a little﴾.

The scholars differed concerning His saying ﴿except a little﴾. It was said that the meaning is: they will never believe, and that such an expression is current in the Arabic language; that is, "none believes except a few" is a negation of the whole. It was also said that the meaning is: except a few of them, so the exception is from the *wāw* (the subject of the verb), meaning they do not believe except a few of them. On this basis they divide into two groups: a believer, who is the minority, and a disbeliever, who is the majority. It was also said that ﴿except a little﴾ refers to the faith, meaning they do not believe except with a little faith.

Then, does the meaning of ﴿except a little﴾ mean except a weak one, or except briefly in time, meaning that most of their time is disbelief, and faith may arise in their hearts but quickly goes out because it has no foundation?

All of this is possible, and the context does not contradict it. It is said that among them are believers and among them are disbelievers, and the disbelievers are more numerous. Then, are the believers themselves steadfast in faith and persistent in it? No. Then, is their faith strong and firmly rooted? The answer is no. On this basis the verse can accommodate all these possibilities.

Let us return to deriving the benefits. God, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And We raised the mount above them by their covenant﴾, and so on to the end.

- In this verse is a demonstration of the power of the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and that when He wills something His command is only to say to it "Be," and it is. Otherwise, who could raise this great mountain? And who could place it above their heads, not upon them so that they would die, nor so far away that they would feel safe, but close above their heads? Is that not so?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Then there is in it evidence of the strength and power of God, Mighty and Majestic.

- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the faith of the Children of Israel was faith under compulsion, because any powerful person who says, "I will drop stones on you from the sky if you do not believe," the one threatened believes. What would his faith be?

**Students:** Compelled.

**Shaykh:** Under compulsion. Accordingly, a believer under compulsion must have a weak, unstable faith; when the compulsion is removed, he may return to disbelief.

- Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is legislated, when cities are conquered, to perform the *ṣalāt al-fatḥ* (prayer of conquest), because of His saying ﴿Enter the gate prostrating﴾. Can this be derived?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** On the basis that the law of those before us is law for us, unless our law has come to contradict it. It has been said that our law has come in agreement with it: when the Prophet ﷺ conquered Makkah, he prayed eight *rakʿahs* of *ḍuḥā* (forenoon prayer) in the house of Umm Hāniʾ. Some scholars said: this is the forenoon prayer. Others said: it is the prayer of conquest, because it is not the habit of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, to pray the forenoon prayer as eight *rakʿahs*, so this is the prayer of conquest. Some of the caliphs acted upon it, so when they conquered a city they performed the prayer of conquest. How close this view is to the truth: that the Prophet's ﷺ forenoon prayer when he conquered Makkah was a prayer of conquest, in gratitude to God, Mighty and Majestic, for the conquest He bestowed, especially if the conquest was of a capital city. The Children of Israel conquered Bayt al-Maqdis, a capital, and Muḥammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, conquered what? Umm al-Qurā, the capital of all the cities.

- Among the benefits of this noble verse: God Most High may make something lawful at one time forbidden and permit it at another time, because He forbade them hunting when?

**Students:** On the Sabbath.

**Shaykh:** On the Sabbath.

- Among the benefits of this verse: the Jews are a people of cunning and deceit, since they transgressed on the Sabbath.

- Among its benefits: whoever devises a trick to get around something forbidden, even by means that appear permissible, is regarded as having actually committed it. How so? Because of His saying ﴿Do not transgress in the Sabbath﴾, and they transgressed in it through this trick. So whoever devises a trick to get around something forbidden by means that appear permissible has committed the forbidden thing, and indeed he has added to it.

- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the complete difference between this nation and the Children of Israel is made evident, and praise be to God. God forbade this nation hunting in the state of *iḥrām* (ihram): ﴿O you who believe, do not kill game while you are in the state of iḥrām﴾ [al-Māʾidah 95]. Then He tested them by sending game to them, saying: ﴿O you who believe, God will surely test you with something of the game that your hands and your lances can reach﴾ [al-Māʾidah 94]. The bird is reached by the lance, and the crawling creature is reached by the hand. What is a crawling creature like? Like rabbits and gazelles and the like, which a person reaches with his hand; he reaches out toward the rabbit and seizes what runs from him. The bird is reached by the lance, not the arrow. The lance, of course, is in a person's hand, and he hunts with it in this way. This was a trial.

God Most High says: ﴿That God may know who fears Him unseen. Whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment﴾ [al-Māʾidah 94]. What did the Companions do? What?

**Students:** They complied with their Lord's command.

**Shaykh:** They avoided it, they complied with the command, they avoided that, even though it was easy for them. But this nation is a nation that says, "We hear and we obey," and praise be to God. May God make us and you among them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verses 154–155 (part 2 of 2):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever employs stratagems (tahayyul, legal trickery) against the prohibitions of Allah from this Ummah resembles whom? The Jews. Any person who uses stratagems against the prohibitions of Allah has in him a resemblance to the Jews, whether in buying or selling, in what Allah has made lawful or unlawful in food, or in marriage. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) named the muhallil (the one who makes a divorced woman lawful again for her former husband); he named him, named him what? 
* Students: The borrowed billy-goat (al-tays al-musta'ar).
* Shaykh: The borrowed billy-goat.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, Exalted and Most High, does not punish His servants except after the proof has been established against them, as in His words: ﴿And We took from them a firm covenant﴾, a strong pact between Him and the creation, and then they broke their covenant. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿And We would never punish until We sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra 15].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of causes. Legislative causes are affirmed, and likewise the decreed (qadari) causes are affirmed all the more so, as in His words: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant﴾, where the particle "bi" (for/because of) indicates causation. Also affirmed is that causes have real influence on their effects, which is a requirement of the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. For if a thing occurred by chance in this manner, it would be foolish. But when a thing occurs bound to its cause, this indicates wisdom and perfection. O brothers, a person who does a thing arbitrarily, without a cause that necessitates it, is not considered wise. Rather, the one who does a thing through its causes and its effective factors, he is the wise one. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has tied effects to what?
* Students: To causes.
* Shaykh: To causes. But we must know that, because of our deficiency and shortcoming, we sometimes know the cause and sometimes do not. So in this there is an affirmation of causes.
People have divided regarding causes into three categories: one group was negligent, one group went to excess, and one group took the middle course. The best of matters is the middle. The first group was negligent and said: there is no influence of causes at all. Even the fire that burns paper has no influence on it; the burning of the paper did not happen by the fire but at the fire. Do you understand? They argued for this by saying that if you affirm that a cause has influence on its effect, you would have associated partners with Allah. Thus they said: any person who affirms a cause is a polytheist. In lordship or in worship?
* Students: In lordship.
* Shaykh: In lordship. The second group went to excess and exceeded the limit, saying: causes have influence by their very nature, necessarily, and causes cannot fail to produce their effects. These also erred; they went to excess.
The third category says: causes have influence, not by themselves, but by the powers Allah has placed in them. These are the people of truth, whether the cause is decreed or legislated. For this reason we find that some lawful matters have causes and also have impediments. For example, inheritance has a cause and has an impediment. Perhaps your father, who would inherit all your wealth if he were alone, inherits nothing despite the existence of the cause. Why? Because of the presence of an impediment. So the cause is not effective now. He who made fatherhood a cause for inheritance made killing, for example, an impediment to inheritance. Is this clear, O brothers?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Likewise the decreed causes. This fire burns, and Allah placed in it the power of burning. When Abraham was thrown into it, Allah said to it: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾ [al-Anbiya 69]. Burning was thus negated, although it is an effective cause by the command of Allah. But why? It did not have effect when Allah said to it: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾, so it became coolness and safety for him.
