He is the Judge over His servants, legislating what He wills for them by His command and prohibition, and He is the Judge among them by His law in this world and by His recompense in the Hereafter. This is ḥukm.
It also comes from ḥikmah, which is the perfecting of a thing and placing it in its proper place. There is no doubt that God, glorified and exalted, possesses consummate wisdom in His legislation and in His decree; therefore we say: wisdom is legislative and decreed.
﴿وَكَانَ اللَّهُ عَزِيزًا حَكِيمًا﴾ The appropriateness, meaning the appropriateness of ending the verse with these two noble names: because these Jews came contending, wanting to kill one of the messengers of God, mighty and majestic. So it was fitting to end the verse with might and wisdom, and here ḥukm is more apparent than ḥikmah; that is, He is the Judge, mighty and majestic, and for this reason He prevented these people from their corruption and from killing the Prophet.
* We take the benefits:
God, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿وَبِكُفْرِهِمْ وَقَوْلِهِمْ عَلَى مَرْيَمَ بُهْتَانًا عَظِيمًا﴾.
* From this verse is derived: the establishment of cause, due to His saying: ﴿وَبِكُفْرِهِمْ﴾.
* Among its benefits: disbelief is a cause of evil, corruption, curse, and distance from the mercy of God, mighty and majestic; because it is connected to an omitted element, as we said regarding His saying: ﴿فَبِمَا نَقْضِهِمْ مِيثَاقَهُمْ لَعَنَّاهُمْ﴾ [al-Ma'idah 13].
* Among its benefits: the Jews accused Maryam with a great slander when they said she was an adulteress and that ʿIsa was the son of fornication—we ask God for well-being—and this is a great slander.
But do we say that they disbelieved by their accusing her?
We say: As for whoever accuses her of that after God has cleared her of it, he is a disbeliever; not for the accusation itself, but for his denial of God's exoneration of her, may He be exalted. So his disbelief in this case is of the type of disbelief by denial (kufr al-juḥud), because he denied what God, mighty and majestic, affirmed. God, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿وَمَرْيَمَ ابْنَتَ عِمْرَانَ الَّتِي أَحْصَنَتْ فَرْجَهَا﴾ [al-Tahrim 12]. So God bore witness to her chastity of womb. Accordingly, whoever accuses her with what the Jews accused her of is a disbeliever, denying God, mighty and majestic. This is not on account of the slander itself; we declare him a disbeliever now because his slander is a denial of God, mighty and majestic.
We move on—though there is no complete connection—if someone slanders one of the wives of the Prophet, peace be upon him, ʿAʾishah, with what God cleared her of, would he be a disbeliever?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, he would be a disbeliever for two reasons:
The first reason: denying the report of God, mighty and majestic. The first thing God mentioned of the story was the slander: ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ جَاءُوا بِالْإِفْكِ عُصْبَةٌ مِنْكُمْ﴾ [al-Nur 11], which indicates that this matter, in its root and its details, is a lie. Whoever accuses the Mother of the Believers ʿAʾishah with what God cleared her of is a disbeliever, denying God, mighty and majestic.
Also, from another aspect: he has defiled the bed of the Prophet, peace be upon him. If the Mother of the Believers ʿAʾishah—and far be it from her that she did what she was accused of—were an adulteress, God forbid, then she would be corrupt, and ﴿الْخَبِيثَاتُ لِلْخَبِيثِينَ﴾ [al-Nur 26]. So it follows from this that he has impugned the Messenger, peace be upon him.
Add to that: he has impugned the wisdom of God, that He would make this adulterous woman a bed for the best of mankind in His sight—we seek refuge in God. Is it from wisdom that He would make His friend, His chosen one, and His intimate, Muhammad ﷺ, lie with an adulterous woman? It is not from wisdom. Those who accuse her of what God cleared her of are without doubt disbelievers; we testify before God that they are disbelievers and have nothing to do with Islam, because they denied God and His Messenger, because they defiled the bed of the Prophet, peace be upon him, and because they impugned the wisdom of God. There is no difficulty in this.
If someone slanders a wife of the Messenger, peace be upon him, other than the Mother of the Believers ʿAʾishah, who died while still married to him or who died leaving them, is it the same?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: The same. The correct view is that he is a disbeliever. Why? We do not say it is because it is a denial of God, since God did not clear any one of them. Rather, it is because he has defiled the bed of the Prophet ﷺ and impugned the wisdom of God, mighty and majestic. Therefore the preponderant view is that whoever slanders one of the Mothers of the Believers is a disbeliever whose blood and property are lawful unless he repents. If he repents, the ruler considers whether to lift the death penalty from him because he repented, or not to lift it because it is a fixed penalty (ḥadd); this is a matter for the ruler's judgment.
* A student: The second category of those who slandered Maryam, may God be pleased with her, before God cleared her.
* The Shaykh: No. If someone slanders her with something other than what God cleared her of, then he is like anyone else who was slandered, because she is not the wife of a prophet, so that we would say he has impugned the Prophet.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: slandering chaste women is a great slander, and for this reason God prescribed for it a fixed penalty. How much is its measure?
* The students: Eighty lashes.
* The Shaykh: Its measure is eighty lashes. Even if someone testifies that so-and-so, a man or a woman, committed fornication, and that he saw this man's member in her private part, and he gave this testimony, we say: now you receive eighty lashes, even if he was one of the most truthful people, even if he was one of the most pure people; we say: you receive eighty lashes. He says: I have another witness, bring him; the second testifies, and we lash him too, eighty lashes along with the first. They say: we have a third witness; we say: bring him, and we lash him also eighty lashes. All of this is protection of honour and of lineage. That is, the lashing of the slanderer is not a protection only for the honour of the one slandered, but also for lineages; because if his adultery were proven, the lineage of the adulterer would mix with the lineage of the husband, and one would not know whether this child belongs to this one or that one, and lineages would be lost. For this reason it is obligatory to impose the prescribed penalty on the slanderer.
Moreover, it is not enough to impose the penalty on him; his testimony is never accepted, not even if he testifies to something worth a single fils, because He said: ﴿وَلَا تَقْبَلُوا لَهُمْ شَهَادَةً أَبَدًا﴾ [al-Nur 4], He emphasized the negation with perpetuity. So if he testifies, even if he is one of the most just of people, we say: it is not accepted. Why? This is God's command: ﴿وَلَا تَقْبَلُوا لَهُمْ شَهَادَةً أَبَدًا﴾.
The third penalty: the loss of his uprightness (ʿadalah); ﴿وَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْفَاسِقُونَ﴾ [al-Nur 4]. Accordingly, every religious or worldly work that requires uprightness, he is never entrusted with it. But God made an exception: ﴿إِلَّا الَّذِينَ تَابُوا مِنْ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ وَأَصْلَحُوا فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ [al-Nur 5]. This exception, by agreement, refers to the last clause, which is the lifting of the status of corruption (fisq) from him if he repents. By agreement it does not refer to the first clause, which is His saying: ﴿فَاجْلِدُوهُمْ ثَمَانِينَ جَلْدَةً﴾ [al-Nur 4]. The scholars differed as to whether it refers to the second clause, which is ﴿وَلَا تَقْبَلُوا لَهُمْ شَهَادَةً أَبَدًا﴾, or not, on two views; and the matter should be referred to the judgment (ijtihad) of the ruling judge.
He said: ﴿وَقَوْلِهِمْ إِنَّا قَتَلْنَا الْمَسِيحَ عِيسَى ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ﴾ and so on to the end.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the Jews bore the sin of killing the Messiah, being held to account by their own confession; for God made confession a testimony, when He said: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُونُوا قَوَّامِينَ بِالْقِسْطِ شُهَدَاءَ لِلَّهِ وَلَوْ عَلَى أَنْفُسِكُمْ﴾. So we say: the Jews killed the Messiah and they did not kill him. What, they killed him and did not kill him? They killed him legally (ḥukman) and did not kill him in actual reality (waqʿan); they killed him legally because they confessed that they killed him, but in reality they did not actually kill him.
* So among the benefits of the noble verse: the ruling of the killing of the Messiah is established against the Jews by their confession.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that they—I mean the Jews—either confessed that he was a messenger and said ﴿رَسُولَ اللَّهِ﴾ to declare upon themselves that they did that out of obstinacy, or that ﴿رَسُولَ اللَّهِ﴾ is a statement of God, as the two views concerning it were mentioned earlier among the exegetes.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: attributing a person who has no father to his mother. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿عِيسَى ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ﴾.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse, a grammatical benefit: when a person is well known by his epithet, there is no harm in placing it before the proper name, because He placed ﴿الْمَسِيحَ﴾ first. Otherwise, the rule is that the name comes first, then the epithet, then the kunyah; but when he is famous by it, the epithet is placed first, as when you say: "al-Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal," or "Ahmad ibn Hanbal al-Imam"? The first, because he is known by it.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that ʿIsa, peace be upon him, is a messenger of God, from His saying: ﴿رَسُولَ اللَّهِ﴾, and he is the last prophet before Muhammad ﷺ was sent; for this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿يَا أَهْلَ الْكِتَابِ قَدْ جَاءَكُمْ رَسُولُنَا يُبَيِّنُ لَكُمْ﴾, what? ﴿عَلَى فَتْرَةٍ مِنَ الرُّسُلِ﴾ [al-Ma'idah 19]. "It is established from the Prophet ﷺ that there was no messenger between him and ʿIsa"[[Narrated by Muslim (2365 / 144) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]; and by this we know the falsity of the reports which claim that Khalid ibn Sinan—who was an Arab—was a messenger. It is said: there was no messenger between ʿIsa and Muhammad.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the nobility of ʿIsa, peace be upon him. How? Because he is a messenger of God, and it is enough nobility for a person that he be a messenger of God, just as it is enough nobility that he be a servant of God, is it not so? But messengerhood is more specific than servanthood.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that ʿIsa, peace be upon him, was neither killed nor crucified, contrary to whom? To the Jews. And the One who said that he was neither killed nor crucified is God, mighty and majestic: ﴿وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ وَمَا صَلَبُوهُ﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the folly of the Christians and their lack of discernment, in that they worshipped the cross and venerated it. If they were sensible they would have broken it. A cross upon which their prophet was crucified, and then they go on to sanctify it! If we took the apparent state, we would say: this is evidence of their hatred for ʿIsa, since they sanctified that by which he was tortured, namely the cross. But they claim that this is an honouring of ʿIsa, peace be upon him.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the perfection of God's power, mighty and majestic, in that the man was transformed into the likeness of ʿIsa, whether we say he was one of those sitting in the house, or that he was the Jew who guided the Jews to the place of ʿIsa. It is evidence of the perfection of God's power, mighty and majestic.
* Among the benefits of the verse—if we say the one killed was the man who guided the Jews—among its benefits: it supports the proverb: "Whoever digs a pit for his brother falls into it," for this man came guiding the Jews to kill ʿIsa, and they killed him instead.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Jews differed after they killed ʿIsa, according to their claim, over whether they had killed him or not.
* Among its benefits: they spoke of this without knowledge; all this disagreement is without knowledge, and for this reason God said: ﴿مَا لَهُمْ بِهِ مِنْ عِلْمٍ﴾; even all the disputants have no knowledge of it, but only conjecture.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: just as knowledge is negated from the Christians because they are misguided, knowledge has also been negated from the Jews in this matter, and they did not truly grasp it.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication of the blame of those who follow conjecture. Its basis: God negated knowledge from them first, and the negation of knowledge implies the establishment of ignorance, and ignorance is blameworthy; so following conjecture is also blameworthy.
But God clarified in Surah al-Hujurat that some conjecture is not blameworthy, when He said: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اجْتَنِبُوا كَثِيرًا مِنَ الظَّنِّ﴾, meaning: do not avoid some conjecture; ﴿إِنَّ بَعْضَ الظَّنِّ إِثْمٌ﴾ [al-Hujurat 12], meaning: but some of it is not a sin. So what is the difference? Conjecture based on strong indicators, not illusions or imaginings, is not sinful; and conjecture that has no basis is sinful.
But if a person suspects his brother of something bad, is it better that he investigate or that he ignore the matter?
* Students: The first.
* Other students: The second.
* The Shaykh: No. If you said the first, you erred; and if you said the second, you erred.
* A student: It depends on the situation.

**The Shaykh:** Yes, it depends on the situation. Sometimes it is in the interest of the listener to investigate until he reaches certainty, either to deny or to confirm. Other times it is better to overlook and ignore. If the matter is between you and this man, then ignoring it is better. That is, if someone conveys to you words about you from another person, it is preferable that you ignore them, so that nothing toward that person settles in your heart. Moreover, you may go to him and quarrel with him. For this reason, a hadith narrated by Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) states that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "None of you should bring me news about anyone, for I love to come out to you with a sound heart."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4860) and al-Tirmidhi (3896) from Ibn Mas'ud, with the wording: "None should convey to me..."]] The hadith has what it has in terms of its chain of transmission, but its meaning is sound. However, if the need arises to inform a person, that is a separate matter. For example, we know that this man has a friendship with that man and confides his secrets to him, and the second man relays his words like a sieve that does not hold water. In that case you must advise him. If you inform about his condition, this is not tale-bearing (namimah), but sincere advice.

The point is that conjecture (zann) now divides into two categories. Some of it has strong indicators, and in that case the sin is removed. Another category has no strong indicators, so conjecture in that case is sinful, ﴿except following conjecture﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the negation of the killing of 'Isa (peace be upon him), and that he was not killed with certainty, based on His saying: ﴿and they did not kill him with certainty﴾, according to one of the two interpretations. Which are they? That "certainty" refers back to the negation of the killing.

If someone asks: what necessitated this emphasis in the matter, ﴿and they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them. Indeed, those who differ concerning it are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it, except following conjecture. And they did not kill him with certainty﴾? What required it? Do we not believe in one word from our Lord, Mighty and Majestic? Yes, but what required it?

What required it is that the Jews have a strong propaganda for what they claim. Because of this strong propaganda, they were met with these affirmations that indicate the Jews did not kill 'Isa. Is it clear? This is from the mercy of Allah and from the wisdom of Allah. As for its being from His mercy, it is so that nothing of this propaganda clings to the hearts of the Muslims. As for its being from the wisdom of Allah, it is so that the matter becomes clear as it is, and is not left ambiguous.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that those who claimed his killing were not certain of his killing, but were in doubt about it. Based on what? 
* Student: On the second [interpretation].
* The Shaykh: The second, who knows? And what is the second possibility?
* The students: (...).
* The Shaykh: That ﴿certainty﴾ is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the subject of "they killed," meaning: "they did not kill him while certain; rather they were in doubt about that." And Allah knows best.
* Student: How do we reconcile the previous lesson with these benefits? In the previous lesson we mentioned ﴿Indeed, we killed the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam, the Messenger of Allah﴾. Is this the speech of Allah? Because the Jews did not admit it with their own tongues, so it was established as the speech of Allah. And we mentioned that it is the speech of the Jews, because they say: "We killed the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam, who claimed to be a messenger"?
* The Shaykh: We mentioned two views in it. We mentioned the two views in the explanation.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shayṭān. ﴿But Allah raised him to Himself, and Allah is ever Mighty and Wise. (158) And there is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him before his death; and on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them. (159) For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things which had been made lawful for them, and for their hindering many from the way of Allah, (160) and for their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it, and their devouring of people's wealth unjustly. And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment.﴾ [An-Nisa' 158–161]
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shayṭān. What do you say about the claim of the Jews that they killed the Messiah?
* Student: They did not kill him; rather they killed the one upon whom his likeness was cast.
* The Shaykh: So this claim is false?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence?
* Student: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they did not kill him with certainty﴾.
* The Shaykh: Good. The word ﴿certainty﴾ here, does it refer to their action, or does it refer to the negation?
* Student: It may refer to both aspects. If we say it refers to the killing, then the killing they carried out was not a certain killing.
* The Shaykh: The one killed.
* Student: The one killed is not 'Isa himself. And if we say it refers to the negation, then it negates that the act of killing was realized from them.
* The Shaykh: It emphasizes the negation of the killing.
And if the verse admits both meanings together, what is the ruling?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, it is interpreted as both meanings together.
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Is there a condition for this, I mean interpreting it as both meanings together?
* Student: That they do not contradict each other.
* The Shaykh: Good, and what else?
* Student: That the wording admits both meanings, and that there is no...
* The Shaykh: This is the meaning of "admits both meanings": that they do not contradict each other. The second?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Its meaning is one and the same.
* Student: That the interpretation is not in a manner (...), meaning a distant manner.
* The Shaykh: That is, neither of them is preferred over the other. If one of them is preferred over the other, then the preferred one is taken.

About His saying: ﴿except following conjecture﴾, how do we describe the exception here?
* Student: Disjunctive (munqaṭi').
* The Shaykh: Disjunctive. What is the rule for the disjunctive exception (al-istithnā' al-munqaṭi')?
* Student: When the excepted item is not of the same kind as the item it is excepted from...
* The Shaykh: When the excepted item is of a different kind from that from which it is excepted. So what is the point of difference here?
* Student: That following conjecture is not knowledge.
* The Shaykh: Because following conjecture is not knowledge.

Then He, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿But Allah raised him to Himself, and Allah is ever Mighty and Wise.﴾
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the refutation of what those people claimed about the killing of 'Isa son of Maryam (peace be upon him), since He negated his killing and then clarified that he was raised to Allah.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the elevation of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, based on His saying ﴿to Himself﴾. The particle "ilā" (to) indicates a limit, so this shows that the one to whom he was raised is above. The evidences for Allah's elevation in His essence are numerous and countless, from the Qur'an, the Sunnah, the consensus of the Salaf, reason, and innate nature. This has been repeated often and we have explained it, praise be to Allah.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that 'Isa son of Maryam (peace be upon him) is alive, based on His saying ﴿But Allah raised him to Himself﴾. This requires that he was raised with his body, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken up with his body through the heavens.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of these two names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, namely: al-'Azīz (the Mighty) and al-Ḥakīm (the Wise). Al-'Azīz is the one characterized by might, and al-Ḥakīm is the one characterized by judgment and wisdom, since it derives from (ḥakama) and (aḥkama). We have already said that Allah's might is divided into three categories: might of rank (ʿizzat al-qadr), might of subjugation (ʿizzat al-qahr), and might of inaccessibility (ʿizzat al-imtināʿ). These are three meanings.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of wisdom to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He does not decree anything except for a wisdom, and He does not do anything except for a wisdom. This wisdom may be known to people, and it may be unknown to them.
* Among its benefits: the obligation for a person to be content with Allah's ruling and to be pleased with His decree. The obligation to be content with Allah's ruling is because when he believes it is for a wisdom, he must be content with it. For this reason, the righteous Salaf did not satisfy the souls when a difficulty arose except with the texts, as 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) did when she was asked: "Why does a menstruating woman make up the fasting but not the prayer?" She said: "This used to happen to us, and we were commanded to make up the fast, and we were not commanded to make up the prayer."[[Narrated by Muslim (335/69) from 'A'isha.]]
As for being pleased with His decree, what is meant is that a person should be pleased with Allah's decree, not merely with the thing decreed, because the thing decreed has detail. But the decree, as the decree of Allah, he must be pleased with it. This is part of the completeness of Tawhid al-Rububiyyah (affirmation of Allah's lordship).
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of judgment to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Judgment belongs to Allah both in the cosmic (kawnan) and the legislative (shar'an) sense. As for the cosmic judgment, it is binding on everyone: Muslim, disbeliever, believer, wicked. Everyone is subject to the cosmic judgment. As for the legislative judgment, some people submit to it and some do not. The believers submit to it, and the disbelievers do not submit to it.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death﴾. ﴿In﴾ here is negating; i.e., there is not any one of the People of the Scripture except that he will surely believe in him.

The particle (in) (inna, here meaning "if/there is not") comes in the Arabic language in various ways:

It comes as a negation, as in this verse, and its examples are many. It is most often a negation when it is followed by (illa) (except), such as: ﴿This is not but clear magic﴾ [al-Ma'idah 110], ﴿This is not but a fabrication﴾ [Sad 7], ﴿This is not but the legends of the former peoples﴾ [al-An'am 25], ﴿This is not but the custom of the former peoples﴾ [ash-Shu'ara' 137]. So (in) is here a negation.

It comes as a lightened form of the heavy (inna), as in: in Zayd la-qa'im (Indeed Zayd is standing), so it is a lightened form of the heavy.

It comes as a conditional, as in: in qama Zayd qama 'Amr (If Zayd stands, 'Amr stands).

As for His saying ﴿of the People of the Scripture﴾, the intended are the Jews and the Christians. As for His saying ﴿but that he will surely believe in him﴾, this is an exception from an omitted element, and the meaning is: "And there is not any one of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him." On this basis, His saying ﴿of the People of the Scripture﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, indicated by the context. What is the omitted predicate's estimate?

* Student: "Ahadun" (anyone).

* The Shaykh: "Ahadun" (anyone).

As for His saying ﴿but that he will surely believe in him before his death﴾, we find the verb here in the fatha form: ﴿la-yu'minanna bihi﴾, although we do not see a particle of nasb. Why?

* Student: Because it is joined to the emphatic nun (nun al-tawkid).

* The Shaykh: That is, it is built on fatha because it is joined to the emphatic nun.

As for His saying ﴿in him before his death﴾: ﴿bihi﴾ means: in 'Isa, peace be upon him. The pronoun in ﴿before his death﴾ refers to 'Isa. It was also said that it refers to the man of the People of the Scripture; meaning that none of the People of the Scripture will be present at his death without believing in 'Isa. Or the meaning is: none of the People of the Scripture after the descent of 'Isa will fail to believe in 'Isa. Both meanings are correct, and the second is more apparent: that the pronoun refers to 'Isa, peace be upon him, because 'Isa will descend at the end of time, break the cross, kill the pig, and accept only Islam; he will not even accept the jizyah.

As for His saying ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them﴾, this is an adverbial phrase whose governing verb is ﴿will be﴾. The meaning: 'Isa son of Maryam, peace be upon him, will be a witness against them on the Day of Resurrection.

The meaning of the noble verse: there is no one of the People of the Scripture who does not believe in 'Isa before 'Isa dies. On this estimate, the meaning is: none of the People of the Scripture who lived to see 'Isa but believed in him before he died. On the second view, that the pronoun refers to the individual of the People of the Scripture, the meaning is: no person of the People of the Scripture will be present at death without believing in 'Isa—what? Without believing in 'Isa. Even the Jews who used to deny his prophethood will believe in him.

As for His saying ﴿of the People of the Scripture﴾: they are the Jews and the Christians, and they were so named because they have living books, even if altered: the Torah for the Jews and the Gospel for the Christians. For this reason they are called the People of the Scripture. No book is known to have survived until the mission of the Messenger, peace be upon him, of what the messengers brought, except the Torah and the Gospel. It was said that the Magians have a book that was revealed, or that they have some doubtful claim, but the correct view is otherwise: no book remains until the mission of the Messenger except the Torah and the Gospel.

As for His saying ﴿he will surely believe in him﴾: it means belief of acceptance and submission, not mere affirmation, because mere affirmation is not called faith. For this reason the faith of Abu Talib is not judged as valid, even though he affirmed it; rather, one must accept what a person believes in and submit to it.

As for His saying ﴿before his death﴾: meaning before the death of 'Isa or the death of the person, and that is when he sees the truth. When the Scripturist sees the truth, whether that is by the arrival of death or by the descent of 'Isa, peace be upon him, he will accept. But this faith will be like compelled faith, because while they were in their choice they did not believe in 'Isa but disbelieved in him.

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them﴾. This is stated in the saying of the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿And [beware the day] when Allah says, "O 'Isa, son of Maryam, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as deities besides Allah?'" He will say, "Exalted are You! It was not for me to say that to which I have no right. If I had said it, You would have known it. You know what is within myself, and I do not know what is within Yourself. Indeed, You, it is You who is the Knower of the unseen." I did not say to them except what You commanded me—"Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord." And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them; but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them, and You are, over all things, Witness﴾ [al-Ma'idah 116–117]. So on the Day of Resurrection 'Isa son of Maryam will testify against his people that he said to them only what Allah commanded him: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord."

In this noble verse there are many benefits:

* Among them: a People of the Scripture may believe under compulsion, either at his death or when 'Isa descends, but does this faith benefit him?

The texts indicate that compelled faith does not benefit, and that faith when the appointed time has come does not benefit, due to the saying of the Most High: ﴿And repentance is not [accepted] from those who continue doing evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now"﴾ [an-Nisa' 18]. However, compelled faith in other circumstances may take root in a person's heart; one may believe first out of fear of the sword, then faith settles in his heart, becomes firm, and becomes true faith for which he is rewarded and by which he is saved from the Fire.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of death for all humans, even the prophets die. Allah the Most High said: ﴿Every soul will taste death﴾ [Al 'Imran 185], and He said: ﴿And We did not grant to any human before you eternity. So if you die, would they be eternal?﴾ [al-Anbiya' 34].

* Student: Shaykh, we have said that 'Isa was raised alive. What is the answer to the saying of the Most High: ﴿When Allah said, "O 'Isa, indeed I will take you and raise you to Myself"﴾ [Al 'Imran 55]?

* The Shaykh: The answer to this is that the saying of the Most High ﴿Indeed I will take you﴾ has several views:

The first: that by death is meant sleep.

(...) The saying of the Most High: ﴿It is He who takes you in death by night and knows what you have committed by day; then He revives you therein﴾ [al-An'am 60]. The meaning is that when Allah wanted to raise him, He cast sleep upon him so that he would not be startled by this raising.

The second view: ﴿Indeed I will take you﴾ means: I will seize you, as one says: "So-and-so took (tawaffa) his due," i.e., he received it in full and took it.

The third view: the verse is not in its mentioned order, and the meaning is: "I will raise you to Me and take you," so the order here is an order of mention, not of meaning.

All of these are sound answers, and the most apparent of them is the first: that what is meant is the death of sleep, and that Allah cast sleep upon him so that at the time of his raising he would be neither startled nor affected.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that death is established for the messengers, peace be upon them, and for those below them a fortiori, and we have already mentioned the evidences for this.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of the Resurrection, due to His saying: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them﴾. We have already explained why this day is called the Day of Resurrection. Who can clarify it for us?

* Student: Because people rise to the gathering.

* The Shaykh: For the people's rising from their graves to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. What is the evidence?

* The Student: His saying: ﴿The Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 6].

* The Shaykh: Yes. And the second?

* Student: The witnesses will stand.

* The Shaykh: The witnesses will be established. What is the evidence?

* The Student: ﴿And the Day the witnesses will stand﴾ [Ghafir 51].

* The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, We will support Our messengers and those who believe in the worldly life and on the Day the witnesses will stand﴾ [Ghafir 51]. Third?

* Student: That it is a day on which justice is established.

* The Shaykh: Yes; due to His saying: ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Anbiya' 47].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the messengers, peace be upon them, bear witness over their nations, due to His saying: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them﴾, and this is general for all messengers, due to His saying: ﴿So how [will it be] when We bring from every nation a witness and bring you, [O Muhammad], as a witness against these?﴾ [an-Nisa' 41].

Will the scholars, who are the heirs of the prophets, also be witnesses?

The answer: Yes; the scholars bear witness over the nations that the message reached them, and they bear witness for the messengers that they conveyed it. For this reason the scholars are the heirs of the prophets.

* We may also say: among the benefits of this verse: that on the Day of Resurrection people will speak, be questioned, and converse privately, or is that not possible?

It is possible, because Allah says: ﴿And [beware the day] when Allah says, "O 'Isa, son of Maryam, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as deities besides Allah?'"﴾ and he answered: ﴿He will say, "Exalted are You! It was not for me to say that to which I have no right."﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 160–161 (part 1 of 2):

(...) ﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them﴾. The (fa') here is conjunctive, linking to what preceded, and the (ba') is causal. Dhulm (wrongdoing) originally means deficiency or diminution, as in the words of Allah: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short therein at all﴾ [al-Kahf 33]. In the sharia, however, it means transgression, whether by neglecting an obligation or by committing a prohibited act.
His words ﴿of those who were Jews﴾ refer to the people of Musa, when they said: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾ [al-A'raf 156], meaning we have repented. Despite their turning back and their commitment to returning to Allah, they wronged themselves.
﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them﴾. This verb is the governing element of the phrase ﴿for wrongdoing﴾; that is, the prepositional phrase ﴿bi-zulmin﴾ is connected to ﴿harramna﴾ (We made unlawful). Tahrim (making unlawful) linguistically means prohibition, as in the term harim al-bi'r (the protected zone around a well), which is the area around it that prevents others from reviving the land near it. From this, women are called harim because they are veiled and protected from transgression against them.
﴿We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them﴾. ﴿Tayyibat﴾ means foods that are good, and it is an adjective of a deleted noun. Tayyib (good) is the opposite of khabith (bad), and khabith has several usages: sometimes it refers to what is impure (najis), sometimes to what is inferior (radi'), and sometimes to what is prohibited in general.
His words ﴿good things which had been lawful for them﴾ mean that they were lawful originally and remained good, but they were made unlawful for them because of their wrongdoing.
﴿Which had been lawful for them﴾: who is the one who makes lawful? The one who makes lawful is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, since the matter is in His hand.
﴿And for their hindering many from the way of Allah﴾. The (wa') is a conjunction particle, and (ṣadd) is a verbal noun that may derive from a transitive verb or from an intransitive verb, because ṣadda can be intransitive or transitive. One says ṣadda al-rajulu 'an kadhā, meaning he turned away from something, and ṣadda ghayrahu 'an kadhā, meaning he diverted another from it. Both are possible here: they turned themselves away from the way of Allah greatly, and they also diverted others, because of the book they possessed, with which they confused and deceived people, saying that Muhammad ﷺ is not the awaited prophet, and similar things.
His words ﴿from the way of Allah﴾: what is meant by ﴿the way of Allah﴾ is His sharia which Allah legislated for His servants. It is called (the way of Allah) because it is a path leading to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and because Allah Himself established it for the servants, and no one else legislated it. It is therefore attributed to Allah in two respects. The first is that it leads to Him, as one says, for example: this is the road to Madina, this is the road to Makka. The second is that Allah established it for the servants and legislated it for them. It is sometimes also attributed to its travellers, as in the words of Allah: ﴿and follows other than the way of the believers﴾ [al-Nisa' 115], where the way is attributed to the believers in respect of their being those who travel it. Accordingly, when the way is attributed to Allah, it carries two senses; when attributed to the servants, it carries one sense.
﴿Much﴾ (kathīran): its i'rab (grammatical analysis) varies with the verb ṣadd. If it is intransitive, it is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, meaning greatly turning away. If it is transitive, it is the object of ṣadd. If you wish, you may say it is an adjective of the deleted object of ṣadd, meaning a great many people. In reality they deserve both descriptions, for they turned themselves away and turned others away.
﴿And their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it﴾. This is the third attribute. He did not say "consuming" (akl), because akhdh (taking) is more general: a person may take usury without consuming it, using it in clothing or building and the like, and he may take it for eating. Sometimes it is expressed with "eating," as in the words of Allah: ﴿Those who consume usury will not stand except as one stands whom Satan has driven to madness by touch﴾ [al-Baqara 275], and sometimes it is expressed with "taking," which is more general. But the expression with "eating" is more severe, because the practice of the one who eats usury is more severe than the practice of one who does not eat it, and more severe than the practice of the one who merely takes it, since the taker may use usury or spend it on other things besides eating.
His words ﴿usury﴾: riba linguistically means increase. In the sharia it means increase in specific items which the Prophet ﷺ explained, six items. What are they?
* Student: Gold, silver, barley, wheat, dates, and salt.
* The Shaykh: And salt. These are six items. What is the evidence?
* Student: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ: «Gold for gold, silver for silver, wheat for wheat, salt for salt, barley for barley, dates for dates, like for like, hand to hand, equal for equal»[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2134) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and Muslim (1587/81), and the wording is his, from the hadith of 'Ubada ibn al-Samit.]].
* The Shaykh: Can anything other than these six be added to them?
We have previously mentioned that the scholars differed on this:
As for the people of the literal reading (Zahiriyya), they said nothing else is added to them, because they reject analogical reasoning (qiyas).
As for the proponents of analogy (qiyasiyyun), they differed:
Some said nothing else is added to them, and it is restricted to what the text has stated, such as Ibn 'Aqil al-Hanbali, may Allah have mercy on him, who said that it is restricted to what the text has stated, although he was among the people of analogy and meanings. But he said that the scholars differed about the effective cause ('illa) and were inconsistent, and there is no clear text to which one must turn. When they differ, they are like the followers differing with the imam about adding or omitting in prayer, and it is known that when followers differ with the imam about adding or omitting, their statements are discarded: neither the statement of addition nor that of omission is accepted. So he says: since the scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, differed about the effective cause of usury in these six items, the cause is void, and we return to the view that it is restricted to what the text has stated.
The second view among the proponents of analogy is that the cause is intelligible, and that things like these six may be added to them.
Then they differed about the criterion of equivalence: is it taste (ta'm), or measure (kayl), or measure and storability (kayl wa-iddikhar)? For this reason the scholars' views on this question are inconsistent and scarcely settle on anything one can rely upon with confidence.
In any case, we say: the usury that Allah and His Messenger have prohibited, whether by way of textual report or by way of reasoning and analogy, is prohibited.
﴿And their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it﴾. The (wa') here is for the circumstantial clause (hal): that is, while they had been forbidden from it and had been informed and the proof had been established against them, yet they took it. The one who forbade it is Allah and His messengers.
The fourth attribute: ﴿And their consuming of people's wealth unjustly﴾. This means they seized the wealth of people. Here "consuming" means seizing, whether they seized it and ate it, wore it, built with it, or did anything else with it.
His words ﴿unjustly﴾ (bil-batil): batil is everything that contradicts the sharia. Whether they took it by deceit, or by lying, or by ignorance of the goods sold, or by concealing the truth, or by claiming what was not theirs, the point is that batil means everything taken without right.
Now remaining is ﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews﴾. We have understood that it is connected to ﴿We made unlawful﴾. What follows, ﴿and for their hindering many from the way of Allah (160) and their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it, and their consuming of people's wealth unjustly﴾, may be conjoined to what preceded, with the governing verb being ﴿We made unlawful﴾; that is, ﴿We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them, for their hindering many from the way of Allah, and their taking of usury...﴾ to the end. It may also be that the governing verb is deleted, the estimate being: ﴿We punished them for their hindering many from the way of Allah, and their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it﴾, which is indicated by His words: ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment﴾.

In this noble verse Allah informs that these Jews who wronged themselves were forbidden some good things, not all good things, as indicated by His words ﴿good things which had been lawful for them﴾, and an indefinite noun does not imply generality but absolute application. So what was made unlawful for them?

Allah, the Exalted, explains this in Surat al-An'am: ﴿And for those who were Jews We made unlawful every animal with claws, and of the cattle and sheep We made unlawful for them their fat, except what their backs carry or the entrails or what is mixed with bone﴾ [al-An'am 146]. So Allah made unlawful for them, from among the classes of animals, every animal with claws. By "every animal with claws" is meant every animal whose feet or paws are not cloven. The one whose foot is not split is called dhu zufr (having claws), such as the camel, the ostrich, and the like; that is, one that has no separate toes and whose foot is not split is called dhu zufr. Accordingly, the camel was forbidden to the Children of Israel.

﴿And for their hindering many from the way of Allah﴾: this means they were hindering from the way of Allah and also hindering others, so they were arrogant and criminal, arrogant toward obedience to Allah by hindering themselves, and criminal in that they transgressed against others and diverted them from the way of Allah.

﴿And their taking of usury﴾: this means their taking it by eating, using, and benefiting from it.

﴿Although they had been forbidden from it﴾: this is more severe in sin and prohibition, because the proof had been established against them.

Likewise, He described them as those who consume people's wealth unjustly, and among this is bribery. They were devourers of illicit gain (suht): bribery in judgment, that is, they bribed the rulers so that they would judge for them by what Allah had not sent down as sharia.

Then the Mighty and Majestic explained that He has prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment, and here you find the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, since He did not say "and We have prepared for them," but said ﴿for the disbelievers among them﴾, and it has already been mentioned that the explicit noun in place of the pronoun has benefits.

* A student: Among them is the indication of the cause of the ruling: He explained the reason, that because of their disbelief Allah has prepared for them a painful punishment.
* The Shaykh: That is, pointing to the cause of the ruling.
* A student: Pointing to the generality of the ruling for everyone who has this attribute.
* The Shaykh: Pointing to the generality of the ruling for everyone who has this attribute.
* A student: Recording judgment upon the referent of the pronoun by what this attribute deserves.
* The Shaykh: Recording judgment upon them by what this attribute requires; that is, by this they became disbelievers. But this meaning does not hold here, because He said ﴿for the disbelievers among them﴾, making them two groups: a group that disbelieves and a group that does not.
Also, alerting the addressee, because when speech departs from the usual style, a person must pay attention. Among this is the shift from address to third person or the reverse, and this requires the attention of the addressee, and it is one of the styles of Arabic.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has explained that this punishment He prepared for them is painful, that is, causing pain. The form fa'il (ʿalīm/alīm) sometimes carries the meaning of mufʿil (causing), and from this is the words of the poet:

Is it from Rayhana, the calling one, the hearing one, that keeps me awake, and my companions are sleeping (hujū')?

Here al-samī' (the hearing one) means al-musmi' (the one who makes hear).

* This verse contains many benefits:
* Among them: the establishment of causes, and that Allah may legislate something for a cause, as shown by His words: ﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them﴾. Among this is that Allah made hardship upon the Children of Israel who were commanded to slaughter a cow, when their prophet Musa, peace be upon him, said to them: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ [al-Baqara 67]. Had they slaughtered any cow whatsoever, it would have sufficed and achieved the purpose, but they made it strict, so Allah made it strict upon them. The establishment of causes has divided people into two extremes and a middle:
Some denied causes absolutely and said: affirming causes implies affirming a creator alongside Allah.
Some affirmed causes as acting by their own nature.
Some affirmed causes as acting by the power Allah placed in them that necessitates their effects, and this is the middle view indicated by both transmitted and rational evidence. What claim is there of a creator alongside Allah when one says that Allah created this thing to be a cause of such-and-such? What claim is valid to deny that causes influence their effects? Everyone knows that causes influence their effects, and for this reason Allah guided those who believed to the truth on which they differed, by His permission, so they affirmed causes on the basis that the One who created and originated them is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason effects may be withheld by Allah's permission, as the burning of the fire did not affect Ibrahim, peace be upon him, although it was a great blazing fire, to the point that it is said they could not approach it, but threw him toward it from a distance with a catapult, and yet it became coolness and safety for him. This shows that the cause does not act by itself but by the will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is also part of the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that He made a cause for everything.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: wrongdoing is a cause for the deprivation of good. This is from His words: ﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them﴾, and wrongdoing is a cause for deprivation of legislated and predestined good. Do you not know that the Messenger, peace be upon him, once went out to inform his companions that the night was Laylat al-Qadr, but two men among the Ansar or others quarrelled, so it was lifted, and he, peace be upon him, was made to forget it? Is this a deprivation of a predestined matter or a legislated one? Legislated, namely that whoever stands in it in faith and seeking reward, Allah forgives his previous sins; yet people were deprived of this good because of wrongdoing, which is contention, dispute, and strife. For this reason forgiveness on Laylat al-Qadr is withheld from those who harbour enmity between themselves, for they are not forgiven, as «deeds are presented on Monday and Thursday, and every person is forgiven except one who has enmity between himself and his brother, and it is said: Leave these two until they reconcile»[[Narrated by Muslim (2565/36) from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.]].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah may make something unlawful through wrongdoing as a predestined prohibition. What occurred with the Children of Israel was a legislated prohibition: ﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them﴾, and ﴿And for those who were Jews We made unlawful every animal with claws﴾ [al-An'am 146]. This is a legislated prohibition.
But a person may be made to abstain from something by predestined prohibition even though it is lawful for him in the sharia. For example, he may be afflicted with an illness for which the doctors tell him: abstain from such-and-such food, because of his wrongdoing.
A person, for instance, may act recklessly and be extravagant in spending. Is extravagance in spending, in eating, drinking, and clothing, forbidden or permitted?
* The students: Forbidden.
* The Shaykh: Forbidden. How is it forbidden? What is the evidence?
* The students: (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿And do not be extravagant; indeed, He does not love the extravagant﴾ [al-An'am 141]. A person may be extravagant and thereby be deprived of this good on which he was extravagant, by predestination not by the sharia: he may be afflicted with an illness that prevents him from eating everything or wearing everything. We call this what? 
* A student: Predestined.
* The Shaykh: A predestined prohibition.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 160–161 (part 2 of 2):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: legislating what is lawful and unlawful belongs to Allah the Exalted, as shown by His words ﴿We forbade﴾ and ﴿were made lawful for them﴾. This is indeed the case: permitting and forbidding (tahlil and tahrim) are not in our hands, nor in the hands of anyone among mankind, but only in the hands of Allah and His Messenger. Forbidding belongs to Allah and His Messenger, and so does permitting, and so does making obligatory (ijab). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely, "This is lawful and this is unlawful," to invent falsehood against Allah.﴾ [An-Nahl 116].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: good things themselves may be prohibited by the Shariah, and this is indeed the case. Good things may be forbidden to a particular person by the Shariah even after the completion of the religion. Shaykh al-Islam said: food is unlawful for a person if eating it harms him, or if he fears indigestion (takhamah), in which case it becomes unlawful for him. For example, a person fills his stomach with food, but the food was delicious and tasty, so he keeps eating and eating until it reaches his throat. Is he harmed by this or not? Without doubt he will be harmed, and perhaps harm will befall him, either immediately or in the future. Shaykh al-Islam said: it is unlawful for him to eat. Likewise if he fears indigestion, which is by the stomach's disturbance and its putrefaction, even if it is not for the sake of harm itself. Sometimes some foods do not agree with other foods, so you find a person eats this with that, and his stomach changes, it gives off a stench and a foul smell. We also say that it is unlawful for him to eat this, because Allah only permitted eating and drinking for the sake of sustaining the body, so if that turns into harm, it becomes unlawful.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning against barring from the path of Allah, whether one bars others directly or bars them by means of others; as shown by His words ﴿and their barring many from the way of Allah﴾.
* Among its benefits: barring from the path of Allah is not restricted to a specific form. Rather, anything that involves barring from the path of Allah, whether by discouraging (takhdhil), by spreading alarm (irjaf), by threatening, by promising, or otherwise, is included in the verse's warning against it. Barring from the path of Allah may occur through discouragement, as when a person comes to someone and says: "O so-and-so, do not burden yourself with calling people, giving advice and counselling them; you are calling the dead."
"You have indeed made them hear, had you called out, but there is no one to hear..."
Although the one being advised has resolve, energy and determination, this person comes and discourages him, and this is barring from the path of Allah.
But if he knows that this person might speak without knowledge, is his discouraging him from speaking a form of barring from the path of Allah, or a form of protecting the path of Allah?
* Students: The second.
* Shaykh: The second; because a person may come who is bold and courageous and wants to call people to everything, but has no knowledge. There is no blame on you if you tell him that it is not appropriate, and that he should not burden or exhaust himself. Whether you attribute this to the fact that people will not accept from him, or attribute it to the fact that he lacks knowledge and will fall into difficulty, there is no harm in it. Indeed this is from protecting the path of Allah, not from barring from it.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: mentioning a description that is more severe in censure, even though it carries no implication of restriction; as shown by His words ﴿and their barring many from the way of Allah﴾. This is the utmost in censure, but if they had barred only a little, they would still have had a share of sin; the point is in the abundance.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: those who engage in usury (riba) from this Ummah resemble the Jews; as shown by His words ﴿and their taking of usury, though they had been forbidden from it﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: taking usury is forbidden, whether it is for eating, drinking, wearing, possessing, or any other purpose; due to the generality of His words ﴿their taking of usury﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: proof is not established except after it reaches a person, and whoever does something without knowing its ruling is not held accountable for it.
As shown by His words ﴿and their taking of usury, though they had been forbidden from it﴾ [An-Nisa 161].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: taking usury is forbidden, whether it is for eating, drinking, wearing, possessing, or any other purpose, due to the generality of His words ﴿their taking of usury﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: proof is not established except after it reaches a person, and whoever does something without knowing its ruling is not held accountable for it, by His words ﴿and they had been forbidden from it﴾. On this basis, if a person engages in a usurious transaction without knowing it is usury, meaning he knows usury in general but does not know that this particular transaction is usury, and then he learns of it afterward, do we say that what he took is unlawful? No, we say it is not unlawful, by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists, for him is what has passed, and his affair is up to Allah﴾ [Al-Baqarah 275]. He did not know that it was forbidden, but if he knew it was forbidden, took it, and then repented, do we say he must return it to the one from whom he took it?
The answer: No. Because if we said he must return it to the one from whom he took it, then the one to whom it is returned would gain it twice. Rather, we say: give it in charity; do not add it to your property, and do not return it to the usurer who knew that usury was unlawful but whose soul tempted him so that he gave you the usury.
And if the usurer from whom usury was taken repents, must he give in charity an amount equal to what he paid in usury? Answer boldly.
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: No; because the one who gave the usury is wronged in reality. When he repents to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, we do not say that he must give in charity an amount equal to what he paid in usury. The discussion concerns the one who took usury.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of consuming people's wealth by falsehood; as shown by His words ﴿and their consuming people's wealth by falsehood﴾. We have mentioned that falsehood is what is not right. On this basis, if a person consumes the property of a belligerent non-Muslim (harbi), is he among those who consume people's wealth by falsehood? No, because the belligerent is permitted in blood and property. Accordingly, if a group who have no strength plunder the lands of the belligerent disbelievers and take property, it is theirs, and there is nothing on them in that, because the property of a belligerent disbeliever is permissible for the Muslims. But if one takes the property of a dhimmi, a mu'ahid, or a musta'man without right, he has consumed people's wealth by falsehood, because these three are protected; their property is sacred and their persons are sacred.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a severe warning against whoever is characterized by these attributes: wrongdoing, taking usury, consuming people's wealth by falsehood, and barring from the path of Allah; as shown by His words ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment﴾.
* Among its benefits: affirmation of the justice of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, in that He mentioned these attributes and mentioned that the one for whom a painful punishment has been prepared is the disbeliever among them.
Then He said: ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them and the believers﴾ up to the end [An-Nisa 162]; its explanation will come, God willing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 160–161 (part 1 of 2):

(...) ﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them﴾. The (fa') here is conjunctive, linking to what preceded, and the (ba') is causal. Dhulm (wrongdoing) originally means deficiency or diminution, as in the words of Allah: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short therein at all﴾ [al-Kahf 33]. In the sharia, however, it means transgression, whether by neglecting an obligation or by committing a prohibited act.
His words ﴿of those who were Jews﴾ refer to the people of Musa, when they said: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾ [al-A'raf 156], meaning we have repented. Despite their turning back and their commitment to returning to Allah, they wronged themselves.
﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them﴾. This verb is the governing element of the phrase ﴿for wrongdoing﴾; that is, the prepositional phrase ﴿bi-zulmin﴾ is connected to ﴿harramna﴾ (We made unlawful). Tahrim (making unlawful) linguistically means prohibition, as in the term harim al-bi'r (the protected zone around a well), which is the area around it that prevents others from reviving the land near it. From this, women are called harim because they are veiled and protected from transgression against them.
﴿We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them﴾. ﴿Tayyibat﴾ means foods that are good, and it is an adjective of a deleted noun. Tayyib (good) is the opposite of khabith (bad), and khabith has several usages: sometimes it refers to what is impure (najis), sometimes to what is inferior (radi'), and sometimes to what is prohibited in general.
His words ﴿good things which had been lawful for them﴾ mean that they were lawful originally and remained good, but they were made unlawful for them because of their wrongdoing.
﴿Which had been lawful for them﴾: who is the one who makes lawful? The one who makes lawful is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, since the matter is in His hand.
﴿And for their hindering many from the way of Allah﴾. The (wa') is a conjunction particle, and (ṣadd) is a verbal noun that may derive from a transitive verb or from an intransitive verb, because ṣadda can be intransitive or transitive. One says ṣadda al-rajulu 'an kadhā, meaning he turned away from something, and ṣadda ghayrahu 'an kadhā, meaning he diverted another from it. Both are possible here: they turned themselves away from the way of Allah greatly, and they also diverted others, because of the book they possessed, with which they confused and deceived people, saying that Muhammad ﷺ is not the awaited prophet, and similar things.
His words ﴿from the way of Allah﴾: what is meant by ﴿the way of Allah﴾ is His sharia which Allah legislated for His servants. It is called (the way of Allah) because it is a path leading to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and because Allah Himself established it for the servants, and no one else legislated it. It is therefore attributed to Allah in two respects. The first is that it leads to Him, as one says, for example: this is the road to Madina, this is the road to Makka. The second is that Allah established it for the servants and legislated it for them. It is sometimes also attributed to its travellers, as in the words of Allah: ﴿and follows other than the way of the believers﴾ [al-Nisa' 115], where the way is attributed to the believers in respect of their being those who travel it. Accordingly, when the way is attributed to Allah, it carries two senses; when attributed to the servants, it carries one sense.
﴿Much﴾ (kathīran): its i'rab (grammatical analysis) varies with the verb ṣadd. If it is intransitive, it is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, meaning greatly turning away. If it is transitive, it is the object of ṣadd. If you wish, you may say it is an adjective of the deleted object of ṣadd, meaning a great many people. In reality they deserve both descriptions, for they turned themselves away and turned others away.
﴿And their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it﴾. This is the third attribute. He did not say "consuming" (akl), because akhdh (taking) is more general: a person may take usury without consuming it, using it in clothing or building and the like, and he may take it for eating. Sometimes it is expressed with "eating," as in the words of Allah: ﴿Those who consume usury will not stand except as one stands whom Satan has driven to madness by touch﴾ [al-Baqara 275], and sometimes it is expressed with "taking," which is more general. But the expression with "eating" is more severe, because the practice of the one who eats usury is more severe than the practice of one who does not eat it, and more severe than the practice of the one who merely takes it, since the taker may use usury or spend it on other things besides eating.
His words ﴿usury﴾: riba linguistically means increase. In the sharia it means increase in specific items which the Prophet ﷺ explained, six items. What are they?
* Student: Gold, silver, barley, wheat, dates, and salt.
* The Shaykh: And salt. These are six items. What is the evidence?
* Student: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ: «Gold for gold, silver for silver, wheat for wheat, salt for salt, barley for barley, dates for dates, like for like, hand to hand, equal for equal»[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2134) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and Muslim (1587/81), and the wording is his, from the hadith of 'Ubada ibn al-Samit.]].
* The Shaykh: Can anything other than these six be added to them?
We have previously mentioned that the scholars differed on this:
As for the people of the literal reading (Zahiriyya), they said nothing else is added to them, because they reject analogical reasoning (qiyas).
As for the proponents of analogy (qiyasiyyun), they differed:
Some said nothing else is added to them, and it is restricted to what the text has stated, such as Ibn 'Aqil al-Hanbali, may Allah have mercy on him, who said that it is restricted to what the text has stated, although he was among the people of analogy and meanings. But he said that the scholars differed about the effective cause ('illa) and were inconsistent, and there is no clear text to which one must turn. When they differ, they are like the followers differing with the imam about adding or omitting in prayer, and it is known that when followers differ with the imam about adding or omitting, their statements are discarded: neither the statement of addition nor that of omission is accepted. So he says: since the scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, differed about the effective cause of usury in these six items, the cause is void, and we return to the view that it is restricted to what the text has stated.
The second view among the proponents of analogy is that the cause is intelligible, and that things like these six may be added to them.
Then they differed about the criterion of equivalence: is it taste (ta'm), or measure (kayl), or measure and storability (kayl wa-iddikhar)? For this reason the scholars' views on this question are inconsistent and scarcely settle on anything one can rely upon with confidence.
In any case, we say: the usury that Allah and His Messenger have prohibited, whether by way of textual report or by way of reasoning and analogy, is prohibited.
﴿And their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it﴾. The (wa') here is for the circumstantial clause (hal): that is, while they had been forbidden from it and had been informed and the proof had been established against them, yet they took it. The one who forbade it is Allah and His messengers.
The fourth attribute: ﴿And their consuming of people's wealth unjustly﴾. This means they seized the wealth of people. Here "consuming" means seizing, whether they seized it and ate it, wore it, built with it, or did anything else with it.
His words ﴿unjustly﴾ (bil-batil): batil is everything that contradicts the sharia. Whether they took it by deceit, or by lying, or by ignorance of the goods sold, or by concealing the truth, or by claiming what was not theirs, the point is that batil means everything taken without right.
Now remaining is ﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews﴾. We have understood that it is connected to ﴿We made unlawful﴾. What follows, ﴿and for their hindering many from the way of Allah (160) and their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it, and their consuming of people's wealth unjustly﴾, may be conjoined to what preceded, with the governing verb being ﴿We made unlawful﴾; that is, ﴿We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them, for their hindering many from the way of Allah, and their taking of usury...﴾ to the end. It may also be that the governing verb is deleted, the estimate being: ﴿We punished them for their hindering many from the way of Allah, and their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it﴾, which is indicated by His words: ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment﴾.

In this noble verse Allah informs that these Jews who wronged themselves were forbidden some good things, not all good things, as indicated by His words ﴿good things which had been lawful for them﴾, and an indefinite noun does not imply generality but absolute application. So what was made unlawful for them?

Allah, the Exalted, explains this in Surat al-An'am: ﴿And for those who were Jews We made unlawful every animal with claws, and of the cattle and sheep We made unlawful for them their fat, except what their backs carry or the entrails or what is mixed with bone﴾ [al-An'am 146]. So Allah made unlawful for them, from among the classes of animals, every animal with claws. By "every animal with claws" is meant every animal whose feet or paws are not cloven. The one whose foot is not split is called dhu zufr (having claws), such as the camel, the ostrich, and the like; that is, one that has no separate toes and whose foot is not split is called dhu zufr. Accordingly, the camel was forbidden to the Children of Israel.

﴿And for their hindering many from the way of Allah﴾: this means they were hindering from the way of Allah and also hindering others, so they were arrogant and criminal, arrogant toward obedience to Allah by hindering themselves, and criminal in that they transgressed against others and diverted them from the way of Allah.

﴿And their taking of usury﴾: this means their taking it by eating, using, and benefiting from it.

﴿Although they had been forbidden from it﴾: this is more severe in sin and prohibition, because the proof had been established against them.

Likewise, He described them as those who consume people's wealth unjustly, and among this is bribery. They were devourers of illicit gain (suht): bribery in judgment, that is, they bribed the rulers so that they would judge for them by what Allah had not sent down as sharia.

Then the Mighty and Majestic explained that He has prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment, and here you find the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, since He did not say "and We have prepared for them," but said ﴿for the disbelievers among them﴾, and it has already been mentioned that the explicit noun in place of the pronoun has benefits.

* A student: Among them is the indication of the cause of the ruling: He explained the reason, that because of their disbelief Allah has prepared for them a painful punishment.
* The Shaykh: That is, pointing to the cause of the ruling.
* A student: Pointing to the generality of the ruling for everyone who has this attribute.
* The Shaykh: Pointing to the generality of the ruling for everyone who has this attribute.
* A student: Recording judgment upon the referent of the pronoun by what this attribute deserves.
* The Shaykh: Recording judgment upon them by what this attribute requires; that is, by this they became disbelievers. But this meaning does not hold here, because He said ﴿for the disbelievers among them﴾, making them two groups: a group that disbelieves and a group that does not.
Also, alerting the addressee, because when speech departs from the usual style, a person must pay attention. Among this is the shift from address to third person or the reverse, and this requires the attention of the addressee, and it is one of the styles of Arabic.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has explained that this punishment He prepared for them is painful, that is, causing pain. The form fa'il (ʿalīm/alīm) sometimes carries the meaning of mufʿil (causing), and from this is the words of the poet:

Is it from Rayhana, the calling one, the hearing one, that keeps me awake, and my companions are sleeping (hujū')?

Here al-samī' (the hearing one) means al-musmi' (the one who makes hear).

* This verse contains many benefits:
* Among them: the establishment of causes, and that Allah may legislate something for a cause, as shown by His words: ﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them﴾. Among this is that Allah made hardship upon the Children of Israel who were commanded to slaughter a cow, when their prophet Musa, peace be upon him, said to them: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ [al-Baqara 67]. Had they slaughtered any cow whatsoever, it would have sufficed and achieved the purpose, but they made it strict, so Allah made it strict upon them. The establishment of causes has divided people into two extremes and a middle:
Some denied causes absolutely and said: affirming causes implies affirming a creator alongside Allah.
Some affirmed causes as acting by their own nature.
Some affirmed causes as acting by the power Allah placed in them that necessitates their effects, and this is the middle view indicated by both transmitted and rational evidence. What claim is there of a creator alongside Allah when one says that Allah created this thing to be a cause of such-and-such? What claim is valid to deny that causes influence their effects? Everyone knows that causes influence their effects, and for this reason Allah guided those who believed to the truth on which they differed, by His permission, so they affirmed causes on the basis that the One who created and originated them is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason effects may be withheld by Allah's permission, as the burning of the fire did not affect Ibrahim, peace be upon him, although it was a great blazing fire, to the point that it is said they could not approach it, but threw him toward it from a distance with a catapult, and yet it became coolness and safety for him. This shows that the cause does not act by itself but by the will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is also part of the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that He made a cause for everything.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: wrongdoing is a cause for the deprivation of good. This is from His words: ﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them﴾, and wrongdoing is a cause for deprivation of legislated and predestined good. Do you not know that the Messenger, peace be upon him, once went out to inform his companions that the night was Laylat al-Qadr, but two men among the Ansar or others quarrelled, so it was lifted, and he, peace be upon him, was made to forget it? Is this a deprivation of a predestined matter or a legislated one? Legislated, namely that whoever stands in it in faith and seeking reward, Allah forgives his previous sins; yet people were deprived of this good because of wrongdoing, which is contention, dispute, and strife. For this reason forgiveness on Laylat al-Qadr is withheld from those who harbour enmity between themselves, for they are not forgiven, as «deeds are presented on Monday and Thursday, and every person is forgiven except one who has enmity between himself and his brother, and it is said: Leave these two until they reconcile»[[Narrated by Muslim (2565/36) from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.]].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah may make something unlawful through wrongdoing as a predestined prohibition. What occurred with the Children of Israel was a legislated prohibition: ﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them﴾, and ﴿And for those who were Jews We made unlawful every animal with claws﴾ [al-An'am 146]. This is a legislated prohibition.
But a person may be made to abstain from something by predestined prohibition even though it is lawful for him in the sharia. For example, he may be afflicted with an illness for which the doctors tell him: abstain from such-and-such food, because of his wrongdoing.
A person, for instance, may act recklessly and be extravagant in spending. Is extravagance in spending, in eating, drinking, and clothing, forbidden or permitted?
* The students: Forbidden.
* The Shaykh: Forbidden. How is it forbidden? What is the evidence?
* The students: (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿And do not be extravagant; indeed, He does not love the extravagant﴾ [al-An'am 141]. A person may be extravagant and thereby be deprived of this good on which he was extravagant, by predestination not by the sharia: he may be afflicted with an illness that prevents him from eating everything or wearing everything. We call this what? 
* A student: Predestined.
* The Shaykh: A predestined prohibition.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 4, verse 160–161 (part 2 of 2):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: legislating what is lawful and unlawful belongs to Allah the Exalted, as shown by His words ﴿We forbade﴾ and ﴿were made lawful for them﴾. This is indeed the case: permitting and forbidding (tahlil and tahrim) are not in our hands, nor in the hands of anyone among mankind, but only in the hands of Allah and His Messenger. Forbidding belongs to Allah and His Messenger, and so does permitting, and so does making obligatory (ijab). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely, "This is lawful and this is unlawful," to invent falsehood against Allah.﴾ [An-Nahl 116].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: good things themselves may be prohibited by the Shariah, and this is indeed the case. Good things may be forbidden to a particular person by the Shariah even after the completion of the religion. Shaykh al-Islam said: food is unlawful for a person if eating it harms him, or if he fears indigestion (takhamah), in which case it becomes unlawful for him. For example, a person fills his stomach with food, but the food was delicious and tasty, so he keeps eating and eating until it reaches his throat. Is he harmed by this or not? Without doubt he will be harmed, and perhaps harm will befall him, either immediately or in the future. Shaykh al-Islam said: it is unlawful for him to eat. Likewise if he fears indigestion, which is by the stomach's disturbance and its putrefaction, even if it is not for the sake of harm itself. Sometimes some foods do not agree with other foods, so you find a person eats this with that, and his stomach changes, it gives off a stench and a foul smell. We also say that it is unlawful for him to eat this, because Allah only permitted eating and drinking for the sake of sustaining the body, so if that turns into harm, it becomes unlawful.
