* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning against barring from the path of Allah, whether one bars others directly or bars them by means of others; as shown by His words ﴿and their barring many from the way of Allah﴾.
* Among its benefits: barring from the path of Allah is not restricted to a specific form. Rather, anything that involves barring from the path of Allah, whether by discouraging (takhdhil), by spreading alarm (irjaf), by threatening, by promising, or otherwise, is included in the verse's warning against it. Barring from the path of Allah may occur through discouragement, as when a person comes to someone and says: "O so-and-so, do not burden yourself with calling people, giving advice and counselling them; you are calling the dead."
"You have indeed made them hear, had you called out, but there is no one to hear..."
Although the one being advised has resolve, energy and determination, this person comes and discourages him, and this is barring from the path of Allah.
But if he knows that this person might speak without knowledge, is his discouraging him from speaking a form of barring from the path of Allah, or a form of protecting the path of Allah?
* Students: The second.
* Shaykh: The second; because a person may come who is bold and courageous and wants to call people to everything, but has no knowledge. There is no blame on you if you tell him that it is not appropriate, and that he should not burden or exhaust himself. Whether you attribute this to the fact that people will not accept from him, or attribute it to the fact that he lacks knowledge and will fall into difficulty, there is no harm in it. Indeed this is from protecting the path of Allah, not from barring from it.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: mentioning a description that is more severe in censure, even though it carries no implication of restriction; as shown by His words ﴿and their barring many from the way of Allah﴾. This is the utmost in censure, but if they had barred only a little, they would still have had a share of sin; the point is in the abundance.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: those who engage in usury (riba) from this Ummah resemble the Jews; as shown by His words ﴿and their taking of usury, though they had been forbidden from it﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: taking usury is forbidden, whether it is for eating, drinking, wearing, possessing, or any other purpose; due to the generality of His words ﴿their taking of usury﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: proof is not established except after it reaches a person, and whoever does something without knowing its ruling is not held accountable for it.
As shown by His words ﴿and their taking of usury, though they had been forbidden from it﴾ [An-Nisa 161].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: taking usury is forbidden, whether it is for eating, drinking, wearing, possessing, or any other purpose, due to the generality of His words ﴿their taking of usury﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: proof is not established except after it reaches a person, and whoever does something without knowing its ruling is not held accountable for it, by His words ﴿and they had been forbidden from it﴾. On this basis, if a person engages in a usurious transaction without knowing it is usury, meaning he knows usury in general but does not know that this particular transaction is usury, and then he learns of it afterward, do we say that what he took is unlawful? No, we say it is not unlawful, by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists, for him is what has passed, and his affair is up to Allah﴾ [Al-Baqarah 275]. He did not know that it was forbidden, but if he knew it was forbidden, took it, and then repented, do we say he must return it to the one from whom he took it?
The answer: No. Because if we said he must return it to the one from whom he took it, then the one to whom it is returned would gain it twice. Rather, we say: give it in charity; do not add it to your property, and do not return it to the usurer who knew that usury was unlawful but whose soul tempted him so that he gave you the usury.
And if the usurer from whom usury was taken repents, must he give in charity an amount equal to what he paid in usury? Answer boldly.
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: No; because the one who gave the usury is wronged in reality. When he repents to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, we do not say that he must give in charity an amount equal to what he paid in usury. The discussion concerns the one who took usury.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of consuming people's wealth by falsehood; as shown by His words ﴿and their consuming people's wealth by falsehood﴾. We have mentioned that falsehood is what is not right. On this basis, if a person consumes the property of a belligerent non-Muslim (harbi), is he among those who consume people's wealth by falsehood? No, because the belligerent is permitted in blood and property. Accordingly, if a group who have no strength plunder the lands of the belligerent disbelievers and take property, it is theirs, and there is nothing on them in that, because the property of a belligerent disbeliever is permissible for the Muslims. But if one takes the property of a dhimmi, a mu'ahid, or a musta'man without right, he has consumed people's wealth by falsehood, because these three are protected; their property is sacred and their persons are sacred.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a severe warning against whoever is characterized by these attributes: wrongdoing, taking usury, consuming people's wealth by falsehood, and barring from the path of Allah; as shown by His words ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment﴾.
* Among its benefits: affirmation of the justice of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, in that He mentioned these attributes and mentioned that the one for whom a painful punishment has been prepared is the disbeliever among them.
Then He said: ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them and the believers﴾ up to the end [An-Nisa 162]; its explanation will come, God willing.

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them, and the believers, believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and those who establish prayer and those who give zakah and those who believe in Allah and the Last Day - those We will give a great reward.﴾ [An-Nisa' 162].

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. We have already mentioned in the verse before this, or rather in the two verses, what indicates the establishment of causes. Is that so?

Student: Because of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews﴾.

Shaykh: What is the indication?

Student: The letter "ba'" (bi) denotes causation.

Shaykh: That "ba'" denotes causation. We have also already mentioned that a person may be deprived of good things, either by a legislated means or by a divine decree, because of his wrongdoing?

Student: Because of His saying: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them﴾; His saying ﴿We forbade﴾ is because of their wrongdoing.

Shaykh: Is this prohibition legislative or decreed?

Student: Legislative.

Shaykh: But by analogy?

Student: There is also a prohibition that is decreed.

Shaykh: A person may be deprived of good things by a decreed prohibition. For example, in our law it is not possible for good things to be forbidden by a legislated prohibition, because the time of permitting and forbidding has ended; but a person may be deprived of them by a decreed prohibition, due to illness or something else.

His saying: ﴿because of their turning many away from the way of Allah﴾. Is (ṣadd) here intransitive or transitive?

Student: Because it is both intransitive and transitive.

Shaykh: Explain it according to both possibilities. If it is intransitive, what is its meaning?

Student: If it is intransitive: they turned away themselves.

Shaykh: If it is intransitive, the meaning is that they turned themselves away.

Student: And if it is transitive, they turned others away.

Shaykh: They turned others away. May Allah bless you. On this difference the parsing of ﴿kathīran﴾ depends. How do you parse "kathīran"?

Student: If we parse it as an intransitive verb, ﴿kathīran﴾ is an object; if it is transitive, then ﴿kathīran﴾ is an adjective.

Shaykh: If (ṣadd) is intransitive, then ﴿kathīran﴾?

Student: Intransitive?

Shaykh: Yes, so ﴿kathīran﴾?

Student: An adjective.

Shaykh: The meaning?

Student: And their turning away from the way of Allah, a great turning away, meaning that their turning others away was a great number of people, so it becomes an adjective of ("people").

Shaykh: But an adjective of what?

Student: Of the omitted ("people").

Shaykh: Of the omitted. The meaning: they turned away from the way of Allah a great number of people, meaning: it is an object. In the first case it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. And if you wish, say: an absolute object.

﴿ʾakhdhihim al-ribā﴾ What is the manner of their taking riba?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: That is, their receiving riba, whether they ate it, wore it, or used it for other benefits. Which is more general: "they eat riba" or "they take riba"?

Student: They take.

Shaykh: Can you explain to us what riba is?

Student: Riba linguistically means increase; technically it is a determined increase in determined items.

Shaykh: A determined increase in determined items, in a determined time, in a determined manner. You have not brought anything.

Student: A determined increase in known items.

Shaykh: An increase in known items, or deferment?

Student: In known items.

Shaykh: If I say to you: what are the known items?

Student: Gold, silver, wheat, dates, and salt.

Shaykh: Five of these?

Student: And barley.

Shaykh: Is anything else analogized upon them?

Student: There is disagreement among them on (...).

Shaykh: Speak, explain.

Student: Some of them said: the effective cause in this matter is...

Shaykh: As for the Zahiriyya, nothing else is analogized upon them, because analogy is not a legislative proof for them. And according to the analogists?

Student: Other things are analogized upon them, but they differed about the effective cause.

Shaykh: Wrong. Yes.

Student: The analogists differed. Ibn 'Aqil al-Hanbali said that: if they differ about the effective cause, we return to the statements and remain on the original basis.

Shaykh: That is, among the analogists, some restrict it to these items, based on their disagreement about the effective cause, and there is no text that clarifies, so the statements cancel each other out.

Student: And among the others, analogy is made upon them, and they differed about the cause.

Shaykh: Yes indeed, well done, may Allah bless you. What is the criterion for consuming people's wealth falsely?

Student: Falsehood is what opposes truth. Anyone who takes people's wealth without right has consumed it falsely.

Shaykh: Fraud: if someone cheats and the goods increase in price, is this consuming wealth falsely?

Student: Yes.

Shaykh: Because...

Student: Because he took it without right.

Shaykh: The excess without right. If he says: the value of this commodity is a hundred, and it was not described, and the buyer buys it for a hundred, is this excess part of consuming wealth falsely?

Student: Yes.

Shaykh: Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said, as an exception to the description of those Jews mentioned above, saying: ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them﴾. So "but" (lākin) here is a particle of exception to the attributes mentioned before. And ﴿al-rāsikhūn﴾ is an active participle from "rasakha," meaning to be established, as in the firmness of a tree, the firmness of the foundation of a building, and the like, because it is fixed and does not waver.

﴿Those firm in knowledge among them﴾. ﴿In knowledge﴾ here refers to legislative knowledge, and the "al" in it is for mental definiteness (al-ʿahd al-dhihnī), because firmness in non-legislative knowledge does not praise or blame its possessor; rather it depends on what that firmness leads to. His saying ﴿among them﴾ means among those who were Jews. We illustrate this with whom?

Students: ʿAbdullah ibn Salam.

Shaykh: With ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, for he was a rabbi among the rabbis of the Jews and believed in Muhammad ﷺ.

﴿And the believers believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾. His saying ﴿and the believers﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿those firm﴾. But is the intended meaning those firm in knowledge whose knowledge yielded faith, so that this is coordination of attribute with attribute, and coordinating one attribute with another is permissible in Arabic, as in His saying, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, and who decreed and guided, and who brought out the pasture﴾ [Al-A'la 1-4]; or is the intended meaning that the believers here are other than those firm in knowledge, referring to the believers among the Emigrants and Helpers, that is, from this Ummah, so that the coordination is of two distinct and different groups?

They have mentioned two opinions on this, and it is not far-fetched that both are correct.

As for His saying ﴿the believers believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾: ﴿what has been revealed to you﴾ is the Qur'an, and the one who revealed it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Say: the Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord﴾ [An-Nahl 102]. So the one who sent it down is Allah Mighty and Majestic, the one it was sent down to is Muhammad ﷺ, and what was sent down is the Qur'an. Therefore "ma" is a relative pronoun referring to what?

Student: To the Qur'an.

Shaykh: The Qur'an. ﴿And what was revealed before you﴾ refers to the earlier scriptures. So they believe that Allah revealed the Torah to Moses, the Gospel to Jesus, the Psalms to David, the scrolls to Abraham, and likewise to Moses (the scrolls).

﴿And what was revealed before you, and those who establish prayer and those who give zakah﴾. "Those who establish prayer": those who perform it in the manner of uprightness and completeness, by performing it with all its conditions, pillars and obligations complete, and completing it with the recommended acts. The word "prayer" here refers to the prayers in general, including obligatory and voluntary prayers.

In the verse there is a grammatical difficulty, since ﴿al-muqīmīna﴾ comes with the ya' ending between nominatives: a preceding nominative and a following nominative. This troubled some people: how does this word come between nominatives in the genitive-form ending? It was said: His saying ﴿al-muqīmīna﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿what has been revealed to you﴾, meaning "and [to] the believers in [and] those who establish prayer," and the intended ones are the angels, because the Prophet ﷺ informed that there is no place in the heavens the size of four fingers without an angel standing, bowing or prostrating [Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (2312) and Ibn Majah (4190) from Abu Dharr al-Ghifari]. So it is as if He said: "and the believers in whom?" In the angels.

It was also said: "al-muqīmīn" here is a general description including everyone who establishes prayer, from the angels and others, and that it was specified for those who establish prayer because of its importance and because it is the most emphatic of physical acts of worship. According to this, it is in the accusative, not the genitive, and it is accusative by way of praise, meaning "I praise those who establish prayer." Its governing verb is therefore omitted, and the estimate is: "and I praise those who establish prayer." The shift to the accusative with an omitted verb serves two benefits:

The first benefit is semantic: to clarify the concern with establishing prayer.

The second benefit is verbal attentiveness: because when speech is in one uniform pattern, a person flows along with it and nothing stops him; but when it changes, he pauses. Why did this word come in this form, differing from the others?

So there are two benefits: one semantic and one verbal. The semantic one is an indication of the importance of prayer and care for it; the verbal one is drawing attention, since when the wording changes, a person pauses and pays attention. This is without doubt better than the one who says this is an error in the Book, as some have said—may Allah protect us—claiming that those who wrote the Mushaf erred by writing "al-muqīmīn," and that the correct reading is in Ibn Mas'ud's reading: ﴿al-muqīmūna﴾. But this is not valid at all. How could an error remain in the noble Qur'an and not be corrected? How does this fit with His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ [Al-Hijr 9]? The truth is that the one who says this is the one who is mistaken; he has strayed far and erred greatly. Rather, the benefit is as I told you.

So the question remains: should we say that ﴿al-muqīmīn﴾ is in the genitive, meaning "they believe in what was revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and in those who establish prayer, who are the angels"? Or is it accusative by an omitted verb? The second is preferable, though the first has some possibility; but the second is more likely. The wisdom in the shift—that is, in the change of case—is what we mentioned: verbal and semantic.

﴿And those who give zakah﴾ is coordinated with what? It was said it is a new sentence, and that its predicate is His saying ﴿those—We will give them a great reward﴾. It was also said that it is coordinated with what came before, by His saying ﴿those firm in knowledge among them and the believers﴾, meaning ﴿and those who give zakah﴾. But the closer view is that it is a new sentence, because of the separation between it and what it is coordinated with, namely His saying ﴿those who establish prayer﴾.

His saying ﴿al-mu'tūna﴾ means those who give it, and ﴿zakah﴾ means the portion specified in zakatable wealth. On this basis, what is meant is zakah on wealth. It was said that what is meant is zakah of the body, based on Allah's saying: ﴿And woe to the polytheists, those who do not give zakah﴾ [Fussilat 6-7], and that what is meant is zakah of the body. But the first is closer to correct, because Allah, Exalted, always pairs establishing prayer with giving zakah.

* * *

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them, and the believers believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and those who establish prayer and those who give zakah and those who believe in Allah and the Last Day—those We will give a great reward.﴾ [An-Nisa' 162]. ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him, and We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Descendants, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon, and We gave David the Psalms﴾ (163). ﴿And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you, and Allah spoke to Moses directly﴾ (164). ﴿Messengers as bringers of good tidings and warners, so that mankind will have no argument against Allah after the messengers. And ever is Allah Exalted in Might and Wise﴾ [An-Nisa' 162-165].

Shaykh: Allah, Exalted and Majestic, says: ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them, and the believers believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and those who establish prayer and those who give zakah and those who believe in Allah and the Last Day—those We will give a great reward.﴾ We have reached the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿and those who give zakah﴾, meaning: those who give it to its rightful recipients. Zakah is a wealth that Allah has made obligatory on specific wealth; it is taken from the wealthy and returned to the poor.

His saying ﴿those who believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾: belief in Allah is not merely affirmation, because mere affirmation is not called faith. For this reason Abu Talib was not a believer, despite affirming the Messenger ﷺ. Rather, faith is complete acknowledgment that entails acceptance and submission. The heart must fully acknowledge, must accept what the Shari'ah has brought, and must submit, for faith to be complete. Belief in Allah includes belief in His existence, His lordship, His divinity, His names and attributes, and His uniqueness in these, which has been explained at length before. Belief in the Last Day: the Last Day is the Day of Resurrection, and it is described as "last" because there is no day after it; it is the final stage of man. For man has four stages after being a human:

The first stage: in his mother's womb; the second: in this world; the third: in the barzakh; the fourth: the Day of Resurrection.

For this reason it is called the Last Day. The barzakh is not "the Last Day," as some people's expression suggests when they describe the dead as having gone to his "final abode." This is not correct; rather the final abode is the Day of Resurrection: either Paradise or Hellfire.

Belief in the Last Day does not only mean believing that people will be resurrected; it has many related matters, which Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, Shaykh al-Islam, defined in his saying: Included in belief in the Last Day is everything the Prophet ﷺ informed of that occurs after death, such as the trial of the grave, the punishment of the grave, the bliss of the grave, and the like; these are included in belief in the Last Day, because death is the last thing for a person in this world, for whoever dies, his resurrection has begun. Belief in the Last Day entails a person's steadfastness upon Allah's religion, because he fears the Last Day and hopes for the Last Day, as Allah said: ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾ [Al-Ahzab 21]. He fears the Last Day so he avoids sin, and hopes for the Last Day so he performs obedience. For this reason Allah, Blessed and Exalted, always pairs belief in Him with belief in the Last Day, because belief in the Last Day is what drives one to steadfastness, or to complete steadfastness.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 4, verse 162 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿Those—We shall grant them a great reward.﴾ There are two readings here: ﴿sa-yu'tīhim﴾ (with *yā'*, "He will give them") and ﴿sa-nu'tīhim﴾ (with *nūn*, "We will give them"). The reading with *yā'* (*sa-yu'tīhim*) follows the established flow of the speech, because the whole context is in the third person. ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them and the believers believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and the establishers of prayer and the givers of zakah and the believers in Allah and the Last Day—those, He will give them﴾, meaning Allah, ﴿a great reward.﴾ The reading with *yā'*, which is a canonical (*sab'iyyah*) and sound reading, follows the context. As for the reading with *nūn*, it involves a shift from the third person to the first person plural, and this shift, called *iltifāt* (shift in grammatical person), has a benefit: it alerts the listener to what follows. When the flow of speech changes, a person must pause and ask what caused the change, and then he pays closer attention to the meaning: ﴿Those—We shall grant them a great reward.﴾ As for enumerating the other benefits that branch from *iltifāt*, each context has its own relevant points. Here, ﴿sa-nu'tīhim﴾ is an explicit undertaking by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that He will give them a great reward. An explicit undertaking, and the attribution of a thing to Himself, is more eloquent than attributing it to a third person.

﴿sa-nu'tīhim ajran 'azīman﴾. Brother, parse for us ﴿ajran 'azīman﴾.

* Student: (...) is a direct object (*maf'ūl bihi*).
* Shaykh: Which one?
* Student: (*ajran*).
* Shaykh: And (*'azīman*)?
* Student: An adjective (*ṣifah*).
* Shaykh: Fine. Do we just say direct object?
* Student: ﴿sa-nu'tīhim ajran﴾, a second object (*maf'ūl thānī*).
* Shaykh: And where is the first object?
* Student: The first object is the *hā'* in (*hum*).
* Shaykh: Fine, the *hā'* or (*hum*). The *hā'* is correct. As for (*hum*), I do not know where it came from.
* Student: According to the view of some of them.
* Shaykh: But (*hum*), and the *hā'* is kasrah (*-him*) in our reading.
* Student: Some of them parse the *hā'* as the first object and the *mīm* as the plural marker, and some parse (*hum*) as the first object.
* Shaykh: But (*hum*) is not the wording of the verse: ﴿sa-nu'tīhim﴾. You say (*-him*) is the first object. In any case, the correct and preferred view is that pronouns of the third person, in non-nominative forms, are parsed as the pronoun alone, and the rest is a marker.

Are these two objects originally a subject and predicate (*mubtada' wa khabar*)?

* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Originally they are a subject and predicate.
* Student: (...) its origin is the subject (*mubtada'*).
* Shaykh: How? Is there anything that governs two objects whose origin is not a subject and predicate?
* Student: (...) If we strip away the verb and the subject, it does not have to be a subject (*mubtada'*).
* Shaykh: A subject (*mubtada'*), fine.

﴿Those—sa-nu'tīhim﴾, meaning, ﴿sa-nu'tīhim﴾: We will give them. ﴿ajran 'azīman﴾: a reward, ﴿'azīman﴾: possessing greatness. Know that when something is great, it exceeds what can be imagined. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said in the sacred hadith: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived."[[Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh); al-Bukhari (3244) and Muslim (2824/2) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

* In the noble verse there are benefits, among them the perfection of Allah's justice, and that when He issues a general ruling, those individuals whose case differs from it must be mentioned. We derive this from the word (*lākin*), the adversative "but," after He had ruled against them, for their taking of usury, which they had been forbidden, and their consuming of people's wealth falsely. He said: ﴿But those firm in knowledge﴾. This is the perfection of justice: to mention both good and evil, whether that good and evil pertains to a group or to an individual. Whoever wishes to correct a person must mention his virtues and his faults. But whoever wishes to refute the falsehood that someone says, here he is not obliged to mention the virtues, because mentioning the virtues in the context of refuting him would weaken the refutation, cause people to incline toward him, and lead to sympathy for him. Thus we distinguish between a person who wants to correct another person, in which case he must mention both the faults and the virtues, and a person who wants to refute another's falsehood, in which case he should mention the falsehood and not the virtues, because if he mentions the virtues, he weakens his refutation.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the virtue of being firm in knowledge. Pay attention to the word *al-rusūkh* (firmness). What does it mean? Stability and steadiness. This is because knowledge is of two kinds: superficial knowledge, meaning knowledge that lies on the surface, which any wind can shake. This is what many students have. You find many students who gather all the sciences at once, so they become like a general physician with no specialty in anything. Other students concentrate and are diligent, and this is the one who truly grasps knowledge and has ability and mastery. Some scholars even claimed that whoever excels in one field of knowledge is capable of grasping all fields.

Some of you are not unaware of what is reported about the debate between Abu Yusuf and al-Kisa'i when they debated before al-Rashid. Al-Kisa'i claimed that whoever perfects one science completely is able to grasp all sciences. Abu Yusuf said to him: "What do you say about someone who forgets in the prostration of forgetfulness (*sujūd al-sahw*)?" He said: "I say there is no prostration upon him." He said: "From where did you take this from your knowledge?" And al-Kisa'i is known for what? For the science of grammar (*nahw*). He said: "I took it from my knowledge, namely that the rule I hold is that a diminutive is not diminished." The prostration of forgetfulness, in his view, is a diminutive, so it is not diminished.

In any case, Allah knows best whether this story is fabricated or true. But it is not authentic; there is no doubt that it is not authentic. My point is only to say that firmness in knowledge is knowledge itself. For this reason I have always told students of knowledge: be diligent about the principles (*qawā'id*) of knowledge and its governing rules, because the particular cases are without limit. Every day a new transaction or a new matter in worship appears among people, and a person cannot judge it correctly unless he has principles and foundations by which he links these particular cases to their roots and rules. As for one who takes knowledge issue by issue, he is like one who gathers locusts from the desert: he tires himself and his bag is never filled. But the person who is diligent about the principles, he is the one who, by Allah's permission, grasps knowledge.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: knowledge is a cause of faith, as shown by His saying ﴿they believe﴾. Without doubt, the more a person grows in knowledge, the more he grows in faith and insight by Allah's grace. So hold to knowledge, hold to knowledge, and beware of doubts and disputation. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "No people were given disputation except that they went astray."[[Reported by al-Tirmidhi (3253) and Ibn Majah (48) from the hadith of Abu Umamah, with the wording: "No people went astray after guidance that they were upon except that they were given disputation." We have not found it from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]] For this reason we find that the people with the most right path and the least artificiality are the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, because disputation was rare among them, and they resorted to it only when necessary. As for a person who, whenever he understands an issue, goes on to raise in his heart or to others objections that do not arise naturally, this is artificiality and excess (*taqallus wa tanaṭṭu'*), and it is a cause of deprivation.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: among the People of the Book there are those firm in knowledge who believe in Allah, as shown by His saying ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them﴾, meaning among the People of the Book.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: faith cannot be complete except by believing in what the Messenger, peace be upon him, brought, as shown by His saying ﴿who believe in what has been revealed to you﴾. So every person who claims to be a believer but does not believe in what was revealed to Muhammad is a disbeliever and a liar in his claim, because the religion of Islam that Muhammad ﷺ brought abrogates all other religions.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the establishment of the prophethood of the Messenger ﷺ. From where?

* Students: (...).

* Shaykh: From (*mā*), or (*unzila*), or the *kāf*?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: From the *kāf*, yes: ﴿what has been revealed to you﴾.

* Among the other benefits of the noble verse: the Quran is the speech of Allah.

* Student: Allah, glorified and exalted, says (...) that the Quran is not an independent entity in itself, but rather it is an attribute.

* Shaykh: Speech is an attribute of the speaker, so it necessarily follows that Allah is the one who spoke it, and this is the case.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is necessary to believe in what was revealed to Muhammad ﷺ and what was revealed before him, as shown by His saying ﴿and what was revealed before you﴾. For this reason, the verse in Surah al-Baqarah says: ﴿Each believes in Allah, His angels, His books, and His messengers; we make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:285].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that there is no prophet after Muhammad. Is it derived?

* Students: ﴿min qablika﴾ (before you).

* Shaykh: ﴿Before you﴾, and He did not say "after you." This is the reality, but the verse contains an indication, not an explicit statement.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the virtue of establishing prayer and giving zakah, because Allah specifically mentioned them above all other deeds. Establishing prayer and giving zakah are paired in the Book of Allah. Were it not for the hadith of Abu Hurayrah concerning the one who withholds zakah, that he "sees his path, either to Paradise or to the Fire,"[[Reported by Muslim (987/24) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] we would say that the one who abandons zakah is a disbeliever, just as we say that about the one who abandons prayer. But we are not permitted to declare disbelief in those whom the texts indicate are not disbelievers, just as we are not permitted to shy away from declaring disbelief in those whom the texts indicate are disbelievers, because we are obligated to follow the word of Allah and His Messenger.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the virtue of believing in Allah and the Last Day, as shown by His saying ﴿and the believers in Allah and the Last Day﴾. It is specifically mentioned although it is included in His saying ﴿who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾, because of its importance. Brothers, the whole of faith depends on believing in Allah, because we believe that the messengers are whose? The messengers of Allah. The books? The books of Allah. The angels? The servants of Allah. And so on. The first pillar is entirely belief in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and what follows is considered branches or various aspects of belief in Allah.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of the Last Day, which has already been discussed.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: Allah, glorified and exalted, promises whoever has these attributes that He will give him a great reward whose greatness cannot be imagined, as shown by His saying ﴿Those—We shall grant them a great reward.﴾

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the high rank of those who possess these attributes, derived from the reference to them with the demonstrative of distance, ﴿Those﴾, and not ﴿These﴾, and not "We shall surely give them." He said ﴿Those﴾. Referring to the one referred to with the distal demonstrative indicates the elevation of his rank, as in His saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:1–2], although it is right before us, but because of its high rank it is referred to with a distal demonstrative.

We ask Allah, the Exalted, to make us and you among those firm in knowledge, who believe in Allah and in what was revealed to us and what was revealed before us.

* Student: May Allah bless you. Regarding His saying ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them﴾ to the end (...) Allah, glorified and exalted, [praised] those who believed in the Messenger ﷺ. Likewise in His saying ﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to those who believe are those who say, "We are Christians"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:82], where He attributed them to the Christians, although they were only praised for their belief in the Messenger ﷺ. What is the wisdom in attributing them to (...)?

* Shaykh: The wisdom is that Allah, in Surah al-Ma'idah, mentioned two groups, indeed three groups: the polytheists, the Jews, and the Christians. So which people are nearest in affection to the believers?

* Students: The Christians.

* Shaykh: They are the Christians. That is, in the verse of al-Ma'idah the intent is not a discussion of the Christians; the intent is a discussion of these groups and that they differ in their relation to the believers.

* Student: Shaykh, the reasoning in the verse of al-Ma'idah is that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, only praised them because they believed.

* Shaykh: No, no. It indicates that among them there are priests and monks, from among them.

* Student: But even if they remained as they were, would they be praised?

* Shaykh: No. If they remained hostile to the Muslims, they would become like the Jews. For this reason we say that the Christians after the mission of the Messenger, peace be upon him, are among those who earned anger, and that the Messenger's description of them as "those who went astray," as in the hadith of 'Adi ibn Hatim that we went over yesterday, refers to their original condition.

* Student: Shaykh, is the praise before the mission (*risālah*) something the verse of al-Ma'idah praises them for in the Quran?

* Shaykh: No, no. He said: ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:83]. Read the rest until His saying ﴿So write us among the witnesses﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:83].

* Student: It is confusing to me, Shaykh, because they believed.

* Shaykh: It is not confusing. They were Christians. For this reason, when they believe in Muhammad they are given their reward twice: the belief in their messenger and the belief in Muhammad. Thus they differ from the polytheists.

* Student: What is your opinion on the saying of the one who says: "The noble Quran is the speech of Allah, and the speech of Allah is eternal"?

* Shaykh: As for his saying "The Quran is the speech of Allah," this is true. As for his saying "The Quran is eternal," which is the second premise, if he means that the Quran itself is eternal in that sense, then it is an error. But if he means that speech as such is eternal, then it is correct. Nevertheless, we do not agree that speech is eternal; rather we say that speech is eternal in its type (*qadīm nawʿī*), not eternal in its individual instances (*qadīm al-ʿayn*). There is a difference between the eternity of the type and the eternity of the individual instance. Allah speaks with speech whenever He wills, but the essence of speech in itself is among the essential attributes.

* Student: Shaykh, what caused the outcry (*al-jihār*) among those who say that the Quran is eternal, as He is eternal, and that Allah spoke it from eternity and then sent it down...

* Shaykh: We say: you have lied. Where did you get that from? These are the ones who say: speech is the meaning subsisting in the self.

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Descendants (al-Asbat), Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon, and We gave David the Zabur (Psalms). And messengers We have mentioned to you before, and messengers We have not mentioned to you. And Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech.﴾ [An-Nisa 163–164].

The Shaykh: We seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾. The pronoun in ﴿Indeed, We﴾ refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and it is in the plural form to express greatness.

His words ﴿We revealed﴾: wahy (revelation) is informing quickly and secretly. What is meant here is Allah informing His prophets and messengers of His law by which He worships His servants. This is wahy: that Allah informs one of His prophets or messengers of the law by which His servants worship Him. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned in Surat ash-Shura that it has three forms, saying: ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or that He sends a messenger and he reveals by His permission what He wills﴾ [Ash-Shura 51].

His words ﴿as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾: "ma" (as) here may be a relative pronoun, and in that case there must be an omitted returning pronoun, the meaning being: like that which We revealed to Noah. It may also be so, but the closer view is that it is a verbal particle (masdariyyah), meaning "like Our revelation", and this is preferable because it needs no estimate: like Our revelation to Noah. Noah is the first of the messengers, peace be upon them, as is explicitly stated in the hadith of intercession, and for this reason He said: ﴿and the prophets after him﴾. What is meant by "the prophets" here are the prophets who were sent to their peoples. Allah has placed prophethood and the Book in the offspring of Abraham and Noah, as He said: ﴿And We had certainly sent Noah and Abraham and placed in their descendants prophethood and the Book﴾ [Al-Hadid 26]. By this we know that there was no messenger before Noah, peace be upon him, and that what the historians mention, that Idris came before Noah, is an erroneous view; the correct view, as it appears, is that Idris was among the prophets of the Children of Israel.

﴿And We revealed to Abraham﴾: "Ibrahim" here has two readings: ﴿Ibrahamа﴾ and ﴿Ibrahim﴾, and both are authentic readings of the Seven, and a person may recite with either. But, as we have previously stated: a person may not recite among the common people with a reading outside what is in their copies of the Mushaf, because that would be a cause of fitnah.

﴿And We revealed to Abraham and Ishmael﴾, who is the elder son of Abraham; ﴿and Isaac﴾, who is his second son; ﴿and Jacob﴾, who is the son of Isaac. He specified him although he is a son because the prophets of the Children of Israel were from the descendants of Jacob. So Ishmael and Isaac are brothers; and Ishmael is the paternal uncle of whom?

Students: Jacob.

The Shaykh: The paternal uncle of Jacob. ﴿and Jacob and the Asbat﴾: it has been said that al-Asbat means the tribes of the Children of Israel, as He said: ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes, as nations﴾ [Al-A'raf 160]. It has also been said that al-Asbat are the sons of Jacob. On the first view it is mentioning the general and intending the specific, because not all the Asbat were prophets, but prophets were among them; on the second view there is no difficulty.

﴿and the Asbat, and Jesus﴾, who is the last of the prophets of the Children of Israel; there is no messenger or prophet between him and Muhammad (ﷺ) either.

His words ﴿and Job﴾, who is from the Children of Israel; ﴿and Jonah﴾ likewise; ﴿and Aaron﴾ likewise, also from the Children of Israel; ﴿and Solomon﴾, from the Children of Israel. ﴿And We gave David the Zabur﴾: David is the father of Solomon, and the Zabur is the book Allah gave to David, and it is mentioned specifically because it contains admonitions that soften the hearts, and because David, peace be upon him, used to chant it, so the birds would hear and glorify along with him, and so would the mountains.

﴿And messengers We have mentioned to you before, and messengers We have not mentioned to you﴾: who are the messengers mentioned in this verse? Who among the messengers is not mentioned here? Jonah, Shu'ayb, Hud, Salih, Lot, Joseph.

﴿Messengers We have mentioned to you before﴾: ﴿before﴾ means before this verse. ﴿And messengers We have not mentioned to you﴾: because Allah did not relate to the Messenger, peace be upon him, except those who were around the Arabian Peninsula. As for those who were far away, like those in America and the far reaches of Asia and what is similar, they were not mentioned, because the purpose of mentioning the prophets is admonition, and if there is no nearness in narratives and in place, the admonition in that is small.

﴿And messengers We have not mentioned to you, and Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech﴾: ﴿Allah﴾ is the subject, ﴿Moses﴾ is the object, and ﴿takleeman﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun for the meaning of the verb before it: "spoke with speech." The mention of Moses was delayed because of his distinguishing feature, speech — "He spoke to him with speech" — just as David was mentioned after Solomon although he is his father, for the sake of specifying the Zabur that Allah gave David. The ordering of prophets in mention follows rhetorical reasons, verbal or semantic, according to what becomes clear from the context.

In this verse there are many benefits. Among them: that the first of the messengers is Noah, as shown by His words ﴿and the prophets after him﴾; this is the truth, and there was no messenger before him. As for prophethood, it existed before Noah, for Adam, peace be upon him, was a prophet, since he worshipped Allah, and one cannot worship Allah except through revelation from Allah; and by the establishment of revelation to him he was a prophet. But he was not sent to his children, because at that time there was no need for messengers, since people were upon one religion, as Allah said: ﴿Mankind was one community, and Allah sent prophets as bearers of good news and warners, and sent down with them the Book in truth﴾ [Al-Baqarah 213], meaning people were one community upon the truth and the upright religion, then they differed; so Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners, and sent down with them the Book with truth to judge between them in what they differed about. But in the time of Adam there was no disagreement, and so he was a prophet and not a messenger.

And among the benefits of this verse: that the revelation to all the prophets and messengers was of one kind, as shown by His words ﴿as We revealed﴾. But does what is revealed agree? We say: it agrees in some things and differs in others. Tawhid was agreed upon by the messengers: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ [Al-Anbiya 25]. This is agreed upon. As for the laws and methods, nations differ, because Allah legislates for each nation what suits its condition, as He said: ﴿For each of you We have appointed a law and a method. And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one nation, but He puts you to trial in what He has given you﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 48]. So laws and methods differ, while the root is agreed upon. All the messengers agreed upon what? Upon tawhid: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ [Al-Anbiya 25]. Thus ﴿as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾ refers to the root of revelation and what the laws agreed upon, which is tawhid; as for methods and laws, they are for each nation according to its circumstances.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the refutation of the claim of some historians that Idris came before Noah; this is a false claim, refuted by the Noble Qur'an.

Among the benefits of this verse: the revelation to these noble messengers, peace be upon them: Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, etc.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah related the accounts of some messengers and did not relate the accounts of others. The wisdom behind that is what we indicated in the tafsir: the prophets far from the region of the message of Muhammad (ﷺ) were not related to us by Allah.

But if someone should ask: Does every nation have a messenger? The answer: Yes, there is no doubt about this, because of His words: ﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24], and His words: ﴿messengers as bearers of good news and warners, so that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah spoke to Moses with real speech, as shown by His words: ﴿And Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech﴾. Those who denied that Allah spoke to him took two paths:

Some distorted the verse in its wording so that the meaning would change, and some distorted it in meaning while leaving the wording as it is. Some said: the correct reading is "wa kallama Allaha Musa takleeman" (and Moses spoke to Allah), making the speaker Moses. This is a verbal distortion that changes the meaning; there is no doubt that it is a crime against Allah and His speech, and it is also false, because of Allah's words: ﴿And when Moses came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him﴾ [Al-A'raf 143]; for no one can say here that the speaker is Moses, because the "ha" in "kallamahu" is an object pronoun, and it cannot be the subject pronoun.

Others said: ﴿Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech﴾ comes from kalm, meaning a wound, as in the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "There is no one wounded (yukkalamu) in the way of Allah, and Allah knows best who is wounded in His way" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5533) and Muslim (1876/105) from Abu Hurayrah with nearly this wording.]], where "yukallamu" means what? It means "is wounded." So they said: "Allah wounded Moses with the claws of wisdom" — distortion, may Allah protect us; they did not make this a matter of metaphor, and this is also false. Rather, the correct view is that Allah spoke to Moses with clear speech, with a letter and a voice that Moses heard, and that His speech to him was of two kinds:

The first: intimate discourse (munajah), and the second: calling (munadah). Allah said: ﴿And We called him from the right side of the mountain and brought him near in confidence﴾ [Maryam 52]. Calling is for one who is far, and intimate discourse is for one who is near. It is known that the distant one needs a louder voice, while the near one is satisfied with a quiet voice.

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Descendants (al-Asbat), Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon, and We gave David the Zabur (Psalms). And messengers We have mentioned to you before, and messengers We have not mentioned to you. And Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech.﴾ [An-Nisa 163–164].

The Shaykh: We seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾. The pronoun in ﴿Indeed, We﴾ refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and it is in the plural form to express greatness.

His words ﴿We revealed﴾: wahy (revelation) is informing quickly and secretly. What is meant here is Allah informing His prophets and messengers of His law by which He worships His servants. This is wahy: that Allah informs one of His prophets or messengers of the law by which His servants worship Him. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned in Surat ash-Shura that it has three forms, saying: ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or that He sends a messenger and he reveals by His permission what He wills﴾ [Ash-Shura 51].

His words ﴿as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾: "ma" (as) here may be a relative pronoun, and in that case there must be an omitted returning pronoun, the meaning being: like that which We revealed to Noah. It may also be so, but the closer view is that it is a verbal particle (masdariyyah), meaning "like Our revelation", and this is preferable because it needs no estimate: like Our revelation to Noah. Noah is the first of the messengers, peace be upon them, as is explicitly stated in the hadith of intercession, and for this reason He said: ﴿and the prophets after him﴾. What is meant by "the prophets" here are the prophets who were sent to their peoples. Allah has placed prophethood and the Book in the offspring of Abraham and Noah, as He said: ﴿And We had certainly sent Noah and Abraham and placed in their descendants prophethood and the Book﴾ [Al-Hadid 26]. By this we know that there was no messenger before Noah, peace be upon him, and that what the historians mention, that Idris came before Noah, is an erroneous view; the correct view, as it appears, is that Idris was among the prophets of the Children of Israel.

﴿And We revealed to Abraham﴾: "Ibrahim" here has two readings: ﴿Ibrahamа﴾ and ﴿Ibrahim﴾, and both are authentic readings of the Seven, and a person may recite with either. But, as we have previously stated: a person may not recite among the common people with a reading outside what is in their copies of the Mushaf, because that would be a cause of fitnah.

﴿And We revealed to Abraham and Ishmael﴾, who is the elder son of Abraham; ﴿and Isaac﴾, who is his second son; ﴿and Jacob﴾, who is the son of Isaac. He specified him although he is a son because the prophets of the Children of Israel were from the descendants of Jacob. So Ishmael and Isaac are brothers; and Ishmael is the paternal uncle of whom?
